items.title: A Magazine That’s Actually a Shop
items.description: Type in shop-magazine.com and you will enter the world of Magazine, an online “destination for divas everywhere” and love letter to wallet-draining excess. It’s a shop, but also a magazine, founded by shopaholic soulmates Coumba Samba and Sylvie Makower. Born
items.author: Marley Wendt
paragraphs: Type in shop-magazine.com and you will enter the world of Magazine, an online “destination for divas everywhere” and love letter to wallet-draining excess. It’s a shop, but also a magazine, founded by shopaholic soulmates Coumba Samba and Sylvie Makower. Born from a friendship stretched between New York and London, Magazine turns a shared fascination with fashionista-dom into a website. It’s a transatlantic affair for a medium that is, fittingly, both nowhere and everywhere: an online space that feels positively physical, practically begging you to swipe your credit card.

From a lime-green 1940s showgirl dress to a pink-and-white Betsey Johnson confection, the colors pop with an almost suspicious perfection. It’s clear that Samba and Makower have a knack for knowing what a girl wants, embracing the fun that comes with acquiring clothes.

But Magazine is not just a place to empty your wallet; it is somewhere to fill your brain, too. Every drop arrives with an online magazine, ranging from essays on a pair of Fall 2011 Lanvin heels, to the quest for the perfect black mannequin. It’s a pink-painted corner of the web where reading becomes wanting, and wanting is very much the point. If you like your money pixelated on a screen, you’ve found your destination, darling!
MARLEY WENDT: What are three colors that capture the spirit of this project?
SYLVIE MAKOWER: Bubblegum pink.

SM: I also love tangerine. Magazine has a very girly, diva-abundance vibe. Neither of us are minimalists by any measure, nor are we into the monochromatic stuff. So, exuberant bright colors, heavy on the pink.
How did Magazine come about?

SM: A year ago while we were having breakfast and drinking coffee Upstate, I was thinking “Oh, Coumba’s being awfully quiet.” She was just on her phone, and seemed to be working. Then I noticed the reflection in her big glasses: Vinted, scrolling by. It was such a beautiful image. It suddenly dawned on me that we are twin flames in being massive shopaholics.

CS: We kind of floated the idea, and I was like, yes, we need that. Especially here in New York, there’s lots of nice vintage places, but sometimes the curation doesn’t really fit with what I’m seeking, so I’ve resorted to online shopping.
The website has a slightly DIY early internet quality to it. Has your relationship to the internet shaped the way you think about Magazine?
CS: It does have this “blog vibe” to it. At least for me, I kind of grew up on Tumblr, so that has a part to play in it.

SM: We like the idea of having this slightly low-stakes, immediate form of online publication where nothing’s too overdone. The actual visual language of the website had a lot to do with our web designer, Alec Mapes-Frances, and also Coumba.

It was quite an organic process. We just kept adding elements. For instance, there’s a sticker of Coumba in a margarita glass in the corner of the website. This links to her many years of writing a personal margarita review. And we also have an agony aunt, Miss Chlo, who you can submit questions to. We wanted to bring many worlds and portals together on the site.
Coumba, what makes a great margarita?

CS: Honestly, I’m a simple girl at heart. I also don’t really like alcohol. The whole reason I started it was because I was looking for a classic cocktail, and wanted to keep tabs on it. I’m just looking for something straightforward, no riff-raff or weird orange juice in it.
On the website, for the listings of the items, there are GIFs of you guys that emulate self-tape videos. Tell me about that.

SM: We thought it would be funny to do a spoof on the walking video that your modelling agency requests, because it’s such a humiliating medium. I modeled for a long time as a teenager, and Coumba still does.
What makes a piece of clothing right for Magazine?

SM: A philosophy that I’ve begun to incorporate is “shop for yourself.” If I Iove something, I’ll buy it. We want to have a mixture of well-constructed, fancy designer pieces, and weird, accessible items. To me, there’s nothing worse than being dressed too well…
CS: You’re spot on. Everything is unique, special, and bright.
Describe your perfect day of shopping together.
CS: We once went to this vintage fair in London called Frock Me!, and just spent the whole day there. I put in my earbuds, walked around for five hours, and spent all of my money. It was beautiful.
SM: Coumba sent me these crazy messages a few hours in telling me I had to come. And when I came, I found her racing around as if she was possessed. I love those fairs so much.
Why did you want Magazine to be an actual magazine as well?

SM: We wanted to print out images of the clothes, like the books of images of counterfeit bags on Canal Street. We thought we could call the shop Magazine because it’s like a magazine. And then Coumba suggested that we make an actual magazine.
CS: It all just clicked. I was also doing zines while I was in uni, so it’s always been an interest of mine.

SM: We wanted somewhere to explore what’s going on in the shop and beyond in greater depth. The magazine is by no means just about the stock though. For our current feature, Fiona Alison Duncan has written a pseudo fictional essay about personal effects.
And if Magazine was an actual shop, what would it look like?

SM: There’s not a moment in my day when I’m not thinking about it! It’ll be very pink. My hypothetical dog, which I intend to own within the next calendar year, will be running around. It’ll be a watering hole for divas, where people can come to shop, but also to congregate and have tea.
What type of music is playing as you walk in?
CS: Probably some classic ’80s dance tracks.
What are your favourite shopping-diva words of wisdom?
SM: I would like to quote our agony aunt, Miss Chlo: “You don’t need to find yourself before getting dressed. Sometimes getting dressed is how you find yourself.”

items.title: Gisele Bundchen Interview: Motherhood, Happiness, Modeling Career
items.description: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
items.author: Steff Yotka
paragraphs: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
photography COLLIER SCHORR

When she was 15 years old, Gisele Bündchen left Horizontina, Brazil, and moved to Tokyo to become a model. It was 1995. She didn’t speak Japanese or English. To reach her parents, grandparents, and five sisters, she used an international calling card on a landline phone. She would speak to them every 15 days, exactly.

“It was, in a way, liberating because I felt like I was living life,” Gisele says, thinking back to getting lost on the subway, navigating teenage growing pains, and learning how to integrate into a foreign reality. “I was experiencing life.”

Thirty-one years later, there is little of life Gisele hasn’t experienced. She walked her first major runway show for Alexander McQueen in 1998, and for the next decade was a regular on the catwalk for Gucci, Dolce & Gabbana, Versace, Valentino, and Marc Jacobs. She signed an advertising contract with Dior, posing for Nick Knight amongst bubbles and saddle bags, then another with Dolce & Gabbana for its glittering perfume The One, and then another with Victoria’s Secret. She routinely wore the brand’s Red Hot Fantasy Bra—estimated to be worth $15 million in 2000.

Gisele was the Forbes highest-paid model for 12 years in a row, from 2005 to 2016. Her own website estimates she has appeared on an unprecedented 1,200 magazine covers (this issue will be her seventh for i-D). She walked the runway during the 2016 Olympic Opening Ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, released multiple singles, and has appeared in a handful of movies, from Taxi (2004) to The Devil Wears Prada (2006). Gisele has fundraised for Lotus House, Save the Children, The Red Cross, and more. In 2016, Taschen published a book commemorating her 20 years of modelling, retailing for $700 and selling out in one day. The cover shot is by Irving Penn of a nude Gisele. (“I still have the note from him saying that it was wonderful. ‘You did great.’”) Inside are now-legendary photographs by Steven Meisel, David LaChapelle, Inez and Vinoodh, and Juergen Teller. Gisele has published one autobiography and one cookbook, which is to say nothing of the digests she posts on Instagram to her 22 million followers. She is so famous and so known, from Brazil to Tokyo to New York to Mars, that it would be impossible for any one of us to calculate exactly where we know her from or how many times we’ve seen her face.

And yet, for Gisele, who turned 46 in July, those wandering Tokyo days are among her most special. “My whole thing is going back to that,” she tells me, tucked into an armchair in a white tank and jean shorts. “How can I create more of that reality in my life?”

You see, despite being the object of so many gazes, Gisele prefers to set hers on the sun, the sea, the sky. She was born on a farm in Brazil, surrounded by her grandparents, parents, sisters, and pets. Now, 6,900 kilometres away, she’s recreated that paradise in Northern Miami with her children Benjamin (16), Vivian (13), and a baby boy (16 months), her husband Joaquim, and a pair of dogs.

“Life is a gift,” she says. “I think I have so much joy in my life because I really see the ordinary as the extraordinary… The sun rises every day. You can walk around and be grateful for it, or you can just be disconnected from all these incredible things. You can be robbed of your life if you think life is this”—she mimics looking down at her phone—“and you forget life is so much more.”
She smiles, sipping from her room-temperature water. “Anyway, I’m sure you have more questions for me.”
Because we got into the meaning of life and Gisele’s very philosophy of being so quickly into our first meeting, here’s what happened in the lead-up—minutes one through seven:
1. I enter Gisele’s small ranch home a couple blocks from her larger, beachfront estate. I am promptly served her homemade granola and her proprietary tea (warming, like dark chocolate and honey).
2. Alfie, her gigantic German Shepherd, comes in first and gives me the once-over. “He’s my protector,” Gisele smiles, kicking off her sandals and wrapping me up in a hug.

3. “You smell amazing,” she says, and I just give her the bottle of perfume in my purse. She asks if it has parabens, and I say I don’t know, and she tells me never to use anything with parabens, especially on your wrists or neck. It’s been three months and I am still too embarrassed to research: Does Maison Louis Marie’s scent Aboukir have parabens?
4. She checks my astrological vibe to make sure this interview will go well: “What’s your sign?” she asks squarely.
“Cancer. I knew we’d talk about it. I read you’re a Cancer, Scorpio Moon. What’s your rising?”

“Oh, go girl! I don’t even know how I ended up doing this job. If you let me, I would just never leave my house, because I’m a crab. And with the Scorpio Moon, for me, if it’s not deep, I don’t want to talk about it.”

That’s the guiding premise of being Gisele: Always searching for depth, connection, and meaning. In some way, modelling was the perfect job for her—homey, crablike tendencies notwithstanding—because it allowed her to find connections the world over. The high-low of the industry, which led to anxiety attacks in her mid-20s, was the impetus for Gisele’s soul searching. “Shit happens to all of us, but I think I don’t stay there,” she says of the down days. “I learned how to meditate. It’s like you can take a step back: You can be having an experience and observing yourself having that experience at the same time.”

Meditation led her to yoga, which she practises routinely, and then to Pilates and then to jujitsu. Recently, she has added weight training. “I do weights three times a week. I do Pilates once or twice a week. I do yoga two or three times a week. I work out every day because, for me, working out—I don’t see it as something I have to do. I see it as something I get to do,” she says. “It doesn’t matter if I’m surfing, if I’m playing volleyball with my daughter, if I’m paddleboarding. Whatever it is, I feel like it’s a moment of being.” She bares a bicep. “Now for the first time in my life, I can do pull-ups.”

Early this summer morning, she took her baby to the park. Much like his older half-siblings, he has picked up on Gisele’s connectivity and generosity. “I have to show you this video.” For the first time, she whips out her phone and opens her camera roll. As she scrolls through—I promise I’m not trying to peek!—I realise almost every photo is of her kids. “He’s so funny,” she says of her son, captured waddling around the park with a paper towel. “I mean, he’s 16 months and he saw that I was cleaning the park—because Miami, it’s so damp all the time!—and he wanted to participate and he felt really good about it,” Gisele beams, watching her tiny son dry off the slide, the seesaw, the swing.

“Kids give us this opportunity to live again, to be more present and to experience life again. To do it maybe differently than we’ve done it before.” She pauses. “I don’t know. I find every little thing so amazing.” Gisele goes on to show me videos of Benny DJing in his bedroom, his baby brother dancing by his side. She has pictures of Vivi playing volleyball (“She’s amazing!”) and dancing with friends. She scrolls to a dancing video. “I mean, what is better than this? This is my daughter and she’s like, ‘Mum, let’s do a dance class.’ So this is us doing a dance class. I’m not so great,” Gisele laughs, “but look at her and her friend—and that’s her mum’s friend.”

She quickly scrolls through about 20 more videos before she chucks her phone away. “By the way, I don’t know if you noticed, my phone doesn’t ring. There’s no alarms. It never rings. It’s liberating.”

A silenced iPhone and spending all day with her family is a far cry from the past 30 years of Gisele’s life. To briefly summarise the lore: Her mother enrolled her, her twin sister Patí, and younger sister Gabriela in modelling classes in Brazil. Gisele was later scouted to participate in the Elite Model Look competition, and in 1995, she placed second. From 1996 to 2016, life didn’t stop—she spent the better part of her 20s and 30s at the white-hot centre of it all: Fashion, fame, celebrity, paparazzi, and money. She was signing bigger contracts than other models, getting bigger media attention, becoming an entity bigger than Gisele Bündchen from Horizontina, Brazil. She was, by 2004, a supermodel, capital S. Everything about her sparkled.

“I’ve experienced the rat race. I was on the hamster wheel in my early 20s,” she says. “I won Model of the Year at 19. I worked so hard from 14 to get to that place, I felt like I couldn’t say no [to major jobs].” And sure, Gisele encountered so much of the bullshit so many models of the ’90s and ’00s did. She tried not to let her industry’s lack of protection faze her. “Even though I wasn’t going to the parties, I was doing 360 days [of work a year]. I wanted to be the best that I could be every day. I wanted to bring my best.”

We start to look through some of her runway fits from her catwalk days and she sparks up with delight. “Girl, it was very tight inside. You couldn’t really move so much—but, I mean, look how he made you look!” she cheers of a supersized Fall 2004 Christian Dior look by John Galliano. “I’m forever grateful to McQueen, I’m forever grateful to John. I was always so excited to do the Dior shows because I never knew what I was going to look like.”

She singles out a Galliano show for Dior held at Versailles. “This was 60 years of Dior and I wasn’t even doing shows anymore. John was like, ‘Please, Gisele. This is all my muses and it’s going to be the 60 years, it’s to be in Versailles.’ I was like, ‘I must do it,’” she remembers. “Look at these shoes. It was like a platform without a heel. I was walking on cement, like bricks. It was crazy. I was like, ‘Am I going to fall and break my ankle?’”

But that’s the thing about Gisele: Even if she’s struggling to walk or struggling to feel beautiful—as she often recounts of that first-ever McQueen show, where she hit the runway topless with a trompe l’oeil white tank painted on by Val Garland, rain falling and her lashes dripping into her eyes—she is always going to do her best. “I didn’t say no or complain because people were giving me the opportunity,” she reflects. “I came in, I did my job, I went home… and I think what I really appreciate and really enjoyed about fashion is that it got me to access and experience different sides of me. I really wanted to be the best canvas for the creatives. I felt like it was my way of contributing.”

But working in the oil-slick glossy world of new millennium modelling meant that few people saw Gisele as a full person—because of her beauty, her chameleonic qualities, and her prowess, she was quickly regarded as an idol. Nice to look at, nothing to say. The first time she appeared in i-D, on the cover in December 1998, she wasn’t interviewed. Instead, the photographer who took the picture was, and here’s what he had to say about the smart and vibrant Gisele: “She’s certainly gorgeous. I’d marry her.”

Her “godfather” in the turbulent fashion industry was Steven Meisel. (Are you surprised that the greatest model of her generation would find kinship with the greatest photographer of his?) In one of the earliest pieces of press about Gisele, a New York Magazine article from 1999, Meisel already saw her as more than a body to stand in front of his lens. He felt her spirit. “Gisele is able to change because she wants to—it’s not in her looks; it’s in her mental process. She is malleable and is willing to be a silent screen star because she understands that modelling is acting,” he told the mag. He later wrote the foreword for her Taschen book, and she still speaks of him as her guardian angel. “I’m grateful for him. I don’t think I would have been the model that I was if it wasn’t for him, for real. We got to play together. I shot with him every week.”

And yet, after weekly Meisel shoots, over 130 Vogue covers, and decades on billboards and TV ad spots, Gisele wanted more. Well—maybe not more in the way you and I might think of it. She wanted to actually enjoy what she’d accomplished, and that meant leaving the fracas behind. After a decade in Boston, she relocated here, to Florida, to co-parent her older children and set up a new world of sea and sun and sand. Being mum, practising gratitude, taking care of herself and her community have become more valuable than any seven-figure ad job: “I say no to 99 percent of the jobs I’m offered because, when I put it on the scale, I’m like, ‘Am I going to miss my daughter’s volleyball game? Am I going to miss going to the park with my son? Am I going to miss my son DJing?’”

That’s why, with the exception of a few trips to her home in Costa Rica, to see family in Brazil, and recently, to Tahiti, Gisele rarely leaves Florida. “Having a baby at this moment of my life is such a gift, because I’m in a different place. I don’t have anything to prove. I don’t feel like I really, quite frankly, care.”
“I’m not defined by other people’s opinions,” she continues, firmly. “I feel like I get to choose how I want to live my life.”

Being alive today can feel like a quest for more: Make more money. Diversify your portfolio. Get PRP+ to be more beautiful and then Ozempic to be more svelte. Become a brand and use that brand to become more famous. Every day of your life can be used to sell something or say something or self-improve. I don’t think I have ever encountered a person more satisfied with exactly how her life is than Gisele. She has a lot, sure, but it’s long been enough. She’s done a lot, sure, but she’s not looking back. She’s been everywhere, yeah, but she isn’t driven by getting in your face.

She’s not a brand. She’s not an entrepreneur. She’s not a self-help guru—even though I tell her she should have a podcast. She’s not forcing Gisele-dom down our throats and, in some way, it seems like she doesn’t really want to be famous at all. That she’s financially well-off, she tells me, is just an opportunity to take care of her sisters and her family. She doesn’t want fancy clothes. She hasn’t been to New York in over two years and she’s not eager to come back.

“At the end of the day, this is your temple, this is your life, this is your journey. How do you want it to look? What do you want it to be? Who defines success?” she asks, as concerned in that moment with my well-being as with her own. “What is success? Some people say success is power, money, fame, more. Some people say success is being able to spend time with your kids, to have food on your table, to have a home to live in, to have great relationships and actually enjoy every day. I find that, quite frankly, much more successful than…” she trails off, not eager to point a finger. “It’s up to each person to define, because when I was in my 20s, success was different than what I feel today.”
“What do you want your legacy to be?” I ask as we’re wrapping up our conversation.

“In the end, I ended up having the best time. I ended up enjoying it all, staying in it, learning from it, and growing up in it. It’s been a blessing. However people see me, that’s okay with me. I want to look back and think, ‘I really enjoyed this journey. I really loved fully. I really experienced every emotion. I really had meaningful relationships. I tried to make the world a better place, and I made my surroundings more harmonious and loving and beautiful.’ I want my kids to feel like I was a great mum and that I helped them become the best version of themselves. I want to feel like I lived striving to be the best version of myself. Hopefully, I can look back and say I did it.”

Today, after I pack up my things and head for Miami International Airport, she’ll go to a birthday dinner. It’s a rare night out for Gisele, and after decades of no carbs and no dairy, she might have some of her friend’s homemade sourdough. “What’s better than bread and cheese? Oh my god, I don’t know!” she laughs. Tomorrow, she’ll wake up early to paddleboard. She’s worried about me not seeing the sea one last time before I get on a plane back to New York, but she’s calmed when I tell her I spent two hours on the beach this morning. As I wheel away my little suitcase and say goodbye, she pops her head out the front door with a final blessing. “Live the life you want to live! Everything else is going to shake out.”

items.title: Reece King on His Career, Mental Health and Social Media
items.description: Model Reece King on His Career, Mental Health and Social Media
items.author: Justin Moran
paragraphs: Model Reece King on His Career, Mental Health and Social Media

Born in the late '90s, 23-year-old British model Reece King was raised by a single mother and family overflowing with aunties. While caring, King's family wasn't very well off, so he began working long retail hours for minimum wage to contribute to their expenses. Once his modeling career took off and stardom came knocking, he left his job to eventually shoot major campaigns for brands like Diesel and grace magazine covers across the globe.

But when the flashing lights subdue, King remains himself. In fact, he is hyper aware of the concept of self. Reserved, and not wanting to reveal too much, he said, "I have such a hard time trying to talk about myself, because I have this situation where I disassociate myself from job. When I'm at home, I don't really check social media. I don't like to focus on it. I don't talk about it. I pretend it's not real."

A model whose image has been seen by thousands but doesn't like attention may seem like the ultimate paradox, but in reality his shyness is not out of the ordinary at all. "I'm just a little introvert, but I think on social media it probably looks like I'm this big, big character that's always doing something, and loves my picture taken, even though I don't," he said. It's true that once you enter the digital sphere, some people will only listen and some people will only look and formulate ideas of what and how public figures should be.

King's Instagram reaches those who are listening and watching beyond surface. Struggling with depression and severe anxiety throughout most of my life, King's posts have been a visual representation of what it means to stand at the intersection. He talks openly about his battle with mental health and how he manages to juggle everything. "It's been kind of hard," he said. "I've had problems with anxiety, and insomnia, even stuff just to do with my weight, and my mental health. I'm the only person in my family that's managed to get a situation, or job, like this. So it's hard to speak to people about what I feel, or deal with, because some people just can't relate from their perspective."

I share with him how as a younger version of myself, I experienced a feeling many young black people across the globe know too well — the idea that constant stress, worry or fear were all just aspects that come with life, an everyday normality we all go through. Now being much older, I see that things I couldn't quite place my finger on before could be diagnosed and treated. King agrees, "I don't think I actually knew anything about mental health. And it sounds crazy, but thinking back, I don't think I've ever had a serious conversation with someone, that's actually explained, 'You're feeling like this, because of this.' Or, 'Your body's like this, because your mind is here.' I never really had that growing up."

King has managed to find a healthy balance and manifest positive energy into most aspects of his life, saying, "I've just had to learn through a lot of lessons, a few bad moments. I've had to learn what's acceptable and what's not. I found that eating and drinking clean really helps me feel better inside. I also found meditating and reading and some time alone helps. I have plants and a little zen garden that I try to do morning and night. I try to stretch and workout a little bit. And I have three dogs, so it's really good energy with them. The best thing that probably helps me is just knowing that everyone is actually going through something as well."

And when things get really rough, there is always one person he can rely on. "My mom definitely has helped me," he said. "But she doesn't really know a whole bunch about what I do. And I still have to explain the difference between a casting and a request casting, and a campaign. Because it's just not her world."

King's most profound advice regards changing ways of thought. "I think it's a personal journey of learning that there's different ways of thinking. That's something that the person, the individual, has to just go through. Sometimes you have to do some stupid things to know that. I don't actually think I actually understood that sort of advice when I was younger, because your mind space just isn't there. With a little bit of age, I kind of understand you are your own world. If you feel good, then it's good. I've had to learn self-care."

Coming to terms with his sexuality as a bisexual black man was a large part of that journey to self-care. For King, understanding his sexuality was not an easy journey. "Just being a bit younger, like 18 or 19, you just don't know. It's very confusing. I think for a year, I was really, really convinced that I was asexual, because I was so confused that I didn't have a preference," he said. But he soon came to understand himself better, realizing, "I don't really care if it's a woman or a man, because it doesn't make a difference if I'm in love. But then I also felt so insecure towards that subject and I had put it off for so long, I didn't actually know who I really was. I knew what I liked in my head, but when it came to real life, I didn't really know how to interact."
"I was really, really convinced that I was asexual, because I was so confused that I didn't have a preference."

He said he kept putting off his feelings until he and then I eventually realized that this is me for the rest of my life, so I don't really have a choice. I can either make peace with who I am or hate myself or lie. So I think the Gay Times interview came at the right time and I was like, 'You know what, people? I've already said that I'm bisexual, but I guess it could be inspiring and helpful if I actually took that and put it into the modeling influences situation of things.''
As a public figure, King battles the negative stereotypes and tropes applied unfairly to bisexual people.

"With the whole picking sides thing," he says, "I've had situations where I've been talking to a girl and then someone will say something like, 'Oh, girl, you can't talk to him because you know he's messed with boys before.' I've had situations where I'm talking to a guy and then it's like, 'Is that girl a friend or is she more?' If I posted pictures with my friends in the past, it would always just get turned into, 'Oh, that has to be someone he's romantically seeing or sexually seeing, because he likes guys and girls.' But I kind of have to tell people, I'm not interested in every human being."

King also addresses society's desire to pigeonhole black men and fetishize them into lustful objects, saying, "Being biracial, I definitely think I've been sexualized a lot. Sometimes, if people know I'm bisexual, they kind of just think, based on the way I look that it's like, 'Oh, he's only interested in one thing.' I guess that's a fetish on their end. I've tried to find more positives in the situation, but when I was younger, it was definitely harder. I definitely had to smile through a lot of uncomfortable situations, but everything comes around."

Throughout his career, King has helped young people all over the world simply by way of being himself. Standing tall at 5'11 inches, he has a unique aura of positivity that draws you in. In a world consumed with the digital realm, he remains centered, introspective and optimistic for the future. "I believe in the law of attraction," he says. "I think I manifested a lot of things that I've wanted in my life where I'm at right now. And I had to learn that not everything I thought I wanted is actually necessary. It's a process of learning who I am and just growing as an adult. I mean 23, that's barely anything, yet."

items.title: Meet the Duo Who Left ‘60 Minutes’ and Launched Their Own Gen Z Journalism Start-Up, ‘Newsgirls’
items.description: Watching a Newsgirls video feels a little like being on FaceTime with a friend—one who’s great at doing winged eyeliner and speaking about Taylor Swift’s musical catalog or the last season of The Bachelor, but who’s also the type to fill you in on the latest g
items.author: Savannah Walsh
paragraphs: Watching a Newsgirls video feels a little like being on FaceTime with a friend—one who’s great at doing winged eyeliner and speaking about Taylor Swift’s musical catalog or the last season of The Bachelor, but who’s also the type to fill you in on the latest global gossip. With grabby headers like “Trump Is Replacing the WH Press Room With a Swimming Pool?!” and “Hegseth’s Wife Spies on His Drinking & Women,” the founders behind Newsgirls hope to stop you mid-scroll for an easily digestible dive into the day’s most mind-boggling news stories.

“When we were launching Newsgirls, we were like, We have to start with a banger, really show people this is a cool thing,” says Wren Woodson, one of the two 30-year-old journalists behind the budding social media news empire. “We delusionally wrote these emails. We wrote [to] Bill Clinton…and we were like, ‘Hi, Mr. President.’”
“No,” her cohost, Mabel Kabani, interjects, “we didn’t say that. We actually said, ‘Hi, Bill.’ The worst thing ever.”
“So bad,” Kabani adds with a good-natured eye roll.

It’s easier to laugh off their naivete now that Newsgirls, their online news start-up aimed at Gen Z, has found an audience of nearly half a million followers across Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok. After bonding as the youngest hires at 60 Minutes—which marked each woman’s first gig out of college—Kabani and Woodson launched Newsgirls in 2024 “to talk to people our age…[who] are just not watching traditional outlets anymore,” Woodson tells Vanity Fair. “We think of ourselves as journalists, but creators too, doing credible investigative work.” They identify with the term “news creator,” says Kabani. “But we really like to go out of our way to tell everyone we’re journalists—because we’re doing the work as journalists. There are so many news creators out in the world that aren’t doing that work.”

Last week they launched Newsgirls Investigate—a YouTube and Substack series devoted to deep dives on substantive issues. “We haven’t seen this [kind of] rigorous, hard work from independent creators,” says Kabani. Their first episode, released last Thursday, features never-before-reported details about Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense from former senior officials.

Before we go further, they address the name Newsgirls. “So many people have been like, ‘Would you consider changing the name? Would you consider not doing pink? Would you consider leaning in differently just to be taken seriously?’” says Kabani. “No, we’re confident in the work, and part of not being taken seriously means maybe more people will watch it.”

Kabani, who won a California press award after breaking the story of a neighborhood brothel in her Beverly Hills High School newspaper when she was 16, admits: “If you had told me in journalism school that picking a thumbnail, or deciding what to wear, or picking the first five seconds of a story was as important as the rest of it, I would’ve been like, This is a really weird and probably bad job. But the worst thing, as a journalist, is to do all the work and not have people watch it. So we’ve been putting so much effort into: How do you coat the broccoli in cheese? Some of that is how you look; some of that is the first five seconds. Some of it is…can you start with something gossipy to get people?”

Woodson, who “grew up in the middle of the woods in Wisconsin” and pivoted to journalism at Northwestern University following the 2016 election, says: “We want you to feel like you’re watching an Unwell podcast or something, but you’re getting Vice content.”

Over the course of their final two years working at CBS, the pair took dozens of pitch meetings “with all of the big outlets,” Woodson says, including Vanity Fair publisher Condé Nast. “Our plan was initially to embed as part of an institution. We believe in institutional journalism,” Kabani says. “The first inclination was never to just break off completely.”

They initially pitched the Newsgirls concept to then 60 Minutes executive producer Bill Owens, who exited his post as leader of the CBS news program in 2025 amid what he described as a loss of editorial independence. “He said flat out, ‘Your show needs to go to a visionary, and CBS is not a visionary. You’ve got to take this somewhere else,’” Woodson recalls. “And we’re very glad we did now.” (Over the weekend, it was reported that Owens will join independent video journalism start-up Newpress, which publishes work from YouTubers and podcasters, as its executive producer when his noncompete with CBS ends next March. VF has reached out to Owens and Newpress for comment.)

The two former 60 Minutes employees find it “heartbreaking” to see the structural overhauls at CBS News. “It’s hard to find news institutions you can trust these days, and it’s sad that that’s all being stripped away,” Kabani says. “It shows you how fragile institutions are—just one year, everything can change. All of these amazing correspondents have been fired or left. I can’t even recognize the place, really.”

Woodson, who worked primarily with veteran 60 Minutes journalist Lesley Stahl and won an Emmy for her very last story on the show—about a hostage who was taken from Israel to Gaza—says she and Kabani “were freaking out” over correspondent Scott Pelley’s headline-making stand for his coworkers during a fiery staff meeting in June 2026. “We didn’t see that as his personality. He, in the most loving way possible, kind of seemed robotic,” Woodson says. “He’s a very kind person, very genuine person, but he could lock in, and he’s such a professional. What you see on TV is who he is off camera. So I didn’t think he’d go up against the leadership, but it’s awesome.”

Kabani, who was interning on Capitol Hill for the Democratic caucus when Trump was elected, says independent news organizations like theirs might not exist without “the splintering of these big institutions—that partially is because of the Trump administration…. People are just so much more skeptical about what they see.”

Their big break at Newsgirls arrived going into 2026, with the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files. The pair had covered the convicted sex offender at CBS. “Mabel worked on the Epstein investigation at 60 Minutes when they got the autopsy photos, so she’s seen all of those,” says Woodson. (“All the naked-dead-Epstein photos are burned into my mind,” Kabani replies with a laugh.) “Exposing corruption was always one of our favorite things to do, coming from 60 Minutes. Those were our favorite stories to work on…. If there’s one type of person that’s the most disliked, that we’ve come across in our reporting, it’s billionaires.”

They channeled their experience covering the story into roughly three videos a day about the Epstein files as they went through them. “There’s millions of documents,” Kabani says. “People wanted it all contextualized in a way that they could just go through really quickly…. That’s when we blew up from 30,000 followers on Instagram to 200,000 in six weeks.” Says Woodson, “I still had the 100K flowers that my parents sent when we hit 200K. It was going so fast.”

The New York City–based creators have since found viral success by going out into the field—such as when they interviewed Staten Islanders supporting Andrew Cuomo before New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s victory in the November 2025 election. “We went to the White House UFC fight, and we snuck our way in because this boy had extra tickets,” Kabani says. More recently, they attended the Charlie Kirk statue unveiling in Times Square. “That one was really scary because it wasn’t just Charlie Kirk supporters; it was overtaken by white supremacists,” Kabani says. “It was the first time Wren and I felt like this could be dangerous.”

They’re less intimidated by the comment-section bullies lurking in their audience of roughly 50% men and 50% women. “A bunch of people think Wren and I are the same person and/or twins, even though we are literally different races,” Kabani says.

“We get so many, ‘Is this the same girl?’” Woodson replies. “Especially when you’re speaking about politics. If we’re just telling the truth, if we’re reporting, ‘Trump did this today’—if there’s no way to come back at that, they’ll just attack us.”

When the Newsgirls founders report on members of the Trump family and their various businesses, those in the comment section inevitably turn their attention to Hunter Biden. “We’ve invited all of the Trump kids to come on. We have tried many times,” Woodson says. When they cold-emailed Hunter Biden, he agreed to a video interview. They wanted to know about his “contradictory” political stances. “Hunter still wants to represent the Democratic Party…. But now he’s going on Tucker Carlson; he’s also saying he loves Candace Owens,” Woodson says. “We’re like, ‘Don’t you feel like you’re validating them by going on?’ And he’s like, ‘When has Hunter Biden ever validated anything?’ I thought it was refreshing that he could poke fun at himself.”

The interview also got a boost from Fox News host Jesse Watters, as they learned from a negative comment. “‘Just saw you two hair-flipping losers on Fox News,’” Woodson recalls with a laugh. “[Watters] didn’t say anything about us; he was just hating on Hunter a little bit. But thanks to the hater.”

Woodson and Kabani hope that Newsgirls will one day become, like Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper’s Unwell empire, a network for other like-minded creators. But first, they’re focused on the upcoming midterms and then the 2028 presidential election, topics that devolve into another survey of the sorry state of things, generally speaking. “I remember the joke during the first Trump presidency was, he’s great for business for journalists. And it really is true, no matter which way you look at it,” Woodson says. “When he won again, we had just launched our show three weeks before, and we were like, Wow, our jobs just got even more important than we realized when we planned this launch.”

items.title: Let Them Eat Olive Spheres: Inside Airbnb’s Star-Studded Charity Gala
items.description: Nothing says billionaire-hosted gala quite like an olive sphere. What’s an olive sphere, you ask? Imagine a bite-sized gelatinous membrane filled with olive juice that is served on a tiny silver platter, and requires two servers—two!—to pass out: one to offer
items.author: Maxwell Adler
paragraphs: Nothing says billionaire-hosted gala quite like an olive sphere. What’s an olive sphere, you ask? Imagine a bite-sized gelatinous membrane filled with olive juice that is served on a tiny silver platter, and requires two servers—two!—to pass out: one to offer guests the savory blobs, and another to collect the discarded platters.

Before taking the stage at Milk Studios in Los Angeles on Wednesday night, Jimmy Kimmel walked past two olive sphere servers and a third handing out caviar. He told me he’d been listening to The Howard Stern Show on the drive over, and something so X-rated came on that he had to quickly turn down the volume when he pulled up alongside another car. Evidently, it put him in a silly mood by the time he welcomed guests to the first ever gala for Airbnb’s independent nonprofit—or “gay-la,” as he put it, “depending on your sexual orientation.”

Kimmel had been tapped to serve as master of ceremonies at the fundraiser for the home-sharing behemoth’s nonprofit, which was created in 2020 to provide free temporary housing to people displaced by disasters and other crises. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky announced a $500 million funding commitment over the next five years, allowing the organization to expand its services to families traveling for medical treatment and survivors of domestic violence.

Among the guests were people who had lost their homes in the devastating Eaton Fire in 2025. They shared a room with a group of people who presumably have little need for emergency housing: Charlize Theron, Serena Williams, Matthew McConaughey, Katie Couric, Joaquin Phoenix, Rooney Mara, Cynthia Erivo, and Demi Lovato, among others. It was a collision of two Los Angeleses: People who had lost everything, and people who wore bling worth as much as a house in Altadena.

Most of the men were dressed in tuxedos. Williams shined in a sparkly animal-print gown. Paul Bettany wore a black Chairman Mao-style shirt. Jaden Smith wore jeans, apparently missing the black-tie memo.

Kimmel, decked out in a perfectly tailored black tuxedo, had some ground rules as the emcee. Guests were expected to wash their dishes. No pets, except service animals, “which we know none of them really are.” “And absolutely no sitting naked on the furniture or on chef José Andrés.”

Chesky, who hard-launched his relationship with girlfriend designer Carly Helfrich on the red carpet, delivered his remarks with the cadence of Vanessa Bayer’s Jacob the Bar Mitzvah Boy Saturday Night Live character, staring down at the teleprompter positioned on the floor. “People are fundamentally good,” he declared, explaining that Airbnb’s business would have never worked otherwise.

On the red carpet, I asked Chesky whether the Trump administration had made it harder for his nonprofit to house people fleeing tragedy. “No, absolutely not,” he insisted, describing emergency housing as a cause that transcends partisan politics. This was a rather diplomatic answer from a man whose company once ran advertisements welcoming refugees in pointed opposition to Trump’s 2017 Muslim travel ban. But Chesky wasn’t taking the bait. “This is a very united kind of issue,” he said.

The night took an emotional turn when Kimmel talked about his son Billy’s three open-heart surgeries before introducing a video of a young boy receiving cancer treatments who was the beneficiary of the charity’s efforts. At that moment, the child, who was in attendance with his mom and grandma, stood on his chair and made a heart symbol using his two hands. The crowd went wild.

José Andrés, whose name appeared on the menu but who was rather noncommittal when asked whether he had actually designed it, insisted that the evening’s charitable mission was more than an excuse for Hollywood to get dressed up.

By dessert, Kimmel was shaking down the wealthy guests. “Don’t cheap out,” he warned, noting that anyone who could afford the new folding iPhone (which retails at roughly $2,000) could surely spare $110 to provide a family with a night of emergency housing. He also accidentally revealed the evening’s secret musical guest: Charli xcx.
“Oh shit!” he exclaimed, realizing his mistake. “Okay, it’s not a surprise anymore.”
Charli eventually took the stage, with will.i.am and Greta Lee dancing from the front row. “That was soooooo good,” Lee said to me on the way out.
And although the set wasn’t particularly long, Charli rocked it, sending heads banging everywhere. She got the Hollywood room doing what it does best: partying for a cause.

items.title: Inside Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s Beloved 730-Acre Country Estate
items.description: On any given day at Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s sprawling 730-acre privately owned estate in Gloucestershire, one might spy the 76-year-old checking in on her prized Highland cows, a scarf tied firmly over her famous bouffant. At the estate’s cutting-edge s
items.author: Hadley Hall Meares
paragraphs: On any given day at Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s sprawling 730-acre privately owned estate in Gloucestershire, one might spy the 76-year-old checking in on her prized Highland cows, a scarf tied firmly over her famous bouffant. At the estate’s cutting-edge stables, her daughter, Zara Tindall, may be riding with her daughter and nieces, coaching them as they jump through courses designed by her father Mark Phillips. Meanwhile, Zara’s husband, rugby star Mike Tindall, may be playing beer pong in the “party barn” with his brother-in-law Peter Phillips, while Princess Anne’s husband Sir Timothy Laurence watches rugby in the cozy, cluttered parlor of the estate’s main Georgian mansion.

The scene is that of an idyllic country estate, a beloved family home that is also a working farm. It may also serve as an example to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle as they search for their own private estate in the British countryside. “Being able to take on a place like this—for me, I’ve got to make it work,” Princess Anne once said. “This is not something that comes free, this has got to pay its way, otherwise I can’t stay here."

Since the ’70s, Gatcombe Park has been Princess Anne’s place of refuge from endless royal duties, a place to live the country life she loves. “Every year, month and day, I realise how fortunate and privileged I am to have grown up and spent most of my life in the countryside,” she told Country Life in 2020. “It’s not only the space, appreciating the seasons, the wildlife, the plant life, the arable crops and the livestock, but, most importantly, it’s the people who live and work there and understand the complexity of their environment.”

The estate was the perfect wedding present from the late Queen Elizabeth to her athletic, no-nonsense daughter and her first husband, Mark Phillips. The two Olympic equestrians first met at a party in 1968, although the meeting was not auspicious. “We had to be told that we’d met in 1968 before we remembered,” Anne recalled.

They later reconnected and found they shared many things, including an obsession with nature, country life, and the world of elite equestrian competitions. “Anne couldn’t marry her horse, so she’s marrying Mark,” the then Prince Charles reportedly joked about his future brother-in-law. Princess Anne approached their upcoming wedding with the same stoicism she did everything. When asked if their relationship could withstand the pressure of publicity and public duties, the Princess was blunt. “Can? It’s got to, hasn’t it.”

The two were married on November 14, 1973, in a lavish ceremony at Westminster Abbey. From the start, Phillips, an active captain in 1st The Queen’s Dragoon Guards, proved to be cut from a different cloth. He refused all the Queen’s offers of titles and was not popular with some royals and their courtiers, with the protective Prince Charles reportedly nicknaming him “fog,” because he was “so thick, according to Kitty Kelley’s The Royals.” British journalist Auberon Waugh (the eldest son of novelist Evelyn Waugh) was even more brutal. He unkindly described him as “Princess Anne’s grinning, speechless husband, who, if you whistle at him, wets himself.”

In spite of naysayers, the couple forged ahead and began searching for the perfect country estate (“I’ve never been a city girl,” Anne noted). In 1976, former Home Secretary Lord Rab Butler, suggested the couple check out Gatcombe Estate, his family home outside of the village of Minchinhampton.

The estate featured over 700 acres of woods and cultivated farmland, stables, a fine herd of Hereford-Friesian cattle and a trout lake, “netting an income of between 14,000 and 18,000 pounds a year.” The five-bedroom neoclassical main house, built with Cotswold stone, was originally built in 1774. In 1820, the famous economist Davis Ricardo had the house redesigned. The exterior was covered in roses and wisteria, and the couple were instantly smitten. The interior was not as picturesque, with one friend describing it as “rather dreary, in some disrepair, with suspicions of dry rot.”

But the couple loved it. “We stood on the front steps and looked out at the view; it was quiet, it was secluded, it was peaceful with woods down each side of a long valley,” Phillips recalled. “I thought to myself—well, whatever is inside, we can change, given time. But this we can never change. This is just what we have been looking for.”

A week later, Princess Anne took Queen Elizabeth to view the property. In June 1976, it was announced the Queen had purchased the home for the couple for a reported 500,000 to 750,000 pounds at the time. Workers on the estate suggested to reporters that Anne could help on a tractor. “Since the Princess can drive a tank, why not?” one quipped.

There was immediate backlash to the private purchase. “When members of the Labour Party government heard that the Queen was buying her daughter and son-in-law the farm and woodland property at such a price, left-wing members called for the introduction of a wealth tax,” the Australian Woman’s Weekly reported. “They pointed out that last year Parliament voted the royal family an extra $600,000 to help it pay its bills.”
MP Willie Hamilton took it a step further. “They’re gold-plated parasites. The lot of them. All parasites.”
For their part, the palace was tight-lipped, claiming the purchase was “an absolutely private matter.” Lord Butler also scoffed at the reported price, claiming it was not nearly as high.

Ignoring the noise, the couple began working to improve their new estate, insisting they would pay their own way. “People never believe me when I say that we’re just like any other young married couple with a mortgage,” Phillips said. Princess Anne did indeed drive a tractor, and Prince Andrew and Prince Edward were said to come down to help during harvest season. While his wife stayed at her apartment working in Buckingham Palace in London during the week, Phillips worked tirelessly on the farm, “so tired that I fell asleep in front of the television.”

Making good on their dream to turn Gatcombe into an A+ equestrian facility, the couple in 1983 hosted the inaugural Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing. The event became a mainstay on the elite equestrian calendar. Held every August, it featured Olympians competing in cross-county (courses often designed by Phillips), jumping and dressage events. Thousands attended the televised program each year, and many more visited at the annual craft fairs and the Gatcombe Food Festival.

Phillips found many ways to monetize the estate, even turning brushwood cleared from the courses into paintbrushes. Meanwhile, the couple raised their children Peter and Zara at Gatcombe, where life revolved around horses. “One enjoys riding, but when you get back there’s still half a day’s work to do just to keep the darn things on four legs,” Anne noted, per The Princess Royal by Helen Cathcart. “You have time for nothing else.”

Tindall has noted that she had an “amazing” country childhood on the estate, far from the hustle and bustle of royal life. “It was a great place to grow up around horses, looking after animals—the respect and partnership that you have to build with the animals, it teaches you so much you know growing up and as a kid,” she said.

But this didn’t mean that growing up on the farm wasn’t hard work. The Phillips children (whose parents declined for them to have titles) were expected to carry their weight. “We had to do everything with them,” Zara recalled. “We had to clean our tack. We had to muck them out.”

Zara, who eventually became an Olympic rider herself, recalled that her parents had very different ways of training. “Mum’s very relaxed. She’s like, Just, you know, just do what you do, whereas my father’s like, More of this, more of that, she said. “My father was quite critical... Very rarely you would get a, Yeah, that was good, out of him. So it was always striving to try and get that comment. He was a tough coach.”

There was also tension inside the home. Both Princess Anne and Phillips were unfaithful (Phillips even had a daughter, Felicity, with a New Zealand woman in 1985) and in 1989 they separated. But Phillips did not go far, moving to Aston Farm on the estate and continuing to run Gatcombe’s events (he finally left Aston Farm in 2013). Princess Anne stayed in the main house with her new husband, Sir Timothy Laurence, who she married in 1992.

According to those who have visited the main house, life there is surprisingly “unroyal” and laid-back, filled with bric-a-brac and cozy, worn decor. “Journalists and biographers who visit Gatcombe for the first time are still struck by the informality of the place,” Anne’s biographer Nicholas Courtney told Glocester Live. Gatcombe Park has become a true family compound, with Peter Phillips and his family reportedly having a cottage there. Zara and Mike Tindall have raised their children at Aston Farm since 2013.

Running the estate has also become a family affair. Peter Phillips helped organize the annual Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing in later years. Princess Anne would present trophies and Zara would compete, as photographers took pictures of Anne’s grandchildren frolicking.

Farming operations have also continued, a practice Anne clearly relishes. “I have lived at Gatcombe for more than 42 years,” Anne wrote in Country Life in 2020. “We were not looking for a farm, but it has been a real privilege to try to work with what we have. Ours is an organic, extensive grass enterprise, usually complicated by running the horse-trial championships in early August. The woodland is a real mix of trees—mostly beeches, but huge numbers of ash of all ages. Who knows how many will survive, but I feel the naturally selected mix could be an important part of the answer.”

That same year, the official royal website also noted the extensive livestock on the property that included 230 Wiltshire Horn sheep, 14 White Park cows, 6 Highland cows, and 2 Gloucester Old Spot sows. There is also a prized herd of rare Suffolk Punch horses, which Anne is passionate about saving. The estate also includes a kitted out party barn, which includes catering facilities, large screens and bar/lounge areas.

The last few years have been eventful, in both good and bad ways. In 2021, Zara gave birth to her third child, Lucas, on the bathroom floor at Aston Farm. In 2023, the estate hosted their last Eventing Festival, citing rising costs and COVID as the reason.

“The horse trials at Gatcombe and more recently the Festival of British Eventing have been a major part of my life for over 40 years when The Princess Royal and I first had the dream,” Mark Phillips said in a statement at the time. “It’s truly a great sadness that the original model and indeed the sport has changed so much. Since COVID, costs, particularly insurance, have risen so much that the numbers no longer add up. It is an end of an era, the next 40 years of the sport will be different, let’s hope it can be equally special.”

In 2024, Princess Anne was reportedly injured by a horse on the property, which resulted in her being hospitalized for a concussion. But there was happier news in June of 2026, when Peter Phillips and his new wife Harriet Sperling reportedly celebrated their wedding reception at the party barn.

Although Princess Anne still continues with her punishing schedule of official engagements, staying in her London apartment in St. James Palace when she must, it is clear her heart lies at Gatcombe Park, surrounded by her loved ones, beloved animals and the crisp country air. “It’s very normal; there isn’t any standing on ceremony, and she’s the only one with a title,” royal historian Robert Hardman told Hello!. “She’s a very good grandmother. She’s hands-on, but like all grandchildren, I think they can get away with things. She dotes on them.”

In fact, the normally tight-lipped Anne has said so herself. “It’s really nice to come back and just be yourself in an area like this.” Former royal courtier Ailsa Anderson agrees. “Gatcombe is her bolthole, where she is not the Princess Royal—she is Anne.”

items.title: Anthony Boyle Talks Sam Bankman-Fried and ‘The Altruists,’ a Tale of Sex and Crypto
items.description: Given how many venal tech billionaires have grabbed our attention over the last several years, you’d be forgiven for having only a hazy memory of Sam Bankman-Fried. He was the cryptocurrency whiz kid whose exchange, FTX, made him one of the richest men in the
items.author: Joy Press
paragraphs: Given how many venal tech billionaires have grabbed our attention over the last several years, you’d be forgiven for having only a hazy memory of Sam Bankman-Fried. He was the cryptocurrency whiz kid whose exchange, FTX, made him one of the richest men in the world, and who forged a charmingly slackerish persona: a shabbily dressed nerd with good intentions. As a believer in the effective altruism movement, SBF planned to donate his riches to charity. Instead, he is now serving a 25-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy.

Anthony Boyle slips under SBF’s skin in The Altruists, the new Netflix limited series chronicling the rise and fall of FTX—as well as the relationship between Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), his on-and-off romantic and business partner. The Belfast-born Boyle is best known to American audiences for his roles in historical dramas like House of Guinness (as 18th-century Irish lord Arthur Guinness), Say Nothing (as IRA leader Brendan Hughes), and Masters of the Air (as WW2 Air Force officer Harry Crosby). He got his break while still in college when he was cast as Scorpius Malfoy in the original cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child in London’s West End.

Ellison’s character would love that. The geek love she and SBF share in the series is complicated and cringe-inducing. She writes Harry Potter fanfic and considers herself polyamorous; he’s a virgin wowed by her brainy sophistication. They egg each other on, bound together by their hunger for risk and their desire to win, whatever the game and whatever the cost. Throughout it all, they remain convinced that they are the good guys.

The Altruists drops November 19, in the midst of a Hollywood tech billionaire reckoning that includes the Sam Altman biopic Artificial, Musk, the Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything, and Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network, The Social Reckoning. Boyle says he hasn’t seen any of those films yet, though he was originally set to play SBF in another movie that fell through. “I was sort of heartbroken,” he tells me, “because I’d spent a couple of months prepping, I had turned down other projects, and then it was taken away from me. I was like, I’m never gonna be able to do that voice that I worked so hard on!”

Yet when his agent called with news of the Netflix project, Boyle was hesitant. “My heart was already broken by [SBF] once,” he says. But the scripts for The Altruist—written by Graham Moore, the screenwriter of The Imitation Game—changed his mind. “It’s so funny and more about the relationship between him and Caroline,” the actor says now, “about their love story and them goading each other to do all this.”
During his initial meeting with Moore, Boyle stayed in character as Bankman-Fried. “I

was complaining about getting off of a Zoom with Mark Zuckerberg, because that’s the tone of the show. It can be quite irreverent at some points, and then other scenes are kind of heartbreaking.” It won him the part. “Thankfully,” he says, “all my prep didn’t go to waste!”
Vanity Fair: It’s funny that you were so eager to live in Sam Bankman-Fried’s head. He is such an anxious figure.

Boyle: There’s a lot of anxiety in him. You can even tell in his speech patterns: He corrects himself and goes back and forth, like his internal metronome is going so quickly at all times. He’s like a hummingbird, like his heart’s beating so quick. But thankfully I didn’t take any of that home with me.

At a couple of points in the series, he says, “I know I’m not a normal person.” There’s an ongoing public conversation right now about a lot of these tech moguls believing they know better than the rest of us. Did you think of SBF as someone with that kind of Superman complex?

I think the opposite. I played him as someone who was profoundly insecure. There’s this thing of broken men building empires. He has this idea of: I am FTX. So if I can make FTX the biggest, the richest, if I can have the most of something…. That’s not someone who’s comfortable in his own skin. I was interested in what possessed someone to become the world’s youngest billionaire. I’m not really interested in money or crypto or finance. It was: What makes them do the things that they do?
Sam is a nerdy guy, but as soon as he gets successful, he hangs giant posters of himself everywhere. Is he burning for the world to recognize him and admire his empire?

Do you know the poem “Ozymandias” [by Percy Bysshe Shelley]? There’s a bit in the show where I’m looking up at this great poster of myself, and it reminded me of that line: “Look on my works, ye mighty, and despair!” I asked Graham, “Can I quote that poem in the show?” And he said, “Originally called that episode ‘Ozymandias!’”

Talking about wanting to be recognized—when I was prepping for this, I went to a crypto guy’s birthday party in Los Angeles. He was paying a DJ a million dollars for one evening, but he built this plinth above the DJ decks for him and his friends so you had to look at him. A lot of these crypto people, who maybe didn’t have buzzing social lives—wallflowers who didn’t know how to communicate—became billionaires. And what this guy had done with it was to throw money at a very famous DJ, and then raise himself above him. It reminded me of the scene where Sam has a 100-foot poster behind him. It was like, Wow, this is that sort of man in his mum’s basement who just wants the world to see him.

In Sam’s case, his roaring egotism is somewhat awkward because he’s also obsessed with the idea of being altruistic. At one point in the show, a leader of the Effective Altruism movement sees this lavish party he’s thrown and says, “Uh, this isn’t very altruistic.”

Yes, he’s spent a lot of money on confetti cannons! That dichotomy is what’s really fascinating about him, because I think both of those two things are true. I think he really is altruistic, and I think he does have narcissistic tendencies.
I read that you corresponded with him in prison. What did you want to know?

Annoyingly for this interview, I promised him that I wouldn’t divulge anything. I asked him to open his heart up to me, and he really did. He was very forthcoming with over 100 questions in emails. He answered, I’d say, 98% of them. Even the ones that he didn’t answer were very telling for me, because you’re like a detective, trying to figure out how he answers them and in what way. And can you trust it?
As we see in the series, he insisted on doing interviews throughout the scandal. Even when his lawyers were telling him to stop.

When I was playing those scenes, it was like: I can outsmart this; I can get in front of it. I can just explain this to them. You know, he went to jail for stealing the money—but if he didn’t go to jail, a year later to the day, all of that money would have been back, and tenfold. He invested in Anthropic. He invested in the biggest AI companies. His argument was: Look, I know the markets. What you all see is a bird falling to certain death. What I can see is that the bird is swooping, and will come back up. I read last week that said Sam might have been the world’s first trillionaire had he not gone to jail, because all the AI companies are now flourishing.
The show frames Sam and Caroline as a love story. But it’s hard to tell if they are egging on each other’s delusions, or if this is kind of a game that’s fueling their relationship.

They’re obsessed with games. Even the first time they meet, they are playing a game. This isn’t in the show, but in my head, the scene that I sort of created for myself to understand him was: He’s playing World of Warcraft, and on the same screen he loses $100 million, and then he dies in World of Warcraft. He’s like, Fuck!, and feels more emotional about the game than about other people’s money.
It does feel like the real-life consequences are very abstract to him. Like he’s busy trying to outplay everyone and not thinking: This is going to cause somebody to go bankrupt and ruin their lives.

I think that’s the great tragedy of it, because people did go bankrupt, and people unfortunately died by suicide through this. Marriages broke up. Families tore apart because all of their money was in this. And that’s something that we have to remember when talking about the show. There were real-world consequences because of this crash.
There’s a whole spate of movie projects this fall that suggest tech bros are the new supervillains. But it sounds like you didn’t approach the character that way at all.

My viewpoint on it is that Sam wants to do good. But I think the best-laid plans of mice and men often [go awry]. It’s easy to say I’m going to give away all these billions—and then suddenly you’re not in your mum’s basement, and you’re hanging out with Katy Perry, and you think, This feels pretty good to me. I don’t think people should have that amount of power.
You are Mr. Period Actor. Is this the first time that you’ve played a character living in the present?

I feel like it is. It’s the first time I had to act with a laptop and an iPhone, and it’s so annoying. There’s no one there that you’re looking at. You’re just looking at a green screen. And then it [causes problems]—like, Oh, we saw the camera in the reflection when you turned it that way. These things that I didn’t have to deal with before because I was, as you said, Mr. Period Man.
Even Say Nothing was set in the 1970s and ’80s, well before cell phones.
That was more handguns than iPhones.

One of your most recent period characters is Arthur Guinness in House of Guinness, and there’s been some buzz about your full-frontal nude scene on that show. I’m just curious if there’s anything that you would not do on screen.

That’s such a funny question. I guess whatever they write in the script, I’d look at it and see if I wanted to do it, but probably not! Like when I did that scene, it was in service of the character and in service of the moment. I wanted that character to feel like he's in control of the world and that these are all peasants that are beneath him and he doesn’t care. Very opposite to Sam, who I think has a lot of body shame.
Somehow, I don’t know that the world wants to think about Sam Bankman-Fried naked.
You never know, man. There’s something out there for everyone.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

items.title: Heidi Klum Teases Her Latest Halloween Costume
items.description: Halloween is just around the corner—and what does that mean? It means that Heidi Klum, the undisputed queen of the scariest night of the year, will soon reveal her incredible new costume. After dressing up as an anthropomorphic worm, an incredibly realistic ET
items.author: Alfredo Toriello
paragraphs: Halloween is just around the corner—and what does that mean? It means that Heidi Klum, the undisputed queen of the scariest night of the year, will soon reveal her incredible new costume. After dressing up as an anthropomorphic worm, an incredibly realistic ET, and a chimpanzee complete with prosthetic facial features and ears, the supermodel is ready to amaze us once again.

Back in September, she revealed to People that she was already hard at work planning her next big costume. While she didn’t reveal any details—which is perfectly understandable—she did hint that it would be a “very, very bloody” look and that it “goes very well with red wine.” She’s given a few clues; the latest one she shared on her Instagram profile.

“What’s my costume?” the supermodel asked her followers, attaching a spooky close-up of some prosthetics ready to transform her into who knows what. The image appears to include a shiny brain, a blue tube resembling a sea creature, fleshy tissue, and a yellow sac that could be a honeycomb, coral, earwax—in short, anything.

Of course, many have tried to come up with an answer. Some suggested it might be Ursula from The Little Mermaid; others noted similarities to the vanity monster portrayed by Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley in The Substance, while another user pointed out that the image resembles the appearance of the zombies in The Last of Us.

In an interview with NBC’s Hollywood ReelTime, special effects makeup artist Mike Marino—who has created some of the model’s most iconic Halloween looks—revealed that this year’s costume is the most complicated one he’s ever worked on.

It seems almost impossible for Klum to follow last year’s incredible costume; on the 25th anniversary of her famous Halloween party, she appeared as the mythological Medusa. Her body was entirely covered in green scales; she had a long tail and moving snakes instead of hair, while her husband, Tom Kaulitz, dressed as a Greek soldier turned to stone.

It’s quite the challenge to top that legendary getup. Yet we’re certain the former Victoria’s Secret Angel won’t disappoint. So mark your calendar for this weekend to find out whom Heidi Klum will be impersonating.
Originally published by Vanity Fair Italia.
