items.title: China’s First Fully AI-Generated Movie Flops at the Box Office
items.description: Just as the first chapter of Elon Musk’s AI-produced version of The Odyssey was turning off viewers in the United States, the first feature-length AI-generated movie widely released in China was flopping at the box office.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: Just as the first chapter of Elon Musk’s AI-produced version of The Odyssey was turning off viewers in the United States, the first feature-length AI-generated movie widely released in China was flopping at the box office.
The film, the sci-fi thriller Sanxingdui: Future Past, was released last week and only grossed an estimated $198,000, according to the French wire service Agence France-Presse.

There have been several other AI-generated feature films in limited release in other countries. But with 10,000-plus opening-day screenings, Future Past marks the first longform AI film to get a true wide release with reported box office numbers in a major territory, arguably marking the first real commercial test of the technology for feature-length projects. The film’s early ticket sales were reportedly about 12 percent of its 10 million yuan budget (about $1.5 million).

According to the AFP, Jiang Defu, CEO of the film’s production company Bona Film Group, told Chinese film outlet Yuli that the film nonetheless represented an important experiment. “We are the first to try it, the first to get a theatrical release permit and the first to be tested by the audience. I think that is not easy at all.”
One moviegoer told the outlet, “In terms of quality, compared with human production, it still falls short.”

That said, the technology is hardly bound to the fate of a single film. In China, AI has taken over the production of short online films (microdramas), with 95 percent being AI-generated, according to Fortune. A feature-length AI-generated hit seems only a matter of time.

Future Past is a 100-minute film inspired by archaeological finds from the Sanxingdui civilization. Appropriately enough, the film is about a future when a superintelligent AI has spread across the globe and humanity has handed control to algorithms, which plunges the world into a crisis.

Previous feature-length movies that gained limited release include India’s Love You, a 95-minute musical, released in May 2025, and Malaysia’s Pirate Queen: Zheng Yi Sao, which was released in January.

In the United States, the first AI-generated feature film is scheduled for limited release Dec. 4. The film is called Gods Don’t Give Gifts, distributed by Fable and created by YouTuber Gossip Goblin, and is an R-rated anthology of four sci-fi stories.

items.title: Patrick Stewart’s Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist
items.description: In the first two decades and change of Patrick Stewart’s distinguished professional career, he spent 16 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, made his Broadway debut alongside Ben Kingsley and Frances de la Tour in a legendary production of A Midsummer Nig
items.author: David Rooney
paragraphs: In the first two decades and change of Patrick Stewart’s distinguished professional career, he spent 16 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, made his Broadway debut alongside Ben Kingsley and Frances de la Tour in a legendary production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream directed by influential theater giant Peter Brook, and became a frequent presence on the storied stages of the prestigious Royal National Theatre.

It’s a telling insight into the hermetically sealed bubble of Hollywood that a renowned classical actor with years of notable work behind him, when cast in 1987 in the sci-fi TV spin-off Star Trek: The Next Generation, was identified in the Los Angeles Times as an “unknown British Shakespearean actor.” Stewart, who died Wednesday at 86, now runs no risk of being called unknown.

That wealth of stage experience was deeply embedded in his layered characterization as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, commander of the USS Enterprise, allowing Stewart to project steely authority without ever losing sight of the man’s kindness and compassion, his mentorship and familial protectiveness toward his crew.

While longtime friend and colleague Ian McKellen urged him not to toss away his prime Shakespeare years — the trajectory that ideally leads from Hamlet and Macbeth all the way to King Lear — Stewart took the Star Trek job. He signed the standard six-year contract despite quiet assurances from his agents and other industry associates that the show would likely last a single season, after which he could pocket his television earnings and return to his first love, the British stage.

But the spacetime continuum has a way of scrambling well-made plans. Not only did the show run for 178 episodes over seven seasons — peaking at 12 million viewers until the 1994 series finale, which was watched by more than 30 million — it also spawned four feature films, plus an additional spinoff, Star Trek: Picard, for which Stewart returned to the role for a three-season run.

The endlessly regenerative sci-fi phenomenon made Stewart a wealthy man and gave him global recognition, but by all accounts, the rigorous discipline he had acquired over all those years treading the boards was instrumental in shaping the work ethic of the entire company. As Picard, he also played a decisive role in making bald sexy.

With his crisp, cut-glass diction, stentorian delivery and regal bearing, it’s hard to believe Stewart grew up in a working-class Yorkshire family, such was his unquestionable natural command. But perhaps that upbringing in an unstable household — where he was often forced in explosions of domestic violence to get between his mother and father, a World War II veteran who suffered from undiagnosed PTSD — was part of what made Stewart such a warmly empathetic screen presence.

That quality, along with his Shakespearean gift for language and dramatic nuance, informed another defining role, that of Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise, starting in the late ‘90s. Back then, the Superhero Industrial Complex was in its infancy, and casting actors of the caliber of Stewart and McKellen gave it a legitimacy that helped turn those films into pop-cultural powerhouse events.

Stewart’s Professor X, like Picard, was a stern but nurturing figure, a telepathic mutant who founded the Xavier School for Gifted Youngsters, providing a refuge for youths displaced or discriminated against and a safe environment for them to better understand and control their extraordinary powers. The professor’s integrity and honor shone brightly when seen alongside the Machiavellian Magneto, the supervillain on a quest to impose mutant supremacy over mankind. Making for what might be the most perfect pairing in Marvel Comics movies, McKellen took on that role.
Between 2000 and 2017, Stewart made seven X-Men features, collectively grossing $3.32 billion, in addition to appearances in two separate Marvel Cinematic Universe films.

While fans of the series will no doubt have a range of personal favorites, for me, Stewart’s best performance as Charles Xavier was his last, in James Mangold’s haunting, Western-adjacent Logan. Starring opposite Hugh Jackman as a battle-weary Wolverine, Stewart brought enormous pathos and heart to the ailing Professor X, his telepathic gifts turned glitchy by an unknown brain disease. The emotional depth and the heavy burdens of the past in both leads’ performances — but Stewart’s in particular — make Logan one of the most unexpectedly poignant MCU films, transcending the comic-book genre to become a moving character study.

I was fortunate to drink in Stewart’s magnificent stage presence in three plays on Broadway. The first was in 2008, in director Rupert Goold’s hyper-kinetic horror-movie reimagining of Macbeth. Stewart was 68 at the time, older than most actors cast in the title role, his advancing age fueling a rich current of resentment at being too long passed over for leadership roles despite his valor on the battlefield. Casting Kate Fleetwood as a ruthlessly ambitious trophy wife some three decades younger added even more tension to that famously conspiratorial spousal dynamic.

Stewart’s Macbeth was absolutely a murderous fiend, willingly goaded into action by his slinky missus, but the actor brought steadily amplified frailty, paranoia and befuddlement to the tyrant that made us see him in a different light. He didn’t go so far as to turn the character from villainous to sympathetic, but he made it impossible not to be touched by this once-great man undone by the encroaching shadows of his treachery.

He returned to Broadway in 2013, reuniting with McKellen in a blistering doublebill of Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land and Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot. Stewart and McKellen first shared a stage in 1977 at the RSC, and their spiky interplay, more than three decades and many adversarial X-Men encounters later, was thrilling to watch.

Absurdist dramas that trace the treacherous limbo between birth and death, the companion pieces assumed the cutting double edge of tragicomic vaudeville. Humor and cruelty consistently overlapped in the actors’ portrayals of two men trapped in an unbreakable cycle of existential unease and futility.

While Stewart’s death is a sad occasion, his legacy is a robust one, demonstrating that classical training and a firm grasp of bardic poetry can enrich even the most seemingly unlikely genre material with dramatic weight, psychological complexity and emotional impact. Not bad for an “unknown British Shakespearean actor.”

items.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’: First Reactions
items.description: He’s back, and he’s angrier than ever! Godzilla Minus Zero had a series of screenings this week for press and the first reactions have been flooding social media. The verdict? We have another kaiju-sized hit on our hands.
items.author: Abid Rahman
paragraphs: He’s back, and he’s angrier than ever! Godzilla Minus Zero had a series of screenings this week for press and the first reactions have been flooding social media. The verdict? We have another kaiju-sized hit on our hands.

Despite having its world premiere at the New York Film Festival on Sept. 26, legendary Japanese studio Toho held more press screenings this week for Godzilla Minus Zero ahead of the film’s Centerpiece gala screening at the Tokyo International Film Festival on Nov. 1. The film is released in theaters in Japan on Nov. 3 and North America on Nov. 6.

Written and directed by Takashi Yamazaki, Godzilla Minus Zero is a direct sequel to the Japanese filmmaker’s 2023 epic Godzilla Minus One, that scored over $100 million at the global box office from a $15 million budget and won an Oscar for best visual effects in 2024.

A synopsis from Toho of Godzilla Minus Zero reads: “War reduced Japan to zero, and Godzilla plunged it into minus. Two years have passed since then, and the country has faced agonizing struggles to achieve recovery and finally reclaim its daily life. Just as humanity managed to cling to a hard-won peace, a new threat strikes, crushing hope in an instant. There is no third time. Everything ends here.”
Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe, Hidetaka Yoshioka and Kuranosuke Sasaki are among the cast returning for the sequel. Newcomers include Min Tanaka and Masami Nagasawa.
Shot entirely in Japan, notably, Godzilla Minus Zero is the first-ever Japanese production to be filmed for Imax.

The Hollywood Reporter‘s David Rooney reviewed Godzilla Minus Zero after seeing it NYFF, and described the film as a “radioactive blast.” In a rave review, Rooney praised Yamazaki for topping the spectacle of his first film. “The resulting clash of the legendary kaiju is a rip-roaring smackdown in a movie that keeps awing the audience with exhilarating action and then continually one-upping itself in the dustups that follow,” Rooney writes. “I’m fairly sure I stopped breathing during a tense scene in which Godzilla bears down on a seaplane attempting a hurried liftoff.”
Godzilla Minus Zero currently holds a score of 92 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 50 reviews. On Metacritic it holds a score of 78 and on Letterboxd it is rated at 4 stars.
See a selection of social media reaction to Godzilla Minus Zero below.

items.title: William Shatner, Seth MacFarlane, Hugh Jackman, Minnie Driver, More Remember Patrick Stewart: “He Was a Singular Talent”
items.description: Patrick Stewart‘s former co-stars and fellow Hollywood notables and executives are paying tribute to the sci-fi icon following his death at age 86.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: Patrick Stewart‘s former co-stars and fellow Hollywood notables and executives are paying tribute to the sci-fi icon following his death at age 86.

The actor, best known for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor X in X-Men, died on Wednesday after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” his longtime rep Kelly Bush Novak previously shared.
Kevin Feige, Ian McKellen, William Shatner, Seth MacFarlane, Hugh Jackman, Minnie Driver, Marvel Studios and Lea Thompson are among those who have taken to social media to remember Stewart.

Feige, the head of Marvel Studios, shared in a statement with The Hollywood Reporter, “I’ll never forget the first time I saw Sir Patrick Stewart on the set of the first X-Men. After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor.”

“It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him,” he added. “His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”

McKellen, who played Magneto/Erik Lehnsherr opposite Stewart in the original X-Men franchise, shared a lengthy tribute on X. “Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love,” he wrote in part.

Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk alongside Patrick in 1994’s Star Trek: Generations, wrote on X, “What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.”

Jackman, who starred as Wolverine in several X-Men films, shared in a tribute on Instagram, “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”

Marvel Studios also shared on social media, “All of us at Marvel Studios are deeply saddened by the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart. Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from X-Men to Logan to Avengers: Doomsday. He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art.”

MacFarlane, who worked with Stewart on numerous projects, including Family Guy, Ted, Blunt Talk and American Dad!, took to Instagram, writing, “Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us. I grew up as a fan, and was later gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend, working with him for many years on “American Dad!”, “Family Guy”, and “Ted”. He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come.”

“I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day 1 of a new film,” MacFarlane continued. “He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, “Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.” We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.”

Minnie, who starred in 2017’s The Wilde Wedding with Stewart, wrote, “Is this year some kind of portal to a much, much better place that all the greatest people know about and so have gently made their exits ? Dearest Patrick. Who always had the best advice, the funniest story, the patience to listen. I’m just bereft. All love to your family, and you, in my heart forever.”

Jonathan Frakes, who played Commander William Riker in Star Trek: The Next Generation series with Stewart, posted on his Instagram Story, “Rest in peace my friend.” Wil Wheaton, who also played Wesley Crusher in the series, shared a photo of him with Stewart on Instagram with the caption, “Godspeed, Captain.”

Thompson, who directed Stewart in two episodes of Star Trek: Picard, shared on social media, “This astonishing actor was kind enough to take a chance on me as a director. Always hardworking intelligent and so very good you could play the whole scene on him. @sirpatstew Patrick Stuart was indeed a Sir. To sir with love. #rip you were one of a kind.”
Kumail Nanjiani shared on Bluesky, “Sir Patrick Stewart was the best. I don’t know what else I can say.”

George Takei, who played Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek: The Original Series, wrote on Threads, “Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”

items.title: This New G-Shock Looks a Lot Like One of the Most Iconic Watches Ever Made
items.description: If we were playing matchmaker for some of our favorite watch brands, we wouldn’t have thought of pairing a Casio G-Shock with Patek Philippe’s iconic Nautilus. However, the Japanese watchmaker’s new GMC-2500 proves that opposites do attract.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: If we were playing matchmaker for some of our favorite watch brands, we wouldn’t have thought of pairing a Casio G-Shock with Patek Philippe’s iconic Nautilus. However, the Japanese watchmaker’s new GMC-2500 proves that opposites do attract.

The 2500 Series is a new collection that “reimagines the design DNA of the watch that started it all,” according to Casio. The brand is nodding towards the original G-Shock ref. DW-5000C from 1983, a watch designed to be tough enough to keep ticking even when dropped. The team famously tested prototypes by hurling them out of the third-floor men’s bathroom of the Casio offices. The new 2500 series is a close descendant of the shock-absorbent watch's original design.

The first G-Shock featured an octagonal digital display, four buttons on the case flanks, and an integrated rubber strap. The 2500 Series incorporates most of those features—but this time, the display is analog rather than digital, and a pair of case “ears” makes the model look a lot like Patek Philippe’s famous flagship luxury sports watch.

Designed by Gérald Genta and released in 1976, the Nautilus is based on a porthole—hence the “ears,” which mirror the hinges/securing mechanism used to open and close a ship’s window against the elements. You may also recall that this isn't the first time that Casio has taken inspiration from a famous Genta watch: the GA-2100 Series (aka ‘CasiOak’), with its octagonal bezel design, bears a remarkable similarity to the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak.

The watch community has been waiting impatiently for the announcement of the 2500 series since Casio’s Japanese website accidentally listed these pieces back in September. In the months since, collectors have already given the watch the “CasioNaut” nickname. (What good is a watch without a clever nickname, after all?) The wait isn’t over just yet, though. The line will officially go on sale through Casio’s website on November 6th.

The 2500 Series is much more than a quartz-powered Nautilus copy. At the center of the design is the Multi-Mission Date function that operates through a three-cell display at 3 o’clock. Besides indicating the date, it can also display the watch’s current mode, elapsed stopwatch minutes, and setting information. Meanwhile, a small-seconds display at 9 o’clock shows passing seconds, but can also be paused and restarted as necessary. (Pausing the function can extend the battery life up to five years.)

The timepiece's tech uses G-SHOCK’s familiar four-button arrangement and comes packed with all the features we've come to expect from the Japanese brand. For starters, the watch automatically keeps rigorous time through 2099 after you input the year, month, and date. LED illumination ensures everything is legible even in low light, while a magnetic system steadies the watch’s hands even if dropped, bumped, or roughed up. Water-resistant to 200m, the 2500 Series is just as capable as you’d expect from a hard-wearing G-SHOCK. Available in simple resin cases with matching rubber bracelets for $145; with metal accents and rubber bracelets for $280-$300; and with full-metal bracelets for $350, the handful of launch references come in a variety of versatile colors and weigh between 47 grams (resin) and 160-180 grams (metal).

Though Casio releases oodles of fresh colorways in existing G-SHOCK families each year, it’s not every day that the world gets an entirely new model family. Fun, streamlined, and much more affordable than the watch it's nicknamed after, the 2500 Series is certainly on its way to becoming a hit.

items.title: Saquon Barkley Is a Luxury-Watch Designer Now
items.description: As a superstar running back for the Philadelphia Eagles, Saquon Barkley has had plenty of opportunities to flex his design muscle. He’s worked on his own shoes and branded apparel, but nothing comes close to his latest project: designing a custom watch with be
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: As a superstar running back for the Philadelphia Eagles, Saquon Barkley has had plenty of opportunities to flex his design muscle. He’s worked on his own shoes and branded apparel, but nothing comes close to his latest project: designing a custom watch with beloved Swiss watchmaker H. Moser & Cie that gave him an even deeper appreciation for timepieces.

“You don’t really get to be too detailed when it comes to designing apparel,” Barkley tells us. “But when it comes to a watch—the little stuff that’s within a watch—it’s just on a whole other level, and you just have a different appreciation of it.” The result of this hyperfocused approach is the new H. Moser Pioneer Cylindrical Tourbillon Skeleton Aventurine Saquon Barkley Edition, a $99,600 watch limited to just 97 pieces.

Barkley discovered Moser while preparing to attend the Met Gala in 2025. He needed a watch to wear and found his way to the independent Swiss house. It’s been a mad love affair ever since. Designing a watch is “something I’ve always kind of wanted to do,” Barkley says. “When you are living this life and setting goals, I want to do stuff that takes me out of the atmosphere of just being a football player. And there aren’t many NFL athletes that can say they have their own watch. And to do it with such a prestigious brand like H. Moser made it 10 times better.”

The Pioneer is Barkley’s first horological baby, and a classic Moser: It blurs the line between a sport and a dress watch and packs specs that are catnip for the biggest nerds. The most critical feature for Barkley was the skeletonized movement—“Being able to see inside was super important,” he says. The single element that prevents you from looking inside the watch is the subdial made of aventurine, a stone that resembles the night sky.

The watch is a tribute to Barkley in more ways than one. There are the obvious touches like the Super-LumiNova-filled numerals 2 and 6, which glow a different color from the rest of the indices in honor of his jersey number. But this wouldn’t be a terribly appropriate watch for someone like Barkley—renowned for his explosive speed and signature backward hurdles—if it couldn’t take some physical abuse. The Pioneer checks those boxes with 120 meters of water resistance and is hardy enough to be worn every day, in any situation.

Designing the new Barkley edition completely changed how the running back thinks about his timepieces. “Before, it was like, ‘How does the watch look? What’s the price on the watch?’ That was how you set the value of a great watch, and I thought about what I want to put on when going out for dinner or an event,” he explains. But designing a $99,600 luxury timepiece changed everything. He brought up hairsprings, tiny pieces of coiled metal that are essential to keeping time, more than once in our interview. “I understand the process behind making a really good watch,” Barkley says, “so my appreciation of it is different.”

items.title: Jacob Elordi's New Cartier Is Secretly Extra Fancy
items.description: Last month, Jacob Elordi did the impossible and made goatees not just socially acceptable but somehow sexy; the month before, the tall Aussie actor wore a suit to The Dog Stars film premiere alongside his canine co-star, and the internet started interrogating
items.author: Mike Christensen
paragraphs: Last month, Jacob Elordi did the impossible and made goatees not just socially acceptable but somehow sexy; the month before, the tall Aussie actor wore a suit to The Dog Stars film premiere alongside his canine co-star, and the internet started interrogating the length of his trousers.

People care a lot about Jacob Elordi and his appearance. That’s one reason he’s in the running to be the next James Bond; it’s also why I don’t think he will be 007. How could we possibly increase our thirst for the 29-year-old? It’s not possible really—unless we talk about his personal watch collection, where there’s quite a lot to talk about.

As a longtime friend of Cartier, Elordi likes to keep things pretty consistently Tank-coded. Over the past year, I’ve spotted him wearing different types of Tanks: a Française, à Guichet, a diamond-set one, green and black Tank Musts, you name it. He wears Cartier very well because, despite his imposing frame, he's comfortable wearing rather dainty pieces of horology.

The man has simple tastes and doesn’t seem to want his watches to do anything other than tell the time in a quaint, uncomplicated way. Second hands? Elordi doesn’t need them. Hour and minute hands will suffice.

Over the weekend, while on a date with girlfriend Kendall Jenner at the Academy Museum Gala in LA, Elordi wore his fanciest Tank yet. Although you really have to study the watch to see how special it is. Zoom in a little on the watch, which could be mistaken for a stainless-steel Cartier Tank, but is actually a new platinum version on a semi-matt burgundy alligator leather strap. The telltale sign is the shinier-than-usual case. Platinum is a heavier, prettier, and more expensive metal than stainless steel.

Unlike some of the vintage Cartiers he’s rocked recently—the majority of which have quartz movements inside—this one is packing a very handy automatic winding, calibre 1899 MC. So it's the real deal, and also makes the watch a tiny bit larger (38.1 x 27.75 mm) than his previous flexes.

No matter what Tank Jacob Elordi has worn, the dials always remain pretty much the same. The word timeless is bandied around far too often in the watch world, but the Tank can legitimately make such claims because the dial design has hardly changed in more than 100 years. Roman numerals, minimalist geometry, and a clear rectangular shape in the centre of the dial inside a very rectangular case make these watches unmistakably Cartier.
This story originally appeared on British GQ.

items.title: I Waited Years for Bvlgari to Make This Watch. It Was Worth It
items.description: It’s been so long that I can’t even remember when I first started asking for a smaller version of Bvlgari’s award-winning, record-breaking ultra-thin watch, the Octo Finissimo. I do remember that it became something of a tradition to badger Fabrizio Buonamassa
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: It’s been so long that I can’t even remember when I first started asking for a smaller version of Bvlgari’s award-winning, record-breaking ultra-thin watch, the Octo Finissimo. I do remember that it became something of a tradition to badger Fabrizio Buonamassa Stigliani, Bvlgari’s product creation executive director and design director. His reaction was always the same. He would flash his signature heavily bearded, friendly smile from behind a desk in the presidential suite of Geneva’s Hotel President and say, “Everybody asks me for this watch!”

This spring, Bvlgari finally made good on my long-standing wish. The brand unveiled a new 37-mm version of the Octo Finissimo, a much more wearable size for most wrists. The new diameter is especially important for this particular model’s shape. “The demand wasn’t driven only by the trend toward smaller watches,” Buonamassa Stigliani told me during an interview in April. “The Octo Finissimo is a square watch, so it wears larger than its dimensions suggest.”

The Octo Finissimo is an icon of modern watchmaking, which made the lack of a Goldilocks-size version even more glaring. Since Bvlgari debuted the OF in 2014, the collection has accumulated 10 world records for ultra-thin watchmaking, including two for the thinnest mechanical watch. The original Automatic, sized at 40 mm, followed a few years later and has since been made available in numerous iterations: sandblasted titanium, stainless steel, 18k gold, ceramic, and more.

Bvlgari rewarded my patience handsomely. The brand debuted three versions of the new OF37: in matte sandblasted titanium; brushed and polished titanium, and yellow gold. Excited beyond what should reasonably stir the emotions of a 36-year-old man, I requested to spend a week with the sandblasted titanium version—which, to my mind, struck a fine balance between graceful futurism and the utilitarian look of a classic tool watch.

Having the OF37 on my wrist really drove home that it looks and feels like nothing else on the market. For almost my entire adult life, I’ve worn a Rolex Submariner, which is in many ways the standard-bearer for modern watch design, and I was immediately struck by how much wearing the OF37 felt like a daring adventure. While I’ve come to love the weight and heft of the Sub, the legendary lightness of the OF was both lovely and slightly alarming. Looking down and seeing this thing—whose matte titanium body completely changes color from steel grey to black to light graphite depending upon the ambient light—is fascinating. On the other hand, I’m a fairly active guy: I’ve taken my Sub swimming and diving without thinking about it, I’ve owned it for 24 years and worn it for 15 without ever servicing it, I’ve donned it during patrols in the military, I’ve banged it into every conceivable surface and (almost) never worried about it. I’m not sure I’d be comfortable wearing the OF37 the same way.

The OF37 is the product of many years of refinement. “We’ve been collecting feedback for years—about the buckle, the case size, the movement finishing, and the needs of both clients and collectors,” says Buonamassa Stigliani. “This watch reflects all of that feedback. We explored several sizes—36, 37, 38, and 39 millimeters. Ultimately, 37 mm was the smallest size that allowed us to preserve the watch’s technical features.”

The change is what made a slightly imperfect watch perfect to me—looking at the older version was like seeing a painting hanging just slightly crooked. I’m of the mind that a well-designed watch should be framed by one’s wrist—not sit right up against the edge of it. This was precisely the quality that the condensed size offered: smaller, incredibly thin, and so comfortable I forgot it was there.

The OF’s similarities to other modern watches begin and end with the fact that it uses three hands to tell the time. You can certainly perceive some of the Gerald Genta-inflected heritage of Bvlgari’s watchmaking division, particularly in the obsession with eight-sided bezels. But compare it to even the luxury sports watch stalwarts out there—timepieces such as the Royal Oak and the Patek Philippe’s Nautilus—let alone to something like a Submariner, and you’re left scratching your head going, this is different.

What distinguishes the design is the clever octagon-within-a-circle-within-a-square architecture. The design starts with one of Buonamassa Stigliani’s famous hand sketches. The angular look is inspired by ancient Roman architecture (and its ample use of the octagon); Italian design; automotive motifs (Buonamassa Stigliani loves cars); and Bvlgari’s own jewelry. In fact, the OF37 wears much more like a piece of modernist sculpture on the wrist than a conventional wristwatch.

The OF37, regardless of material, boasts the brand-new Bvlgari BVF 100 movement. Measuring just 2.35 mm thick, it uses a platinum micro-rotor activated by the movement of your wrist to automatically wind the watch. The case itself at 6.45 mm is actually thicker than the 40mm version’s case at 5.15 mm, though you likely wouldn’t notice this given its smaller diameter and the fact that it’s only as thick as a few credit cards stacked together. The power reserve on the 40-mm version is 60 hours; impressively, that of the 37mm—a watch 20% smaller in volume—is 20% higher, at 72 hours.

The OF is almost a victim of its own success in differentiating itself from the rest of the market. I’m almost certain that the watch couldn’t be my personal daily driver. But could it be a part of my rotation? Hell yes. I can’t wait till the first celeb pairs one of these with black tie, frankly. Josh O’Connor, can you help me out there? The list price warrants discussion here: $16,600 for the sandblasted titanium version ($17,300 for the satin/polished titanium version and $48,300 for the gold version) is no joke. This probably won’t be someone’s first watch but rather the province of somebody for whom watch collecting is already a practiced sport.

Once or twice while wearing the OF37, I caught a glimpse of its sleek angles and strange profile in the window reflection of a parked car, or even the mirror in my bathroom. That it looks quite unlike anything that came before it means that it doesn’t have simple answers to simple questions: Is this an everyday watch? A dress watch? Something for serious collectors or splashy newcomers? What makes the OF37 special is that it refuses to be any one of those things.

items.title: 5 Products That Changed My Life in October
items.description: Late October officially lands us at the start of the holiday season, a typically chaotic period I have never been very effective at managing. There are costumes to plan, parties to throw and attend, and between it all, many end-of-year deadlines to meet. A lit
items.author: Alyssa Bereznak
paragraphs: Late October officially lands us at the start of the holiday season, a typically chaotic period I have never been very effective at managing. There are costumes to plan, parties to throw and attend, and between it all, many end-of-year deadlines to meet. A little push and pull between my full calendar and the routine that keeps me steady is inevitable. But there’s no reason to white-knuckle through it without some help. The products that spoke to me this month are all stopgaps in some way or another—handy ways to fortify against, or work with, the busy stretch ahead.

While I’m still working my way through the stash of sunscreens I bought in Europe and Asia during recent travels, I am nonetheless stoked that US formulas are finally catching up to their superior foreign counterparts. A quick recap for context: This past June, the Food and Drug Administration approved its first new sunscreen ingredient in over 25 years, a chemical filter called Bemotrizinol, or BEMT for short. It’s a standard part of most SPFs abroad, valued for its stability when exposed to UVA and UVB rays, its gentleness on sensitive skin, and its low potential for skin penetration—meaning, it’s less likely to be absorbed into the bloodstream in comparison to other chemical UV filters. As of September, a few sunscreens with the ingredient have begun trickling out into the marketplace—and more are surely on the way. I got my hands on the version from La Roche Posay, the brand I usually search for in European drugstores, earlier this month. I’m happy to report that it’s extremely lightweight. It rubs in easily and leaves no white cast or excessive grease behind—just a punch of hydration, thanks to some welcome glycerin. Also, for those of you with facial hair, La Roche-Posay’s (notably bearded!) head of brand engagement Justin Ollivierre assures me it plays nice with scruff, and doesn’t create the flaking effect common with other formulas. Wearing it while walking or gardening under the strong, persistent Los Angeles sunshine, my skin hasn’t experienced even a hint of redness. And given my dear city’s reputation for polluted air, I’m also grateful for the concoction’s Litchiderm and Exo-P extracts, which are meant to protect the skin barrier from oxidative stress. It’s not quite the next-level skin care product that sunscreens are abroad, but it’s a significant step up. Go get a bottle immediately.

Extremely caffeinated energy drinks are becoming the norm at the office and in the gym, but I personally can’t handle a cold brew without getting the jitters. If I drank a Celcius Heat, packed with an eye-popping 300 mg of caffeine, I think I might implode. But I still lean on caffeine to focus at work and lift better, like everyone else. I just prefer to get it from various types of green tea, both to protect my sleep and sensitive stomach. I make an Ippodo matcha in the morning, buy jugs of jasmine Tea’s Tea to portion out throughout my workweek, and when I really need a pick-me-up, I down an Ito En Sencha Shot. While an espresso shot contains approximately 60 mg of caffeine, these only have about 40 mg. It’s a tamer, more refreshing option to put a little pep in my step. Not to mention each one is infused with a healthy helping of vitamin C. One of these, in fact, may have had a hand in helping me write this column.

Whenever I travel, I always seem to either forget my razor at home or leave it behind in a hotel. Over the years, this bad habit has left me buying flimsy, plastic razors as replacements—not ideal! Schick’s new limited-edition Hydro Razor is a nice in-between travel option—not quite the quality of your at-home shaving setup, but also far more elevated than what any hotel toiletry kit has to offer. It has a weighty metal handle with some grip to it, and comes with a sturdy magnetic stand to place on a countertop. And it delivers a precise shave without irritating the skin. A nice little upgrade for your Dopp kit during a chaotic holiday season.

If you follow skin care as closely as I do, you probably already know that PDRN stands for polydeoxyribonucleotide, which—gasp!—is a small DNA fragment of salmon sperm. Over the past few years, it’s become a popular ingredient across Korean skin care brands eager to capitalize on the fascination over the more invasive, painful, and, I must say, very effective salmon sperm injections or microneedling, which center around polynucleotides (PN), also found in salmon sperm. Funny enough, many brands are now developing plant-based versions of PDRN, all but stripping it of the original reason it earned so much attention in the first place. But that doesn’t mean it’s not effective. Case in point: Dior’s new silky smooth PDRN shot. This patented formula combines a plant-derived PDRN with vitamin Cg and niacinamide to plump, brighten, and smooth skin. I can dab this at my elevens, crow's feet, and dark spots before bed, and no matter how little sleep I get, I emerge in the morning with fortified, radiant skin.

As long as I’ve exercised, I’ve been locked in a never-ending endeavor to prevent post-workout breakouts. The reality is, if I go for a long hike, or catch an evening yoga session, I’m not always able to shower off my sweat immediately afterward. When I finally am able to spritz off, I find it can be helpful to counteract the dirt and sweat seeping into my skin with a little extra exfoliation on my back, neck, and chest. I loathe a harsh “peel” wipe, but these exfoliating sheets from Prequel are gently effective. They use a mix of different acids to lift dead skin cells without sacrificing any moisture, thanks to an infusion of squalane. Since using them I’ve noticed fewer exercise-induced blemishes. They’re a nice, light option to tuck into a backpack, Dopp kit, or gym bag.

items.title: 'Backrooms' Director Kane Parsons on What Scares Him the Most
items.description: Backrooms, your anxiety-inducing horror film about a man trapped in an endless world of portals leading to disturbing environments, earned a staggering $118 million globally on its opening weekend. You are 21 now, and were a teenager in 2022 when you started t
items.author: Lynn Hirschberg
paragraphs: Backrooms, your anxiety-inducing horror film about a man trapped in an endless world of portals leading to disturbing environments, earned a staggering $118 million globally on its opening weekend. You are 21 now, and were a teenager in 2022 when you started the project as a series on YouTube; after it went viral, A24 signed you to develop it into a feature film. You’re the youngest director ever hired at A24, and Backrooms is the biggest hit in the company’s history. And yet you’re back at home in your childhood bedroom in Petaluma, California. Do you still have posters on the wall?
No posters. My childhood bedroom looks like a CIA agent lives here—there’s film equipment everywhere in an empty white room.
You made your first film in eighth grade, and it won an award.
It was called Late for School, and it was kind of sci-fi. It won the Five Minute Film Festival award here in Petaluma. I later extended the film to 30 minutes— I wanted to increase the quality.
Backrooms has the feeling of found footage, like The Blair Witch Project. Were you influenced by that film?

I watched Blair Witch only one time. I was more influenced by body-cam footage on YouTube. You can find video content of dynamic situations in people’s lives. As creepy as that sounds, there’s nonfiction footage of emotional moments; environmental footage where people are alone in a room. I would watch 30 minutes of people walking in dead malls or empty parking lots. Spatial anxiety fascinates me.
Although your bedroom walls are white, you seem to be intrigued by the color yellow—Backrooms is suffused with that shade.

When I was growing up, my walls were yellow. The yellow in the film was influenced by the short story “The Yellow Wallpaper,” by Charlotte Perkins Gilman. [“The Yellow Wallpaper” is a horror fiction story from 1892, about a woman confined to a room; obsessed with the yellow wallpaper, she descends into madness.] I spent a lot of time fixating on creating a sickly, suffocating, gross yellow. Interestingly, when we’d post thumbnails on YouTube of “Backrooms” videos, if they didn’t have yellow in the background, they would get much less traffic. There’s an efficacy in yellow.

Most horror directors your age work with young, relatively unknown actors in their films. Instead, you cast Academy Award nominees such as Renate Reinsve and Chiwetel Ejiofor. Was there a reason you chose them?

In terms of characters, I prefer people with more life experience. If an external idea hits a young person, they are immediately vulnerable. But when a person has a history and a set of beliefs and views, banging up against something new and unsettling causes a tectonic change. An older person evaluates an obstacle in a different way than a young person does—they have to weigh what they are seeing against their life experience. You couldn’t tell the same story with younger individuals.
I’ve experienced things that people might call ghostlike, but I prefer to think the ghost is in my own brain.

I’m most frightened of violence against consciousness. And, of course, that fascinates me also. I don’t like the idea of brains being grown in petri dishes. And I can be afraid of darkness. But isn’t everybody?
You have said that you often prefer television to films. Which shows do you love?
My brain goes to Mr. Robot, Better Call Saul, and Barry. I love Bill Hader.
Barry is a dark comedy. Would you ever direct a comedy?
I think I could! I’m not a funny person, but I think I could navigate that world.
Did you watch Backrooms with an audience in a theater on the opening weekend?

Yes. I watched it in the one theater in Petaluma where I saw films as a kid. It was great to see the poster in front. They were selling Backrooms merchandise in the lobby. It was quite wonderful, and also surreal.
You’re an original! Who is an original to you?

The musician Gary Wilson. My director of photography and I carpooled to set every day on Backrooms, and we’d play Gary Wilson in the car. On the days that we didn’t play a Gary Wilson song, we’d have a bad shoot day. So that became our superstition. Without Gary Wilson, there would be no Backrooms.
Grooming by Michael Moreno for Oribe at The Only Agency; Photo Assistant: Jordan Zuppa.

items.title: Amanda Seyfried Is Ready to Ring in the Holiday Season With Tiffany & Co.
items.description: It is never too early to get into the holiday spirit. Everyone knows the Christmas season can be stressful, but the more you prepare ahead of time, the more you can enjoy all the magic. So while it may seem too early to start considering your gifts, in reality
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: It is never too early to get into the holiday spirit. Everyone knows the Christmas season can be stressful, but the more you prepare ahead of time, the more you can enjoy all the magic. So while it may seem too early to start considering your gifts, in reality, you’ll just be saving your future self a lot of stress. And luckily, the brands are, once again, ahead of schedule, already rolling out their holiday content for our benefit. Ferragamo, Dior, Chanel, and more have released their 2026 holiday campaigns, and the images are getting us in the yuletide mood. So while the leaves may just now be falling off the trees, soon they’ll be on the ground, covered in snow—and there’s no time like the present to dive into the 2026 holiday campaigns.

Fresh off her buzzy turn in You Can See Everything, Amanda Seyfried has returned to New York from Texas, just in time for the holiday season. The actor is Tiffany & Co.’s newest House ambassador and the star of its holiday campaign, “Love Is a Gift.”

As part of the campaign, Seyfried acts in a short film, “You & Me,” which tells the story of two different Christmas celebrations: one taking place in the present day, and one in 1992. Between these two moments passes a Bird on a Rock ornament, originally gifted decades ago and still a prized possession all these years later. It’s a story of tradition, holiday memories, and the connection between generations.

“I’m thrilled to join the Tiffany & Co. family as their newest House ambassador and to be part of a campaign that celebrates love, family, and the traditions we carry with us through generations,” Seyfried said in a statement. “‘You & Me’ captures beautifully how a meaningful gift can hold memories and become part of a family’s story. It was incredibly special to bring that idea to life with Tiffany this holiday season.”

The holidays are all about family, so it makes sense that Kim Kardashian enlisted her very famous sisters to star in the Skims Holiday campaign. Shot by frequent Kardashian collaborator Nadia Lee Cohen, the campaign takes inspiration from nostalgic holiday portraits, placing Kim, Kourtney, Kylie, Khloe, and Kendall in scenes you may recall from your own home videos.

The sisters are styled in pieces from the Skims holiday shop, wearing outfits with varying degrees of coziness. Khloe and Kourtney are covered head-to-toe in their respective patterned onesie and red long johns. Kylie and Kendall, meanwhile, show off more skin in bras boasting classic holiday prints. All the girls don retro glam—bouffants and old-school glasses. The result is a vintage scene with no clear time stamp. But it doesn’t matter, because Santa still clearly approves.

Gigi Hadid, Louisa Jacobson, and more gather in a grand townhouse to celebrate the holidays. The polished wood walls are covered in wreaths, the tree is bedecked with ornaments, and everyone is dressed in Miu Miu.

The wardrobe highlights contrasts between lifestyle archetypes and seasonal themes. Silk dresses are paired with upcycled knits and sportswear-inspired zip-front blousons. Cropped sweaters reveal button-down shirts, and utilitarian cotton canvas separates are layered over sequined bralettes.

But the models are not alone in this uptown space. They are joined by plush toy bears, rabbits, geese, and more. Treated like treasured guests, these additions provide whimsy to the scene, a composed portrait of bourgeois behavior subverted by humor and play.

Friendly furry creatures are not unique to the Miu Miu campaign this season—they pop up in the Prada world as well. This time, though, the woodland pals are hand-drawn by a team of artists led by cinematic animator John Pomeroy.

Sadie Sink gets down on the ground with a trio of mice to admire a patterned, calf-hair loafer. Maya Hawke faces off against a sly fox as she braves the elements of a frozen setting. There is a whimsy to these wintertime scenes, which emphasizes Prada’s humanity and a connection to craft that lies at the heart of the brand’s approach to creation.

Kris Jenner is the matriarch of the Ferragamo family in the brand’s 2026 holiday campaign, The Joy of Loving. “Ferragamo is all about family,” says creative director Maximilian Davis. “And when I design, I am always thinking about that, too: how a collection can be worn by different generations, but also how pieces you love will be held onto and passed down through them.”

The momager stars as the director of a fictional film, leading screen tests featuring the campaign’s various faces. There’s Paloma Elsesser and her brother, Sage; girl group The Womack Sisters; and Sofia Testino with her dog, Syko. Actress Joan Chen is joined by her daughter, Audrey Hui, while acting coach Nancy Banks poses with her son, actor Benny Buckley.

The campaign connects back to the roots of Ferragamo, and founder Salvatore Ferragamo’s original desire to build a better life for his family through his love of invention and creativity. “One of the founding values of Ferragamo has always been of beauty that develops from craftsmanship, humanity, and joy,” says Salvatore’s son, Leonardo Ferragamo. “This campaign is telling that story.”

Loro Piana invites you to a weekend at the cabin, where the elegantly falling snow outside matches the chic inhabitants’ wardrobes. Models are dressed in the brand’s holiday collection, an expression of style that plays out across textures, hand-finished prints, exclusive patterns, and elaborate stitches.
Loro Piana’s usually muted color palette is realized once again, this time in the form of dark greens and earthy browns. They are highlighted with pops of winter-white and marigold.

Warm jersey tops and trousers form the foundations of these après-ski looks. On top, classic Loro Piana outerwear like the Spagna jacket and Konny vest are crafted in wool and finely detailed with needlework; the wearer stays warm while also making an enviable sartorial impression.

Chanel is hitting the slopes for its 2026 Coco Neige collection. Bright-red knits and colorblocked puffers stand out against snow-capped mountains. The images have a retro flair, but the clothing is distinctly modern.
A snowball fight adds even more joy to this already playful campaign, while penguin and polar bear-shaped purses and earrings provide the perfect amount of whimsy.
Shearling caps keep ears warm, while winter whites are embraced with aplomb. It’s a reminder that dressing for warmth does not mean sacrificing style or charm.

Indulge in your sweet tooth with Dior’s 2026 holiday campaign, which sees the brand’s famous 30 Montaigne store reimagined as a sugar-dusted gingerbread house. Anya Taylor-Joy and Deva Cassel star in a joyous musical video. The house’s ambassadors prance around the store, snacking on Dior cookies, spritzing the brand’s famed fragrances, and trimming the icing-lined cookie Christmas tree.
This article was originally published on

items.title: Pierpaolo Piccioli on His Vision for Balenciaga & the Power of Starting Over
items.description: It takes less than a minute for Pierpaolo Piccioli to steer a conversation about fashion into one about philosophy. More than a year into his tenure as creative director of Balenciaga, during an interview on the day after he showed his first couture collection
items.author: Eric Wilson
paragraphs: It takes less than a minute for Pierpaolo Piccioli to steer a conversation about fashion into one about philosophy. More than a year into his tenure as creative director of Balenciaga, during an interview on the day after he showed his first couture collection for the house in July, Piccioli explains how he has navigated a role that is both familiar and foreign to him by first quoting Friedrich Nietzsche and the concept of oblivion—oblio in Piccioli’s native Italian.

“Oblio is a moment when you are aware of your past, but you kind of forget everything for a moment and you see everything with new eyes,” says Piccioli, seated at a large conference table in his office suite on Avenue George V, in Paris. “And that’s what actually happened to me.”

For most of his career, over a quarter century, Piccioli was associated with one designer: Valentino Garavani, who made a lasting impression on his life and his eye. Starting in 1999, Piccioli, then in his early 30s, and his longtime collaborator, Maria Grazia Chiuri, rose through the ranks at Valentino, becoming co–creative directors in 2008, a year after Valentino announced his retirement. Then Piccioli led the Roman house solo from 2016 to 2024, while Chiuri served as creative director at Dior. He knew the seamstresses by their names, their skills, their peculiarities, and their very Italian way of working, and he adopted the rhythms and rituals, if not the formality, of Valentino himself. This would have been a lot to leave behind for a designer taking on the mantle of another legendary brand—let alone that of Cristóbal Balenciaga. That house’s own rich history includes two wildly successful modern interpretations, first under Nicolas Ghesquière, then under the now mononymous Demna. But in the words of Nietzsche, “Man will desire oblivion rather than not desire at all.” “I didn’t want to come here to find the same people with the same experiences,” Piccioli says. “I wanted to face something new.”

At his couture show the day before, under the blazing sun in a garden on the outskirts of Paris, Piccioli showed 52 looks that were captivating in their strange beauty. Some of them were outrageously glamorous in the bold style that Piccioli had once championed at Valentino: He opened with a cloud-shaped jacket trimmed with a flock of intense red feathers, worn over a white oversize silk duchesse satin T-shirt and voluminous beige trousers; another look consisted of a dark red shirt styled with big pink pants. But many others represented new territory for the designer, like a floor-length coat the color of a yellow highlighter, which he showed backward, slung over matching pants. There was a fluorescent pink silk “balloon bolero” dress trimmed with feathers made of tiny strips of curled organza. The designs seemed to demand close inspection to be fully understood.

“It felt like a real celebration of artistry,” said the actor Lily Collins, who has known Piccioli for more than a decade, since they first attended a Met Gala together. “Pierpaolo and Balenciaga are the perfect mix.” Naomi Watts headed backstage, where she raved about a tailored black dress adorned with a white ribbon scarf. “That’s the sort of dress I look forward to wearing in my 50s, 60s, 70s, and then some,” she said. Demi Moore, who wore a Piccioli-designed Balenciaga couture ensemble at Cannes in May, circled the boards showing photographs of the models in each of their looks, while Hudson Williams, who appeared in one of Piccioli’s first Balenciaga advertising campaigns, stood nearby, waiting to offer his congratulations.

“This collection is the result of a feeling,” Piccioli wrote in a printed program composed of 20 narrowly spaced pages, including detailed descriptions of all the looks, along with the names of the members of his atelier who helped realize them—Victor, Thomas, Léa, Margherite, etc. “We worked while getting to know each other, learning to understand one another,” Piccioli wrote. It was part of his broad effort to humanize the couture-making experience, which can feel cold and anonymous to anyone living outside that bubble.

The week before the show, Balenciaga wiped its social media history and then posted portraits of some 40 members of its atelier, all dressed in their white Balenciaga Couture work coats. Many of them appeared to be quite young, though a few were established hands and familiar faces, including Bruno Sialelli, formerly the creative director at Lanvin. Philip Treacy, the milliner, was also credited in the couture program for contributions that included a pink ostrich-feather headpiece that spiraled from the crown and around the torso, turning the model who wore it into a swan.

This meeting of minds, among Piccioli, his seasoned collaborators, and his younger team, has become as much a part of his vision for Balenciaga as the clothes seen on his runway. “When you don’t know the rules, you are more open to experiment,” he says. “And that is the key for me to interpret Balenciaga. I didn’t want to go back to any of the old shapes but to try to invent a new shape that could have been that of Cristóbal.”

The day after the show, the couture salon is packed with visitors examining the looks. Patti Wilson, the stylist, has been there for more than an hour. Amal Clooney is spotted among the mannequins. When he arrives, Piccioli, who is 59, is dressed in his usual uniform of a black T-shirt and trousers, with a necklace of coral amulets worn as protection from bad energy. He has a pack of cigarettes in hand and is still very much the picture of a Roman designer who cooks his own pasta most nights, now at his new home just across the Seine. “I’ve got my Roman ways in Paris,” he says. “It’s a sort of effortless approach that is maybe less formal than expected, more direct and more human.”

On his first day at Balenciaga last year, Piccioli traveled to Getaria, the tiny fishing village in the Basque region of Spain where Cristóbal Balenciaga was born in 1895, and where a museum dedicated to the master’s work today offers access to an enormous array of designs collected by his staff and clients. As Piccioli immersed himself in Balenciaga’s world, he began to understand that designs he had perceived through images as austere or strictly linear were, in fact, quite light. That would be his starting point for Balenciaga couture. “In every one of his silhouettes, the body was the protagonist,” he said.

To achieve similar results in new ways became an obsession for Piccioli, and this is where having a younger atelier was an advantage—the team was willing to experiment with techniques that break with the strict traditions of couture. Perhaps the biggest change was replacing standard Stockman mannequins with custom forms created from 3D scans of models’ bodies. Those ghostly plastic forms were used to shape fabrics through a complex process of layering cashmere upon leather that had been washed, stretched, and allowed to dry in place to hold its shape. Each mold took as long as a month to create, but eliminated the need for darts or seams. Piccioli also wanted to play with new fabrics and materials, using a lab-grown silk called AMSilk that purports to be fossil fuel–free and stronger than steel.

Despite these technical innovations, Piccioli believes in the classic model of couture as the pinnacle of fashion. “When you talk about couture, you talk about an approach in which there are no maps. A 3D conversation with the body can then apply to denim, T-shirts, and tailored jackets from prêt-à-porter. To me, a T-shirt has to be a T-shirt, as much as a pair of jeans has to be a pair of jeans. But if you meld couture and industrialization, you can make a more modern garment.”

Like most designers of his generation, Piccioli was raised to worship at the altar of the great Cristóbal Balenciaga, who worked in Paris from 1937 until his retirement, in 1968. The first image Piccioli posted on his personal Instagram account, in 2018, was of a 1967 Balenciaga wedding ensemble that had been included in the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute exhibition “Heavenly Bodies” that year. “Simplicity is a solved complexity,” Piccioli wrote in his caption, paraphrasing the sculptor Constantin Brâncusi. It did not escape Piccioli’s attention that the wedding dress had been designed by Balenciaga the same year Piccioli was born. And although his reverence for Balenciaga is rooted in the maestro’s innovations, Piccioli made clear upon his arrival at the house that he respected the label’s more recent history as a modern luxury brand as well. Balenciaga is now a commercial behemoth that has been redefined by other famous designers. Ghesquière gave Balenciaga heat in the new millennium; Demna brought the house to the street over the past decade, and his flair for disruption ultimately drove Balenciaga well past $1 billion in sales. Both are difficult acts to follow.

With his initial ready-to-wear shows, Piccioli laid some of the groundwork. His spring 2026 collection was based on Balenciaga’s 1957 sack dress, which had a lightweight and unrestrictive shape that was revolutionary at the time; the following season was an ode to “finding lightness in the dark,” as illustrated by inky black skirts and coats, a few pieces rendered with imagery from Sam Levinson’s Euphoria. Piccioli also alluded to his personal love of sports with a techwear-meets-couture pre-fall collection, and with the introduction of a collaboration with the NBA in January that included four-figure varsity jackets, as well as hoodies and sweatpants that would not have looked out of place in the luxury streetwear oeuvre of his predecessor.

As Piccioli steers the future of Balenciaga while learning to embrace his own, he is facing change on a personal level. Valentino Garavani, to whom Piccioli remained close long after his retirement, died in January at the age of 93. Piccioli’s former design partner, Chiuri, has since left Dior and returned to Rome, where she made her couture debut for Fendi the same week Piccioli was presenting his for Balenciaga. His children, Benedetta, Pietro, and Stella, are all now adults and starting their own lives. Just as before, he returns to Italy to spend his holidays with his wife, Simona, and their family at their seaside home in the small beach town of Nettuno, near Rome, but their days there are more limited than they were before.

In Piccioli’s loose interpretation of Nietzsche, a designer might be able to forget his history out of necessity for a moment, but the past remains around him all the same. Acknowledging as much, Piccioli has kept the office he inherited mostly untouched. Its decor is aggressively gray, just as Demna left it last year when he was tasked with righting the ship at Gucci, which, like Balenciaga, is owned by the luxury goods conglomerate Kering. Piccioli layered some brightly colored rugs on the floor and retrieved from his own storage a three-person desk designed by Gio Ponti. Against the far wall is a billboard-size poster of a famous photograph of the same Balenciaga 1967 wedding ensemble Piccioli posted on Instagram, which shows the dress in such stark black and white contrast that its sharp silhouette forms an almost perfect triangle. Leaned against the photo is a bright pink surfboard designed by Piccioli for Zara’s 50th anniversary last year.

“I’ve added some elements and taken out others, but this is kind of metaphorical of what I’m doing here at Balenciaga,” Piccioli says of the office. “They are contradictory in the space, but in a way I feel that they have found their own harmony. I didn’t want to deny what has been done before me. I’d rather layer on top of that and create a bridge so that Balenciaga can go somewhere else.”

Hair by Benjamin Muller at MA+ Talent; makeup by Lucy Bridge at Streeters; manicure by Fanny Santa Rita for Essie at Call My Agent. Model: Lydia Hall at Ford Models Barcelona. Casting by Ashley Brokaw Casting. Set design by Rafael Medeiros at the Wall Group.
