items.title: The ‘Pain in the Ass’ Math That Could Save Vibe Coding From Itself
items.description: Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually.
items.author: Paresh Dave
paragraphs: Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.

For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.

Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.

“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”

&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.

And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.

The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.

The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.

Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.

Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.

Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.

Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.

But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.

Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.

Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.

Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.

Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.

Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”

Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.

But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

items.title: Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
items.description: A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now
items.author: Joel Khalili
paragraphs: A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.

The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.

“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”

The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.

The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)

Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.

Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.

“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”

According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.

“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

items.title: This App Brutally Shames You by Tracking How Many Hours You’ve Lost to Scrolling
items.description: You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a health
items.author: David Nield
paragraphs: You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a healthier relationship with your device.

One of the newer ones, which takes a slightly different approach to the norm, is Oh My Hours for iOS. (There's no sign of an Android version yet.) Rather than giving you a mass of menus and options to wade through, it simply splits each day into blocks of hours that you can either waste or use productively, then puts a black mark next to the hours during which your phone has distracted you.

It's simple, it's effective, and it just might work. Rather than seeing how long you spent on X and Instagram, you see the hours you've lost to social media algorithms and the infinite scroll. Here's how Oh My Hours works on your iPhone, plus some other apps to check out if you’re looking to develop healthier phone habits.

You can get started with Oh My Hours for free on iOS. But to really make the most of it, a $10-per-year or $20 lifetime payment is required. This lets you customize what counts as a “lost” hour or day, and it gives you access to month and year views, which provide the best insights into how you're spending time on your phone.

Here's how it works. First, you indicate which apps you consider distractions, either by category (social media apps and games, for example) or by selecting apps individually. If you use any distracting app for a certain amount of time—this can be customized in settings—then that hour of the day is marked as “lost.”

The main interface shows each day as a straightforward series of circles representing hours. Every circle that’s filled in black is an hour you’ve lost to an app that has pulled you away from something more worthwhile.

It’s quite a brutal and minimalist approach, but I like it. It really brings home how much time you can spend on apps that aren’t really all that good for you, especially when you start looking at your progress (or lack of it) over entire weeks or months. However, I did find that once I’d lost a particular hour, my brain wanted to cram in as much absent-minded scrolling as possible during the rest of that hour.

By default, an hour is marked as lost if only if you spend seconds inside a distracting app. It's quite a harsh approach, but it needs to be—otherwise I think there would be the temptation to use up any allotted free time after every hour resets. You can extend this threshold period through settings, if you pay for the app.

Another handy feature here is the ability to set designated quiet hours. These are times when you really, absolutely do not want to look at your phone unnecessarily: Any use of a distracting app here blackens the boxes for all the hours in the quiet zone, not just one. Again, this can be customized, whether or not you’re using the app for free.

There’s one more option here, which is to reset an hour if you think it’s been marked incorrectly. (Maybe your finger slipped and you really didn’t mean to launch Instagram.) It’s all very simple and easy to use, and there’s an export tool here that gives you a CSV file of your stats if you want to do more with them.

As I’ve already mentioned, if you’re in the market for an app that’ll gently nudge your habits toward spending less time on your phone, there are abundant options that look at the problem from a variety of angles. These are in addition to the Digital Wellbeing (Android) and Screen Time (iOS) tools you’ll find on your phone, which can be accessed from the Settings screens.

One Sec for Android or iOS takes a simple approach to phone addiction. For the apps you specify, it will load up a breathing exercise for you to complete before giving you the choice to continue to the app or back out. It’s a small tweak, but it’s surprisingly effective, and it’s backed by science. You can get started for free, while $20 a year gets you more features, including full app blocking and more advanced time tracking.

Then there’s Forest, for Android or iOS, which I’ve found to be useful whenever I’ve wanted to try to encourage myself to spend less time on my phone. The longer you ignore your handset, the bigger your virtual forest grows, and the app developers invest in real tree planting to further incentivize you. The main focus timer can be used without paying, while upgrades like customizations and allowed lists will set you back at least $6 a month.

ScreenZen, available for Android or iOS, is comprehensive and completely free (though you can donate to the developer if you find it helpful, which I’d recommend). You can set up a variety of barriers between you and your distracting apps, depending on your preference, including customized pauses (with motivational messages) and math challenges. Conventional app and timer blocks are also included.

One of the most thorough options here is Roots, though it’s available only on iOS. You’re able to schedule phone-free periods, block specific apps, and set up phone detox challenges that you can take on with friends and family. Like Oh My Hours, the app is also really good at giving you a breakdown of how much time you’ve saved by staying out of certain apps. Basic blocks and limits are free, with more advanced customizations available for $10 a month.

Also worth considering is Brick, which combines the free Android or iOS app with a small physical device that’ll set you back $59. The Brick itself is an NFC transmitter (it works like tap-to-pay), and when you want some distraction-free time, just press your phone against it to block (or unblock) specific apps. The controls are all managed in the Brick app. It’s incredibly simple, and that’s what makes it effective.

items.title: I Did Push-Ups With Snap’s Chunky AR Glasses
items.description: I hadn’t expected to be doing augmented reality push-ups in the middle of the mall. Yet there I was, wearing bulky Snap Specs while facing the ground.
items.author: Boone Ashworth
paragraphs: I hadn’t expected to be doing augmented reality push-ups in the middle of the mall. Yet there I was, wearing bulky Snap Specs while facing the ground.

The Lens (what Snap calls apps on its augmented reality headset) is called Thirty Ups. It is in Halloween mode now, so when I look down, a virtual cartoon Jack-o’-lantern sits right next to where I’m supposed to start working out. I’m not trying to get jacked right now, but my goal is to see if these gigantic smart glasses will fall off when I’m staring straight down and moving up and down.

I get into position and start my workout. When I go down and back up, a little virtual circle on the ground below me starts counting up. I don’t get to 30 push-ups. I’m surrounded by people, many of whom are now staring at me, and it feels too hot outside to keep going without feeling gross. I get in 12 reps before giving up. The glasses only count 11 because it tells me I “skipped” one. Great.
The nearby Snap representative is thrilled. “You’re the first person who’s tried that one,” he says. I’m also pleasantly surprised. These glasses seem huge, but they stayed on my face just fine.
Snap announced its Specs in June. They cost $2,195 and will start to ship in the coming weeks. It took a few months for Snap to share what actual features would be available on the glasses

WIRED’s Julian Chokkattu and I both tried out Snap’s Specs last week. He got a dedicated demo with the company. I was offered one, too, but instead I happened to stumble upon the Specs First Look demo at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles. The space has been here for just a couple of weeks.

It was a warm Sunday afternoon, and a steady stream of people came through the mall’s demo zone. Snap reps handed out Specs to anyone curious enough to register and hang out. Kids were running around, and the glasses looked especially large on their faces. When people left the demo, they got a free cup of ice cream with a small, Specs-shaped chocolate cookie.

The Specs had a dozen or so Lenses available for testing. Aside from the push-ups, the Specs let you finger paint in midair, see navigation directions overlaid on the real world, or engage with the physical environment by drawing on a notepad or analyzing text in a print book. They also have some sporty features, like one that allegedly helps with golf and another through a partnership with the NBA that guides you through shooting hoops.

You may have noticed that the glasses look pretty chunky. That’s true, but I was pleasantly surprised by how lightweight they felt and how well they stayed put. (The glasses come in two sizes, so if the small is too tight, try the larger model.) Another surprise was how well the virtual digital elements held up in bright light. I made a point of walking into direct sunlight to test out the screen. With the brightness turned all the way up, the onscreen elements were still visible. The glasses had automatically switched into “sunglasses mode” and dimmed to block the sun. The Snap rep said the lenses protect the eyes from UV rays at all times.

The problem, though, is that Snap is really trying to make the case that these glasses—or at least future, smaller iterations—are the holy grail of consumer tech. But I still don’t care to wear them in public. Walking around with the AR elements on can be distracting. Even if you turn it all off, the waveguides on the lenses still have a rainbow shimmer in your vision as you move. I wouldn’t want to wear these while driving or even walking when I really need to see where I'm going. At one point in the demo, I had to dodge a kid wearing a pair of Specs who was wildly swinging punches at something on the screen only he could see.

Most of the device features are controlled with your hands, like pinching two fingers together to open a lens or move something around. You can play Beat Saber-esque games by moving your hands around. But the controls can be finicky, and I found myself clawing at the air repeatedly to move or open something. Chokkattu tried writing in Google Docs—a demo showing the Specs as a computer you can work with anywhere—but the connected Bluetooth keyboard had a severe input lag, making typing a chore.

It also feels odd that some Specs features really just feel like advertising. A Harry Potter spell-casting experience is a fun idea, but really it just comes across as an ad for the upcoming HBO show. The Specs also have a shopping feature which lets you browse stores online. It’s a reminder that one day your augmented vision will be bombarded with pop-up ads.

I have a hard time imagining who these glasses are for. Given the price, it’s clearly aimed at developers and early adopters. But I tried the developer version of the Specs in 2024. The new glasses are much more comfortable and slightly less chonky, but the software hasn't changed much since then. Snap has shown off the same finger painting demo every time I’ve tried them, and every time it works until it doesn’t. The Specs are interesting but lack a killer feature, and Meta and Xreal both have more polished mixed-reality glasses that cost less. That’s going to make Specs a hard sell.

“We see consumer adoption as a process—the hardware, software, available experiences and price all need to develop together,” a Snap representative wrote in a statement to WIRED. “Specs bring computing into the world without pulling you out of it.”
For now, Snap’s most compelling pitch might be the free ice cream.

items.title: Liquid Glass Finally Makes Sense on the iPhone Duo
items.description: Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.
items.author: Craig Grannell
paragraphs: Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.

“With all major design updates, there’s a natural process where we take a bold leap forward, and then we continue to iterate,” said Apple's human interface designer, Shubham Kedia, during a predictably sleek keynote video. “Our team really appreciates your feedback, and we considered it deeply as we refined the new design.”

Not quite “Sorry, everyone, we messed up,” but for Apple, practically an apology tour. The subject was Liquid Glass, Apple’s most divisive interface design since at least iOS 7. Apple's Vision Pro mixed-reality headset (which itself flopped) inspired the translucent design language, and the company brought it to millions of other Apple devices.

The result was a mess—at odds with Steve Jobs’ famous line, “Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.” Liquid Glass started obsessed with gloss and effects, despite promises it would bring your content to the foreground. Yet Apple’s own press release showed interfaces with illegible text. Worse, users found constant reflections and flickering color shifts distracting, and a lack of clarity across devices hurt accessibility.

But iOS 27, alongside updates to Apple's other software platforms, signaled a shift in priorities after Kedia’s mea culpa. Kedia spoke of reincorporating design cornerstones in what was, if not quite a U-turn, then at least a rediscovery of a core principle: how it works. Instantly, interface elements across Apple devices gained greater clarity and structure, making it easier to tell apps' components from content. The most obvious change, though, was a slider.

Apple said it tuned Liquid Glass to diffuse complex content more effectively, keeping elements legible when above imagery and text. But it also acknowledged that not everyone wants the same thing—some users might prefer a more tinted look, and others “would like Liquid Glass to be even more clear.” You can now decide for yourself with the Liquid Design slider in Settings. For a company known for being opinionated, such bet-hedging was surprising but not unwelcome. Choice isn’t a bad thing, and now users had more of it.

“I immediately pushed that slider all the way to the most tinted setting, and pretty much all the legibility issues vanished,” Ben Rice McCarthy, an indie developer behind popular apps like Obscura and Indigo, tells WIRED. McCarthy has long criticized Liquid Glass. Now? Not so much.

“Liquid Glass introduced a lot of issues without adequate solutions, but this year’s operating systems solved or improved a lot of them,” McCarthy says. “There’s the adaptiveness of the interface. Buttons can grow into menus. Controls merge and divide like cells as you transition between views. Toolbars can expand and contract smoothly as the view changes size.”

Flexibility matters when resizing windows across any device. But while announcing its updates, Apple also dropped major hints that all but confirmed new hardware—it showed iPhone apps running on an iPad or a Mac could resize to a suspiciously specific shape that matched the rumored inner display dimensions of Apple’s upcoming folding phone.

When Apple showed off the iPhone Duo, everything clicked. Its passport-shaped display bucks the trend of iPhones and their rivals growing taller over the years. The Duo is wider and almost squat, and when opened, it naturally defaults to landscape, echoing the iPad Mini display.

Apple being Apple, it wanted to avoid the jarring jolt between displays that’s often evident on rival foldables, so it made content appear to move seamlessly from one screen to the other. That begins with the hardware. As Molly Anderson, Apple's vice president of Industrial Design, said at the September keynote: “To achieve this continuity, we designed iPhone Duo around a consistent aspect ratio that is the same across both displays.” But it’s the software—rooted in Liquid Glass—that sells the illusion.

The most arresting element is a fancy animation, which various folks in the Android space are now busy being “inspired” by. It reinforces the idea of a flowing interface. Meanwhile, Liquid Glass freed Apple from being prescriptive about where essential controls live. On the Duo, they sit at the side. When the phone’s closed, that frees up space for content. When it’s open, the controls stay in a consistent spot, so you never have to hunt for them. Reorient the device, and everything settles into the most appropriate place.

That’s form following function, not function being subservient to form. This device and its flexible interface don’t strictly need the Liquid Glass design language, but the two feel made for each other. Liquid Glass finally makes sense on the iPhone Duo—and with Apple’s other refinements, it’s starting to make sense elsewhere, too.
How much of this is happenstance is hard to say. Given Apple’s lead times, pure coincidence seems unlikely. And even if Liquid Glass wasn’t made with the Duo in mind, it adapts to it.

Liquid Glass feels more considered. It’s increasingly tuned for individual devices rather than governed by a “universal” aesthetic forced onto them all. The result is operating systems that feel solid rather than fragile, with interfaces less likely to fight content for your attention. On Macs and iPads, the Liquid Glass revamp now looks more like a love letter to Aqua—Apple's water-themed interface introduced in 2000. On the iPhone, it’s usable again. On the Duo, it’s a delight.

That’s not to say it’s perfect. “There’s some weirdness that hasn’t been fully resolved, and there needs to be a consistency to all these materials or the metaphors break down,” McCarthy says. “But overall, Liquid Glass is vastly improved.”

And it’s worth remembering that while the Duo is new, Liquid Glass is relatively young, too. As developer Steve Troughton-Smith wrote, “For some iPhone apps, even with keen developers, it will take six months to a year of work to properly support iPhone Duo. A lot of developers are still trying to finish the Liquid Glass transition they started last year.”
A useful reminder that transitions take time. But at least now, Apple’s vision looks clear.

items.title: 10 Breakthrough Technologies 2026
items.description: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies

Our reporters and editors constantly debate which emerging technologies will define the future. Once a year, we take stock and share some educated guesses with our readers. Here are the advances that we think will drive progress or incite the most change—for better or worse—in the years ahead.

Sodium-ion batteries, made from abundant materials like salt, are emerging as a cheaper, safer alternative to lithium. Backed by major players and public investment, they’re poised to power grids and affordable EVs worldwide.

AI coding tools are revolutionizing how we write, test, and deploy code, making it easier and faster to build sophisticated websites, games, and other applications than ever before. Just be sure to double-check what they come up with.

Nuclear power already provides steady electricity to grids around the world, without producing any greenhouse-gas emissions. New designs rely on alternative fuels and cooling systems or take up less space, which could get more reactors online faster.

Every day, millions of people interact with AI chatbots. Some of them form what feel like close, personal bonds with the bots. There’s mounting evidence that this can be dangerous, and politicians are finally waking up.

When he was just seven months old, baby KJ became the first person to receive a personalized gene-editing treatment. A clinical trial is now planned, and bespoke gene-editing drugs could be approved within the next few years.
Growing banks of gene information on extinct creatures are providing clues to new treatments and suggesting solutions to climate change—and may help save endangered species.
Mechanistic interpretability

Nobody knows exactly how large language models work, which means we don’t have a clear idea of their limitations. But that’s changing: Clever research techniques are giving us the best glimpse yet of what’s really going on inside the black box.

Space tourism may seem fanciful, but this might be the year paying customers can finally check into a room with a galactic view. The shiny new modules will also support research missions by scientists and space agencies.

Screening embryos for genetic diseases is relatively common practice in fertility clinics today, and it can give potential parents some peace of mind. Now, though, new startups are making bold claims about using similar techniques to predict certain traits, including intelligence.
Hyperscale AI data centers

The race for AI supremacy has supercharged data centers. Hyperscale AI data centers pack powerful computer chips into synchronized clusters that work like giant, high-speed supercomputers—sizzling hot, power-hungry behemoths pushing infrastructure to its limits.
10 Breakthrough Technologies

MIT Technology Review’s annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies aims to help our audience know which emerging technologies are really worth paying attention to right now. Our editors and reporters pitch advances that they think should make the list, and we discuss and debate the merits of each over the course of several months.

We look for breakthroughs that will have a broad impact and make meaningful differences in our lives and work. We give equal consideration to those that we think will have a positive effect or bring negative consequences. Every year, we have to pass on many worthy candidates. Here’s what didn’t make the list this year.

This is the 25th year we’ve produced this list. Predicting the future is tough and we don’t always get it right. Look back through our archives to see what’s worked out—and what hasn’t. Or read this special analysis by an MIT researcher about some of the flops.

items.description: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthr
items.author: Michelle Kim
paragraphs: Brace yourself: It turns out AI is being optimized for cheating. OpenAI’s agents hacked into Hugging Face to get the answers to a cybersecurity test. Next, they solved a prestigious math problem (or just stole from two top mathematicians’ answer sheets). Anthropic’s models have also hacked into other companies’ systems four times already. And that’s only what we’ve caught so far.

Freaking out? You’re not alone. AI lab researchers are quitting their jobs and issuing dire warnings that if we keep going this way, AI might eventually kill us all. Bill Gates is sounding the alarm. Bernie Sanders has teamed up with Steve Bannon, of all people, to call for curbs on AI. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is urging a slowdown, and other top US AI executives agree. But fear not: President Trump has a plan. He says the only guardrail AI needs is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

items.title: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
items.description: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.
items.author: Jessica Hamzelou
paragraphs: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.

A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders.

What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue.

Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says.

Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others.

It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson.

Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps.

That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost).

The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai.

Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people.

It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says.
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here?

Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says.

Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content. But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result.

When researchers at the University of Melbourne investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders. They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising. Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month. Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders.

The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders. Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020.

Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023. But anecdotally, things seem to be getting even worse. “There are more eating disorders, more severe eating disorders… and we’re seeing earlier ages of onset,” says Levinson. “We’re seeing eight- and nine-year-olds with eating disorders.”
“From what I’m hearing and seeing, I am not going to be surprised if that number isn’t at least doubling again,” she adds.

Levinson particularly worries about the impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which have exploded in popularity in recent years. A Gallup survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 15% of Americans had used one of these drugs for weight loss. And they’re becoming more accessible—drug companies are working on new formulations that are both easier to take and more effective, and many people can buy versions of these drugs from compound pharmacies or dubious online sources.

In a small study published earlier this year, Levinson and her colleagues found that 30% of people with eating disorders had used GLP-1 drugs. The drugs might benefit some of those people. But 10% appeared to have misused the drugs. And Levinson thinks that figure is also an underestimate.

Levinson says she and her colleagues have seen children develop eating disorders after being prescribed GLP-1s for medical reasons. They’ve seen others—even children as young as 11—buy versions of these drugs over TikTok.

“We’re very concerned that GLPs will lead to even faster and more extreme weight loss in people with anorexia nervosa, and that patients will come to us in even more advanced stages of illness that become difficult to reverse,” says Bulik.

Both Bulik and Levinson are continuing to study the impacts of these drugs in eating disorders. In the meantime, both urge medical professionals to consider the risks GLP-1s might pose to people with those disorders. Bulik contributed to a set of research and clinical guidelines, published earlier this month, that recommends doctors screen for eating disorders before prescribing the drugs, for example. The guidelines also recommend more patient education and more robust monitoring of people who take GLP-1s.
If you think you or someone you know might have an eating disorder, you can find information and support at the National Eating Disorders Association.

items.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
items.description: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI
items.author: Madhulika Srikumar
paragraphs: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.

Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.

With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.

The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.

Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.

Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.

OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people.

Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.
No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.

AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.

Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.

No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.

Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.
Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

items.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
items.description: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reducti
items.author: James Temple
paragraphs: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.

Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.

Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.

items.title: Hillsong’s Former Pastor Is Rehashing His Beef With the Biebers
items.description: Remember Carl Lentz, the former Hillsong NYC pastor whose infidelity rocked the celebrity-megachurch community in 2020? Well, he and his wife are back with a new book, in which they revisit some old beef with their former congregants Hailey and Justin Bieber.
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: Remember Carl Lentz, the former Hillsong NYC pastor whose infidelity rocked the celebrity-megachurch community in 2020? Well, he and his wife are back with a new book, in which they revisit some old beef with their former congregants Hailey and Justin Bieber.

Lentz became a big name for anyone keeping track of the extended megachurch universe in the late 2010s, when he emerged as Bieber’s swaggy spiritual adviser. (He was also the lead pastor and co-founder of Hillsong NYC, the East Coast branch of Bieber’s beloved church, which was frequented by Chris Pratt, Selena Gomez, and NBA star Kevin Durant as well.) Lentz and Bieber seemed to have fallen out in 2020 after Hillsong’s then–global senior pastor Brian Houston wrote in a newsletter that Lentz had been dismissed from the church due to “leadership issues and breaches of trust, plus a recent revelation of moral failures.” Houston, another founder of Hillsong, resigned in 2022 after two women accused him of misconduct. Lentz admitted to both an affair with his family’s nanny and an Adderall addiction in the 2023 FX documentary The Secrets of Hillsong.

The Biebers unfollowed the Lentzes on social media in the wake of the scandal, fueling speculation that they wanted to distance themselves from their pastor and his transgressions. Now, Carl and Laura Lentz have co-authored a book about it all — it’s called Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations to Help Heal the Hurt, naturally — that offers more details about what happened between them and the Biebers. According to the Lentzes, once Carl’s infidelity began making headlines, Hailey and Justin forced them to move out of the NYC apartment the Biebers had lent them.

Per “Page Six,” Laura wrote that the family had been planning a move to Brooklyn “for months” when the Biebers stepped in with an offer to let them stay at their place in New York while they looked for their new home. The couple allegedly told the Lentz family to “use their place as long as needed” and to “take [their] time.” After Carl’s extramarital affair surfaced, however, the Lentzes claim the Biebers rescinded their hospitality with a righteous quickness.
“Somebody on Justin’s team [called] to say we needed to be out of his and Hailey’s apartment in the next 24 hours,” Laura wrote. “We hastily packed our things and loaded them into a rented U-Haul.”

Per “Page Six,” Carl felt the Biebers’ decision was unfair to his wife and kids. “I deserved to be kicked to the curb,” he wrote, “but I felt Laura and the kids were just innocent bystanders suffering once again for my sins.” Carl and Laura share three children, the youngest of whom was 11 at the time. The Biebers haven’t yet commented on the Lentzes’ fickle-landlord accusations.

Meanwhile, Carl and Laura are busy promoting their book, which was published last week. The 208-page book, which is marketed as an “unfiltered” look at the couple’s journey to “rekindle their love,” appears to be the Lentzes’ attempt to get back into the good graces of the megachurch community after both were fired from Hillsong in the aftermath of Carl’s affair. They also want the Biebers to know they’re not harboring any bad feelings.

Carl wrote that he totally understands now that he put the couple “in a precarious place on multiple levels” following the scandal, and that their relationship with the Lentzes dragged them into a “publicity nightmare they never asked for.” But you know who wasn’t afraid of the PR maelstrom? (Whoever you guess is going to be wrong.) It was Tyler Perry.

Apparently, Perry offered the Lentz family a port in the storm, allowing all five of them to move into his Manhattan Beach mansion after the Biebers kicked them out. That same year, Perry also lent one of his residences to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle after they stepped down as working royals and left the U.K. He was also recording Paw Patrol: The Movie at the time — you can’t accuse him of slowing down during the pandemic. (And if you’re wondering, Perry loves the Lentzes’ new book.)

These days, Hailey and Justin Bieber attend Churchome, another celebrity-loved megachurch with a Beverly Hills congregation that happens to have ties to Hillsong. But I’m sure everything there is fine!

items.title: How to Have Sex When You Also Have Roommates
items.description: This article first ran in The Cut’s Personals newsletter, which features new sex and love stories — and date-wanted ads from interesting single people — every week. Sign up to receive the latest issue in your inbox.
items.author: Emily Leibert
paragraphs: This article first ran in The Cut’s Personals newsletter, which features new sex and love stories — and date-wanted ads from interesting single people — every week. Sign up to receive the latest issue in your inbox.

Imagine for a moment that, by the grace of Venus, you’ve reached the end of a successful date and you’re ready to see if the connection carries into the bedroom. So begin the negotiations: Your place or mine? However, you have roommates, and they are, to your abject horror, likely home and wide awake.

That’s not so hard to imagine for a lot of us. Rent is expensive, and moving into a solo apartment where one can dazzle with postcoital martinis from the bar cart might be out of reach right now. What do you do when you’re trying to do it despite the fact that your housemate who enjoys cat-forward TikToks at full volume won’t vacate the couch? Whether you’re in a relationship or bringing home a stray from the bar, we’ve gathered some advice about how to have good sex without becoming the nightmare roommate. Enjoy!

There’s nothing worse than finding Magnum wrappers (or their used contents) in a communal trash can, but leaving no trace extends to more than sex-related garbage. Ask Maria, a 25-year-old living in Lisbon who isn’t fond of her roommate (Maria finds her fussy and difficult to talk to and says she’s “always, always at home watching the same two shows”).

Maria noticed a jagged crack in their bathtub a few months ago. When Maria asked about it, her roommate seemed nervous but said she had no idea what happened. Hm! A few weeks later, Maria caught up with a friend who had recently crashed on their couch. He had apparently run into the roommate on the street, and for some reason, she “decided to describe every place she’s had sex in this house to him,” Maria said. The roommate admitted to having sex with a partner in the tub, and its acrylic sealant “ripped” under the strain. “For a month and a half, I couldn’t shower in my bathroom,” said Maria. Don’t be like Maria’s roommate. If you break something, fix it. Your housemates will respect the honesty.

It can be awkward to talk about sex with your partner, let alone with a platonic roommate. But there are benefits to giving your housemate a heads-up about hookups — like, say, avoiding a situation where you don’t hear your roommate knocking and they wind up catching you naked in the middle of performing oral.

Ruby Rare, a writer and intimacy expert for the dating app Feeld, says they are always “banging on about open and honest communication” and thus have a solution. They suggest that you don’t have to spell out the NC-17 details ahead of time — instead, a subtler approach works well. You can play it coy, like “Hey, just letting you know [partner] and I are retreating to the bedroom for some alone time.”

If you’re friends with your roommate, this might be easier — and could be especially important if you have the kind of open-door policy where you’re always barging in to hang out or borrow clothes. “My roommate and I waltzed into each other’s rooms whenever,” says Lauren, a 24-year-old living in Raleigh in a “tiny, tiny” apartment with friends. “One time, I walked in on one of my roommates and her then-boyfriend nude, mid-foreplay. He screamed ‘Get out!’ repeatedly, and I ran out in horror.”

Via trial and error and a few conversations, Lauren and her roommates agreed on some house rules: If a guy is coming over, send a warning text. If a door is shut, knock. No sex in common areas, no exceptions. “If a boyfriend is over, we have to be there, too, or at least keep him in our room,” she said. “I don’t want to wake up or get home from work and find some man sitting on my couch.”

Even if you can’t address it outright, being a good listener will get you far in all aspects of life and particularly in the quest to fuck. Paying attention to your roommates’ calendars and general whereabouts works both ways: You’ll be a more engaged, caring friend … and surreptitiously get intel to inform your hookup schedule. When they mention upcoming work trips and dinner dates, see if you can time any hot encounters to align with their out-of-the-house obligations. Do they have a Democratic Socialists of America meeting to attend Thursday night? Use that time too.

The most common roommate sex gripes are noise-related. While mutual respect is enough of a motivator for some to keep it down, others might need further seducing. Try creating tension by playing the silent game, placing a consensual hand over your partner’s mouth, or whispering dirty talk. Being called “such a good girl” for staying quiet equals real-life audio erotica.

If you really can’t keep your mouth shut (and your partner can’t shut it for you), there are work-arounds. Rosa, a 20-something in Brooklyn, said that at her last apartment, the laundry machine was just outside her room. She timed her hookups to when she was washing clothes to mask her moans. Chelsea, a 25-year-old in Manhattan, has two roommates. She leans on a common-sense approach: If someone’s home, muffle your gasps with a pillow. If the headboard creaks, secure it to the wall. If that’s not an option, hook up on the floor. If all else fails, Rare recommends minimizing movement by prioritizing oral, fingering, or hand jobs with only one person receiving at a time. “That’s quieter than anything penetrative, where two bodies are colliding,” Rare said.

Finally, to the more kink-inclined among us: If your roommate is home, your self-installed sex swing can wait. “I want people to have fun and let go in the moment, but we have a responsibility to not overtly impose our sexuality on others. If you’re in close proximity to others, it’s probably not the time to get the flogger or cane out,” Rare said. That doesn’t mean you have to totally sacrifice freaky sex. “You can lean into pain in quieter ways, like biting, pinching, or scratching,” they said. Okay, hot!
Employ a strict “no losers” policy.

Try as you might to keep your visitor out of sight, sometimes your roommates will run into your hookup anyway, e.g., fishing the Brita out of the fridge at dawn. Bring only the good ones home so any encounters are polite.

Lauren knows what it’s like when a loser makes it into the inner sanctum. Once, when she was living with four other girls, one brought a guy over. It wasn’t hard to clock him as bad news when he immediately gave a long, politically charged lecture to Lauren and the rest of the girls. He called one a “commie” because she was voting for Joe Biden, then played beer pong on their kitchen island by himself for two hours before disappearing into her roommate’s bedroom.

Around 3 a.m., Lauren heard the couple having sex in the next room — as in he repeatedly yelled “Oh yeah!” and banged around. She requested they keep it down. The suitor yelled at Lauren to “shut the fuck up” while slamming his fist against the wall. Later, the roommates discovered via Instagram that he kept a cardboard cutout of Donald Trump in his living room. Lauren’s roommate was on probation from sleepovers for a long time. They’re all still friends, though they’re haunted by this encounter over six years later.

And for the enthusiastic supporters and practitioners of first-date sex and one-night stands among us: Josh, the 24-year-old fintech intern from Tinder whom you never plan to see again, doesn’t need to sleep over. You can insist on a no-sleepover rule or blame it on one of the classics: an early Pilates class, an 8 a.m. meeting, or an ob-gyn appointment. Try this template to kick someone out with grace: “I had such a lovely time with you, but I need to wake up early for this presentation I’m giving — do you need any help figuring out how to get home?”
Be a stellar person to live with in every other respect, and you’ll get away with more.

Act like your roommates are the people to impress rather than your sexual partner. If the apartment is sparkling and you’ve taken on extra chores that week, your roommates will be more inclined to be chill if they hear something they shouldn’t have. Consider the alternative: When Maria, the 25-year-old in Lisbon, found out about the broken bathtub, she said, “If she was my friend, this would probably have been really funny. In this context, it’s annoying as hell.”

Chelsea, the 25-year-old in Manhattan, is nonconfrontational and prefers saving face over communicating directly with her roommates about sex, so she does whatever she can to keep the peace more generally — including by being understanding toward her roommate about her hookups. “Is dealing with this an inevitability if you’re not completely chaste and you live in tight quarters with people?” Probably, but trying to be a decent person outside of what you’re doing in bed will go a long way in terms of how irritating it is.
If all else fails: Just have sex with your roommate.
Angela is in her mid-30s but was once a grad student having trouble affording rent. She and a friend from her program had only known each other for six months but decided to move in together anyway.

Though they pretended otherwise, there was immediately a vibe. “There are all the obvious reasons that sleeping with your roommate can be a bad idea,” Angela said. “If a feeling emerges, there are rational reasons to suppress it.” For five years, they did … until they went to a party, took molly, and made out. Even though Angela was seeing three guys at the time, her roommate declared that if they had feelings for each other, they shouldn’t hold back.

At the time, Angela and her roommate had started watching the lesbian TV touchstone The L Word together. “It’s just too on the nose,” Angela laughs. “We’re watching The L Word in her bed. We started the series as friends, and when it ended, we were sleeping together.” Suddenly, they had a guest bedroom. “Moving into her room solved every issue in my life,” Angela said. “It solved the real-estate question. It solved my tension with my roommate. And it solved the love question too.” A year and a half ago, Angela and her roommate got married. While she can’t fully recommend fucking your roommate, it might be better than just listening to each other hook up and getting mad about it.

items.title: When the ‘Mommune’ Isn’t All It’s Cracked Up to Be
items.description: When Anilese Haney and her best friend, Nicole, were growing up outside of Eugene, Oregon, they used to fantasize about what their lives would be like when they were older. They wanted to be in each other’s weddings and hoped they would be pregnant together. B
items.author: Erica Schwiegershausen
paragraphs: When Anilese Haney and her best friend, Nicole, were growing up outside of Eugene, Oregon, they used to fantasize about what their lives would be like when they were older. They wanted to be in each other’s weddings and hoped they would be pregnant together. But by the time they were 25, Nicole was divorced with 3-year-old twins and a baby; Anilese was living with her boyfriend and her 3-year-old, but her relationship was on the rocks. “I told Nicole, ‘If we break up, I need you to move in with me.’ We’ve always wanted to live together. We’ve always wanted to raise our kids together,” Anilese says. Her apartment had four bedrooms, and they could each have their own bathroom. A few weeks later, Anilese and her boyfriend split, and Nicole moved in. “We were so excited. It was kind of like a dream come true,” says Anilese.

For the two mothers, living together wasn’t just a way to save money on rent. Combining their households under one roof made their lives easier in all sorts of ways. “My daughter’s dad was not helpful at all,” says Anilese. “He drank a lot, and he barely worked. He didn’t have a lot of motivation. My mom was helping us pay for diapers.” Moving in with Nicole, she felt as though she suddenly had an extra set of hands. The moms split groceries and shared clothes, and in the mornings, they helped get each other’s kids dressed and loaded up in the car. They dropped the kids off at their gym day care so they could work out together, and they decided to start a cleaning business. Anilese and Nicole both had split custody, so when the kids were with their dads, they would work long days and then lie around watching Love Island. When the kids were there, they had built-in playmates for crafts and movie nights. The arrangement seemed ideal for everyone — at least at first.

The economics of raising kids as a single mom has always been brutal. With inflation and soaring rents, moving in with another mom just makes sense: You can split the bills, switch off cooking dinner, and have someone there to watch the kids when you need to run an errand. On TikTok, plenty of women are taken with the idea. This summer, 38-year-old single mom Bernie Sinclaire went viral documenting her life sharing a three-bedroom apartment in Harlem with her best friend and their three kids, an idyllic-seeming living situation she calls “the mommune.” Sinclair is adamant she’ll never go back to living with a man. But even if you can find a mom willing to sign a lease with you, sharing a kitchen and a living room with another parent and their brood is a complicated proposition. What if your kids don’t get along or you have wildly different approaches to discipline? How do you avoid becoming a de facto babysitter? What if your roommate’s boyfriend decides to move in too?

For Kristen Dill and Rachel Zachry, becoming roommates was a last-ditch attempt to avoid having to live with their parents again. After she split with her husband, Rachel bought a four-bedroom house in Fort Worth, Texas. But once she moved in with her kids, who are 13, 11, and 9, she felt overwhelmed by the realities of homeownership. Her ex lived across the country, and she was working full time waiting tables. Between property taxes, insurance, and utilities, the bills were endless. She felt she was constantly behind. “I would wake up in the mornings completely anxious. Like, How am I supposed to do this without a man? My lawn needs to be mowed. I don’t even know how to fix a sink if it’s leaking.” Rachel was on the verge of selling the house when Kristen — who was going through a divorce of her own and had been crashing with her mom and stepdad — asked how she would feel about her and her 9-year-old daughter moving in. “I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, absolutely,’” says Rachel.

At first, they were just going to try it out for a week. Two months later, it still feels like the honeymoon phase. Sure, there were some kinks to work out early on; now, they don’t go into each other’s rooms without asking, and Kristen stays out of Rachel’s way when she’s trying to get her kids out the door in the morning. “It takes a lot of communication, just like a marriage would,” says Kristen. But as longtime friends, they take pride in anticipating each other’s needs. Someone is always there to move the laundry to the dryer, and they can tag-team cooking dinner and helping with homework. Kristen bakes sourdough and packs all the kids’ lunches the night before. She set up a Skylight smart calendar with a morning checklist to remind the kids to brush their teeth, wash their faces, and remember their water bottles and Chromebooks for school. “As the wife, you feel like you’re solely in control of taking care of the house and the kids, and also you still have to work. The dynamic between two moms or two best friends is so different,” says Kristen. “And there’s no sexual tension, like, After this I’m gonna have to go and have sex with my husband.”

But no matter how well you get along with your roommate, living with someone else’s kids comes with its own set of challenges. With babies and toddlers, noise is a constant, and even a house that seems spacious can quickly start to feel cramped. When a friend of a friend needed a place to stay, Shannon Foote was happy to let her and her 4-year-old move into a spare bedroom in the house she shared with her four kids outside of Reno, Nevada. But the woman’s daughter had a hard time going from being an only child to suddenly being one of five. They ended up having to stagger their custody schedule so the kids were together only a few days a month. In the end, the other woman decided living with four more kids was just too chaotic. “She was like, ‘I want to read a book in quiet,’” says Shannon, who adds that she gets it. “I mean, she was also sharing a bedroom with her daughter. That sucks.”

And like any living arrangement, when it goes wrong, it can really screw up your life. After Heather, a 37-year-old single mom in New Jersey, got divorced, she started renting a house with her son, who was 5 at the time. When she found out a childhood friend was getting evicted, it seemed like a no-brainer to invite her and her 4-year-old to move in and split the rent. “I said to her, ‘Neither of us have men, so why not?’” At first, everything seemed fine. Her new roommate worked long shifts as a nurse, so Heather would help out with day-care drop-off and pickup. Then things started to get weird. The roommate accused Heather’s son of hitting her daughter and wouldn’t let it go. One morning, her car was blocking Heather’s, but she refused to move it until Heather’s son apologized to her daughter. “She was yelling at me, and I started laughing,” Heather says. “She got really close to my face, and I bumped her, like, Back up.” The next thing she knew, they were on the ground wrestling in front of their children, who were terrified. After that, Heather told the woman she would have to move out — but she refused and called child protective services on Heather. In the end, she had to get a temporary restraining order to force the other woman to leave.

Then there’s the question of where men fit into the arrangement. Kim Cosby, a mother of four in Georgia, has lived with multiple single mothers, and she always tells them up front she doesn’t want boyfriends around. “I love to be half naked, in a spaghetti-strap shirt and leggings,” she says. She doesn’t want to “get fully dressed” just because her roommate’s boyfriend is coming over — and she doesn’t want men who aren’t family around her kids, either. She does a “heavy vetting process” before moving in with anyone. “I have rules and regulations: I don’t smoke, I don’t drink, and I don’t want those influences around my children.” She hasn’t had any problems yet. But others aren’t so lucky.

If you don’t take a hard line on keeping men out of the house, you may suddenly find your roommate’s boyfriend crashing there all the time. For Anilese and Nicole, things fell apart when Nicole started dating someone. “He was kind of a bum, in my opinion. He was basically homeless,” Anilese says. Since he didn’t have anywhere to go, he started staying with them — and brought along two kids of his own. The women had already been struggling to make ends meet; adding three people to the mix just felt impossible. Then Anilese also started seeing someone. “We were like, ‘What are we gonna do? We can’t all live here.”’ Finally, they had a blowout fight and Nicole moved out. The friends eventually made up, but they don’t plan to live together again.
