Kristen and Rachel told me, as much as they love it, they know their current roommate situation won’t last forever. Kristen would be happy never to date a man again, but Rachel really wants another husband. When she starts dating someone, she’ll be up front about her lifestyle. “Like, this is what my household looks like. No, we’re not lesbians. We’re best friends trying to make this economy work.” She wants to make sure a man doesn’t come in and expect to kick out Kristen and her daughter: “And he better respect that. If he doesn’t, then that’s an absolute ‘no.’”

Still, as much as Rachel would like to remarry, she has yet to meet the “mature, fabulous” man of her dreams. “So it’s, like, either settle for a man I don’t like or have my best friend move in,” she says. “It was an obvious answer.”
- ‘I Wish I Could Move Out, But My Parents Need the Rent Money’
- How to Have Sex When You Also Have Roommates

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

items.title: How Vaginal Fillers Gave Me My Life Back Postpartum
items.description: I hit my breaking point on a Monday night outside a club in Hollywood.
items.author: Casey Gates Frey
paragraphs: I hit my breaking point on a Monday night outside a club in Hollywood.
I had been riding high, emerging in the afterglow of the dance floor. I bet no one even knew I was a mom, I thought, strolling back to my car-seat-filled SUV.

Then I looked down. A puddle of urine had spread across my crotch, identical to when my toddler refuses to stop playing and has an accident. I had been savoring this moment of rare freedom from my responsibilities, but my body once again betrayed me.

I began to struggle with incontinence after the birth of my older daughter in 2020. At first, I thought the liquid that sometimes dribbled out of me without warning was leftover amniotic fluid. At my postpartum checkup, though, my doctor told me I was actually peeing myself. She referred me to pelvic-floor physical therapy and assured me that would likely solve the problem.

But soon I was pregnant again. My second daughter, whom I delivered vaginally, weighed a whopping ten pounds, ten ounces. After her birth, my incontinence got even worse, but with two young kids, I had my hands full.

I wasn’t entirely passive about the problem. I followed my doctor’s advice and did physical therapy — my bird dogs, my squats, and my bridges. I did my effing Kegels. I told myself that because I experienced incontinence only on occasion and managed it relatively well by modifying my activities, I probably wasn’t eligible for any other treatment. Oh, you had a kid and now sometimes you pee when you sneeze? Welcome to the club, I told myself. For three years, I accepted sporadic urine leakage as my new normal.

But my new normal began to weigh on me. Not long after my little “oopsie” on the dance floor, I was mindlessly scrolling social media hoping to stumble upon some hidden gem that would change my life. I found a post from a woman who said she had also struggled with postpartum incontinence and had gotten vaginal fillers to solve the problem. I was sat.

At my annual physical, I brought up the idea with my primary-care physician. After I assured her that I didn’t mean “labial puffing” — a.k.a. restoring volume of the labia for aesthetic purposes — she referred me to a urogynecologist named Dr. Michele Torosis. At my first appointment, Torosis listened to my symptoms and performed a cough stress test. She then formally diagnosed me with stress urinary incontinence, or SUI, the involuntary leakage of urine caused by sudden physical pressure or strain on the bladder and urethra. SUI can occur after having kids because pregnancy and childbirth stretch, weaken, and sometimes damage the complex system of muscles, nerves, and tissues that normally hold urine in the bladder, Torosis told me, adding that you’re at higher risk if you’ve had a vaginal delivery.

I was also given a more thorough explanation of these so-called fillers, which are officially called “bulking agents.” The treatment consists of injecting a soft gel into the walls of the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the bladder.
This solution to my woes is relatively new. The material used for the treatment was approved by the FDA only in 2020, and Torosis says it has made the procedure much easier to do.
“We’ve actually seen on a national scale the rates of bulking have gone up,” she says.

Not until Torosis performed a pelvic exam on me during my appointment did I realize how much shame I’d been carrying over my incontinence. She confirmed that my pelvic muscles felt strong and that I had good control. It was liberating. I’d done weeks of physical therapy, Kegels, and everything else I was supposed to do to prevent leaks, then blamed myself when it didn’t work. But the problem wasn’t just my pelvic muscles.

Torosis tells me that while pelvic-floor physical therapy can be hugely helpful in regaining strength postpartum, it alone can’t cure more severe cases of incontinence. Johanna Hanley, the Los Angeles–based physical therapist I worked with, agrees. She says she sees patients racked with “shame and guilt” about birthing experiences over which they had no control.

“Sometimes, it’s just how we’re made and the size of our baby — a confluence of factors we can’t necessarily control in the moment,” Hanley tells me. “We do the best we can, but at some point, we may need more of an intervention. And that’s also okay.”

After years of adapting, avoiding, and modifying how I moved through life, solving my SUI took only about 15 minutes. The doctor inserted a numbing jelly into my urethra, followed by a local anesthetic before the fillers, and the pain was mostly tolerable. The sensation felt similar to having an extremely full bladder. No one directly said “Wow, what a champ” in response to my bravery, but I could tell they were thinking it.
The immediate discomfort subsided within a couple of hours, and I was back to weight lifting the very next day. But the real triumph for me? It worked.
Two days after my procedure, I went dancing and stayed magically dry. I tried jogging for the first time in years. No leaking.

According to Torosis, the treatment is expected to last about two or three years, at which time I can go back and get the fillers again. But I’ve also learned I am now in a position to train my muscles in a way I wasn’t able to before the treatment, so it’s possible I may be able to restore better control.

Either way, I am thrilled to know I will be out on those streets running, dancing, and doing dry-ass dead lifts for decades to come. Last week, I even said “yes” to a moms-only potato-sack race at my daughter’s preschool — an act of public-facing jumping I would never have done pre-fillers. And I won.

items.title: The Case For Doing A Couples Costume With Your Situationship
items.description: The weeks leading up to Halloween are always full of bone-chilling frights. There are vampires lurking in the dark waiting to suck the life from their next victim, oozing mummies rising up from their coffins with vengeance, and ominous black cats scampering ac
items.author: Sophie Fishman
paragraphs: The weeks leading up to Halloween are always full of bone-chilling frights. There are vampires lurking in the dark waiting to suck the life from their next victim, oozing mummies rising up from their coffins with vengeance, and ominous black cats scampering across your path. Yet, when the days get shorter and the autumn breezes start to blow, there’s only one thing scarier than skulking creatures of the night: commitment.

Dressing up together is about as hard a hard launch as you can get, and proposing the idea means laying your intentions for the relationship bare. When you don’t have a crystal ball to read your partner’s mind, is there anything more awkward than asking them to be Santana to your Brittany? If you want to make things official, proposing they be the Ilya to your Shane can feel like putting your still-beating heart on a silver platter for the taking.

Nicole, 24, (whose name, like others in this story, has been changed to avoid an awkward conversation) has been in an on-and-off situationship for almost three years, and the pair is planning on doing a couples costume as Anora and Vanya from the movie Anora. When I call her, she’s outside looking for a place to sit. “Sorry, I was literally just at Brandy Melville looking for a shirt to buy him for this,” she says.

The idea was meant to be tongue in cheek. Two years ago, the two had an explosive public fight over the status of their relationship on the subway coming home from seeing the film. Now, several fights later and still non-exclusive, she thought it was a fun call-back. With some playful begging, he agreed.

When I ask if Anora and Vanya’s toxic and ultimately tragic relationship is an apt comparison to hers, she laughs. “It definitely fits him. The guy from Anora is very haphazard and kind of boyish and immature,” she says. “But he also goes through the phase of being obsessed with someone for a period of time and then moving on from it. And that's exactly who he is.”
She’s not worried about her friends’ reactions. “I think they'll just think it's funny.” According to Nicole, “You should be doing a couples costume with your situationship as soon as possible.”

Lauren, 25, just became exclusive with her partner a few weeks ago. Still, she was nervous to pop the question to her beau. “It’s just so awkward!” she says, laughing. “You just don’t want to be the one to have to do it first.”

Thankfully, he beat her to it. “I think I’m just traumatized. Back in college when you start ‘dating’ someone at the beginning of the year, you always think, ‘Obviously by the time Halloween comes around, this is going to be real serious,’ and then it's most definitely not,” she says. “So when he was like, ‘Should we do a couples costume?’ I was like, ‘Oh wait, I'm out of jail!’”

Though she’s starting to feel more confident about where they stand as an item, Lauren is looking at their Princess Buttercup and Westley outfits as an opportunity for the ultimate test of their status: telling the world. “If anybody happens to take a picture of us, will it go on Instagram? Probably.”

That said, even for couples in it for the long haul, couples costumes aren’t sacred. Sarah, 23, has been dating her boyfriend, John, for over two years. Recently he’s been blowing up her phone with inspiration pictures of Spider-Man and MJ, Mario and Princess Peach, and The Office’s Jim and Pam. She’s yet to break the news that she’d already been planning for weeks to dress up with her best friend as Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes. “I honestly don’t want to see you in a couples costume unless you’re married,” she says. “Halloween just feels like a girl holiday and it’s cringe to pick your boyfriend over your friends.”

So to couples costume or to not couples costume? If you’re on the same page and it’s fun, absolutely. If the getup is a substitute for an honest conversation about your future? Absolutely not. And if you’re worried that not showing up as Edward and Bella means they’re going home with Jacob, maybe it wasn’t meant to be after all.

items.title: Exclusive: 'SNL' Star Grace Reiter Wants To Bring Back This Weird TikTok Trend
items.description: SNL’s Grace Reiter Wants To Bring Back Weird TikTok
items.author: Samantha Leal
paragraphs: SNL’s Grace Reiter Wants To Bring Back Weird TikTok
The comedian talks Saturday Night Live, chaotic voice memos, and Venmo etiquette.

Grace Reiter is having a pretty big year. The comedian, who first found an audience on TikTok with absurdist sketches and recently on YouTube with parodies of The Hunger Games (with Twilight up next), has officially made the jump from the FYP to Saturday Night Live. But if you’re imagining a cinematic moment when the Wisconsin native got the call, think again.

“I was in LA, and there was a mix-up with the place I was staying,” Reiter, 25, tells Bustle. After a chaotic day of hotel mishaps, she got the call that she’d been cast on Saturday Night Live. But between the early morning, unexpected travel logistics, and sheer exhaustion, it was almost too much to process in the moment.

It wasn’t until the announcement went public on Sept. 16 and the congratulatory texts started rolling in that the magnitude of it all began to sink in. “I always think my life is The Truman Show, and at any point they’re going to be like, ‘OK, and cut! That was fun, wasn’t it?’” she says. “I think it’s real now.”

Now, a few shows into her SNL tenure, Reiter is already juggling live television, internet fame, and, apparently, a second, unexpected gig. “I think my part-time job is answering emails,” she says. She’s also taking on another very 2026 problem: Venmo ghosting.

Just in time for Halloween, the comedian has partnered with the mobile payment app as its official “Venmo Ghost Medium,” a crystal-ball-wielding psychic who helps people confront the friends, dates, and acquaintances who mysteriously disappear when it’s time to split the check. As part of the campaign, launching Oct. 28, people can share their own Venmo ghosting stories in the comments on Instagram for a chance to have outstanding requests covered by the company.

And while she might be helping people recover their money, Reiter admits she’s not entirely innocent when it comes to the occasional unpaid request. Recently she saw her roommate’s two-month-old request in her Venmo. “I was like, ‘Oh, oops.’ So I have been that person for sure. Then I’m like, ‘OK, we do live together,’” she says, laughing. “‘You could also tell me.’ But that’s my bad.”
Below, Reiter talks about the TikTok trends she wants to resurrect, her chaotic voice notes, and why she could probably give a PowerPoint presentation on The Sims 3.
The Fast Follow With Grace Reiter
Are you the type to send a Venmo reminder, or do you suffer in silence?

I don’t even really do it. If it’s in your requests, I imagine you see it and ignore it for a reason. It’s there, and it won’t go away unless you decline it, but then you get notified anyway. Maybe money is hard to talk about. So I’m like, “Well, we’ll get to it.” They’ll pay me! They’ll pay me!
Do you ever snoop on other people’s Venmo transactions?
All the time. Honestly, I’ll have to scroll through my Venmo and see because I feel like people are always just lying about what they’re actually paying for because they know other people can see it.
Who’s your dream SNL host?
I said Jack Black and Melissa McCarthy before, but I’d love it if Jennifer Lawrence came on again.
What’s one internet trend you desperately want to bring back?

Honestly, the duet feature was so prominent in 2020. People would do duet chains, or if their arm went off frame, the person on the other side would make the rest of their arm. There was so much comedy to be had with that feature. Nobody uses that anymore, and I think it’s because the algorithm doesn’t favor that type of video. I’d love to see people bring back duetting in a comedic way.

Or I would say, oh my gosh, the Mafia stuff in 2020. Everyone decided to dress up as Mob bosses, but it was like a YA romance Mob-boss kind of thing where they were just looking sexy and walking in place. They’d all duet and be like, “We’re the family, meet the family.” And I’m like, “This is just awesome. This is what we should be using the internet for.”
What’s the most used app on your phone?
I feel like mostly email and Google Calendar.
Are you a Notes app comedian, or do your best ideas live somewhere more chaotic?

Probably Notes app or voice memos, because my stream of consciousness is more like pacing and talking, and the only way to know if any of it is usable is to record it and listen back. That seems to be the most natural way for ideas to come out.
So are your voice notes quick thoughts or full-length sagas?
Oh, it’s rambling. It’s a podcast. It’s a complete waste of phone storage that never really gets looked at again. But it just makes me feel good knowing that if I want to go back to it, I can.
What’s the last thing you Googled? No judgment.
An internet speed test, that Thanos quote where he’s watching the sunset in Avengers, a comedian, and then I think I was looking up the definition of “stoic.”
What’s a topic you could give an entire PowerPoint presentation on with zero preparation?
There was a time when I could give you a PowerPoint on Sims 3, go through each expansion pack, and tell you the different clothes and features. I was a big Simmer back in the day.
I also play Overwatch, and the characters have a lot of lore. So maybe a shipping chart of the characters in Overwatch — who ships to who. I could easily do that.
What’s your current internet rabbit hole?

The Atomic Twins on YouTube. I watch them react to Love Is Blind. When I’m eating food, that’s the YouTube video I’m putting on. Then I have this other guy I watch who recaps the episodes. So I’m getting double: I’m getting the clinical, just-the-facts take, and then a funny one.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: 11 Hair Icons To Know, From Zendaya’s Hairstylist To TikTok’s Fave Trichologist
items.description: There’s a reason so many people reach for the kitchen scissors after a breakup: Hair is one of the most personal ways to change how you look — and how you feel. But it’s also a space for some of beauty’s most exciting experimentation, from gravity-defying updo
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: There’s a reason so many people reach for the kitchen scissors after a breakup: Hair is one of the most personal ways to change how you look — and how you feel. But it’s also a space for some of beauty’s most exciting experimentation, from gravity-defying updos and intricate braiding designs to colorists challenging our ideas about aging.

The pros behind those transformations don’t all work the same way. Some create the celebrity looks that take over your FYP; others are rethinking the products, techniques, and traditions that shape how we wear our hair. From wigmakers to scalp specialists, lash and brow artists, and entrepreneurs, the honorees of Bustle’s 2026 Beauty Icon Awards are pushing their respective crafts forward.
Ahead, meet the 11 experts helping shape the future of hair and beyond.
The Internet’s Trichologist: Abbey Yung

Dealing with dry ends, an oily scalp, or hair that just won’t grow? Abbey Yung has a routine for that. The certified trichologist and social-media star, who’s amassed nearly 5 million followers across TikTok and Instagram, shares tips and product recommendations for just about every hair concern. (And many of her favorites are drugstore finds.) Her recommendations come with something more useful than hype: an explanation of the science behind them.
The Celebrity Lash Queen: Alanah Sahaba

The hair on your head isn’t the only thing worth thinking about — at least, according to Los Angeles-based lash artist Alanah Sahaba. After leaving college in 2020, she started doing lashes full time, quickly building a celebrity clientele that includes Kehlani, Quen Blackwell, and Megan Thee Stallion. From barely-there fox eye sets to colorful, anime-inspired designs, her work is about more than just adding length and volume. She treats lashes like another form of self-expression, creating looks that feel like an extension of each client’s personal style.
The Red-Carpet Trendsetter: Coree Moreno

If you’ve found yourself obsessing over Zendaya’s hair lately, Coree Moreno may be the reason. The goddess braid that sparked countless TikTok tutorials? He was behind it. He also created her piecey pixie cut. But Zendaya isn’t the only star who trusts him with her hair: His client list includes Hollywood names like Chase Infiniti and Madison Bailey. With a knack for working with natural texture, Moreno isn’t just following trends — he’s helping set them.
The Ayurveda Advocate: Diipa Buller-Khosla

Most people pick up a beauty trick or two from their mom, but Diipa Büller-Khosla got a whole brand’s worth. Raised by an ayurvedic doctor and dermatologist, she grew up surrounded by traditional Indian beauty rituals — and in 2021, turned those childhood lessons into Indē Wild, a hair and skin care brand that combines ancient wisdom with modern science. Five years later, it’s landed on Sephora shelves, introducing those 5,000-year-old traditions to a whole new audience.
The Editorial Architect: Guido Palau

Cher, Madonna, Beyoncé — some people are so iconic they don't need a last name, and in the fashion world, hairstylist Guido Palau is one of them. He got his start at London’s legendary Vidal Sassoon salon in the early ’80s, before a gig with George Michael put him on the map. Since then, he’s become a defining force in editorial and runway hair, creating everything from architectural updos for Schiaparelli to old Hollywood waves for Lana Del Rey’s W Magazine cover. With bombshell blowouts among his recent credits, Palau continues to shape the looks that define beauty's biggest moments.
The Gray Hair Guru: Jack Martin
Follow: @jackmartincolorist

Gray hair isn’t something to hide — just ask Jack Martin. The Arizona-based colorist has built a career out of helping women embrace their silver strands, counting Andie MacDowell and Sharon Osbourne among his celebrity clients. Using his signature French blending technique, he weaves together shades of silver, gray, and white for results that look every bit as dimensional as any good blond or brunette dye job. In an industry that often treats aging as something to disguise, Martin offers a different vision — one that doesn’t begin with covering up.
The A-List Brow Artist: Kelley Baker

Even if you don’t know Kelley Baker by name, you’ve almost certainly seen her work. Based in Beverly Hills, she got her start as a makeup artist before finding her niche in brows. Now, she’s responsible for some of Hollywood’s most recognizable arches, working with everyone from Kim Kardashian and Megan Fox to Drake. Whether she’s carving out a bold brow or a softer, more natural frame, her work is proof that a few strategically plucked hairs can do a lot of heavy lifting.
The Hollywood Hairstylist: Mara Roszak

For hairstylist Mara Roszak, inspiration has always been close to home. Growing up in L.A.’s Laurel Canyon, hairstylist Mara Roszak developed an appreciation for the laid-back, California-cool aesthetic that’s since become her signature. Her clients include Emma Stone, Zoe Saldaña, and Sandra Bullock, but there’s more to her perfectly undone looks than meets the eye. Roszak has been honing her craft since her teens, landing her first celebrity client, Sarah Michelle Gellar, before she even got her license. More than two decades later, she’s channeled that experience into her own hair care brand, Roz, with a simple premise: Effortless hair should actually be effortless.
The Wig Whisperer: Noah Scott

The Internet loves a wig allegation — but when Noah Scott is behind the hair, good luck spotting the lace front. After teaching himself how to make wigs through YouTube tutorials at just 8 years old, he got his big break creating Ariana Grande’s signature extra-long ponytail for her 2019 Coachella performance. Since then, his celebrity clientele has grown to include everyone from Lindsay Lohan to Zara Larsson, all turning to him for custom hairpieces. But you don’t need to be an A-lister to get in on the fun. Through his online store, WhatWigs, he’s making red-carpet-worthy hair transformations available to anyone who feels like switching up their style.
The Braid Specialist: Tashana Miles
Follow: @tasha_worldofstyles

Tashana Miles isn’t just a stylist — she’s an artist whose medium is braiding. Whether she’s creating sculptural Bantu knots or geometric cornrows, she approaches each style as an opportunity to experiment with shape and design. That creativity, paired with meticulous technique, has made her a favorite of A$AP Rocky and Beyoncé. For anyone looking for inspiration for their next protective style, Miles offers a reminder that braids can be as individual as the person wearing them.
The Extension Innovator: Tendai Moyo

Tendai Moyo thinks synthetic braiding hair is overdue for an upgrade. As co-founder and CEO of Ruka Hair, she’s challenging the industry’s reliance on conventional plastic-based fibers with Synths 2, a collagen-based alternative designed to look and feel like human hair. The patent-pending material is also designed to be biodegradable and withstand heat styling. With Ruka expanding its retail presence, Moyo is pushing the conversation beyond how braiding hair looks to how it’s made.

items.title: Exclusive: Joe Amabile Shares His Thoughts On That 'Bachelor' Casting Rumor
items.description: Bachelor Nation’s Joe Amabile Is Sprinting To The Finish Line
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Bachelor Nation’s Joe Amabile Is Sprinting To The Finish Line
The reality TV star opens up about recovering from brain surgery, marrying Serena Pitt, and a Bachelor casting rumor.

Joe Amabile has had quite the eventful summer, to say the least. The Bachelor Nation alum (aka Grocery Store Joe) had to undergo brain surgery after doctors found a “blueberry-sized” tumor. However, through his recovery, the 40-year-old refused to lose sight of one of his goals: running the New York Marathon on Nov. 1.

“When I got my unexpected diagnosis of having a brain tumor and having to go through brain surgery, it was a goal that I set for myself to just keep me motivated and keep my mindset positive,” he tells Bustle. “Brain surgery is out of your control. I’m not going in my own head like the doctors are, so it was just nice to give myself that control.”

Naturally, Amabile’s medical crisis made him reflect on many aspects of his life, from friendships to his financial situation. He partnered with Northwestern Mutual to share why getting your finances in order is essential. “It’s so important to be flexible and able to switch things when something unexpected happens,” he says. “That’s what Northwestern Mutual does so well.”

Marrying his Bachelor in Paradise costar Serena Pitt gave him a new outlook on saving. “Before getting married, I don’t think I had any financial goals,” he says. “It’s just so important to save money and put it away for a family. You’re trying to build a life together, and regardless of what people wanna say, money is very important.”

After a gradual but successful recovery, Amabile looks forward to reconnecting with some of his fellow reality TV star runners. “I run it with Zac Clark every year, and Matt James is running it again,” he says. “I’m friends with Dylan Efron, and he’s running it.”
Below, Amabile opens up about his marathon journey, his wife’s support, and his thoughts on Bachelor Nation’s future.
After your recovery, what has become a bigger priority in your life, and what new goals have you set for yourself?

Being vulnerable is one. I wasn’t really vulnerable on social media at all, and once I decided to share, it’s honestly helped me so much. It’s comforting to hear other people’s stories about going through something similar and having good outcomes. Right now my goal is not to do too much, because I tend to overdo it.
Tell me how Serena’s been supporting you during this marathon journey.

[Laughs] Uh... I don’t know if she is so happy that I’m running the marathon. She is OK with it and will support me, but she’d rather I didn’t run it, if I’m gonna be completely honest. But she’s been wonderful. I’ve never been through [a major health scare], and neither has she, but she’s always been by my side. Her resilience and strength are a testament to who she is as a person.
You two are one of the few couples who are still standing from Bachelor Nation. What do you see for the future of the Bachelor franchise?

Oh, that’s an interesting question. It depends on who they choose as the Bachelor and the way they cast the women. There’s a lot of competition out there, but there’s still only one Bachelor and Bachelorette, so I think the show will be OK.
What do you think of the rumor that producers are eyeing Dr. Mike to be the next Bachelor?

That would be a great pick. He doesn’t need it financially, and his social following is already massive, so I’m sure that’ll help. If you’re looking for someone who is there for the right reasons, I think it’s him.
How has Bachelor Nation supported you during this health journey, whether it’s the fans or your fellow contestants?
So many people have just showered me with love and support. So many Bachelor alumni have reached out and sent me Uber Eats and DoorDash. Honestly, it’s almost been too gracious.
Your fellow Bachelor Nation star Joey Graziadei just returned from filming The Traitors. Would you ever consider doing that one day?
If they asked, I would be lying if I said no.
Do you want to be a Faithful or a Traitor?
I don’t have a preference. The way the show’s set up right now, it takes a lot of luck at the beginning, no matter if you’re a Traitor or a Faithful. It’s a little bit of a popularity contest.
How do you hope you’ll come out of the marathon, and what message do you hope to send?

I hope to finish. I don’t think I’ll beat my last two scores, but I want people to get that you can do anything. As long as you set that goal, something unexpected happening doesn’t necessarily have to change the outcome. It just changes the path.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Sophia Bush Has Gifted Cheryl Strayed’s ‘Tiny Beautiful Things’ More Than 30 Times
items.description: One Nightstand With Sophia Bush
items.author: Charlotte Owen
paragraphs: One Nightstand With Sophia Bush
The actor and activist, who’s just released a new memoir, shares four books that have shaped her worldview, including works by Gloria Steinem and Cheryl Strayed.
In One Nightstand, celebrity readers and writers join us at the blond in 11 Howard to discuss some of their favorite books, allowing us to learn about their tastes and lives in the process.

For activist and actor Sophia Bush, writing her memoir, And I Will Tell You Mine: Notes from a Life in Progress, proved a surprisingly challenging experience. “When you are a thinker, a writer, when you’re privileged enough to have regular therapy, you really think you know your sh*t and then your book drags you,” she says. “It’s horrible. I called a few friends who are writers and I was like, ‘Why do we do this? Who let us do this?’”

Bush has been in the public eye since being cast as Brooke Davis in One Tree Hill in 2003, bringing the added complication of fame. “If you are a gorgeous writer, like a personal hero of mine, Cheryl Strayed, and you write the bone marrow of your life and that book becomes famous, you’re allowed to do that,” she says. “If you are someone the world perceives as famous in whatever way they do, you don’t get the same carte blanche to talk about your life.”

For that reason, Bush returned to the fundamentals she learned while studying journalism at the University of Southern California. “I wrote the New York Times piece, the investigative reporting of some of my life experiences to get them out, and then I had to decide what to reduce,” she says, nodding to intimate chapters that cover her divorces and what she describes as workplace sexual harassment. “Over a hundred pages of my book I pulled out and literally burned. I had a little ritual all to myself and I burned them. It didn’t feel like something I owed to everyone else. I don’t think you have to give someone your whole heart.”

For the chapters about her experience shooting One Tree Hill, she also sought consent from those involved before moving forward. “We’ve got an incredible group chat, but I chose to have individual conversations with every single person and individual dissemination of pages and things because I didn’t want anybody to feel swayed by the group,” she recalls, adding that she even anonymized two people who she “smushed into one.”

The goal was to protect the relationships they’d built with each other, despite the odds. “When I started working on TV in the early aughts, the machinery loved to input women and chew them up and spit them out,” she says. “The benefit to the machine itself is to cast you, the woman, in a role that they can then clickbait to death, but that’s not who you are. The hours are crazy. If you have a not particularly great boss, like we all didn’t, you’ll be taught to compete instead of collaborate. You’ll be pitted against each other and then won’t understand why suddenly everything feels weird. And you can’t talk about it because you can’t have a fight with your friends at work. So then it buries and it festers and it just cements.”

Bush, stepmother to the two children of her wife, former US soccer goalkeeper Ashlyn Harris, compares the craft of writing to raising a child. “Everyone I know who’s a parent has thoughts about what parenting will be, and then they meet the person their child is in every stage and they are that person,” she says. “Nothing you do is going to change who they intrinsically are. You hope to raise them well, you hope to make them feel confident, you hope to love them enough that the world doesn’t break them, but they are who they are.” Her book proved to be similar.
“The book is going to be what it wants to be,” she says. “You think you know the book you’re going to write, and then it pulls you on a journey.”
Keep reading to discover four of Bush’s favorite reads.

Bush’s first selection is Gloria Steinem’s 2015 memoir My Life on the Road, tracing the activist’s life from childhood through the 2010s. The morning Bush joins One Nightstand, she’d learned of Steinem’s passing at 92. “It was just such a surreal thing to sit and read over these gorgeous articles. I knew she hadn’t been feeling well,” she says. “Strangely, some friends of ours were talking about the next talking circle we wanted to host with her. And I said, ‘I know she’s not well, but she’s Gloria.’ I think we really thought she would just be with us forever.”

Steinem’s memoir made an impression on Bush when it came out, but it became a true North Star while writing her own. “It’s very surreal and it’s an interesting thing having just finished my first memoir to think about the memoirs and the life stories like hers, like this book that truly shaped me,” she says. “I think about the fact that I grew up a fan of hers and she became a friend. She became a person I could text. I will never not be so grateful that I got to be in her orbit.”

Steinem’s work also informed Bush’s own activism. “One of the things I learned from her was that I’ll show up for the small organization that’s working in one town on a border in Texas to protect migrant children in the same way that I’ll show up for a federal election,” she says. “It’s so clear for me how the political is, in fact, personal. And that’s her whole thesis. I think when you know it, it doesn’t have to feel overwhelming. It actually is so empowering. You realize that each of us has a hand on a lever of change, and that makes me feel optimistic rather than pessimistic.”

One of the last conversations she had with Steinem was on FaceTime. “She held a talking circle on women’s health, and I was working in Los Angeles and I couldn’t be there, but my partner was there and a group of our best friends were there,” she says. “It was so lovely just to see her, and she grabbed my partner and was like, ‘I love her.’ I said, ‘I know, right?’ She was like, ‘I’m just so happy for you two.’”
Her second choice is Tiny Beautiful Things, a collection of responses from Cheryl Strayed’s advice column “Dear Sugar.”

Bush has purchased and gifted the book more than 30 times. “There are things from running the gamut of Eastern and Western tradition that I understand to be universally true about humanity,” she says. “I believe Cheryl’s book to be one of the most spiritually sacred texts that any of our peers has ever written, because what she’s doing is modeling love out loud and in the hardest moments and in some of the most beautiful, and it is so exacting and yet so gentle.”

Some of Strayed’s advice has had an enduring effect on her. “We are all so much more than the worst mistake we’ve ever made or the greatest success we’ve ever had. We’re human beings in the center of all of that,” she says. “I think especially for women, the world encourages us to just self-obsess about our failures, or to wonder what everyone thinks of us, or to be so ashamed for existing or speaking, God forbid. We have to figure out how to divest from that, and I think we do that in community.”

That said, she’s judicious about giving advice. “I'm a little on the spectrum,” she says. “I've had to learn that my neuro-spiciness that goes like, ‘You're not alone. I have a thing.’ Calm down. Slow down. Like a Cheryl, I want to make people feel seen and know they're not alone. I also know that the immediate, ‘You're not alone. I can also offer you a terrible thing or a hard thing or a bad boss or whatever.’ It’s not always helpful.”

She continues: “As a person who has crazy pattern recognition because of the way my brain is wired, I can go big 30,000 feet: ‘Well, this is the system and this is what's going on with you and this is what women are dealing with in the workplace,’” she explains. “Also not always helpful. I love the data. Not everybody needs it.”

Her third pick is The Bitter Southerner, a triannual magazine coming out of the American South. Although Bush is California born and raised, she feels a strong connection to the region. “I spent 10 years in North Carolina. I’ve lived in Texas, and I’m madly in love with a woman from Florida,” she says.

It’s also been at the center of much of her activism. “The South is so culturally rich and has also been so historically under-resourced and taken from,” she says. “In all of my travels everywhere, some of my favorite fellow organizers, some of the most hilarious radical minds I know, come from my Southern friends that are like, ‘It’s f*ck this sh*t o’clock, and we're going to fix America.’ And, I’m like, ‘OK!’”

Bush says living in North Carolina while filming One Tree Hill was an enlightening experience. “It was very strange to move somewhere and be walking down a sidewalk downtown next to my neighbors of color and have to pass Confederate statues,” she says. “Interestingly enough, moving there enabled me to begin on the journey of having conversations about disparity in real time, not talking about what happened historically, but about: What were the patterns of our history that still exist today?”

Her final pick is Parable of the Sower by Octavia E. Butler. Written in 1993 and set in 2024, the novel follows a California on the brink of collapse due to climate change and social decay. “In the year 2026, it’s weird to revisit it because you realize she’s a gorgeous writer and perhaps a psychic,” she says. “One of the things that inspires me most about her is she wrote her lead female to be someone who is willing to ask the questions that most people are too scared to answer, that most people want to ignore because they are on the precipice of something scary and they're trying to cling to what was, but what was will never exist.”

Strangely, Bush says Butler’s dystopian world has a hint of optimism. “What I think it encourages is readers to be bold enough to envision something we can build together,” she says. “We only survive in community. The only way through is to build together and everyone’s experience — the diversity of race, generation, economic status, all of it — is actually what gives a community the amount of thought and the different experience levels to be able to build something together.”

paragraphs: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn compensation.

Anyone can run to the store and grab a gift card, but the best gift givers know that the most-appreciated presents start with giving it some real thought. Whether you’re shopping for your bestie who’s been checking in with FaceTime calls every week or that special somebody you gave your number to while leaving the gym, gifts that come with intention are always the winners of the holiday season.

Of course, you could spend hours opening a million tabs just to find the right item. Or you could get a lil’ advice from a veteran shopping director (hi, it’s me!). I’ve been on the search for the most thoughtful finds this entire year, so the holidays are like my Super Bowl. I get joy out of people asking me, “Where can I find the best personalized gifts?” or “What are some impressive finds that won’t blow my budget?” So, ahead I’m breaking down the meaningful, fun finds that deserve to be wrapped this season. And because we’re always going to be financially smart sirens, start with what you’re comfortable spending, then find something that feels just right for your person. Each item is available for purchase with Affirm, you can pay over time with no late or hidden fees—and keep the surprises where they belong: in the gift giving. It doesn’t matter if you’re giving the gift of a fancy beauty product you discovered at Neiman Marcus, a unique trinket from an Etsy seller, or a hero home essential on Wayfair, Affirm makes checking everyone off your nice list easy peasy.
Take our holiday quiz to find your gifting match or keep scrolling for the Refinery29 edit of thoughtful presents.

She has impeccable taste, sends you links before you’ve even heard of the brand, and somehow already owns everything you were considering. The move? Get personal. An embroidered zebra-print pouch with her name on it gives her everyday essentials a very cute home, while a photo jewelry dish turns that picture of you two into something she’ll actually use. Yes, the one from the night you still talk about. If she loves a beauty treat, Dior lip oil or a bottle of one of Tom Ford’s fragrances brings a little luxury to her getting-ready routine. You know your friend. Pick the gift that proves it.

You’ve seen their kitchen. You’ve admired their table settings. You’ve wondered whether you should start bringing your own containers because even the leftovers leave looking chic. Pink checkered canisters from Wayfair make keeping the counter tidy considerably more fun, and Jonathan Adler’s lip-motif coasters give guests something to comment on between sips. An olive oil gift set from Williams Sonoma is another good call: they can taste their way through it, then casually make you the best salad of your life. And for the host who does all that cooking and washing up? A Jo Malone hand cream trio feels like a little thank-you for their hands.

Maybe they’ve had a year. Maybe they always take care of everyone else. Maybe you simply love watching them open something they would have talked themselves out of buying. Here’s your chance. A Saint Laurent card case makes even pulling out a loyalty card feel a little fancy, while a Dyson Supersonic Nural is a generous upgrade for someone who takes their hair routine seriously. For the person whose signature scent is practically part of their introduction, the Parfums De Marly’s viral perfume puts a favorite fragrance within reach. Start with something you know they’ll love, then give them the version they’ve been eyeing.

“We should do that” has been sitting in the group chat for six months. Let’s give it a little momentum. A pasta basket packed with gourmet treats makes choosing a Saturday very doable, while a personalized passport holder and luggage tag give your buddy something to unwrap before you two settle on a destination. For the friend who keeps promising cocktail night, a gold bar-tool set from Wayfair says, “Great, I’ll bring the limes.” Add a travel journal for the person who wants to remember every meal, wrong turn, and surprisingly good hotel recommendation. You may still have to send the calendar invite, but at least you've got an opening.

Your gift budget also has rent, groceries, and your own holiday travel to consider. Fair enough. A personalized hairbrush feels chosen just for them, and colorful stemware can make their usual Friday-night pour feel like an occasion. For your friend who treasures a good night in, consider a checked pajama piece or a candle in a playful, colorful vessel. Just think about the small pleasures they return to every day, then find something that makes one of those moments a little sweeter.

items.title: I'm 29, I Make $110K & I'm Deep Into The Wedding Season Of My Life
items.description: A Week In Denver, CO On A $110,000 Salary
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In Denver, CO On A $110,000 Salary
This week: a data scientist working in politics who makes $110,000 per year and spends some of it on a ginger stick-on moustache and eyebrows that she ordered for her sheriff costume. YEEEEHAWWWW!

If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.
Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We'd love to hear your thoughts here.
Editor's note: This is a follow-up diary. You can read the previous one here.
Location: Denver, Colorado

Joint Income/Financial Setup: My boyfriend and I moved in together about a year ago and are working towards combining our finances in a way that feels right for us. We have a joint RocketMoney account where we create a monthly budget and can generally monitor whether we are spending more than we take in. We split things proportionally to our income (he has been laid off twice in the last year #journalism and cobbles together several recurring freelance jobs while job searching for a full-time role in the brand content space), so I pay more in rent, I pay for his healthcare and I help subsidize his therapy (it's his first time going and I wanted to make sure he had as few barriers as possible!). I cover more of the dinners, entertainment, and such, but we split groceries equally. Given that we don't have any joint accounts or anything, I'll report on just my spending!
IRA (old 401k rolled over): $72,951
Various investments (managed by Merrill Lynch): $280,004
Paycheck Amount (2x month): $2,938.32

Housing Costs: $1,100 (my boyfriend and I have a sweet deal on a two-bed in Denver. He pays $575 and I pay $1,100, not including utilities. It's not our dream apartment by any means, but it's amazing for the price and allows us a great lifestyle).
NYT subscription: ~$10 (news, games and food).
Local mutual aid organization: $17
Colorado abortion fund: $20
Phone: $0 (yes, I continue to mooch off my parents).
Fox One: $21.82 (going to cancel this as soon as the World Cup is over!)
Health insurance: $0 (luckily my company pays).
Health insurance for my boyfriend: $~230 (pre tax, my company covers 70% as he is listed as domestic partner).
Therapy: $400-600 (I pay out of pocket $200 a session, which is steep, but I've been working with this therapist for years and I love her).
Therapy for my boyfriend: $75-100 (his copay is $50 per session so I split with him).
401(k): $231 (pre-tax, employer matched 75%)
Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?

Yes! I grew up between Brooklyn and Westchester, New York — both affluent communities in which everyone I knew was on the college track. My parents and stepparents and grandparents and everyone else had attended college, and many had master's or PhDs. When I was a senior in high school, I learned that my grandparents and parents had been saving for my college education since my birth but that I would still have to take out student loans. In my affluent community, no one talked about needing to take out loans, only “dream schools” and “following your heart,” so I was really ashamed (which I now know is stupid. Financial transparency is empowering!). However, my mom worked at NYU at the time so if I went there I got a 90% discount. I was on the fence but ultimately decided to go to NYU over other private and public schools and it was the best decision my 18-year-old self ever made. Graduating without any debt, and with money that my parents had left over, has changed my life and I'm incredibly lucky to have had that option.
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

Going to school in Westchester, I often felt less privileged and a bit different than my peers. My mom was the breadwinner in the family and got on the train to NYC early every day with the dads, while many of my friends' mothers were stay-at-home moms who played tennis and were involved in PTA. My friends took international vacations every year and had multiple Juicy tracksuits (tbt to 2006) but we had to ask my grandparents to help out with my flute lessons, and I only ever got one Juicy tracksuit because it was on major discount at Filene's Basement (lol). That being said, I never wanted for anything serious and am so grateful that my mom instilled the value of budgeting in me early. Starting in high school, I got a sizeable allowance ($100!) every month for doing chores but that was it; there was no asking for movie tickets or pizza money. This taught me to save for the things I wanted and I do feel like I have a better grasp on money now than many of my friends who were raised more privileged than me. My dad is a documentary filmmaker who had his own production company, but had to close it when my stepmom got sick in my early high school years. He then did odd jobs (filmmaking-related), while always pursuing 3-4 personal projects at a time. When I was <12 he told me he was in $70K+ debt, but between an inheritance from his parents and help from my stepmom's very affluent parents, they were able to provide for my brothers and me. His lack of job stability (and my stepdad's, who is also in the film business) always made me want to get a steady job and definitely shaped my relationship to money and career.
What was your first job and why did you get it?

When I was 12, I got a summer job as a counselor at a day camp in the Hamptons. I was paid $100 a week under the table but I was SO excited. My older cousin worked there and we spent the following five summers chasing after other cute counselors, going to the beach and engaging in standard teenage mischief. Although I wasn't paid great, I was able to charge an outrageous amount for babysitting ($25 an hour as a 15-year-old in 2011?!) because of the wealth in the Hamptons and therefore had plenty of money for groceries, eating out and even saving. Over the five summers I saved a few thousand dollars, which helped immensely in college.
Did you worry about money growing up?

Not really. I always had food on the table, lots of clothes, and a new gadget at Hanukkah. As mentioned above, growing up affluent in a VERY affluent community definitely made me feel less than sometimes, but I never seriously worried.
Do you worry about money now?

Yes and no. A few years ago (during my previous Money Diary!) I went on medical leave from my job due to depression and burnout and ended up working for over a year doing odds jobs: front of house at a local bakery, babysitting/dog walking, and data collector at a museum. My salary during that time went from ~$115K to ~$30K and I learned A LOT about myself and how to be happy with way less. I worked harder than I ever had before (4:30 a.m. wake-up calls!!), and met incredible people who were grinding to put themselves through college, etc. It really put my privilege into major perspective and made me realize how much of a bubble I had been living in. Last summer, when my boyfriend got laid off, I kicked my "white collar" job search back into high gear and ended up back working as a data scientist (similar work to what I had been doing before I burned out). Though I initially took the job because we needed it and was apprehensive about going into politics, I have come to really really enjoy the day-to-day and my team. I have much better appreciation for my salary, and save ~$800-1000 a month easily, while treating myself and my loved ones (in large part because of my low rent). That being said, I do worry about my future goals and how to get them to come to fruition financially. I really really really want to own a small house or townhome, and even with a down payment ready to go (and I am SO lucky for that) the month-to-month costs seem forever out of reach. I look at 2-bed, 2-bath listings near me in the $450-550K range and see that the monthly expenses would be over double what I pay now, which does not feel justifiable. I also want a child or children and simply don't know how it would be possible with my boyfriend and I's current earning potential. (My boyfriend works in a field where lay offs happen A LOT, especially with AI, and he believes he won't ever make $100K+ a year). He wants to get married and have a wedding and I can't see how we'd justify 10s of thousands of dollars on a party — let alone how he would afford a ring. I'm incredibly financially lucky and I do not worry about our day to day in the slightest, which is such a blessing, but as an everlasting worrywort and pragmatist, I do worry about our future goals and how to make them achievable.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

Six months after college, I moved in with a roommate in NYC and became responsible for everything except healthcare and phone bills. I had a decent paying job and could cover all my expenses fairly easily. My financial safety net is primarily myself and I have a few months of expenses saved and much more in stocks. When I was making less than my boyfriend he treated me to dinners and paid more in rent, so we do lean on each other financially in that way, which I love, it feels great to have that mutual support. That being said, I could always move back in with either of my parents if I really needed to. While I love living in Denver and definitely do not want to move back to NY any time soon, it wouldn't be the worst option and I would likely do that over liquidating my investments.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.

Yes, quite a bit and I'm incredibly privileged. In college, my step-grandpa passed away, and since my stepmom had passed as well, $80,000 of his life insurance payout went to me. In addition, post-college my mom and dad gave me the remainder of their college funds for me ($40,000 and $20,000, respectively). All of this has gone into investments and remains untouched. And of course, my parents paid for my college tuition, books and housing. Last year when I was working odd jobs my parents paid for my plane tickets home, and when I faced a particularly tough string of job rejections my mom sent me ~$200 bucks to cheer me up. After many years of feeling less privileged than my peers, I realized just how privileged I am and how rare of a situation I am in! I want to fight for others to have safety nets (at the very least lets get medicare for all) and have dignified lives in the way I've been able to.
10:00 p.m. — Take my dog out again and head to bed by 11:30 p.m.

I usually track my spending pretty closely through the Rocket Money app, but I enjoyed the experience of thoroughly journaling about my day, and I hope to do that part a bit more consistently. Adding up my bills and net worth and such at the beginning also helped to reinforce just how lucky I am, and how much of a safety net I (and to a lesser extent E.) have. Helped alleviate some of the anxiety and rumination I experience around our long term financial future. Sure — we might not be as well off as my friends who have a $300K+ joint income, we might not own a house or have money for a wedding, but we're doing alright, and for that I'm very grateful.
The first step to getting your financial life in order is tracking what you spend — to try on your own, check out our guide to managing your money every day. For more Money Diaries, click here.
