items.author: Raquel Reichard
paragraphs: I consider myself a pretty private person. I’m a journalist. My job, as my j-school professors drilled into my head, is to tell other people’s stories, not mine. On social media, I mostly post career highlights, leaving my romantic relationships and other intimate details of my life a mystery. It’s intentional. It’s protective. It’s how I want it. And maybe some of it is cultural. After all, Latinas are often taught not to air our dirty laundry in public. And yet, come July 2027, some of the darkest and hardest moments of my life will be sitting on a bookstore shelf near you.

My debut memoir, The Best Love Stories Are Between Friends, will be out in the world, and in its pages, strangers and relatives will read about experiences I never shared with anyone. Why? Because the grief of losing my best friend, Angelica Alvarez, to stage 4 small-cell carcinoma lung cancer four years ago nearly killed me, too. And talking about her, our friendship, and the life-affirming power of girlfriends that sustain us, even in their death, is what helped pull me back to life.

Sometimes, shamelessly allowing our grief to be seen, even in a culture that tells us to suffer in silence and move on, is what helps us carry it, and what allows those around us to carry theirs, too.

Monica Veloz, aka Monicastylemuse, understands this, too. The beloved Dominican-American content creator and beauty influencer is used to being honest about the challenges she faces as an Afro-Latina or her journey through motherhood. So when her own mother, Mama Muse, died of stage four gastric cancer, she mourned publicly, out loud, as her community of more than 400,000 followers on Instagram and Youtube (respectively) bore witness.

In this episode, we speak with Monica about losing her favorite person, the loneliness of grief, and what it means to mourn out loud and in public without shame or fear of judgment. We explore the power of grieving on your own terms, honoring your loved ones unapologetically, and finding ways to keep those relationships alive long after death.

items.title: I Was Never Allowed To Go To Camp. So I Signed Up In My 30s
items.description: I Was Never Allowed To Go To Camp. So I Signed Up In My 30s
items.author: Raquel Reichard
paragraphs: I Was Never Allowed To Go To Camp. So I Signed Up In My 30s
"I wanted so desperately to go away to camp for myself, to play tug-of-war, toast marshmallows, and then whisper under covers to a group of girlfriends I only saw a couple weeks every summer."

"I stood amid the towering trees, taking it all in, grateful for the younger body that carried me up the trail and the older, more mature mind that knew to pause and appreciate the beauty around me. "

"I remember watching the sunset that last night and how my campmates and I ended our trip by singing Camp Rock’s “This Is Me” — just as we would have if it was 2008, when the Disney Channel classic dropped, when we were all still teens just imagining camp days like this one."

items.title: My ER regulars spat at me. And opened my mind | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: I’m bent over a patient, starting an IV. I hear the steady beep of monitors, the constant hum, and then a scuffle and profanity. The commotion lands on the other side of the curtain. I finish taping up the IV, excuse myself, and slip out.
items.author: Anita Lambert
paragraphs: I’m bent over a patient, starting an IV. I hear the steady beep of monitors, the constant hum, and then a scuffle and profanity. The commotion lands on the other side of the curtain. I finish taping up the IV, excuse myself, and slip out.

There, surrounded by paramedics, nurses and police, I find a yelling, kicking, spitting woman who smells of a long day of drinking. ‘Grab that leg, Anita!’ someone calls. I move quickly, dodging a surprisingly well-aimed kick by inches, and grab her shin with both hands, holding it to the bed. She’s strong. Staff members hold her other limbs while a coworker gets the leather restraints in place.

Here I am, I thought. I wanted to be in the big city. I grew up in a smaller town where our experience was limited to what we saw on TV and read in newspapers. By the time I was a teenager, I had such a narrow worldview that barely anybody else belonged in it and an ego so loud that barely anyone else could be heard over it. I proudly spouted ‘personal responsibility’ to anyone complaining about whatever rut they’d become stuck in. ‘Drag yourself out by your fingernails,’ I’d advise. I carried that attitude with me to Chicago in the 1990s, when I began working in this ER.

I watched the woman urinate on herself and then taunt us about having to clean it up. Meanwhile, my patient on the other side of the curtain waited for the asthma medications still in my pocket while another patient held pressure on a wound in the waiting room.

‘Meet Charlene,’ said Frank, grinning. I huffed and looked at my paramedic colleague in disbelief. Frank had lived and worked in Chicago his whole life. Charlene’s mask had slipped off in the scuffle, and she used the opportunity to spit at me.
So that night went. And the next. Always stitched through the chaos were the regulars. Every ER has them, and I was introduced to ours by name every night.

One evening, during a lull, I sat beside June catching up on our charting. She was a seasoned ER nurse and one of my favourite coworkers. I groaned as I heaved myself onto my aching feet. ‘I have to go check on Charlene.’

‘You know she was a teacher?’ June said, glancing up from her chart. ‘Her son drowned, and she never really recovered. Lost her job, lost the rest of her family. She’s been coming here for years like this.’
As I slipped past her curtain, Charlene turned her face toward me. I noticed how hollow her gaze was. How had I never seen that before? How had I never wondered?
She never seemed to remember the night before and apologised bashfully when reminded
‘Hi, Charlene.’ I stood a safe distance away, prepared to duck if she spat. She didn’t.
I pulled up a stool and sat next to her bed, as I’d done before.

‘Is it safe to take these off?’ I asked. She nodded. I slowly loosened the leather straps, limb by limb, watching for signs of attack. I paused, just for a second, and gave her hand a soft squeeze. I’d never done that before. Then I sat back down.
With her limbs free, she turned over on the bed to face me, eyes closed. She whispered: ‘I haven’t always been like this.’

‘You’re not always like this now,’ I said. I’d seen sober Charlene leave the ER in full high spirits, giggling and flirting with Frank. She never seemed to remember the night before and apologised bashfully when reminded.

In the ER, we lived by one rule: work hard, play hard. Together, we developed a perverse sense of humour that only we appreciated. Sometimes we saw obituaries of our regulars pinned to the break-room wall.

Long, challenging shifts were broken up by nights out together, when we drank, got silly, played pool, ate bar food and laughed over jokes that would turn anyone else’s stomach. We also raised a quiet toast to our deceased regulars. We were bonded by what we did in a way I had never experienced before.

A few years into my ER career, by then more experienced and cynical, I attended a required class. The instructor opened with a lesson on compassion as a cure for burnout. She reminded us that our kindness might be the last kindness a person in our care receives. Those words have knocked around in my thoughts ever since. I remembered times when I should have been kinder and more patient, and I vowed to improve my approach to all patients, no matter how many times I’d triaged and discharged them that day. I began to wear compassion like armour, and our toasts to dead regulars took on more weight.
June no longer had to give me insights into our patients; I learned their stories on my own.

The armour of compassion worked – until it didn’t. As the years pressed on, and I gained experience in emergency departments all around the US, the ER became more difficult. C-suite executives with business or finance degrees but no medical training loaded nurses with more and more non-patient-care tasks: fill out this extra form for someone in a back office doing metrics here, ask these five extra questions to all patients to ensure we can bill for screenings that have nothing to do with the patient’s chief complaint there, spend an extra 10 minutes searching for a computer, and sign into it only to find the scanner broken, then repeat. As the pace accelerated, the goalposts for success moved farther away. I couldn’t be in enough places at once, let alone spend three minutes connecting with a patient and addressing their fear or discomfort.

The number of regulars increased, but we didn’t have time to get to know them. Nobody wants to feel like they’re failing day in and day out, so in December 2019, I planned my exit. I enrolled in Spanish classes in Colombia and intended to stay for a year on a student visa, teaching English on the side. I hoped the move would lead to other opportunities away from the United States healthcare system.

Around that time, I began to catch rumours of a new, unnamed illness overseas. I checked with the hospitals I’d worked in before and, aside from a few other concerned coworkers, they seemed largely unaware and certainly weren’t taking any precautions. For them, it was business as usual (making money). For me, it was a race to go where my savings would last longer, and my stress would be lighter.

By the time entire villages in Italy were singing and cheering out their windows for healthcare workers, it was still business as usual in the US. When the virus hit US hospitals, they were already filled to the brim in the name of ‘efficiency’ and caught with their proverbial pants down. Then borders closed, and I was trapped in the US.
Whatever the signs said, we weren’t heroes in the hospitals’ eyes

With my savings dwindling and a growing sense of duty, I jumped in again. Something about the need, the fear and the desperation of so many people rekindled the compassion I’d worked so hard to cultivate years earlier. I wanted to help.

I arrived in North Carolina for work and secured housing, but my job was cancelled before it even began. Next came New York and then New Hampshire. I knew that our presence meant something to scared people. Somehow, we brought comfort – and that felt worthwhile.

At first, cheers for nurses and doctors filled the empty streets. Hospitals hung ‘Heroes Work Here’ signs while administrators stayed far away. Whatever the signs said, we weren’t heroes in the hospitals’ eyes. Real heroes would have been given proper personal protective equipment. I had one N95 mask, pulled repeatedly from a crumpled brown paper bag, and single-use face shields I washed, hung and reused until they were scratched and foggy. The worn-out equipment and closed doors made it nearly impossible to hear alarms or see monitors. Once again, I wasn’t meeting my patients’ needs, and compassion quickly morphed into despair.

As the coronavirus swept across the US, a family tragedy brought me to northwest Florida. There, the bars and restaurants were in full swing, masks were scoffed at, and the pandemic seemed real only for families of the dead. Everywhere, people talked about the COVID hoax and loved to exclaim: ‘If you think you’re at risk, YOU wear a mask and stay home!’ Eventually, the first pandemic wave seemed to die down, and I cautiously took a job in a nearby ER.

As in other emergency departments where I’d worked, the staff were stretched thin. But here, each nurse carried a heavier patient load, and staff members, often traumatised themselves, had little time to laugh together or bond.
Then the Delta variant swept through. These patients were younger, many of them previously healthy, and it was disturbing to see so many of them in such a serious condition.

I was rushing through discharge instructions one day when I saw a new patient wheeled into one of my rooms, his lips blue, his skin sweaty and pale. I immediately excused myself and headed toward him. He didn’t have time to waste. He was in his 40s, and too short of breath to speak more than a few words at a time. He denied any history of asthma or other health issues.
My regulars were the intoxicated, psychotic, lost, and forgotten, the ones who had broken down doors inside me I’d never known were there

He refused to keep his mask on, which I had come to expect by then. Double-checking my own mask, I put him on oxygen, listened to his lungs and hooked him to the monitor while scanning the nurses’ station for a respiratory therapist and the attending physician. He was agitated, which commonly happens as oxygen levels drop. I asked him the standard questions, including whether he had been exposed to COVID-19 recently. At that question, he began to sputter about the hoax we were all perpetrating. Fatigue squashed his outrage, and he grudgingly allowed me to collect a sample for a COVID-19 test while I guarded against a possible attack.
His colour and oxygen levels improved on high-flow oxygen therapy, but his anger didn’t abate. I wasn’t looking forward to breaking the news that his COVID-19 test was positive.

When I did, he glared at me and used what little energy he had to call me a liar. As I backed out of his reach, he tore off his monitor leads and oxygen, yanked out his IV, and made for the exit, blood dripping down his arm. He made it several steps toward the exit before nearly collapsing, and we helped him back to bed, panting. Back in the room, I called for a tight-fitting breathing mask that would push air into his lungs as I pressed gauze over his dripping IV site and reattached his monitor. Then he took a feeble swing at me and spat. I don’t remember his name. He wasn’t a regular.

The people spitting and swearing at me in this ER believed that safeguarding oneself from illness was a matter of personal responsibility, but that responsibility ended with themselves. They were sealed inside an echo chamber that confirmed everything they believed. I recognised what I used to be, and what I might have become had it not been for the ER, Chicago, Frank, June, Charlene. The thought sickened me.

Nah, these weren’t my ER regulars. My regulars were the intoxicated, psychotic, lost, and forgotten, the ones who had broken down doors inside me I’d never known were there. Working with them in the chaos of that Chicago ER, I learned that personal responsibility didn’t mean just taking care of yourself. They helped me see that a world of people responsible only for themselves will never improve.
I put in my notice that day, and scoffed at the ‘Heroes Work Here’ sign on my way out.

items.title: When giving up teaches you more than persevering ever could | Psyche Ideas
items.description: After three years and more than 20 rejections, I asked myself a difficult question: should I give up? The evidence seemed clear. American universities did not want me as a philosophy graduate student. The world was telling me that an academic life was nothing
items.author: Mario I Juarez-Garcia
paragraphs: After three years and more than 20 rejections, I asked myself a difficult question: should I give up? The evidence seemed clear. American universities did not want me as a philosophy graduate student. The world was telling me that an academic life was nothing more than a teenage dream. My lifelong goal of becoming a professional philosopher appeared to founder on the shoals of academia. It was time to decide whether it made sense to continue pursuing what the world told me was an unachievable project. But how does one decide when it’s time to give up?

In theory, there is a tidy formula to know when to abandon a goal: when the expected utility of quitting becomes greater than the expected utility of pursuing it. But, of course, the clean theoretical answer dissolves in the strange complexities of life. When we face the question of giving up in reality, expected utility is really just an arbitrary personal estimation. The moment for giving up is messy, determined more by one’s idiosyncratic criteria and personality than anything that could reasonably be considered objective. This opens the door to further questions: what if the next try is the successful one? Am I letting all of my past efforts go to waste? What kind of person am I if I give up?

It is especially difficult to abandon goals when we are surrounded by stories of victorious grit. Popular culture adores portrayals of unlikely success, of those who experience setbacks, keep trying, refuse to surrender, and then, despite the overwhelming odds, win. ‘Losers’ and ‘quitters’ are insults in a society that prizes those who never give up. But the value of persistence not only permeates popular culture. It has also prompted moral philosophers to stress the virtues of grit.

Philosophers have recently been animated by the challenge of grasping the nature and rationality of persistence. One important thinker about persistence was the American philosopher Robert Nozick, who held that honouring our past efforts builds a commitment that helps us overcome the temptation to quit and may push us to achieve long-term goals. In a similar line of thought, Jennifer Morton and Sarah Paul invite readers to always start long-term projects with the strong belief that they will succeed despite evidence to the contrary, which in favourable circumstances can overcome deadening inertia. Others, like Elizabeth Jackson, underline hope as fundamental for rationalising the pursuit of long-term goals despite evidence of failure and temptations to give up. Philosophers thus contribute to a culture of perseverance.

Despite its virtues, an important problem of a culture of perseverance is that it hides exactly what it denies: the positive value of giving up. Grit is all well and good, but in real life, abandoning goals is crucial to discovering who we are. This is what I call the exploratory value of giving up: quitting may reveal skills, limitations and passions that could not have been known prior to failure.

To grasp the exploratory value of giving up, we must understand the process of choosing goals. Rational choice theory distinguishes between means and goals. Goals fall beyond the purview of rationality; they are chosen according to our preferences. Once chosen, goals provide the fixed point from which the means can be rationally chosen. But mere pursuit of preference is not the only way to choose goals. They can also be selected according to the means that are available through a process of exploration and improvisation. Saras Sarasvathy, a theorist of entrepreneurship, explains these two ways of choosing goals with a mundane illustration: deciding what to have for dinner. We can choose a dish from a cookbook, buy the ingredients, follow the recipe, and voilà! This is normally how we think about pursuing goals: we choose one, develop the necessary skills, and strive to achieve it. The goal determines the means. In a culture of perseverance, any goal we choose is supposed to be achievable – and, if we fail, it is because we did not try hard enough.
What are the chances that we get the right combination of ingredients on the first try?

But there is another way to choose what to have for dinner. You can first look at the ingredients you have in the cupboard and improvise. This is a different selection process. The ingredients determine the dish. Sarasvathy holds that the second strategy is the way entrepreneurs build successful businesses: they try and fail until they figure out what they do well, and only then do they persevere. They give up on bad business ideas before choosing the right one. This framework allows us to grasp the exploratory value of giving up: we discover ‘the ingredients in our cupboard’ through our failures. Giving up is often a step toward self-knowledge.

Consider the choice of long-term goals. These goals are like unknown ingredients in the cupboard: we need to try them first to see what can be useful. What are the chances that we get the right combination of ingredients on the first try? Likewise, what are the chances that the first goal teenagers choose will fulfil them as adults? The earliest life goals one adopts are often chosen from a place of ignorance and childish illusion. But if we acknowledge that those goals are temporary and are attentive to the reasons for our failures, we are likely to gain knowledge about ourselves.

Initial goals are what the philosopher David Schmidtz, in his article ‘Choosing Ends’ (1994), calls maieutic ends, those ‘end[s] achieved through a process of coming to have other ends’. Maieutic ends are provisional and hence can orient the search for other goals. We might realise that we were not talented enough to become musicians, that we sabotage romantic relationships that feel too close to be safe, or that we do not want to spend years writing a dissertation, and so on. Being attentive to failure is being alert to one’s skills, talents and drives. The search is not easy, and it might need to restart many times throughout a lifetime, not always because the lessons are not learned, but because we change with the circumstances.

Other times what is learned from failure is not something about ourselves, but about the context of our life. An ambitious young woman from rural West Virginia realises that she lacks the means to go to college; an Indigenous writer from Chiapas who works in his mother tongue accepts that his texts will not be read by many; the chair of the literature department of a small university comes to terms with the fact that the administration is gradually eliminating the humanities. Failure helps us learn that our conditions are not right for the goal we are pursuing. Yet reality is not so malleable. When our surroundings are working against us, the right strategy is not always to change them. Sometimes it is better to change ourselves. That wisdom can be found in René Descartes’s words: ‘my … maxim was to endeavour always to conquer myself rather than fortune, and change my desires rather than the order of the world.’ Maybe that ambitious young woman from rural West Virginia must find ways to succeed that do not involve college; perhaps the writer from Chiapas needs to learn to write some texts in English; and the literature professor may need to find a way to make a living outside academia.

Consider again the original question. How do we know when one should give up? In theory, the answer is straightforward; in reality, asking for the optimal point for abandoning goals seems to be the wrong question. The right one is different: would I know myself better if I gave up? This is what ultimately helped me decide to quit trying to become an academic philosopher. I did not renew my adjunct contract at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and took over the old office job of a good friend. It wasn’t much, but it was a place to start reimagining my life. Then, after a week of taking the new job, I couldn’t tolerate how unmotivating the office job was. It was worse than the sting of rejections. So I confirmed that what moved me was doing philosophy. What I really had to give up on was the office job – and what I had to persist with was the PhD applications. For two more years I applied. The first year I was rejected. Then, one day, I was accepted at the University of Arizona. The risk paid off. But it might not have done. Giving up on philosophy might have led me to a better place. I doubt it, not because I persevered, but because, for one week, I did not. That is how I learned what moved me.

Friedrich Nietzsche’s aphorism ‘What does not kill me makes me stronger’ has become a cliché at the core of a culture of perseverance. But it implies an often overlooked truth: what does not make us stronger may also teach us who we are.

items.title: Ellah Wakatama, the godmother of African books | Psyche Portraits
items.description: Not long ago, a group of East African writers gathered at my house in Nairobi for a writing weekend. We were all working on manuscripts – novels set in Kenya and in Kazakhstan, histories of people in Ethiopia and Uganda, works we each imagined would be our mag
items.author: Carey Baraka
paragraphs: Not long ago, a group of East African writers gathered at my house in Nairobi for a writing weekend. We were all working on manuscripts – novels set in Kenya and in Kazakhstan, histories of people in Ethiopia and Uganda, works we each imagined would be our magnum opus – but the problem, invariably, was how we might turn these into published books. Over beers and pizza, we brainstormed. Maybe what we needed was to be agented in London or in New York. Maybe what we needed was to move to London or New York. Maybe we simply needed to support each other, edit one another’s manuscripts. (But how would that help us get published?) Then, a Somali author who’d won some of Africa’s most important literary prizes for shorter work, chimed in. What we needed, he said, was to be adopted by Ellah Wakatama.

To be an African writer today – especially one writing in English, especially one younger than 40 – is to reckon with the idea of Ellah. Born in Zimbabwe when it was still under the Rhodesian flag, and now based in Britain, she is an editor-at-large at Canongate, an independent publishing firm. But it is more accurate to describe her as the most powerful woman – person – in Anglophone African literature today. From friends whose books she has touched, one hears of the fury of her red pen, of what they describe as the best editing they’ve ever experienced. From those who’ve worked with her, one hears of a person who doesn’t suffer fools, nor clichés like ‘suffer fools’. No other individual has so influenced the 21st-century African canon, if there is such a thing. Wakatama calls it ‘the bookshelf that my grandchildren will refer to’. Her lifelong project is to shape that bookshelf, to turn it into a library unto itself.
The night went on, as did the weekend. We’d all laughed when he said it, but beneath our laughter were three uneasy truths:
- There were no publishers in East Africa who would put out our work.
- We were doomed to try and find our own way into publishing networks in the West.
- Having a literary godparent was what had worked for generations of African writers.

In the beginning was Chinua Achebe. It is a rule of African literature that any exegesis has to begin with him. Achebe is famous as a novelist – Things Fall Apart (1958) really is one of those great books that everyone should read before they die – but he was more important as an editor of Heinemann’s African Writers Series (AWS), which introduced Western readers to an array of African authors, fledgling and established alike. Novels by African writers had existed before Achebe but, for writers of a certain generation, the AWS was arguably the only publishing vehicle for their work. The great Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, for instance, had his first book published because he gave his manuscript to Achebe. Now we needed to give our manuscripts to Wakatama. She was editor, agent, publisher and godparent, all rolled into one.
But how had she become this person? How did a kid from Harare grow up to wield such influence? I, a kid from Kisumu, a city in Kenya, was determined to track how this had come to be.

The idea of Ellah is different from Ellah in person. In June 2025, I met Wakatama in Accra where she was leading a writing workshop for Pfumo, a Pan-African literary collective she’d recently co-founded. Who was this person in front of me, smoking a cigarette she’s rolled herself? So giggly, so cheery, a bit frilly. She squealed when we passed the store of her favourite Ghanaian designer. I wanted to gossip with her. She exuded fun.

I put to her my Achebe comparison, although I could already see holes: Wakatama’s hair is far more glorious and, unlike the grand old man of African letters, she’d never been a novelist, though she’d briefly tried to be a poet, and co-authored a book of short stories when she was 21. Wakatama, laughing, wouldn’t agree with the Achebe analogy – we both knew that would be in bad taste – but said she could see the throughline of my logic. She was, after all, a child of the age that the AWS represented and sought to shape: Africa after empire.

The second child of Winnie Ndoro and Pius Wakatama, Ellah spent her first four years in a village south of Harare with her grandparents. Winnie and Pius had met at work: she, educated, was a secretary; he, a township boy who sold newspapers, had, Ellah told me, very much ‘married up’. Pius didn’t finish high school but he could write in English; he’d read the short fiction in DRUM, a South African magazine he sold, and thought to himself: I can do that! He could, and did, and then became a novelist in the Shona language, well-known enough that he was invited for a residency at the University of Iowa.
‘I feel I have been looking for Narnia ever since. Every book I open, I’m looking for Narnia’

This time, the whole family went. In Iowa, little Ellah struggled to make friends, partly because she barely spoke English. Once, she saw a group of Black girls playing outside but they wouldn’t speak to her since all she spoke was Shona. That people who looked like her couldn’t understand her was deeply unsettling; soon after, Ellah stopped talking altogether for six months. When she resumed, she stuttered badly in English. Her mother, Winnie, enlisted a speech therapist who used C S Lewis’s The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe to help her. If you can read this word w-a-r-d-r-o-b-e without stuttering, the therapist once told her, we will have a peach melba. Ellah thought and thought, said the word without tripping over it, then snarfed down her reward.

Perhaps that’s where it started – the belief that books could be a salve against the world. A few years later, when her class went on a field trip to see a wardrobe that had once belonged to C S Lewis, Ellah packed spare socks, a sandwich and a flashlight because she was going to Narnia and not coming back. But when they opened it, it was just an empty wardrobe. ‘I was really disappointed,’ she told me. ‘And I feel I have been looking for Narnia ever since. Every book I open, I’m looking for Narnia.’

In 1976, the family moved back to Zimbabwe, where a war of liberation was being waged. A year before Ellah was born, the white minority in Rhodesia had seized power, declaring independence from Britain. Consequently, two liberation groups – ZANU and ZAPU – had started a resistance war, rejecting rule by a clique of white settlers. Pius and Winnie wanted to be home when it was won. Ten-year-old Ellah, no longer mute, had forgotten how to speak in Shona. Winnie enrolled her in the best private elementary school in Zimbabwe at the time. Only white girls were students at Bishopslea but Winnie saw no reason why her daughters shouldn’t get the best education. Neither did the school’s British headmistress. But the Rhodesian government was angry this had happened, and they deported the headmistress.

All the while, the war continued. Some of Ellah’s relatives were either fighting or living in villages fenced off because of the war. Her classmates were told to support their soldiers; one year, they had to knit balaclavas for the prime minister Ian Smith’s forces, so Ellah went home and asked her mother for green yarn. Winnie was furious; no daughter of hers was going to make balaclavas for the Rhodesians. Ellah cried and cried; all she wanted was to fit in with the other girls. As a compromise, Winnie bought her brown wool – nothing but the green of the Rhodesian flag would fit the Rhodesians.
‘It had a profound effect on me … this idea that your life has to have meaning, that you can’t just exist, that you have to be impacting the world’

This is one part of what shaped Wakatama. The memories of the war. The race laws in Zimbabwe. The fury with which her mother disregarded them while ensuring that her children were equipped to navigate them. The other part is books. Ellah moved from Nancy Drew and The Hardy Boys to Hermann Hesse and Taban Lo Liyong, working through her father’s library. She wrote Liyong a fan letter; to her delight, he responded. She and her best friend forged their mothers’ signatures so that they could borrow Georgette Heyer paperbacks from the adult library. Then, in 1980 – the year of the first free elections, of Zimbabwe’s independence, of the start of high school – she was assigned to read Doris Lessing in class.

Lessing’s The Grass Is Singing (1950) – the story of the relationship between Mary, a poor white farmer’s wife, and Moses, a Black servant on the homestead – was the first book Wakatama read that was set in Zimbabwe. She found it shocking – and confusing. ‘As a girl, I wanted to become a woman who stood at the vanguard of the battlelines that Lessing had set out, the questions she asked about selfhood and a woman’s place in the world,’ she would later say. ‘But Moses was the one who was my relative.’ It was a challenge in newly independent Zimbabwe to hold both those stories: ‘Lessing, on the one hand, speaking for my gender, and her boldly imagined Moses, on the other hand, bearing witness to my people’s dispossession.’

Enflamed by Lessing, she started writing fiction. A magazine called Moto had a monthly short-story competition, top prize $100, which she entered and won. Her story was about a prison inmate suffering an existential crisis – full of ‘deep emotion, injustice and pretty sentences’. With her prize money, she bought a pair of shoes, grey snakeskin. ‘My brother was at school with a Kenyan boy I really liked,’ she added. ‘So I took him and his friends out to lunch.’ When her father read the story, he said: ‘Yes, Miss Ellah, it’s very good.’ But he was a traditional writer; he believed stories should have a beginning, middle and end, and a moral lesson. Hers didn’t have any of that. ‘The next month, he sent in a story and he won,’ Wakatama told me. ‘It’s something a therapist would have a field day with but, in our house, it was a massive joke.’

Pius Wakatama was a man of strong opinions and believed all his children should have opinions, too. He would argue with them and expect them to argue back. ‘Are you a man or a mouse?’ he once asked Nhamu, Ellah’s younger brother, when he refused to engage. ‘Dad, I’m a mouse,’ Nhamu responded. (Ellah laughed at the memory.) Pius was also extraordinarily large-hearted, often bringing home people who were in a tight spot: struggling relatives, street families, hitchhikers. ‘I grew up with that kind of thing,’ Wakatama said. ‘I think it had a profound effect on me … this idea that your life has to have meaning, that you can’t just exist, that you have to be impacting the world.’ Once, at the school where he taught, he heard a student crying in the girls’ bathroom because her parents wanted to marry her off. ‘Don’t worry,’ Pius told the young woman. ‘Bring your suitcase with you tomorrow.’ He went home and told Winnie he was bringing her a new daughter. The next day, he knocked on Ellah’s bedroom door and said: ‘This is Florence, she’s your sister.’

Wakatama went to the same college as her mother, a small Mennonite school in rural Indiana. There, in her final year, she declared that she would not read. Specifically – and ‘with all the irritating self-riotousness of youth,’ as she once put it – she announced that she would not be reading any dead white males. Craft your own reading list, her professor told her. This was a turning point. ‘Even though it would be years later that I started working as a publisher, it defined how I approached publishing,’ she told me. ‘The bookshelf was wrong; I knew there was more to it. My professor challenged me to find that “more” – and I did.’
She put James Baldwin on her list, and Alice Walker. Then she discovered Tsitsi Dangarembga.

Dangarembga’s Nervous Conditions (1988) was the first book published in English by a Black Zimbabwean woman. It follows 13-year-old Tambu at a mission school and confronts the ‘nervous conditions’ – a phrase taken from Jean-Paul Sartre – of being caught between traditional African culture and Western colonial influence. The novel’s opening sentence – ‘I was not sorry when my brother died’ – jolted Wakatama, not least because Tambu’s brother had almost the same name as Wakatama’s brother, Nhamu. It felt as if, in exploring the dissonance of social mobility in Zimbabwe, Dangarembga was writing about Wakatama and her peers: she ‘felt that the author had peeked inside our most secret diaries and written us into being.’

More than a decade would pass before Wakatama found her way back to books. After college, she married Richard Allfrey, a British boy she’d met in the US, and, while in grad school, decided to have a child because she was ‘curious about motherhood’. She wrote her dissertation with little Gabrielle on her lap. (‘I’d breastfeed and type, breastfeed and type.’) Afterwards, the family moved to England, where she worked a series of jobs in the education sector. ‘I hated every single one,’ she said. The racism in England rankled her but, more than that, she was bored. One day, on holiday in Zimbabwe, her parents sat her down. Pius asked what she was doing with her life. Her mother added: ‘You’ve been sitting on your brain so long you’re going to forget to use it.’
‘They didn’t recognise me as a member of the tribe. I would hang out with the guys in the post room because they were Black’

Ellah cried after that intervention. She felt she was letting down her family, letting down Zimbabwe – in those early postcolonial years, the feeling was that your education was meant to improve things. Then her daughter unwittingly spearheaded another intervention. ‘We can’t live with you because you’re so unhappy,’ Gabrielle, seven at the time, told her after she returned from work one day. ‘You spend all your time and money on books,’ Richard chimed in. ‘Why don’t you just work in books?’

Gabrielle, now 34 years old, doesn’t remember giving her mother this advice, though she told me it must have been very good advice for a seven-year-old. She and her sister Rujeko, born 10 years after Gabrielle, were also in Accra. She was enjoying seeing her mother work with writers. Wakatama knew how to talk with writers in a way she hadn’t instinctively known how to talk to babies. When Gabrielle was born, Wakatama – unsure of how to interact with an infant – would read her the paper. This was the 1990s and the Soviet Union had crumbled, so she read Gabrielle stories about Boris Yeltsin. What Gabrielle remembers is struggling with dyslexia
and her mother encouraging her to read, being patient, open and supportive.

After that second intervention, Wakatama worked for a year as a temp at Penguin’s offices in London, before being hired as an assistant to both the editor of the Ancient Classics series and the editor of the Modern Classics series. She was 30. There were books everywhere, piles on the floor, spilling out of cabinets, teetering stacks on desks. I’m home, she thought to herself. But the trouble with being home is that sometimes not everyone there accepts that it is your home. ‘I knew I was with my tribe of people,’ she told me. ‘But they didn’t recognise me as a member of the tribe. I would hang out quite a bit with the guys in the post room because they were Black. Nobody was cruel to me – it just never occurred to them at the time.’
She paused. ‘I didn’t look like an editor because none of the editors looked like me.’

She’d sit at the desk looking at the Modern Classics: there were Russian writers, and Japanese writers, and French writers. She began to wonder where the African writers were. ‘How can you say you have a Modern Classics list, and you don’t have Achebe? You don’t have Ngũgĩ? It made absolutely no sense to me.’ Encouraged by her boss, she reached out to people who’d worked at the African Writers Series, and licensed some of those authors: Dambudzo Marechera from Zimbabwe, Bessie Head from Botswana, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o from Kenya. She became interested in Black writers from elsewhere, for instance championing the work of the Jamaican-born Linton Kwesi Johnson, who became the first Black poet, and the second living poet, to be included in the Penguin Modern Classics series.

‘I wasn’t at this point thinking I’m out to change literature,’ she told me. ‘I just thought this bookshelf is wrong. As a child of independence, you know you’re supposed to be changing the world, you don’t just submit and do your job. Plus, I was ambitious as fuck.’

It’s hard to write about editors. Who profiles editors? Writers are easier, at least published ones. Why did you say this 40 years ago, you might ask them; Why does the structure of your novel resemble Flaubert? While talking to Wakatama – we were discussing Wole Soyinka’s hair (‘like a cloud!’) and that time in 2010 she interviewed him – my own early obsessions returned to me: Peter Abrahams and the world of 1940s Johannesburg he created in Mine Boy (1946), Gustave Flaubert’s Parisian aristocrats in Sentimental Education (1869). I knew from an early age that I was going to be a writer; I’d been trapped by literature, deriving pleasure ever since from moments when I could do what those writers did: bring an idea in my head to life on the page, turn a half-formed thought or image into a sparkling sentence.

None of these moments would have been possible without an editor. Only a specific kind of obsessive understands Andy Elisburg’s role in the Miami Heat’s NBA championships, or Elvira Nabiullina’s in Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine, and it’s the same with editors. Writers know. Without an editor who ‘gets it’, we have little chance of succeeding – a sentence my editor most certainly did not force me to write. Or, think of musicians and their producers: there was no Michael Jackson without Berry Gordy, or Kendrick Lamar without Dr Dre. I mentioned Dre to Wakatama, specifically the way she stopped trying to be a poet and began publishing other writers, just as he killed his own rap career, and she cackled.
‘No one’s ever compared me to Dr Dre before!’

The books she is drawn to are ones ‘that feel like they had to be written’, she tells me later, when I ask about the bookshelf she is building, the one her grandchildren will refer to. ‘There has to be a message, a question, an exploration. This works best when filtered through character and place – so the story is equally important.’ In this, she has come to agree with Pius: a story needs a message and a plot. But she remains drawn to beauty. ‘It’s the layers underneath that will keep me reading and re-reading,’ she added. ‘I remain obsessed with beautiful sentences, that delicate crafting of the thought until it becomes poetry.’
Western readers should have to do the work that the African reader has always done

After Penguin, Wakatama moved to Jonathan Cape, an imprint of Random House. Among the first big writers whose books she worked on were Julian Barnes and Ian McEwan. She said: ‘I copyedited On Chesil Beach, which has one mistake in it.’
I said I would read the book to try to find it.
She laughed and said: ‘You won’t know the mistake. If you find it, tell me. Ian said it was his fault, not mine, but I still blame myself.’

Although she now had more room to commission books, her acquisitions budget was still tiny. She scoured the list of writers awarded grants by the Arts Council of England, reaching out to them to see if they had anything to publish. That’s how she published Biyi Bandele’s Burma Boy (2007), about African soldiers in the Second World War, and Nii Ayikwei Parkes’s debut novel Tail of the Blue Bird (2009), a thriller that blends forensic science and Ghanaian folklore. Both challenged the way she thought about editing. In a multi-lingual book, for instance, the non-English parts are usually italicised. But Ayikwei Parkes refused to submit to this; in Blue Bird, this convention is flipped. Typically, ‘English is the standard and the rest of us are deviations,’ she told me. But in Blue Bird, a lot of the narration is by a man who doesn’t speak English: only when he uses a non-Akan word (particular to English) do italics appear. Ayikwei Parkes’s insistence on italicising these individual words of English, rather than those of Twi or Ga, was an assertion that the centre of the world was where the writer said it was, that Western readers should have to do the work that the African reader has always done.
‘That was really, for me, political,’ she said.

Ayikwei Parkes told me how unexpected it had been to find an editor willing to change her mind about editorial style. ‘For most conventional editors, it might be baffling to accommodate such a conceit,’ he said. ‘But she fully grasped the political thrust of my stylistic choice and supported its use, protecting me from the clutches of standard copyeditors.’ When I mentioned the Achebe-Wakatama comparison to him, he disagreed. ‘I sort of resist the idea of godparents for African writing, a notion that doesn’t exist for Western writing. What I will say is that Ellah is, like Achebe, certainly interested in the dignity and autonomy of the African personality and perspective. She believes and understands that Africa is a continent from which the world can be observed, made sense of, influenced and remade.’

Growing up in Zimbabwe, Wakatama says, made her a better editor. ‘Because as an African, for my generation at least, you grow up in an education system that doesn’t include you in the literature; therefore, you have to fill in the gaps yourself. So almost any African, if they were a reader anyway, is going to be a better reader than an English person – because we’re always reading outside ourselves, as well as within ourselves.’ She paused. ‘Which I don’t think we acknowledge enough. I think, now that I’m older, especially post-menopause, and also senior enough not to care what anyone thinks, I can just say it out loud.’

It has taken decades of being dismissed for her to speak so freely: of working under bosses who paid lip-service to diversity, of going to award ceremonies and realising the only other Black people in the room were waiters, of having smaller purchasing and marketing budgets than her colleagues. She recalls trying to acquire a book once, championing it fiercely, but being turned down – mere months later, it was bought by another editor in a different division for five times the price. ‘I told them: This is nonsense – you could have had this book for five grand six months ago when I found it, but because someone else says that it’s good, you’re now going to take it. What the fuck?’

Above her desk at Random House, she’d put up a picture of Toni Morrison, previously an editor at the company. ‘I used to look at that picture and think: She survived and I can too.’ But it was after the death of Nhamu, her younger brother, that she decided things could not go on as they had. Nhamu had suffered a series of strokes, and his death a decade later catapulted Wakatama into a deep depression, a depression that would be matched in depth only by the one triggered by her later divorce from her husband. ‘[Nhamu] was one of the true loves of my life,’ she told me, dabbing her eyes. ‘I was a completely different person after he died … his dying made me think: If he’s gone and I’m left behind – if his life has ended, what am I gonna do with mine?’
‘My feeling is that, if I am sitting at that table, to not sit at that table for too long’

Shortly after, she joined Granta as deputy editor of the literary magazine. She loved its international scope and finally had what she’d always wanted: a proper budget for commissioning writers. She also began to commission authors for Granta Books. She said: ‘I am driven by a mission, I really am. I’m not a religious person, but I grew up in a religious family. Part of that is about what are you here on earth for? The most important thing to me is books. My daughters will absolutely tell you that they had to fight for my attention. And I want others to have the chance to experience what I’ve experienced. Granta finally gave me that opportunity to do that level of commissioning.’

She started doing workshops – in Nigeria, China, Sri Lanka – to train other editors, as well as more public talks and radio. Her first big interview was with Wole Soyinka. She read him a poem on stage; it was a poem he had written when younger about what he’d be like when his hair was silver. Ellah told him: ‘Look at you now, you’re pretty much all silver. You know, what do you think about the poem?’ The great man laughed.

In 2011, she was awarded an Order of the British Empire for her services to the publishing industry. Somebody noticed, she thought to herself, somebody noticed the work I’m doing. Meanwhile, some colleagues asked: Well, what are you getting that for? ‘We now call these microaggressions, which are never microaggressions,’ she said. ‘My answer was always, for surviving this.’

What does it mean to be the only person of your kind in a room, constantly having to prove you belong? For Wakatama, the cost was psychological. ‘I wish someone had said to me: This life that you’re living is really fulfilling your soul but beware of the damage it will do to you,’ she said. It is tempting to buy into the hoopla of being the first this-or-that, of having a seat at the table, ‘to get sucked into that sense of, Oh, I’m special,’ she warns. ‘My feeling is that, if I am sitting at that table, to not sit at that table for too long.’

Part of her mission, therefore, is to continue to facilitate the entry of gifted writers into the global publishing infrastructure. In this regard, the English writer Max Porter, who worked alongside Wakatama at Granta, describes her as ‘a proper writer’s editor, deeply committed to and connected to her writers, not necessarily just the one book she is working on.’ As someone new at the time to the publishing world and ‘a little suspicious of it already’, Porter was inspired by how Wakatama nurtured and protected the writers she worked with ‘in the line and on the page and in the world.’

In 2020, after the murder of George Floyd forced a new racial reckoning in the United States and beyond, Wakatama watched white agents rush to sign Black writers. ‘I was like, you’ve got to be kidding me,’ she recalled. ‘After 20 years of saying: Publish Black writers now, you have this.’ Young writers were suddenly being offered massive advances. ‘On one level, that’s great – I’m thinking: Baby, take the money and run! But when you pay half a million for a book and the book sells 10,000 copies, it’s a failure. Remember, it’s an advance against your royalties. So, the next time, you’re starting off in debt.’ The result is that the publisher thinks these books don’t sell and ‘you’ve made it impossible for those authors to be successful.’

In Accra, I sat in on some of the Pfumo sessions. One reason Wakatama co-founded the collective was her concern about how few African nonfiction writers were published internationally. As the participants discussed writing craft, she listened closely, her head tilted towards the speaker, her legs crossed. When she talked, she leaned back, her hands a vital part of her speech. Books surrounded us. (‘It’s overwhelming to realise how many of these I edited,’ she told me.)
When a participant read out her work softly, Wakatama told her to read it again because she wanted ‘a big voice’. Here are other things she said to the writers presenting their work:
‘How do you feel about that?’
‘You’re not being brave enough. I need you to be brave.’
‘Greener pastures, no. That’s a cliché. We don’t use them.’
‘I don’t want you to run away. I want you to try. I think you’ll get it.’
‘I know I said lean into the poetry, but maybe you leaned too much.’

One evening in 2017, Wakatama saw a post on Facebook by Dangarembga, the author of Nervous Conditions. That book’s opening sentence – ‘I was not sorry when my brother died’ – had shocked Ellah, but when her own Nhamu died, she returned to the novel in her sorrow. How astutely Dangarembga had written of what Ellah herself had to grapple with: ‘the psychic trauma of fitting into a world that seems to demand an erasure, a forgetting of the self before.’ Dangarembga’s second novel, The Book of Not, had come out in 2006. She was now seeking an editor for her third, which she would self-publish.

That Dangarembga would struggle to find a publisher despite her success was an indictment of an industry that still struggled to recognise African writers. Wakatama didn’t know Dangarembga personally but she reached out anyway. ‘Your writing is so important to so many of us, why are you self-publishing?’ she asked. ‘If you do self-publish, please can I offer my services for free as your editor?’

The new book – This Mournable Body (2018) – was remarkable, Wakatama thought, and she offered to introduce Dangarembga to a friend who ran Graywolf Press, an American indie publisher. Wakatama flew to Harare; Dangarembga came to the family house for lunch. Some years before, Dangarembga recalled, she had corresponded with a Zimbabwean writer called Pius Wakatama. Was he a relative, Dangarembga wondered. Pius laughed. It was him.

Graywolf bought the book. Wakatama, who had, till then, been editing it for free, added a clause in the contract stipulating that the publisher would pay her an extra fee if the book made it to the Booker shortlist. ‘Everyone was fine with it because it was never going to happen,’ she recalled, smiling. But by now Wakatama knew to bet on herself. ‘When she got shortlisted and the money hit my account, I was, like, Yeah. I told you all.’

items.title: Why the dilettante is the anti-hero of our over-optimised age | Aeon Essays
items.description: Why, of all people, defend the dilettante? An amateur at best, a flighty rascal at worst: why take an interest in someone whose own interests are never more than a passing hobby? These are serious times – why take seriously someone for whom nothing is serious?
items.author: Jay Miller
paragraphs: Why, of all people, defend the dilettante? An amateur at best, a flighty rascal at worst: why take an interest in someone whose own interests are never more than a passing hobby? These are serious times – why take seriously someone for whom nothing is serious?

Merriam-Webster defines the dilettante as ‘a person having a superficial interest in an art or a branch of knowledge’. Encyclopedia.com calls the dilettante someone who cultivates an interest ‘without real commitment or knowledge’. Cambridge settles for someone whose understanding ‘is not very deep or serious’. Collins gives us someone who ‘seems interested in a subject … but does not really know very much about it’. None of it is flattering.

Clearly, the dilettante is no aspirational character. No university markets itself as training the next generation of dilettantes; no magazine runs a ‘dilettante of the year’ issue (except, perhaps, for the excellent Idler publication). He – for the dilettante is, historically and in popular imagination, so often a ‘he’ – is in essence an amateur, a role defined by wide interests and narrow expertise.

Such is the reputation of the dilettante, assigned and maintained by a culture that treats a single-minded devotion to one pursuit as the only route to a meaningful life. Pick something and stick with it, we are told. It’s not so much an explicit campaign against dilettantism I’m challenging, but rather the diffuse yet relentless pressure to narrow one’s interests, to specialise, to gain expertise, to forgo breadth for the sake of depth. We hear it in the barrage of imperatives to follow your dreams or find your passion uttered at graduation speeches, in self-help guides, and similarly corporate-sounding pep talks. Under this scheme, the specialist is the hero and the dilettante is but a cautionary tale: the person who never committed, never finished, never got good enough at any one thing.

But what if the scheme has it backwards? What if the dilettante’s perpetual movement from one thing to another is not a failure of nerve but a different and defensible way of being, one whose exploratory zeal turns out to be just what a hyper-specialised, over-optimised and all-too-serious world needs most? Then the dilettante would turn out to be not a capricious buffoon but a kind of modern anti-hero. That, I argue, is a dilettantism worth defending.

First, let’s consider how ‘dilettante’ relates to some of its conceptual cousins: the amateur, the dabbler, the jack-of-all-trades, etc. First, the dilettante is by nature an amateur, ie, a non-expert, a non-professional. But amateurism is a necessary though not sufficient condition of dilettantism. Anyone can be an amateur at any particular thing: woodworking, birdwatching, astronomy, etc. The dilettante’s amateurism is wide-ranging over several interests, and tends to orient around the production and/or appreciation of art and beauty. Like the jack-of-all-trades, the dilettante is a multi-dimensional amateur. But the dilettante’s amateurism is typically of the aesthetic variety.

Further, the dilettante is no dabbler. The dabbler scratches the surface of interests, whereas the dilettante, I argue, can and does go deep – without, however, anchoring a sense of self in any one interest. This also sets the dilettante apart from the flâneur, Charles Baudelaire’s urban wanderer strolling through the city’s offerings, sampling everything, invested in none of it. The dilettante is deeply engaged in interests, and more an active participant than a passive spectator.
The term originally referred to someone who pursues an interest, particularly an artistic one, for the sake of ‘delight’

In this respect, the concept is closest in spirit to the ‘Renaissance man’, minus the gender specification and historical context. The dilettante is one who is moved by enjoyment rather than necessity, professional obligation or the pursuit of credentials, and who purposefully cultivates a plurality of distinct, often aesthetic interests beyond mere surface familiarity.

One reason to defend the dilettante, then, is for lexicological justice. The term has been unfairly burdened with an overly negative connotation. It wasn’t always this way. From the Baroque-era Italian dilettante, the term originally referred to someone who pursues an interest, particularly an artistic one, for the sake of pleasure, or ‘delight’. Even as the term evolved, it stayed largely neutral, distinguishing enthusiasts from professionals in a given practice. The pejorative connotation familiar to us today is more recent, shaped by what I’ll call a ‘deficiency’ model, in which amateurism is viewed negatively as a lack of something: skill, seriousness, focus, expertise. This is the meaning ascribed by cultural gatekeepers like Theodor Adorno, who in 1929 dismissed the dilettante as one ‘unable to establish any standards’.

The more important aim, however, is to show dilettantism as a way of living that offers more than we might think. It is a life liberated from specialisation, instrumentalisation and meritocratic bean-counting, as well as from a Protestant work ethic that is suspicious of pleasure for pleasure’s sake. Arguments denigrating specialisation in education and vocation are well known, as are those championing well-roundedness and the virtues of the liberal arts. Though similar in spirit, this defence of dilettantism is less about the purpose or outcomes of academic or professional life and more about making the mental switch away from the socially conditioned pressure to find your thing and stick with it to an open and exploratory pursuit of pluralistic interests. Reclaiming this sense of joyful experimentalism is intended to show dilettantism as a mode of abundance rather than deficiency.

A good place to start is the essay ‘On Dilettantism’ (1799) by J W von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller. This fragmentary, never-completed project by the literary dream-team of Weimar-era Germany paints a deeply ambivalent portrait of dilettantism, praising the dilettante over here for ‘cultivat[ing] something serious in man’ and condemning him over there as a ‘plagiarist’ and a ‘bungler’. Viewed retrospectively, however, its almost scientific treatment of the ‘advantages’ (Nutzen) and ‘disadvantages’ or ‘harms’ (Schaden) of dilettantism helps give a clear-eyed view of the potential virtues and vices of dilettantism today.

Crucially, Goethe and Schiller’s analysis is squarely situated in the cultural context of Weimar classicism. This means that, first, the question of the dilettante arises (as it does in its original Italian usage) exclusively in relation to the arts. They treat the dilettante as a distinctly aesthetic figure, ‘a lover of the arts who wishes not only to contemplate and enjoy them, but also to participate in their production.’ This aesthetic dimension has (regrettably, I think) faded from the meaning of ‘dilettante’ over time. But nor does it need to be narrowly inscribed in 18th-century anxieties about who can and cannot properly be called an artist. Artistic engagement isn’t essential to dilettantism. But it is worth reasserting, maybe even foregrounding, the sense in which the ‘delight’ of dilettantism involves, to some extent, the experience of aesthetic pleasure, broadly understood. The dilettante, that is, pursues what Søren Kierkegaard calls an ‘aesthetic life’: the ongoing, everyday activity of observing, valuing, and participating in art and beauty.
The dilettante is comfortable in the garb of an amateur. For the dilettante, every night is karaoke night

Though rooted in classicist aestheticism, some of Goethe and Schiller’s criticism of the dilettante still resonates today. They worry, for example, that the dilettante ‘jumps over the steps’, gliding too glibly through the creative process and claiming victory too early. There’s something to this. Similar to Oscar Wilde’s concern about the ‘sentimentalist’ in his 1897 epistolary essay, De Profundis, who ‘desires to have the luxury of an emotion without paying for it’, the authors voice a reasonable objection to those willing to cut the line in chasing laurels. Progress is earned through practice, and those of us who have put in the work are right to protect it, as any trained therapist, frustrated with the quackery that passes for therapy on YouTube and TikTok, will gladly testify.

But due to their idealisation of the ‘true artist’ as a manifester of Truth and Beauty, Goethe and Schiller cannot help but view the dilettante as lacking in both aim and ability. To be fair, no practice is a total free-for-all, and some practices are less permissive of dilettantism than others (who wants to live in a house built by a dilettante architect?). But the notion that the dilettante tries and fails to follow the ‘true objective rules’ of art and beauty the way legit artists do rests on outdated and Eurocentric assumptions about what both artists and dilettantes are actually up to. In other words, take away the neo-classicist presumption, and suddenly the dilettante appears less like an imitator and more like a liberated creator. It’s not that the dilettante falls short in any given practice but, rather, has a different orientation toward it. Indeed, an overly goal-oriented attitude, especially in the realm of pastimes and pleasures, cuts against the very spirit of dilettantism. Part of its appeal is its ethos of open-endedness, its willingness to do something for the sake of delight rather than achievement. The dilettante is comfortable in the garb of an amateur. For the dilettante, every night is karaoke night.

From our Germans, we glean a sense of where the dilettante goes wrong. But they can also help us make the corrective mental switch from seeing the dilettante as a wannabe practitioner to someone who chooses a more experimental, exploratory orientation toward a given practice.

The key to perceiving dilettantism as abundance instead of deficiency is to appreciate the sense of freedom it affords. It is, in the first place, a negative freedom, a freedom from the constraints that otherwise bind professional practitioners. More precisely, it is a freedom of mobility within a practice.

First, the dilettante has greater freedom to engage in a given practice. For Goethe and Schiller, one of the most important ‘advantages’ of dilettantism is that it ‘stimulates a certain taste for art, and extends it to where the artist would not be able to reach’. Generalising a bit, the point holds well beyond art: the dilettante can act as a liaison between expert and layperson, closing the gap between high practice and everyday curiosity, introducing otherwise cloistered practitioners to wider audiences and extending an invitation to anyone who might otherwise feel shut out.

A personal example. A few years ago, I joined Mountain Haulers, a cycling group that meets on Tuesday evenings for a ride through Asheville, North Carolina. It is a ‘no drop’ ride: cyclists wait at points along the way for everyone to catch up, however slow or struggling, and the first ride of the month is always a chill ride along the river. This openness sets the group apart from a cycling culture of notorious cliques of devotees clamouring to outdo each other’s worship of the sport. Welcoming the less-experienced and the less-committed seems a more genuine way of loving the thing you claim to love. If biking is your thing, surely you want more butts on bike seats. The dilettante cyclists who show up for Tuesday-night rides make cycling better.
The modern admonition to ‘stay in your lane’ stems from assumptions about the commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own

The further sense of the dilettante’s freedom involves mobility between different practices – a freedom from the barriers dividing them. The dilettante maintains a certain detachment, or intentional separation, between who one is and what one does, to live the life of a cultural itinerant. Painting, gardening, MIG welding, beekeeping, language learning, comic-book collecting, dancing, swimming, printmaking, powerlifting, pickleballing, sourdough baking, accordion playing, brisket barbecuing – all exciting destinations to travel and explore without seeking citizenship or even permanent residence in any one. The dilettante is a wayfaring cosmopolitan whose sense of freedom is found in never being stuck in one place.

And yet, this mobility is also part of a positive freedom to satisfy the basic human need to explore and make one’s mark on the world. Goethe and Schiller credit the dilettante for activating this natural impulse toward curiosity and creativity, a drive they compare with children’s innate desire to playfully imitate their surroundings. Going further, I would say that dilettantism offers not only the satisfaction of scratching the Homo faber itch; making and exploring for the simple sake of joy and curiosity is a freedom that is every bit as valuable to self-discovery as any commitment or singular pursuit.

However, from the outside, mobility may look like mere lack of commitment. No doubt this drives some of the allegations of superficiality commonly lodged against the dilettante. Pulling up anchors and moving on from an interest gets flagged as surface-skimming. I’m speculating here, but such criticism seems rooted in a work ethic that tells us that investment in certain interests ought to yield dividends: authority, credibility, permission to enter culturally guarded spaces, etc. Just as the neo-classicist wants to set the ‘true artist’ apart from the poseurs, the modern admonition to ‘pick a lane’, or (more aggressive) ‘stay in your lane’, stems from assumptions about the level and length of commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own.

Dilettantism rejects this quasi-capitalist mindset. The petty territorialism common to social, academic and cultural spaces (think record stores, cocktail bars, art galleries, philosophy classes, etc) is unnecessary but, more importantly, at odds with a genuine interest in the thing itself. A crucial part of the switch from deficiency to abundance is learning to see the dilettante as an asset to a given practice rather than a threat to it. Even Adorno, snob par excellence, allows a version of this, arguing that the expert critic needs the dilettante around ‘in order to prove to himself that he isn’t one’.
More than simply escaping sickness, the dilettante’s movement is a headlong rush at vitality and vigour

Also crucial to making this mental switch is seeing the dilettante’s curiosity as equal in intensity to the expert’s, but different. Picture the dilettante as the love-child of two very different philosophical figures: Kierkegaard’s aesthete in Either/Or (1843) who finds and cultivates interests with an intensity that is abandoned before it hardens into obligation, and Friedrich Nietzsche’s ‘free spirit’, the fiercely curious, light-footed nomad whose restless pursuit of intellectual and artistic treasures provides a profound, if rootless, freedom. From Kierkegaard, the dilettante acquires an innate aversion to boredom (‘the root of all evil’) which is achieved by what he calls ‘rotation of crops’: perpetually changing ‘the method of cultivation and the kinds of crops’. From Nietzsche, the dilettante inherits a rejection of convention coupled with perpetual motion, a sense of permanent ‘homelessness’ that propels an unfettered perusal of interests. Passionate enough to go deep, detached enough to eventually leave, such a figure shows the possibility of being intensely invested in various ways of knowing, doing and making, but never content to let a sense of self form too firmly around them.

In a memorable scene from the Spike Jonze film Adaptation (2002), the journalist Susan Orlean (Meryl Streep), who is writing a book about the orchid thief John Laroche (Chris Cooper), is at once intrigued by his hunt for a rare hallucinogenic ‘ghost orchid’ and baffled to learn that it is only the latest in a lifetime of obsessions: turtles, prehistoric fossils, 19th-century Dutch mirrors, etc. How can he detach so abruptly from something in which he’s invested so much? He can only offer an anecdote. A profound and consuming love for tropical fish ended suddenly with the realisation that the passion had simply run its course. ‘Fuck fish,’ he tells her, disrupting her assumption that loving something means sticking with it forever.

The difference is that, unlike Kierkegaard’s aesthete, the dilettante doesn’t rotate crops out of despair. Dynamism, detachment and insatiable curiosity are constitutive of the dilettante’s free and full subjectivity, rather than a stage on the way to achieving selfhood. The dilettante chooses aesthetic life over the life of commitment that Kierkegaard’s ‘either/or’ dichotomy presents, and fully owns that choice. Nor is the dilettante simply recovering from existential illness, as Nietzsche’s free spirit seems to be. Rather than running the risk of relapse – or worse, the ‘cankerous vice’ of pessimism – dilettantism is a healthy embrace of this freedom; more than simply escaping sickness, the dilettante’s movement is a headlong rush at vitality and vigour.

In the dilettante’s genes is a compulsion to pursue passions, deeply coupled with a refusal to shape a life or identity permanently around any one of them. The dilettante possesses a unique capacity to dive deep into an interest, then surface and plunge into the depths of the next, each one an exploration, an adventure, but not a lifelong, life-defining project. It is precisely to hold open the possibility of the next reconnaissance mission that the dilettante rejects any dogmatic principle of stick-to-itiveness. Sometimes, the dilettante is a devout hobbyist parked on one interest for years at a stretch; sometimes, a juggler of several overlapping projects at once; and sometimes, a serial enthusiast on the hunt for the next novelty – what holds these modes together isn’t any fixed duration or rhythm of arrival and departure, but a disposition toward perpetual motion. The dilettante’s talent, energy and passion are constantly rechannelled through new outlets. Far from deficiency, dilettantism is a constant quest for abundance.

The life of the dilettante, so described, is not an especially easy one. It is a life of perpetual searching and fleeting satisfaction, in which accomplishment often arrives without accolades. Until breadth of interest is held in higher esteem, today’s dilettante will largely have to forgo public recognition and settle for a private life of pursuits and pleasures. Rarely is the dilettante widely celebrated as such. Consider someone like Susan Sontag, a novelist, critic and political activist whose wide-ranging work has earned both praise for its unconventional contributions to the intellectual life of 1960s New York and criticism for lacking rigour, for lacking substance. A ‘Win’ in the dilettante’s column, in other words, often comes with an asterisk – a conditional victory at best.

Further, the dilettante is also no pack animal; however much a part of a group one may feel, the dilettante will likely always be something of a tourist within it. The dilettante has to be comfortable travelling as a lone wolf at the margins of any community organised around a shared interest.

No, dilettantism is not for everyone. For anyone whom the universe has called to pursue a single passion – congratulations! Stay the course! But for those of us compelled by something closer to FOMO for the sheer variety and abundance the world has to offer, the dilettante’s path can lead to a genuine quality-of-life upgrade. If courage means overcoming the fear of new beginnings, without the reassurance of a title or a track record to show for it, then dilettantism may have much to offer. After all, not every crop is a monoculture, sowed and tilled to maximise output. Some of us need to cultivate our gardens through crop rotation. A defence of the dilettante is thus a call to follow the forked path of varying interests to a life made meaningful through abundance rather than acclaim.

items.title: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies | Aeon Essays
items.description: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in a
items.author: Melanie Challenger
paragraphs: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in and out of wakefulness myself, I take hold of my phone. With scarcely a thought, I switch from one app to another, scrolling through images and opinions and adverts for no discernible reason beyond habit.

Later, I head for my office and open my laptop to a slew of half-completed documents and an inbox brimming with emails. My stress levels begin to nudge upwards. I have vague memories of what my professional life felt like before smartphones and video calls. I used to do my writing by hand. And I could concentrate for hours at a time, getting little upticks of arousal from lifting my head from the page, letting the hold on my pen loosen, and gazing at the life beyond my window, the light softening on my skin and eyes like snowfall on warm tarmac.

Nowadays, my productive bursts come from caffeine and sugary or salty snacks, even if I try to pick the healthier ones, and from checking my emails or picking up my phone to update my inbox. By the end of the day, the sheer volume of work I expect myself to do, now that digital tools make so much possible, has kept me nailed to my seat. Another day has passed and the hope I’d had that I might have time for a run or a hike outside has been dashed again. I wish I could say that this is atypical. Yet, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I went from hours spent in nature and on physical activities to a passive, phone-addicted individual, meeting people first and sometimes only online. I am not alone.

We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.
Algorithms that regurgitate patterns and recommendations can release us from the effort of exploration and disrupt the play and curiosity from which preferences are formed and understood.

This is a strange turn of events for an animal whose success comes mostly from the extraordinary ability to learn through experience. It would be easy to blame our deskilled bodies on the machines themselves. But, for centuries, modern human societies have been sold the lie that we are machines.

Long before the digital revolution, René Descartes described the body as a machine governed by physical laws, declaring that animals such as ‘worms and flies and caterpillars move mechanically’. But he treated rational thought as a separate and uniquely human power. The body might behave like a machine, but the thinking mind stood apart from it. Build something correctly, and its function follows.

By the middle of the 20th century, the comparison between organisms and machines had been recast in the language of information. During the cybernetics revolution of the 1950s, the US computer scientist Norbert Wiener envisaged a future in which ‘messages between man and machines, between machines and man, and between machine and machine, are destined to play an ever-increasing part’. Writing in The Human Use of Human Beings (1950), he warned against wholesale automation, while also noting that ‘we are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves’. A person could be imagined as a pattern of information surviving in another form.
If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Mechanical language also persisted in the study of living behaviour. In The Foundations of Ethology (1981), the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz wrote that animal behaviour was as rigidly programmed as a sequence of movements in a clock.
