items.author: Zahaan Bharmal
paragraphs: The senior partner didn’t waste any time. ‘I’m sorry, Zahaan,’ he said, ‘your services are no longer required at the firm.’ We sometimes called him the Burger King behind his back, because he ate a Whopper Meal at his desk every day. I’d never spoken to him before, and now I never would again.

It was the summer of 2001. I was fresh out of university and nine months into my first job as a management consultant in London. My parents had allowed me to move back into my old room, where I routinely collapsed after getting home from the office well after midnight. Professional life was punishing, but I gave it my all. For a brief time, I felt like I was flying: at my first performance review, I was told I had ‘partner potential’.

But then I got a phone call, telling me that one of the senior American partners wanted to meet me. That was unusual; but then again, I’d been working so hard and getting such good feedback, I figured it couldn’t be anything too bad. I was directed to an office on the first floor, several levels below where I usually sat.

After he fired me, my ears buzzed and my chest tightened; I don’t remember much else, except being told that I shouldn’t even return to my desk. It became apparent that the location of the meeting had been chosen because it would allow me to take a single flight of stairs down to the ground floor. No one would need to see me, and I wouldn’t need to speak to anyone.

The decision felt cruel and unfair. But more than anything, it seemed to violate the laws that for many years had been my way of making sense of the world: the laws of physics. Cause and effect, action and reaction. What followed was an unlikely journey – one in which the equations I thought I’d left behind at university became, unexpectedly, a companion through the messiest parts of life.

Before work, before university, I attended a competitive and prestigious all-boys school in London. While I’ll be forever grateful for the opportunities my education afforded me, life still felt tough for me as a lonely and anxious teenager. The school’s social currency was confidence, quick comebacks, and an effortless cool I never quite mastered. I often felt like I was watching from the edges, trying to decode the rules of a game that everyone else grasped intuitively.

The only thing that got me through was physics. The most fundamental of the sciences, physics represented a world that was perfectly ordered. It offered structure, rules and predictability. There was no social speculation; I could just work hard and try to figure things out. Problems and solutions, equations and outcomes. It didn’t matter how popular I was – what mattered was whether I understood the system. Slowly, the chaos of the world developed a sense of form and structure.

That clarity stayed with me, through school and into university. I read physics at Oxford, convinced for a long time that I wanted to become a scientist. It wasn’t always easy; there were late nights, bitter struggles with problem sets, moments I wondered if I’d ever get it. But when it clicked, it was wonderful: entropy, quantum mechanics, cosmology, all those deep, strange laws that govern the Universe. Physics seemed like it had a purpose, and I thought we’d go the distance.

But at some point in my final year at university, things started to change. Physics still fascinated me, but I found myself drawn to other subjects too – politics, economics, business. I wanted to understand not just how the Universe worked, but how people did. So after graduating, I decided to leave physics behind and see where those other interests would take me.
For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist

As it turns out, when I stepped away from physics, many others did too. In the years after I left university at the turn of the millennium, physics began to fade from view in the English classroom. In 2006, physics A-level entries (post-16 qualifications in the UK) were down 37 per cent from where they were in 1991. The absolute numbers have since rebounded – but not for everyone. Today, the gender gap remains stark: only 23 per cent of A-level physics entries in 2026 came from girls, a figure that hasn’t budged much in decades. And more than half of GCSE physics classes in England (taken by 14- to 16-year-olds) are taught by a non-specialist, with a shortage of some 3,500 physics teachers nationally.

Research looking at why students choose or reject physics has found that it’s seen as abstract, difficult, and disconnected from real life – a perception that’s remained steady, even as enrolment has recovered. Meanwhile, newer fields – computer science, behavioural economics, even data journalism – have felt more immediate, more applicable. They speak the language of now.
What’s strange is that this perception problem has happened at the same historical moment in which physics has begun popping up in other surprising places.

Dominic Cummings, the strategist behind Brexit and later Boris Johnson’s chief adviser, gave physics a fair share of the credit for the success of his campaigns. In one of his highly popular newsletters, he paraphrased the theoretical physicist Richard Feynman: ‘The most important thing is not to fool yourself and you are the easiest person to fool.’ Then there’s Elon Musk, who credits the success of his many business ventures to physics and ‘first-principles thinking’: discard convention, start from fundamental truths. And for decades, the legendary investor Charlie Munger made the same case in finance, saying that the ‘logic and power’ of physics had helped him enormously.

For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist, praised by public figures whose decisions affect millions of lives. But look closer, and the picture is more complicated.

In the first instance, billionaires and political operatives make for awkward ambassadors; Cummings, Musk and Munger might be brilliant, but they’re also extremely divisive. But more than who they are, what interests me is how they’re putting physics to work – whether they’re truly thinking with the discipline, or just brandishing it for rhetorical effect. Is ‘physics’ simply a shorthand for cutting through complexity, for stripping down problems to their most basic parts? Or does it genuinely offer something distinctive that other sciences and ways of thinking cannot?

Philosophers call the first approach ‘reductionism’: the idea that if you break any system into small enough components and trace them far enough, you eventually arrive at physics. That view can be powerful, and explains why so many people find it attractive.

It’s also been spectacularly successful. When 19th-century physicists showed that heat was simply the motion of atoms – that temperature, seemingly its own phenomenon, was actually just particles bouncing faster – an entire science collapsed into physics. Years later, that same approach helped particle physicists break matter into smaller and smaller pieces until arriving at something apparently irreducible. From the reductionist instinct came quarks, leptons and the Higgs boson. Their catalogue blueprint, the Standard Model, remains one of the greatest intellectual achievements in human history.

But reductionism has its limits. Take politics: a radical reductionist might say that this too comes down to physics, because politics is about the behaviour of groups of people; groups are made of individual people; people are made of atoms; atoms are governed by physics. But does this mean that we could predict the outcome of, say, a national election by studying the behaviour of individual atoms inside the brains of every registered voter? Unlikely. Putting aside issues of practicality, what would be the point? Economists already have economics. Psychologists already have psychology. Politicians have political theory. Physics has value only if it’s additive and illuminating.

For me, the real value of physics had never been as a cudgel for smashing things up into their smallest bits, but as a framework for navigating systems – for recognising patterns, probing assumptions, and testing whether the models we rely on actually work as they’re meant to. We see this way of thinking throughout the history of science. When cholera swept through Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow didn’t know its cause. But he mapped the cases, identified the pattern, and traced the outbreak to a single water pump on Broad Street. The founder of what we now know as epidemiology, Snow worked by constructing and interrogating mental models of the world, probing their assumptions, and following the data wherever they led.

The question, then, is not simply whether physics can be borrowed as rhetoric, but whether it really helps us to see the world more clearly, in ways that complement and benefit other disciplines. That, at least, was what stayed with me after I stopped studying it formally. Not equations or textbooks, but a way of thinking that I found myself reaching for when my world was falling apart.

Getting fired was one of those moments. I had worked so hard, yet somehow I’d still failed. Everything I understood about cause and effect told me this shouldn’t have happened. But here I was, after months of working flat out, with nothing to show for it.
An infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance

While some might have turned to therapy or career counselling, I turned back to physics to try to move on. The immediate cause was clear enough. The dot-com bubble had burst, sending ripples across the global economy that eventually reached my desk. Belts tightened, and the harsh rule in such circumstances tends to be last in, first out.

The dot-com bust was not the first nor last time something like this would happen. In 2008 came the subprime mortgage crisis; in 2011, the eurozone crashed; in 2013, the rupee tanked; in 2015, there was turbulence on the Chinese stock market; and in 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic. All these crises had two things in common. First, almost no one saw them coming – at least not precisely when or where or how. Second, they weren’t triggered by some enormous dramatic collapse, but by small, seemingly innocuous failures that cascaded into something far larger. For example, it just took a few small incidents that might otherwise have passed unnoticed – like the failure of a local mortgage lender in Southern California – to precipitate the subprime mortgage crisis.

All these events are examples of what physicists might call chaotic systems – deterministic in theory, but in practice so sensitive to initial conditions that tiny variations can spiral into radically different outcomes. A well-known example is the ‘three-body problem’, popularised by Liu Cixin’s 2008 novel of the same name and a 2024 Netflix adaptation. If you have two planets orbiting each other, you can write down neat equations to predict their paths forever. But add a third planet, and suddenly the maths explodes into unpredictability. The three bodies are still governed by clear laws, but an infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance.

The mathematician Edward Lorenz discovered something similar in 1961 when running weather simulations. His first attempt entered starting values rounded to six decimal places. His second try was rounded only to three. Yet the results diverged so dramatically that he initially suspected it was a computer fault. In fact, tiny differences in initial conditions had cascaded into entirely different weather systems. The atmosphere, like the economy, like a career, was deterministic in principle and unpredictable in practice.
As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do

Understanding the crash was one thing, but physics also helped me think about what came next. I had believed that inputs led to proportional outcomes; logically, in that world, the way to get ahead was to work as hard as possible. But physics teaches that chaotic systems play by different rules. They call instead for surge capacity, an extra buffer that allows them to absorb shocks. Without it, even small failures can lead to total collapse.

Think of a power grid. Most of the time it hums along without problem. But during an unexpected surge, such as a heatwave when millions of air conditioners are switched on at once, the system can overload and shut down. To prevent this, engineers design grids with slack in the system and extra capacity to handle unexpected spikes. Without it, a minor disruption can cascade into a blackout.

That was my mistake. As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do. We optimise everything from our schedules to our to-do lists – convinced that if we just push a bit harder, we’ll be fine. But the more we operate at our limits, the more fragile we become.

Physics provides a different lesson. Rather than relentlessly maximising, resilience is about building the capacity to withstand outlier events when they come. That might mean time slack, leaving space in our lives to recover rather than scheduling every minute. It might mean career slack, developing new skills, side projects and networks, rather than relying on a single path. Surge capacity might not prevent a crisis, but it sure helps survive one.

After my brief and bruising spell in consulting, I joined the civil service and spent most of the rest of my 20s working in government. I loved the sense of purpose, the colleagues and the privilege of shaping policy. Yet, if I’m honest, I still carried a small canker of resentment and jealousy towards my former consulting colleagues.

Compared with the UK national average, I know I was paid well as a civil servant. But with friends on six-figure salaries, it felt like I was failing at something. They could afford nicer clothes, cars and apartments. And then there was the magic trick of turning money into more money by buying assets, further widening the gap between their bank balances and mine. What stung wasn’t the inequality itself, but the perceived unfairness of the circumstances. I felt like I’d worked just as hard and still fallen behind. That distinction between inequality and unfairness became important to me.

Psychologists have shown that we’re wired to make this distinction from a very young age. In one Yale study, children were asked to split 10 coins between two people based on their performance on a task. When the two people performed equally, the children split the coins five-five – equal and fair. When one person did better, the children split the coins six-four – unequal but still fair. The interesting result happened when the children were told that both people had performed equally, but they now had to split 11 coins. With no way to maintain fairness, what could the children do? They decided to simply throw away one coin. Time and again, the children prioritised fairness.
People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged

This distinction is also evident in physics. Inequality, in the literal sense of unevenness, is built into the fabric of the Universe. In the very beginning, the cosmos was smooth and equal, a uniform fog. Only when tiny imperfections appeared – quantum fluctuations that allowed matter to clump in some places more than others – did galaxies, stars and planets emerge. Without that inequality, there would have been no structure, no possibility of life. In that sense, inequality is not always a flaw. Sometimes it is the condition for growth and diversity.

We see the same principle in natural systems. Rivers branch into unequal tributaries. Lungs and blood vessels evolve into networks with a few large arteries feeding many smaller ones. That inequality of size isn’t corruption or greed, but a kind of efficiency. It allows flow. Yet when the flow is blocked, like when a river silts up or a vessel clogs, the system fails. The problem, in other words, is not inequality itself, but unfairness: the obstruction of flow, the stacking of rules, the blocking of opportunity.

I think this is true in human systems, too. A society where some are richer than others may be tolerable, even healthy, so long as opportunities and resources can still move freely. But a society where opportunity is blocked, where the rules are stacked, where unfairness rules – people reject that instinctively. Just as I did when I looked at my friends’ consulting careers and wondered why I’d been cast out. Physics, then, suggests that a lack of justice is the real problem, rather than inequality per se. People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged.

Suddenly I saw this dynamic about fairness everywhere I looked. The financial crisis of 2007-08 wasn’t just about banks making risky bets, but about the perception that ordinary people paid the price while bankers walked away with bonuses intact. The eurozone crisis wasn’t just about debt, but about southern European countries being squeezed by rules they hadn’t set. The Occupy protests, the Arab Spring, Brexit, Donald Trump – all, in their different ways, were rebellions against unfairness.

Looking at the world through a physicist’s lens, these moments resemble phase transitions. You can heat water gradually and nothing seems to change – until you reach a critical threshold, a boiling point, and suddenly the whole system transforms from liquid to gas. Human societies, too, can bear strain for a while. But once unfairness feels systemic, the pressure builds until the system flips.

Small wonder, then, that in an age of tumult and transition, physics has found new admirers – especially among those who want to catalyse radical change, for better or worse. Musk speaks of first principles, Cummings of complexity. Their examples show how the tools of physics can shape thinking far beyond the laboratory. But in their hands, physics can feel more like a weapon than a framework, a way of bulldozing nuance in the name of clarity. For the rest of us, the challenge is not simply to borrow the garb and glamour of physics, but to carry forward its mindset – one that values humility as much as boldness, and curiosity as much as certainty.

That, I think, is where physics can still make its greatest contribution. Not by giving us ready-made answers or comforting illusions of inevitability, but by training us to question ourselves and live with the resulting uncertainty. Public discourse is saturated with physics, yet we need a deeper grounding in what it really teaches us about how to ask better questions, to test our own blind spots, and to admit what we don’t know. That need feels more urgent as new technologies only increase the temptation to reach for shortcuts.
We need artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both

So what would it take to embed this shift? My journey with physics began when I was a teenager, and that’s where I believe we need to start now. Too often, we present physics to young people as dry and technical. We teach them equations but not frameworks, facts without wonder. We rarely tell them that physics can help with the messiest parts of life, bound up as they are with uncertainty, resilience, decision-making.

In the UK, we make things worse by forcing students to choose just three or four subjects to study for the final two years of school. In practice, this often forces a split between being on the ‘science’ track or the ‘arts’ track. That false binary deprives us of exactly the kind of multidisciplinary thinkers we need: artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both.

When I visit schools now, I try to show physics as a kind of superpower. I want young people to feel that physics is something they can use, not something that excludes them. More than anything, I want them to feel it’s theirs.

I started this essay as a young man being shown the door by a superior. I ended it somewhere else entirely, with physics as a way of making sense of the messiest parts of life. But, really, what I’ve been edging up to is a story about how certain hardwon habits of mind can help us find meaning in the messiness and unpredictability of reality. For those of us who are not professional scientists, maybe the real task isn’t to love physics uncritically, or wield it carelessly, but to use it wisely. Physics shouldn’t be a shortcut to rock-solid certainty, so much as a way to live more humanely without it.

items.title: Drew Starkey’s Disappearing Tricks
items.description: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:
items.author: Emma Madden
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:

At 3am, the insomniac is most awake. His mind raves, his heart thumps against the pillow, and the rest of the world falls silent somewhere else. “In a real dark night of the soul, it is always three o’clock in the morning, day after day,” wrote F. Scott Fitzgerald in a 1936 essay. Drew Starkey posted that quote to his Facebook, among others about sleeplessness from Walt Whitman and Albert Einstein, when he was 17. In his own dark-souled hour, Starkey would smoke some weed, read Tolkien, and say to himself over and over: “I can’t sleep.”

Starkey was plagued by several ailments as a teenager. He’d lie awake at night, seething with extreme stomach pain from a hiatal hernia. His doctor advised him to stick to a paleo diet. Starkey has never publicly discussed either the stomach pain or the insomnia. “I don’t know how you found out about this. It’s so wild to me. I haven’t thought about it in ages, but I know exactly what you’re talking about,” he says. He is referring in particular to a piece he wrote for his university’s literary anthology about his sleeplessness. I read it and immediately felt I understood him better. “Years of difficulty sleeping sent me out in to (sic) a black sea without any direction. The distinction between me and the world outside of my thoughts became blurred during the night. In this process, I lost myself,” he wrote.
“I’ve been an insomniac since I was 13,” he tells me today. “I still have a lot of trouble sleeping. I become much more creative and alive at night, and maybe I do lose something of myself at night.”

There is something about this loss of self that resembles his understanding of acting. He views his work, ultimately, as an act of sublimation: “In every way, you have to submit yourself,” he says, paraphrasing a Kristen Stewart quote. In the long, wide night, he fantasised about putting himself somewhere else. He became obsessed with the slow drip of time.
“I still ruminate on it quite a bit. I have a weird skill of guessing what time it is.”
Without looking, I ask him to tell me the time.
“3:38pm,” he says, cold as a clock.

So: it is 3:38pm in New York City. Starkey has just wrapped a day of press for the final season of Outer Banks. For hours, he has been subject to the glamorous indignities of today’s press junket. “Yeah, it was a lot of playing games with my castmates,” he says. All day long, he has been playing the role of “Drew Starkey.” He goes to places he wouldn’t ordinarily go, wearing clothes that aren’t his. Usually, that means head-to-toe Dior; Médaillon loafers, which he tries to wear as often as he can get away with. (“I just love those buckles.”)

He has gone from the teenager who wore beige chinos to the best-looking version of himself: groomed and styled by professionals. His sandy-blond hair is spiked at the back of his head; he has a closely shaved beard. His lips are pinkish memory foam, his husky-dog eyes forever sparkling and limpid. Physically, he is absurdly suited to male superstardom. Temperamentally, he appears resistant to it.

As Starkey climbs higher up the Hollywood food chain, this might be the last time we speak before he reaches the loftiest echelons of fame. “The trick is to treat it all like you’re playing a character, because you are,” he says. And, to ensure he “stays sane,” he says, “there are things about myself that I want to keep for myself. So while I’m presenting myself, I’m also protecting a version of myself. It feels like an unnatural process to let millions of people know your actual nature.”

Starkey understands that all of us perform ourselves for one another; he’s just doing it on a much larger and more literal stage. The character “Drew Starkey” that exists onscreen transfers to parties, red carpets, fancy rooms where he might not otherwise go. “You have to lean into a specific version of yourself,” he says, “as opposed to, say, the person you are at home.” Today, back in his hotel room, he seems closer to that back-home self. His voice is low and largely unemotional, but warm. His energy has a low-key gravity to it, a kind of inwardness that seems remote without quite becoming aloof. If he took one of those aura photos, I’d imagine the colour around him would be a soft duck-egg blue.

After a long day as Drew Starkey, he has changed into a blue-striped shirt and dark-blue jeans. Nearby, his publicist wears a pair of sunglasses jewelled with Claire’s gems, the letters R A F E spelled out in friendship-bracelet beads. It was gifted to him by an Outer Banks fan. Hundreds have been following Starkey all day. They still wait outside his hotel room as we speak.

For seven years, Starkey played Rafe Cameron in Outer Banks, a character he says he knew “inside and out. I could defend him, make cases for him.” The last scene he ever filmed as Rafe was a pickup shot of him walking through the woods and breaking through a treeline. “Then I heard, okay, Drew, that’s a wrap,” he says, “and then I walked about 20 yards away and just started crying.”
He describes it as grief. “It was the last time that I was gonna get to play this person. It felt like losing someone.” I wonder if some of that grief was also for the loss of home.

The show was filmed in Charleston, South Carolina, close enough to his hometown that he could spend his summers back at his family home. “I didn’t know if I’d get that time again,” he says. “It’s where I’ve spent most of my time these past seven years.”

Starkey grew up in Asheville, North Carolina. His first memory is trailing through the apple orchards near his Appalachian home. His first word was “apple.” His first, and perhaps most enduring, dream was to own a little piece of land in Asheville and tend his own orchard.

For years, Outer Banks allowed him to remain relatively close to that life. Now, the farther he gets from home and into Hollywood, the farther he reaches for roles that take him outside himself. In his breakout film role as Eugene Allerton in Luca Guadagnino’s Queer, he played an American expatriate in Mexico City who becomes the fixation of William Lee, played by Daniel Craig. The performance required a vanishing act from him: Eugene is self-effacing and withholding to the point of opacity. Starkey played him with great restraint, not allowing any of the character’s interiority to peek through onto the surface. It was the inverse of Rafe, whose every feeling overpowers the characters around him.

In every role, Starkey appears an actor of great charm, imagination, surrender, and command. He can play good and evil. He can play both top and bottom. He is drawn to characters who fuck, or, as he puts it, “Characters who have their own kinks about life.” Since he has played characters who are both submissive and dominant, I ask whether he sees acting as a kind of power play – not only sexually, but in the more fundamental sense of determining who controls a scene and who yields to it.
“Absolutely. There’s a sub and dom in every scene,” he says. “And I think the more you lean into who has control in the room, the closer you can get to the truth of what a scene and what a story is.”

In his latest role as Cyrus in Adam Wingard’s A24 slasher-action movie Onslaught, he plays a government agent who leans a little leather daddy: bleach-blond hair, dyed eyebrows, almost unrecognisable as Drew Starkey. Starkey relished the transformation. “I wanted to take it as far as he could,” he says. “I would like to seek things out that are as far removed from myself as possible.”

His recent roles have carried him farther and farther away from the YA version of himself that made him famous. As he was wrapping the last season of Outer Banks, he quickly started learning how to play guitar and piano and sing for Deep Cuts, A24’s adaptation of Holly Brickley’s novel about a music-obsessed couple. Now, he can play four or five songs “really well,” he says. He studied with Blake Mills, the virtuoso guitarist and producer, while director Sean Durkin made Starkey and castmate Cailee Spaeny a playlist to get them into the 2000s of it all, filled with Wilco, the Strokes, and Red House Painters.

Then there was King Snake, Jeff Nichols’ Southern Gothic film, which he wrapped in July in Arkansas alongside Margaret Qualley. They play a young couple who inherit a haunted farm. The material brought him back to the old folk tales his Appalachian relatives told around campfires – the stories that made the mountains feel eerily mythical and thick with lore.

Qualley, who also grew up in Asheville, North Carolina, turned out to belong to that world, too. “Acting with her felt like cosmic intervention,” he says. Starkey had first met her when he was nine, when he spent time at her mother’s house, a family friend. Years later, they found themselves in the same orbit again.
“I went up to her at a party and was like, I met you when we were nine,” he says.
“Our parents were friends,” he told her, before eventually getting the recognition he was waiting for: “Ohhhh.”
It sounds like the sort of anecdote that will eventually calcify into a story Starkey tells over and over during the film’s press run.

For now, Starkey comes without the Hollywood lacquer. He is forthcoming and gracious in conversation, but contractually faithful. Can he address the rumours that he’ll play Cyclops in the upcoming X-Men reboot? “Can’t do that,” he says. American Psycho? “Nope.” What about the film he wrapped in early October? “Nope” again.

Every topic besides those is a concession. He says he still gets nervous in the days leading up to a press appearance or a day on set. But once the cameras are rolling, something else happens. “Disappearing into characters feels like a protective layer,” he says.

In every single role, just like in the grief he felt when he finally had to let go of Rafe after several years, there is “a sacrifice.” “I view the work like I’m some kind of martyr. I use the work to lose myself,” he says.

He says he’s been this way his entire life, a martyr to his passions. “If I didn’t do well at a basketball game in school the world would literally feel like it’s ending,” he says. “For me, I have to perform at the highest level, or it’s nothing to me.” Now, approaching 33, he says he feels like he’s “maturing.” “Like I’m realising my old way of thinking isn’t sustainable.”

He is also now trying to figure out what is left when he is not working. “For the past few years, I’ve been in a constant rotation of projects,” he says, “and I feel like the only thing I’m able to pull from now is my work experience, and not from life. I’m in need of a psychological break.”

When it comes to maintaining a sense of self off set, he says, “that’s still a skill I’m having to learn.” Now, with projects coming one after another, the problem is beginning to look less like how to lose himself and more like how to keep something in reserve. It all reminds me of what he wrote about his insomnia while he was in college: “In this process, I lost myself.”

But near the end of that piece, after thousands of words describing himself caught between the white consciousness of waking and sleep, he wrote how he’d finally “found myself in those shipwrecked hours.” He had spent the night trying to lose himself, and take the world away with him – “the distinction between me and the world outside of my thoughts became blurred during the night” – and then on the page, he found a way back to himself. “I knew I’d find land. I just didn’t know how long it would take for me to get there.”

In trying to regain himself and reach landfall, he’s remembering how much he loved to write, something he struggles to do while acting. As a student, he learned from the masters of minimalism and elision, Raymond Carver and Ted Chiang. “I always thought that’s what I’d end up doing, writing,” he says.
He dreams of picking it up again, maybe writing under that tree in his future orchard. “One day I’ll take writing seriously,” he says.
“What would you write?” I ask.
“I don’t know,” he says. “I love short story fiction and short story creative nonfiction… But I don’t know what I’d write. I need to start so I can find out.”

Photography Collier Schorr. Styling Ellie Grace Cumming. Grooming Melissa Dezarate at A Frame Agency. Digital tech Travis Drennan. Lighting Taylor Schantz. Photographic assistants Anna Rhody and Amelia Hammond. Styling assistant Charlie Edwards. Production Will Foster at Farago Projects. Production manager Christine Carreira. Production coordinator Elissa Graddy
This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man, which is on sale from 5 November 2026. Pre-order here

items.title: Naomi Ackie on Female Friendship, Hollywood and I Love Boosters
items.description: As she stars alongside Keke Palmer, Taylour Paige and Poppy Liu in Boots Riley’s anarchic new film I Love Boosters, Ackie talks finding her feet in Hollywood and the thrill of taking on a new challenge
items.author: Hester Underhill
paragraphs: As she stars alongside Keke Palmer, Taylour Paige and Poppy Liu in Boots Riley’s anarchic new film I Love Boosters, Ackie talks finding her feet in Hollywood and the thrill of taking on a new challenge

With every new film, Naomi Ackie finds herself wondering the same thing: will she click with her fellow castmates? “It’s a gamble every time you get a job. You’re like, am I gonna like everyone? Are they gonna like me?”

With her latest film, I Love Boosters, Ackie struck gold. Cast by rapper-turned-director Boots Riley as part of a shoplifting girl gang – alongside Keke Palmer, Taylour Paige and Poppy Liu – the chemistry between the actresses extended well beyond the set. “Boots knows how to pick them. I felt so bad for him sometimes because we would just be chatting and chatting. It was like herding cats. But he was just like, ‘Let the women do what they need to do.’”

A follow-up to Riley’s 2018 debut Sorry to Bother You, the film stars Palmer as Corvette, the ringleader of a crew of shoplifters (or ‘boosters’) who become hellbent on taking down an evil fashion corporation run by designer Christie Smith (played by Demi Moore). The film sees Riley take his playful visual style into hyperdrive to create a psychedelic vision of the Bay Area, with candy-coloured costuming by Shirley Kurata – the stylist behind Everything Everywhere All at Once – and an equally zany soundtrack from Oakland band Tune-Yards. “He’s an auteur; no one can do what Boots does,” says Ackie, who plays Sade, Corvette’s straight-talking best friend who gets sucked into a mysterious pyramid scheme. “He’s a director who has such a strong vision, and yet he also sits back and really allows you to explore it the way you want to.”
“I don’t really look for scripts in terms of whether they pass the Bechdel test, but I think that because I’m a feminist I naturally gravitate to things that speak to me” – Naomi Ackie

When it comes to the Bechdel test (a measure of female representation in film, based on whether two female characters have a conversation that isn’t about a man), I Love Boosters passes with flying colours. So do two other of Ackie’s recent films, Eva Victor’s Sorry, Baby and Zoë Kravitz’s directorial debut Blink Twice, both of which place female friendship at the heart of their stories. “It’s rare to find a film where men aren’t centre stage,” says Ackie. “I don’t really look for scripts in terms of whether they pass the Bechdel test, but I think that because I’m a feminist I naturally gravitate to things that speak to me.”

Growing up in Walthamstow, north London, Ackie attended an all-girls school, an experience that taught her a lot about the complexities of female friendship. “There’s so much school politics. And there is nothing like a girl bully. They get into your mind, man. So I experienced both sides – incredible friendships and also very difficult ones.”

After leaving school, Ackie attended London’s Royal Central School of Speech & Drama. She graduated in 2012, landing a string of theatre roles and television bit parts before making her 2016 film debut in Lady Macbeth. Playing the maid to Florence Pugh’s titular character, the role earned Ackie a British Independent Film Award (BIFA) for most promising newcomer. But it wasn’t plain sailing from there. A steady trickle of film and television work came Ackie’s way after her win, but by the age of 26 she was still living at home with her dad in Walthamstow and working part-time at the West End’s immersive Crystal Maze experience. She was seriously considering giving up acting when she was cast as former stormtrooper Jannah in Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker (2019), JJ Abrams’ closing chapter of the sci-fi sequel trilogy. The role thrust Ackie into the Hollywood limelight, opening the door to a string of high-profile projects. In 2022, she played Whitney Houston in the biopic I Wanna Dance With Somebody, and in 2025 starred as heroine Nasha in Bong Joon Ho’s sci-fi comedy Mickey 17.

Despite making a name for herself in Hollywood, Ackie still lives in the UK. “LA is fun, but I’ve always associated it with work. London is just a vibe, isn’t it?” On set, though, she sticks to an American accent as a way of remaining in character between takes. “I’m not trying to fool anyone; it’s just so I can stay in that part of the brain. But I’m not method by any means.”

But as with Mickey 17, where she played opposite Robert Pattinson, and The Rise of Skywalker – which starred Daisy Ridley and John Boyega – Ackie often finds that she’s not the only Londoner on set. “The cultures are very, very different, so sometimes you do feel slightly homesick. So I think whenever I get the chance to work with a fellow Brit, I'm a happy girl.”

It’s been a busy year for Ackie, who has other high-profile releases coming up, including DC body horror Clayface and They Follow, David Robert Mitchell’s eagerly awaited sequel to his cult horror It Follows. She’s also just finished shooting Sugar Raye, a British indie drama in which she plays a former boxing champion attempting a comeback. For the role, Ackie spent eight months training in the sport. Taking on a new skill has become something of a theme in her career; in preparation to play Whitney Houston, Ackie spent around six months in vocal training, and for Star Wars she had to master archery and horse-riding. When it comes to what’s next, she’s already cooking up some ideas. “My new thing is dancing. I want to find a film that’s about burlesque or ballroom dancing. Something where I have to learn something new. Because it’s a really fun way of upping the challenge.”
I Love Boosters will release in UK and Ireland cinemas on 30 October

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.
