But restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches, anxiety to panic attacks, sadness to depression, or pleasure to ecstasy – it is taking the most extreme instantiation of something and making it the essence of that thing.

If grief isn’t just about death, what is it about? What do all these cases of grief share? A good way to answer this question starts from the observation that every emotion has a characteristic thing it is about. Fear is about danger or threat; anger is about offence or injustice; happiness and joy are about flourishing or harmony between self and world. What is grief about? If you say ‘death’, you are doing something weird: you are defining the emotion by the particular thing that sets it off, rather than by what that thing means to us. In technical philosophical jargon, you are making the mistake of conflating an emotion’s material object with its formal object. Fear of sharks, fear of public speaking and fear of heights aren’t three different emotions – shark-fear, public-speaking-fear and heights-fear. All three count as fear because they are about danger: their aim is to tell you something is threatening.

Grief clearly has something to do with loss. Although this gets us somewhere, it doesn’t get us far enough. Mere loss is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a pen or an old sweater, I am not experiencing any grief. If I have any emotional reaction at all, it will be a slight ripple of annoyance. Perhaps we should add that for there to be grief we must lose something we care about or love, but, again, this is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a book I really like or don’t get a dream job I applied for, what I experience is frustration or disappointment, sadness perhaps, but not grief.

What sets grief apart is how deeply the loss reaches into the fabric of your life: grief begins where your identity is disrupted. What is lost in the case of grief is not just some concrete, historical object, but a cluster of (future) possibilities that are tightly woven into your sense of identity, life structure or experiential world. When they go, you don’t just lose something: you lose a version of yourself, your life is turned upside down, and you come to inhabit, in a real sense, a different world. This is why death is grief’s most extreme instance, rather than its only one. When someone we love dies, every possibility – not only our own possibilities with them, but their possibilities too – is wiped out. As Matthew Ratcliffe and Louise Richardson, academic philosophers at the University of York, put it in their paper ‘Grief Over Non-Death Losses: A Phenomenological Perspective’ (2023):

Grief is thus distinctive insofar as it involves recognising and comprehending the implications of lost possibilities for the structure of one’s life or world, and – over time – coming to reorganise one’s life accordingly.

This reorganisation is not merely cognitive. It lives in many other places: in the body (the hand that still reaches for the phone to text someone who no longer answers your messages), in how you experience your surroundings (the café you used to visit together that now feels alien or even hostile), or in your autobiographical memories (the shared joke that simply doesn’t land with other people).
‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to’

My mother is still alive. No one has died: there is no concrete, historical object that has been pulled beyond my grasp. But a whole set of possibilities that had been woven into the structure of my life and world, all bound up with having a mother who was present, responsive, good enough – those are gone. It has become impossible to call her and poke that mind of hers, so unusually free and unusually deep.

The same goes for my father. Sure, he survived the stroke. But the man whose restless mind needed to cycle to make his thoughts liquid – the future I had with that man, the shared cycling trips in the south of France, the conversations that needed repetitive, cyclical movement to come alive – that future was negated. The same structure holds for the woman whose disappearance collapsed an experiential world that felt like a home I had only just found, and for the academic identity I had built over almost two decades. As other vocations began to call more insistently, a single, all-consuming way of being in the world – the thinker, the life of the mind, the person whose future would be organised around reading and writing – loosened its hold.

The case that makes this way of thinking about grief most compelling, though, is one where there is no concrete object of loss at all. Ratcliffe and Richardson’s central example is involuntary childlessness – grief for a child who never was, a future that was imagined, anticipated and deeply woven into one’s sense of self, but that never materialised. Here, no one died and no one left. There is nothing tangible to point to: no grave, no anniversary, no recorded name, no memorial service, no shared practices to give words or meaning to the loss. And yet, as one respondent in their study put it: ‘No one can understand what it’s like to carry this loss. In their minds, no baby meant no loss.’ Another respondent simply called their grief by its name: ‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to.’ And a third spoke, chillingly, of ‘the death of a future life’.
They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience

‘No baby meant no loss.’ Many forms of non-death loss are what the family therapist Pauline Boss calls ‘ambiguous loss’. These are losses without clear boundaries, without a definite beginning or end – cases where someone is physically present but psychologically gone, or physically gone but psychologically still there. Think of an Alzheimer’s patient whose self has been erased by the disease or of a soldier missing in action. Because many non-death losses are ambiguous, the grief that follows them is not openly acknowledged, socially validated or publicly mourned – what the grief scholar Kenneth Doka has called ‘disenfranchised grief’.

Those whose grief is disenfranchised because their losses are ambiguous don’t just lack scripts or rituals or traditions. They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience. When we lack the concepts to name what it is like to be us, what it is we are going through, we suffer what the philosopher Miranda Fricker calls a ‘hermeneutical injustice’ – an inability to make our own experience intelligible to ourselves and to others. This is not because we are confused, but because the shared language or conceptual apparatus – the frameworks we use to make sense of ourselves – hasn’t caught up. As two of Ratcliffe and Richardson’s respondents put it: ‘It took me a while to understand that what I was feeling was grief’; ‘I never realised this was grief until I found others in a similar situation.’

The same happened to me: when the magical stranger disappeared, my loss was ambiguous – she still existed, we were never officially together, I had another partner – and my grief went into hiding. In a culture where the end of a relationship is ‘just a breakup’ and monogamy is the unspoken rule, I lacked the rituals to digest the grief and the hermeneutical resources to conceptualise and communicate what had happened to me. For ‘self-interpreting animals’ like us, in the words of the philosopher Charles Taylor, the result is that we end up in the dark, as strangers to ourselves.

The narrowing of grief to bereavement is more than a conceptual mistake. It does real damage. What the writer and grief counsellor Stephen Levine called ‘unattended sorrow’ doesn’t dissolve but goes underground, hiding in the shadows, later resurfacing as unexpected symptoms. I have been there. A mechanical tightness in the chest and a hard belly, like wearing a harness to brace against life. Harrowing dreams. Attempts to numb what is too painful to feel alone. And, worst of all, cynicism and a slow erosion of trust. Not just in other people, but in your own feelings, your own intuitions about the depth, sustainability and future of any new connection. When no one around you recognises your grief, you begin to wonder whether you were wrong to feel it at all.

Sigmund Freud understood this, though he read it as pathology. In the essay ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (1917), he contended that grief is healthy and normal, but only if it is intelligible and bounded. The job of mourning, he argued, is to detach you from the lost object and reinvest your emotional energy elsewhere. If you can’t complete that job, if the loss is unclear or unnamed or ambiguous, you are no longer mourning. Instead, you are suffering from an illness called melancholia. For Freud, grief that cannot do its work calcifies into something darker, something more elusive.
If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to themselves

But the damage runs deeper than that. When we cannot grieve a loss, we lose something else along with it: the chance to register what mattered to us. Grief is how we come to know what we loved in the presence of its absence. Or as the psychotherapist and grief worker Francis Weller puts it in The Wild Edge of Sorrow (2015):

Grief and love are sisters, woven together from the beginning. Their kinship reminds us that there is no love that does not contain loss and no loss that is not a reminder of the love we carry for what we once held close.

Your grief tells you that you had the courage to love, that you allowed someone or something else to enter ‘the core of [your] being and find a home in [your] heart’. If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to what they loved and valued, which is to say that you deny them access to themselves. You don’t just rob them, then, of their love; you also rob them of self-knowledge.

The tradition I spent most of my life in – the lineage of Western thinkers who asked how a human being should live – was the first place I looked to understand what was happening to me. These thinkers had a lot to say about grief, but most of it was suspicious and sceptical. Plato believed a good man is the most self-sufficient of all, and least shaken by loss. In the Phaedo, Socrates’ wife Xanthippe is led away wailing before the philosophy can begin, and towards the end of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes his weeping friends for behaving like women. A similar sentiment can be found among the Stoics. Epictetus, in the Enchiridion, compares the loss of a wife or child to a jug breaking. And Marcus Aurelius, who lost many of his own children, reminds himself in his Meditations not to pray that he might keep his child, but to pray that he might not fear losing him.

Behind this way of thinking lies an expensive belief: that attachment is a liability, and that a wise person – someone who has figured out how to live the best possible life – does not need anything that can be taken away from him. If grief is love with nowhere to go, a tradition that treated such love as an error was never going to know what to do with it.

Christianity kept the verdict the ancients had arrived at. In his Confessions (397-400 CE), Saint Augustine looks back on his devastation after a friend’s death, and diagnoses it as a spiritual mistake: ‘Why had that grief penetrated me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand, loving someone who would die as if he never would?’ Baruch Spinoza – not religious in any conventional sense of the word – reached the same conclusion. Sadness, he writes in his Ethics (1677), is the mind’s move to a lesser perfection, a loss of its power to act. This means it can never be a good in itself, and its typical source is too much love for things that are impermanent. The cure for grief – and this puts him squarely back into the ancient intellectualist tradition – is understanding: the moment it dawns on us that what we lost could never have been kept, our grief will relax.
The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder

Arthur Schopenhauer, unlike many before him, did not despise grief. In The World as Will and Representation (1818), he values sorrow for one reason only: great personal suffering breaks the will and leads to self-renunciation (Selbstverneinung). Grief is worth having, then, because it has the power to cure us of wanting the world at all, which means that, in the end, he is not so far from the thinkers who came before him. A good life, for all of them, is a matter of loosening our attachments to what is impermanent and fragile.

What began as a doctrine of philosophers leaked into the wider culture. In his landmark study Death, Grief, and Mourning in Contemporary Britain (1965), the anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer found that mourning was increasingly seen as ‘a weakness, a self-indulgence, a reprehensible bad habit instead of as a psychological necessity’. In the 1970s, the historian Philippe Ariès traced the same shift across the industrial West: death, once familiar, had become shameful, something to be hidden. Meanwhile, medicine had entered the debate. In 1961, the psychiatrist George Engel asked, half provocatively, whether grief was a disease. In 2000, the philosopher Stephen Wilkinson answered: yes. In one of academic philosophy’s leading journals, he argued that even normal, healthy grief qualifies as a mental disorder because it meets the standard definition of one. Like all mental disorders, it involves significant distress and interrupts normal functioning. In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders removed the clause that had excluded the recently bereaved from receiving a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Then, in 2022, the revised edition added prolonged grief disorder, whose possible symptoms include identity disruption, such as the feeling that part of oneself has died. The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder – though, tellingly, only when someone has actually died.

But the Western tradition had it backwards. Suppressing, eradicating, denying or pathologising grief doesn’t protect the good life; it sabotages human flourishing by cutting us off from the things we love. More than that, it cuts us off from each other. Grief named and disclosed is grief that can be met, grief that can be placed between you and another person, where the two of you can look at it and hold it together. That shared vulnerability lets one person recognise another in their common humanity. Grief, as Weller reminds us, was never meant to be carried alone; it was meant to be held and processed by a whole village. Strip it of its name and you strip people of the possibility of being seen in their loss, of discovering that the wound they thought was theirs alone is in fact shared by those around them.

Recently, while in the Netherlands, I visited the Kröller-Müller Museum with my father, the same father whose future was negated by a stroke. I looked at him from a distance, the man who once built his life around cycling – to France, to Rome, to Spain’s Santiago de Compostela – now hunched behind his rollator. We stood together in front of Vincent van Gogh’s painting At Eternity’s Gate (1890): an old man, face buried in his fists, clearly hurting. A sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man painted by a sorrowful man. Years before he painted it, when he first drew the same figure for a lithograph, Van Gogh wrote that there can be an ‘unutterably moving’ quality, ‘something precious, something noble’, in the expression of an old man like that.

I didn’t know my father loved Van Gogh as much as I do. We stood there for a long time – somehow in contact with the magic of grief – and something opened up between us that had no name but felt important, exquisitely alive. We didn’t talk about my mother, or how our family had unravelled, or what the stroke had taken from him. We didn’t have to. The painting said what neither of us could.

items.title: Lucy Bridge Wants To Bring Colour Back to Beauty
items.description: As her debut book Colour Mode is released, the make-up artist talks us through her technicolour world
items.author: Dominic Cadogan
paragraphs: As her debut book Colour Mode is released, the make-up artist talks us through her technicolour world

Lucy Bridge has always lived her life in full colour. When she was at school, the make-up artist dyed her hair a new shade every week, much to the despair of her teachers, and after moving to London in 2008, it was her affinity for popping to the shops with neon pink blusher and green glitter eyebrows that turned the head of famed photographer Tim Walker – who scouted her for a shoot in i-D after spotting her on the 55 bus.

Today, she is one of fashion’s most prominent talents, known for colouring outside the lines and a roster that includes Jean Paul Gaultier, Mugler, Dries Van Noten and Tom Ford, where she is now global make-up artist for the brand under Haider Ackermann. A scroll through her kaleidoscopic oeuvre reveals crimson lacquered lips that deepen to merlot at the edges, acid green eyeshadow and licks of molten silver and gold. It’s an urgent antidote to the neutral tones of the minimalist ‘clean girl’ who currently reigns in beauty.

It comes as no surprise, then, that her debut book Colour Mode, created over three and a half years in collaboration with creative director Veronica Ditting, is a smorgasbord of shades. A trip down the rabbit hole into the make-up artist’s mind, alongside ten commissioned shoots – featuring photographers Paolo Roversi, Oliver Hadlee Pearch and Thurstan Redding – ‘Looks in Process’ captured by Jean Marques offers a glimpse into the fantastical creations as they come together.
Here, Bridge talks us through the inspiration behind three of the stories in Colour Mode and her collaborative process with each photographer.

“This shoot really represents my head as a make-up artist and what goes on in my brain. It’s totally bonkers, so abstract and very out there. I must admit it’s my favourite one out of the whole book, all the wacky colours. We started with beads on the face and we needed another beaded element somewhere. I tried them on the eyes; it wasn’t quite working. We tried the hands, it didn’t work. I was like, ‘Right, one of these models needs to give me one of their feet’ and honestly it was incredible. After I did the foot, Lauren Michelle Pires tested out a few different colours and then actually put fake toenails on. On the day, Carlijn was like ‘I didn’t really understand the foot when you were doing it, but my agent is obsessed’ and anyone I’ve shown this shoot to has been mesmerised by the foot. I don’t really know where it came from, it just sprang from my imagination. I need it blown up one day and put up in my house.”

“I’ve been working with Tim on and off for the past 15 years. He’s been so nurturing. He’s really helped me throughout my whole career and given me a platform. He was inspired by the psychedelic hippie group from 1970s San Francisco, The Cockettes and I did some wacky make-up inspired by them. There’s a lot of trust between me and Tim, so we didn’t have too much back and forth before the shoot – we had a cup of tea in the morning and a little discussion and then we cracked on. I knew I wanted a simple white background so the make-up was the focus and then we worked with Gerry O’Kane to create these characters. Tim has been in the game for a long time and he knows what he wants to do, so I knew we were going to get something incredible.”

“Jack was actually the last photographer to shoot for the book, it took us about two years to get together. I’d only worked with Jack once previously, but Veronica had a long-standing relationship with him – she calls him the magician. I always go into a shoot with a very methodical and clear idea of what I’m going to do, whereas with Jack, it was much looser because I don’t even think he knows what he’s getting on the day. I love his world, it’s so surrealist. We wanted the shoot to look really timeless and you can’t quite place it, it could have been shot in the 1920s, but it also feels so modern. We were shooting and all of a sudden he started projecting my make-up palettes onto the model. I didn’t know Jack had taken a picture of them when I was doing the make-up and it was genius and that’s what made the cover. It’s not technically make-up, but it’s showing my practice as a make-up artist and it’s nice that Jack brought it into the shoot so elegantly.”
Lucy Bridge Colour Mode is published by Thames & Hudson and out now

items.title: Lance Oppenheim on His Feature Fiction Debut, Primetime
items.description: The 30-year-old Floridian’s feature fiction debut Primetime, with an “operatic” performance from Robert Pattinson, taps into a culture war that’s still raging and at times, he says, felt more like making a documentary than some of his documentaries
items.author: Miriam Balanescu
paragraphs: The 30-year-old Floridian’s feature fiction debut Primetime, with an “operatic” performance from Robert Pattinson, taps into a culture war that’s still raging and at times, he says, felt more like making a documentary than some of his documentaries

Between his fiction feature debut Primetime and his Nathan Fielder collaboration You Can See Everything, Lance Oppenheim, a 30-year-old from Florida, is behind two of the buzziest films of the year. The day I talk to him over Zoom, his three-hour Elizabeth Holmes doc has been slapped with an R rating for “graphic nudity” – fanning the flames of online speculation about a film Oppenheim insists should be experienced with “no context”.

What he will say about the enigmatic doc is that, together with Primetime, this is a new stylistic chapter for his filmmaking. Oppenheim rose through the ranks of Hollywood with the documentaries Some Kind of Heaven (about America’s largest retirement village) and Spermworld (following unregulated online sperm donors). Oppenheim’s Robert Flaherty-inspired “docu-fantasias” would involve spending sometimes years with his subjects and using “the tools of narrative filmmaking” to recreate subjective experiences.

“Primetime was different. And I would say [so was] You Can See Everything. That was made in a completely new style [...] very rigorously vérité documentary. With Primetime, by saying that in some cases it felt more like making a documentary than my documentaries themselves, I mean [in terms of] the process. On a documentary, because the crew is so small, normally I’m able to control the image, to wait and see how I want to shoot something. If I don’t get it right, I’ll go back and do it the next day.”

By contrast, Primetime was a sprawling shoot: 780 people were involved, 20 different camera formats were used, and shot listing and rehearsing were avoided. At the epicentre of Primetime and You Can See Everything are two slippery subjects. The former follows Chris Hansen, the television host who spearheaded To Catch a Predator, played by an exquisitely slimy Robert Pattinson. The NBC show would document sting operations baiting would-be child predators to a stage house, and turn Hansen’s confrontation with them (and their arrests) into peak viewing entertainment. Like Hansen, Oppenheim calls Holmes a “cipher”. The Theranos fraudster invited Oppenheim’s documentary crew into her home days before her prison sentence in a seeming bid to outsmart Fielder and his team.

Primetime begins as Hansen’s flagship show is programmed in competition with Lost, upping the pressure for Hansen and his producer Andie (a brilliantly nihilistic Merritt Wever). A new “decoy” is recruited – Daniel (Skyler Gisondo), a Rent-singing adult actor posing as a minor. And Hansen’s marriage (to Anna Faris) starts to unravel once his affair is discovered by the press. These personal dramas unfold amid the carnivalesque television set, inhabited on and off camera by Oppenheim’s own crew. “I liked that we were living a parallel existence as the characters were in the movie,” he muses.

It is Pattinson’s exacting, “operatic” embodiment of Hansen – as Oppenheim puts it – that brings the film truly into a hyperreal dimension, however. The actor, who also produced Primetime, approached Oppenheim with Ajon Singh’s script for the film but didn’t initially plan on starring. “[Robert and I] talked so much ad nauseum about the script,” says Oppenheim. “My wife gave birth to our son five days before production started, and he was in the delivery room with me on FaceTime, calling mid-delivery with ideas for the script.

“We spent Christmas together, staying up until three in the morning, drinking beers and talking about the character, watching Hansen vs Predator together.” He adds: “This is more of a media collage than anything else. He’s essentially playing every version of Chris Hansen that’s ever existed [...] stitching all that stuff together with something very vulnerable and human, which I think comes from Rob’s experience dealing with essentially becoming an overnight celebrity. He was struggling to make sense of how to be himself, but also give people what they wanted.”

Amid QAnon paedophile ring conspiracy theories and the rise of “predator hunters” in the manosphere, Primetime taps into a culture war that’s still raging. “There was still so much anger and confusion post-9/11 that the regimented concept of being a Democrat or Republican, this binary, started to exist,” reflects Oppenheim. “Because of all the anger and fear and anxiety, it almost felt like the show, when it arrived in the early 2000s, was the perfect receptacle for all of this stuff. It’s to me a very Bush-era concept of politics of ‘if you’re not with us, then you’re against us.’”

Despite Hansen’s dubious methods – and his threats to sue Oppenheim for making the film – the director maintains that he is still a fan of the TV show personality. “Chris’s reaction to the film itself, in a lot of ways, feels exactly like the sort of behaviour we were trying to trace. It’s actually proving the thesis of the movie,” he urges. “When the movie was first announced, [Hansen] was at the Crime Con convention, and I think he said something to the tune of you may have thought that Robert Pattinson was going to be here, but it’s me. He’s gone from journalist to crusader, and then from crusader to vigilante [...] an almost messianic person cleansing the world of an ancient evil” – all the while hijacking the film’s publicity to nail a book deal and an autobiographical series.

“He kind of reminds me of Batman or something,” says Oppenheim. “He’s doomed to living a lifestyle where he has to fight crime for the rest of his life. Like in The Dark Knight Rises, Bruce Wayne, you see that it’s taking a toll on his body physically and spiritually.” Oppenheim says he eagerly awaits Hansen’s reaction to actually seeing Primetime: “I want to go on his podcast with Rob. Ideally I’d even love to do the A24 podcast with him and talk about the movie and have a seat together.”
Previews for Primetime start from 28 October, before arriving in UK cinemas on 30 October

items.title: When Is a Monastery Like a Calvin Klein Store? When John Pawson Gets to it
items.description: How should we live? What is space? How minimal can a building or room be? These are some of the questions architectural designer John Pawson brings up in his book The Minimal Home, and which come up in his commissions. The designer behind the Calvin Klein Coll
items.author: Sami Reiss
paragraphs: How should we live? What is space? How minimal can a building or room be? These are some of the questions architectural designer John Pawson brings up in his book The Minimal Home, and which come up in his commissions. The designer behind the Calvin Klein Collections Store in Manhattan, London’s Design Museum, and a number of monasteries, he is minimalism’s ambassador if there ever was one. A Pawson building tends to be stripped down to its essence and spacious. Even his apartments are cavernous; work is both demanding and light.

Such simplicity and directness of purpose didn’t happen overnight. Pawson, raised in Yorkshire, and who worked formatively under Shiro Kuramata, the generationally important Japanese designer, and founding member of Memphis Group, entered the Architectural Association School of Architecture in his late 20s already converted to minimalism, then opened his practice in 1981. At the time, maximalism was popular; but Pawson’s projects weathered the trend, and created a new language for minimalism. The Calvin store, Pawson’s first commission of scale, veered retail design into the radically minimal. The 30-foot high windows—suggested in jest to Klein by Pawson—that didn’t display any jeans or clothing made waves in the industry; so did the phenomenon of people coming in just to experience the store. The same reverent, spare and straight aesthetic would appear in churches and monasteries his firm later designed. 40 years in, it makes for a broad body of work, that is minimalist on the surface with a maximum of effort below. Work that is easy to look at, but hard to create.
We spoke to Pawson from his London office about his new book, sacred spaces, Calvin Klein, and the difference between designing buildings and clothes.
You worked with Shiro Kuramata at a young age and discovered Domus and Mies van der Rohe as a youth. How'd architecture show up for you so early?

For Mies, I must have been around mid teenage years. Kurumata I found at about 18. I left school at 17, traveled the world for a year or two. I was in Newcastle, and the gallery there had Domus. There was also a furniture magazine called Mobilia, which had lots of things I liked. I devoured those. When you spend time reading, all your experience comes from photographs or magazines. I found Kuramata in Domus in 1968 and thought this is a living architect who does work. It was Mies and Kurumata, and that was it. Still is, actually.
I think of that story where you asked Philip Johnson, the great architect, about his mentor, Mies, and he brushed it off. What was it about Mies’ work that struck you so early and stayed with you?

With Mies, every single thing you saw was an edited work. The Farnsworth House [in Plano, Ill.], the Barcelona Pavilion, the Seagram Building, the [Promontory] apartments in Chicago. They were all as near to perfect as I could think, really. And the works just got stronger over time. Spending time at the Farnsworth House, [van der Rohe’s seminal 1951 modernist house in Illinois] being able to enjoy it personally was fantastic. It was also quite surprising. I didn't realize how generous the proportions were.
Everything was wider and taller and more spacious than you saw from the photographs. Even his Barcelona chair is big enough for two people.
I'm curious how your own work has evolved in the past 40 years. Is it more minimalist? Is the approach different with a team?

It's a bit easier. My clients are young now, and before I was a young guy and they were mature. But nothing's really changed. It’s been very consistent. It’s surprising to me. I'm not completely blinkered, but I tend to keep my head down and get on with the work. You can't ignore what happens, but it's not a fashion thing, driven by trends. Things are a bit different than 40 years ago. But not our approach. The tenets are still there.
I read you keep up quite a bit with engineering projects, like bridges and roads. What draws you to these structures?

I'm not sure if you could draw a direct line to it, but architecture with a single purpose, like a bridge, or a motorway, or a dam, there's something spare about the form. They have a single purpose and their engineering makes them visually simple, which is also pleasing. You tend to only be able to do that if you’re doing a bridge. A house is always very complicated; it’s not a single form.
Are the monasteries and churches you made closer to that?

The interior of a church should be simple enough, so it doesn't distract you from the job at hand, to get closer to God, or to at least pray, and have a few moments of silence. The rest of the monasteries, the cloister, and the refectory and all the other rooms are designed as visually simple. They have to function.
At the beginning of your career, was it tougher to get your minimalist ethos across to clients?

It was very difficult to get across to the teachers. But there were early adopters. Doris Saatchi, an American in London, was a great patron. And then Calvin Klein, who was introduced to me by Ian Schrager, the hotelier. That set the whole thing on a different scale. It changed my life, actually, not just my career. It's hard to overestimate the impact.
Did Calvin have a specific vision of how he wanted the shop to look like? Or were you directing it?

He's an architect manqué and was interested in architecture and designing it together. He had very strong ideas. You can identify Calvin a lot in the finished product. He likes black and white and contrast. I said as a joke to make the windows one piece of glass, which is quite hard—36 feet high, the biggest piece you can get. But that was him. And there are things I wouldn't have done, but luckily I saw sense.
What would you not have done? What did you change your mind about?

Minor things. I wouldn't have had so much contrast or detailed the handrails as they are. But I'm quite happy now, especially how successful the store was. I didn't realize how fresh and new it was for people in New York. It wasn’t life or death for me.
What is it about the details of a bare minimalist work that makes it affect people?

There is a feeling walking into spaces like the ones we do, where people expel air, feeling something different. And of course, there people walk in and have no idea at all, or who think it's a lot of nothing, or it's empty, or there's something strange going on. But creating that atmosphere is hard work, and is far from minimal. It’s not a question of painting the walls white or putting a wood floor down. It’s the whole complete thing. Even the placement of the furniture.
Is it because you're trying to maximize space, or light?

Trying to make people feel good is the biggest thing. And space. The feeling you get in space is important. People aren’t necessarily relaxing, but feel stimulated or excited. It's a visceral feeling.
Your architecture work can be collaborative, but is it different with object design? Is it a collaboration with the object company, or a brief, or a lark?

We're all architects here, we're not product designers. The products we occasionally design are approached from an architectural point of view. We rely on the manufacturer to develop the object and produce it. It can take a long time, getting from the idea to the table is a long process. The cooking pans we did [with Demeyere, in 2007] took about nine years. We approach them as if they're buildings a bit.
The objects are complex. There are a lot of parts. It’s small architecture, for me. It’s also not two different teams in our office. The best architects make the best objects.
I have to ask because this is a fashion magazine. Are you minimalist with your own clothing? Are you taking the same architectural approach—fewer seams, fewer lines—to dressing?

Yes, but not in a design way. The shirts are white, the trousers are gray, the pullover is grey. Shoes are black. Socks are black. Overcoat, black. But it's not all black. My wife likes very colorful dresses, which I've learned to keep my mouth shut about. It's like the painting on the wall. It’s her dress, it's their house. I wouldn't want everyone dressed like I think. it would be terrible. And for architecture as well. Thank God for variety.
John Pawson: The Minimal Home by John Pawson and Deyan Sudjic is published by Phaidon, £39.95 (Phaidon.com)

items.title: Xavier, So Blessed
items.description: In our cover story from Issue 38 of Hypebeast Magazine, Xaviersobased opens up about protecting his independence, taking underground rap mainstream, and why caring about people matters more than playing the part.
items.author: Hypebeast Newsroom
paragraphs: In our cover story from Issue 38 of Hypebeast Magazine, Xaviersobased opens up about protecting his independence, taking underground rap mainstream, and why caring about people matters more than playing the part.
It’s late August on the New York City subway. You’re on your way to interview an artist, and when you look up from your phone, what do you see in a video ad, but that very artist posing a question.

“Have you considered Gibsonton?” Xaviersobased asks me, right there on the L train. New York’s quintessential young hip-hop producer and rapper of the 2020s, matter-of-factly promoting travel to a town on Florida’s west coast that was heretofore best known as a winter haven for circus performers, part of an Airbnb campaign aimed at Gen Zers on a budget. Random? Casually cool? Kinda weirdly Orwellian? Yes, yes, and yes.
In other words, pure Xavier.

A short time later, I am meeting the real Xav. He’s as warm and affable as his reputation and is in the middle of a fitting at Hypebeast HQ for a photo shoot the following day. It’s another busy week for him — two music videos, the release of a tour promo, the announcement of a one-off show in LA, and a performance with the brothers of his 1c34 collective, on the rooftop of Bushwick’s Elsewhere, all as he prepares for a month on the road as support on Ken Carson’s fall tour. Only the latest chapter in what has been an underground-to-increasingly-overground milestone year for the rapper.

2026 began with the release of his first studio album, Xavier, and was followed, in approximate order, by: a string of inspired music videos, including a collab with Skrillex; the second and third legs of his Riverside headline tour; a memorable car dealership-themed set at Rolling Loud; his first trip to Australia and two to Europe. Not half bad for a Golden Birthday year: Xav turns 23 on October 23rd.

“It feels insanely different,” says Xavier, as we settle into a lounge area at the Hypebeast office. “But in a way, it kind of feels normal. Cause this is what we were building towards.” A big part of this year’s leveling up had to do with Xavier’s 2025 signing with Atlantic Records, a deal that he and his larger-than-life DJ, manager, and greatest champion, DJ Rennessey, did not rush into. “Me and Ren was going back and forth with different companies,” Xav recalls. “We were kind of just preparing everything. From the beginning, we were like, ‘Yo this music shit is working, let’s just keep pushing it and see how far we can take it.’ In the beginning we were definitely avoiding the labels, the majors. Because we knew we didn’t have that leverage.”

Xav and Rennessey watched as some of his peers jumped at that first, fast money, but they held out for autonomy: a low-pressure, two-project deal. Under their own O1-chance imprint, along with longtime supporter Evilgiane’s Surf Gang and Atlantic, the agreement allows Xav to also drop singles and videos independent from the label. “We fought for that,” says Ren. “That was the biggest thing. We fought for a lot of our freedom.”

Xavier’s come up is both familiar in internet rap, and singular. A New York City native, Xavier Lopez from West 109th grew up in the aughts and teens as a Dominican kid obsessed with hip-hop and skating. His passions were fueled by his mom, a DJ, and his older brother Alex, the musician and visual artist known as Nurse, who Xav credits for his more experimental impulses. His influences ran the gamut, from Lil B and Chief Keef, to Bladee and Drain Gang, and as for many in Gen Z hip-hop, the COVID era proved suffocating, but formative. Xavier was 16 when the pandemic hit, and with online friends he created the gaming clan-turned-music collective 1c34. He quickly grew into a prolific local phenom, dropping a ton of music from 2020 on, including the seminal “Patchmade” — which anointed Xavier as a leader in a “nu-jerk” explosion, and a blueprint for music soon to come from YT, Nettspend, and fakemink.

On a pivotal night in 2022, Rennessey caught Xavier performing at an especially turnt outdoor DIY rap show, and had a lightbulb moment. The rest is underground history that is still being written: Xavier as artist, producer, and burgeoning NYC icon with Rennessey as manager, learning the ropes together, a formidable team. When tastemakers heaped praise on Xav’s irresistible 2024 tapes Keep It Goin Xav and With 2, the pair bided their time. “We were just waiting, patiently staying down until we got a good situation,” Xavier recalls.
“In the beginning we were definitely avoiding the labels, the majors. Because we knew we didn’t have that leverage.” – Xaviersobased

This year, with the Xavier LP and Riverside tour, there have been new and unexpected eyes on Xavier. Rolling Stone, iconic New York station Hot 97, and the hip-hop desk at Billboard — outlets populated by rap traditionalists not known for their progressivism, who would likely never give the time of day to some of his more “aura-first” peers — all welcomed Xavier. It’s put him in a curious dual-track situation: certified A-lister in underground rap, but effectively introducing himself as a newcomer to more mainstream audiences, repeatedly retelling his backstory and often being asked to “describe” his label-resistant sound. And that’s OK with him. “I don’t mind it, because at the same time, I am a new person on these platforms,” he says. “The average Billboard reader is not listening to me, you know what I mean? A lot of these publications, their audience is not my base. So that’s why I completely understand it, and Ren helped me put it in that perspective.”

About that sound: Xavier is a palpable epitome of a New York kid, with all the self-possession that implies. You cannot grow up in our sui generis city and not be a product of it and its music. But just as true is that he’s an internet native, born two years before YouTube. So while it’s not unfair to see him as a latter-day Max B, bootstrapping a crazy run of mixtapes from COVID on, he is equally a product of the haze of Bladee and Drain Gang, the ethics of Lil B, and many more spaces he discovered growing up in the age of the algorithm. He’s a collage artist whose music pulls from cloud, low-end, electronics, and sampled internet flotsam.

What does he mean for the legacy of “New York rap,” which has in truth never been one thing, anyway? Xavier has just lurched it forward more radically. When he is asked how his music fits into the city’s musical lineage, as he has been, especially this year, he seems flattered by the inclusion, but a little flummoxed by it. When pressed to “describe” his sound, he will often default to simply “experimental.” And he credits some of that impulse to his older brother Alex, who records as Nurse.

“A lot of the things my brother used to listen to, a lot of noise music, black metal, and all those like subgenres like grindcore, all that,” Xavier recalls. “It was very experimental stuff. And – I never really liked those styles of music? But I loved the experimental-ness of it, and so I was thinking, ‘How can I make the stuff that I listen to even more experimental than what it already is?’” Anyone who thinks this year’s Xavier LP is “left field” ought to give a spin to his 2021 Store tape, more throw-it-on-the-wall-and-and-see-what-sticks essays in sound that play more as ambient than hip-hop. “I was making all those kinds of tracks where I was just like, ‘try anything,’” he says. “Like you said, kind of an ‘anything goes’ type of mentality.” He obviously identifies first and foremost as a rapper, but as a producer and writer he has no problem upending its conventions.

Those soundcrafting skills and a clear sense of where he’s headed musically — he’s described the Xavier LP as a “steppingstone” to what’s next — may help explain why he’s peaking mainstream interest when others in the Gen Z underground are not. The other reason is realness. In a world where fantasy often rules, with Xavier, what you see is what you get. Rhode Islander Demetri Demetropoulos, aka @poortfolios, is Team Xav’s videographer, in-house documentarian, and consistent creative collaborator. “In one word or phrase, I would say Xav has due diligence,” Demetri says. “I think that’s something that is noticeable from afar. I don’t think there’s ever been anyone to doubt his authenticity.”

Xavier is also authentic in his choice of restaurants. We’re off to La Dinastia, a Chino-Latino spot on 72nd St that Xav has been going to since he was a kid. To get there, it’s a nearly hour-long drive from the LES to the UWS, in traffic and a torrential rainstorm, with six of us, plus a driver packed into a luxe SUV. The good news is, that gives us plenty of time for real talk, starting with success. In a FADER documentary late last year, Xavier defined “making it” as “financial stability” and being set up “for the rest of your life,” before adding, “as long as I am enjoying the music I am making, that’s all that matters.” Fast forward six months, in an SSENSE piece, Xav was said to be considering an upgrade from an “entry-level Mercedes.” When I point out the two comments, Xavier asks me if I think one “goes against” the other. I tell him no, that both can be valid. But I do wonder, as someone who’s more known for t-shirts, skating, tagging, and good times than Rick Owens, Pateks, and fancy cars, whether he now wants things he didn’t care about before.

“Nah, I feel like I am getting stuff that I always cared about, but that’s why I feel like I didn’t make it yet though,” he says. “I know exactly what you mean, that it seems out of character with the way that I’ve been coming up. But at the same time, I’m from the trenches! I grew up seeing a lot of n*ggas come around, pop they shit, and being like, ‘Damn, I wanna do that. I want something like that for myself, I want to do this, that, and a third.’ Just cause I come from damn near nothing. My crib is crazy cause the house I grew up in felt more like a hallway without any doors. So, coming from a situation like that? I know I’ve just got to get more money.”

However much he makes, he will likely never lose his compassion for those with less — another trait that unquestionably sets Xavier apart. While the vast majority of young artists and their bottom-line-focused handlers avoid divisive topics like a third rail, Xav has zero problem speaking out: for Palestine, for LGBTQ+ fans, or to call out America’s systemic “soft slavery,” in which people with less are kept down so that the rich get richer. On 2022’s install, he said he’d slap the shit out of a “classist” and on “Patchmade,” from the same tape, declared he “can’t fuck with n*ggas if they right-wing.” He’s clearly not doing it for pats on the back, but he deserves them, nevertheless. “I don’t think you are overstating it at all,” Demetri says of Xavier’s humanitarian side. “I think Xav just has a big heart. He really does want the best for people, whether it’s the homies making music, or something in the world. It’s in the name. It comes with being based, I think.”

Indeed. He walks the based walk. But Xav is quick to dispel any idea that he is a tapped-in socio-political activist. “As far as me talking about these issues and all that bro, I’m not even that political of a person,” he admits. “But like you said, I just care about people. That’s it. And if there’s a way that I can speak for these injustices, and express how I feel on ‘em, I’mma do it. If I have a platform then why not? Why not express these things?”

He adds that there are some who question his social commentary. “Like, there are certain fans that do find it weird that I talk about certain issues, because I’m a rapper,” he says. “And I’m getting money. I don’t really know what to say about that.” I tell him there’s nothing to say about it, except that the notion that you can’t have money and still care about people is ridiculous. “Facts,” he replies. “But there are certain people who will just call it bullshit.”

As we head up FDR Drive in rain so hard it feels like we’re in a car wash, I remind Xavier that the first time we met was a brief hello at a Nettspend show in late 2024. I distinctly remember seeing him exiting Irving Plaza that night, and spending so much time chatting and taking pictures with the crush of fans outside that all I could think was, “Man of the people.” It tracked with the accessible way in which he’s generally moved over this past half-decade. But as his star has risen, sometimes the man of the people needs his space. “When I am up to it, I try to take every opportunity to chill with the fans,” he explains. “But I’ll be honest, sometimes I’m not feeling up to it. And I feel like the fans will be mad at me like they’re being disrespected. Sometimes it is a lot for me, though.”

He’s also no stranger to parasocial fans. “I experience it a lot. For sure,” he says. “And they be crazy, too. You ever met someone that’s a fan of you, but then they kind of stuck around for too long?” Um, yes. “I don’t mind when people say, ‘What’s up?’ But then some people don’t get the gist of when you meet someone for the first time, it’s like, ‘hi’ and ‘bye’ you know?”
“The average Billboard reader is not listening to me, you know what I mean? A lot of these publications, their audience is not my base.” – Xaviersobased

The Pride of 109th will soon get his personal space – and maybe upgrade that ride. He is planning to decamp for “six months” to — yes — Los- fucking-Angeles. When I express concern about our homegrown Gotham king, young rap’s perfect embodiment of Mamdani-era New York going Hollywood, Xavier laughs.

“It’s funny you should say that,” he says. “Because I probably hate LA as much as you do. But I like the idea of being able to live in a house. I never lived in a house, I always grew up in apartments. And I feel like LA is one of the places where I feel like I can get more work done. I can pull up to Atlantic [Records], you feel me? Go talk to them, see what’s up. There’s hella studios — more than here. That’s really the reason why, and I feel like it’s a good place to be out the way.”

Well then. That means this may be Xav’s last trip to venerable La Dinastia for a while. The monsoon has subsided by the time we pull up to the restaurant, get a table for six in the back, order up, and talk touring. Ren is looking forward to the upcoming Ken Carson Xperimenting tour in September, as a chance for Xavier to win over the rage-heads with a full throttle opening set. “We can show a different side of him,” he explains. “Just to say, ‘I can do it too.’ But I can do it my way, and with my music.” Xavier is more blunt about what awaits him with the Carson faithful: “I feel like there’s a good portion of them that hate my guts. For sure.” But I’m inclined to agree with the team’s publicist, Sam, who offers, “I don’t even know what a Xavier hater would look like!”

The next day, everyone has reconvened at a three-story house in Ridgewood, Queens. I’m told the building once hosted Sunday school for a nearby church, though some of its nooks feel more Shining than sanctified (one creepy bedroom is empty except for a lone rocking horse). Hypebeast’s Nayquan Shuler is putting Xav through his paces, shooting on the stoop, in a stairwell, a blue-tiled bathroom, even doing some ironing — good practice, perhaps, for Xavier, now that he’s on his own and doing adult things. When he lived at his grandma’s, he says, she would not let him do anything for himself: “She’d be like, ‘No you’re gonna do it wrong, you’re gonna fuck everything up. Let me do it.’”

Downstairs I catch up with Ren, who doesn’t let on too much about the year ahead, although the LA stint offers possibilities, not least because Xav is signed to talent agency behemoth CAA. Could there be film and TV in Xavier’s future? It’s not hard to imagine. “Everything happens at the right time,” Ren says. “It’s not about how fast it happens.”

One thing is for certain: the music won’t stop. Whether it’s single drops on Soundcloud, videos on alt pages or — eventually — another full project for Atlantic, Xaviersobased has held onto the freedom needed to keep flexing his experimental muscles. And what about chart-chasing at the behest of someone in a corner office? I ask him whether he would draw a line at, say, a feature with Sabrina Carpenter. “Bro, I’ll knock out a whole album with her,” he laughs. “I’m down for all types of things, but it just has to feel right and be done in a certain way.”

2026 has already proven to be the most blessed year yet for a young artist whose singular ear, willingness to push the rap envelope, and thoughtful, deliberate approach to career choices is getting its due. Time is on his side, and I don’t know anyone who’s not rooting for him.

items.title: lululemon’s Clean-Cut Outerwear Collection Arrives at Zalando
items.description: Just in time for the new season, sportswear label lululemon brings its technically built outerwear to Zalando. The latest collection applies the label’s refined blueprint to functional styles, giving coats and jackets a versatile edge for everyday wear.
items.author: Angelee Kholia
paragraphs: Just in time for the new season, sportswear label lululemon brings its technically built outerwear to Zalando. The latest collection applies the label’s refined blueprint to functional styles, giving coats and jackets a versatile edge for everyday wear.

With puffer jackets often adopting large silhouettes, lululemon provides a unique alternative through an array of sleeker shapes. Helping to achieve this aesthetic, the label incorporates innovative insulating materials to keep silhouettes tailored while ensuring warmth and weatherproofing.

In the Featherweight line, a noticeably weightless feel encompasses outerwear. Made with 900-fill-power RDS-certified down, coats are able to lock in heat with the addition of cinchable cuffs and hems. The material also offers unique compressibility so tall collars can be folded over, or the entire coat packed away in a removable sack.

Among its short and long-length styles, the Mac coat becomes the defining piece of the ThermoZen line. Appearing at first as a smart jacket, the new design proposes a cozy feel with PrimaLoft® Gold insulation. Enhancing the stylish design, lululemon kits out the coat with two-way zippers, a zippered hand, and internal pockets.

Elsewhere, the Wunder Puff line builds on its previous silhouettes, introducing new bomber-style cuts and vests. Like the aforementioned Featherweight pieces, outerwear comes to life with RDS-certified down, while the outer SoftMatteTM shell attributes a water-repellent quality to drop-waist pieces.

For the launch of the new collection, the label’s ambassador collective is captured in a street-level campaign. They show how performance outerwear can adapt to different looks, reinforcing the everyday focus of the range.
Discover the campaign in the gallery above featuring Lewis Hamilton, Ayan Broomfield, Marc Tortell, and more.
Be sure to shop lululemon at Zalando by visiting the dedicated webpage.

items.title: Опера «Русалка»
items.description: Написанная по мотивам неоконченной драматической поэмы Пушкина «Русалка» стала важным этапом в развитии русского музыкального театра — переходом от романтической условности к психологической драме. Сохранив пушкинские стихи, Даргомыжский дополнил либретто новы
items.author: Анна Данилина
paragraphs: Написанная по мотивам неоконченной драматической поэмы Пушкина «Русалка» стала важным этапом в развитии русского музыкального театра — переходом от романтической условности к психологической драме. Сохранив пушкинские стихи, Даргомыжский дополнил либретто новыми эпизодами и трагическим финалом, а народные песни, пляски и хоровые сцены превратил в неотъемлемую часть действия.

В центре сюжета — трагедия Наташи, преданной возлюбленным и доведённой до гибели: оказавшись в подводном мире, она становится русалкой, которая ничего не забыла и не простила, а орудием её мести князю оказывается их дочь.

В постановке Александра Тителя замыслы Пушкина и Даргомыжского соединяются с эстетикой Достоевского: режиссёр переносит народные сцены в пореформенную эпоху и закольцовывает сюжет, предлагая новый взгляд на известную историю. Партию Мельника — одну из легендарных ролей Фёдора Шаляпина и трагический центр оперы — исполнит заслуженный артист России Дмитрий Ульянов. В главных партиях также Мария Лупарева, Чингис Аюшеев и Лариса Андреева. За дирижёрским пультом — Тимур Зангиев.

items.author: Анна Данилина
paragraphs: Показ фильма «Отверженные»

В прокат выходит «Отверженные» — масштабная экранизация культового романа Виктора Гюго от создателей «Графа Монте-Кристо» и режиссёра Фреда Кавайе. Главные роли исполнили Венсан Линдон, Тахар Рахим, Камилль Коттен, Вассили Шнайдер и Бенжамен Лаверн. По сюжету Жан Вальжан, когда-то осуждённый за кражу буханки хлеба, сбегает с каторги и пытается стать достойным человеком: получает должность мэра и берёт на воспитание Козетту, дочь погибшей бродяжки. Но инспектор Жавер не оставляет его в покое. Мировая премьера прошла в основной конкурсной программе 74-го кинофестиваля в Сан-Себастьяне. Приглашаем на всероссийскую премьеру.

items.title: Показ фильма «Навар»
items.description: В прокат выходит «Навар» — режиссёрский дебют выпускника Московской школы нового кино Артура Григорьева. Шуст и его друзья промышляют мелкими махинациями и навариваются на каждом шагу. Встреча с бывшим чемпионом СССР по метанию ядра Ульяновым и его дочерью мен
items.author: Анна Данилина
paragraphs: В прокат выходит «Навар» — режиссёрский дебют выпускника Московской школы нового кино Артура Григорьева. Шуст и его друзья промышляют мелкими махинациями и навариваются на каждом шагу. Встреча с бывшим чемпионом СССР по метанию ядра Ульяновым и его дочерью меняет представление Шуста о том, как можно жить. Но под давлением банды он использует Ульянова, чтобы спланировать ограбление бурятской коммуны, торгующей нефритом. Главные роли исполнили Илларион Маров, Елизавета Базыкина, Геннадий Блинов и Евгений Сидихин; рэпер Icegergert появился в камео и записал оригинальный саундтрек.

«Идея фильма родилась, пока я поднимался по лестнице за призом за свой короткометражный фильм на фестивале “Дух огня”. Тогда было не лучшее время для меня, время сомнений, самокопаний и растерянности, но как только я услышал своё имя и названия фильма со сцены, всё вдруг изменилось: я почувствовал прилив сил, было такое ощущение, что мне дают второй шанс. Так и родилась идея фильма про потерянного парня, который встречает другого человека и эта встреча меняет вектор его жизни», — рассказывает режиссёр Артур Григорьев.
Приглашаем членов клуба на премьерные показы в Москве и Петербурге. В Москве перед фильмом выступит Icegergert, а после показа в обоих города состоится разговор со съёмочной группой.
