items.title: ИИ научился определять возраст и риск смерти по одному селфи — Reminder
items.description: Ученые из американских медицинских центров Mass General Brigham разработали две нейросети: одна определяет возраст человека по фотографии, другая прогнозирует выживаемость пациентов с онкологическими заболеваниями. Точность первой проверяли на общедоступных на
items.author: Анна Аскарян
paragraphs: Ученые из американских медицинских центров Mass General Brigham разработали две нейросети: одна определяет возраст человека по фотографии, другая прогнозирует выживаемость пациентов с онкологическими заболеваниями. Точность первой проверяли на общедоступных наборах фотографий, а связь обеих моделей с выживаемостью — на снимках более 40 тысяч онкопациентов из США и Нидерландов, которые проходили лучевую терапию.

Первую модель, FAHR-FaceAge, обучили определять возраст человека по фотографии. На общедоступных наборах снимков алгоритм в среднем ошибался на 5,1 года — по данным авторов, точнее предыдущих моделей оценки возраста .
Однако для медицины важнее не точность определения возраста сама по себе, а связь между тем, насколько старым выглядит человек, и состоянием его здоровья (ее проверяли уже на онкопациентах):
Эта связь сохранялась после того, как исследователи учли возраст пациентов, пол, тип опухоли и лечение.

Вторая модель, FAHR-FaceSurvival, не определяет возраст, а сразу рассчитывает показатель, связанный с риском смерти. По результатам ее оценки пациентов разделили на четыре группы. В верхней четверти риск смерти оказался примерно в 3,2 раза выше, чем в нижней, даже с учетом других факторов риска. Среди 122 пациентов с самыми высокими показателями 64 умерли в течение 90 дней после съемки. В группе с самыми низкими показателями за тот же период умерли около 2% пациентов.
Две модели не дублируют, а дополняют друг друга: каждая улавливает свою часть информации, поэтому вместе они прогнозируют выживаемость точнее, чем по отдельности.

В основе обеих моделей лежит одна нейросеть, обученная на более чем 40 миллионах фотографий лиц. Во время обучения на каждом снимке скрывали большую часть изображения, а нейросеть училась восстанавливать недостающие фрагменты. Так она усвоила общие закономерности строения лица, от пропорций до расположения отдельных черт. Затем ее дообучили под две задачи: одну копию — определять возраст на почти 750 тысячах общедоступных снимков, другую — прогнозировать выживаемость на 34 тысячах фотографий онкопациентов.

Алгоритмы обращали внимание на разные участки лица. Возрастная модель учитывала, среди прочего, носогубные складки, область лба над глазницами и виски — зоны, где с годами меняются объем и распределение мягких тканей.

Модель выживаемости больше ориентировалась на область под глазами и вокруг переносицы. Исследователи обнаружили, что эти участки сильнее влияли на прогноз модели, но не установили, какие именно биологические процессы объясняют эту связь.
У пациентов старше 40 лет возрастная модель придавала больше значения вискам и лбу, а модель выживаемости смотрела на одни и те же зоны независимо от возраста.

Исследователи также проверили, связана ли оценка возраста нейросетью с образом жизни участников. Оказалось, что курильщики по оценкам алгоритма выглядят старше тех, кто бросил курить, а бросившие — старше тех, кто никогда не курил. Употребление алкоголя и наркотиков также было связано с более высокой оценкой возраста. Однако эти результаты сами по себе не доказывают, что именно эти привычки вызвали наблюдаемые различия.

Отдельно ученые проверили, можно ли обмануть нейросеть с помощью внешних условий съемки. Для этого ей показали наборы парных фотографий одних и тех же людей. В одном наборе были снимки с макияжем и без, в другом — фотографии анфас и вполоборота, с улыбкой и с нейтральным выражением лица, при ярком и приглушенном свете. В проверенных условиях эти различия не приводили к существенным изменениям оценки возраста.

Также нейросеть проверили на снимках до и после пластических операций. Большинство проверенных вмешательств не приводили к существенным изменениям оценки возраста. Исключением стала ринопластика: после нее модель в среднем оценивала людей на 1,1 года старше. Все эти проверки проводили на возрастной модели; устойчивость модели прогнозирования выживаемости к таким изменениям отдельно не проверяли.
Важно: это статистический прогноз, а не индивидуальный диагноз. Исследование не показало, что использование модели в клинической практике помогает выбирать лечение или улучшает исходы для пациентов.

items.title: Почему надежда важнее счастья? — Reminder
items.description: Кэрол Грэм — экономист, исследовательница благополучия и автор книги «Счастье во всем мире: парадокс счастливых крестьян и несчастных миллионеров». В начале карьеры она занималась экономикой развития, работала приглашенным научным сотрудником Всемирного банка
items.author: Анна Аскарян
paragraphs: Кэрол Грэм — экономист, исследовательница благополучия и автор книги «Счастье во всем мире: парадокс счастливых крестьян и несчастных миллионеров». В начале карьеры она занималась экономикой развития, работала приглашенным научным сотрудником Всемирного банка и входила в экспертную группу ООН, которая искала способы оценивать прогресс общества не только по ВВП.

Сегодня Грэм — старший научный сотрудник Института Брукингса, профессор Мэрилендского университета и старший научный сотрудник Gallup. Среди прочего она изучает, почему одни люди смотрят в будущее с надеждой, а другие впадают в отчаяние, и почему бедность в богатых странах может переживаться особенно тяжело.
«Раньше я занималась счастьем, а теперь, кажется, все больше изучаю отчаяние, — рассказала она Fortune. — Не самое приятное положение дел, но такова наша реальность».

Первые книги Грэм были посвящены бедности и рыночным реформам в Латинской Америке. Но со временем ее стали больше занимать экзистенциальные вопросы: как общество влияет на душевное благополучие людей и почему одни чувствуют себя счастливыми, а другие — несчастными.
Эту эволюцию отражают даже названия ее книг:

В своем недавнем исследовании Грэм и ее коллеги проанализировали данные Gallup по 44 странам за 2006–2024 годы. Выяснилось, что в США доверие к правительству упало на 31 процентный пункт, к судам — на 24, а доля людей, которые чувствуют себя свободными выбирать образ жизни, сократилась на 19 пунктов. При этом в США рост доходов влияет на благополучие людей слабее, чем в других странах. Исследователи называют это парадоксом несчастливого роста, или парадоксом изобилия.

Объяснение Грэм начинается с Латинской Америки. «Я родилась в Перу и вначале занималась экономикой развития, — рассказывает она. — И я могу сказать вам, что такое настоящая бедность». Этот опыт до сих пор влияет на то, как она интерпретирует американскую статистику.

«Бедные люди в Латинской Америке гораздо больше надеются на будущее, чем бедные в США, — говорит Грэм. — И я пришла к выводу, что в очень богатой стране быть бедным тяжелее: там на тебя смотрят свысока. К тому же сама идея американской мечты способствует такой стигматизации».

Ярче всего этот парадокс проявился в Китае. В исследовании Грэм, опубликованном в журнале World Development в 2017 году, она с коллегами обнаружила, что в годы самого быстрого роста, с середины 1990-х до середины 2000-х, удовлетворенность жизнью в стране резко упала. «Перемены затронули все стороны жизни, — объясняет Грэм. — Изменился образ жизни, появилось неравенство, которого раньше не было».

В США похожий процесс развивался медленнее. За последние два десятилетия американская экономика росла быстрее, чем экономика почти всех других богатых стран. При этом неравенство постепенно увеличивалось — до такой степени, что стало разрушительно влиять на общество, подчеркивает Грэм.

В экономике счастье называют субъективным благополучием. Для его измерения экономисты используют как субъективные данные — в основном опросы, — так и более объективные: долголетие, уровень образования, доход. Но становится ли богатое общество пропорционально счастливее с ростом доходов?

Теория относительного дохода гласит, что экономическое поведение человека в большей степени определяется его доходом по отношению к другим, чем абсолютным заработком. Если вы хорошо зарабатываете, но живете в самом дорогом районе города среди сверхбогатых соседей, вы будете чувствовать себя хуже, чем с тем же доходом в квартале среднего класса.

Это помогает объяснить парадокс Истерлина, который был сформулирован в 1974 году: в долгосрочной перспективе экономический рост, даже влекущий за собой рост дохода, не всегда влечет за собой рост благополучия населения.

Дело в том, что экономический рост обычно ведет к увеличению доходов всех людей. В краткосрочной перспективе каждый человек ощущает рост дохода и уровня жизни, а потому становится счастливее. Однако усилия всех других людей по повышению уровня жизни приводят к увеличению средних показателей, оставляя всех на одном и том же уровне с точки зрения относительного дохода.

Значит ли это, что бороться с неравенством бессмысленно? Нет. Психологи Сигэхиро Оиси, Костадин Кушлев и Ульрих Шиммак проанализировали данные опросов американцев за 1972–2014 годы. Оказалось, что в годы более прогрессивных налогов люди с низкими доходами чувствовали себя счастливее. Самые обеспеченные при этом несчастнее не становились. Авторы объясняют это так:
Когда неравенство снижается, люди чаще считают жизнь справедливой и больше доверяют друг другу.

В книге «Счастье для всех?» Грэм показала, как американская мечта влияет на отношение людей к собственным неудачам. Если успех считается результатом упорного труда, то бедность легко принять за личную неудачу.
«Если ты отстаешь от остальных и беден, значит, сам виноват: недостаточно много работал, чтобы добиться успеха. Никто никогда не говорит о невезении», — отмечает исследовательница.

Эта идея уходит корнями в один из главных мифов американской культуры: человек способен добиться всего самостоятельно, благодаря трудолюбию и упорству. Классический пример — романы Горацио Элджера о бедных мальчиках, которые выбиваются в люди. В его самой известной книге, «Рваный Дик» (Ragged Dick), нью-йоркский беспризорник, который чистит обувь на улице, спасает тонущего сына богача и получает в подарок новый костюм и место в торговой конторе.

«Даже у героя знаменитой истории Горацио Элджера был покровитель, — напоминает Грэм. — Но когда эту историю пересказывают, об этом почему-то не говорят». По мнению Грэм, снижению уровня счастья в США способствует не только неравенство, но и культура индивидуализма, в которой люди меньше полагаются на социальную поддержку.

Однако надежда — это не просто вера в то, что все сложится хорошо. Она связана с ощущением, что человек может влиять на собственную жизнь и справляться с трудностями. Это подтверждает недавнее исследование, которое Грэм провела совместно с Редзо Муйчичем из Уорикской бизнес-школы. На протяжении 14 лет они наблюдали за 25 тысячами взрослых австралийцев. Люди с более высоким уровнем надежды впоследствии добивались лучших результатов в здоровье, образовании и работе. Они также легче переносили жизненные потрясения и быстрее восстанавливались после них.
«Надежда отличается от счастья и оптимизма. Она предполагает ощущение, что ты способен влиять на происходящее, — объясняет Грэм. — Это то, что я называю внутренним локусом контроля».
По словам исследовательницы, уровень надежды остается удивительно стабильным с течением времени. Похожая закономерность может проявляться и в удовлетворенности жизнью.

В своих исследованиях отчаяния Грэм обращает внимание на людей, которых обычно не учитывает официальная статистика. В первую очередь это мужчины трудоспособного возраста, которые потеряли работу или перестали ее искать.

В исследовании 2021 года Грэм обнаружила, что такие мужчины в США «очень несчастны и крайне пессимистичны». Среди них также непропорционально много людей, употребляющих опиоиды. Многие из них, по словам Грэм, до сих пор живут с родителями или по соседству с ними и не смогли начать самостоятельную жизнь. Без высшего образования им сложнее найти хорошую работу, а значит, и переехать туда, где есть подходящие вакансии.

При этом речь необязательно идет о людях, которые полностью лишились средств к существованию. Проблема шире: «Система оставляет позади большие группы населения, — говорит Грэм. — И это не обязательно люди, которые совсем остались без работы или без гроша».

Британское исследование 2015 года показало, что благополучие снижается и у тех, кто перегружен, и у тех, кому работы не хватает. Обычно этот эффект кратковременный. Но если переработки продолжаются в течение двух лет и дольше, уровень благополучия остается сниженным.

Безработица негативно влияет не только на самих безработных, но и на их окружение: высокий уровень безработицы по стране повышает тревожность у трудоустроенных — они начинают беспокоиться о потере работы. Исследования показывают, что нематериальные потери превышают денежные: человек лишается признания, общения, распорядка дня и контроля над своей жизнью. Частично эти потери может восполнить волонтерство, но лишь отчасти и при условии, что у человека нет острых финансовых проблем.

Сомнения в том, что прогресс можно измерить одним ВВП, появились довольно давно. За последние полвека экономисты и правительства предложили несколько альтернатив. Самая известная — индекс человеческого развития, который ООН рассчитывает с 1990 года. Его автор, пакистанский экономист Махбуб уль-Хак, хотел сместить фокус экономики развития с национального дохода на людей. Индекс складывается из трех составляющих:
В 2011 году Организация экономического сотрудничества и развития запустила индекс лучшей жизни. Он оценивает 11 сфер:

Дальше всех пошел Бутан. Понятие «валовое национальное счастье» ввел в начале 1970-х четвертый король страны Джигме Сингье Вангчук, тогда еще подросток. Он ставил под сомнение, что один ВВП способен обеспечить обществу счастье и благополучие. У идеи глубокие корни: еще в бутанском своде законов 1729 года сказано, что правительство, которое не может сделать людей счастливыми, не имеет смысла. В 2008 году, когда Бутан перешел к конституционной монархии, принцип закрепили в основном законе.

Статья 9 конституции обязывает государство создавать условия, при которых люди могут стремиться к валовому национальному счастью. Еще одна статья требует от правительства обеспечивать благополучие и счастье народа. Опирается концепция на четыре принципа:
Прежде чем принять закон или программу, власти проверяют, как они скажутся на жизни людей. Конституция требует и того, чтобы не менее 60% территории страны составляли леса.

Счастье в Бутане измеряют по 33 показателям в девяти сферах, от психологического благополучия и здоровья до использования времени, культуры и жизни сообщества. Человек считается счастливым, если у него все в порядке хотя бы по 66% этих показателей.

В опросе 2022 года участвовали 11 052 человека, и по его итогам счастливыми назвали 93,6% бутанцев. Правда, ни один из 33 показателей не измеряет счастье напрямую. А в международном Докладе о мировом счастье за 2019 год, где людей прямо просят оценить свою жизнь, Бутан занял лишь 95-е место из 156.

items.title: The Silver Lining of Israel’s Historic Election
items.description: Shaima Kaabneh, a young Palestinian activist who lives in the West Bank village of Taybeh, has been visited twice daily for months by a particularly violent settler named Yedidya Cohen. Early yesterday morning Kaabneh posted a photo to her Instagram story of C
items.author: Celeste Marcus
paragraphs: Shaima Kaabneh, a young Palestinian activist who lives in the West Bank village of Taybeh, has been visited twice daily for months by a particularly violent settler named Yedidya Cohen. Early yesterday morning Kaabneh posted a photo to her Instagram story of Cohen crouched on the ground outside her home clad in his typical camo face-covering and baggy T-shirt with prayer-shawl fringes swaying above dirtied jeans. Over the the photo, Kaabneh wrote the following message in English:

Today is election day, and all our hopes are that the government will change and that the situation will improve. WE hope this day marks the beginning of a new chapter filled with hope and positive change. We dream of a day when everyone can live in safety and dignity, when people’s voices are heard and their rights are respected, and when decisions are made for a better future for everyone. 🕊️❤️
We hope these elections will bring hope for a future with more justice and peace, and mark the beginning of a better reality and a dignified life for every human being.

The election to which Kaabneh referred was not an election in which she can participate. She is not a citizen of Israel. But it is the only election that can meaningfully impact whether or not Cohen continues showing up each day to terrorize her and her family with the intention of pushing them off their land.

The debate leading up to this election was dominated by the usual diametrically opposed worldviews. Many mainstream outlets described the election as the most significant in Israel’s history. The argument was made repeatedly that Israel’s democracy was on the ballot. On the other side, anti-Zionists, especially those in the diaspora, insisted that no matter the results of the election, Israel’s government will hasten no significant changes for Palestinians either in Israel or on its borders. Everyone predicted that there would be no clear winner, and in this they were vindicated. But no one foresaw the shocking voter turnout of the Arab-Israeli parties — even the highest turnout projections for that electorate were exceeded. In an election that broke turnout records across every demographic, the Arab-Israeli electorate was the highest of all with 78.8 percent.

According to all exit polls, Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won the most seats — 27, according to mainstream outlets — but it lacks a clear path to the 61-seat majority it would need to establish and lead the next government. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party trails Netanyahu with either 21 or 22 seats, but it isn’t evident how he could form a majority coalition either, especially if he keeps his campaign promise not to sit with the Arab parties. All told, the Netanyahu bloc has an estimated 53 seats to the opposition’s 49. There will be enormous pressure on Eisenkot to form a unity government (that is, a government with the two largest parties that ran against each other) with Netanyahu. Already, commentators are theorizing about the possibility of Eisenkot and Netanyahu establishing a rotating premiership till the next election four years from now. Eisenkot also swore before the election that he would never agree to sit with Netanyahu. Campaign promises are made to be broken. Let’s hope he breaks the right ones.
In either case, there is a glimmer of hope for the Arab population.

It is no secret that Bezalel Smotrich, who has served as finance minister in Netanyahu’s coalition since 2023 and who also oversees settlement affairs in the West Bank, has established a regime of impunity for settler terrorists like Cohen who operate as key actors in Smotrich’s plans for the region. Last September, Smotrich held a press conference with settler leaders at which he presented what he called a “Sovereignty Plan” map, which showed how he intended to use settlement expansion to annex 82 percent of the West Bank and to eliminate Palestinian communities in Bethlehem, Salfit, and Qalqiliya. The plan Smotrich unveiled at that meeting called for the expulsion of about 450,000 Palestinians. So far, he has succeeded in expelling 42,322.

Voters also registered a protest against Netanyahu, whose fascistic policies and projects will outlive his tenure in office — in Gaza most of all, but also in the West Bank and inside Israel itself. In the days preceding the election, he unintentionally made it very clear that the existential threats Israel faces stem from his disastrous stewardship. In an interview on the Friday afternoon before the election, he sounded alarms about the threats of impending sanctions for settler violence. He conceded that Israel must prepare for the inevitability of these sanctions, which could crush the Israeli banking system. He also warned of the impending loss of American military and civilian aid, which has numbered in the billions of dollars annually for years — two shocking concessions that imply Netanyahu knows his policies have damaged Israel irrevocably. Netanyahu explained that Israel would have to create a “circumventing economy” based on cryptocurrencies — a proposal so idiotic that it in itself would have been enough to upset the national economy.

At the same time, Netanyahu made overt, desperate attempts to provoke an attack from Iran before the elections, which would have forced the country to reschedule the vote (at the potential cost of Israeli lives). And as if all these antics weren’t enough, he also posted an AI-generated image of Tel Aviv beneath a nuclear mushroom cloud and warned that nuclear destruction is what awaited an Israel without him at its helm. All this served to cement the opposition bloc’s distaste for the havoc Netanyahu brings.

Opposition-bloc voters want normalcy, and if they cannot have it, they at least want its mirage. Netanyahu spent much of his campaign boasting that he has led Israel into a seven-front war since October 7. This was an apparent expression of certainty that he had not run his own population ragged by forcing much of the country to serve in reserve units for wars that never end. When opposition bloc voters described this election as the most significant in Israeli history, they meant that it would either secure an exit from Netanyahu’s hamster wheel of eternal battle or else strap the country in forever.

Neither the Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc includes Palestinian citizens of Israel, who account for 20 percent of the Israeli population. Each bloc has accused the other of being a Trojan horse for Palestinian citizens. Netanyahu spent much of election day warning that the Arabs were surging into the polls — a racist attempt to galvanize his supporters to get out the vote. And he wasn’t wrong. Many Palestinian Israelis have stayed home on election days in the past. Since the advent of the State of Israel, Arab-Israeli parties have averaged between three and 15 seats each election. Exit polls indicate that this year they will have secured 19. If either one of the two blocs would sit with the Arab-Israeli parties (and if the Arab-Israelis would agree to sit with them), that bloc would glide to an easy victory. But, as of this writing, that seems unlikely.

Over the next few days, the president of Israel, Isaac Herzog, will have the duty of deciding who gets to try to form a government first. Herzog’s responsibility is to try to oversee a transition that is as seamless as it can be. His influence can go a long way in pressuring either bloc leader to make serious concessions to its opponent or to the smaller parties that are in play. If, within the next 90 days, neither bloc can manage to form a government, then the country will be forced to schedule another election. (Who can forget the streak between 2019 and 2021, when Israel was forced to schedule four elections in half as many years?)

Where does all this leave Kaabneh and her family? The good news from Monday is that neither Smotrich nor his fellow hard-liner Ben Gvir is likely to be a part of any governing coalition. The opposition bloc will not sit with them, and Netanyahu will not be able to fit them into a coalition that would secure 61 seats. The money that Smotrich has used to outfit settler terrorists with drones, guns, and ATVs, and to secure them with farms with sprawling fields that once belonged to Palestinian shepherds, was money secured in the direct aftermath of the last elections in 2022. At the start of each government, the premier essentially bribes the heads of the various parties in his coalition with slush-fund money from the national budget, which they are empowered to use for their pet projects in exchange for promising to remain inside the government. It makes a great deal of difference that, as a result of this election, both Smotrich and Ben Gvir have no way to serve in the next government, barring another election that produces different results. Over the next 90 days, it will become clear whether their expulsion will stick.

The majority of Israelis voted on Monday to oust Netanyahu. But, as Americans know too well, the popular vote is not always decisive. The pioneers who divined a coalition government for the first Jewish state had a wicked sense of humor. It is almost inevitable in such a configuration that small parties secure outsize power. Perhaps the Palestinian Israeli electorate will be rewarded for evincing astonishing faith in democracy by voting on behalf of their brothers and sisters who have no such power.

items.title: This Is the Dumbest Culture-War Fight I’ve Ever Seen
items.description: I last visited the Cheesecake Factory in 2025 during a brief visit to Washington, D.C. I did not go there because I wanted cheesecake or anything else on the menu. The restaurant was attached to my hotel, and I felt ill, impossibly ill, so anything more ambiti
items.author: Sarah Jones
paragraphs: I last visited the Cheesecake Factory in 2025 during a brief visit to Washington, D.C. I did not go there because I wanted cheesecake or anything else on the menu. The restaurant was attached to my hotel, and I felt ill, impossibly ill, so anything more ambitious was out of the question. I have vague memories of walking through an empty lobby to the Factory itself, which was so gaudy I thought I hallucinated it. I picked up an order of chicken Alfredo, ate most of it in my room, and collapsed on the bed. Six months later, I learned I had type 2 diabetes. By then, my blood sugar was so out of control that I did ask myself if the pasta had something to do with it. Perhaps, by entering that monument to carbohydrates, I dealt my pancreas such a blow that it will never truly recover. Can you absorb diabetes from the air? From the sight of dessert in a refrigerated case? My endocrinologist says no. Whatever the truth, I know the Factory is closed to me. Not even the SkinnyLicious menu is safe. I am out of touch with the people now, if The Wall Street Journal is correct.

You see, Barack Obama made a joke. Last weekend, he said Donald Trump’s White House redecorations look like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” That was mildly funny, which is the best we can expect from a politician on the stump, and most people snorted and moved on. Not the right wing. “Making fun of chain restaurants is quite an angle for Democrats, who keep insisting that they haven’t forgotten the working man in Middle America,” sniped the Journal, that champion of the American worker. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent, net worth $600 million, dined at a Cheesecake Factory in protest. (He ordered the French Dip Cheeseburger, or the Diabetic’s Bane.) Obama’s comment “goes exactly to why Democrats lost the middle class, why they lost blue-collar voters,” Martha MacCallum said on Fox. Clay Travis, a right-wing sports commentator, apparently made up a story about visiting the Cheesecake Factory as a child.

Somehow, it gets dumber. Evan Barker, an UnHerd contributor who quit Democratic politics to rebrand as a contrarian working-class whisperer, has tweeted almost incessantly about the Obama joke since last weekend. “When I got to go there as a kid a few times it was a big deal, a fancy treat,” she posted. Barker says this is proof of her bona fides; as she would later inform Hasan Piker, she is “the real-deal bitch” who “lived in the trailer parks of Missouri.” At this point, I laughed in a way I hadn’t at Obama’s speech. I don’t know anyone who talks like that in real life, and I’m from rural Appalachia, which usually ranks near the top of the right wing’s taxonomy of Places That Get to Be Real America. Again, we don’t have any Cheesecake Factories back home. The closest location appears to be in Knoxville, Tennessee, which is quite a drive, and it opened in 2013, when I was 25 years old. I didn’t go to a Cheesecake Factory or even know what it was until I moved to D.C., Satan’s own metropolis, for work. In fact, many Factory locations are in the suburbs. On X, reporter Natalie Fertig observed that most rural Americans probably “live hours from any Cheesecake Factory and just see it as another urban chain with a comically long menu located in some high-end shopping center you’d probably hate parking in.” Olive Garden is another story, but I digress.

There is almost no point in fact-checking a manufactured outrage. Barker isn’t posting about the Cheesecake Factory because she has a unique vantage on working-class America and its preferences. I didn’t grow up with much money either, but personal experience is not an argument on its own. Sometimes it doesn’t even provide much insight. After all, Obama wasn’t making a joke at the expense of working-class aesthetics; the punch line is Donald Trump, a wealthy would-be authoritarian who spends more time on renovations than on governing. Barker — and Bessent, and MacCallum, and the editorial page of the Journal — are performing a style, not making a point. They miss the joke so they can stir up an outrage cycle, which can only survive on social media, and only for a few days. They’re dancing for the algorithm and a handful of cable TV bookers who should know better by now. One of Barker’s latest posts abandoned any pretense of public concern. “My Cheesecake Factory tweets have made the national news,” she boasted, because MacCallum had mentioned her on Fox.

That’s the American Dream to this crowd. Not universal health care or paid family leave or a living wage, but chicanery that pays. A thousand snake-oil salesmen lurk offstage, dreaming of their big moment and the McMansions they’ll buy. (I can make fun of McMansions because I’m a Real American who grew up in a snake-infested ranch home.) And why shouldn’t they dream? J.D. Vance is the vice-president of the United States. Clearly anyone can call themselves a tribune of the people and make it work, as long as they attack the same religions, ethnic groups, sexualities, and gender identities their patrons happen to despise. Nothing is real because nothing has to be real.

In the right’s fantasyland, the Cheesecake Factory is a temple to American values. The failed Cracker Barrel rebrand was an offense to Mamaw and Papaw, for whom it is a cherished third space. Bud Light betrayed the working class because of a single brand partnership with a trans woman, who received death and bomb threats after conservatives made an example of her. The Obama presidency was itself a catalyst for so many fake outrages that I can hardly remember them all. Remember when Michelle Obama wanted healthier school lunches for children? A horror, because “there must be recognition that parents — not the first lady or Congress — know what’s best for their children,” a Heritage Foundation analyst complained. Remember when Obama wore a tan suit? The beer summit?

Of course, this kind of thing goes much farther back. I was an Evangelical kid in the 1990s and early 2000s; I remember when Jerry Falwell said Tinky Winky, the Teletubbies character, was gay because he was purple, which is “the gay-pride color,” and wore a triangle, which is “the gay-pride symbol.” I remember the Disney boycotts. I remember a frenzy over The Lion King because the stars in a night scene allegedly spelled “sex” to corrupt America’s children. I know that in 2015, an influencer named Joshua Feuerstein filmed a video wearing a Jesus shirt and a handgun to accuse Starbucks of taking “Christ and Christmas” off its holiday cups. The outrage never ends. It never gets smarter and or more factual. The snake will keep eating its tail as long as someone has a book to sell, or a career to launch, or an office to win, so: forever.

Nevertheless, I do think our cheesecake defenders are beginning to exhaust the well. At some point, there is a bottom. They may dig through it, hoping to unleash a subterranean monster, but if nothing happens and they bore their audience, the effort won’t matter. People have other things to worry about. The Cheesecake Factory cycle is so detached from human experience, so half-hearted an outrage, that I feel a kind of embarrassment for the people who are trying to keep it alive. Karoline Leavitt says that Democrats “can’t appreciate beauty.” Okay? The White House called the Cheesecake Factory “a great American institution” and threatened a surprise of some kind. I considered many possibilities but not the inevitable dull reality, which turned out to be an AI-generated video of Trump waving to a crowd in front of a yassified Cheesecake Factory.

But no circus can improve Trump’s historically low approval numbers or his party’s chances of retaining the House next week. Many Americans can’t afford groceries, let alone a meal at the Cheesecake Factory. Because of the war on Iran, gas prices have risen to an average of more than $4 a gallon nationwide. Diabetes keeps me out of most chains, but it does remind me that 41 percent of households surveyed by the American Diabetes Association in 2026 had to ration, delay, or skip insulin because of costs over the last 12 months. Outrage may keep a grift going, but voters can’t eat it or save their lives with it. Reality still matters — to most of us.

items.title: Every Way Trump Might Mess With the Midterms
items.description: In Donald Trump’s mind, elections anywhere, in America or around the world, have only two possible outcomes: victory for him, his party, and whomever he regards as a friend or ally, or a fraudulently stolen result. He famously took the country to the brink of
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: In Donald Trump’s mind, elections anywhere, in America or around the world, have only two possible outcomes: victory for him, his party, and whomever he regards as a friend or ally, or a fraudulently stolen result. He famously took the country to the brink of a constitutional crisis after refusing to accept defeat in 2020. He made claims of Democratic ballot-box stuffing after the 2018 and 2022 midterms. Even when he won his breakthrough victory in 2016, he argued (without a shred of evidence) that Hillary Clinton’s popular vote victory was the result of millions of “illegal votes.” His bizarre boasts of a landslide victory in 2024 also depend on the false theory that his opponents massively cheated.

A Washington Post analysis this week found “nearly 300 statements in speeches, in press remarks and online that question the integrity of elections” by Trump during his second term. He has signaled repeatedly that barring radical changes in voter rolls and voting methods, the 2026 midterm elections will be fatally tainted. He said that “we won’t have a Country any longer” if Congress did not pass his SAVE America Act, which would have federalized election administration overnight and imposed stringent new voter ID requirements along with restrictions on voting by mail. The bill was not passed, but that was just one of many, many steps Trump has taken and will yet take to avoid and reverse any adverse 2026 election results. Here’s an overview of what’s happened and what to watch out for.
What Trump has already tried and failed to do

Aside from the SAVE America Act, Trump has been battling since regaining the presidency to insert the federal government into constitutionally assigned state and local election administrations by executive order. A March 2025 EO sought to impose new proof-of-citizenship requirements and ban receipt of mail ballots after Election Day; it was knocked down by the U.S. Supreme Court in June of 2026. A March 2026 EO sought to set up a scheme whereby the U.S. Postal Service would refuse to deliver mail ballots to voters not certified by the Trump administration as eligible to vote. That too was struck down by SCOTUS in September of 2026, partly because of the proximity of the midterms and partly because only states and Congress can regulate elections.

Most recently, a federal judge has blocked Trump administration efforts to force California to reject mail ballots cast by voters it deems possible noncitizens (based on dubious federal data). The administration is now making a similar demand of the state of Washington, which is also likely to be rejected by the courts.

The administration also attempted a preemptive strike on Alaska’s certification of its Senate election. As our contributor Elie Honig has explained, the Justice Department sent out what looked like a feeler to gauge the tolerance of courts for a future gambit by preemptively challenging any future certification by the state of Alaska of a U.S. Senate victory by Democrat Mary Peltola on grounds that the state impermissibly allowed someone with the same name as incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan to remain on the general election ballot. The DoJ’s lawsuit is flimsy on multiple grounds and again appears to ignore the Constitution’s clear consignment of election administration to the states and to Congress. A federal judge has already signaled likely rejection of the suit. But it could be a harbinger of things to come.

As far as what to watch out for, there are still multiple ways to potentially undermine the integrity of the midterms — before, on, and after Election Day. Trump and his administration and allies may yet try to:
Undermine confidence in election integrity and justify possible interference

Though the president’s most blatant efforts at election interference have so far been blocked by Congress and the courts, he and his allies have kept up a relentless drumbeat of ill-supported claims that Democrat chicanery is underway, as the Washington Post reports:

Nearly 600 high-profile, right-wing social media accounts, podcasts and other online media have published more than 7,000 statements questioning the election’s integrity so far this year, a Washington Post analysis found. That messaging has, in particular, pushed overstated claims that noncitizens are on voter rolls and that mail-in ballots enable widespread fraud — themes that are twice as prevalent as they were during the 2024 election cycle, The Post’s analysis found.
Interfere with the voting process

While denying they have any plans to disrupt voting around the country, Trump administration figures and local Republican activists have refused to rule out efforts to interfere with what they regard as suspicious people trying to vote. Possible interventions that worry election officials include ICE agents carrying out immigration-enforcement sweeps at or near polling places, federal law-enforcement personnel or even National Guard or Army troops being deployed to deal with “disturbances” while voters are voting, and private- or public-sector election “observers” behaving in an aggressive or intimidating manner. As the New York Times reports, such possibilities are dominating the run-up to Election Day in many parts of the country, though “the tricky part, officials said, is predicting what shape that interference might take while also recognizing that it might not materialize at all.”
Prematurely declare victory on Election Night

If the past is prologue, early returns based on Election Day voting are likely to tilt Republican despite the near-certainty that later-counted in-person early votes and mail ballots will tilt the other way. If it plays out that way, everyone should prepare for an Election Night victory claim by Trump modeled on what he did in 2020. He would almost certainly describe subsequent ballots as manipulated either by massive noncitizen voting or (in blue jurisdictions) outright ballot-box stuffing, setting the stage for future challenges to the results while inflaming supporters over the alleged “steal.”

Only a big and immediate Democratic tide could forestall this gambit, and even then the president can be expected to allege fraudulent voting as he has all year and, indeed, all of his political career.

You can expect the administration, and in some red jurisdictions, state and local election officials, to react to reports of election irregularities aggressively, perhaps by the seizure of ballots or voting machines. Again, the number of ballots in question could be less important to Team Trump than creating the general impression of a “troubled” or “rigged” election. You can also expect a lot of agitation on MAGA social media over each and every case.
Mess with certifications of results

At the same time, the first step toward official certification of the results will begin as counties (or in a few states, towns) send results certifications to state-election officials. This process will continue for weeks in some jurisdictions, particularly those with heavy voting by mail and/or post-election day receipt of postmarked mail ballots. Post-election audits of election equipment are required prior to local certification in many states, and in very close elections recounts can delay certification as well. All such procedures might offer opportunities for Trump and his allies to allege illegal voting, vote tampering, or improper canvassing of results. We can expect all the vast resources of the Justice Department to be made available to legal challenges to Democratic victories in congressional and statewide races.

As was evident in the last truly disputed national election, in 2020, once elections are certified by the states (most often by secretaries of state, occasionally by governors or judicial panels), they are very difficult to dislodge legally. As with local certifications, the timelines vary significantly, with some states (e.g., Florida) certifying elections within two weeks of voting while others (e.g., California) with more elaborate vote-counting procedures not certifying results until well into December. It’s worth noting that 25 states have Republican secretaries of state and 22 have Democrats (three states do not have that office).
Set up another early January showdown

When it comes to control of Congress, the key date to remember is January 3, 2027, when the Republican-controlled 119th Congress ceases to exist and the 120th Congress begins. The general assumption is that every state-certified new member of the House and the Senate will be sworn in. But there are asterisks that must be noted. The Senate is the judge of its own membership, and theoretically the Republicans who control the Senate could refuse to seat new Democratic senators (potentially Mary Peltola, on the shaky grounds asserted in DoJ’s rejected lawsuit) initially and maintain control. In the House, the clerk — an appointed, nonpartisan employee of the chamber — prepares a roster of new members and swears them in. There are scenarios where outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson could fire the clerk just prior to January 3 and install a hireling who would not observe state certification of enough Democratic House members to flip control.

Such a coup is possible, particularly after weeks and months of disinformation about stolen elections and perhaps another encouraging mob of “patriot” rioters in Washington. But it would be difficult to pull off and at a minimum would require an extraordinary degree of Republican Party discipline around maneuvers clearly designed to thwart the judgement of the American electorate.

Donald J. Trump would not hesitate to turn January 3 into another January 6 and this time carry out the coup to a successful conclusion. But would the rest of his party do this dangerous favor for a lame-duck president? Democrats would be well advised to lawyer up and perhaps make all this talk irrelevant by winning a victory so large on November 3 that it cannot be overturned.

items.title: John Early and Kate Berlant Are Totally Unbelievable
items.description: John Early and Kate Berlant are the most influential, forward thinking comedians of the 21st century.
items.author: Joan Summers
paragraphs: John Early and Kate Berlant are the most influential, forward thinking comedians of the 21st century.

I might even say they're visionaries of the filmic medium, although one or the other might roll their eyes at the thought. Less effusive sentences tend to fail when entertainment writers in the know attempt to describe the cosmic pull they've had on art and comedy over the last 14 odd years.

Their latest gift to the world is Early's genre-shifting Maddie's Secret, an homage to the daytime film of the same name. Melodramatic to the point of complete absurdity, it is a singular work that pulls together every loose thread of combined comedic output. In full sincerity, I have thought about it every single day since. Not just because of the film's naked humanity, uncovered through the absurd, but through the fulfillment of what feels like prophecy between them. "This whole movie was like that for me. I very innocently thought I was playing with these archetypes or these genres or these references that felt so far away from me. I thought I was safe, in other words," Early tells me. "And then before I knew it, I was like, 'Oh my God, this is profoundly personal.' It was a very emotional experience."

A bit on the nose, I arrive to our interview with my hair in rollers and a half-face of makeup on, nearly ready for a work event that follows and a living commentary on online media culture and beauty standards, which the film excavates to depths never seen before. Early laughs and Berlant waves off my apologies, and all together, we're off to the races.

On that film: Maddie's Secret follows budding social media chef Maddie, played by Early, as a childhood eating disorder circles the block amidst her rapidly accelerating online fame. Berlant plays Dina, an archetypal lesbian with a keen interest in Maddie's wellbeing, for better or worse, alongside a host of familiar faces to the combined Early-Berlant comedic multiverse. Kristen Johnson and Vanessa Bayer among them deliver career high performances as Maddie's bewitching mother and eventual rehab bunkmate respectively.

"I tend not to like when movies very self-consciously try to correct for the ills of past films by being like, 'Let's give Dina a hopeful arc.' There is something funny about being like, "No, this is opera." This is a Greek tragedy," says Early. "I wanted the stakes of this movie to be Greek. I didn't want them to feel educational or like some sort of corrective."

Thrillingly, longtime fans will also see unintentional nods at their perfect recreation of the iconic dance sequence from Showgirls, alongside the omnipresent dread in the short film Rachel and Early's unabashed love of getting up in drag for characters like Vicky, the queen of denim. In the case of that Showgirls nod, I seem to surprise them both that there is a near 1:1 dance movement that occurs in both. Early laughs, admitting "
For more on Charles Busch, the naked humanity of melodrama and Kate Berlant's least favorite tacos in Los Angeles, read our full interview below.

I want to start by saying I loved your guys' movie. It was transcendent. I'm a huge Douglas Sirk fan and Charles Busch fan, so this was a real treat for me. I've been following your work for so long, and I was immediately reminded during the dance sequence of your Showgirls recreation, which is a staple in my household. Movement comes back a lot in your collaborations together. Even in your special, you play two indignant dance toddlers.
Why dance? Where does dance come into your friendship?

John: To me, the reason why I choose dance in our various projects is there's something very audacious about it. It's kind of like a dare. It's like we're going to learn choreography, actually. You think this is just a little sketch, or you think this is some low-budget ass movie? No, we're going to have a full dream ballet in the middle of the movie. We're going to learn choreography. We're going to execute it. We're going to hire professional dancers. There's something about choreography that immediately, I think, telegraphs a certain kind of, maybe this is totally defensive or desperate of me to do this, but it tells people that a certain amount of care went into this. And I think that is on some level important to me. It's like a kind of showmanship thing, where it's like I'm not making some fucking mumble core indie where we're sitting on a fucking couch with too much head room. I'm not doing that. I want to make something that requires some effort. I mean, sometimes I feel like it's possible that it feels almost aggressive or too dense or heavy for the audience. Jesus, we get it. But I would like to think that people hopefully go, oh, they care about us. They wanted to give us an experience.
Kate: Totally. I'm reminded that we've done that on stage too, John. John and I have done so many choreographed dances on stage from Marfa, Texas to-
John: And we choreographed that, right?

Kate:I know. We did a choreographed dance to "Can't Feel My Face", when that was top 40, you were like, "That's a fun kind of ironic choice."... I was going to say, I have a personal aversion to learning choreography. It really frustrates me. Actually, John, did I tell you about the workout class I went to? I didn't know they were teaching you choreography.
John: Oh yes, you did, but you have to say it, though.

Kate: Well, it was a workout class. Then one day, it was like, oh, it's like dance workout. And I was like, okay, sure. And I went, and then I quickly realized, okay, so we're going to learn a couple moves. And I was so pissed. The entire class I was working up the courage to leave, and I was like, "Just go.” I was like, "Just leave. What is this? You're hostage?" The main reason I couldn't leave is because it was curtains to leave, and I didn't want to get lost in the curtains and then make too much of a show of leaving. But I stayed. There was one other girl who clearly was like, "I thought this was fucking Pilates." Anyway, it's because of various learning and spatial disorders that I have, but I love to dance, and dance is a huge part of my life.
John: No, it is. Kate and I do have this thing where it's like we can mimic certain dance styles without training.
Kate: I've been asked if I have dance training several times. I've been asked if I have acting training several times.

It was one of those moments where, when you reach out your hand to John's character and pull him into the dance, I was with my boyfriend watching the screener, and I kind of did the pointing at the screen Leonardo DiCaprio thing. They did that in the Showgirls bit. Literally.
John: Oh yeah. [laughs] I didn't even think about that.
I was like, “it must be unintentional”, just because it makes the scene. But just as a longtime follower, I was like, “Guys, they did the thing. They literally did the thing.”

You begin the film with this beautiful monologue about all of these things that are happening in LA. You're talking about the jasmine, the Filipino and the Mexican food, and they're making cacio e pepe in the back. As two LA people, also New York too — let's give credit to New York and honor to New York. But in the context of LA, what are some things you want not to be happening in LA right now?
John: I mean, lines. I mean, everyone's talking about it, but-

Kate: Well, it's the biggest thing. It's like Tito's Tacos. The line is around the block. The food's inedible. I'm from LA, so I get to say that. And then it's like next door, this taco place that has zero line and the food-
John: Just go to that place.
Kate: Listen, I'm a matcha girl. Sorry, not sorry.
It's sad that you have to apologize for liking it.

Kate: I won't apologize for matcha because I've been doing macha for a long time. But I will say, and this is my own thing, I gasped with excitement because I saw that there was a new matcha. It's called rock. But the point is the cream top matcha. I do a cream top matcha as a fun treat a couple times a month. I'm not getting cream top once a month, once every five weeks. I don't know. But I guess I'm feeling a little bit — it's so obvious to even say it, fatigue for the cream top, but Maru, they took away their cream top for matcha. You can get it for coffee! Don't worry. They took away their cream top matcha, because they were clearly like, "We don't want this culture." And I thought that was worth noting.

John: I mean, I guess LA does have so much. I mean, when I first moved to LA, and this is where so much of this movie is born out of, I was shocked by this very kind of Jonathan Gold thing of, “Oh my God, the beauty of the restaurant that's actually in a strip mall. Oh my God, it's a hole in the wall, and there's fluorescent lights. Yet it's the best sushi you've ever had.” And it was very exciting when I first moved there, to explore these things earnestly and to feel like you were stumbling upon these genius restaurants. And now, of course, there's just a little bit of a sadness where it all feels very algorithmically determined, and it's very hard to feel like a kind of organic relationship to a restaurant now. It's all on a list.
Kate: The state sanctioned places to go.
One of the things that I was really struck by, just obviously so much of it takes place within the office and the lighting in that office, I know obviously we're–
Kate: We were just talking about it.

I was like, “How intentional was that?” It felt so Sirk-ian to me, just this insane backlighting and the glow around everything. Obviously, there's stuff happening with the filmmaking there, but I would love to know how much of that was intentional and how much was it that the space literally just looked like that?

John: Well, it was totally intentional. There ended up being some unintentional elements that made it extremely exaggerated. But the key reference point for the Gourmaybe space was Adrian Lyne and Flashdance, 9 ½ weeks, and Unfaithful, even. Adrian Lyne has all these big, beautiful old warehouse spaces in his movies, and there's always tons of giant shafts of sunset light.

In Flashdance, there's fans that create a moving shadow. And so I was with the DP and the grip and electric department, I was like, “Don't be polite. Really pump it up. Turn it up.” I want it to feel artificial. The big thing with Adrian Lyne is haze, even in apartments. There's lots of unmotivated haze in his movies, and it just makes everything feel more dreamlike and beautiful. And so again, we were a bunch of amateurs. This was so many people's first feature. And so we were pumping rooms full of haze any chance we got. Unfortunately, the treatment center did not let us use haze, but every space where we were allowed to use haze, we would use it.

And then what happened actually was that it made the image so murky. We used too much haze. And so then in color correction, in order to see the people clearly, we had to brighten everything even more. It's many layers worth of artificiality that makes it as extreme as it is. But yeah, I mean, that's the thing, I wanted to make these kinds of miserable jobs, these kind of media food content influencer jobs that all live inside our phones. I wanted to make them feel more romantic and cinematic.

It's playing so much in past melodrama, TV and movies, which you've talked about extensively. One of the things I always love about Douglas Sirk movies is this sort of naked humanity that melodrama exposes, where in the extremity of the emotions, it gets at something much truer. Dina's arc in the film was very unexpected to me, and it took it to a place of, speaking of Sirk, you become an eye surgeon so you could fix the woman you accidentally blinded after her husband dies. I'm curious how you threaded that needle with Dina. What was the inspiration there?

Kate: It's John's movie! I just showed up, hit my mark. But oh my God, I mean, I remember John telling me about the character and it was like, it's such an archetype. There's no, “send me reference images of what this looks like.” We all know her.
John: Kate is obviously just so gifted and was able to immediately tap into this archetype with very little discussion, but...
Kate: I love what you said about it being heightened.... It's like our philosophy in life and in work always, it's like the artifice is the way to the reality and there isn't this-
John: Exaggeration is even a pathway.
Kate: That feels more like what life feels like.
John: That's the job of a movie, it is not to represent some texture of real life, some sort of subdued texture of real life. You push in and go-
Kate: And it's like a perversion of what actual real life feels like. Or it's like, “How dare you tell me life doesn't feel like that?”
John: No, I know. I'm like, if I could punch the wall right now, I would.

That is what it feels like. That is how it feels, all the time. And I think that's what your comedy really plays into. By heightening it to such an extreme, you're getting at something almost more honest than if it was just a cut and dry movie about an influencer's life gone wrong.

John: Well, this whole movie was like that for me. I very innocently thought I was playing with these archetypes or these genres or these references that felt so far away from me. I thought I was safe, in other words. And then before I knew it, I was like, "Oh my God, this is profoundly personal." It was a very emotional experience writing it, acting it, and it's still emotional for me to watch it.

I think Kate's character is such a vessel for a lot of the emotion in the movie. It's all in Kate's eyes. But in terms of the queer tropes, I mean, I was concerned about that and also completely titillated by the idea of going deep into it. I mean, there was something quite funny to me actually about not being cautious about it — of the tragic queer character. Because also, it's like, I'm queer, and yet I'm playing a straight cis woman — a blonde girl, a very kind of normal girl, just some ally. I tend not to like when movies very self-consciously try to correct for the ills of past films by being like, "Let's give Dina a hopeful arc." There is something funny about being like, "No, this is opera." This is a Greek tragedy. I mean, that's the thing, it is Greek. I wanted the stakes of this movie to be Greek. I didn't want them to feel educational or like some sort of corrective. And it's not just Kate's character, people go through hell in this movie.

It's very Dante's Inferno like that, where everyone here is in hell. I wanted to say too, films really struggle with technological cues like phones, Siri, TV. And I really love the way you did it in this film. There's a moment that calls to mind a crossfade, with the TV. Or when she's on the phone with her mom and goes “Hey Siri, call mom,” with the dramatic lighting in the back and the sound cue. Maybe that's all we need to make texting believable — ireally blown-out dramatic lighting.

Kate: Thank you. I love that because it's so true. Every movie now, it's like, the texts. And John, today I actually thought of the movie, because I was on a beautiful walk, and I texted my mom. And I said, "It's so beautiful outside, exclamation point, send." And I was like, "That is- "
John: Well, to me, one of the funniest lines of the movie is, "Hey, Siri, call Mom."
I wrote that line down to ask about it because I loved it so much.

John: I've been in a few screenings where people really laugh at that. I've seen haters comment on the trailer, “There are no jokes.” And I'm like, that to me, is a joke that's hard to define. There's something that's very funny about me very sincerely saying, "Hey, Siri, call mom." And it's also like, it's true. I mean, she's trying to build up courage to speak to her mother, and yet she's using this blunt, ugly technological language of our moment.
And how polite you are to Siri in that moment was what really came through. The politeness, I love that.
Kate: It's like when you feel yourself obeying.

In the spirit of Maddie’s Secret, you both should find a film on the Lifetime original channel called Stalked by My Doctor. There's seven of them. When I was watching this film, I was like, I just have to introduce you both to the Stalked by My Doctor franchise.
Kate: I'm going to look it up right now.
Yeah, it's a franchise. Julia Roberts' brother is the lead in all of them.
And it's always like a girl breaks her ankle, and then she finds this nice doctor at the ER who becomes a little bit too involved in her life—
Kate: By the way, he looks like a predatory lesbian, in the poster that I'm looking at.
It's very melodrama. It's very Douglas Sirk.
Kate: This is a real gift.

items.title: 'Artificial', Andrew Garfield, Olivia Wilde, and Seth Rogen Join Vanity Fair’s Slate of Screening Room Programming
items.description: Vanity Fair is pleased to announce its second wave of programming for its Screening Room event series in Los Angeles and New York.
items.author: John Ross
paragraphs: Vanity Fair is pleased to announce its second wave of programming for its Screening Room event series in Los Angeles and New York.

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will be held at LACMA’s Peter Zumthor–designed Steve Tisch Theater from November 13–15. On Saturday, November 14, the weekend’s marquee screening will be Luca Guadagnino’s highly anticipated new film, Artificial. Guadagnino’s story follows OpenAI and the two-decade artificial intelligence arms race; as AI becomes more powerful, a battle wages in Silicon Valley over who gets to control this important technology. Director Guadagnino, Andrew Garfield, Yura Borisov, and Monica Barbaro will participate in a Q&A after the film.
Scene Selection Live will return with The Invite costars Olivia Wilde and Seth Rogen revisiting some of their pivotal work in film and television.

John Malkovich, the latest winner of the Volpi Cup for best actor at the Venice Film Festival, will join the Q&A for Wild Horse Nine. Penélope Cruz and Miguel Bernardeau will join Friday night’s La Bola Negra Q&A.

Just a few weeks later, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will come to New York, where screenings and events will take place at the Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6. Alex Gibney, the director of Musk, will participate in a conversation with esteemed tech journalist Kara Swisher about covering the richest man on the planet.
Naza, the winner of the Special Jury Prize at this year’s Venice Film Festival, will screen in New York City with a special introduction.
For more information on Screening Room and to see the schedule of events, click here.

items.title: A Highly Opinionated Guide to the Best Horror Movies to Watch This Halloween
items.description: Halloween is a special kind of holiday, and it requires a very specific kind of film. It needs to scare you in the moment, give you a couple of laughs, satisfy (but not depress) you with its ending…and boomerang back to give you the creeps the next time you’re
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: Halloween is a special kind of holiday, and it requires a very specific kind of film. It needs to scare you in the moment, give you a couple of laughs, satisfy (but not depress) you with its ending…and boomerang back to give you the creeps the next time you’re alone in the dark.

But when you’re dealing with a candy-based month like October, you don’t want to mess with anything that feels like homework (sorry, Robert Eggers’s Nosferatu) or leaves you feeling worse about the world than you did before you pressed play (like David Gordon Green’s second and third Halloween films). You can watch gore for the sake of gore, nubile teens being tortured, or small children and pets die the rest of the year. The best horror movies for Halloween need to offer something a little richer, that mix of shivers and catharsis that makes this time of year so darned fun.

Below you’ll find our guide to the best horror movies available on streaming right now, all of which tick those Halloween-specific boxes. So fire up the popcorn popper, turn down the lights, and nestle into your favorite spot on the couch.
Available on: Netflix and Fubo

Ridley Scott had no idea what he was kicking off when he pulled together this ragtag crew of blue-collar workers awoken from stasis sleep to investigate a derelict ship. It’s easy to forget what a stunning and fresh film this was when it was released just two years after Star Wars. (My parents, assuming it was a similar film, took me to see it in the theater when it dropped. That experience I had at eight years old is probably why I am writing this article for you now, so parents, be warned.) The franchise has taken a lot of directions, some of which were ambitious failures (Prometheus) and some of which remain potential-filled side stories (Alien: Earth). But the OG, with the revelation that is Sigourney Weaver’s Ellen Ripley and the artist H.R. Giger’s innovative creature design, still feels relevant, vital, and terrifying.

Is Kane Parsons’s big-screen debut prepared to stand the test of time? Maybe not, but like its classmate, Curry Barker’s Obsession (now on Peacock), this extremely strong debut of a young YouTube auteur seems just as historically significant as some of the other innovations here. Obsession picks comedy and gore over Backrooms’ claustrophobic dread, which is why the A24 hit made the list—I suspect that in the long run, its striking depiction of trauma and toxic masculinity will have more staying power than Obsession’s villainous (and yes, Michael Johnston, he’s villainous) Cat Person. You know what? We can answer the question of comparable impact in a couple weeks, by tallying how many Halloween partygoers are dressed as Pirate Clark against how many are wearing this sad sack hoodie. Let’s circle back then.
Available on: Starz and Philo

Before dorks were hashtagging everything with #SnyderCut—gosh, before there were even hashtags—Zack Snyder rebooted George Romero’s mall-centric zombie movie with a level of style, humor, and scares that he hasn’t exhibited since. (Netflix’s Army of the Dead is fun, but comparably toothless.) A preretirement Sarah Polley, a post–Pulp Fiction Ving Rhames, and Phil from Modern Family go up against Olympic-sprinter-level zombies, a concept launched just two years before with 28 Days Later (Apple TV+). 28 Days is good, but Dawn is supersized in an especially American way. It’s the movie I go back to most often when I think about what to do—and not to do—when the zombie apocalypse comes.
Available on: AMC+, Roku, and Kanopy

Director Neil Marshall followed his promising 2002 werewolf film, Dog Soldiers (Amazon Prime, Fubo, and Shudder), with this all-female cave exploration movie that ruined me—both for driving behind trucks loaded with pipes and doing anything underground ever again. It’s got the one-two punch of spooky monsters and human ones, and it doesn’t argue that the supernatural beasts are the worst ones in the yarn. Oh, one thing that’s important to note is that the film had one ending when released in the UK and another for its stateside drop; as a depressed citizen of the US, I prefer the happier North American version.
Available on: Hulu, Peacock, and Philo

Has there ever been a more lankily beautiful offscreen-onscreen couple than Jeff Goldblum and Geena Davis? The former famously read David Cronenberg’s script for this movie while lying in bed with the latter, who was so intrigued by his visceral reaction as he read that she pursued her own role in the film. It’s sexual jealousy that drives Goldblum’s scientist to take his ill-advised teleporter ride with an insect stowaway, and his growing realization that the experience didn’t make him miraculously healthier, but instead is killing the best parts of him, is body horror at its finest. You’ll never look at your medicine cabinet—or a box of doughnuts—in the same light ever again.
Available on: Fubo, Philo, and AMC+

Here, let me save you a lot of time: The only Halloween you really need is John Carpenter’s original, especially when it comes to legitimate scares. Sure, you can do what my husband and I did last Halloween and watch them all in order, including the Paul Rudd–starring Halloween: The Curse of Michael Myers (Cinemax and HBO Max) and Josh Hartnett’s film debut, Halloween H20 (same). But stop before you get to Rob Zombie’s 2007 iteration and let Michael Myers rest. He did such a great job of scaring us just by driving down the street (best not to ask how he learned to get behind the wheel) or standing amid some falling leaves in the first film. The rest are increasingly warped and inferior attempts—Pirate Clarks, if you will—to capture John Carpenter’s early brilliance.
Available on: Kanopy and Tubi

Three years before he directed the slightly too cuddly Gremlins (HBO Max), Joe Dante brought us this dark werewolf tale, which takes on 1970s encounter-group culture, marital infidelity, and the cannibalistic nature of broadcast journalism. Now, I know what you’re thinking: All werewolf movies are inherently cheesy. You are not wrong! Transformation scenes can be unintentionally laughable, and no one has fully figured out how to make a wolf-human hybrid look less like a fall-season impulse buy at Home Depot and more like a terrifically terrifying beast. (Maybe Eggers will crack the code with his upcoming Werwulf, which drops on Christmas Day?) Dante and practical-effects master Rob Bottin get pretty close, though—but the scariest moment, in my opinion, involves only the werewolf’s hand.
Available on: Amazon Prime

There’s nothing supernatural in this Paul Walker–starring road movie, but that doesn’t mean it’s not scary as hell. The late Fast & Furious lynchpin got back in a car for this thriller just a few months after the now ubiquitous franchise made its debut, but this time he—alongside Steve Zahn—is a hapless near-victim of a rage-filled truck driver pissed off after the pair catfish him via CB radio. It’s all made even more intense because you never see the driver pursuing them, you just hear his voice, provided by the great Ted “Buffalo Bill” Levine. Director John Dahl made his mark in the early 1990s with a series of desert-set noir films, detoured into whatever Rounders was (Oreo spon?), and you could feel him exhaling and having a blast with this very funny, very scary film. Ever made a cross-country road trip and been unsettled when you see the same driver again and again? This movie is the worst-case version of that.
Available on: Netflix, Peacock, and Kanopy

While some prefer the original Japanese version, Ringu (AMC+ and Kanopy), Gore Verbinski’s English-language adaptation streamlines the scares to a stiletto point. For many Americans, this movie was the first time they were exposed to the “creepy pale girl with long hair” trope, now common to the point of parody. But the story of a cursed video tape somehow manifested by an evil kid named Samara holds up, jam-packed with unsettling images backed with an actual plot (yes, friends, it’s possible). Even after 22 years of rip-offs, Samara’s final reveal is still best viewed through one’s fingers.
Available on: Hulu, Peacock, and Kanopy

Ethan Hawke’s author/shitty person, Ellison Oswalt, is my favorite horror movie scribe, and I’d wear all of his writerly cardigans in a heartbeat. (I’m not counting Jack Torrance of 1980’s The Shining—available on HBO Max—as a writer; that guy never managed to produce.) Oswalt somehow manages to move his family into an infamous murder house without them finding out, then assumes he’ll be forgiven once his book about the case makes its inevitable splash. Surprise, surprise, the crime had a supernatural basis—and is linked to a number of others, all brutally depicted in reels of film left in his attic. Over a decade before Weapons’s Aunt Gladys (Amazon Prime and HBO Max) was luring kids to the basement, Sinister’s monster was enticing them to do far worse.

Jordan Peele’s Get Out (Peacock, Fubo, and FX) confirmed he was the real horror deal, and two years later, Us suggested his ambitions were more aligned with Stanley Kubrick than John Carpenter. What is this movie—about a trip to the Santa Cruz, CA, seaside that ends in a pair of Lupita Nyong’os in a bizarre and violent dance set to an instrumental version of Luniz’s “I Got 5 On It”—actually about? Is it about the people who make all the stuff we privileged classes thoughtlessly consume? Or is it an examination of the nasty, brutish, and short lives of the animals we eat? You can debate questions like that if you’re feeling clever, but you can also just dig how terrifying it would be to look down the driveway and see yourself, but in a set of red coveralls and driving gloves.
Wes Craven’s New Nightmare (1994)
Available on: AMC+ and Philo

I don’t think you need me to tell you that the late Wes Craven’s 1984 classic Nightmare on Elm Street (HBO Max, Philo, and AMC+) is a pretty big deal—you are reading this article, after all. But is it scary in a way that haunts you after? Even at his launch, Freddy Krueger is pretty corny, and a little too quick with a locker-room-level pun. New Nightmare is for grown-ups, Craven said at the time, a work aged up for his original audience, then a decade older. Marketed at the time as the horror genre’s take on Robert Altman’s Hollywood meta-take The Player, New Nightmare featured the original’s actors and director as themselves, exhibiting varying levels of comfort with their cult fame. This challenge is complicated when Freddy somehow makes the trip from the silver screen to the real world. Eventually, things get kind of goofy, as they always do in dreams. But it’ll be a while before you get Craven’s speech on the power of fiction to infect our real lives out of your head.
Available on: Amazon Prime, Roku, and Kanopy

Godzilla guy Adam Wingard bummed out legions of horror fans with his reboot of The Blair Witch Project, 2016’s completely unnecessary Blair Witch (I don’t recommend you watch it on Cinemax or HBO Max, but it’s a free country). But three years before, he thrilled them with this film, an elegant evisceration of the cliché of the final girl that plays like a Treehouse of Horror–style episode of Succession. It’s got terrifying animal masks, the worst-ever (and still kind of funny?) decapitation, and the hookiest earworm of a throwback signature tune, the Dwight Twilley Band’s “Looking for the Magic.” No ghosts, ghouls, or demons here, just the evil things that greed makes people do, at least until the little guy starts fighting back.

items.title: ‘Swipe Right on the Devil’ Exposes a Real-Life Tinder Murder
items.description: It’s been almost a decade since 24-year-old Sydney Loofe disappeared after connecting with a woman named Bailey Boswell on Tinder. After a single in-person date, Loofe would later learn that she had actually been messaging with a man named Aubrey Trail, who re
items.author: Savannah Walsh
paragraphs: It’s been almost a decade since 24-year-old Sydney Loofe disappeared after connecting with a woman named Bailey Boswell on Tinder. After a single in-person date, Loofe would later learn that she had actually been messaging with a man named Aubrey Trail, who referred to himself as a “powerful warlock,” at the head of a “coven,” which was, in reality, a coercive sex cult and criminal enterprise with Boswell as one of his “witches.” Boswell and Trail were in a romantic relationship themselves, a Bonnie and Clyde of online dating in small-town Nebraska. Within days of their first Tinder messages, Loofe was killed as a “sacrifice” by the coven’s leaders, her body dismembered and dumped in trash bags around a plot of rural land in small-town Nebraska.

In Swipe Right on the Devil, a new Ron Howard–produced, three-part true-crime series now streaming on Hulu, filmmaker Brian Biegel recounts the story of “witchcraft and its sister, black magic” in Wilber, Nebraska, as it “meets the modern-day digital dating world,” he tells Vanity Fair.

As part of the police investigation into Loofe’s death, authorities discovered that she had been recruited as the 13th member of Trail and Boswell’s “coven,” in which various women they met on dating apps were used for local thefts and sex in return for “love” and some money. “The headline is witchcraft, cult. But at its core is this more universal story of looking for belonging,” says producer Christopher St. John. “Obviously there’s the cautionary tale about tech.”
“With AI, it’s only going to get worse,” says executive producer and fellow Imagine Entertainment exec Sara Bernstein. “You really don’t know who you can trust.”

The documentary features interviews from multiple women who were scammed by Trail and Boswell, one of whom speaks in the third person to distance herself from the PTSD of her memories. “As documentarians, you want there to be a greater social value or conversation that can come,” says Bernstein, “as opposed to just retelling, frankly, what can be really graphic and gory details and having people relive their pain and suffering.”

In the documentary, Sydney’s sister Mackenzie Loofe expresses regret that she and her family didn’t offer more support regarding her sister’s sexuality. “Dating as a queer woman in middle America, there’s not a whole lot to choose from. Their way of coming out was through a dating app,” says Biegel. “So that alone made them vulnerable, because they really wanted to find their person. They wanted to feel a sense of belonging, and Sydney did. But what they couldn’t know, what was on the other side of the screen, was basically a trap waiting for them.”

The Loofe family “appreciated the opportunity to set the record straight” about Sydney, given what they felt was misleading press coverage around the case at the time of her murder, says St. John. “Sydney was misrepresented in their eyes as someone who was either involved in a crazy sex ring or involved in some sort of witchcraft, which she wasn’t,” he says. “She didn’t know these people, hadn’t met these people. It was this web of lies.”

The director spoke to Trail “on a daily basis for over a year until he agreed to give us audio and then eventually some video,” says Biegel. “Look, I watched the interviews the FBI had done with him, and he’s a game player. I also know he loves praise. So in order for me to build a rapport, I knew he was an artist, so I’m like, ‘Oh man, would you send me a painting?’ And his eyes opened up. I won him over.”

Once they had secured Trail’s participation from behind bars, they had to ensure it was used responsibly. “It’s a constant questioning, frankly, of everything he says, anything he’s promising,” says St. John. “We didn’t want to be another group of people manipulated by this guy, even from death row.”

Trail was sentenced to the death penalty following his trial in the summer of 2019. Boswell was convicted of first-degree murder and improper disposal of human remains in the fall of 2020 and was sentenced to life in prison the following year. “Bailey, we can say safely and without any doubt, is an incredibly complicated character. She wouldn’t talk to police, she wouldn’t talk to reporters, she wouldn’t talk to us,” says St. John. “She is a phantom at the center of this case. Since the trial, it seems she’s found it better to keep her cards close to her vest.”
