As for those who escaped Trail and Boswell, “after experiencing a very harrowing issue in their lives, the girls in Aubrey’s group and even the Loofe family—everyone involved in this case—have gone on and lived happy, successful lives,” says Biegel. “And there’s an important message in that. People are more resilient than you think—they overcame a lot, and continue to do so.”

items.title: ‘The Pet Cemetery Murders’: HBO’s Latest True-Crime Tale Is a Microcosm of American Trauma
items.description: Stephen King’s horror novel Pet Sematary (1983) was published roughly two years before the real-life death of Dorothy Thompson, who owned and operated the St. Bernard Parish pet cemetery until her 1985 murder. Strangled, suffocated, wrapped in chains, and thro
items.author: Savannah Walsh
paragraphs: Stephen King’s horror novel Pet Sematary (1983) was published roughly two years before the real-life death of Dorothy Thompson, who owned and operated the St. Bernard Parish pet cemetery until her 1985 murder. Strangled, suffocated, wrapped in chains, and thrown in the Mississippi River, mere miles from the popular pet burial spot she ran, it would take nearly three decades to catch and convict groundskeeper Brandon Nodier, who in July 2014 pleaded guilty to manslaughter as part of a plea agreement and was sentenced to 10 years in prison for Thompson’s death.

When introduced to Thompson’s story about three years ago by true-crime writer Mikita Brottman, then working on a book about the case, documentarian Philip Cairney was struck by the amount of “historic trauma” that could transpire on one piece of land. “It became a litany of tragedy,” says Cairney, “the more you looked, the more you found.” So begins HBO’s The Pet Cemetery Murders, airing through October 25, in which Cairney unearths decades of death and dysfunction on one plot of rural Southern property.

“The killing occurred after Nodier duped Thompson into transferring possession of the property to him, then feared he would lose it after she sued to have the transaction voided,” St. Bernard Sheriff's Office colonel John Doran said at the time, as reported by Reuters. Police reopened the case in 2009 after a witness came forward saying Nodier had told him he was the killer and that Thompson’s ghost was haunting the witness’s dreams, Doran said in the documentary. “People genuinely almost fall down a foxhole when they become involved with this bit of land,” Cairney says, “because it does seem to suck you in and not let you go.”

Decades before the documentary’s central crimes, the Louisiana land was tied to racial violence—first against the region’s Indigenous population by white colonizers, then the dozens of formerly enslaved Black people murdered by mobs of white men during what became known as the Reconstruction-era 1868 St. Bernard Parish Massacre. “These are America’s original sins—enslavement, Native American genocide, women’s role in society,” Cairney says. “It’s that rich, fertile soil—to use a terrible metaphor—that means any story, if it’s got those layers, is interesting.”

Twenty years after the investigation into Thompson’s death went cold, in 2005, Hurricane Katrina wiped out key evidence from the case and decimated much of the pet cemetery. Touring the resulting land, “you’re forced to look Katrina in the eye,” says Cairney, who says being from Scotland offered him the right amount of distance from and perspective on the American atrocities tangled up with the place. “As an outsider, I wasn’t coming with the same cultural, social, political baggage that Americans might,” he tells VF. “The trauma of America is in the land, and whether that’s a metaphor or a literal fact you can decide for yourself. But the people in these areas with histories of enslavement, colonization, opioids, they’re dealing with the trauma, and it’s getting passed on from generation to generation.”

Even production on The Pet Cemetery Murders faced some paranormal activity, “from cameras jamming during interviews, to ghost sightings,” the director says. “The director of photography, whenever he put his camera on the ground, it would flip between stills and video. When he would pick it up, it would be fine. So you’re forced to reconcile an empirical rationalist worldview with something far more inexplicable.”

There are plenty of spirits who could be lurking around. In addition to the residents of the cemetery (a snake named Sarita that performed on The Johnny Carson Show was among the more famous pets laid to rest), a string of other deaths occurred on the property while Thompson had run of the place with her mother, Grace. As recounted in the docuseries, two men who were married to Dorothy died on the same plot of land—the first was fatally shot by Dorothy in 1970 in what authorities determined was an act of self-defense, and the second death, in 1978 by two gunshots to the back, was ruled a suicide by police.

Cairney was intrigued by the idea of exploring Dorothy as an “imperfect victim” still deserving of justice. “That was really important to remember: You can have a woman who died a horrible death, but she also can be a complicated character, and they can both sit side by side,” he says.

That duality was best embodied by the presence of Dorothy’s estranged daughter Kristine Wood, who was raised by her paternal grandparents in the wake of her mother’s substance abuse issues and is interviewed in the documentary. “We’re conditioned to want, especially female victims, to be ‘pure.’ This is a woman who had a really, really difficult life, and a really difficult death,” says Cairney, “and you have a daughter who’s been forced to reckon with that intergenerational trauma and to stop the cycle of it. That kept me committed to telling this story.”

There are more mysteries to unfurl in future episodes of Pet Cemetery Murders, starting with the isolated Grey Gardens–esque dynamic between Dorothy and her own mother, Grace, who opened the pet cemetery in 1946. “When we meet Grace, she looks like this kindly old lady sitting on a rocking chair,” Cairney says. “Then you realize she managed to reconcile a devout Christianity, with a pet cemetery, with mafia connections...I mean, you couldn’t make it up.”

The Louisiana land where remnants of the pet cemetery still stand invites plenty of local intrigue. “It’s one of those places locals go with a metal detector trying to find a hidden treasure supposedly buried there,” says Cairney. “It does attract an audience, even without us making the series.” But now that the filmmaker has become part of the land’s story, “you feel embroidered into the fabric of it,” he adds. “I’m never going to escape the tentacular grip of this place and this land, because it kind of gets inside your head, the story, and you can’t really get it out. So even though the series is done, dusted, and delivered,” Cairney shrugs a little, “it feels like it’s not done with me yet.”

items.title: ‘Widow’s Bay’ Creator Katie Dippold Would Marry Freddy Krueger, F Jason, and Kill Hellraiser
items.description: “I think this is a great way to start a podcast,” says Widow’s Bay creator and showrunner Katie Dippold. “If you can bring up semen in any way. That’s the publicity rule: The quicker you can get to that, the sooner you hook them.”
items.author: John Ross
paragraphs: “I think this is a great way to start a podcast,” says Widow’s Bay creator and showrunner Katie Dippold. “If you can bring up semen in any way. That’s the publicity rule: The quicker you can get to that, the sooner you hook them.”

Dippold has been telling me about sneaking into a movie theater when she was a kid and watching 10 minutes of The Silence of the Lambs. It was the scene when Hannibal Lecter first meets Clarice Starling; lucky for Dippold, she missed its ending, when Lecter’s cellmate flings bodily fluids at Starling as she walks away. “I remember seeing that part a couple of years later,” Dippold says. “[I was still] too young to understand it.” Eventually, Dippold saw the whole movie; she now counts the film as one of the greatest ever made, alongside Halloween and Jaws.

On paper, Dippold is a comedy writer. She worked on Mad TV, then Parks and Recreation, then started writing major studio comedies including The Heat, Snatched, and the all-women Ghostbusters remake (more on that later). But her love of horror has been a theme throughout her career, including a viral tweet of her dressed as the Babadook at a Halloween party filled with people in normal clothes. She marries her two loves in Apple TV’s word-of-mouth hit Widow’s Bay, a horror-comedy for which Dippold initially drafted the pilot in 2008.

The television business has evolved since Dippold first took the show’s pilot script to buyers. Initially, she says, Widow’s Bay “was more like a show you would see on network TV. I don’t think in that kind of show you would do a flashback from centuries ago.”

On this week’s Little Gold Men, Dippold reflects on the success of Widow’s Bay—which is currently up for 19 Emmy awards, including best comedy—the defining features of a comedy, her career thus far, and the internet’s love of all things Patricia.
Vanity Fair: Do you find comedy in horror films? For example, Ari Aster thinks that Midsommar is a dark comedy.

Katie Dippold: I completely get that. I saw Midsommar and I laughed so hard. The parts of the movie where the boyfriend is gaslighting her were so perfectly on the money. So I agree with him. I thought it was hilarious and terrifying. And then there are horror movies that are done by people I can tell just have a really good sense of humor. Jordan Peele and Zach Cregger are making horror movies, but they’re very playful and fun in moments. They are also brilliant comedy writers, even if they’re not making a comedy.

You know what’s funny about Jordan? I worked with him at Mad TV, and I remember he had a poster of The Descent in his dressing room. I remember he was telling me later about Get Out, and I just immediately assumed, “It’s like a horror-comedy?” And he said, “No, it’s a horror movie.” There are so many ways he could have done that movie where it was more of a comedy, but he loves horror.

It would’ve been so easy for him to get a comedy made. I remember I tried for years. I had a horror movie that I was trying to direct, and I just went down such a rabbit hole of it where every time it went somewhere, the place got shut down.
You have been working on this show in some form or another for 20 years. Can you talk a little about how it’s evolved?

I would say, first and foremost, TV has changed so much since I wrote the pilot. I just really hadn’t fleshed out the world or thought seriously about what this would be like as a full series. It was a little bit spoofier. It was just jokier. And it would’ve felt more like a parody.

Over the years, I kept thinking about Widow’s Bay as a real place. What would this island really be like? And what are the kind of scary things that I would want to see on the screen? I remember then TV started changing. I was watching shows like Atlanta and then Barry, and I just loved the stuff they were doing. It opened up the world to me of imagining all the different kinds of episodes you could do.

Then I sent it to Hiro Murai, who was my dream director for it because I loved Atlanta. He came on board—to my shock, because I was such a huge fan of his. Then we brought it to Apple and then Matt Cherniss [Apple TV’s head of programming] bought it in the room, as they say. He said, “Okay, great. Let’s do it.” And that is not something I had experienced before, and don’t know if I’ll ever experience again.
You shot this show on location in Massachusetts. Do you have a connection to Stephen King’s New England?

I grew up loving Stephen King. Growing up in New Jersey, I always romanticized New England. I like writing things where you just want to be there. Some people will write painful experiences, but I tend to write situations that I wish I were in. So when we scouted in January, you could still just feel all these buildings were real. It adds this authenticity that I think is so crucial. Because that’s the thing about the show, as ridiculous as it is: You have to buy everything that’s happening, or any false moment really takes you out of it.
Let’s talk about Kate O’Flynn, who plays Patricia. She’s become a favorite on the internet. What did she do in the audition that made you think that she could be Patricia?

Her audition was not what I expected. If you read the scripts, you wouldn’t imagine this person, if I’m being honest. I almost had to shake off what I thought Patricia was going to be and embrace what Kate did because it was so special. Patricia was a little bit based on my mom. There are some things about my mom that are in there. This sort of passive aggressiveness. I think Kate O’Flynn just made that her own.

Patricia is the conduit for a lot of jokes about gender on the show, which I thought really worked. Do you think that’s part of why the internet has just fallen so in love with her? I feel like there’s this underdog aspect to her that people relate to.

There is. I feel like she wants to be seen and heard, and she tries to do the right thing, but she’s also not self-righteous. There’s something authentic and real about her. There’s something about her that’s very inviting.

This is a weird thing to say. It’s a theory I have that I have not said out loud: People bring up that Babadook tweet of me and then relate it to the show. I feel like the connection is that there’s something inviting about these characters. Patricia puts herself out there in the way that the Babadook photo does.

This is a weird story—but I remember when I was in fourth grade, I was allowed to have a Halloween party. My parents said you have to invite everyone in your class. But there was this one kid who was the outcast, and I was like, “I can’t invite him. Then no one will come.” Which is terrible. But my parents made me invite him. I went around to every student and gave them their invitation. I remember this moment; it’s burned in my brain for the rest of my life. When I gave him his invitation, he welled up and was in shock and said, “Really, I’m invited too?”

That just stuck with me forever. Part of me loves Halloween because it is something everyone can do. Anyways, it’s a long, weird, emotional way to say there’s something about Patricia that would invite you in, and would never want you to feel bad.
When you wrote the Ghostbusters remake, were you shocked by the sheer amount of discourse about having an all-female cast?

When Paul Feig [the director of Ghostbusters] said he wanted to do a reboot with all women, even as a Ghostbusters fan, I was looking forward to a sequel with the original cast passing down the baton. I had friends working on versions of that movie, and I knew it wasn’t going to happen. So when Paul brought it up, I had a mixed reaction. I knew people aren’t going to like the reboot part of it. To be honest, I knew we were asking for it.

The reaction was more hateful than I would’ve anticipated. But it’s also Twitter. Sometimes a hundred people on Twitter feels like the entire world. It became this thing where if you said you didn’t like the movie, you were sexist. And that’s not true. You can not like the movie. But then there were also people who were very sexist. So both things were true.
We’re going to play a fun game: Fuck, Marry, Kill, horror-movie edition. First, final girls: Sidney Prescott from the Scream series, Laurie Strode from Halloween, Maxine from the X series.

This is painful to me because I don’t want to kill anyone, and I love all these people. But you have to marry Laurie. She’s the icon. It’s Jamie Lee Curtis, Halloween. That’s everything. I guess I would spend time with Sidney. I was 16 when Scream came out, so that was a real touchstone for me. I don’t want to kill Maxine. I love the X movies. I love Ti West. But that wasn’t a formative year for me when I saw those movies. So if I had to get rid of one, I would sadly have to. Sorry, Ti West.
Freddy Krueger, Jason Voorhees, Hellraiser.

I don’t want to marry any of these guys. But if we’re talking about who meant the most to me, then I would marry Freddy Krueger. Just the poster alone terrorized my childhood before I ever saw the movie. He seems like he would be a lot to deal with, but I would marry him. I would have sex with Jason because it’s like a summer-fling kind of movie. And I would kill Hellraiser. Even though there’s something fundamentally about Hellraiser that scares me the most, I would have to kill him.
Finally, quirky witches: Minnie Castevet played by Ruth Gordon in Rosemary’s Baby, Anjelica Huston in The Witches, and Fairuza Balk in The Craft.

Oh, that’s very hard. I have to marry Ruth Gordon. Yeah. I love that performance so much. She’s so incredible. Gosh, the other two? I can’t. I’m having sex with them both. I’m cheating. I can’t. I can’t kill all of them. I refuse.

items.title: Therapy Helped Jim James So Much, He Wrote a Book About His Breakthroughs
items.description: Jim James has spent the past few years working through decades of memories and experiences in therapy. The My Morning Jacket frontman’s breakthroughs inspired him to write a book, One Wonders, out April 13, 2027.
items.author: Larisha Paul
paragraphs: Jim James has spent the past few years working through decades of memories and experiences in therapy. The My Morning Jacket frontman’s breakthroughs inspired him to write a book, One Wonders, out April 13, 2027.

“Perhaps if I illustrated my journey, and how I began to deal with my own struggles with mental health, it could help people take a step toward getting out of their own darkness and depression,” James said in a statement about the origin on the project.
One Wonders will be released in all formats via Simon & Schuster and comes in at 336 pages. James will narrate the audiobook recording.

The memoir will span the musician’s life and career as he reflects “on finding my voice — both as a singer, songwriter and musician, and as a person wandering the earth wondering… what do I really want to SAY with my life overall?”
Raised in Louisville, Kentucky, the singer-songwriter formed My Morning Jacket in 1998. The band has released nine studio albums together, while James’ solo discography spans five albums.

“As I reflect on my own musical journey (from first learning to play the guitar to creating music in the present day) and navigating the complexities of life in general, I have been thinking a lot about my elders,” James said in a statement. “For so many of them, tradition was to never speak about yourself. You carried your victories and failures, your joys and horrors, quietly. A thought kept making its way into my mind: wouldn’t things be lighter for all of us if we shared more with other people?”

He added, “If nothing else, I hope the main thing someone takes away from this book (aside from learning more about the joys and challenges of being a working artist and musician) is that it’s okay to ask for help. Everyone is going through some sort of challenge in this crazy world. IT IS POSSIBLE to find your way out of darkness and despair, and begin to enjoy the subtle, beautiful, everyday victories of simply being alive.”

items.title: Guided by Voices Welcome 2027 by Announcing 'Speculation and Gossip'
items.description: While working on Guided by Voices‘ 45th studio album, Speculation and Gossip, frontman Robert Pollard developed an obsession with Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. “[I watched it] over and over,” he says. “I’ve almost learned the dialog like R
items.author: Brenna Ehrlich
paragraphs: While working on Guided by Voices‘ 45th studio album, Speculation and Gossip, frontman Robert Pollard developed an obsession with Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. “[I watched it] over and over,” he says. “I’ve almost learned the dialog like Rocky Horror Picture Show.” The record drops January 22 via the band’s Rockathon Records.

Pollard has also been immersed in surrealism and dada, fitting genres for a musician and visual artist who has a knack for bending words and images to his will — either via hallucinatory lyrics or collages that mesh realms both physical and meta.

The first single off of the new album, “Designed for Use,” is a barreling, muscled track that turns a piece of mundane packaging copy into a motto: Pollard was designed to be a musician, to play “in most stereophonic atmospheres.”

While the band’s last album, Crawlspace of the Pantheon, was recorded in the studio with the full band, GBV went back to the old ways for number 45. “We went back to doing things remotely with each individual coming up with his own approach to sound, fidelity and instrumentation instead of playing all together,” Pollard says. “I wanted more audible separation of the instruments and overall I was after more diversity in song structures, musical styles and lyrical content. I also wanted it to be much brighter, less heavy in overall tone than Crawlspace. On this one I just gave them genre references. Post punk, pop, prog, psych or combinations.”

Heading into 2027, Pollard caps off a year of artistic success — including his largest-ever show of his collages — and, in addition to Speculation, has a few other surprises on the horizon. “I work on collages everyday. It’s an addiction,” he says. “[There’s] special releases in the works for 2027 but I can’t divulge them yet.”

items.title: Ozzy Osbourne's Last Black Sabbath Concert Will Be Available On Vinyl
items.description: When Ozzy Osbourne died on July 22, 2025, the music world mourned the loss of a generation-defining artist and the defining heavy metal pioneer.
items.author: CT Jones
paragraphs: When Ozzy Osbourne died on July 22, 2025, the music world mourned the loss of a generation-defining artist and the defining heavy metal pioneer.

But 17 days earlier, fans, loved ones, and Osbourne’s greatest collaborators met for a star-studded and highly emotional farewell tribute concert. Over 44,000 fans swarmed Osbourne’s hometown of Birmingham, England, and watched groups like Metallica, Mastodon, Slayer, and Guns N’ Roses bid a musical farewell to Osbourne in the Villa Park stadium. It was also Osbourne’s final performance, a bittersweet solo moment and the reunion of Black Sabbath’s original lineup playing together for the first time in almost 20 years. The 10-hour event became the two-hour concert film Ozzy Osbourne & Black Sabbath: Back to the Beginning, out in theaters today.

Those without tickets — or fans desperate to relive the concert again and against — don’t have to fret. Mercury Studios announced Wednesday that the full-length film version and soundtrack of Back to the Beginning will be available in digital and physical forms on December 11, including 4K Ultra HD, Blu-ray, CD, and vinyl. Physical versions of the film will include behind the scenes footage of the event and video tributes from Dolly Parton and AC/DC. You can preorder copies here.

In a rare interview earlier this month, Sharon Osbourne told Rolling Stone that Osbourne was incredibly proud of the concert and while it was difficult to watch, she believes it will be an important musical artifact. “It’s bittersweet. It’s amazing. Everything about the show was amazing and just a joyous occasion and one that will go down in music history,” she said. “It’s just something that will stand the test of time. It was groundbreaking for what it was. Like everything with Ozzy, he’s the first.”

According to Sharon, Osbourne’s medical team advised him against doing the concert but the heavy metal legend insisted. “They advised us not to do the show. They said it would kill him. We were all together and Ozzy said, “It’s not an option. It’s what I want.” He said, “I know I’m dying. If I miss a few months of my life, I want to go this way. This is what I want.” It was his wishes and we went through it,” Sharon said. “He was very, very emotional. But you know what? It was beautiful too. It was amazing. How lucky was he to go out that way? I say he went out like a Viking. It was the way he wanted.”

items.title: Below Deck Recap: Exposure Therapy
items.description: Nothing exposes the shortcomings of a yachting crew more clearly than a group of demanding guests. This week, the Azul V team finds their first real challenge of the season in primary Carolyn and her life partner, Robby, who are bringing Robby’s super-chill si
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Nothing exposes the shortcomings of a yachting crew more clearly than a group of demanding guests. This week, the Azul V team finds their first real challenge of the season in primary Carolyn and her life partner, Robby, who are bringing Robby’s super-chill sister Melani onboard, along with “trained healers” in Carolyn’s “inner circle.” These spiritual beings are nothing if not preoccupied with the state of material things, such as the temperature of the wine, for example. Seeking to understand them, Kaylee explains that they are rich hippies, which are, of course, the worst kind of hippie. They want fruit for breakfast, but it must be “artistically cut,” “like it’s gonna make it taste different,” Moe quips.

In other words, they are annoying people with CVS-receipt-long preference sheets. Unfortunately, though, they are within their paying right to request ridiculous things, especially if they prepare the crew well in advance. Is it weird that Melani requests a glass of wine for her turndown service so she can gulp it down when she wakes up in the middle of the night and needs to go back to sleep? Yes, but this nationally televised weirdness shouldn’t stop the interior team from complying. Is it annoying that Melani’s drunken hunger for salty snacks grossly surpasses the rabid, raccoonlike spirit that used to possess me when I got back to my college apartment after consuming unadvised amounts of vodka-cranberry at the townie bar? Yes, but she is a guest, and as such, she is entitled to the nuts and chips.

Given last week’s minor chip incident, it’s a bad sign we’re having this conversation again. The interior team’s failure to fulfill some of the guests’ requests points to a lack of standards, which I’m afraid is coming from Fraser. This week’s mistakes are not grave, but they’re adding up as quickly as Alex’s mistakes on the deck team, which are starting to freak out Kerry. The captain gathers the deck team for a pep talk the day before they pick up the new guests, urging them to be more efficient now that they’ve had their practice run with the first charter. So far so aligned with Alex: That morning, in a bid to be more assertive, he called out his hungover team for showing up late to their morning meeting.

But Alex can’t seem to do anything right. He is strikingly calm about how often he’s falling short of the captain’s expectations. Even his initiative to figure out how to get the slide set up more quickly before the guests arrive doesn’t go over as well as it might have because Alex interrupts the captain mid-sentence. Still, he soldiers on, determined to rely on Matt’s experience with the slide for the best results. His trust in his lead deckhand would have created an atmosphere of collaboration within the team were Matt’s ego not so gigantic. On the first night of the charter, Kerry sends Alex to accompany the guests on their twilight kayak excursion, during which the guests are spared any paddling. In the meantime, Alex instructs Matt and James to deflate and put away the slide. Matt resents that Alex gets to do “the fun stuff” while they’re stuck doing the heavy work, apparently forgetting that he is Alex’s subordinate and ignorant of the fact that it was the captain who sent out Alex. Despite admitting that Alex is a better people manager than he is, Matt maintains that Alex needs to “prove himself as a bosun.” My guy, you are not the captain of this vessel. Alex needs to prove himself to Kerry, it’s true, but not to Matt. The fact that he is constantly underestimating Alex has only made me root for Alex more. Let’s show him!

Meanwhile, in the galley, Moe endeavors to prove himself both to the captain and to the guests. The night before they arrive, while the crew watches a beautiful sunset, Moe uses the time to get ahead of prep. He is nervous because the guests have requested a fine-dining experience when he’s more of an “ugly-delicious” guy. It’s clear he’s feeling the pressure when the provisions arrive the next morning — he gets some containers confused and, were it not for Fraser, would have sent back the caviar Carolyn requested for breakfast (my eyes are rolling into my skull) — and when he decorates the welcome charcuterie board with many beautiful slices of strawberry, forgetting Melani is allergic to the fruit.

But Moe pulls it together in time for dinner and nails a menu that includes Thai crab salad, a beautiful piece of kingfish with curry, and a chocolate matcha cake. Knowing service will push the chef, Kerry comes down to the galley to lend a hand with the dishes. Moe does his part; it’s service that becomes strained under the guests’ demands. They start complaining from the moment they arrive — the Champagne isn’t cold enough (“not drinkable”), and Melani keeps asking for “super-salty” snacks, ideally a can of anchovies, an item that was not on her preference sheet. During dinner, Fraser keeps a list of their complaints: “Wine too warm; stabilizers not working?; salt not good; lime not great; wine glasses not nice,” and so on. Some of these misgivings are serious enough to warrant getting up from the table — Robby finds Fraser in the pantry to ask him to adjust the temperature of the wine.

These guests are obviously grating, but just because they’re difficult, it doesn’t mean Fraser shouldn’t care to appease them. Let us go over what happened with Melani’s turndown wine request. Rosa got confused and brought up the glass of red to Carolyn’s cabin instead. No problem there; we all make mistakes. Before going to bed, Melani asks Rainbeau for some more chips and nuts to take to her room — no wonder she’s so thirsty — an order that seems to slip Rainbeau’s mind. A little over half an hour later, Melani comes out looking for Rainbeau and finds Rosa, who wasn’t told about the chips order. While she has a stew’s attention, Melani complains about the absence of her requested glass of wine, which Rosa is still under the impression was actually Carolyn’s request. But Melani still gets everything she needs: Carolyn hands off the misplaced wine, and Rosa brings up her chips and nuts.

Rosa doesn’t feel bad about these mix-ups because, one, this lady sucks, and, two, it was Rainbeau who forgot about the chips, so it’s not her problem. But the misplaced wine was Rosa’s mistake, which she doesn’t realize until later. To be fair, going over the whole thing with Fraser while pulling her own espresso shot, Melani exaggerates their interaction, saying Rosa told her “emphatically that only Carolyn gets wine next to her bed,” which is not entirely true. But Fraser’s response is also off. In a confessional, he says he trusts Rosa over “this witch” and he doesn’t really care what went on between them. Well, he should. However annoying Melani might be, Rosa did make a mistake, albeit a small one. Talking over the incident with Fraser, Rosa owns up to her mistake, but Fraser then says she “did nothing wrong,” which is simply not true. He could still take Rosa’s side and acknowledge how rude Melani is while also encouraging Rosa to be more attentive. As Aesha always says, appeasing rich people is a huge part of the job. At least Fraser demonstrates a bare-mininum interest in the guests when he gets spun in the air by Jason, who “invented acro-yoga” (?).

Even amid so many absurdities, one of the strangest things that happens this week is Rainbeau suddenly developing an English accent. I’m talking about Rainbeau, the Dutch girl with an Americanized accent and a sorority past. She tells Kaylee and Rosa that their own accents are rubbing off on her, but it weirds out Fraser and for good reason. It comes out when she’s talking to the guests, and she even brings it into her cabin when she’s calming herself down after Fraser criticizes her golden age of Siam tablescape. It reminds you of those kids who went to study abroad in France and came back saying croissant differently.

On the morning of the second day of the charter, Alex has the whole team up and ready to haul anchor in an adjustment of what went wrong last week. But because nothing can be easy for the Azul V’s Charlie Brown, Sen accidentally drops the harness that attaches the Jet Ski to the crane in the water. Learning what happened, Kerry flushes red from head to toe, not necessarily because Sen dropped the strap but because Alex didn’t react quickly enough. According to the captain, it’s basic protocol when you lose something to drop a floated weight behind it so that a searchable area is immediately marked. In the galley with Fraser, Kerry worries he’ll have to “make changes,” which should make Matt foam at the mouth.

It can’t be good for Matt’s overinflated ego that Kaylee is acting obsessed with him. I saved all the boatmance stuff for last because it’s the most boring part of this week’s episode. I will be very surprised if Matt doesn’t break Kaylee’s heart. I felt the need to cover my ears with my hands and go la la la hearing Kaylee tell Rosa she “loves giving people second chances.” Despite venting to James about Kaylee’s eagerness — within the first 72 hours of knowing him, she’s talking about marriage — Matt tells her he wants to be exclusive. Apparently, he is on a journey of self-improvement and means to redeem himself from cheating on a girl he loved for reasons that are not entirely clear to him. We know he can’t be that serious because just a few hours before, he told James he won’t stop “having banter with the other girls” just because he’s exclusive with Kaylee. Then he backtracks and says he’s not interested in anyone else on the boat. What could possibly go wrong?

James understands Matt’s dilemma — he loves flirting, especially with Rainbeau, who calls him eye candy (she should have gone for “quite fit,” maybe, to stay in character) and is always around for a hug. (Rosa, look alive!) But he also tells Matt that being on the boat has made him realize the “girl [he travels] with” may be his person after all. Excuse me, what? Everyone disclosed their relationship status on the first day of the season. Now, all of a sudden, we learn James is in an open relationship with ground rules, like no cuddling and no sex. Later, Matt relays the information to Kaylee, who is suspicious James might be a fuckboy. Oh my God, open your eyes, Kaylee! So far, the only couple conducting themselves normally is Sen and Alex, who made out a little, then put on their professional hats, which they will maybe take off again once the charter is over.

items.title: Russell Brand Takes the Stand in Rape Trial and Reveals No One Agreed to Testify on His Behalf: ‘My Entire Life Has Been Consumed by These Allegations’
items.description: Russell Brand took the stand in his criminal trial in London on Wednesday, denying all accusations against him and revealing that he was not able to convince anyone to testify on his behalf.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Russell Brand took the stand in his criminal trial in London on Wednesday, denying all accusations against him and revealing that he was not able to convince anyone to testify on his behalf.

He was called by his lawyer, Ian Winter KC, as the first and only witness as his defense began to lay out its case, according to Sky News. Winter began by asking Brand if he had committed each of the alleged offenses he is being accused of, to which he repeatedly replied: “No.” Questioned about his prominence in the mid-2000s, Brand said that his marriage to Katy Perry in 2010 brought about “staggering fame.”

Brand then revealed that not a single person with relevant information agreed to testify on his behalf in the trial. “My entire life has been consumed by these allegations,” he told the Southwark Crown Court. “I have devoted myself to these matters.”

He called the 2023 Channel 4 documentary about him “devastating” and claimed that he was not able to visit his sick son in the hospital because he had been publicly accused of rape. “The reason given by Great Ormond Street Hospital when my son was receiving open heart surgery and subsequent treatment was due to the material published,” he said, according to Sky News.

On Tuesday, judge Mr Justice Bennathan reduced one of Brand’s seven charges from indecent assault to attempted indecent assault, telling jurors that there was “insufficient evidence” regarding an alleged 2001 incident involving a MTV employee. He has also been charged with three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and has pleaded not guilty to all charges. The case involves six female plaintiffs, all of whom are given automatic lifelong anonymity according to U.K. law, and relates to alleged offenses that occurred between 1999 and 2009.

Outside the courthouse on Wednesday, Brand told journalists (via Sky News): “Due to the circumstances of today, I think it would be inappropriate for me to say anything other than I am very grateful that today’s a day for truth and justice and we are blessed that as yet we have a system that can accommodate such things.” He was accompanied by his wife, Laura Gallacher.

On the stand, Brand was then questioned by the defense about the first allegation, concerning a woman who alleged he raped her at the 1999 Labour party conference. After meeting at his cabaret show, Brand said the woman “suggested we go to her hotel room” and he thought there may be a “possibility of sex.” In the room, he said there was “messing about, some kissing on the body and sex with a condom.” Asked about her claim that he forced her to take the photos, Brand responded: “I don’t know how you can make someone take photographs.” Further questioned on the importance of consent, he said, “Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary, and in many ways more important than sex itself.”

Moving on to the second accusation, involving a woman who claims Brand grabbed her and tried to pull her into a toilet while she was working at MTV in 2001, Brand said he has no recollection of the alleged incident. Regarding the third complainant, who alleged Brand squeezed her breasts at a party in Soho in 2004 and then orally raped her in a toilet, he said he was introduced to her by the host of the party as a “bird” who “really wants to meet you.” He said he “absolutely” did not grab her breasts and said the toilet she claimed he orally raped her in “was unsuitable for me to meet the goal… of getting it off.” He also denied the fourth woman’s allegation, who claimed he allegedly pushed her against a wall and “aggressively” kissed her while she was working at Capital Radio in 2004/2005.

Regarding the fifth accuser, who alleged that Brand anally raped her in 2009 after they had consensual vaginal sex, he claimed that she did not say “no” or tell him to stop. He also said he believed that taking off his condom before the alleged anal rape was a “consensual act,” according to Sky News. He denied sexually assaulting the sixth complainant as well, who alleged she was forced to give him a massage at work in 2009.
“I’m innocent,” Brand said as the defense’s questioning ended.

The prosecution has set out its case over the past two weeks. In her opening statement at the start of the trial, Riel Karmy-Jones KC called Brand a “predator,” adding that he was “ruthless and calculated” with an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact.

Cross-examining Brand on Wednesday, Karmy-Jones asked him if he blames the women who have come forward against him, and Brand said he does not. He also denied that he had a “goal” of sleeping with 5,000 women, as he allegedly told a friend at the time; however, he admitted to being “obsessed” with sex when he was younger. Asked if he ever said he wouldn’t leave a woman alone until he slept with her, Brand referenced a quote from Woody Allen, the director who has also faced his own allegations. “That sounds specifically like a riff on a Woody Allen joke, when he said, ‘The only advice my dad ever gave me on his death bed was always try and fuck the waitress,'” Brand said, adding: “It was a joke.”

Questioned about the specific alleged offenses, Brand responded often with “I don’t remember” or “I have no recollection.” Asked by Karmy-Jones if he is being “selective” with his memory, Brand said he was doing his “best” to remember the events being discussed. He later added, when asked about inconsistencies in his police statements, that hearing the complainants’ allegations during the trial has caused an “escalating recollection” of events.

“It’s been a deeply traumatic episode of my life,” he said. “I’ve focused on it at the expense of my marriage, my children and health. I ask your forgiveness — well, not your forgiveness. I recognize that this recollection includes small details which are inconsistent, and I recognize that.”
Asked generally about his past behavior, via Sky News, Brand said he was “in the position of fame” and “misused that commodity very selfishly,” which was “wrong in retrospect.”

“As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong,” he continued. “I do recognize I have been a very determined and focused man … With women — of course, which is the subject of my trial — I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless, philandering and idiocy.”
He later restated that “not guilty is my plea to all the charges on the indictment.”
Brand’s defense will continue on Thursday. The jury is expected to start deliberating a verdict on Tuesday.

items.title: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ First Reactions Call Prequel the ‘Rogue One’ of the Franchise and Praise Joseph Zada as Haymitch
items.description: “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” has officially premiered, and members of the film press are already calling the sixth installment a “perfect adaptation” that breathes “new life” into the franchise. “Sunrise on the Reaping” is the second “Hunger Game
items.author: Zack Sharf
paragraphs: “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” has officially premiered, and members of the film press are already calling the sixth installment a “perfect adaptation” that breathes “new life” into the franchise. “Sunrise on the Reaping” is the second “Hunger Games” prequel movie following 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.”

Film critic Griffin Schiller hailed the movie as the “Rogue One” and “Andor” of “The Hunger Games” franchise, adding: “It’s [a] sobering, yet powerful story of devastating loss and the necessary cost of rebellion for a sunrise we may never see. As a massive fan of the series and especially this book, I couldn’t have asked for a more perfect adaptation.”

Filmhounds Magazine editor-in-chief and Tomatometer critic Gavin Spoors praised the film’s third act as “stellar,” writing that it “pulls the rug out underneath you.” “Anchored by terrific performances (Zada is a star), this emotional thriller nails the themes of the cost of revolution and how we all need to play our part,” he wrote on X.

Matt Neglia, Next Best Picture editor-in-chief, wrote that the film “features some of the best casting of the year” in his review. “Many of the actors breathe new life into familiar characters, making them their own, while preserving the qualities that made them so compelling in the first place,” he continued. “Glenn Close, with her horror-inducing face, is a scene-stealer as is Jesse Plemons embodying the spirit of the late great Philip Seymour Hoffman. Joseph Zada is beyond impressive in a highly demanding role that pushes him to the limit physically and emotionally, perfectly capturing the essence of Haymitch with all the sympathy, charm and bitterness Woody Harrelson brought to the role. I’m continually blown away by how Francis Lawrence continues to find more layers in this familiar structure thematically and stylistically as the production and costume design continue to be dazzling highlights. If this is to be the end of his time working on these movies, it’s a good way to go out as this latest installment brings the franchise full circle with the character that’s always been the beating heart at its center.”

“The rebellion is sparking with SUNRISE ON THE REAPING,” wrote fellow Next Best Picture editor Lauren LaMagna. “Francis Lawrence continues to breathe new life into this world. The unique production design doesn’t let familiar beats get too dull. Joseph Zada is heartbreakingly radiant as Haymitch. A star is born role.”

“One of the biggest highlights? Joseph Zada,” wrote Collider’s Perri Nemiroff. “I had high hopes for him after watching We Were Liars, but he had my jaw on the floor time and time again during Sunrise on the Reaping. His ability to capture Haymitch’s warmth and charm and then weave that into the rage and heartbreak the Hunger Games sparks is superb. SO much of this movie is on his shoulders, and he soars tackling every ounce of it. This is only the beginning for Zada.”

She continued: “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes bolstered my rewatches of the original films, and I have no doubt the same will be true of Sunrise on the Reaping. Sparking real change can take time and demand great sacrifice. This film franchise is better off for having added Haymitch’s.”

Static Media writer Nina Starner also championed Zada’s casting, saying that it “couldn’t be better.” “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is a worthy addition to the franchise,” she wrote. “It looks and feels terrifyingly real, and it bridges the gap perfectly between the original stories and Ballad. A from me.”

Based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest “Hunger Games” movie centers on a young Haymitch (Zada, taking over the role from Woody Harrelson) as he fights to survive while competing in the 50th Hunger Games. The cast also features Jesse Plemons as Plutarch, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman, Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket, Maya Hawke as Wiress and Kelvin Harrison Jr. as Beetee. New characters in the film franchise are played by the likes of Mckenna Grace, Glenn Close and Whitney Peak, among others.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” takes place 24 years before the start of the first “Hunger Games” movie. Frances Lawrence, who has directed every “Hunger Games” movie except for the first installment (that was Gary Ross), returns to helm the latest prequel movie.

Much of the buzz surrounding “Sunrise on the Reaping” has been related to the franchise returns of Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Harrelson as Katniss, Peeta and Haymitch. Book readers know that Suzanne Collins’ novel ends with a flash-forward epilogue featuring the trio, so it appears the film adaptation is following suit.

“It was unbelievable,” Lawrence said on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast about reprising Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional. Josh and I didn’t walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other. It was so beautiful.”
“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” is set to open in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate. Check out first reactions to the movie below.

items.title: ‘Smile 3’ Sets David Bruckner to Direct While Franchise Creator Parker Finn Helms ‘Possession’ Remake (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Put on a happy face, because “Smile 3” is officially in the works.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: Put on a happy face, because “Smile 3” is officially in the works.

Paramount has hired David Bruckner to direct and Nick Antosca to write the screenplay. They’re taking over for Parker Finn, who created the series and will remain involved as a producer alongside Temple Hill. (Finn pitched the framework for the third installment.) Jonathan Fass will executive produce.

Bruckner’s credits include the 2022 “Hellraiser” reboot, 2017’s psychological thriller “The Ritual” and 2020’s supernatural horror film “The Night House.” Bruckner is particularly in demand as of late: he’s currently writing and developing a reboot of the sci-fi horror classic, “The Blob,” for Warner Bros., as well as Universal’s adaptation of “The Caretaker,” starring Sydney Sweeney, plus he’s set to direct “Mice” for A24.
Antosca is best known for creating Apple’s miniseries “Cape Fear” and co-creating Hulu’s “The Act,” as well as writing 2021’s “Antlers” and the most recent Colleen Hoover adaptation “Verity.”

Plot details for the third “Smile” movie haven’t been revealed. The first film stars Sosie Bacon as a therapist who becomes haunted by hallucinations after witnessing a patient die. In the second, Naomi Scott plays a pop singer who begins to experience a series of disturbing events as she embarks on tour. Since each “Smile” movie has functioned as a standalone sequel, with a separate story and new stars, it’s unclear who will appear in the threequel.

Finn wrote and directed 2022’s “Smile” and the 2024 sequel “Smile 2.” The original film — commissioned for streaming before pivoting to a theatrical release — became a sleeper hit, with $105 million domestically and $217 million globally. The follow-up wasn’t quite as big at the box office but became a commercial win, with $69 million domestically and $139 million globally against a modest $28 million budget. In total, the franchise has earned more than $350 million worldwide.

Although Finn isn’t spearheading “Smile 3,” he’s still working closely with Paramount, having signed a first-look deal with the studio after the first “Smile” became a theatrical success. Finn is directing a remake of the 1981 supernatural thriller “Possession,” starring Callum Turner and Margaret Qualley and set for June 11, 2027.

items.title: After the Cast and Creator’s Comments, ‘Nobody Wants This’ Can No Longer Ignore Israel and Gaza
items.description: For the past few weeks, the cast and creator of the Netflix hit comedy “Nobody Wants This” have been trading takes on the Israel-Palestine conflict via the press. First, star Adam Brody, who plays “hot rabbi” Noah Roklov and one half of the show’s central coup
items.author: Alison Herman
paragraphs: For the past few weeks, the cast and creator of the Netflix hit comedy “Nobody Wants This” have been trading takes on the Israel-Palestine conflict via the press. First, star Adam Brody, who plays “hot rabbi” Noah Roklov and one half of the show’s central couple, told GQ that he considers Israel’s actions in Gaza to be a genocide, and that he supports a free Palestine. Creator Erin Foster, who based the show on her experience converting to Judaism after meeting her now-husband, then stated in a podcast appearance that “I disagree with [Brody], and that’s OK,” keeping her own stance vague but reiterating that she considers the series “a love letter to Judaism.” Actor Tovah Feldshuh, who plays Noah’s overbearing mother Bina, went much further in her own response, outright condemning Brody’s comments to the New York Post as “right out of Hitler’s playbook.”

One could argue that the media is not an ideal forum for co-workers to work out opposing stances on complex geopolitical issues that also touch on religious identity. You know what could be? A television show that theoretically celebrates Judaism in all its forms!

Of course, that’s not the kind of show “Nobody Wants This” actually is, nor has it ever been. The rom-com began as a featherweight diversion, and remains as such in its recently released third season. Brody’s Noah is a fantasy of a sexy, saintly man who inexplicably thinks Kristen Bell’s self-absorbed podcaster Joanne walks on water, and the ostensible core conflict of their relationship — it’s important to Noah that his partner be Jewish, while Joanne isn’t so sure about conversion — repeatedly dissipates in the warm fog of a romantic kiss. Conflict is more likely to arise from Joanne and her sister-slash-podcasting-partner Morgan (Justine Lupe) squabbling over who the real star of their show is, or Noah’s brother Sasha’s (Timothy Simons) new dye job than any deep-seated disagreements over values or lifestyle.

To watch too many episodes of “Nobody Wants This” in one sitting is to get the same kind of stomachache one develops after eating too many KitKats on an empty stomach. (Maybe that’s why Season 3 dropped so close to Halloween?) Such a sugar rush may be poorly suited to address spirituality and ideology as a matter of disposition, but “Nobody Wants This” further damaged its ability to fully represent the Jewish community with some early creative choices.

Season 1 was widely criticized for a seemingly antagonistic and stereotypical depiction of Jewish women like Bina or Noah’s sister-in-law Esther (Jackie Tohn), who came off as shrewish, possessive obstacles to Joanne and Morgan’s happiness. Subsequent seasons have partly adjusted and brought on new behind-the-scenes voices like co-showrunners Jenni Konner and Bruce Eric Kaplan (“Girls”), but “Nobody Wants This” trends toward lessening friction, not increasing it. (Bina is weirdly chill about Noah proposing to Joanne approximately two seconds after they move in.) And there’s no greater source of friction among American Jews right now than how to feel about the Jewish state in the aftermath of the Hamas attacks in October of 2023.

“Nobody Wants This” premiered nearly a year after that horrific event, and Israel’s total absence from conversations around the Roklov household has always been glaring. If my own life is any judge, it’s pretty much bound to come up at any holiday or family gathering, with opinions falling along predictable generational lines. If part of Noah’s personality is that he’s a more hip and chill kind of religious leader, then him offering a critique of the ongoing occupation would be a perfectly reasonable way to establish that. The last time I opened Instagram, I saw a video from a progressive rabbi based on the Eastside of Los Angeles — basically real-life Noah Roklov! — providing protective presence around the olive harvest in the West Bank. I’d wonder how Bina might feel about her son doing the same, but I’m certain Feldshuh’s statement is the closest I’ll get to finding out.

To be fair, that vacuum is part and parcel with how “Nobody Wants This” approaches Judaism in general: as a minor and easily overcome source of difference, rather than a religion or culture with internal divides of its own. In Season 3, Joanne finally starts taking Jewish education classes as a potential precursor to conversion. But the courses, taught by guest star Sarah Silverman, have almost no substance and disappear for long stretches of the season; they’re mostly there to introduce Andrew Rannells as Joanne’s catty new nemesis. Even the Holocaust, a much more longstanding and less controversial source of Jewish trauma, is almost entirely absent lest its shadow puncture the bubbly mood.

Nor is “Nobody Wants This” the only Jewish show — or even the only Jewish show on Netflix! — to avoid the issue. The animated series “Long Story Short,” from “BoJack Horseman” creator Raphael Bob-Waksberg, didn’t mention Israel in its first season, a deliberate choice to give the characters a chance to establish themselves without becoming proxies for their politics. “I have found that when we talk about it, it takes all the air out of the room,” Bob-Waksberg said in an interview with Variety last year. But “Long Story Short” is set entirely before the Oct. 7 attack, and if that show goes two more years without naming the elephant at the oneg, I’d fault it as well.

“Nobody Wants This” can avoid Israel all it likes. Now, though, the inevitable has happened: Israel has come to it. In the same podcast where she politely distanced herself from Brody, Foster said that “our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing.” The comment is a tacit admission that, in representing those very dinner tables, Foster is making a massive omission, knowingly sacrificing realism for the blandness of safety. That empty space was always going to fill up eventually; now, it’s happening outside the control and potential catharsis of the show’s crafted narrative.

To be frank, I’m not sure I’d want to see what the “Nobody Wants This” version of that conversation might look like, in part because my own feelings on the matter hew far closer to Brody’s than Foster’s, and certainly Feldshuh’s. “Nobody Wants This” has never been a Norman Lear-style forum for airing the arguments of the day, and would be jarring if the show were to suddenly become one. But if “Nobody Wants This” is a proudly escapist fantasy, there’s a line between a transportive entertainment and a story whose distance from its supposed subject is too great to maintain even a pretense of plausibility. If Foster and her collaborators don’t want to talk about a painful and acrimonious, yet central part of Jewish American life, then they don’t really want to make a show about Judaism as actual Jews live it. And if “Nobody Wants This” doesn’t want to live up to its creator’s stated aim of representation, then maybe it’s time to wrap things up.

items.title: YouTube Q3 Ad Revenue Growth Slows, Rising 9% to $11.2 Billion, as Alphabet Misses Earnings Estimates
items.description: YouTube continued to vacuum up digital ad dollars in the third quarter of 2026, but the video platform’s advertising business grew at slower pace than in recent quarters. YouTube’s growth also was lower than Alphabet overall, given a sales boom in the internet
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: YouTube continued to vacuum up digital ad dollars in the third quarter of 2026, but the video platform’s advertising business grew at slower pace than in recent quarters. YouTube’s growth also was lower than Alphabet overall, given a sales boom in the internet giant’s Google Cloud division, which saw revenue double. Meanwhile, Alphabet came in below Q3 analyst estimates on the top and bottom lines.

For Q3, YouTube ad revenue was $11.21 billion, an increase of 9.2% from the year prior, below analyst projections. That’s compared with growth of 15% in the year-earlier period and 13% in Q2 and 11% in Q1 of this year. Total advertising revenue for Google (including from YouTube) was $80.0 billion, up 10.6%.

In addition to advertising sales, YouTube also generates a massive amount of subscription revenue, which Alphabet said topped $60 billion in 2025. In the third quarter, YouTube surpassed 150 million YouTube Music and Premium subscribers globally (including trials), according to the company. It previously crossed the 125 million mark in March 2025.

On the Q3 call, Philipp Schindler, Google’s chief business officer, said YouTube’s subscription revenue is now growing faster than the ad side of the business. In the quarter, connected-TV viewing accounted for more than one-third of total YouTube ads revenue globally (in the U.S., YouTube says the majority of viewing is on TVs). Schindler also said more than 20 million videos are now uploaded per day to YouTube.

Overall, Alphabet posted revenue of $127.6 billion (up 25%) and net income of $26.17 billion (down 25%), translating to earnings per share of $2.12. That fell short of Wall Street consensus estimates of $128.2 billion in revenue and EPS of $3.02, per LSEG data. Alphabet’s Q3 2026 loss included a net loss on equity securities of $8.7 billion. Google Cloud delivered record growth as revenue increased 103% to $30.7 billion.

“We had a strong quarter and are now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate,” Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google and Alphabet, said in announcing the earnings. “Our deep full stack approach is driving momentum across the business, with Alphabet revenues growing 25% year-over year. Our AI investments are driving overall Search query growth, including commercial queries. In fact, our year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.”
In addition, according to Pichai, the Gemini AI app has reached 1 billion users, which he said makes it the fastest-growing product in Google’s history.

On the call, Pichai said that at the “Made on YouTube” event last month in New York, the platform introduced more than 30 new products, including a “custom feed” feature that lets users create new channels with recommended videos on topics they request to see.

Like other AI “hyperscalers,” Alphabet is spending heavily on building out capacity for artificial intelligence applications. The company’s capital expenditures in Q3 totaled $51.36 billion, up 114% year over year. In July, the company raised full-year 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion-$205 billion, up from its previous projection of $180 billion-$190 billion, driven by AI data center buildouts. That capex guidance for 2026 remained unchanged while Alphabet continues to expect capital spending to “significantly” increase in 2027, according to CFO Anat Ashkenazi.

Amid the ramped-up spending on AI, Google reported a bigger dent in free cash flow in Q3 than analysts expected. FCF was negative $9.07 billion in the September quarter versus negative $5.86 billion in Q2.

items.title: TV Ratings: Why Fox News Suffered Its Largest Pre-Election Month Drop in the Past Decade
items.description: In the “two things can be true” category: Fox News still holds sizable ratings leads in cable news over CNN and MS NOW. It also suffered the largest year-to-year ratings drop in the month before an election in the past 10 years.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: In the “two things can be true” category: Fox News still holds sizable ratings leads in cable news over CNN and MS NOW. It also suffered the largest year-to-year ratings drop in the month before an election in the past 10 years.

Nielsen ratings for October show Fox News averaging 1.68 million viewers in primetime and 1.01 million for the full day. Both are comfortably ahead of MS NOW (925,000 primetime, 588,000 full day) and CNN (598,000, 402,000). In the key news demographic of adults 25-54, things are a bit closer, but Fox’s totals of 145,000 in primetime and 98,000 for the total day still lead. CNN had 107,000 in the demo in primetime and 60,000 for the full day to 95,000 and 62,000 for MS NOW.
Fox also had the five most watched cable news shows, led by The Five at 2.7 million daily viewers.

Fox News is also touting its online strength, citing 3.8 billion YouTube views for 2026 so far (as measured by social media analytics firm Emplifi) to 2.96 billion for MS NOW and 2.36 billion for CNN.
As for the second true thing: In the past decade, none of the three biggest cable news outlets have suffered a decline in the month before a national election as big as Fox News did this year.

Compared to October 2025, Fox News slipped by 28 percent in primetime viewers and 27 percent for the full day. The networks’ adults 25-54 audience fell by more than 30 percent. MS NOW and CNN both had double digit percentage gains in primetime vs. a year earlier; MS NOW also did so for the full day, while CNN had a more modest 3 percent bump.

Pundits and media analysts have suggested that President Trump’s low approval ratings and an election cycle that seems to favor Democrats may have contributed to the drop at Fox News. Nielsen data doesn’t explain why people watch or don’t watch certain programs or networks, obviously. But the change is a stark one.

The Hollywood Reporter analyzed October cable news ratings for the past six national election cycles — presidential contests in 2016, 2020 and 2024 and midterms in 2018, 2022 and 2026 — and compared each to the previous October (2015, 2017, etc.). Unsurprisingly, all three networks showed huge year-to-year gains in October 2016 and October 2020. Fox improved substantially in October 2024 as well, with total day ratings up about 20 percent vs. October 2023. MS NOW was flat and CNN declined in October 2024 total day ratings (though both grew in primetime).

Midterm years are more of a mixed bag: Before this year, biggest improvement was a 25 percent year-to-year boost in primetime viewers for Fox in October 2018, and the steepest fall was a 20 percent drop in primetime adults 25-54 for MSNBC (MS NOW’s predecessor) in 2022.

October 2026 set new marks for the biggest swing in both directions. Fox News’ declines have no recent precedent in the month prior to an election. On the other end, CNN had 40 percent growth in its primetime adults 25-54 audience vs. a year ago, and both of MS NOW’s 25-54 averages grew (30 percent in primetime, 38 percent in total day).

Month-to-month numbers weren’t as drastic for any outlet, but Fox News was down a bit from September (off 2.5 percent in primetime and 1 percent all day) and MS NOW (up 10 percent in primtime, 8 percent all day) and CNN (up 11 percent in primetime, 8 percent for the full day) grew.

items.title: Cate Blanchett Warns Against “Unthinking Certainty” as She Accepts Japan’s Praemium Imperiale
items.description: Two-time Oscar-winner Cate Blanchett added to her stack of global honors on Wednesday, accepting Japan’s prestigious Praemium Imperiale award at a black-tie ceremony in Tokyo.
items.author: Patrick Brzeski
paragraphs: Two-time Oscar-winner Cate Blanchett added to her stack of global honors on Wednesday, accepting Japan’s prestigious Praemium Imperiale award at a black-tie ceremony in Tokyo.
At a news conference ahead of the presentation, the actress used the occasion to reflect on the value of creative uncertainty — and the destructive hubris of its opposite.

“In an uncertain world riddled with unthinking certainty I believe doubt is vital to the creative process,” Blanchett said. “It’s what starts the challenge, the questioning, the exploration. It allows conversation and connection. It allows change.”

Presented by the Japan Art Association, the Praemium Imperiale recognizes lifetime achievement across five disciplines: painting, sculpture, architecture, music and theater/film. Often described as the Nobel Prize of the arts, the honor places Blanchett among good company — past theater and film recipients have included Federico Fellini, Akira Kurosawa, Jean-Luc Godard, Martin Scorsese, Judi Dench and Catherine Deneuve. Ang Lee was the last Hollywood-associated recipient, taking the prize in 2024.

Japan’s Princess Hitachi presented Blanchett with her medal at the Meiji Kinenkan in Tokyo’s Moto-Akasaka district. Each laureate also receives a testimonial letter and an honorarium of 15 million yen (just under $100,000). This year’s other recipients were American artist Jenny Holzer, British sculptor Andy Goldsworthy, American architect Daniel Libeskind and Swedish conductor Herbert Blomstedt.

Blanchett used her acceptance speech to offer a meditation on the limits of language and how artistic work finds its power in the inexpressable. Opening her remarks with a reference to surrealist artist Leonora Carrington, she described acting as “a profession that at its worst sinks into a quagmire of literalness but at its best can leave people speechless.”
Her creative starting point, she explained, is often the mysterious gap between what a character says and what they can’t seem to convey with language.

“I always look for meaning, for opportunity in the spaces between what is said, in what is not said, in what people are trying to say, in what they wish they had said and in what they wish they had not,” she said.
That search, Blanchett suggested, requires a willingness to remain unsure, even when uncertainty is read as weakness.

“The doubt that I will ever fully communicate is always with me. And as a woman that doubt is often interpreted as a lack of confidence. It is not. That doubt is my artistic starting point,” she said. “It’s what allows me to hear, it allows me to see, it allows me to sense.”
Continuing to take artistic risks over a long career, she added, requires courage and rigor — qualities she praised in her fellow laureates.

Former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who serves as the prize’s U.S. international adviser, was also present at the press conference. Clinton is part of the international advisory network whose committees recommend candidates, with the final selections made by the Japan Art Association.

Clinton said the prize makes “a global declaration that artists and culture are essential pillars of our societies,” arguing that its role has only become more important amid threats to democratic values and the anxieties surrounding artificial intelligence.

“It’s also, I think, even more essential that we bolster the arts in a time when we are facing the transformations being brought about by artificial intelligence,” she said, making a call to rein in the technology’s risks while preserving the human capacities of imagination and connection.

Blanchett’s visit to Japan will next include appearances at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, which runs through Nov. 4. On Friday, she is scheduled to join filmmakers Mohammad Rasoulof and Shahrbanoo Sadat for a Q&A following the Japanese premieres of five shorts supported by the Displacement Film Fund, the initiative she co-founded and leads to support displaced filmmakers.
Later Friday, she is due to appear with directors David and Nathan Zellner for a discussion accompanying their alien comedy Alpha Gang, in which she stars.
Blanchett concluded her Tokyo remarks on Wednesday with characteristic poise.

“I am profoundly grateful to have this honor bestowed upon me,” she said. “It’s an Olympus of sorts that I never conceived of even touching. It’s a beautiful, soul-soaring surprise, and a deep honor indeed.”

items.title: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim Go Deep on the Twisty Ride of ‘You Can See Everything’ — and How Audiences Are Reacting
items.description: [This story contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.]
items.author: David Canfield
paragraphs: [This story contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.]

Less than two months ago, the world did not know the existence of You Can See Everything. In the time since, the A24 production has opened as one of the most successful documentaries of all time at the North American box office and made a strong case to become the first documentary to ever be nominated for the best picture Oscar. The three-hour film, helmed by Nathan Fielder (The Rehearsal) and Lance Oppenheim (Primetime), has captured the zeitgeist in its combination of extensive, intimate access to its subjects; its newsmaking revelations; and its audacious formal choices, from the dynamic cinematography to the structural twist that defines the movie’s back half.

It’s also been a product of true discovery for audiences: Ever since its secret screening at the Telluride Film Festival over Labor Day weekend, You Can See Everything has generated deafening buzz while keeping its biggest surprises hidden.

Viewers went into cinemas likely knowing that the film would depict the final month of Elizabeth Holmes’ life with her husband, Billy Evans, and their children, before the start of her 11-plus-year prison sentence for fraud. But the surreal nature of Holmes and Evans’ dynamic, both with each other and with Fielder (who appears on camera), could hardly have been anticipated. Ditto the final act’s flash-forward that finds Fielder and Oppenheim’s access to Holmes, now incarcerated, slipping away — leading to the introduction of Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy for her portrayal of Holmes in Hulu’s The Dropout, to help them complete the film and re-enact key scenes and conversations from the time spent together.

In one of their first public Q&As since You Can See Everything’s theatrical release, Fielder and Oppenheim joined yours truly at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival for a wide-ranging conversation reflecting on those big surprises — while still clearly processing the years-long saga of making a film deep in the bubble of a “real-life human optical illusion.”

You guys had a seven-person crew moving into their household. How did you think about the way you were going to shoot this and capture this? I know whether Nathan would even be on camera was a conversation, too.

LANCE OPPENHEIM When we first started this, we didn’t think Nathan was going to be on camera. It was Elizabeth and Billy: When we were filming in the early days, they kept asking questions of Nathan. It almost felt like they wanted him to gravitate from behind the camera, in front of it. So it happened sort of organically. One of our operators, Jonathan Mitchell, who’s worked with Nathan for a long time, just panned the camera to Nathan, and I was watching on the monitor. I actually thought maybe this could be useful, in a way — if Nathan was becoming this accidental investigator of these everyday moments, he could try and pull Elizabeth from whatever version of reality she was living in and try and pull her back into the one that we were in.

The first stint of it was seven people. I usually shoot with one camera, with David [Bolen], and on this, it didn’t work at all because we kept missing these moments, especially when Nathan would ask a question — if we were panning from Nathan to Billy or Elizabeth, we would lose the first nonverbal reaction of what happens on somebody’s face when a question is posed. Nathan was like, “That’s unacceptable.” No, he wasn’t saying that. (Laughs.) But he was like, “We’ve got to get that stuff.”

NATHAN FIELDER For something like this, where you’re evaluating honesty and sincerity on someone’s face, their response even before they answer me is so important, in terms of trying to gauge if someone’s honest or not, or just what’s going on with them. … Because they would move around the house, it was a process of trying to continuously incorporate the things we were missing. We needed to pull the cameras back more, and we only had two operators for three cameras in that house; it was only two to three people maximum besides me and Lance in that house at any given time. We had the wide [shot] that would cover the whole house, and then we had these zoom lenses that could also go wide, so that we could cover anything that was happening and [we] could zoom into a tight [shot] from really far away.

Then what started happening is, before we were even rolling, they’d start talking to us. They’d try to catch us off camera and be like, “OK, this is what we’re doing today,” or, “Do you want to film this?” We thought, “Well, this is relevant because if they want something filmed, then that’s their idea of what’s going on.” We were like, “We need those process conversations.” We started coming in before they even woke up because they didn’t lock the door of their house, and we’d set up the cameras wide to cover the whole thing. You see it in the film when Billy’s like, “We’re going to the gym,” or whatever. It’s a totally different scene if you know he thinks that’s something that would be important for this documentary — to film him at the gym — as opposed to it coming from us.

OPPENHEIM Ironically for us, what felt new to us in some ways was embracing the oldest tenets of documentary filmmaking — like vérité film. As we were responding to the situation where we had less and less access to Elizabeth, that led us to embracing other modes of filmmaking, like a director on camera or even where we go later on with the re-enactments. It’s amazing seeing the way people are talking about the movie, saying it’s this new formal thing, but I’m like, “Oh no, this is actually the oldest. We’re channeling all of the different ways that documentaries have been made.” Ultimately, we’re doing that because we’re dealing with a real-life human optical illusion. That’s who she is.

You’ve mentioned some healthy disagreements between the two of you, just about what was happening and how you were interpreting it. Let’s take the “who’s on first” scene as an example: Nathan, what it was like to be there for a bizarre moment like that, and how would you two then talk about it in terms of how it would inform the movie? And how do you reflect on them now?

FIELDER There were so many things that we were tracking all at once. Sometimes these little moments would sit in your mind for a bit, but we were there constantly for a month, so some we would sort of forget about — and then be reminded when we reviewed the footage in the edit. That “who’s on first” moment, everyone was like, “What was that?” We knew these moments that we couldn’t make sense of were interesting because we would talk about them a lot. It’s hard because you’re just there and you’re observing and you can’t cultivate anything. You can’t make anything happen. You’re just documenting.
OPPENHEIM There are also so many moments in this where Nathan would be like, “I think you’re guilty. Why are we here? Do you want us to leave?” And they’d be like, “No, no, stay.”

FIELDER I didn’t say that in the same sentence, hold on. (Laughs.) I did not say, “I think you’re guilty. Do you want us to leave?” I said it very early on to her; I laid out so she knew how I felt. But yeah, we were conscious that this was a mother’s last month with her children. If tensions would ever run high and we sensed that our presence wasn’t wanted, I’d say, “Look, if you guys are regretting this decision, we’ll pull the plug. We’ll go.” It wasn’t a thing where we were saying, “You have to do this,” or trying to convince them to be a part of this.
OPPENHEIM It was the opposite.
FIELDER We always were saying, “We will leave anytime.” And they were very much like, “No.”
OPPENHEIM “Stay. Stay for this.”
FIELDER That was part of the mindfuck of it all. Sorry for swearing. I don’t normally swear in professional settings or even private ones a lot of times.

OPPENHEIM Before we started shooting, Billy showed us a video — because he would sometimes video things on his phone, like just of him and Elizabeth on a couch. He’d be like, “Look at this moment.” It’d be a video of Elizabeth crying, and he’s like, “We just watched Pride and Prejudice. This is so good.” I’m just like, “Are these the type of moments that you are interested in having us show? What do you want us to see? What is the object of your guys’ inquiry with this?”

FIELDER Why us? Why are we there? I mean, I like myself enough, but I would not want me there for my last month of freedom, if that makes sense. What was also weird about it is we felt like there was some game going on that even we couldn’t make sense of, but we were like, “Well, let’s just go along with this and see what comes out, I guess.”
Do you feel like you have any more clarity on that now?

OPPENHEIM Seeing it with audiences is always really different for me. I feel like I end up having a completely different reaction to the movie. It’s like it’s this evolving Rorschach test. But I do feel like we witnessed something. We saw a pattern of behavior emerge over the time we had. Other documentaries I’ve made, I’ve spent a lot of time with people — years — but sometimes you don’t really notice as much of a change.
