It felt like there were things that were going on, and there are times where I watch this movie and I feel like the behavior is totally unconscious and she’s not aware of it. And there are times where I’m like, “No, she’s totally aware of it.” It’s hard to operate fully in the world of binaries. It’s somewhere in between, somewhere deep, lost in the void or something.

FIELDER This is an interesting time because there are a lot of reactions to this, and I have time to look at some stuff. There is this phenomenon that happens that is related to proximity. When you’re in their bubble, you’re in a different mindset than when you step out of it and you’re in the world of everyone else. We weren’t talking to anyone about this project; no one had seen it, we were just talking amongst ourselves for so long. And now the conversation is so all over the world, I’m gleaning new things from just hearing what other people are saying. Also, it does feel like people bring to this a lot that’s inside them. It’s not just what’s on the screen, or else everyone would have a consensus. There’s something coming from people, individuals, and it’s hard sometimes for me to separate that from what we’re objectively looking at.

We should talk a little bit about the back half of the movie, as you were losing access to Elizabeth but decided to continue telling the story. How did you decide on the shape of it, and how did you know when to end it?

OPPENHEIM We both were interested in seeing what was going to happen with the business. Nathan said to Billy, “Let us know when you have something you can show us,” and he’s like, “I’ll have it in 365 days.” It turned out to be two years instead of when he had initially suggested it would happen. But then it felt like once we were out of the bubble of San Diego and we were seeing Billy work on the thing, there were these questions that kept coming up for us. We wanted to go to even more people. We reached out, but so many people we tried to talk to that were out of the bubble didn’t want to talk to us because they thought that Elizabeth was this toxic personality. So that led us to [Amanda Seyfried].

FIELDER When we watched everything and put together that first half, even though something felt complete with her going to prison, the picture didn’t feel complete because we were still having conversations where we were trying to make sense of it that were being informed by other stuff that happened off camera. We didn’t know where we were going to go. And like Lance said, we reached out to a bunch of people and then when we reached out to Amanda, she was like, “Come over, bring cameras.”
OPPENHEIM We didn’t know Amanda before this.

FIELDER And when we eventually realized we had something complete, that was just a decision that was made in the edit. We felt like there was enough, or the conversations that were being informed by things that the audience wouldn’t have been privy to were now part of the film. Once we felt like you guys had all the information basically that we had, it felt like, “OK, this is sort of as far as we can go with it.” We didn’t even know if it felt complete. It just felt like the end of the road for this, a little bit.

OPPENHEIM The Amanda piece — she maybe knew who Nathan was, but they’d never met each other before. That first moment when we’re in her apartment, that’s the very first time any of us had really spoken with her in person, when she’s watching the footage. She even says in the scene, “I have no interest in doing this again.” Then she started imitating her, and that suddenly led to us being like, “OK, well, this is interesting.” It almost felt like she had this unfinished business, this desire to do it again. That led us down a whole different path. She brought her own baggage into the process too. It was amazing. It’s a testament to the way we made the film.

items.title: Free IP and Fresh Eyes: How Hollywood Is Reinventing the Classics
items.description: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.
items.author: Lexy Perez
paragraphs: Some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

East of Eden showrunner Zoe Kazan has had her eye on adapting John Steinbeck’s family saga since she first read it at 15. “Somebody has to put the thing onscreen that I see in my head,” she told The Hollywood Reporter. And after “a good 20 years” of carrying that feeling, the opportunity to translate the story to screen finally came to fruition, with Kazan’s vision unfurling as an eight-episode Netflix limited series.
Hollywood has never been shy about mining the classics, with Pride and Prejudice, To Kill a Mockingbird and Little Women among the staples of film and TV’s page-to-screen catalog.

This year, Kazan’s dip into the classic canon is joined by the likes of Christopher Nolan, who has taken on Homer’s The Odyssey, Emerald Fennell’s adaptation of Emily Brontë’s Wuthering Heights, and new versions of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility and Charles Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities. Steinbeck, Austen and Dickens come with name recognition, a built-in audience and, as Sense and Sensibility screenwriter Diana Reid puts it, “free IP.” But the prestige and name recognition only get a project so far with audiences desperate for something fresh.

This year, the writers behind Netflix’s East of Eden, Focus Features’ Sense and Sensibility and MGM+’s A Tale of Two Cities used that audience demand to do something different: leave the novels’ worlds intact and rebuild the people inside them.
For Kazan, that meant rereading Steinbeck’s Cathy. For Daniel West, it was giving Dickens’ Lucie a pulse. Reid let the Dashwood sisters Marianne and Elinor each grow into a bit of the other.

And while a famous novel might spark initial curiosity, it offers no inherent road map once development begins. So rather than reimagining these books through a modern lens, each writer chose to lean into the ways the stories already transcend time.
“You don’t need to spoon-feed the audience the modernity of it,” West says.
Why a Classic Novel Already Has Appeal

Reid is the first to admit the commercial logic of adapting a classic. “I think they are classic for a reason,” she says. But the appeal runs deeper. In an era of surface-level connection, she argues, audiences crave something that feels substantial.

“There’s nothing more satisfying as an audience than encountering someone who’s superficially very different from you — they live in another time, they have different values and customs, they dress in a bizarre way — and then realizing that emotionally you have the same inner life.”

She also knows she won’t be the last to take on Austen. “It’s nice to be part of such a big catalog. On one hand, it’s an honor and on the other, it takes pressure off, because it’ll be one of many. It doesn’t need to be definitive.”

West’s pitch for A Tale of Two Cities, a four-part series that premiered on MGM+ last month, started with what he calls a “unicorn”: a book with a huge cultural footprint that, by his account, hadn’t had a major screen adaptation in nearly 40 years. He and star and executive producer Kit Harington had been talking about adapting Dickens’ 1859 novel for roughly a decade, noting that there “hasn’t really been a seminal TV or film adaptation” of the story.

“It was done quite a lot in the first half of the 20th century, but then it petered out. So a large part of the draw was the opportunity: There was this huge built-in audience that already knew the book, or at least knew of it,” he says.

“The story itself is incredibly timely,” he adds. “It’s about a disenfranchised, broken society that is pushing back and reaching a crisis point. Within that, there’s a very personal, intimate love story.”

Kazan has a personal tie to East of Eden — her grandfather, Elia Kazan, directed the 1955 film — but part of her motivation for making a series was to tell more of the novel than that film did. Though Steinbeck’s book was published in 1952, she says, “there’s this beautiful continuum between us and the past,” which is part of what makes revisiting a classic so appealing.
Looking backward and forward at the same time, she adds, “is a profound part of what makes us human.”

“It’s the opposite of AI. It’s not regurgitation, not spitting back up what we’ve already digested,” she says. “It’s why we should read these books. They’re like a bow shot across time from one human to another.”
Rethinking the Novels’ Protagonists

Still, none of the three writers treated an established title as a safety net. Instead, their adaptations declined to modernize the novel’s setting and embraced finding new ways into the protagonists.

While developing A Tale of Two Cities, West and his producers considered a contemporary reimagining early on before dropping it. “The issues these characters are dealing with, the injustice and the way it bleeds into vengeance and cruelty, already feel very 2026,” he says.

What he changed instead was characterization. In Dickens’ novel, heroine Lucie Manette is “prone to a lot of weeping” and “quite a lot of fainting,” West says. “She’s not the most compelling heroine in large passages of it. So we made some fundamental changes. We made her much more intentional.”
He wanted Lucie to be “the central pivot of the entire story” and “the investigative force” of the opening episodes, pushing against the walls of “buttoned-up Georgian London.”

“That was a fairly big modernization from the book,” he says. Of Mirren Mack, who plays Lucie in the series, he adds: “Lucie is the central component of the whole thing, the sun at the center of the solar system, and then an actor arrives who delivers all of that and more and elevates it through her own interpretation.”

He also replaced Jarvis Lorry and Miss Pross — who he felt were “serving a similar purpose” and were too “big and colorful” for the series’ taut, volatile tone — with a new character, Hester (Sharon Duncan-Brewster). “She isn’t a proxy father figure to Lucie. She’s an inherited family member, almost an inherited stepmother. … As the story goes on, they discover that they mean a lot to each other and are more than just inherited relations. They really are family, but they come to that on their own terms. That gives them a larger emotional distance to travel.”

Thérèse Defarge (Roxane Duran) marks another departure. “We wanted to see somebody become, for want of a less anachronistic word, radicalized,” West says. “She starts as part of her community. She has a warmth and generosity. Because of what happens to her within the story, we see that crack begin to metastasize into something really sinister and ugly, and by the end, murderous. When we meet her in episode one, she’s a completely different person from what we see at the very end of the show.”

Dickens’ book centers on a couple, but West wanted to “intensify that” and “twist it slightly into much more of a triangle and make it more live and more complex” between Sydney Carton (Harington), Lucie (Mack) and Charles Darnay (François Civil). “That way we don’t really know which way Lucie is going to go until she does, toward the back end of the story. I also wanted both men to be equally attractive, equally intriguing and volatile, each speaking to a different side of her, so we really feel the pull, the tension and the dilemma she’s wrestling with.”

Kazan’s rereading centered on Cathy Ames (Florence Pugh), the character who first hooked her in Steinbeck’s story. Writing the series, which released on Netflix on Oct. 1, she realized something she hadn’t anticipated: Cathy “is almost always telling the truth.”

A fresh perspective also helped Kazan see the story as a love story between brothers Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles (Mike Faist), one that Cathy interrupts. “By watching Chris and Mike interact, I understood how much these characters loved each other,” she says.
Respecting the Literary Blueprint — and Knowing When to Change It

Creative liberties, the writers insist, aren’t changes for the sake of it. Reid describes her approach as “respect rather than reverence.” Her biggest liberty is a duel between Herbert Nordrum’s Colonel Brandon and Frank Dillane’s John Willoughby, which Austen mentions but keeps offstage. “Hearing about things secondhand in a novel is not so confusing, but onscreen, hearing a character describe it isn’t very interesting,” she says. “You need to see it to reveal the drama.”

Austen’s voice also served as a guide for balancing drama with wit. “When I read the book, I made a note of the lines that made me laugh, and a lot of those ended up verbatim in the film. Jane Austen’s just really funny,” Reid says.
Kazan’s challenge was the opposite: too much book. She was only interested in adapting it as a series because “the book is simply too big,” and even with seven episodes, “half is not in our series.”

For A Tale of Two Cities, West’s key structural decision was genre. “I always wanted it to be a thriller: a very taut, limited story,” he explains. “Four episodes felt like the perfect length to keep the pace and stakes up, and to never let any of the characters settle. I really wanted to make sure that all the characters, whether they’re in London or Paris or moving between the two, are always in a state of agitation. Their feet are never quite on solid ground, so we feel the jeopardy and the volatility of their world.”

Asked why classics keep returning, each offers their own perspective. West points to archetypes and longevity. A Tale of Two Cities, he says, “is the archetypal sacrificial story,” with “strong parallels in that act of sacrifice to the Bible and all the stories that form the basis of our narratives and our emotional map of the world.”

Classics “still feel timeless, and they still feel as resonant today,” West adds. “The key thing for us as creatives is to find a new way of telling those classic stories, an angle and something new to say about them. That doesn’t mean reinventing the wheel. It just means giving yourself the license to look at them with fresh eyes.”

Reid returns to the idea that classics are “classics for a reason.” She explains that “when an audience doesn’t feel patronized” and an adaptation allows “the classic to exist in its own time, that makes for incredibly powerful viewing.”

Kazan sees adaptations as a way to lower the barrier for new readers. “One thing these adaptations can do is make a general audience feel they have access to East of Eden, The Odyssey, Wuthering Heights.”

While they have differing ideas about what keeps the classics coming back, all three writers share the same hope: that viewers will pick up the book. Classics haven’t disappeared from school reading lists, but students are reportedly reading significantly fewer full-length books than in past decades.

“As long as we don’t ban and burn these books, everybody will continue to have access to them,” Kazan says. “There are so many books I came to as an adult that changed my life, and if I’d read them in high school, I wouldn’t have cared or understood. The most important thing is to let kids feel they can have pleasure in reading.”

There’s already evidence that these adaptations are sending people back to the page. Since the series’ Oct. 1 debut, sales of East of Eden have risen nearly 200 percent across all formats, according to publisher Penguin Classics. The novel also hit No. 1 on Amazon’s best-sellers list — 74 years after it was published. The Economist reports that U.S. sales of The Odyssey have quadrupled this year, while Wuthering Heights topped Britain’s best-seller list.

“Anything that can nudge people back toward bookshops and toward discovering those works again can only be a good thing,” West says. “The reason the work of classic storytellers like Dickens, Shakespeare and Austen still resonates is that they’re saying something about the human condition, about what we’re all struggling with, yearning for and reaching for.”

“It would be amazing if people went back to the book,” Reid says. If Sense and Sensibility “could make Austen and the classics feel less intimidating, and encourage people to see themselves in it and find emotional truth in a story they thought was too remote, that would be amazing!”

items.title: Are Men Ready for the Return of the Shiny Dress Shirt?
items.description: The designer Julian Louie remembers the first shiny dress shirt he ever saw: an iridescent purple number worn by director Todd Haynes during the press tour for his 1998 film Velvet Goldmine (fittingly, a movie about 1970s glam rock). Louie came across that ima
items.author: Tyler Watamanuk
paragraphs: The designer Julian Louie remembers the first shiny dress shirt he ever saw: an iridescent purple number worn by director Todd Haynes during the press tour for his 1998 film Velvet Goldmine (fittingly, a movie about 1970s glam rock). Louie came across that image of Haynes in the 2000s, and something about the shirt stuck with him. That rakish, slightly decadent menswear became central to Aubero, the label he launched in 2022. Earlier this year, Pedro Pascal showed up on the red carpet in a shiny Aubero shirt that rivaled the juicy, luminously green interior of a freshly cut lime.

Pascal isn’t the only movie star embracing a little sheen these days. Riz Ahmed delivered a one-two punch on the recent Digger press tour, during which he sported both a black silk habotai shirt by Lemaire and a silk chartreuse tee under a gray Saint Laurent suit. Last month, the actor-skateboarder Nico Hiraga showed up at the Toronto International Film Festival in a supremely shiny mauve shirt, worn unbuttoned to his sternum. Heated Rivalry’s Connor Storrie, who is a Saint Laurent brand ambassador, has made a habit of wearing the label’s silky shirts. Meanwhile, Resident Evil star Austin Abrams took it a step further and opted for a shiny two-piece suit from Maison Valentino. Hollywood’s leading men, it seems, are looking a whole lot glossier.

Anyone old enough to remember the early 2000s knows this isn’t the first time shiny shirts have had a moment in Hollywood. Think of Brad Pitt’s wardrobe as Rusty Ryan in the Ocean’s franchise, which basically mirrored the actor’s own red-carpet fashion at the time (and sometimes even in the present day). Or the bros on Entourage, whose fondness of shiny “going-out shirts” sometimes seemed eerily interchangeable with the actors who played them. The glossy dress shirt has a documented history of appearing both impossibly cool and slightly ridiculous, so even as other Y2K styles surge through menswear, it’s little surprising that the shiny button-up has come around again. (Proceed with caution, though: A few wrong turns and guys will be back in bedazzled jeans and gelled faux hawks.)

Sophie Jordan, the menswear buying director at luxury retailer Mytheresa, points to the spring 2026 collections as a turning point. “Gucci’s first collection under Demna showcased this shiny evening shirt in a sexy way but still a strong edge of masculinity,” she says, noting that Haider Ackermann’s Tom Ford—always the proprietor of sexy, nightlife-ready clothes—also offered printed silk shirts that same season, which were a hit with Mytheresa’s shoppers. Since then, designers (including Demna) have just kept ’em coming.

Jordan places the shiny shirt within a broader category she calls the “evening shirt,” which encompasses everything from silk and sequins to velvet and sheer fabrics. The appeal isn’t necessarily to dress like, say, the Roxbury Guys of Saturday Night Live fame, but rather to tap into some of menswear’s more sensual currents. “This style of shirt plays into that without being too over the top. Fundamentally, the shape and silhouette is very classic,” she says. “When styled with a pair of tailored pants, it’s very easy to wear and adds an evening feel to the styling without being overdone.” In other words, a little shine can is a relatively low-lift way to make an impression.

“I like the pairing of a very expressive material used on a super straightforward silhouette,” says Louie, the Aubero designer. For some of his label’s earliest designs, Louie deconstructed mid-century silk taffeta cocktail dresses and turned them into board shorts. “It was about taking a material that has always been associated with a more feminine couture sensibility and applying it to a men’s wardrobe in an unexpected way,” he says.

But, as with most things, the shiny dress shirt never truly went away. It’s a perennial fixture on the runway of labels like Tom Ford and Dolce & Gabbana. Dries Van Noten elevated the garment with prints and patterns into something approaching high art, while the cult Swedish brand Our Legacy continues to turn out the wonderfully weird shirting that has continually wooed menswear’s more adventurous dressers. But what’s changed is how many guys seem willing to give the look a shot. It certainly helps that shiny dress shirts slide into today’s slouchy tailoring as well as the sexier, more retro fare à la Anthony Vaccarello’s final work at Saint Laurent (as seen on Storrie) or the French breakout label Husbands.

For those curious but are perhaps afraid of veering too close to “lounge lizard” territory, there are plenty of halfway steps. Many labels, including Auralee and Tom Ford, offer dress shirts in cotton-silk blends that feature more dull cotton than shiny silk, for a finish that catches the light without going full disco ball. For newbies, “it’s a smart idea to build up to it,” says Jordan. A little texture and a little sheen will go a long way for guys who don’t typically spend their evenings walking red carpets.

In recent years, the stronghold of “quiet luxury” and tasteful neutrals has been so enduring that it’s easy to forget that clothes are allowed to be a little ridiculous, a bit sexy, and hell, even fun. Perhaps that’s what all these newfangled glossy dress shirts are getting at. Or as Louie put it: “Maybe this means we’ve moved on from a moment of banal clothing.”

items.title: NASA’s Oldest Martian Spacecraft Have Been Running for Decades. Here’s How
items.description: NASA’s Mars Odyssey spacecraft has been operating for so long, it can rent a car without any fees. The spacecraft arrived at the Red Planet on October 24, 2001. It, along with its 20-year-old sibling, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), have operated longer
items.author: Meghan Bartels
paragraphs: NASA’s Mars Odyssey spacecraft has been operating for so long, it can rent a car without any fees. The spacecraft arrived at the Red Planet on October 24, 2001. It, along with its 20-year-old sibling, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), have operated longer than anyone watching their launches could have dreamed possible.

Having such a long record of observations from above the Martian surface has rewritten the story of water on the planet, past and present alike. Keeping the wizened orbiters going for so long has been possible only thanks to great engineering and constant problem solving—and a little luck. But scientists wonder whether, despite their storied legacies, Odyssey and MRO will be the last of their kind, at least for the Red Planet.

“Both Odyssey and MRO are some of the most productive spacecraft that have ever existed,” says Briony Horgan, a planetary scientist at Purdue University who isn’t affiliated with either mission, calling them “critical” to NASA’s overall Mars research program. Odyssey’s observations of the planet’s ice, for example, and MRO’s ability to see surface features change over time have each given scientists unprecedented insight into Mars as a vibrant planet rather than a lump of rock. Odyssey and MRO also connect humans to every NASA rover, which can’t communicate with Earth directly. It’s an impressive legacy for a pair of orbiters that were only meant to last just a few years.

Space is a notoriously harsh environment that takes luck and resilience to survive for decades. Particularly tricky is the barrage of high-energy particles hitting machinery; a powerful enough strike to a delicate enough apparatus can be fatal. And whereas engineers can keep constant tabs on satellites orbiting Earth, bandwidth to Mars is more limited—science spacecraft might only check in once or twice a week, says Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, who has worked on a range of more recent Mars orbiters.
“A Mars craft has to be able to manage by itself,” he says.

Losing an instrument is bad, but losing the power or computing systems can brick the whole craft. NASA often doubles up on vital parts of a spacecraft to ensure that if something important fails, the mission can run off the spare until engineers can troubleshoot a problem.

In the MRO’s case, one challenge it’s faced is ironically due to its staying power. The orbiter determines its precise location and orientation by comparing what its cameras see with a stellar atlas onboard—with just one hiccup. “MRO is actually old enough that some of those stars have moved across the night sky—very slightly, but they have moved,” says Paul Fieseler, an engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and chief engineer for MRO. The tiny misalignments confused the spacecraft, and last year, engineers had to send up an updated map to keep MRO oriented into the future.

Odyssey’s greatest risk right now is simply running out of propellant it uses to make tiny adjustments to maintain its orientation in space. The spacecraft doesn’t have a fuel gauge–without gravity to push the fuel down, there’s no volume to measure–so NASA can’t be sure how much juice it still has. Engineers have improvised new ways to fully operate the spacecraft on just a few drops at a time in a bid to extend its life.

Experts say both spacecraft benefited from failures during NASA’s infamous “faster, better, cheaper” era. In 1999, NASA lost two missions arriving at Mars: First the Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in the atmosphere, and then, just months later, the Mars Polar Lander botched its arrival and slammed into the surface. Each catastrophe, investigations determined, was caused by what might in more pedestrian realms be dubbed careless mistakes. The first was due to miscommunication between a ground system relying on imperial units and the flight system using metric, while the second was due to a software error not caught during testing.

“Those failures were very much on the mind of the team pulling together the Odyssey spacecraft,” says Glen Havens, an engineer at JPL and project and mission manager of Mars Odyssey. With those losses stinging, NASA invested more in perfecting the Odyssey and MRO spacecraft before launch, designing each to be as resilient as possible and testing every tiny component and every system configuration.
One key principle is what NASA calls “margin”—the spacecraft equivalent of carrying a snack, just in case.

“Unexpected things might happen, and you want to make sure the spacecraft will survive,” says Nilton Renno, a spaceflight engineer at the University of Michigan who hasn’t worked on either mission. MRO launched with a larger battery and more propellant than it strictly needed, Fieseler notes, and that margin is now keeping the mission going, with NASA hoping to operate it for another decade.

But orbiting Mars, it’s wise not to take anything for granted. Just last year, NASA lost the 11-year-old Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution—its youngest Red Planet orbiter—after the spacecraft unexpectedly lost power on the far side of the planet. As Odyssey and MRO continue to age, questions linger about what Mars orbiters come next for NASA.

The agency has hired Blue Origin to build a dedicated communications satellite to beam scads of data back to Earth for at least five years—but unlike its forebears, which began as science missions before turning to communications work, this orbiter will only relay signals for other spacecraft.

NASA’s Mars science agenda includes only relatively limited projects. One mission, which Lillis leads, features two orbiters currently on their way to study how the planet responds to the constant stream of charged particles flowing off the sun. But even he calls the mission “right on the edge of being too small to do good science.” Then, there’s Skyfall, the trio of small helicopters meant to launch aboard the first nuclear-propelled spacecraft within just two years—a shockingly rapid timeline, and for a mission with minimal ability to answer meaty research questions.

To scientists, none of these initiatives quite build on the legacy of Odyssey and MRO and may even raise the specter of the infamous Mars failures that came before. “Certainly they’re pushing for faster, cheaper,” Horgan says. “It’s going to be a lot more challenging to do good science in that environment.”

items.title: The Best Last-Minute Halloween Costumes That’ll Arrive Before the Weekend
items.description: Okay, so while everyone else was crafting their elaborate Wicker costumes, you were busy with work and life and everything in between and didn’t have time to plan an outfit for Halloween this weekend? Don’t worry, you still have time to pull something together
items.author: Chinea Rodriguez
paragraphs: Okay, so while everyone else was crafting their elaborate Wicker costumes, you were busy with work and life and everything in between and didn’t have time to plan an outfit for Halloween this weekend? Don’t worry, you still have time to pull something together that’s more creative than a sexy cat (thanks to the magic of two-day shipping).

I made it extra easy for you by rounding up some of the best last-minute Halloween costumes, below. Keep scrolling for easy ideas that’ll arrive before Saturday if you have an Amazon Prime account, plus options from other retailers that also offer two-day shipping, like Revolve, Zara, and Shopbop.

It’s a little too late to DIY Kylie Jenner’s million-dollar Fantasy bra, but with a pair of wings, you can still pull off a runway-worthy look. You can make this as dramatic or subtle as you want with a pink silk robe or lingerie-esque top. The key part of the look (and the part that’s easiest to pull together on a time crunch) is the bombshell glam, courtesy of Pat McGrath and Guido Palau this year. Consider high-shine glitter shadows and glosses from the makeup artist’s brand.
Zendaya at The Odyssey premiere in New York City

If you want to channel Zendaya this Halloween, skip the variations of Rue from Euphoria and the infamous large hat and try out one of her viral press-tour looks instead. The actress and her longtime stylist, Law Roach, had a legendary red-carpet-fashion run while promoting The Odyssey, which included this angelic Matières Fécales haute couture look. To get the look without an appointment at the brand’s atelier, you can recycle your VS angel wings and grab a strapless white dress. For your glam, make sure to read our interview with Zendaya’s makeup artist, Ernesto Casillas, for tips on how to re-create the soft makeup look at home.
Jordyn Woods, a.k.a. the ultimate NBA WAG

Someone, somewhere is making a costume that looks like Jordyn Woods’s lucky bag. While you don’t have that kind of time, you can make use of the bag and jersey you already own to dress up as New York City’s favorite WAG and brand founder. Lean into her courtside glam by dressing in the Knicks’ blue and orange, denim, faux fur, and her signature bag (if you were lucky enough to snag the orange version before she retired it).
The all-powerful Etsy witch

Whether or not you’ve used an Etsy witch to land a job interview, lure in a lover, or ensure perfect weather on your wedding day like influencer Jaz Smith, you can easily create this TikTok-favorite costume last minute. All you need is a witch hat, a printer (for your Etsy label), and a dream — maybe even throw accessories you already own that have witchy vibes, like a black bag or flameless candle.
The queen of country music

I’m sure there will be many costumes honoring the late great Dolly Parton this year. But since she was such a style star, you don’t have to worry about showing up to your party in the same costume as someone else; she has so many famous looks to choose from. Whether you opt for a casual denim look or one of her sequin-embellished dresses, make sure to go big or go home with this platinum-blonde wig — it’s what Dolly would’ve wanted.

You probably won’t be the only deer at the party, but the perk of this look is that it relies almost entirely on trends you already own and can wear again. If you missed out on the Sandy Liang x Gap deer-print fleece, you can still find something just as cozy, like this zip-up hoodie from Urban Outfitters. Layer it over a brown dress or wear it with jeans, then take your costume a step further by pairing the look with split-toe Tabi shoes. With all the time you’ll save putting the outfit together, you can spend a few minutes watching and re-creating one of the many deer makeup tutorials on YouTube.

It would be easy enough to re-create one of the everyday looks Harry Styles wears as he walks the length of Brooklyn and Manhattan. But if you’ve attended his 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden, you probably already have what you need to pull off dressing like the star during a show. Don’t let that feather boa and sequins you bought go to waste.

items.title: 'One Tree Hill' Star Bethany Joy Lenz Wrote A Terrifying Novel
items.description: Note: This story discusses violence and emotional abuse.
items.author: Sophie Fishman
paragraphs: Note: This story discusses violence and emotional abuse.

Bethany Joy Lenz was just 12 years old when she penned her first novel on her family computer. “We just got a new Mac when they first came out, and the unit was massive. It was like I’m on my AOL dial-up, and then I was on the computer writing this book,” she says. “It was about a girl named Lucretia who I called Luke, and she had a best friend who was a guy, and there were bullies at school. I mean, I was just processing my own life, I’m sure.”

Lenz never published Luke’s story, but 33 years later, her debut novel, The Betrayal of Cora Wexford, hit shelves this week. It’s historical fiction inspired by real events: a string of 11 killings in London’s East End between 1888 and 1891 known as the Whitechapel Murders, with at least some attributed to Jack the Ripper. The story follows Cora, an American expat and postmortem artist painting intricate portraits of the city’s most marginalized women as a serial killer terrorizes London. On the eve of her 39th birthday, she meets Miles Vale, a handsome and suspiciously charming stranger. As their relationship develops, Cora finds herself in a twisted game of psychological manipulation and gaslighting.

“It became clear to me that the best way to tell this story was to parallel the horrendous psychological and emotional violence that so many of us still experience today,” she says. “It’s an unspoken thing that we don’t have language for. It’s unseen, right alongside also very real violence that is seen because it’s physical. The courts don’t know what to do with it.”

For those who read Lenz’s bestselling 2024 memoir Dinner for Vampires, aspects of Cora’s story may sound familiar. At 20, two years before she began starring as Haley James Scott on One Tree Hill, Lenz attended a Bible study with a friend. What would follow was 10 years in a high-control religious cult that would extort her of more than $2 million and coerce her into a marriage.
Many of Cora’s experiences of confusion and isolation came from Lenz’s own experience. “I put myself into her as much as I felt was appropriate,” she says.

That’s not to say the work was easy. “There was a heavy lift writing this book in a short period of time: all the research I had to do, all the characters that needed full development, the world that needed to be explained in a luscious and attractive way so that readers didn’t feel like they were slogging through one heavy theme after another,” she says.
Below, Lenz opens up about the research process, painting her own book cover, and feeling rebellious.
How did you know you wanted to dip your toes into fiction?

It’s all I’ve ever really wanted to do except sing and dance. It’s how I express myself, even if nobody else gets to see it, because I just need to get things out of my body. Having something on paper helps my neuro-spicy brain remember things and keep them in order. This is just a total, total dream come true, and I’m really excited I got the chance to do it.
You write about London with such precision. How did you go about researching the scenery?

I did a lot of online research. I also went to London. I’m familiar with the city from hanging out with friends, so I wasn’t trying to get my bearings, but I’d never gone as a tourist. So I’d walk down the streets and put in my noise-canceling earbuds and listen to a three-hour loop of Victorian London street sounds I found on YouTube.
One of my favorite lines from the book is when Cora adds a detail to a painting and says: “Quiet rebellions, I get away with them all the time.” What kinds of quiet rebellions do you get away with?

Every time I hold my tongue, that feels empowering for me as someone who grew up feeling like I had to constantly say things six different ways to make sure I wasn’t misunderstood, because that would make me feel rejected and unworthy. But for me to recognize that what I say probably won’t be very meaningful to a combative or closed-off person, and to instead try to listen and leave it at that — that feels like a rebellion to the part of myself that wants and needs attention or to be seen.
How was the process of painting your own book cover?

I loved art in high school and was really good at sketching, but I could never quite figure out paint. And then I moved to Manhattan, and where do you set up an easel in a little matchbox apartment? And then two or three years after I left the high-demand group, I just decided, why not? Who cares if I’m any good at it? Nobody’s looking.

We’re so used to commodifying everything we do. We have to hustle and sell. And I kind of was like, “Actually, no, I need something that’s just for me.” So I was an abstract painter for years and would’ve been embarrassed for real artists to see my work.

Then my editor was like, “You paint, right? Why don’t you just paint the cover?” I’m like, “I don’t paint people. I don’t know how to make stuff look real.” But I gave it a shot, and I’m just so grateful that for whatever reason, God gave me all these gifts of creativity.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Jennifer Lawrence's Haircare Brand Is Here To Give You "Floof"
items.description: Jennifer Lawrence's Hair Care Brand Is Here To Give You "Floof"
items.author: Rachel Lapidos
paragraphs: Jennifer Lawrence's Hair Care Brand Is Here To Give You "Floof"
Everything to know about Mes° Beauty, a line designed for healthy, styled hair without the high-maintenance routine.

The rumors you may have read about are true: Jennifer Lawrence is launching her own hair care brand. Mes°, which launches Oct. 27 on mesbeauty.com, is a biodesigned line built around a deceptively simple premise: Hair care should work without requiring a complicated routine.

If you’re rolling your eyes at yet another celebrity beauty brand, I hear you. The Oscar-winning actor came to the hair care space with a familiar frustration: She couldn’t find products that made her hair look good while also prioritizing its health.

After dyeing her hair dark brown for The Hunger Games and cycling through colors for other roles, Lawrence cut her lengths into a pixie as a fresh start — a transformation that marked the beginning of her hair health journey. “I found that, with the products I was using, it was always an either/or: either my hair is styled, which means hairspray and hot tools and teasing. Or it’s healthy, which means it’s listless and flat and damp,” she said at a preview event ahead of the launch.

This trade-off became the mission behind Mes°: high-performance hair care that helps you get the look you want without turning your routine into a second job. Delivering on that promise, however, requires smart formulation.

After hearing a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a beauty industry veteran and MIT-trained chemical and biological engineer, Lawrence knew she'd found the right person to help bring her vision to life. Aganovic, who also founded biology-based beauty brand Arcaea and fragrance brand Future Society, wasn't immediately convinced. At the preview event, Lawrence recalled calling Aganovic multiple times, insisting she'd wait until the engineer was ready to work with her.

Together, the duo built Mes° around three core concepts. In Situ° Design is about creating products that work with hair in its real-life context, including helping a style last beyond wash day. The brand’s “unbothered beauty” philosophy prioritizes multifunctional formulas that deliver results without a complicated routine. And Creative Biodesign uses biology as a starting point for rethinking familiar hair care challenges.

The brand’s debut comes with three products: a reparative mask, a volumizing mist, and a restyling serum. Each tackles a different hair frustration, but the common thread is making a good hair day a little less labor-intensive.

Traditionally, hair masks come with a whole production: shampoo, treatment, rinse, style, repeat. It’s the pain point Lawrence and Aganovic aimed to address with the Multitask Repair Mask. Apply it to dry hair before shampooing and leave it on for five minutes or overnight.

The magic lies in the biomimetic tri-lipid complex and olive squalane, a combo that helps protect and replenish hair's lipid barrier. According to the brand, it delivers up to 158% more lipids in hair and reduces protein loss during washing.

And since every product in the line is multifunctional, it doubles as a styler: Use it to create a sleek wet-hair look (instead of lube, which Lawrence quipped was the only thing that truly worked for her in the past).
The Good Roots Volume Mist

Lawrence has a particular beef with volumizing sprays. “I’ve always been looking for a better option,” she said, noting that she’d never purchased the same one twice. Enter: the Good Roots Volume Mist, a root-lifting formula made with the brand’s ARC-5™ Technology and Mediterranean Microalgae.

Rather than focusing on volume alone, the mist is designed to help balance excess scalp oil while lifting hair at the roots. The brand says clinical testing found a reduction in scalp oiliness over 14 days, while its styling claims include up to 2.5 times more volume with heat styling compared with air-drying.

Lawrence’s main requirement was that the formula deliver lift without the usual crunchy, product-y finish. “It never gets crunchy,” she said. “Your hair is soft and fluffy and it stays for days because it’s actually a scalp treatment.”
In other words, the goal isn’t just to make hair look bigger for a few hours — it’s to give roots a lift without leaving lengths stiff or crispy.
The Off-Duty Restyling Serum
Rounding out the trio is the Off-Duty Restyling Serum, a product Lawrence describes as “a hot tool replacement styling serum.”

“I get photographed pretty much every time I leave my house, but I don’t have time to give myself a blowout,” she said. “And I don’t want to be putting hot tools on my hair every day. So I wanted something where I could brush my hair and put something in and give it that floof.”

The bi-phase formula combines a lightweight oil phase to smooth frizz and restore shine with a serum phase designed to strengthen hair and help reshape it. “It goes on and almost looks a little wet, but doesn't change your hair texture,” Lawrence said. “You can add as much as you want because there isn't any buildup. You can even put it on your roots because it doesn't make your hair flat.”
The idea is to revive day-two or day-three hair without starting an entire wash-and-style cycle. Think of it as a multitasking zhuzh.

items.title: Exclusive: The 'Wicker' Stars Actually Insist You Dress Like Them For Halloween
items.description: The Wicker Stars Actually Insist You Dress Like Them For Halloween
items.author: Rachel Chapman
paragraphs: The Wicker Stars Actually Insist You Dress Like Them For Halloween
The cast and crew break down the behind-the-scenes details you need to make the characters your own.

The internet's response to Wicker was something no one could anticipate — especially the cast. “The fact that this quirky, independent original movie that’s not based on a famous IP got that reaction when the trailer came out, and that people seem excited to go see this movie, just made me very happy and thrilled,” Alexander Skarsgård tells Bustle at the Los Angeles premiere.

But the pre-release hype didn't stop there. Fans are already taking their enthusiasm for the romantic comedy about a fisherwoman marrying a basket man to the next level just in time for Oct. 31 — planning full costumes based on the film — and the cast is completely obsessed with the prospect. In fact, Olivia Colman is hoping to see many Fisherwoman and Wicker Husband ‘fits this year.
“When we were filming, I thought this would be great for a couple [...] or two buddies doing Halloween,” she says. Her one regret? “I wish we’d sort of got in on the merch beforehand."
“There’s no greater honor than to be in a Halloween costume for your movie.”

Wicker’s writers and co-directors, Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, had actually hoped the film would come out around spooky season "just in case" people wanted to copy the styles. "That's the dream," says Wilson, revealing that the costume trend is already taking off online.
For the creative duo, seeing audiences bring these characters to life is such a compliment. “There’s no greater honor than to be in a Halloween costume for your movie,” says Fischer.
If you find yourself inspired to re-create the looks after watching the film, below, the cast breaks down exactly how to pull off the Wicker aesthetic yourself.
Olivia’s Essentials For The Fisherwoman

The one word Colman would use to describe her Fisherwoman costume is “heavy.” There isn’t a specific time period when the movie is set, but the villagers of Wicker don medieval-like garb with tons of layers, including peasant skirts, billowy sleeves, and corsets.

To properly channel your inner angler, the actor says there are three non-negotiables: a “monobrow, a little bit of mud, and [to] carry a fish.” Pro tip: Opting for a rubber bass will save you from smelling like a harbor all night.
Alexander’s Look Requires Some Serious Hot Glue

The Wicker Husband might be the harder costume to conjure. If you don’t know a basket weaver, like Peter Dinklage’s character in the film, you’ll need to get creative with some woven elements. You could even repurpose old wicker furniture and piece the fragments together to construct his look.

Skarsgård’s costume in the film was also “multi-layered,” according to the directors. “It was constructed so that he could move with some rigidity,” says Wilson. “[Alexander] was able to do most things. I don't think he could lift his arms very high above his head, but who needs that?” (At the very least, it'll stop your counterpart from hogging the dance floor.)
Elizabeth’s Tips For A Wicker Villager

The fairy-tale wardrobe comes courtesy of two visionaries. “The costume designers [András Dániel Tóth and Godena-Juhász Attila] are geniuses,” says Elizabeth Debicki, who plays the Tailor’s Wife. “They actually come from a fashion background, so their attention to detail, even about color and shades and skin tone, was unparalleled, just incredibly complementary.”

Even though the The Crown star has plenty of experience with historical garments, this attire felt like a completely different world. And while the fantasy look was "dreamy" at first, the actual wearing experience took some getting used to. “It was not the most comfortable,” she says. “The woolen corset type things are very heavy and quite restrictive, but look great.”

Still, for a single night of holiday fun, a little fashion-induced discomfort is a small price to pay to pull off such a stunning ensemble. Plus, channeling Debicki’s style in the film gives you plenty of choices. “The Tailor’s Wife has four different looks — a spring, summer, autumn, and winter,” she says. “It’s very important because no other villagers have a change of outfit.” Just don’t forget a wicker corsage to complete the getup, and your Halloween wardrobe is sorted.

items.title: Margot Robbie & More Cool Girls Just Revived Your Fave Messy ’00s Jacket Trend
items.description: Military, Napoleon, band — whatever you want to call it, fall’s most dramatic jacket trend is impossible to ignore. Everyone from Margot Robbie and Daisy Edgar-Jones to Jenna Ortega and Lola Tung is completely obsessed with the style right now, making the orna
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: Military, Napoleon, band — whatever you want to call it, fall’s most dramatic jacket trend is impossible to ignore. Everyone from Margot Robbie and Daisy Edgar-Jones to Jenna Ortega and Lola Tung is completely obsessed with the style right now, making the ornate outerwear one of this year’s buzziest obsessions.

Military jackets typically lean into sharp, fitted silhouettes packed with maximalist details — think rows of shiny metal or braided buttons, baroque embroidery, and sometimes a high Mandarin collar for added drama. A favorite from the indie sleaze era of the late 2000s (Tumblr girlies know this well), the look made its comeback on the Spring/Summer 2026 runways of McQueen, Burberry, and Ann Demeulemeester before quickly cementing itself as a full-blown staple.

While the OTT vibe looks intimidating, this piece is actually surprisingly easy to wear. It can instantly elevate even the simplest tank-and-jeans combo into a polished street-style moment, and brings a sleek, tailored edge to wardrobe basics like black trousers. To help you build your own autumn uniform, Bustle’s fashion team rounded up the best celebrity takes on the closet veteran with tips on how to copy the looks without feeling like you're wearing a costume.

Margot Robbie was actually way ahead of the curve on this trend. Back in May, she stepped out for the West End opening of 1536 in London wearing a Napoleon-style military jacket embellished with intricate gold embroidery. To offset that heavy metallic detailing, she relied on an ultra-simple base, pairing the statement piece with black trousers, a tee, pointed-toe heels, and a clutch.

The all-black ensemble allowed the jacket to do the talking — a chic reminder that a loud, vintage-inspired piece can easily transition from a spring night out straight into your heavy fall rotation. — Naomi Ludlow, fashion closet freelancer

BRB, recreating this look from Bella Hadid’s Miss Sixty campaign. It perfectly balances the trend, chicness, and quality. Spotted on the FW26 runways, the military-inspired silhouette is poised to make its way from the runway to the streets, and I can’t wait to see how the It girls (that means you) style it this fall and winter.

I sourced two pieces worn by Miss Hadid herself, alongside a selection of statement jewelry to elevate the look this season. The boots are a bonus, but truly tie everything together, capturing the mood of this autumn’s moment. — Noelia Rojas-West, Fashion Market Assistant

Contrary to popular belief, the military jacket isn’t as authoritarian as its name implies. You can give it a soft-girl spin by wearing one in ivory. Daisy Edgar-Jones wore one during her Sense and Sensibility press tour, and the resulting ‘fit was so romantic, it was downright Austen-ian.

Take a page from her playbook and keep everything light: a white tank, cream shoes, and lighter-wash jeans will make the attire dreamy instead of harsh. Bonus points if you add a messy, low pony. — Alyssa Lapid, style writer

Jenna Ortega went sleeveless with the trend at Dior’s Spring/Summer 2026 show. Reminiscent of the Napoleon-style jackets that defined Kate Moss’ indie sleaze era, the military vest brings edgy 2000s nostalgia without the extra layers.

Though this look was from last fall, it’s still wearable today. Whether dressed down with denim or paired with low-rise trousers, it’s an easy way to take the trend from day to night without breaking a sweat. — Isabel Choi, fashion closet freelancer

If you’re looking for a more relaxed take, consider a Napoleon jacket in denim. Better yet, give it a Y2K-inspired Canadian tuxedo update by pairing it with jeans in a similar shade. It’s perfect for giving off that effortless cool-girl vibe.

Lola Tung serves as major inspo for this styling hack. She stepped out in a matching indigo set, accessorized with bold blue sunglasses to lean all the way into the monochrome palette. Not blue enough for you? Commit to the bit and wear denim shoes, too. — A.L.

items.title: AnOther Loves: A Storied Slip-on
items.description: The clog is a shoe with as much practical history as fairytale lore. These ones from the Chloé Autumn/Winter 2026 collection only continue that legacy
items.author: Rose Dodd
paragraphs: The clog is a shoe with as much practical history as fairytale lore. These ones from the Chloé Autumn/Winter 2026 collection only continue that legacy

One doesn’t look at a clog and think of it as a practical shoe per se. And yet that’s its origin story: dating back to the Middle Ages, clogs were carved from a single block of wood for farmers and fishermen, miners and factory workers. Adopted and renamed across Europe – le sabot by the French and Belgians, lo zoccolo by the Italians, the clog by the Brits – it’s a famously Dutch shoe, de klomp. In Holland, clog dancing is something of a named tradition, klompendansen. The shoe makes its cameo in fairytales, too. European folkloric tales collected by the Brothers Grimm; in Carlo Collodi’s 1881 serialised novel, Pinocchio, the titular fibber wears shoes made of tree bark. Then there’s Hans Christian Andersen’s The Red Shoes – the clog precedes those fateful red slippers. Granted, those were a symbol of the protagonist’s lowly status betoken to her subsequent transformation. Less humble but fairytale-fitting, this Chloé pair epitomises the boho charm of Chemena Kamali’s world. Knocked up a few inches, with an almond-shaped toe and in black leather bedazzled with floral metal studs, these clogs from the Autumn/Winter 2026 collection conjure the blossoming prairies of stories old. Sure, you might not wear them for fishing, but, sturdy, easy to slip on with plenty of wiggle room for a thick seasonal sock, they’re perfect for a little klompendansen. So there, the clog – both practical and magical.
The Chloé Talis studded leather clog is available to buy now

items.title: Lee Chang-dong: “Is Love Even Possible?”
items.description: Eight years after Burning, Lee Chang-dong returns with a masterful fable of class envy, corporate trauma and hidden desire
items.author: Miriam Balanescu
paragraphs: Eight years after Burning, Lee Chang-dong returns with a masterful fable of class envy, corporate trauma and hidden desire

Near the start of Lee Chang-dong’s searing chamber piece Possible Love – his Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize-winning follow-up to the 2018 cult film Burning – the wife of a laid-off factory worker and a dashing, married business magnate have what could be called a meet-cute. Mi-ok (veteran Korean actor Jeon Do-yeon), having lost weight due to stress, drops her wedding ring in a car park and Sang-woo (Jo In-sung) comes to her rescue. “I would love for it to be in a romantic comedy,” chuckles Jeon when we meet in a hotel during the London Film Festival. “You can really see in this scene the extreme degree her anxiety and fear of what it might be like to lose her husband and her family.”

This encounter sets in motion the treacherous entanglement of the two couples. Co-written by Lee and Oh Jung-mi, the plot takes loose inspiration from the 2009 labour strike in Korea, which is increasingly familiar thematic terrain in Korean cinema. (Think Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice.) Two years before the film begins, Mi-ok’s husband Ho-seok (Lee’s long-term collaborator Sul Kyung-gu) is brutally, traumatically fired amid mass lay-offs ahead of the company’s sale, leaving the family reeling and Mi-ok the breadwinner. When Sang-woo’s wife, filmmaker Ye-ji (Parasite’s Cho Yeo-jeong), asks to feature them in her documentary about dwindling labourers’ rights, the ever-optimistic Mi-ok leaps at the opportunity despite her withdrawn husband’s resistance, “trying to borrow the strength of Ye-ji and the strength of the documentary in order to get some help for her husband,” Jeon explains.

Opening with a title card bearing the Tenth Commandment, Lee’s film was initially conceived as an homage to Krzysztof Kieślowski’s Dekalog Ten. (Lee also tipped his hat to the late Three Colours director by naming Ye-ji’s dog Blue.) “‘Thou shalt not covet’ is about human desire,” says the director, “whereas all the other nine commandments are about the human act, and so I thought it would be intriguing to think about what it means to not covet in the capitalist society that we live in today.”

Through the slippery dynamics of this quartet, Lee probes the divisions of class, gender and wealth. “I wanted the discomfort and unease between these characters’ relationships to be naturally revealing the incongruence of our lives,” he says, noting the unexpected humour that arose from the chasms between his characters. “Going through many film festivals recently, I realised that audiences tend to laugh a lot more than I expected them to laugh – especially the bigger the screen.”

Though each feels deeply human, the four characters take on symbolic dimensions. Lee considers Sang-woo, for example, capitalism incarnate. Early on, Mi-ok likens the good-looking charmer, who married down and may or may not be financing his wife’s films, to Apple founder Steve Jobs. “The technological revolution that is symbolised through somebody like Jobs feels like it’s going to solve all of your problems, that it’s all-knowing, and that it’s going to liberate you,” Lee insists. “However, when the tech revolution is married with capital, the power that it gains is so immense that it will completely change all of our futures as well as our daily lives without us even being aware of it. However, Mi-ok continues to have that fantasy.”

However, when Mi-ok and Ho-seok are invited to stay in the rich couple’s mansion, reality hits. In one memorable scene, Mi-ok “protests” capitalism (aka Sang-woo) “with her entire body”. “There was a lot of fear around shooting that scene,” Jeon recalls. “Her desire is for freedom. When she’s younger, she’s spraying water on the car in order to clean it, and she’s told off and then restrained by her mum. She must have always dreamt of being free to do what she wants and hoped that that was what life was going to be like for her.”

In contrast to Sang-woo’s ‘new money’, Ho-seok embodies old-world values. “When I first encountered this story, I felt that Ho-seok was just like me – not as an actor, but just like a typical Korean male in East Asian society,” says Sul. “Many also commented that Ho-seok is just like my dad, who worked really hard for his family. Regardless of where you’re from and your nationality, I think he really resonates with a lot of men out there.”

That repressive masculinity carries over to the next generation in their ten-year-old son Cheol (Jung Seop). “You can see that his son doesn’t have a lot of expression on his face throughout the film,” explains Sul. “That was one way of signalling Cheol’s own pain and hurt that he experienced during this process.”

Possible Love spent decades in the pipeline, Lee hesitant about telling the story of those so different to himself. It was when co-writer Oh suggested the framing device of the documentary that things clicked into place. Cho herself was constantly filming: “I think it directly made me live in that character,” she reflects.

While many possible loves are explored in the film, the one between filmmaker and subject is the most poignant. Lee adds: “The character Ye-ji is closest to my own identity. I always find myself trying to love the people whose story I am telling through my work, and I always hope to be on their side. I always ask myself, is it possible to be on their side, and am I worthy of telling their story?

“This is something that I’ve always felt, not just as a filmmaker, but from my novelist days,” Lee continues, pointing towards the incomprehensibility of others’ pain. “Can I even say that I am close to them, or can I say that I truly love them? Is love even possible? I think these are questions that not only filmmakers but any storyteller or creators of a narrative that deal with others’ lives should think about.”
Possible Love is out on 23 October

items.title: Norman Foster has designed his first watch, and it's a lesson in precision
items.description: Developed by Lebond, an independent watchmaker based in Switzerland that realises designs by leading architects, Sir Norman Foster has made his first foray into creating timepieces.
items.author: Felix Bischof
paragraphs: Developed by Lebond, an independent watchmaker based in Switzerland that realises designs by leading architects, Sir Norman Foster has made his first foray into creating timepieces.

‘What is particularly interesting about a watch is that you wear it, you travel with it and it becomes part of your everyday life,’ says Foster. ‘The opportunity to reconsider something so familiar as a complete object made the challenge especially interesting.’

The result, which Foster conceived in partnership with the Design & Innovation Unit of the Norman Foster Foundation, is a duo of automatic, mechanical timepieces. One case is matte black, the other micro-sanded matte metallic; both are made from Grade 5 titanium and feature integrated straps. Grade 5 titanium is a material Foster selected with everyday use in mind. ‘The choice of titanium came from performance,’ the Pritzker Prize-winning architect and urbanist explains. ‘Grade 5 titanium has an exceptional strength-to-weight ratio, as well as excellent resistance to corrosion and wear. For something that is worn continuously on the wrist, that combination of strength, lightness and durability is particularly valuable. ‘

The choice of material echoes Foster’s overall, cross-genre approach. ‘I have always been interested in materials that perform rather than materials that are simply decorative,’ he says. ‘Grade 5 titanium allowed us to reduce weight without compromising strength, while giving the case a very precise and refined character. The material is therefore integral to both how the watch performs and how it feels.’

Aviation has long been an interest of Foster's and the two Lebond watches feature details that nod to airborne travel. Bidirectional, rotating 12-hour bezels allow a second time zone to be read using the main hour hand. On the dial, typography is clear and restrained. Hands are coated in Super-LumiNova for legibility.

‘I have always been interested in the relationship between design, engineering and precision, and a watch brings all of those things together in a very small and personal object,’ says Foster. ‘What is particularly interesting about a watch is that you wear it, you travel with it and it becomes part of your everyday life. The opportunity to reconsider something so familiar made the challenge especially interesting.’
The Lebond Norman Foster, in black and titanium, are available to buy now from lebond.com at €3500.

items.title: Model's Own: The Louis Vuitton Talent Whisperer Whose Bag Probably Weighs 10 Kilos
items.description: Model’s Own showcases our favorite friends’ favorite things. For more recs on fashion, beauty and tech, visit the Shopping tab or subscribe to our newsletter.
items.author: Maximilian Migowski
paragraphs: Model’s Own showcases our favorite friends’ favorite things. For more recs on fashion, beauty and tech, visit the Shopping tab or subscribe to our newsletter.

Still yet to turn 30, Ira Tassouli has already built a career out of helping brands like GANNI, A.P.C., and now Louis Vuitton not only present themselves well to the world, but also to connect with the right tastemakers. She's a talent maestro, a bona fide influence-monger, a community conjoiner — and, as a result, a kind of alpha influencer in her own right who can often be spotted in Copenhagen, Paris, and wherever else the fashion industry's moveable feast might be on any given day.

Today, as the manager of global talent relations at the biggest luxury house in the world, Tassouli steps out from behind the scenes to offer us a primer on her own personal style. As our latest "Model's Own" subject, Tassouli told us all about the "grown woman" watch she gave herself, her go-to LV bags, and her perfect airport outfit formula.
What is an item or garment that you regret having gotten rid of?

There is a pair of Dries Van Noten loafers that I sold. I don't know why, I was having a moment, and then I later repurchased them — in a different color though, if that makes any difference. I was like, you know what? I'm going back for another pair. Otherwise, I'm pretty good with getting rid of things and that being the end of it.
What's the most you've ever paid for an article of clothing or an accessory?

I think the most expensive thing that I've gotten for myself is a Cartier Panthère watch that I bought last year to celebrate a milestone. It was an “I'm an independent grown woman with adult money”-move, and I wanted to get myself this watch. And it definitely started an itch for me to continue this tradition of attaching sentimental value to objects, of connecting purchases to life moments.
Who's the most stylish person you grew up around?

I would definitely say it's my mom. Ever since I was really young, she would see things in magazines and make her own patterns and recreate what she really liked. And so, when I was a kid, I had like a fully custom wardrobe of just things that she would see and be like, “Let me make a version of this for you.” I think so much of my overall taste, not just in clothing, comes from all the things she exposed me to from a young age. She's probably one of the best-dressed people in my life.
What item do you own multiples of?

Amy, who owns Nhỏgirl in Amsterdam, is a close friend, and she recently released the Nhỏgirl Classic line, where she does streamlined basics, and they're incredible. They're made for layering, and when she did a pop-up in Paris, I bought the long sleeves in every single color. I wear them practically every single day. It's been a month or even more, and I have not stopped wearing them. I've literally just been waiting for them to restock so that I can repurchase the white one in particular, which I've worn and washed so much.
What has the algorithm recently convinced you to buy?

Something I bought recently was a pair of Thistles sunglasses. It's not necessarily the product, specifically, but the style of it. Everybody's got a pair of big aviator sunglasses, or at least I was seeing them everywhere, and eventually I felt like, “Okay, I think I want a pair." The algorithm will create a need for me to buy something, and then I'll look into what kind of version of something I want.
Tell me about your everyday bag.

I know I'm biased, but I actually do wear an LV bag every single day of my life — an Express bag currently. It's one of the more subtle bags that we've released lately. I have the medium size, and it fits my laptop even though it looks like it wouldn't, which is the perfect size of bag for me. It's, like, big but not gigantic. So you see it and you think, “What can she fit in there?” The answer is: a lot. I usually make it weigh about 10 kilos a day. I love her and wear her crossbody too, because I bike a lot in Paris, and we love functionality.
What's the last thing you bought in person?

I went to the store two days ago to buy a new Rimowa suitcase. And the other purchase that I did make in-store was in the US recently over the summer. If there's one thing I do when I'm in the US, it's go to multiple vintage shops and hunt and dig. I got two Ralph Lauren Made in USA vintage shirts at some secondhand store in Portland.
Are you more of an impulse shopper or deep researcher?

I wouldn't say that I'm a deep researcher, and I wouldn't call my shopping impulse either, but I would say it's like I'm somewhere in between. I'll see a movie and someone's wearing incredible jeans, or see someone outside and be like, oh, that looks great — “What would that look like within my universe and like my kind of wardrobe, myself interpreting that?” If I can think of a million ways to style this and wear something, I'll buy it. I won't put too much thought into it or be like, “Oh, let me look at other options.”
What do you wear to the airport?

I have a great airport formula: Sweatpants styled in an elevated way. This means: gray sweats with a loafer, a nice sock, and I'll do a flannel layering situation. Like a sweats by way of Ralph Lauren, let's call it. Add a cap and plus a hoodie shoved down a bag, in case.
What about your wedding guest get-up?

“Wedding guest” is more nuanced. As a person that works in the fashion industry, a lot of weddings with quite extravagant and fun dress codes happen around me. As such, I always try to just come through with something fun and playful that feels true to what the bride or groom would expect. If you tell me to dress up, I will dress up.

As a woman, if the dress code allows, something that I think is underrated is wearing a pant to a wedding, like a very chic pant look. I did that for a friend's wedding: a feathered off-shoulder top and a simple black pant and a pointed heel. If the bride and groom have something more traditional, don't challenge that. That said, I do a lot of black, which I think can be controversial because a lot of people don't like black for weddings. But I would suggest checking with the person first, if they care or not, about the whole good luck / bad luck thing. There's a lot of cultural nuance, too. There's something somewhere about how wearing red means you're sleeping with the groom? Anyways, check with the bride and groom.
What goes on your face in the mornings?
SPF. Always. Every single day. Of course. Like a broken record.
Evening is where we cleanse and moisturize. If I have to name a specific product, I would say Dr. Althea 345 Relief Cream. It absorbs really quickly. It's very lightweight.

For healthy, shiny hair I have this Shiseido hair oil bought in Japan and have not stopped repurchasing since. Fino Premium Touch is what it's called. Not expensive, super affordable, and just works wonders on dry hair, it's just amazing.
And lastly, what do you pick up from the infamous French pharmacies?
La Roche-Posay Cicaplast Baume B5. It's just never not in the house, always restocking if I'm near a pharmacy.
