items.author: Barton Gellman
paragraphs: Now and then, not often, Deidre Henderson will still work up the nerve to drive herself to the market for milk or bread. She will sit in the parking lot in her big S.U.V., engine running, doors locked, ruminating on risk. Generally, she heads home without getting out of the car.

Henderson, who is fifty-two years old, is the lieutenant governor of Utah, a Republican midway through her second term. That makes her the state’s chief election officer. (Elsewhere, the responsibility most commonly falls to a secretary of state.) It also makes her a target. Along with her counterparts in dozens of other states, Henderson has refused to allow the Trump Administration to obtain state voter rolls and to oversee the removal of voters it deems unqualified, in advance of the midterms, on November 3rd. For that resistance, election conspiracists have deluged her with threats of sexual violence and murder.
“It’s scary,” she told me late this summer. “It’s horrible. Honestly, I’ve had to have counselling just to function, to deal with the burden of fear that comes from the threats I’ve been getting.”

Many of the messages, however disturbing, are protected speech under the First Amendment. Some, though, have been treated by law enforcement as posing a credible danger to Henderson’s life or safety. In Utah, a lieutenant governor does not routinely get a security detail. But in Henderson’s first term, when she opposed Donald Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 Presidential election, she received threats that were so intense and specific that the Department of Public Safety placed her under protection for more than two years. The protection resumed before the 2024 election for a period. Henderson said that at times she has hired other protection. (The D.P.S. declined to comment on Henderson’s security detail.)

It was not always this unnerving to be an election official. But persistent lies about voter fraud, a centerpiece of Trump’s political narrative, have set loose torrents of hostility toward the men and women who oversee balloting nationwide. There are more than ten thousand voting jurisdictions in the United States, ranging from townships to states. In a national survey of local election officials this year, a third of them reported that they had personally been subjected to threats, harassment, or abuse because of their work. Half said they feared for the safety of their colleagues.

In this election season, the familiar threats, online and often pseudonymous, have been accompanied by new ones from federal authorities. The Department of Justice has warned Henderson and her counterparts that they may face criminal prosecution and imprisonment if they fail to surrender state voter rolls and purge them as the President directs.

Never before, not even when Trump tried to nullify his defeat by Joe Biden, six years ago, has an American President marshalled the coercive authority of the executive branch to reshape an election for his own benefit. Trump fought in court, in Congress, and in state legislatures to reverse the results of the 2020 election, but, as Brendan Nyhan, a Dartmouth political scientist who studies democratic erosion, told me, “he did not use his powers to try to undermine that election in advance.” And Trump ultimately failed to persuade high-level subordinates, such as William Barr, who was then the Attorney General, to wield their government power on his behalf. This year, multiple federal agencies, following Trump’s directives, attempted to strong-arm state election officials long before the first votes were cast. Trump, Nyhan told me, has tried “to tilt the playing field the way authoritarian populist leaders do in countries around the world.”

Article I, Section 4, of the Constitution reserves for the states the power to prescribe the “Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives,” with the proviso that Congress may change the rules by statute. The Framers granted the President no role in elections. Trump has declared otherwise. In an August, 2025, post on Truth Social, he wrote, “Remember, the States are merely an ‘agent’ for the Federal Government in counting and tabulating the votes. They must do what the Federal Government, as represented by the President of the United States, tells them, FOR THE GOOD OF OUR COUNTRY, to do.” Trump is open about his motives. He has warned Republicans that if they fail to purge the “millions and millions” of noncitizens who, according to his fantastic claims, are voting, they “will never win another election as a Republican.”

Early in his second term, Trump issued an executive order to restrict voter registration, impose new standards for voting machines, step up prosecution of “election crimes,” and forbid state authorities to count ballots that are mailed on time but arrive after Election Day. This past March, he issued another executive order with fresh instructions for election oversight, including a call for the Department of Homeland Security, in concert with other agencies, to “compile and transmit to the chief election official of each State a list of individuals confirmed to be United States citizens” and eligible to vote. The same order outlined new restrictions on voting by mail, specifying that the U.S. Postal Service “shall not transmit mail-in or absentee ballots from any individual” who does not appear on a U.S.P.S. list of eligible voters. How that list would be compiled, and by whom, and under what criteria, was left unclear. A coalition of states, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, and voting-rights groups separately filed suits. (The Brennan Center for Justice at N.Y.U. School of Law, where I am a senior adviser, is a co-counsel in two of the legal challenges.) For now, courts have blocked the most consequential provisions of both orders, primarily on the ground that the President has no lawful authority to impose them.

Meanwhile, the Justice Department set to work on a separate path. In a string of nearly identical lawsuits, filed beginning in September, 2025, it accused chief election officers in thirty states and the District of Columbia of violating Title III of the Civil Rights Act by failing to hand over electronic copies of their unredacted voter-registration lists. All but one state fought the lawsuits, including seven that had Republican chief election officers. (Oklahoma agreed to submit to the D.O.J. demand in exchange for dismissal of the case.) In response to United States of America v. Deidre M. Henderson, the Utah lieutenant governor, like most of her counterparts, cited privacy laws that obliged her to protect the personal information of voters, and said that the Trump Administration had no legal power to demand access in any case.

Since the litigation began, twenty-seven U.S. district judges and one appellate panel have reached decisions. All of them ruled against the Trump Administration. The case against Henderson was dismissed on October 23rd. One representative opinion, by Judge David O. Carter, in California, held that the D.O.J.’s declared purpose was “contrived” and that its demand for voter lists “wholly disregards the separation of powers.”

As its civil lawsuits foundered, the Justice Department reached for another weapon to compel obedience from state election officers. In a letter dated July 7th, the Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon warned Henderson and her counterparts that the D.O.J. was “also authorized to prosecute criminal violations” of the relevant statutes. Winning the civil litigation, in other words, would not prevent a state election official from being indicted for unspecified crimes. None of the election officials surrendered to that threat. “Garbage—I’m not breaking the laws,” Arizona’s secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, a Democrat, told me. Trump, he said, is “trying to pick his own voters, because he doesn’t believe in the American people. He believes in preserving his own power.”

The following week, the Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, issued a warning of his own. His department had repurposed a program called SAVE(Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements), which previously had been used only to check immigrants’ eligibility for federal benefits, and pressed state election officials to use it to verify citizenship. A federal judge had blocked this use of SAVE. Mullin, however, warned that election officials who failed to use SAVE to screen voter rolls for noncitizens could face “prison time.” (The Supreme Court later stayed the district judge’s order but noted that it was too late to make large-scale changes to voter- registration lists.)

The Trump Administration’s efforts to cull the electorate before the midterms have, by and large, failed. Courts stripped the President’s executive orders of meaningful impact. At least sixteen states, all Republican-controlled, voluntarily agreed to turn over voter rolls to the Justice Department, but only three—Alaska, South Carolina, and Texas—signed agreements allowing the D.O.J. to oversee the removal of supposedly ineligible names. Twenty-eight states have voluntarily registered to use the SAVE data to check their voter lists for noncitizens, but it is unclear how many have relied on it to remove voters. In any case, it is too late for further purges: the statutory deadline to “systematically remove” ineligible voters is ninety days before a federal election.

In a last-ditch effort, the Justice Department brought a new lawsuit on October 15th, asking a California judge to require the state to set aside the ballots of about twenty thousand people, who the Administration alleged were “likely noncitizens.” The following day, the acting Deputy Attorney General, Trent McCotter, sent a letter to Los Angeles County election officials, threatening them with prosecution if they knowingly count the alleged noncitizens’ votes. On October 19th, McCotter said that twenty-eight California residents had been charged with violating federal voting laws.

Similar D.O.J. claims of widespread voter fraud elsewhere have proved spurious. In Nevada, the Administration alleged that there were nearly sixteen thousand noncitizens on voter rolls and produced the names of a hundred and eighty-five people, saying that it had manually verified their alien status. In September, state officials established that all of them were U.S. citizens. (A spokesperson for the D.O.J. said that the department continues to investigate individual cases of alleged noncitizens who voted in recent Nevada elections. A White House spokesperson said that, though “extreme Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive action to protect our elections, including prosecuting election crimes.”)

In another late-breaking intervention, this one even more extraordinary, the Trump Administration asked a federal judge on October 23rd to prevent certification of the Alaska Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Daniel S. Sullivan, loses narrowly. D.O.J. lawyers argued that the presence of a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot may deprive the senator of votes intended for him. (The Alaska Supreme Court had already ruled, in June, against an effort by the senator and the state G.O.P. to disqualify the challenger.)

Michael Waldman, the president of the Brennan Center, told me, “It turns out that our backstop is the fragmented nature of our political system, and federalism—that the election isn’t run by decree by any President, good or bad.”

If one thing has been decisive in safeguarding the nation’s electoral machinery, it is the tenacity of state officials who willingly accepted the political, financial, and personal risks of defying the President. They did so in a strong majority of states, including some under Republican control. “In order to protect democratic institutions,” Nyhan said, “we still depend on politically ambitious people sacrificing their careers.”

Henderson is among the most intrepid of the chief election officers who have stood in Trump’s way. For months, not a single Utah G.O.P. leader offered her public support. Yet, even as other Republicans who were resisting federal orders avoided open conflict with Trump, she spoke out against unlawful intervention from Washington. “It sure looks like they’re trying to take over control of elections to make sure only people they want to vote are voting,” she said recently. “To me, as an American and a Republican, it’s offensive.”

The Justice Department launched its campaign to seize control of voter rolls in May, 2025, when it began sending letters to state election officials which alleged that they had “anomalies” on their lists. Henderson received a letter that July, citing the Attorney General’s authority to bring “enforcement actions” under the National Voter Registration Act and questioning whether Utah was obeying the law. “Utah has the lowest rate in the nation for voter registration records removed” from the rolls, it alleged. The letter directed Henderson to “produce for inspection” a full electronic copy of Utah’s voter rolls, which contain sensitive personal information such as driver’s-license numbers, partial Social Security numbers, full dates of birth, phone numbers, and e-mail addresses.

It was unexpected and perplexing, Henderson said, to “get a letter from the U.S. Attorney General’s office citing all sorts of federal code.” Scott Cheney, a Utah assistant attorney general who serves as her principal legal adviser on elections, was out of the country. Henderson requested help from the office of Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown. Brown sent over two lawyers, who, Henderson said, seemed to believe that she had no choice but to comply.

Henderson was skeptical. “I knew there were other federal statutes that applied,” she said, including the Privacy Act and the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act, which limit the release of personally identifying details. Henderson and the lawyers decided that the D.O.J. had overstepped. Their ensuing correspondence with the department began politely but devolved into threats and demands emphasized in italic type. She declined to hand over personal information about voters, citing state and federal privacy laws, and instead offered “the most current version of the public statewide voter registration list.” The next letter came from Dhillon, the Assistant Attorney General. Henderson’s reply was unacceptable, she wrote: “The Attorney General is demanding an electronic copy of Utah’s complete and current” voter rolls, and “Utah must ensure that it contains all fields.” Any contrary obligations that Henderson thought she had under Utah election and privacy statutes, Dhillon wrote, were “clearly preempted by federal law.”

Months later, the D.O.J. explained for the first time precisely why it was seeking the voter rolls. On December 2nd, a new D.O.J. lawyer, Eric Neff, sent Henderson a proposed “memorandum of understanding,” which disclosed that the D.O.J. intended to do a complete analysis of the rolls. Neff, a longtime legal warrior on behalf of election conspiracy theories, explained that the department would notify the state of any “insufficiencies, inadequacies, deficiencies, anomalies, or concerns” that it found. Utah would have forty-five days to “clean” its voter rolls and send back an updated list proving that “proper list maintenance has occurred.” The existence of this agreement between the state and the federal government, according to the memorandum, could not be publicly disclosed. The Justice Department sent a similar memorandum of understanding to many of Henderson’s counterparts in other states. Henderson decided to disregard the request for secrecy. She made all the correspondence public and announced that Utah would not comply with the D.O.J.’s demands.

On September 16th, the Justice Department filed lawsuits against the chief election officers of Maine and Oregon. Later that month, it did the same in California, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New York, and Pennsylvania. In January, at a conference of the National Association of Secretaries of State, Henderson denounced Dhillon’s contention that states needed federal help to clean up their rolls. (Dhillon had claimed that the D.O.J. had “found two hundred and sixty thousand plus dead people” on state registration lists.) “The things that have been said publicly, frankly, are quite appalling,” Henderson told a White House official, Jared Borg, in open session, adding, of Dhillon, “She’s pretty much slandered all of us.”

By the time Dhillon’s office filed suit against Henderson, on February 26th, the Justice Department had already lost three of the cases against state election officers. Henderson began to taunt the Trump Administration.
“0-8,” she posted on Threads on May 21st, after judges dismissed five more of the D.O.J.’s lawsuits.
“0-9,” she posted on June 22nd, when a Maryland judge did the same.
“Persistence in the face of defeat is usually an admirable quality, but not in this case,” she posted on July 14th, when the count was 0–13.
I asked Henderson one day why she had chosen this provocative tone.

“Am I provoking?” she replied, sounding a little annoyed. “Now, it’s interesting that the person bringing the conflict into the light, highlighting the injustice of the situation, the unconstitutionality and illegality of the situation to the public, is the one that’s considered provocative.”
Had other Utah Republicans urged her to turn down the heat? I asked.
“Not to my face,” she said.

Many of them, though, including the highest-ranking state legislators, criticized her for refusing to coöperate with the Trump Administration. Some, notably the former gubernatorial candidate Phil Lyman, accused her of being involved in election fraud. “I don’t think that her voter rolls can withstand scrutiny,” he told me. Others privately expressed fear that Henderson would provoke retaliation from the President, perhaps causing the state to lose pending federal grants to build nuclear power plants and to restore the Great Salt Lake.

For years, Henderson had told her staff that her No. 1 rule was “If it feels good, don’t say it.” She wanted to do her job and stay out of political combat. But that stance was changing. Utah’s governor, Spencer Cox, has said that he will not seek a third term in 2028, and Henderson told me that she is “seriously considering running.” I asked whether she thought her public conflict with Trump would hurt or help that campaign. “I have no idea, and I don’t care,” she said. “If discharging the duties of my office with fidelity means that I am unelectable in 2028, I am O.K. with that.”

Renae Cowley, a Republican political consultant who admires the lieutenant governor, said that she did not doubt Henderson’s commitment to principle but thought another consideration might also be on her mind. “I think that Deidre is strategically poking the bear, and it is both a brilliant political strategy and exactly what her voters want her to do,” Cowley said. “We’re Westerners for a reason,” she continued. “We wanted to be able to live our lives and do so free from the all-seeing eyes of the government. Of all the things to push back on, this is perhaps the most palatable, strategic, winningest issue that she could pick.”

In mid-August, I visited Henderson in Utah. As I rode with her to her office, she steered her S.U.V. onto the capitol grounds and edged toward what appeared to be a blank granite façade. An unmarked entrance opened to reveal a dimly lit parking bay, just big enough to accommodate side-by-side vehicles, for Henderson and Governor Cox.

In an hour, at Henderson’s request, a team of election and law-enforcement officers from across the state would gather in her conference room for a crisis-management exercise. She had asked an outside consultant to devise scenarios for the midterms to test the preparedness of her team. Election officials around the country run similar tabletop exercises before each voting cycle, to plan for contingencies ranging from extreme weather and power failures to bomb threats and foreign interference.

First, Henderson convened her senior staff for an update on the workaday operations for the election: auditing certification procedures, offering assistance to voters, unsnarling data conflicts, interpreting obscure rules. They met in the lieutenant governor’s private office, which is outfitted with polished dark wood, green curtains, and tan leather chairs. A painting on one wall depicts Seraph Young, who in 1870 became the first woman to cast a ballot in the Utah Territory. It is a point of pride for Henderson that voting rights for women there predated the Nineteenth Amendment by half a century.

Ali Majid, the state director of election systems, told Henderson that his quarterly audit of voter rolls had been updated to comply with a Utah statute that required a passport, a birth certificate, or similar proof of citizenship to vote in state races. He reported that thirty-five hundred people would soon be disqualified from voting in state elections because they had not responded to requests for that documentation. (Most states have no such requirement.)

Henderson was disturbed by the number. She had been mistakenly disqualified a few years back, because she was born in the Netherlands, where the Air Force had stationed her father. “Are we making sure clerks are actually reaching out to voters?” she asked.
In one database, Majid said, the list of registered but inactive voters included “thirty-three voters that were unconfirmed and ten voters that were likely noncitizens.”
“None of them ever voted,” Henderson said, in what seemed like more of a statement than a question.
“None of them ever voted,” Majid confirmed.

Next, Henderson and her staff discussed a new D.H.S. rule, announced in July. Mullin’s department had said that it would cut twenty per cent of FEMA homeland-security grants to states that did not comply with “election security” requirements. No one at the table was sure what the state attorney general planned to do about the rule, but they hoped that Utah would join lawsuits by other states to challenge it.
“Because we’re going to lose all the funding, not just twenty per cent,” Henderson said, sounding resigned.

“There’s the nonsense of it,” Ryan Cowley, Utah’s election director, replied. “You have FEMA, who knows nothing about elections, now dictating not just, like, ‘You have to have secure elections.’ Now they’re dictating exactly how.”
On September 28th, a federal judge ruled that FEMA could not withhold the funds.

The President’s campaign to seize control of the midterms has gone far beyond voter purges and threats to withhold federal funding. Ranging widely across the executive branch, it has included F.B.I. raids to seize election and voter-registration records, and menacing suggestions that Trump may send armed ICE agents to the polls.

One of Trump’s earliest attempts to “take over” elections, as he has put it, was the 2025 executive order on voting, which would have required, among other things, that people show a passport or comparable proof of citizenship in order to register. A national survey found that at least twenty-one million Americans do not possess or have no ready access to those documents. The House had passed a similar requirement, called the SAVE (Safeguard American Voter Eligibility) Act, but Republicans in the Senate were struggling to wrangle enough votes. Trump tried, unsuccessfully, to bypass Congress and impose the rule himself.

The same executive order directed the Election Assistance Commission, an independent federal agency, to “rescind all previous certifications of voting equipment” and establish new standards to address some of the claims that Trump and his allies had made about rigged election machinery in 2020. This provision of Trump’s order was among those struck down by a federal judge.

The President also enlisted law-enforcement agencies to produce new evidence of voter fraud, past and present. This past January, Kurt Olsen, a prominent election denier and at the time the newly appointed White House director of election security and integrity, asked the F.B.I. to launch a criminal investigation in Fulton County, Georgia, according to an F.B.I. affidavit, and the Bureau did so with uncommon dispatch. Trump had brought unsuccessful lawsuits alleging extensive fraud by Fulton County election officials in the 2020 Presidential election. The F.B.I.’s mission was to revive those allegations. In Georgia, dozens of F.B.I. agents—accompanied by Trump’s director of National Intelligence, who called the President immediately afterward—seized more than six hundred and fifty boxes of ballots, tabulator tapes, electronic ballot images, and other records from the 2020 election.

Five months after the Georgia raid, about a hundred F.B.I. and D.H.S. agents descended on the Cleveland offices of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a left-leaning group that advocates for voting rights and organizes voter-registration campaigns. The agents seized records and electronic devices, looking for evidence of unspecified criminal behavior. Last year, the President also ordered the D.O.J. to launch a criminal investigation of Chris Krebs, a former director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, in part on the ground that he had publicly disputed Trump’s claim that the 2020 election was rigged.

Federal law-enforcement agencies have also been involved in what amounts to a psychological operation ahead of the midterms. Trump’s subordinates have been hinting for months that ICE agents or other federal officers may turn up at polling places on Election Day. Federal law forbids the presence of “troops or armed men at any place where a general or special election is held.” But in March, Todd Blanche, who was then the Deputy Attorney General, said that he saw nothing wrong with it. “Why is there an objection to sending ICE to polling stations?” Blanche asked at the Conservative Political Action Conference. “Illegals can’t vote.” Mullin has raised the prospect several times, saying that ICE is not restricted from conducting enforcement operations at polling places, and may even be needed to protect them. (In a statement, D.H.S. said that it has no plans for operations “targeting polling locations.”)

Voting-rights advocates regard these statements as thinly veiled efforts to intimidate lawful voters. “They make headlines to use them as deterrents with no intention of deploying” on a large scale, Maria Teresa Kumar, the founding president of Voto Latino, said, noting that Latino voters have seen a lot of ICE violence in their communities, and that millions of citizens live in “mixed-status families,” with relatives who are vulnerable to deportation. Kumar said that the spectre of illegal voting was a pretext for the ICE threats, citing a study that found that fewer than 0.0001 per cent of ballots in the 2016 Presidential election, or one in a million, were cast by noncitizens.

The Trump Administration, for all its efforts, has failed to establish a commanding position over the federal voting landscape. No indictments or evidence of voter fraud have emerged from the raids in Ohio and Georgia. A Trump-appointed judge blocked a subpoena to collect what he called a “staggering” amount of personal information about election workers in Fulton County. Senate Republicans never found enough votes to pass the SAVE Act.

David Becker, a former senior trial attorney in the D.O.J.’s voting section and the founder of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said that he saw “no coherent strategy” in the disparate attempts to carry out Trump’s wishes for the midterms. “There’s malevolence, but there’s a lot of incompetence,” he said, citing competing directives from the D.O.J. and D.H.S. and the stunning record of setbacks in court. “They don’t have a single success.”

Becker continued, “I think there’s a lot of people within the conspiracy-theory ranks—within the economy of grift that’s grown around election denialism—who are seeking approval from President Trump. And they’re all doing their thing to do that. And often those things conflict.”

Control of the House and the Senate will be decided by some very close races. Even the marginal success of Trump’s effort to disqualify voters in states that agreed to use D.H.S. citizenship data might tip one or more of these contests. And there is still a hypothetical risk, election experts say, that the President could do something new and outlandishly lawless on or close to Election Day.

In Henderson’s conference room, a test of nightmare scenarios commenced at 10 a.m. with a cheerful slide that read “Ready for Anything.” Cowley and Majid, the state election officials, were there. So were several lawyers and the election clerks of two of Utah’s twenty-nine counties.

The consultant who wrote the scenarios said she had devised “scary situations” that Utah’s previous contingency planning might not have addressed. About nine in ten Utah voters cast ballots by mail, but most of the scenarios would involve federal agents dispatched to Utah polling places or tabulation centers.
“I will just let you know they’re a little bit provocative, and that’s intentional,” she said. “I want to drive up the temperature just a little bit.”

Utah, which has long been represented exclusively by Republicans in Congress, might seem an unlikely place for conflict with Trump over elections. But in 2025 court-ordered redistricting created a strongly Democratic-leaning First Congressional District centered in Salt Lake County, where Kamala Harris beat Trump by ten points in 2024.
In one scenario, the consultant said, “the President announces that federal agents are going to ‘flood the zone’ on Election Day in certain areas with large immigrant p

items.title: How ‘Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’ Tees Up Taylor Sheridan’s Movie
items.description: November will bring arguably the most highly anticipated piece of media of all time in Grand Theft Auto VI, but October’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 release on Xbox and PCs was no indie drop. The latest CoD game will also serve as unofficial ambassador for
items.author: Tony Maglio
paragraphs: November will bring arguably the most highly anticipated piece of media of all time in Grand Theft Auto VI, but October’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 release on Xbox and PCs was no indie drop. The latest CoD game will also serve as unofficial ambassador for Xbox’s newest division, XP, to the broader entertainment ecosystem.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 came out on Oct. 23 — it has been well-reviewed and well-monetized. As of this writing, Metacritic has aggregated critics’ takes to an 86 Metascore, which is quite strong; IGN gave it a 7 (of 10) and Game Informer rated it an 85 (of 100). Modern Warfare 4 quickly pushed the CoD franchise beyond the $40 billion lifetime revenue mark, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed on Monday. (At our last update in 2025, the games had combined for $35 billion in sales.)

Worldwide, Call of Duty games crossed half-a-billion units in sales two years ago, when the series became the best-selling first-person shooter franchise ever. We’re way beyond that today. (The mobile game alone, which is what exactly nobody thinks about when talking CoD, has been downloaded more than a billion times.)
It’s music to Sharma’s ears and catnip for Kayleen Walters, the president of XP.

XP is the new division dedicated to pairing owned Xbox IP with Hollywood producers to adapt popular video games and franchises for film, television and beyond. (Theme parks, experiences, events, etc.) Crossing thresholds in a big way in 2028 will be a Call of Duty: Modern Warfare feature film from Peter Berg and Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone universe).

“The greatest gaming franchises are more than stories. They’re worlds people belong to, help shape, and carry with them. The connection between players and these expansive worlds is unlike anything else in entertainment,” Walters told The Hollywood Reporter. “With XP, our ambition is to honor what makes these worlds extraordinary and work with the best creative partners to bring their magic to life in new ways, for the communities who love them today and the audiences who will discover them next.”

Given the Call of Duty games’ regular rotational cadence, Modern Warfare 4 ought to be the last major in-universe game before the movie comes out. So there was additional pressure here to get it right.

“You kind of got your heart in your throat and you’re just waiting for it to go live,” Jack O’Hara, the co-head of Call of Duty video game studio Infinity Ward, told THR. When it finally did, it was “surreal.” Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 was in development for four years.
O’Hara says he had “a feeling” the game would be well-received. Now it’s his job that keep the good times rolling.

Today, major AAA video game releases are living organisms. When he first worked with the Call of Duty team in 2009 (joining them full time three years later), the life cycle of video games was very different. For starters, they usually stayed as video games only. When development was done and all the tests passed, you’d “print a disc” and “everybody would go on vacation,” O’Hara said.

Not anymore — there are hardly even discs. These days, the “sense of relief” of publishing a game at long last linger for “about eight hours,” O’Hara said. O’Hara and his team will be updating and supporting the live Modern Warfare 4 for the next year.
It “can be exhausting,” he said.

Just wait until the movie enters production. O’Hara says he won’t be personally involved in the blockbuster film, a collaboration between Activision (the Microsoft subsidiary that directly owns Infinity Ward) and Paramount Pictures — but he’s there if you need him.
It’s “important” for the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare movie “to stand on its own,” O’Hara said, and it’s equally crucial “for people who own a creative project to own it.”

For Xbox, it’s important to find new audiences and revenue streams. The company has recently laid off thousands of employees and consolidated or outright shuttered numerous development banners. Console sales are down, profit margins are on GLP-1s and subscriptions are carrying the world on their shoulders. It’s a war zone out there. Sharma says Xbox should be back on a growth path “by the end of 2027.”

The Call of Duty movie is just one piece of Xbox’s plan to invade Hollywood. The deployment of intellectual property predates the formation of XP. It even predates Sharma’s succession of Phil Spencer.

Last year’s biggest film in terms of box office ($960 million worldwide) was A Minecraft Movie, a Microsoft and Warner Bros. feature film. A sequel, A Minecraft Movie: Squared was wisely rush ordered and will come out next year. Though it already has a studio (WB, now owned by Skydance, will remain the label), XP will shepherd the franchise’s expansion into theme parks and a coming Netflix animated series.

To a lesser — but not unimpressive — degree, Fallout (the Xbox-owned Bethesda Studios in collaboration with Amazon MGM Studios) has found success in TV form on Amazon’s Prime Video platform. Next to try the jump are the extensions of Gears of War (as a Netflix movie), Wolfenstein (a TV series at Amazon) and Diablo (a Netflix animated series). Down the road a bit is a collaboration with Kojima Productions on PHYSINT and OD, two new gaming projects with Hideo Kojima (Kojima owns the IP) that also include film and TV rights, and at least another half-dozen unannounced adaptations of Xbox games in the works, THR is told. Other popular Xbox-owned franchises include Warcraft, Candy Crush, Forza, The Elder Scrolls, Halo and Spyro.

Halo, we should point out, already tried and (mostly) failed as a television show. The Showtime-turned-Paramount+ series, a joint effort that also included Steven Spielberg’s Amblin Television, was plagued with issues from the jump. Following 10 years(!) of development, Halo ended up with a first time showrunner and not enough in common with the popular game. Season two would bring a new showrunner and a disappointing end to the series. Halo wasn’t a bad show per se — Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic both have more positive than negative reviews — but its lack of authenticity to the world the games had created turned off established fans.
Fallout learned from the sins of its cousin.

Todd Howard’s approach to adapting Fallout was “full authenticity — treat it the same way we would any major game entry,” the Bethesda Game Studios head and TV show’s executive producer tells THR. “Finding a creative partner to do that is the essential element, and we found that in Jonathan Nolan (Westworld) and a team who have done an absolutely mindblowing job.”
Fallout has been renewed for a third season and has an unscripted competition companion series set to premiere on Jan. 13.

Clearly, good games can make for good film and TV. There are also reciprocal returns. During season one of Fallout on Prime Video, hours played across Fallout titles on Xbox Game Pass increased 5x, Xbox says, and following A Minecraft Movie, the Minecraft video game saw a 75 percent year-over-year increase in weekly active users.

items.title: Selena Gomez and Demi Lovato Are Inducing Major Nostalgia With Their New Beauty Campaign
items.description: Selena Gomez and Demi Lovato have reunited to take fans back in time.
items.author: Tiffany Taylor
paragraphs: Selena Gomez and Demi Lovato have reunited to take fans back in time.

The pair have joined forces for a new campaign for Gomez’s Rare Beauty brand titled “Still Making Each Other Blush” that introduces The Delena: Soft Pinch Blush Bundle, which includes Rare Beauty’s Soft Pinch Liquid Blush in the stars’ respective favorite shades of Hope and Virtue, as well as a Soft Pinch Blush Brush.

Delena, of course, is the joint name fans gave the duo who commonly referred to themselves as “best friends” during the height of their Disney Channel fame in the late 2000s, before they publicly distanced themselves from each other over the years. Gomez and Lovato famously became pals on the set of Barney & Friends as child actors ahead of their respective star-making roles in Disney’s Wizards of Waverly Place and Camp Rock.

The campaign sees the pair pay homage to the movie poster for their 2009 Disney Channel Original Movie Princess Protection Program, in which they co-starred as a princess forced to flee her country and a regular girl now tasked with helping her conceal her identity.
As part of the campaign, the duo released a roughly four-minute clip reminiscent of the vlog-style YouTube videos they routinely made together back in 2008.

In the new video, Gomez and Lovato answer questions, recall their go-to red carpet pose (as pictured above), and lip-sync and dance to “One and the Same,” the song they recorded together for the Princess Protection Program soundtrack.
“I felt like that was our moment when we felt like Avril Lavigne,” Gomez said, reminiscing on the pair’s experience shooting the music video for the track. “We were so into it.”
“And Kelly Clarkson,” Lovato chimed in. “Always Kelly Clarkson.”
In May 2020, Lovato said she wasn’t close with Gomez during a cover story interview with Harper’s Bazaar.
“When you grow up with somebody, you’re always going to have love for them,” Lovato said. “But I’m not friends with her…”
The pair first publicly reunited when Gomez attended a concert on Lovato’s It’s Not That Deep Tour in Orlando in April of this year.

“There have been different chapters throughout our lives, and naturally, friends are in each other’s lives heavily at times, and then sometimes you’re not in constant communication,” Lovato told Elle in a new interview. “But Selena is someone that I’ve always loved and adored. It’s really great to be in a place today where we can collaborate on things, but also just hang out and spend time together.”
The Delena: Soft Pinch Blush Bundle is currently available on the Rare Beauty website.

items.title: Whoopi Goldberg Has Little Use for Pretense
items.description: In 1984, your one-woman show, Whoopi Goldberg, premiered on Broadway and launched you into stardom. A recording of the show—in which you portray various eccentric characters, ranging from a young Valley Girl to a Jamaican woman—aired on HBO in 1985 and earned
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: In 1984, your one-woman show, Whoopi Goldberg, premiered on Broadway and launched you into stardom. A recording of the show—in which you portray various eccentric characters, ranging from a young Valley Girl to a Jamaican woman—aired on HBO in 1985 and earned you a Grammy. This summer, it was revived as The Whoopi Monologues, starring several actors, including Kerry Washington and Kara Young. Why did you decide that 2026 was the right time to bring the show back?

I didn’t. Kerry Washington came to me and said, “I have this idea. I would like to revive your show with five actors.” And I said, “Fantastic.” I didn’t want to be part of it at all, but I recommended one woman, Kara Young, to play Fontaine, the junkie. I didn’t want to go to rehearsals, and I didn’t want to talk about the show with the cast, because I wanted them to make it their own.

You’ve been revisiting several of your old projects. Sister Act 3 is officially underway, which means you’ll revive Deloris, a nightclub singer forced to take refuge from the Mob in a convent. The first two Sister Act movies came out in the early 1990s. What’s it like to return to them after all this time?

I had hoped to do it before Maggie [Smith] passed, but we weren’t able to get it done. I don’t want to say it’s closure, because that sounds so esoteric. It’s like, You know what? Let’s put a button on this. People love Sister Act. As I’ve traveled around the world, I’ve discovered it airs almost on rotation in so many countries. Nuns come up to me everywhere and say, “We’ve done the same thing that you did, but we did it for real.” Chinese nuns, Spanish nuns.
What makes you say yes to a project?

The truth of the matter is, very few times has anybody said, “Do you want to be in this movie?” I know and you know that I’m Black. Apparently, this comes as a surprise to people. So I would say, “Gee, I’d love to read for that.” And they’d go, “Oh, no, there’s not a part for you.” Most of the movies I have made, I got the job because some bigger star said they didn’t want to do it. Jumpin’ Jack Flash was for Shelley Long. Sister Act was for Bette Midler. Burglar was for Bruce Willis. I know all the names.
You’ve been on The View with a panel of women discussing the day’s topics for almost 20 years. What keeps you coming back?

That’s really what it is. I’m well-paid, and I do a good job. I earn my dough, and sometimes people like it, sometimes they don’t. No one is going to pay me guy money to be in a movie. I get what I can, have as good a time as I can, and I don’t really worry about it too much.
Weighing in on politics opens you up to criticism. Are you ever scared to speak out?
No. Barbara Walters gave me the job, which is something I take very seriously. She hired me to say what I think, and that’s what I do.
Of all your careers and projects, what do you want to be remembered for?
Just for being a decent person who maybe made mistakes but didn’t run from anything.
What about your EGOT? You’ve received an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar, and a Tony Award—and became the first Black person to achieve that feat. What does that distinction mean to you?

Not a lot. I had never heard of such a thing until I did Tracy Morgan’s show 30 Rock [in 2009], where his character is looking to become an EGOT. I said to him as we were shooting, “Can you explain what this is?” He said, “You don’t know what this is?” I didn’t know I had done that.
When was the last time you surprised yourself?

I did a very crazy animated show called Kevin this year. I played an old, filthy, bald cat named Cupcake. And when I say “filthy”—she has a dirty mouth. It surprised me how much fun I had, because people get very nervous if you curse, but everyone seemed to be very happy when I was doing it.
You’ve been doing a lot of voice work. What do you enjoy about that?
The fact that I can do it in my underwear.
Is there anything you wish you could go back and tell your younger self?
No. You know why? I wouldn’t have listened. Also, I think it’s much better to—pardon my French—step in shit. That’s how you learn.

items.title: Scientists Trapped an Antimatter Particle for Months to Study Its Secrets
items.description: Antimatter is not known for being easy to get ahold of. That’s part of why these particles remain so cryptic. But recently, a team of physicists at Northwestern University managed to trap a single antimatter particle for months. Cooling it to temperatures near
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: Antimatter is not known for being easy to get ahold of. That’s part of why these particles remain so cryptic. But recently, a team of physicists at Northwestern University managed to trap a single antimatter particle for months. Cooling it to temperatures near absolute zero, they could control its quantum states with great precision without even touching it. The experiment, published in Physical Review Letters, represents a breakthrough in our understanding of one of the great mysteries of physics.

In theory, antimatter should be everywhere. Mathematics predicts that every particle of matter has an equivalent antiparticle, a fact that scientists have verified experimentally. The universe should therefore contain similar amounts of both, but almost everything we observe is made up of ordinary matter, and we still don’t know why.

It is possible to produce antimatter particles in laboratories, but studying them is still incredibly difficult. When an antiparticle comes into contact with ordinary matter, the two annihilate each other and release energy. To prevent research facilities from exploding, scientists use vacuum chambers and electromagnetic fields that suspend the antiparticles in isolation. But this only partially solves the problem. Studying these particles, especially experimenting with their behavior on a quantum scale, remains challenging.

For this experiment, researchers at Northwestern trapped a positron, the antimatter counterpart of electrons. The team, led by Gerald Gabrielse, developed a device known as a single-positron quantum cyclotron, which used electric and magnetic fields to hold the positron in a vacuum at a temperature close to absolute zero. This means the antimatter particle was at its lowest energy state, allowing the researchers to induce controlled changes in its quantum behavior. Unlike other methods in particle physics, this approach didn’t destroy the particle. The researchers were therefore able to keep the single antiparticle trapped for months, allowing them to repeat measurements.

So what can taming antimatter particles actually teach us? Scientists know that matter and antimatter have very similar properties. For example, an electron and a positron have exactly the same mass, although their electric charges are opposite. However, questions still remain about exactly how similar these two forms of matter are and whether there are small differences that have gone unnoticed in experiments conducted to date.

To this end, researchers want to compare the magnetic properties of both particles. Physicists have already made very precise measurements with electrons, but achieving the same level of precision with positrons has proven more difficult. According to the American Physical Society, the new device could enable measurements of antimatter particles about 30 times more precise than scientists were capable of before.

So far, the experiment has not revealed any unexpected differences between the two particles. What the researchers have achieved is an improvement in their ability to detect these differences in antimatter particles. If future measurements find that a positron responds to magnetic fields differently than an electron, scientists would have to revise some of the laws they use to explain the behavior of matter and antimatter.
This story originally appeared in WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Will the real Anthropic please stand up
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
items.author: Will Douglas Heaven
paragraphs: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.

It also warns that there’s a fair chance that its tech could “erode trust, harm society and destabilize the geopolitical order” and, if things don’t go to plan, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

“We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms,” the company writes. “We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.”

This kind of public messaging is a master class in narrative capture. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here.

Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers.
Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation.

And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience.

The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?)

If you skim through the long sections about risks in the IPO prospectus, it’s clear this is no ordinary offering and no ordinary company. The way Anthropic tells it, business success depends not only on the firm’s ability to translate its technology into profitable products but also to save the world from what it has made.

Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”

Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. This view of its technology makes its way into the prospectus as one more risk to its business. Anthropic states that: “In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications.”
In other words, if Claude wakes up, it could be a problem.

I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this (although it’s pretty wild to read about machine sentience in an IPO prospectus.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum. When so little seems certain, what it says is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship.
It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think.

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation. Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked).
Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said. But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked.
Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.

But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that. As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free. Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because they have big egos.

In fact, Anthropic is all of these things. As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post: “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”

Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard. There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.)

Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us. They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs. They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light.

But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra. Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy. In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.
This article has been updated with additional details from the IPO prospectus.

items.title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
items.description: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have exist
items.author: Sam Hiner
paragraphs: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling.

We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.

A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines.

A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms.

Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states. The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable.

We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka, and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war. The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world.

AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place.

Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own.

We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline.

Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list.

Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 28, 2026
items.description: Mismatched energies between the sun and Uranus (in focused Scorpio and capricious Gemini, respectively) could leave you feeling off-balance today. You might be inclined to second-guess yourself — especially if you’re not sure what you really want. The more unc
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Mismatched energies between the sun and Uranus (in focused Scorpio and capricious Gemini, respectively) could leave you feeling off-balance today. You might be inclined to second-guess yourself — especially if you’re not sure what you really want. The more uncertain you feel, the more you might hope to avoid any significant changes or challenges today. But with unpredictable Uranus in the mix right now, that’s simply not going to be possible. You don’t have to go out of your way to force change (if anything, it’s probably best if you don’t), but try to stay adaptable when it comes for you anyway.

You probably won’t be in the mood to take things slow today; it’ll feel too inefficient and unsatisfying. You’d rather try your hand at multitasking: If you can do everything at once, why wouldn’t you? In reality, though, trying to juggle numerous projects will only make all of them take longer. You’ll run the risk of making preventable mistakes or of getting so distracted you end up accomplishing nothing at all. For now, try to choose just one project to focus on. You’ll have time to tackle the rest later.

You can avoid unnecessary stress today by assuming change is inevitable. Don’t waste your energy trying to prevent it. There’s no point in trying to keep your life exactly as it is right now, because that simply isn’t in the cards. You can’t control change itself, but you can control how you respond to it. Try to focus on making the most of whatever comes your way.

Some days it’s best to be daring, even brash, operating on instinct and nerve. But today probably isn’t one of those days. Your instincts likely aren’t as sharp as they usually are, and what seems like a great idea in one moment could look like a big mistake the next. Make a point of slowing down and thinking things through before you act. Everything might feel urgent right now, but, in reality, there’s no reason to rush.

Sometimes — maybe without realizing you’re doing it — you approach interactions with a clear expectation of how you want them to unfold. You might script your conversations in your head beforehand, determining unspoken rules about how people are “supposed to” respond. Today, though, try to let go of any assumptions about how others should or should not behave. Don’t imagine that you already know what they’re thinking or what they’ll say — leave space for people to surprise you. If you let your interactions be open ended, you’ll have much more fun.

Dreaming about a better future can sometimes make your present problems feel less intense. When you remind yourself that things won’t always be this way, the challenges before you might seem more manageable. But today, imagining future possibilities might only make your current frustrations more acute. So instead of fixating on a hypothetical in which everything in your life is “better,” remind yourself of what’s going right in the here and now. Even if your situation isn’t perfect, there are almost always still pockets of joy to be found if you seek them.

In general, you try not to worry about being “easy” to work with. It’s more important to you to be honest, conscientious, and competent, rather than simply agreeable. But today, it’s worth putting some extra effort into getting along with the people around you. That doesn’t mean you have to bend over backward to avoid making waves — you can still express your genuine opinions, even the unpopular ones! — but consider that a polite approach might be better received than an aggressive one. Giving your relationships this additional care will pay off in new opportunities and better results for everyone.

As much as you think you want the freedom to do whatever you want, you’re sometimes more stressed when you’re given free rein. The fewer limitations placed on you, the more responsibility you bear for your own life and your own choices. Part of you wishes someone else would just tell you what to do! Today, your challenge is to make the most of the freedom you have. You don’t have to make only perfect choices, or live a big, dazzling life — you just have to live a life that’s authentic to you.

Indecisiveness isn’t typically a problem for you. You rarely struggle with confidence, and most of the time you know what you want (and what you don’t). Today, though, you might be quick to second-guess yourself. You’re hyperaware that saying “yes” to any one path means saying “no” to the others, and you’re hesitant to close any doors yet. So for now, allow yourself to put off any big decisions until later, if possible. With another day or two to weigh your options, you might find more clarity about what’s next.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

Exciting opportunities could land in your lap today. But if you’re not paying attention, or if you’re too focused on sticking to preexisting plans, it’ll be easy for you to miss out on them. Today, keep your eyes and your mind open to the world around you. Don’t assume you know what’s going to happen next — your life might get wilder and more interesting than you initially counted on. Futures you hadn’t even considered might suddenly be in the realm of possibility, but it’s up to you to seize opportunities when they arrive.

If you’re unsatisfied with the direction your life is heading in, you might be tempted to do something drastic to change it today. If you’ve felt stuck in a rut lately, you’ll tell yourself that bold, even reckless, action is the only way out. But right now, impulsiveness is more likely to create new problems than to solve your existing ones. This is a time for taking steady, incremental risks, not huge swings. Those little risks will still make a meaningful difference as they add up over time.

In some cases, the quickest and easiest way to achieve your goals is to play by the rules: to be hardworking and patient, refusing to overcomplicate the process. In others, though, your best bet is to take a more creative approach. Today, either strategy might serve you best, so pay close attention to what your gut tells you. This isn’t the time to break rules just for the sake of it — but if you can sense that they’re only holding you back, don’t be afraid to try something new and daring.

Sometimes, you hold others to more stringent standards than you hold yourself. You don’t necessarily do this intentionally, but you nevertheless need to step back and notice when it happens. If you want to have absolute freedom to do whatever you’d like, but you want others to follow a specific set of rules, you’re setting your relationships up for failure. Try to notice when you’re being unfair to the people around you, and adjust your expectations. You and the people you care about will be better off for it.
