The opening of Frieze London is casting the world’s art market in a positive light – and catching the eye of eager buyers.
Forget the usual business books. If you really want to get ahead, take some advice from Cruella de Vil, Tom Ripley and other entrepreneurial characters from the world of fiction.
Part workspace, part residence, the communal facility by Jan Garde and Henning Weiss is bringing people in all stages of life together in style.
This month’s highlights include an irreverent novel about contemporary art, an exhibition of one of today’s most exciting fashion photographers and a Tom Cruise disaster movie.
To help you pick the right books for your summer reading list, we asked an array of cultural figures to share the titles old and new that have inspired them.
The preview week of the world’s most prestigious exhibition of contemporary art was an unruly spectacle – charged by political dissent, moments of beauty and works shining brightly through the chaos.
In recent years the art world’s largest commercial fair has painted itself into a corner. But satellite shows and new initiatives at this year’s event are helping to offer fresh perspectives.
The world’s biggest space dedicated to illustration has opened in London. Can it help to protect the art amid rising threats from AI?
There’s more to collecting than following markets and speculating on value appreciation. We meet the people at the heart of the action, from a veteran auctioneer to a design-fair director.

items.title: How DC's Progressive 'Absolute' Line Has Reinvigorated Modern Comics
items.description: O n a sunny day at the city zoo, a group of fifth graders excitedly gather for a field trip. Their chaperone, Thomas, isn’t just a teacher but a proud parent whose son’s first-place win in a science competition afforded the whole class this excursion. The joy
items.author: Christopher Cruz
paragraphs: O n a sunny day at the city zoo, a group of fifth graders excitedly gather for a field trip. Their chaperone, Thomas, isn’t just a teacher but a proud parent whose son’s first-place win in a science competition afforded the whole class this excursion. The joy is cut short when shots ring out. It’s unclear who’s firing; it’s indiscriminate. Amid the havoc, the children flee into an enclosure, their teacher slamming the door from the outside. One last shot echoes before the end.

It’s the type of scene that’s become a horrific norm in modern America, one played out so often people have become ambivalent to the news. But in this instance, it serves a singular purpose: It’s the origin story of Batman. At least, a version of him.

Conceived by writer Scott Snyder and artist Nick Dragotta, Absolute Batman reimagines the seminal tragedy of DC’s most popular superhero as something even darker, evoking themes ripped from the headlines that reflect the fears and anxieties of today’s readers. In the process, it’s kicked off an entire line of series that has rejuvenated interest in superhero comics — specifically in a newer, younger audience.

“The idea came about four years ago, during the malaise after the peak of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and it felt like there was this cultural conversation going on about how superheroes were over,” Snyder — no relation to Justice League director Zack — tells Rolling Stone. “It came from a place of anger about it. Those moments when [the] larger popular culture feels as though they’re tired of superheroes, that’s usually when comics reinvent them.”

Snyder’s pitch was for an entirely new DC universe, adjacent to the main one where most of the brand’s comics take place. Here, he could recruit a roster of writers and artists to “strip [the characters] down to the absolute core, then rebuild them in a way that makes them feel even more heroic, more resonant, more exciting [than] they have been,” as Snyder puts it. These heroes may look or act differently than readers expect, but their essential characteristics — be it their militaristic conviction or capacity for hope — remain intact.

Absolute Batman launched in October 2024, and it was swiftly followed by Absolute Wonder Woman, from writer Kelly Thompson and artist Hayden Sherman, then Absolute Superman, by writer Jason Aaron and artist Rafa Sandoval. Of DC’s Big Three, Batman led the pack as the highest-selling comic of 2024 with nearly 400,000 copies sold, although all titles performed well enough for DC to rapidly expand the Absolute line with versions of Flash, Green Lantern, and Martian Manhunter arriving in 2025.

In two years, DC’s Absolute Universe has dominated the sales charts — on top of racking up multiple nominations and wins at the industry’s Eisner and Hugo Awards — with a cultural footprint that seems outsized for this era. We expect superhero movies to rake in billions at the box office, but people flooding brick-and-mortar stores for paperbound products almost feels unreal.

“Week after week, people are lined up outside the door waiting for us to turn that key at 10 a.m.,” says Jermaine Exum, owner of Acme Comics in Greensboro, North Carolina. “I’ve been behind the counter here for 30 years. I’ve seen a lot of Number One relaunches, but I’ve never seen anything quite like what is happening with the Absolute material.”

What’s driving the fervor for Absolute comics is arguably twofold: a freedom from the constraints of decades worth of continuity, and something deeply cultural — a socially conscious bent to most of the titles in this new DC world. Batman’s nemesis is a billionaire with his own personal island for committing atrocities; Superman is traveling the world combating corporate abuse of laborers; this year’s new addition, Green Arrow, flat-out hunts CEOs.
By getting more political than mainstream comics usually allow, DC may have found the key to reaching an entirely new generation of readers.

This isn’t the first time Snyder’s been tasked with reintroducing the world to Batman. From 2011 to 2016, he shepherded the character through a company-wide relaunch — one of several DC’s done throughout the decades — as the lead writer on the mainline Batman series during a crossover narrative event called The New 52. His take on Batman cherry-picked aspects from older versions while inventing plenty new, from the Illuminati-like Court of Owls to a terrifying version of Joker who wears his own degloved face like a mask.

But Absolute Batman is a different beast entirely; it’s the flagship of an all-new DC universe. The conceit of the Absolute Universe is that it exists parallel to the primary one, and was directly created by DC’s greatest villain, Darkseid. Under his influence, the cosmic scales are tipped in favor of darkness, and everyone’s fate, from superheroes to regular Joes, turns out much more grim. That context is set up in the one-off issue, DC All In Special, which depicts the birth of this new reality — but it’s nonessential. Each book offers its own fresh starting point, and all readers really need to know is that, for our heroes, everything is fucked.

“[Darkseid] is sort of God of this world, and it’s like, ‘What if God isn’t helpful?’ God is against you, to some degree,” Snyder explains. “This is the kind of a world where you don’t do an arc and they win and it’s a triumph, and then you go onto the next arc. It’s more like they win, but it’s one step forward, two steps back, because the point isn’t to win. The point in this world is to fight.”

As envisioned by Snyder and co-creator Dragotta, Absolute Batman’s a beast: a 24-year-old who’s six feet nine, pushing 420 pounds, and wrapped in spikes. He’s hyper-aggressive, crunching bones and gouging eyes while screaming expletives. His iconic chest symbol even doubles as a detachable ax for severing limbs. Lacking the billions, this Bruce Wayne comes from a blue-collar background, raised by a teacher and social worker, before his dad’s untimely death in a mass shooting. And if this Batman is big, his villains are even bigger, more violent, and, frankly, smarter than they’ve ever been. This world’s Joker more closely resembles the mainline Batman: a billionaire philanthropist on one hand, and a demonic horror on the other.

This kind of inversion extends to all the depictions of classic heroes in the Absolute line. Rather than growing up on the paradise island of Themyscira, Kelly Thompson’s Wonder Woman is raised in hell by the witch Circe — historically one of her greatest enemies. To adapt, she’s become skilled at magic in addition to combat, and often uses spells to solve problems, in addition to a skyscraper-size sword. She’s also an amputee, having sacrificed an arm to help a mortal escape the underworld; the one she uses is conjured — a weakness that can be exploited.

But true to her mainline counterpart, Absolute Diana is a more hopeful character than, say, the broodish Batman. “I see a lot of people going, ‘Oh, Diana is just having a good time while everyone else is struggling,’” Thompson says. “And, I want to be like, ‘This bitch cut her arm off before she even showed up! Don’t tell me she’s had it easy.’ It’s a matter of perspective. One of the tricks that we have that works incredibly well for the character, but we do have to fight against, is that she’s pretty unflappable.”

In contrast to the physically larger takes on Batman and Wonder Woman, Jason Aaron’s Superman almost seems quaint. Shorter than his peers (with Diana the tallest), Absolute Superman is more reserved and less confident than them — but just as tortured. Raised until his teens on Krypton, this Kal-El mourns its demise, and arrives on Earth nowhere near Kansas or the Kents. Stripped of the traditional Clark Kent persona and the accompanying American upbringing, he’s burdened with assimilation to an alien world. With a deeper sense of cultural memory that informs his perspective, Kal-El’s story leans further into the immigrant identity that originally defined the character, and he’s left to fend for himself with no people to call his own.

“I wanted him to embrace some of those dichotomies. He fully remembers Krypton. He was a teenager there, so he [had] somewhat of a fully formed personality,” Aaron says. “Things he loved, things that were difficult for him. I wanted him to break away from the traditional Superman setup where the Clark Kent persona is a role that he’s playing, an affectation. This guy is not that. There’s no lie to him at all.”

Perhaps the most surreal deviation from the mainline DCU is writer Deniz Camp and artist Javier Rodriguez’s Absolute Martian Manhunter. Originally created in the Fifties, the Martian is a stoic, shapeshifting powerhouse who’s been popular in shows like the animated Justice League, but doesn’t quite have the mainstream recognition of his peers. Taking extensive liberties, the duo transformed the character into a more esoteric being, living inside the head of a down-on-his-luck FBI agent named John Jones — who, after surviving a suicide bombing, is left emotionally detached from his family and humanity itself.
“This is a world where you don’t do an arc and they win and it’s a triumph. The point isn’t to win. The point in this world is to fight.”
Absolute Batman co-creator Scott Snyder

“In the normal continuity, Martian Manhunter is an alien who’s pretending to be a man and, in this case, he’s an alien. He’s a combination of a man, a human man, who’s been invaded by another world, the alien,” Camp says. “I wanted to enhance the alienness of him while also enhancing the humanness of him — so, splitting them into two and having them become a buddy-cop situation, the ultimate odd couple. Outside of that was all this other stuff that I’ve been reading for years about consciousness, free will, the illusion of free will, what that means for guilt and innocence and punishment in a world like ours if there is no free will.”

Camp and Rodriguez’s Martian Manhunter tackles these themes by positioning real-world horror in a visual fever dream. The second issue in their miniseries run depicts a man named Trigger Taylor who, radicalized by conspiracy theories, becomes convinced that extraterrestrials are replacing humanity — leading him to slaughter Syrian refugees in a neighborhood named Little Damascus. The gunman has internally dehumanized his victims, convincing himself they’re aliens, but the root is unearthed as the Green Martian probes the killer’s psyche. Taylor has been conditioned by media and institutional racism to harbor prejudice; his perception has been easily weaponized by an entity called the White Martian, the villain of the book, who embodies a contagious nihilism that lives in the back of every person’s mind.

The creators choose to represent the bad Martian as a seemingly innocuous white circle for much of the story, and it’s in that simplicity where the terror lies. “We [were] talking about how to create this enemy that [is] scary, and at the end of the day, we realized that there is nothing more scary than a white circle — because it’s the void,” Rodriguez explains. “The void is the thing that scares us the most, because it means nothing. Nothing is possible. In my case, I’m the kind of guy that believes, when you die, there isn’t anything else. So, this void, the most scary thing is that there is no life.”

Two years in, it’s clear that the Absolute lines have been a hit, but pinning down the exact reasons why isn’t easy. For some, it’s the break from continuity that’s appealing. Will Osgood from Dragon’s Lair Comics & Fantasy in Austin champions the accessibility of an all-new universe. With the mainline series, “it’s just like, where do you start? Spider-Man is almost on Issue 1,000,” Osgood says. “With these, you start at Issue Number One and you read through to the newest issue. It’s been helpful for new readers and helpful for us.”

But rebooting continuity or creating all-new universes from scratch, while fine tactics for giving newcomers an on-ramp, have become routine. To create the kind of groundswell seen by DC today, there needs to be a deeper hook. What separates Absolute comics from their mainline counterparts is a decisive politicism that appears to resonate with audiences. The trick has been deftly weaving in heavy material without devolving into preaching or stunts.

“Anyone reading [these stories] can feel like their views, themselves, they’re just represented in a way that I don’t think is done very well in a lot of other comics,” says Asher Wilson, 20, from Greensboro. “They’re coming after topics that, obviously, people are afraid of, but also afraid to talk about.”

It all stems from the initial pitch by Snyder, which saw Bruce’s origin centered on a school shooting — which was later relocated to the Gotham City Zoo. But, contrary to many comics that trade in shock value, Snyder’s inspiration came more from a place of lived experience.
“It’s drawn from real life. My kids have red dot drills where they huddle at the one point in the classroom a bullet can’t pierce through. Addressing that makes the book more relevant.”
Absolute Batman artist Nick Dragotta

“I wrote Batman the first time around as though it was me, and I was younger; it was like Batman is me going up against my own fears,” Snyder explains. “But now, 15 years later, I’m a lot more afraid of the world that my kids are entering. You just see a much more difficult, more challenging, more fraught, much more frightening world [that] they’re entering on every front. Whether it’s the pragmatic aspects, like the job market, or the more existential worries like everything from climate change to political turmoil.”

Steeped in uncomfortable parallels, the Absolute world often expresses the very real issues writers — and readers — are facing daily. It’s a bold swing to hinge a character like Batman on something as emotionally fraught as a mass casualty incident, but is it unrealistic? Obviously not. “It’s drawn from real life,” Dragotta adds. “I remember the first time I realized [my kids] have red-dot drills. They all have to huddle around this red dot because it’s the one point in the room where a bullet can’t pierce this one spot through a window or a door. And you start to realize our kids are growing up with certain things we didn’t. Addressing that makes the book more relevant.”

For many readers, comics can be a form of distraction or wish fulfillment, with larger-than-life heroes performing godlike feats to save the day. But over the past few years, it’s become harder to hide from the dire straits of everyday life. Inundated by never-ending doom scrolling and a grim and relentless news cycle, fans are just looking for some semblance of vindication that illustrated fantasy can afford.

“I first picked up the line in the winter of 2025 after the Trump administration took office,” says Nikita Kohomban, 31, a comics reader from Brooklyn. “I’m a trans woman, [so] right away it felt like my entire world had been thrown upside down. Honestly, I felt super lost and scared on a daily basis. It was actually seeking some escapism as a coping mechanism that led me to get back into comic books. [Absolute Wonder Woman] and, later, Martian Manhunter, have really kept me afloat the past couple of years.”

To their credit, the creative minds behind the Absolute series don’t bother masking their politics — an especially bold move for anyone working in an industry with an often reactive and volatile fandom. Snyder himself is very open and active on social media (“I’m a big lefty New Yorker,” he says), and Thompson affectionately compares her Wonder Woman’s quest for positive transformation to the work of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani: “Not everything can be a win, but I do think it’s the right attitude to cut through the cynicism and sarcasm,” she notes.

This isn’t the first time real-world politics have informed comic writing. Snyder points toward Frank Miller in the Eighties, whose seminal work The Dark Knight Returns (1986) basically re-created the character post-Bronze Age into the unrelenting vigilante we know today. Miller’s depiction of Batman’s world featured then-President Ronald Reagan in a critical light, with Superman as his stooge. In the 2000s, the specter of Sept. 11 hung heavily over the industry, inspiring works like Marvel’s Civil War (2006-07), wherein superheroes faced an allegorical issue of defending civil liberty over security.

For Jason Aaron, writing an authentic Superman story meant looking back at the character’s inherently political origins dating back to the Thirties. “What choices would you make differently in terms of Superman than [Jerry] Siegel and [Joe] Shuster made in 1938?” Aaron says. “Some of it was looking at what that character meant to them as the sons of immigrants. That was very much an ideal immigrant story.”

From his inception, Superman reflected the trials of immigrants and everyday people. “He wasn’t running around fighting super-scientists all the time; he was going after a guy who beat his wife,” Aaron adds. “It was very much Superman solving the problems of real people down on the ground before he evolved into this guy who’s flying around the cosmos punching gods.”

For those like Aaron, with a deep historical knowledge of comics, it shouldn’t be surprising to see politics and current affairs bleed into the medium. Younger readers might be drawn to Absolute because it’s aligning with the here and now, but seasoned fans can connect the dots back to the industry’s early days. “It does take comics and superheroes back to their fundamentals,” says Earl Rufus, 41, a fan from Brooklyn. “In modern words, [they] are essentially social justice warriors.”

Beyond racism, sexism, corruption, and institutional failures, some of the Absolute stories tackle more abstract issues. Sure, a hero like Superman or Wonder Woman can personally clock a president or executive, but how do we address the ways in which individuals are failing each other? That’s a hill Absolute Martian Manhunter hopes to climb.

“We have a loneliness epidemic in this country [and] internationally right now, for a lot of different reasons. The lack of connection with people makes you angry, and it makes you sad, and it also allows others to dehumanize groups very easily because you don’t have connections to them,” Camp says. “When I look at some of the fearmongers around right now, the way that they’ve had success is [by] just how isolated everyone is, and how difficult it feels to be vulnerable. That’s a universal thing.”

Camp isn’t wrong about the plague of isolation. The ways in which we consume and discuss media now are at arm’s length; people are watching, reading, and listening on their phones, and if they’re engaging with each other, it’s all on social media. And yet, to some degree, that always-online mindset might be one the strongest drivers for audiences getting into comics today. After all, where does word of mouth spread these days, if not through virtual discourse?

“There’s just been a big trend on social media,” Osgood says. “It’s like, ‘Oh, my God, Absolute Batman just revealed their version of this character, and it’s insane and the scariest thing you’ve ever seen.’ They’ll just spread one picture of it around and that’ll get people really hyped.”
“It does take comics and superheroes back to their fundamentals. In modern words, [they] are essentially social justice warriors.”
Earl Rufus, Absolute comics fan

It’s true that the viral, and often shocking, imagery pulled from the Absolute stories have an instantly recognizable appeal of their own. On TikTok, it’s easy to find clips of creators explaining the widely circulated panel of Batman football-punting a child off a yacht from Issue Six (it’s OK, he had a life preserver!). Perhaps the most visceral of Absolute Batman’s exploits come from Absolute Batman 2025 Annual #1, i.e., the one where Batman takes down a group of white supremacists in one of the comic’s anthology-styled short stories.

The segment, written and illustrated by Daniel Warren Johnson, has a two-page sequence that depicts a demented-looking neo-Nazi raising his arm in salute, followed by his howls of “white power” cut short as an enraged Batman breaks the limb backward at the elbow. The next page then sees Batman pile-driving masked police, who have glibly sided with the agitators as they wreak havoc on a homeless encampment. Even for the squeamish, the scene is bound to draw some secondhand feelings of vindication. The one-shot issue arrived in October 2025, shortly after President Trump began sending ICE agents in unprecedented numbers to U.S. cities, and just under two months before the controversial Operation Metro Surge was enacted — which led to the deaths of citizens like Renée Good and Alex Pretti in January 2026.

While the creators of Absolute stories usually express their real-world frustrations with a slightly subtler touch (“There’s a push away from representing anyone specifically,” Kelly Thompson says), the directness of the 2025 annual took root in social media zeitgeist. Johnson himself shared online a revised concept sketch in October 2025 showing Batman gripping an ICE agent in a headlock — drawing even greater attention. “That issue by Daniel Warren Johnson, that was another one that got people in the door,” Jermaine Exum of Greensboro’s Acme Comics says. “They’re like, ‘I saw something’s going on with some new type of Batman. Do you have it?’ And that was some people’s very first issue, not Issue One.”

Without hard data provided by DC, it’s tough to say precisely where younger readers are discovering Absolute comics, but anecdotally, the biggest trends do appear to be word of mouth, propagated by social media. “I think one of the most interesting things about it, culturally, is it’s been almost a revolution for the comics world because it’s created a whole new audience on TikTok and Instagram,” Asher Wilson says, “and it’s brought in people who have never even considered comics before.”

Brooklynite Neil DeGondea, 26, also points toward social media as a driver: “I’m sure TikTok has played a big part in drawing in younger readers,” he says. “I think being a part of a fanbase and reading a book as big as Absolute Batman gives people that sense of community online.”

Regardless of what’s bringing people in, the biggest ripple in the current comics surge is how long it’s actually lasted — with sales and presales for upcoming issues matching or dwarfing earlier ones. Anyone who knows the industry understands how rare that is. “What usually happens with comic book orders is the numbers go down,” says Dimitrios Fragiskatos, owner of Anyone Comics in Brooklyn. “No store in their right mind would order more copies of Issue Number Two than they would of Issue Number One, but my orders for Number 25 are much higher than my initial orders for Number One were. I would even say triple that.”

“We got a giant reorder of the trades on Wednesday or Thursday, and they were all gone by Monday morning,” says Mitch Cutler, owner of Brooklyn’s St. Marks Comics. “We’re stocking this stuff deep, and it wasn’t enough. For something to have this kind of velocity at this late date is unusual.”

The two-year explosion in popularity has been a boon for moving volumes, stemming from a surprising excitement in younger readers who are adamant about buying tangible copies. Although, perhaps it shouldn’t come as a total shock; it’s become a popular trend among Gen Z to seek out legacy and retro media in a potential rejection of our all-digital and subscription-based culture. “We’re definitely looking for escapism on [some] level,” artist Hayden Sherman adds, “but people are looking to engage with the world around them through the media they intake.”

At the moment, it doesn’t seem like the Absolute boom is slowing down. But as with most media trends, especially those appealing to younger, savvier audiences, the comics will continue to live or die on authenticity. What Snyder and his peers have built has lit a fire that’s drawing in a growing fandom. It’ll be up to DC to keep it going.

“I hope people can tell we’re trying to do it sincerely; it’s not about going on a soapbox or about bringing them in a way and thinking you necessarily have the only answer to something,” Snyder says. “The guiding principle and the secret of the series [is] that Batman, in this world, needs to learn that power is in collectivism. Power is in letting more and more people in.”

items.title: The Real Housewives of Potomac Recap: A Friend to All is a Friend to None
items.description: Over the last eleven seasons of The Real Housewives of Potomac, Gizelle Bryant has slowly evolved from a participant in the show’s social ecosystem to its unofficial director of intelligence. She is like Lord Varys in Game of Thrones: she gathers rumors, excha
items.author: Shamira Ibrahim
paragraphs: Over the last eleven seasons of The Real Housewives of Potomac, Gizelle Bryant has slowly evolved from a participant in the show’s social ecosystem to its unofficial director of intelligence. She is like Lord Varys in Game of Thrones: she gathers rumors, exchanges confidences, and negotiates allegiances, then distributes the resulting information at whichever moment it best advances the plot for peak entertainment, while Gizelle largely evades the line of fire herself. It’s an operation that Gizelle has managed to maintain with relatively little interference over the years, thanks in no small part to the unwavering loyalty of Robyn Dixon and the enthusiastic scheming of Ashley Darby — and once Robyn left the camera lens to tend to her overexposed marriage, Ashley proudly served as Gizelle’s faithful go-to minion.

But now that Robyn has returned to the fold, the Green-Eyed Bandits are experiencing something of a succession crisis. Ashley has grown accustomed to being Gizelle’s principal deputy, but Robyn has no intention of surrendering her seniority, creating a power struggle of sorts. It’s just like Mean Girls: everybody wants to be Regina George’s No. 1 lackey, because they all recognize that being constantly subservient to her is easier than enduring her wrath. Now Gizelle has to decide whether that person is her longtime friend in real life or the woman who has spent the past several seasons doing much of her dirty work. There’s just one wrinkle: Robyn’s time touching grass seems to have come with a strong dose of basic common sense, and the ladies of Potomac have abandoned anything resembling rational consistency at least four seasons ago.

It’s only been three episodes so far, but Robyn is demonstrating a novel willingness to not only hold Gizelle accountable and express her disagreement with her friend on camera, but also acknowledge that she never truly cared for Ashley. It seems that a couple of years away from the confessional chairs has allowed Robyn to realize that her castmates’ collective obsession with producing compelling reality television has blinded them to the elementary principles of friendship, as she points out that Gizelle handled the allegations about Tia’s husband remarkably poorly. Considering this woman spent years defending Gizelle’s most questionable interventions, I am inclined to regard it as a minor miracle.

The conversation is purportedly around Gizelle’s ethics, but what Robyn is really confronting is the shifting ways that Housewives have to circulate information in the Bravosphere. Before, the verboten activity was “calling the blogs,” from Lisa Vanderpump being accused of leaking puppygate to RadarOnline to the Atlanta girls having relationships with B Scott and Funky Dineva. Then the girls cozy up to podcasters and leaker accounts while pretending to be above them, the ultimate contradiction of Monica Garcia’s exposure, for example: she knew so much of the SLC cast’s business precisely because they sent her snark account information all the time. Now, there’s no need for a third-party pretense whatsoever, as the housewives build gossip platforms themselves, and openly speculate about their respective shows and other franchises to their true-crime-addled listeners, eager for any bits of information that will help them unravel the next Scandoval or Summer House fiasco. One podcast at a time, the ladies of Bravo are smudging the increasingly blurry line between reporting on their castmates’ public lives and manufacturing the very conflicts they subsequently monetize on camera. Apparently Robyn is the only one who has inhaled enough fresh air to recognize the friction.

(As a brief aside: it’s interesting too how differently the women in Tia’s life have approached her marital crisis. Wendy has encouraged her to reject the shame and insist that Rob carry the burden of explaining his behavior to their daughters. Gizelle has focused on helping her navigate the emotional humiliation and get back in control. Her mom is obsessed with the aesthetics, which lines up with everything Tia has told us about her. Robyn, perhaps the most pragmatic of the bunch, has advised Tia on how to bring her children into the conversation. It’s a revealing little survey of how women process betrayal.)

Gizelle also attempted to repair that fragile ceasefire between her and Wendy that is now at risk. Wendy is understandably furious to find out that Gizelle has been referring to her as a scammer, particularly because the term carries a specific cultural weight when directed at a Nigerian person. But while Wendy is right to point out that the accusation doesn’t exist in a cultural vacuum, I am not entirely convinced that invoking the broader history of a xenophobic prejudice is sufficient here when she is facing serious allegations of fraud. While I don’t think insurance schemes are the most immoral offenses in the world, Wendy’s tendency to collapse criticisms into a single argument about persecution is one of her more frustrating rhetorical habits, and one that I don’t think they’ll give her much room to get away with this time around. For now, though, Gizelle is playing ball, and promptly apologizes for saying “the S word,” which sounds more damning than just saying scammer and being done with it.

Speaking of scams, Gizelle and Ashley are attempting to breathe new life into GNA, their nebulous venture whose latest iteration involves a “workout wellness situation.” At this point, I’m not entirely sure what GNA is supposed to be beyond a logo in search of a business model; neither are its founders. Nothing says luxury wellness quite like taking a HIIT circuit class in an industrial art studio rented by the hour for a corporate team-building retreat. At one point, Ashley brings up the “coochie sweat leggings,” which I believe was from back when GNA was supposed to be the Jack & Jill version of LuLaRoe. Somewhere, a branding intern is quietly weeping into a mood board as they try to understand what sound bowls have to do with the National Brain Tumor Association.

As the gang debriefs after the event, Robyn reveals that Gizelle had made yet another reference to Tia’s marital troubles during a podcast recording, teasing that listeners would learn more in six months. Robyn, who apparently is the only one on the podcast with working reasoning skills, removed the comment from the final edit to save Gizelle from being raked over the coals yet again. Ashley, however, is eager to try to turn this minor tension into her advantage in retaliation for Robyn discussing her kissing Jackson on the podcast while she was desperately trying to tamp down the backlash, and promptly informs Tia of the podcast joke that never was before their next group get-together. The tension follows the women to Courtney’s event celebrating her husband’s birthday, where the real entertainment for the evening was Tia and Gizelle lacing stepping in the ring.

Gizelle strikes first and approaches Tia to express her displeasure that Tia is playing telephone, only to have the game flipped right back on her as Tia cuts her to the quick over making jokes about her marriage on the podcast. Suddenly, Gizelle finds herself in the unenviable position of having to explain something she clearly said while standing directly in front of the person she said it about. Her response is a spectacular display of selective amnesia: she stammers and sputters like an old car engine attempting to turn over. It’s obvious that Gizelle didn’t expect to have the disadvantage here, as she scrambles to distinguish between the offenses by arguing semantics.

Unfortunately for Gizelle, we have already watched her acknowledge to Robyn, Ashley, and Kal that the podcast remark was inappropriate, making her indignation ring hollow. And on her end, Tia is having none of it. “As long as you can get a check, anybody’s pain, anybody’s family, that is free game for your success,” she tells Gizelle. “And that kind of friendship, my dear, I don’t want it.” By the time Robyn joins the conversation, her bestie is on the ropes, feebly trying to insist that the entire matter is a misunderstanding. It’s a claim that is immediately undone when Robyn reveals that Gizelle said: “You’ll hear about it in six months.” It’s easily one of the most effective confrontations Gizelle has faced in years. (Poor Alexis. Imagine inviting your wife’s friends to celebrate your birthday, only to discover that you’ve inadvertently hosted a Housewives summit on the ethics of podcast production.)

It’s been a while since Gizelle has been forced to withstand a sustained attack from someone who isn’t easily intimidated by her social standing. Stacey has been a great sparring partner so far, but she has yet to really nail her to the wall on her misdeeds the same way Tia seemed willing to this week. We already know that Tia has since reconciled with Gizelle, so this uprising is inevitably going to falter at some point, but for the time being, it’s fascinating to watch Gizelle slowly recognize that she may have lost her grip on all of the moving pieces around her, even if it’s only for the short term. With Robyn increasingly willing to challenge her, Gizelle can no longer enjoy the luxury of operating from a relatively secure position.

Eventually, Wendy redirects the interrogation back to Ashley, who is the ultimate mastermind behind everyone’s frustrations at the table. This time around, Ashley couldn’t even attempt to muster up a plausible defense for her impish penchant for chaos, feebly insisting that her issue was with Robyn’s decision to discuss the podcast incident on camera instead of burying it once and for all the way that Monique did for her ex-husband. Robyn, understandably irritated, points out the absurdity of being accused of messiness by a woman who was the first one to circulate allegations about Tia’s marriage in front of a live audience. It’s the kind of circular argument that Ashley thrives on stoking on the show, making everyone so preoccupied with establishing the chain of custody for a rumor that the original harm becomes almost incidental. Normally, these sorts of acrobatics early on are a bad omen for the season, but Robyn, Tia, and Stacey are clearly willing to cut through the hemming and hawing and force the group to address conflicts head-on.

For now, it seems that all of the show’s increasingly elaborate attempts to exploit conflict within people’s marriages over the years have finally come home to roost. We are at a year where multiple marriages are explicitly in flux, and Gizelle is not only being forced to acknowledge head-on what she feels her moral responsibility is to respect the cast’s privacy, but is being held accountable to that standard. I would honestly respect Gizelle if she pulled a Tamra Judge and freely admitted that she is only loyal to the cameras and the audience that she serves her theatrics to. But for all of Gizelle’s bluster about being unfazed by the constant criticisms over her machinations, she so clearly wants to be seen as a good person, and a good person could never admit that Tia’s read on her was 100 percent correct. That said, our green-eyed bandit will never take a beating lying down. She may be licking her wounds for the moment, but this is only a strategic retreat; I do not doubt that despite being caught slipping, she will end the season right back at the top of the heap like always. Gizelle Bryant has survived far worse than an uncomfortable birthday party.
There was so much to get into that we’ll cover the taglines next week, as we get a closer look at the cracks in everyone’s marriages and get more of an introduction to Courtney. See you all then!

• Congrats to Stacey and Thiemo on their re-engagement, but I am firmly against bringing non-service dogs into restaurants, even for romantic purposes. I don’t know what happened during the pandemic that convinced people their pets were entitled to accompany them into every establishment in America, but I would like to eat a meal without a golden retriever’s hair shedding in my peripheral vision, thank you very much! The ring is cute, I suppose.

• We finally meet Tia’s mother, Yetunde, who arrives at Dulles looking like she has just stepped out of a leisure catalog with her tailored white pantsuit and the kind of gently aristocratic you only get at British boarding schools. Can’t wait to see more of her on camera.
• At this point, Cynthia seems to be operating as the Housewives equivalent of a diplomatic attaché, appearing wherever scenes demand her carefully neutral expression.

• Gizelle looks extraordinary in her new confessional ensemble. The bronzed makeup, golden wig, and sunflower bandage dress are all working for her. In another life, she was definitely a Dallas Cowboys WAG — which, to be fair, isn’t all that far off from a megachurch wife.

• Monique is back, which only made me realize how little I notice of her presence right now. Now that Angel and her husband are gone and Stacey is back with Wonder Bread, I’m unclear what reason we really have to integrate her with this group.

• Courtney is understandably irritated that none of the women have brought men to socialize with her husband, although I have to wonder why the guest list for a grown man’s birthday party appears to depend so heavily on the romantic availability of his wife’s castmates. An NBA coach can’t find any friends willing to appear on camera? They’ve already got to do it at least 82 times a year!
• Gizelle may lack Wendy’s academic pedigree, but if anything, Congress could probably learn a thing or two from her about evading direct questions.
• Karen’s admission that a lack of money and sex can destroy a marriage may be the most revealing thing she’s said about her marriage with Ray in years.

• Karen explains that her therapeutic journey will remain off camera, a decision I support wholeheartedly. Reality television has produced enough questionable on-screen therapy sessions to make me deeply suspicious of any clinician willing to conduct treatment in front of a Bravo camera crew. Only time will tell us how much of what we’re seeing is genuine self-examination; Karen has certainly always understood that vulnerability can be a powerful tool for maintaining audience sympathy.

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: The Dinner Guest
items.description: Just when you thought Lord Lovat couldn’t get any more vile, we get “Small Mercies.” It remains enraging that we are well aware this guy lives well into the 1740s, where he is still the greatest of dicks. Here’s hoping that whatever Brian does (and maybe Colum
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Just when you thought Lord Lovat couldn’t get any more vile, we get “Small Mercies.” It remains enraging that we are well aware this guy lives well into the 1740s, where he is still the greatest of dicks. Here’s hoping that whatever Brian does (and maybe Colum and Dougal and definitely Murtagh) once he learns what his father has done to Ellen is at least somewhat satisfying. Ellen deserves it, and we deserve it too. Remember last week when I asked if anyone on this show would ever know peace? Well, not this week, certainly!

Can you tell I’m stalling? This episode is devastating. It all begins once Balloch delivers Ellen to Castle Leoch. You know immediately that Lord Lovat must be up to something truly dastardly because (1) he wants to speak to Ellen privately, before Julia meets her, and (2) he isn’t cruel but rather does this whole little number about how Brian painted the wrong picture when he spoke of him. And oh, aren’t they both just so worried about Brian making it home from the war alive, and hey, he actually sent Balloch to protect Ellen — didn’t he come in handy when she was attacked by that MacKinney guy? I really want not only Ellen’s instinct but her trust in Brian to kick in a little harder here. She is obviously hesitant to believe Lovat could be sincere — she does remind him that he’s the one who caused all the hubbub about her virginity — but not hesitant enough. Sure she’s in a precarious position being in this guy’s home, and surely once Julia walks into the dining room she must believe Julia would never let harm come to her, but also, come on, girl! You literally just rode across the Highlands because Lovat was a traitor to his Jacobite allies and was going to get Brian and Dougal killed. Use your head, Ellen!

You’d think Julia’s spidey sense would be set off, too. After she and Davina return to Leathers following a cute little girls’ trip in which they bury Seema’s body out in the mud and chat about being haunted by death, they find Lovat has returned. He proudly confesses to switching to Team Crown and gets irate when the women ask about Brian — he abandoned his father for honor, and honor might just get him killed. He says words that make it seem like he doesn’t care if Brian lives or dies, but the anger is clearly stemming from feeling hurt by his son. Still, does he seem like a guy who would welcome that son’s best girl? Plus, Julia and Davina find Maisri in the kitchen making a spiced wine for dinner, and they just accept that like it’s totally cool and normal. When Julia finds Ellen at dinner and watches as Lovat is suddenly very pro-unification of Frasers and MacKenzies, she should’ve known right then that something was afoot.

Because friends, something is very, very afoot. As the dinner goes on, Ellen looks sicker and sicker. She’s pale and sweating and clutching at her stomach in pain. Not long after, Julia has many of the same symptoms. This is when Maisri arrives to do a reading, and while she says that Brian is alive, she also notes that death is coming. Almost on cue, Ellen is in so much pain that she wants to leave. Lovat seems more than happy to oblige in getting her back to Leoch. And soon we know why: Ellen begins bleeding — she’s having a miscarriage. When Julia realizes she and Ellen both had Maisri’s wine and Lovat hardly touched his, she confronts him, and it doesn’t take long for him to admit his plan: Maisri’s prophecy about Simon (William) included that fun little caveat about this baby having to be the last in his line for him to become king. Lovat had Maisri make a potion that could destroy a womb. He wants Ellen, and Julia, for that matter, unable to have children. Julia is horrified. Lovat yells at her with such righteous indignation — he’s doing this for his (Henry’s) son. Lovat’s not just a dick; he’s a madman.

Julia can barely form the words to tell Ellen what’s been done to her. Ellen is devastated. She is broken. It’s Davina who gets her back to Leoch, but she is not the same Ellen as before. Mrs. Fitz and Jocasta take her into their arms, clean her, and let her rest. When Colum demands to talk to her to find out what happened, Mrs. Fitz mercifully persuades him to leave her be for now. “Her body will mend,” she tells Colum, “but her spirit, I’ve never seen it so broken.”

All the MacKenzies are pretty much having the worst day of their lives. When the men return from Sheriffmuir with the bodies of their fallen comrades, Colum has to grapple with his role in their deaths. This man is struggling under the weight of being a laird, and it is straight up paralyzing him. When he learns that Dougal has been captured, he doesn’t even pretend like he’s going after him. He has to think of the clan first, and sending people there would be a suicide mission. Ned is dismayed by the inaction. But our sensitive lawyer is even more disgusted by Colum’s reaction to the news of Ellen being taken — he doesn’t rage until he gets more information about who may have taken her; instead, he begins to spiral about what it could mean for their plan to keep Leoch safe from the crown if she dies. Have we ever seen Ned so horrified by the callousness Colum displays here? Colum claims it is his job to put the clan first, and I fear this inclination to put clan before family is only going to get worse now that he’s carrying the guilt of all those dead clansmen. That, paired with his complete ineptitude when MacKinney tried to coup his ass, has really shattered Colum’s sense of self.

So, if Colum won’t even make an attempt to save his brother’s life, who will? Brian and Murtagh, of course. These two are almost too good at stealthily murdering soldiers in the dead of night. The two best friends you ever did see. And they arrive just in time. Dougal is being beaten within an inch of his life as Lord Gerard Grey demands information on Jacobite plans. Things get absolutely wild when a young redcoat asks if he can take a turn torturing him and almost uses a coal to first burn Dougal’s tongue and then his dick before being called off. If you were watching this and thinking, What a sadistic little fuck, you were probably not at all surprised to learn that this man is actually young Jack Black Randall. A sicko through and through. Dougal’s saved from Randall’s mad lust for torture, but then he and Old Angus are tossed into “the vault,” which is a hole that fills up with water from the ocean tide coming in, ultimately drowning those inside. A very cool and not at all horrifying way to go.

Thankfully, Brian and Murtagh find their way to the vault just as the water is reaching the top and, using all of their strength, pry the lid open. Old Angus dies in the escape attempt, but they manage to get Dougal out. In one gasp-worthy moment, the men bump into Randall on the way out. Dougal wants to kill him on the spot, but Brian sees Randall is so afraid that he’s peed himself, says he’s just a kid, and they spare his life. I mean, they shove him into a trunk, but still, how infuriating? How gutting? It’s Brian who shows Randall mercy, letting this man live and go on to spend much of his adult life terrorizing Brian’s future family. Friends, I know this is stating the obvious, but the Outlander-verse is bleak as hell.

• Anyone else get the shivers when John Cameron returns and embraces Jocasta, but looks directly at Grace when he tells his wife how lucky he is to come home to her. Someone save Grace … and Jocasta, for that matter. That woman looked downright disappointed when she saw her husband was one of the few who survived the battle.

• I did have a little chuckle when Lovat invoked the Capulets and Montagues while making a toast about the Frasers and the MacKenzies coming together. Uh, dude, do you know how many people had to die for those families to stop feuding?

• We get the smallest sliver of hope for a happier future when Arch Bug agrees to help Henry be with Julia. For now, he gets Henry to Leathers so the husband and wife can reunite for a few moments, but he also promises to deliver letters back and forth between the two while Henry searches for the gemstones needed to travel back to their time. There’s zero chance this goes off without a hitch, but for a moment, it feels like the tiniest of wins.

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Recap: Puddings Pop
items.description: This was a shockingly British episode of this quintessentially British show. While we have to reckon with bread-and-butter pudding and more custard than is good for a healthy heart, the most English thing is everyone calling Gary by the nickname “Gazza.” It’s
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: This was a shockingly British episode of this quintessentially British show. While we have to reckon with bread-and-butter pudding and more custard than is good for a healthy heart, the most English thing is everyone calling Gary by the nickname “Gazza.” It’s common here with any name that ends that way (Barry becomes “Bazza,” Sherry becomes “Shazza”), and I always get an absolute kick out of it. You can call me Brazza as much as you like. As my father says, call me anything, just don’t call me late for dessert — and we got plenty of those this week.

Dessert week is always a little bit odd because I don’t know how it differentiates itself from all the other weeks. Can’t many of these sweet bakes be dessert? This season it definitely seemed mostly like things you would order in a restaurant rather than bake at home, at least for the signature and showstopper challenges. The signature is to make eight “self-saucing” puddings, which makes them sound like they have some kind of medical condition. Many of the bakers are going with a variation of a chocolate lava cake, and at least four of them are going with the chocolate-orange flavor combination. While it’s not common in America, it is everywhere here in King Charles’s formerly European island. And not just the famous Terry’s Chocolate Orange Americans can buy around Christmas (which is available year-round here). When you go to the cookie shop, the ice-cream store, and any place where fine desserts are sold, you’ll find something chocolate and orange flavored. That combination, along with sticky toffee puddings, is one of the best things about having the honor of paying His Majesty’s taxes every year.

Because these types of desserts are best served straight out of the oven, they staggered the bakers’ start times so that the judges can get them hotter than Gabe and his two boyfriends at a polyamory convention. Connie, one of only two remaining females in the tent and the third baker to finish, wows Paul and Nigella with her (yes) chocolate-orange fondants and gets a handshake. I feel bad for everyone involved in this. No one gets to appreciate Connie’s handshake because everyone but Gazza and Clazza (that’s Clara’s new nickname) is still working. Also, how disruptive that must be. Everyone’s cheering and clapping, and they’re just trying to make cake with sauce oozing out of it in under two hours. I am glad for Connie, especially since she forgot to set the timer on her bake and has to figure it out by eye.

Gary also gets high marks for his (yes) chocolate-orange fondants. Though Tom’s apple-crumble puddings look like blobs, the judges still say they’re disgusting. Paul absolutely loves Mo’s fondant inspired by the free cookie he got in his meal deal but says the sauce was a little too grainy. Clara’s “doce de leite” looks runnier than a nose on a cold winter’s day, and Nigella says they’re more like liquid with a bit of cake floating in them. Gabe’s have no sauce, which is ironic because he pumped his (yes) chocolate-orange fondants full of orange liqueur. The worst has to be Yannis, who makes apple-strudel puddings, which are so big they don’t bake. You know that his apple-strudel puddings are common in Austria. Did you know that Yannis spent his childhood in Austria? Yeah! It’s true! I don’t think we’ve ever heard this before.

The technical is to make bread-and-butter pudding, which is even more English than getting drunk, screaming football songs at the top of your lungs, and then pissing against a wall straight onto the sidewalk — sorry, straight onto the “pavement.” As you see in the technical, it is made by buttering stale white bread, slathering it in custard, and then plopping the whole thing in the oven. It is a cultural institution, and it is … a cultural institution. I do not love it. It’s sort of like having French toast for dessert. Mo says that it sounds like a war recipe and he’s totally right, but it actually dates all the way back to the 18th century, so it is the only thing in the tent older than Paul’s entitlement.

What’s even worse than the pudding itself is that Nigella tells them all she wants them to soup it up and add things to it. No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. This is not how a technical works. We went over this two weeks ago. The entire point of the technical is that everyone is making the same thing so that they can rank those bakes. Here they are asking them to make something different again. I find this as annoying as top-ten lists that include “honorable mentions.” No. Someone set the arbitrary number at ten, and the whole point of the exercise is to whittle the list down to ten. Just like with the technical. The arbitrary designation is that everyone makes the same thing. If the author of the list wants 11 titles, just make it a top-11 list. No one cares. If the producers want the technical to be different, then change the rules. But these are their rules and they should play by them.

Not surprisingly, Gary and Connie make the best bread-and-butter puddings because they’re the only two who have made them regularly, because it’s a bit of a fuddy-duddy dessert. Moyin, Yannis, and Mo are at the bottom for, respectively, not using enough custard, adding too many additional flavors, and not really caring about anything because that is his whole shtick.

The showstopper is a very cute idea where each baker has to make a dessert cart with at least three classic desserts on it. While they keep talking about all of these retro desserts, I still regularly see these carts with just these types of desserts on them all over London. Well, maybe not all over, but they’re not entirely uncommon. There are lots of Black Forest gâteaus (which there often are on Baking Show) as well as sticky toffee puddings, which are the best dessert invented by the Anglican Jesus and something that I desperately miss when I’m back in America. Also trifles. The English love a trifle. Why they always be trifling? Mo even makes a STP trifle, and I would really like to get my hands on that.

Unlike with Bread Week last week, it seems like everyone is quite successful in their creations. Well, they all look fantastic, and everyone works harder than J.Lo worked the pole in Hustlers. Tom goes one further and decides to make four desserts, all of them inspired by his favorite cocktails, and his drinks-and-dessert cart might as well be Michael B. Jordan’s backside because I want to bury my face in it. Even Nigella gets a little worked up eating his mojito-inspired pavlova, and she asks if she can steal the recipe. Make that the new Hollywood handshake, the Lawson larceny. They also go gaga over Mo’s mango mousse that he makes in the shape of a mango. (Can he make it in the shape of Michael B. Jor … Oh, never mind.) Nigella asks him if he made the recipe, and he says he did, and both she and Paul are astounded by how good it is. Mo seems to finally care about something, and it’s this mango. After these two winners, I thought for sure one of them would take Star Baker, but instead it goes to Connie. She makes a classic trifle, an apple-and-pear tart, and a pineapple upside-down cake. The judges don’t love all of her desserts (as they didn’t with Mo and Tom), saying that her cake was overbaked and that her pie needed custard. However, they love the trifle so much, and she ranked so highly in the first two challenges that she gets to make a call home to her very cheeky husband, who asks when she’s going to arrive home, probably so she can whip him up one of those trifles.

Gazza, who has been cruising along all episode, doesn’t bowl the judges over with his treacle pudding or his Black Forest gâteau, which is a little bit shocking. Clara continues to be in the bottom, rare for her, with her macarons and frangipane tarts. Yannis decides to go for STP, a Black Forest gâteau, and a Mary Berry’s recipe for Queen of Desserts, which is a mix of breadcrumbs and custard with jam and topped with meringue. I don’t know, guys. I don’t think I would make that queen of anything. Though I would throw Paul out of my kingdom for the face me makes when Yannis says he is going to use Paul’s old co-judge’s recipe over his. Yannis doesn’t seem to score with any of these confections, and he is sent home. Actually, no. Noel personally drove him to the train station, gave him a fresh sausage roll, and sent him on his way. As Yannis stood on the misty platform, saddened and slightly shivering, he pulled back as the train screeched into the station. The doors opened, and he approached just as the conductor said, “Next stop, Vienna!”

items.title: Skydance TV Co-Chair George Cheeks Reveals Executive Structure Following Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger
items.description: Skydance TV co-chair and chief content officer George Cheeks formalized his division’s executive structure. In a memo to staff, Cheeks shared the specific titles for his direct reports, as well as how Skydance TV will now operate post-Warner Bros. and Paramoun
items.author: Michael Schneider
paragraphs: Skydance TV co-chair and chief content officer George Cheeks formalized his division’s executive structure. In a memo to staff, Cheeks shared the specific titles for his direct reports, as well as how Skydance TV will now operate post-Warner Bros. and Paramount merger.

“Reporting to me, these accomplished leaders will work together to advance our strategy and help shape the next chapter of our division,” Cheeks said in his memo, confirming his Skydance TV Studios trio: Channing Dungey as head of Warner Bros. TV Group and of the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery cable networks; David Stapf as head of CBS Studios; and Matt Thunell as head of Paramount TV Studios. Also, David Berson leads Skydance’s Global Sports Group, including CBS Sports, TNT Sports and WBD Sports.

Also, Amy Reisenbach continues as CBS Entertainment president; Tom Cibrowski as CBS News operations head; Byron Rubin as chief operating officer; Laurel Weir overseeing research and programming insights; Mike Benson leading marketing; and Chris Ender as head of communications and publicity.

The news isn’t a surprise; it had previously been understood that divisional bosses who will report to him include Warner Bros. TV Group and U.S. networks chairman/CEO Channing Dungey, CBS Studios president David Stapf and Paramount TV Studios topper Matt Thunell. It had also already been reported that Dungey — who took on overseeing the Warner Bros. Discovery networks a year ago — would be given oversight of the Paramount cable networks as well.

Alongside Cheeks, JB Perrette (previously WBD’s CEO/president of global streaming and games) serves as co-chair of Skydance TV, as well as chief business officer. Perrette additionally holds those roles for the Skydance DTC streaming division.

Prior to the merger, Cheeks most recently served as Paramount TV media chair — a job he was given last year when Skydance first took control of Paramount. Prior to that, Cheeks was one of the three co-CEOs of Paramount Global (previously known as ViacomCBS) — and was the only one of that triumvirate to make the transition to the new company.

In a previous memo sent to the team after the deal closed, Cheeks spelled out how the divisions would be set up, including Warner Bros. TV Group, CBS (and CBS Studios) and Paramount TV Studios. “This newly formed Skydance Television group is an unmatched mix of networks, studios, platforms and programming genres,” he said in the previous memo, noting TV studios Warner Bros. Television Studios, CBS Studios and Paramount Television Studios; the CBS broadcast network; CBS Sports, TNT Sports and Warner Bros. Discovery Sports; CBS News; CBS stations; and the cable portfolio. “There are too many standout shows to name individually, but one thing is clear: the breadth and quality of programming across this group is unrivaled, spanning some of the most watched, most acclaimed and most award-winning in the industry,” he wrote at the time.
To: All Skydance TV Employees

The excellence and scale of our entertainment, news and sports businesses, combined with the talent and expertise across our organization, position us well for the road ahead.

While each of us has a distinct role to play, our success will depend on all of us working together at every level, sharing expertise and leveraging the full strength of our portfolio. I’m a firm believer that a collaborative culture generates strong creative and business results.

- Channing Dungey will continue to lead the Warner Bros. Television Group and its portfolio of scripted, unscripted and animation studios. Warner Bros. TV Studios is home to the Emmy Award-winning series ‘The Pitt’ and an impressive slate of acclaimed series. She will also oversee the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery cable roster of 50+ brands such as HGTV, Food Network, TNT, BET and MTV. For cable channels outside the U.S., Channing will report to me for programming and to JB Perrette for operations.

- Matt Thunell oversees Paramount Television Studios, home to premium series for streaming and broadcast, with blockbuster franchises including ‘Reacher,’ its spin-off ‘Neagley’ and the Taylor Sheridan universe that spans ‘Dutton Ranch,’ ‘Landman’ and ‘Lioness’ on Paramount+ and ‘Marshals’ on CBS.
- Skydance Sports Entertainment will be part of the Skydance TV Studios Group with details to follow.

David Berson leads Skydance’s Global Sports Group, with oversight of our live sports portfolio, led by CBS Sports, TNT Sports and WBD Sports, across all platforms and in partnership with JB and the International team for outside the U.S. Combined sports rights for the new division include the NFL, UEFA Champions League, NHL, MLB, March Madness, PGA Tour, The Masters, WNBA, NASCAR and college football, among many others.

Amy Reisenbach leads CBS Entertainment, a cornerstone of our multiplatform strategy and home to the most-watched primetime schedule on television that consistently delivers the biggest new hits year after year – including this season’s Rotten Tomatoes 100% Certified Fresh drama ‘Cupertino.’

Tom Cibrowski will continue to oversee operations across CBS News’ broadcast, streaming and digital businesses, while leaning into his deep experience in morning television to bolster ‘CBS Mornings,’ and sustain the ratings momentum at ‘CBS Evening News.’
The following leaders will support our broader Skydance TV organization as we bring together and grow our group:

- Bryon Rubin will be our Chief Operating Officer (COO) working with all divisional leaders on strategic and operational matters while maintaining his leadership of CBS’ domestic syndication. Bryon will expand his remit to include oversight of the CBS Television Stations group, working closely with division president Jennifer Mitchell, who will also have a dotted reporting line into me and will be part of my Skydance TV SLT.

- Laurel Weir will oversee research and programming insights across Skydance TV broadcast, cable and studios. She will work closely with creative and marketing leaders in all areas to help shape our strategy through a deep understanding of audience insights and consumption trends. Laurel will continue to oversee her content strategy, scheduling and content acquisitions teams for the Paramount cable networks while we work through integration planning.

- Mike Benson will lead marketing across our portfolio, bringing our talented teams together to strengthen our brands, elevate audience discovery and eventize and promote our programming launches through all forms of traditional and emerging media. Mike will have a dotted reporting line to Rebecca Mall, Chief Marketing Officer, Skydance.

- Chris Ender will oversee all communications and publicity. He will serve as the spokesperson for Skydance TV and lead best-in-class comms teams in each division that will shape our narrative, elevate brands and programming and help define the voice of our combined group. Chris will have a dotted reporting line to Melissa Zukerman, Chief Communications Officer, Skydance, and support JB Perrette on any Skydance TV business and operations topics.
I know many of you have questions about our structure and what comes next. We will continue to share more information when possible.

We’re still early in this journey and process, but I’m confident in the strength of this team and in the extraordinary talent and capabilities across our business. As I’ve said, the work ahead is significant, and so is the opportunity. Together, we’ll build on our strengths and shape an even stronger future.
Thank you for everything you do.

items.title: ‘Pride and Prejudice’ Trailer: Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden Reboot Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy’s Love Story for Netflix
items.description: Netflix has released the trailer for its upcoming “Pride and Prejudice” limited series, starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden as adversaries-to-lovers Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy.
items.author: Giana Levy
paragraphs: Netflix has released the trailer for its upcoming “Pride and Prejudice” limited series, starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden as adversaries-to-lovers Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy.

The six-part series is a faithful adaptation of Jane Austen’s 1813 novel penned by “Everything I Know About Love” author Dolly Alderton, centering on the will-they-won’t-they love story of Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy as they navigate the social landscape of 19th-century England. It’s directed by “Heartstopper” helmer Euros Lyn.

The cast also includes Olivia Colman (“The Crown”) as Mrs. Bennet, Rufus Sewell (“The Diplomat”) as Mr. Bennet, Freya Mavor (“Industry”) as Jane Bennet, Jamie Demetriou (“Stath Lets Flats”) as Mr. Collins, Daryl McCormack (“Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery”) as Mr. Bingley, Louis Partridge (“House of Guinness”) as Mr. Wickham, Rhea Norwood (“Heartstopper”) as Lydia Bennet, Siena Kelly (“Black Mirror”) as Caroline Bingley and Fiona Shaw (“Killing Eve”) as Lady Catherine de Bourg. Hopey Parish and Hollie Avery also make their debuts as Mary Bennet and Kitty Bennet.

They will be joined by Anjana Vasan (“We Are Lady Parts”), Sebastian Armesto (“Gangs of London”), Rosie Cavaliero (“KAOS”), Saffron Coomber (“Three Little Birds and Die Zweiflers”), James Dryden (“Deadpool”), Justin Edwards (“The Thick Of It”), James Northcote (“The Last Kingdom”), Eloise Webb (“The Queen’s Gambit”) and Isabella Sermon (“Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom”).
Executive producers include Corrin, Laura Lankester, Alderton, Lyn and Will Johnston and Louise Mutter for Lookout Point. Lisa Osborne serves as producer.
“Pride and Prejudice” premieres on Netflix Dec. 3. Watch the trailer below.

items.title: Kathleen Kennedy Replaces Peter Rice as Head of Ceremonies and Content for L.A.’s Olympic Games (Exclusive)
items.description: When news broke that Netflix had tapped Peter Rice to replace Bela Bajaria as chief content officer charged with overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more in all territories across the globe, it didn’t take long for insiders to wond
items.author: Chris Gardner
paragraphs: When news broke that Netflix had tapped Peter Rice to replace Bela Bajaria as chief content officer charged with overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more in all territories across the globe, it didn’t take long for insiders to wonder how he could lead such a massive portfolio while continuing on with a role as head of ceremonies for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

Question no more: Hollywood veteran Kathleen Kennedy has been tapped to replace Rice as head of ceremonies and content for LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games. The executive producer role will find the iconic producer helping shape the opening and closing ceremonies for back-to-back Games in four separate events that will be viewed by an audience of billions across the globe.

LA28 confirmed the appointment today and revealed that Rice won’t be bowing out completely, as he will stay on as executive producer. Kennedy is expected to dive straight in and work from early development toward production and execution alongside a team that includes executive producer and creative director Ben Winston and veteran Olympic and Paralympic ceremonies producer Scott Givens, who serves as executive producer of production. The production of the Olympic and Paralympic ceremonies is being supported by FulFive, a new entity composed of Fulwell Entertainment and FiveCurrents.

Kennedy is among the most accomplished and successful producers in Hollywood, with more than 100 credits on her résumé dating back to the early 1980s. She’s an Oscar winner whose films snagged 120 Academy Award nominations and 25 wins, and she’s steered special-effects-heavy blockbusters in the Star Wars universe to character studies and comedies, as well as dozens of projects alongside her husband, Frank Marshall, at their Kennedy/Marshall Company. She recently became something of a free agent after departing her post at Lucasfilm earlier in 2026 after 14 years at the helm leading one of the biggest American film franchises.
LA28 chairperson and president Casey Wasserman had plenty of praise for his new head of ceremonies.

“Kathleen is a legend. She is one of Hollywood’s all-time greats, with a rare gift for storytelling,” said Wasserman. “When the stars align to focus the world’s attention on Los Angeles for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, I can’t think of anyone better to conjure the magic of Hollywood than Kathleen.”

In response, she credited Wasserman for having a “bold vision” for what the Games “can mean for Los Angeles and the world.” And she’s thrilled to play a part in the Olympics, which have been a big part of her life for decades.

“The Olympics have been a touchstone in my life. My husband, Frank Marshall, and I have attended virtually every Games since Los Angeles in 1984, and sport remains one of the great unifying experiences we share,” Kennedy said. “Peter Rice has laid a terrific foundation, and I can’t wait to get to work with Ben Winston, our creative director, and the whole LA28 team. These Games are rooted in Los Angeles, but with events from Oklahoma City to LA28’s six incredible soccer/football cities, all of America gets to host the world’s finest athletes, and I’m honored to help celebrate every Olympian and Paralympian who comes to compete.”

It’s also worth noting that Kennedy produced a short documentary titled Olympic Glory that covered the 1998 Olympic Games in Nagano, which was directed by Kieth Merrill. And when she mentioned that the Games had been a touchstone for her in her life, they’ve also been very important to the household: Husband Frank Marshall was presented with an Olympic Shield in 2005 in honor of his contributions to the Olympic and Paralympic movements for serving on the executive committee of the U.S. Olympic Committee for more than a decade.

It’s not a surprise that Rice was replaced by another Hollywood heavyweight. Not long after he stepped into the role in 2025, Wasserman detailed the expectation of having the Olympics in this particular location. “When you think about what we expect of ourselves and what the world is going to expect of us, clearly we’re the creative capital of the world and Hollywood is a big piece of that, but we better knock people’s socks off,” Wasserman told The Hollywood Reporter at the time, adding that Rice was his No. 1 “overall” pick among candidates. “Peter is the one we started with, and we didn’t have to engage in meaningful conversations with anyone else.”

As for Kennedy, who is coming off the release of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu with the anticipated Star Wars: Starfighter starring Ryan Gosling on the horizon for 2027, she recently appeared onstage at Bloomberg’s annual Screentime event in Los Angeles. She offered some comments on her tenure at Lucasfilm that apply to her new LA28 role.

“I think that that’s the challenge that all franchises [face], certainly something that’s been around now for 50 years. You’ve got people where this means a lot to them,” she said. “But at the same time, the challenge is to try to create something new, something original.”

Kennedy’s work will be on display when L.A.’s Olympic Games kick off with an opening ceremony on July 14, 2028, and wrap up on July 30, 2028, hosted at venues including Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum and 2028 Stadium (aka SoFi Stadium). The Paralympic opening ceremony is set for Aug. 15, 2028, with the closing to take place at the Coliseum on Aug. 27, 2028.

Kennedy, whose long list of credits includes work with filmmakers like Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, Robert Zemeckis, J.J. Abrams, Rian Johnson and Shawn Levy, has produced E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, the Indiana Jones franchise, Back to the Future, The Color Purple, Arachnophobia, Hook, Jurassic Park, Congo, Twister, The Sixth Sense, A Map of the World, A.I. Artificial Intelligence, War Horse, Lincoln, Star Wars: Episode VII: The Force Awakens, Rogue One: A Star Wars Story, The Last Jedi, The Rise of Skywalker, The Mandalorian, Ahsoka, The Acolyte, Andor and many more.

In other LA28 news revealed Wednesday, there’s a new official slogan: “Stars Align.” It’s designed as “both a rallying cry and an invitation for athletes to compete on the world’s biggest stage,” per the organization, and it sits alongside the official Olympic motto of “Faster, Higher, Stronger — Together” and the Paralympic motto of “Change Starts With Sport.” Previous slogans of the games include “A New World” for Rio 2016, “United by Emotion” for Tokyo 2020, and “Games Wide Open” for Paris 2024.

“Los Angeles is the place where dreams take flight, and the Olympics show us what’s possible when the world unites. ‘Stars Align’ is a call to action, whether you’re an athlete at the peak of your skill, a volunteer welcoming the world to these Games, or a fan cheering passionately from the stands,” said Wasserman of the slogan, which also debuted in short promo that features the hit “Can’t Stop” by homegrown superstars Red Hot Chili Peppers.

items.author: Naked Beauty Podcast
paragraphs: All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.

Nina Parker knows pop culture. The Emmy-nominated television host, podcaster, fashion designer, and reality television host has led pop culture coverage for the past two decades. Nina has built her journalism career on E!, TMZ, VH1, CBS, and now Crooked Media’s Keep It. Her work has given us a front-row seat to the biggest moments and full access to Hollywood's biggest names. Whether she’s interviewing A-listers on the Met Gala’s red carpet or mediating disagreements on Love & Hip-Hop, Nina brings her expertise and signature style to every moment. But before she commanded screens across multiple television and podcast shows, she learned what it meant to be powerful in Sacramento, California. Nina shared how her parents taught her to prioritize her brilliance by encouraging her to pursue higher education and enrolling her in competitive public speaking.

Nina learned her strengths and how to use her voice against misogyny in the newsrooms where she eventually worked. She shared which beauty and pop culture icons sparked her interest in the entertainment industry, and why. Nina’s relationship with beauty wasn’t as straightforward as her building her personal power. Nina was open about how she used her power to push back against misogyny at TMZ and, inadvertently, impress her newsroom bosses. We also discussed the heightened standards of beauty and professionalism placed on Black women, which are only further complicated for plus-sized women. Nina walked us through the behind-the-scenes of building a strong glam team that always delivers and how the business has changed with the influx of influencers. Nina also shares her favorite thing about Gen Z, her well-researched skincare journey, and her decision to get Botox at 44.
