At the start of the project, though, Bowick had expressed her anxiety to Robertson. “I remember when we turned on the Zoom cameras for the first meeting, Mia and her husband David looked at each other, and they inhaled and exhaled, and said, ‘We’re nervous,’” Robertson remembers. “Then I inhaled and exhaled, and I said, ‘We’re nervous too.” That was the beginning of a really beautiful connection.”

But the series almost didn’t happen. After the release of Perry’s 2022 memoir, “Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing,” Robertson and her Maxine Productions team reached out to his publisher and several people within his inner circle about making a documentary. They never heard back. It wasn’t until Perry’s tragic passing in 2023, from the acute effects of ketamine, that she renewed her efforts and ultimately got traction among those close to him.

Bowick was not the first to sign on, but ultimately became the lynchpin for Robertson to feel it could be a substantial project. Also important were the voices of Perry’s closest friends, Roger Castillo and David Pressman. Robertson says Castillo signed on first, after many calls and conversations, and they flew him out to Los Angeles for the interview. Only after that did she get to plead her case to Pressman.

“After Roger’s interview, we all had dinner with David, and Roger sat there with David and said, ‘It went really well,’” Robertson says. “I understand that Matthew’s life was harvested for content by tabloids for many, many, many years, and his friends and his loved ones were fiercely protective of Matthew. That was their trained response, and a completely understandable one. They’d never met me before, so we had to, through time and through experience, come to a place where they believed that my intentions were correct by them.”

Robertson confirms the team did reach out to Perry’s “Friends” co-stars to participate, but “they chose not to,” she says. Still, they are present throughout the series, in archival behind-the-scenes footage and press interviews. But fans of the series will hear Bowick’s account of Perry’s being taken directly from rehab to set to film Monica (Courteney Cox) and Chandler’s wedding in Season 7; and a particularly poignant memory of his funeral, when the “Friends” cast arrived together holding hands, and stood together crying at his open casket to say goodbye.

The documentary also features Warren Littlefield, the former entertainment president of NBC, who talks about casting Perry as Chandler and navigating, from the network’s perspective, his repeated visits to rehab while the series was filming.

Much of Perry’s story has already been chronicled by the actor himself in his memoir. Robertson read it one sitting, and was floored by his willingness to share the depths of his addictions. “I remember the blue couch that I was sitting on, and the trees that I saw at the window as I read it,” she says. “I remember that he begins his book by saying, in essence, he should be dead. I couldn’t stop thinking about it when I was done.”

Despite how important it was to her origins with the project, she doesn’t include anything from the memoir in the documentary, except for that opening page, which reads, “Hi, my name is Matthew, although you may know me by another name. My friends call me Matty. And I should be dead.”

When asked why she didn’t at least try to use Perry’s darkly funny audiobook narration to give more space for his voice, she explains that the documentary is about the perspective the book can’t offer. “We wanted to craft a text that enriched what Matthew delivered through the memoir,” she says. “His memoir delivers something that, by definition, is first person, and doesn’t include the accounts of those who can describe what it was like to love someone who is completely brilliant and generous and loving, but also grappling with this enormous monster that he carried on his shoulder for most of his life. This is their account that’s missing from the memoir.”

Perry does speak for himself though, through a grainy-quality but insightful interview he did with actor and friend Kevin Pollack in 2009 for the YouTube series, “Kevin Pollack’s Chat Show.” The raw footage of the interview, which Pollack granted to Robertson, winds through the documentary, giving Perry the chance to narrate his own story up to that point, which was just five years after “Friends” ended.

The Pollack interview is different from the others that appear in the doc, including stops on the late-night circuit. It’s more casual, jovial and reflective of a life, a career and how the latter had taken over the former. Robertson says getting access to the raw, long-form footage was another moment when the potential for the documentary became clear.

“There’s something really distinct about the quality of that interview, in that it is between two friends,” she says. “It’s not a talk show host who’s been prepped for the interview, and everyone knows exactly what they’re going to cover. They knew each other well, and they loved to make each other laugh too. Making each other laugh was their sport, so it was really transformational for our project to be able to use it.”

But inevitably, the docuseries has to shift from looking back on Perry’s life to exploring his death, which is not uncharted territory for Robertson. In recent years, she has explored the intersection of celebrity, mental health and criminality with series like “Framing Britney Spears” for FX and “Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV” for Investigation Discovery. The former sparked a significant conversation about the nature of conservatorships and had a hand in freeing Spears from her own controversial one. The latter was an Emmy-nominated hit that let former Disney Channel and Nickelodeon child stars share their stories of abuse behind the scenes. While Robertson insists that “The One About Matthew Perry” is not an investigative piece, those two series certainly helped guide her focus here on excavating the perils of celebrity.

“Celebrities are reflections in so many ways of our ideals,” she says. “They’re the mirror that we hold up to ourselves. They show us who and what we want to be, and who and what we are allowed to be. I believe that popular culture is tantamount to the air that we breathe. It fills our lungs and bodies, and shapes our health.”

But for a subject like Perry, who so many people think they know intimately, there is still confusion surrounding his death, which ultimately led to the conviction of five people involved with supplying him the cumulatively lethal doses of ketamine.

“As much as his final days and hours were heavily covered, there’s still some misunderstanding and mystery around what happened,” Robertson says, acknowledging the early conflicting reports of how he died and that people were indicted for their part in it. “Truth and accuracy are always our North Stars, so on some basic level, the assignment here was to render his last hours and the subsequent investigation, indictments, and sentencing with accuracy.”
The series leans on law enforcement to help explain the details, simply because those closest to Matthew were excluded from the side of his life driven by addiction.

“Certainly some of the people that we interviewed knew Kenny, Matthew’s assistant, who was ultimately indicted, but they were not in the house the night that Matthew passed away,” Robertson says. “They were not in the midst of these transactions, which were ultimately understood to be criminal.”

“The One About Matthew Perry” is the mode in which Robertson wants to operate moving forward, promising more investigative portraits in the vein of “Quiet on Set” as well. She also continues to explore with Maxine Productions the branches of power and criminality, particularly with the new financial crimes-focused series, “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers” for Peacock and “The Real Wolf of Wall Street” for Paramount+.

Citing the smash-hit documentary “You Can See Everything,” Robertson says she’s excited “The One About Matthew Perry” is arriving at a time when people are actively seeking out boundary-breaking additions to the genre. While Perry’s story is told traditionally as it moves through his life, she hopes there is room to evolve the genre with renewed interest, thanks to subjects that are beloved, polarizing or a bit of both.

“We’re entering a really interesting era of documentary filmmaking, and documentary that is roughly biographical in nature — and part of that is projects like the Elizabeth Holmes film,” Robertson says. “We’re always in dialogue with the projects that have come before us, and I think we’re at a moment of evolution in the genre, where maybe we get to be more expansive now with our understanding of what that can be.”

items.title: Connor Storrie in Talks to Play Villain Opposite Ryan Gosling in Marvel’s ‘Ghost Rider’
items.description: “Heated Rivalry” star Connor Storrie is in talks to play the villain opposite Ryan Gosling in Marvel’s “Ghost Rider” movie.
items.author: Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: “Heated Rivalry” star Connor Storrie is in talks to play the villain opposite Ryan Gosling in Marvel’s “Ghost Rider” movie.

Shawn Levy is directing the film, from a script by “Star Wars: Starfighter” screenwriter Jonathan Tropper. “Ghost Rider” is slated to release on July 28, 2028. Levy and Gosling also produce the project alongside Marvel Studios chief Kevin Feige, Louis D’Esposito and Stephen Broussard. Executive producers are Richie Palmer and Jessie Henderson.

Landing a Marvel movie would be a big win for Storrie, who shot to pop culture prominence by starring as Russian hockey hunk Ilya Romanov on “Heated Rivalry.” As the story goes, the Texas native was waiting tables at Laurel Grill in Culver City before being offered that game-changing TV role; he’s since parlayed that attention into a Primetime Emmy-nominated turn as guest host of “Saturday Night Live,” and a supporting role opposite Billie Eilish in Sarah Polley’s “The Bell Jar” movie for Focus Features. The much-anticipated second season of “Heated Rivalry” — which centers on the rivals-to-lovers journey between Storrie’s Ilya and Hudson Williams’ Shane Hollander — is now filming and will premiere on HBO Max next spring. Storrie is represented by CAA, Linden Entertainment, Shelter PR, and Yorn Levine.

As for “Ghost Rider,” the project is coming together quickly, with plans to begin shooting in New York next year. Feige made the surprise announcement about the movie during Marvel’s Hall H presentation at San Diego Comic-Con this summer.
“As you know, this is a character I’ve wanted to play for a very long time,” Gosling told the excited crowd.

For years, Gosling had been Marvel fans’ top choice to star in a “Ghost Rider” movie after Nicolas Cage previously played motorcycle stuntman Johnny Blaze in a 2007 origin story movie and its 2011 sequel. In the comics and those movies, Johnny sells his soul to the devil Mephisto in order to cure his father’s cancer. When the rights reverted to Marvel Studios following those movies, Gabriel Luna played the Robby Reyes version of the character — a younger, Latino man — on the ABC TV show “Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.”

That said, Marvel has yet to confirm which version of Ghost Rider that Gosling will play, so it’s also unclear which villain Storrie would embody. Mephisto was recently introduced into the MCU, played by Sacha Baron Cohen, in the Disney+ series “Ironheart.”
THR broke news of Storrie’s potential involvement in the film. Marvel Studios does not comment on casting.

items.title: ‘Crystal Lake’ Hits 1.3 Billion Minutes Watched in 11 Days, Becoming Peacock’s No. 4 Scripted Debut Ever
items.description: According to Peacock, “Crystal Lake” is its fourth-most-watched scripted original series of all time.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: According to Peacock, “Crystal Lake” is its fourth-most-watched scripted original series of all time.

The “Friday the 13th” prequel series was watched for 1.3 billion minutes in its first 11 days of streaming. Divided by the series’ 398-minute runtime, that comes out to a total of 3.3 million estimated views. But in terms of overall minutes watched on Peacock, it ranks behind only “The Best Man: The Final Chapters” (2022), “All Her Fault” (2025) and “The Five Star Weekend” Season 1 (2026).
Per Nielsen, “Crystal Lake” ranked as the third-most-watched streaming original series and the third-most-streamed first-season series across all of television during the week of Oct. 19.
The series also boasted strong social engagement, garnering 1.8 billion impressions in one day and more than 7.6 million video views in 11 days, as measured by Sprout Social.

“Crystal Lake” was created by Brad Caleb Kane, who also serves as showrunner. According to the official logline, the series follows “single mother Pam Voorhees (Linda Cardellini) who has been unable to shake her grief after her young, sickly son Jason (Callum Vinson) tragically drowned in the town lake almost a year before. When two strangers arrive at Pam’s door digging into her past, a disturbing chain of events is set into motion, leaving the townspeople of Crystal Lake wondering: Just who is Pam Voorhees?” The cast also includes William Catlett, Devin Kessler, Cameron Scoggins, Gwendolyn Sundstrom, Nick Cordileone, Joy Suprano, Danielle Kotch and Phoenix Parnevik.

Executive producers of “Crystal Lake” include Kane, Marc Toberoff, Victor Miller, Robert M. Barsamian, Robert P. Barsamian, Stuart Manashil, Tyson Bidner, Michael Lennox and Roy Lee. Michael Lennox, Celine Held, Logan George and Quyen Tran serve as directors. A24 is the studio.

items.title: Skydance Is Offering Employees Voluntary Buyouts Ahead of Layoffs, Adopts 5-Days-per-Week In-Office Policy
items.description: Skydance, as it embarks on the work to integrate the businesses of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is offering certain employees a voluntary buyout in a “one-time offer.”
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Skydance, as it embarks on the work to integrate the businesses of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is offering certain employees a voluntary buyout in a “one-time offer.”
The new program was outlined by chairman and CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz in a memo to staffers Monday.

“As we bring our teams together, we recognize that not everyone will see their future here, and we respect that. To give eligible employees the option to move on in a way that works for them, we are introducing a Voluntary Buyout (VBO) Program,” the execs wrote. “Those who qualify will receive an individual communication with their personalized details and terms, and a window to decide whether to accept this one-time offer.”

They added, “Please know we don’t take any of this lightly. We are clear about what we’re building: a company that tells the stories people around the world love, embraces new ways to connect with audiences, and leads the next era of media and entertainment. We have the talent, the creative firepower and the ambition to do it, and we will get there together.”

Across Skydance, there are different eligibility criteria and deadlines by which employees must confirm they’re taking a buyout (for example, if the jobs are union or non-union or if a staffer is on contract or an at-will employee), according to sources familiar with the situation. In general, the buyout opt-in deadlines fall around the second week in November.

Paramount’s massive $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery closed on Oct. 6. In their “Day One” memo to employees that day, Ellison and Kreiz (who was the CEO of Mattel before joining the new Skydance earlier this month) acknowledged that layoffs will be part of the process. “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce,” the execs wrote in that memo. “We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully.”

In the Oct. 26 memo, Ellison and Kreiz also said the new Skydance is moving to a mandatory five-days-per-week in-office policy across the company. “We believe in-person collaboration is vital to our culture and to the success of our business. Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems,” the execs said. “We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We’ve seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them.”

Skydance execs have said they are shooting to achieve more than $6 billion in cost savings on an annualized basis within three years, and part of that will come from layoffs. The company has not revealed at this point the extent of the job cuts it expects. According to a report issued by Los Angeles County in August, the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger could result in the loss of some 4,500 film and TV jobs over three years in L.A. alone.
Read the full memo sent by Skydance’s top brass Monday, a copy of which was obtained by Variety:

At Skydance, our goal is to build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology. We are creative-first, audience focused, tech-forward and globally scaled. And in a world of endless choice and fierce competition for attention, we don’t just want to succeed. We want to win.

To do that, we must be a strong, connected and agile company. Among our business and creative priorities, none matters more than building a strong culture, because it’s the foundation of everything we want to achieve. Winning requires us to work as one team: one company, fully aligned. That means communicating openly and collaborating efficiently across every part of the organization.

We believe in-person collaboration is vital to our culture and to the success of our business. Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems. Being together isn’t just about showing up. It’s about inspiring one another, learning and coaching, forming friendships and having the casual conversations that spark something great.

With that in mind, we will adopt a five-day in-office policy across all of Skydance. We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We’ve seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them.

While many of you are already in the office five days a week, we understand this may be a significant change to the daily routines of others. To give you time to plan and adjust, we will take a phased approach by location. You will receive ample notice before changes take effect, and we will work closely with managers to support you through the transition.

As we bring our teams together, we recognize that not everyone will see their future here, and we respect that. To give eligible employees the option to move on in a way that works for them, we are introducing a Voluntary Buyout (VBO) Program. Those who qualify will receive an individual communication with their personalized details and terms, and a window to decide whether to accept this one-time offer.

We recognize this is a significant decision, and we want you to feel informed and supported. If this applies to you, please review your materials carefully and reach out to your leadership or HR representative with any questions. FAQs and other resources are available on the Skydance Integration Hub, and HR support is also available through My Paramount (legacy Paramount employees) or Ask Employee Connection on WBD One (legacy Warner Bros. employees).

Please know we don’t take any of this lightly. We are clear about what we’re building: a company that tells the stories people around the world love, embraces new ways to connect with audiences, and leads the next era of media and entertainment. We have the talent, the creative firepower and the ambition to do it, and we will get there together.
Thank you for your commitment, and for the creativity and passion you bring to your work every day.

items.title: Academy CEO Bill Kramer Makes the Case for a More Global Oscars at Tokyo Film Festival
items.description: The U.S. may be growing ever more isolationist under the “America First” rubric of President Donald Trump, but the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences remains steadfastly global in its outlook and ambitions.
items.author: Patrick Brzeski
paragraphs: The U.S. may be growing ever more isolationist under the “America First” rubric of President Donald Trump, but the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences remains steadfastly global in its outlook and ambitions.

That was the thrust of Academy CEO Bill Kramer’s comments at the Tokyo International Film Festival on Wednesday, where he spoke at length about his organization’s ongoing efforts to bring more international filmmakers and film lovers into the Oscars fold.

“The Academy is becoming more and more global across programs, and as part of that, you’re seeing a great increase in the number of academy members who live outside of the United States,” Kramer said. He noted the oft-cited fact that a decade ago just 5 percent of Academy members were based outside the U.S., compared with 25 percent today. And in a hat tip to the local crowd, Kramer said the Academy has about 70 Japanese members, but that he expects that number to climb.
“This is all part of our drive to create a more diverse and inclusive academy,” he said.
Kramer also underscored that Oscars nominations have already begun to reflect the increasingly cosmopolitan tastes of the member base.

“At the last Oscars, every category had international representation. It’s not just found in the international feature film category — this trend includes our best picture category,” he explained. “Of course, everybody remembers the moment when Parasite won best picture. That was sort of a pivot, or a shift, I think, in our thinking about what was possible with global cinema at the Oscars, and that continues.”

Kramer asserted that the Academy’s somewhat controversial deal with YouTube was inspired by this same desire to cultivate deeper ties with filmmakers and film lovers across the globe. The agreement gives YouTube exclusive global rights to the Oscars from 2029 through 2033, making the ceremony available live and free worldwide after ABC’s final telecast in 2028.

“In two years, the Oscars will be available on YouTube for free to 2.5 billion people around the world in over 30 languages,” he explained. “So, for the first time, everyone around the world will have access to the show at the same time and in the same format — and that is a huge, intentional move by the Academy to reach a bigger global audience.”

As part of its multifaceted international push, the Academy has brought a substantial leadership delegation to the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival. Kramer’s remarks came Wednesday during a panel discussion in a sleek high-rise in Tokyo’s Hibiya district. The Oscars chief was joined by Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and Meredith Shea, the organization’s chief membership, impact and industry officer. Tokyo film festival director Takeo Hisamatsu moderated the conversation.

The Academy leaders also highlighted the new festival-winner pathway into the race for the best international feature film Oscar. Beginning with the 99th Academy Awards, eligible non-English-language films can be submitted for consideration by winning a designated major festival prize, without having to secure their country’s official selection. The route supplements the longstanding system under which approved national and regional committees each select a single entry on behalf of a country. The new program’s six qualifying festivals and their designated awards are Cannes, for its Palme d’Or; Venice, for the Golden Lion; Berlin, for the Golden Bear; Busan, for the Busan Award for best film; Sundance, for the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize; and Toronto, for the Platform Award.

During the Q&A session after the panel, Kramer was quizzed twice by audience members on whether the Tokyo International Film Festival will soon be added to the list of qualifying festivals under the new program.

The inclusion of regional rival Busan in the program and Tokyo’s omission have been received as hard news by many involved in the Japanese festival. But Kramer hinted that Tokyo might not have to wait long.
“We’re looking to expand the universe of film festivals that will help a film qualify for the international feature film category,” he said, adding: “Stay tuned, we’re just beginning.”

items.title: Russell Brand Trial: Star Takes the Stand and Tells Court No One Will Touch Him “With a Bargepole”
items.description: Russell Brand took the stand for the first time in his ongoing rape and sexual assault trial on Wednesday and revealed that no one else has agreed to testify on his behalf.
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: Russell Brand took the stand for the first time in his ongoing rape and sexual assault trial on Wednesday and revealed that no one else has agreed to testify on his behalf.
At London’s Southwark Crown Court, the prosecution has completed presenting its case and Brand’s defense team, led by Ian Winter, are set to detail their arguments for the jury.

The prosecution ran the court through all of the charges against the presenter and comedian (also star of St. Trinian’s and Forgetting Sarah Marshall). He is accused of three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault, with six women alleging offenses dating from 1999 to 2009. The final charge was reduced from indecent assault to attempted indecent assault by the judge, Justice Bennathan, on Tuesday afternoon.

Among the claims is a woman who says Brand raped her in a Bournemouth hotel room in 1999 following one of his comedy gigs. Another says he grabbed her breasts and pushed her into a toilet in a bar in Soho, where he orally raped her, in 2004. A separate woman alleges Brand anally raped her at his home in Hampstead in 2009, after consensual vaginal sex. Brand vehemently denies any criminal wrongdoing.

According to Sky News coverage, there was a “significant shift” in the courtroom on Wednesday as Brand took the stand as the defence’s first witness. After taking his oath, his barrister began probing Brand on the “sea of change” brought about in his life after marrying U.S. pop superstar Katy Perry in 2010. “It did,” replied the defendant. “Staggering fame.”

Brand was asked about the documentary that prompted the police to first investigate him in 2023. Made by Channel 4’s Dispatches and followed by allegations in The Sunday Times, Brand was accused of rape and assault. “It was devastating,” he told his barrister, who then asked: “Were you able to persuade a single person with relevant evidence to come to give evidence on your behalf?”

Brand replied: “I have not.” When Winter asked if anyone “would touch him with a bargepole,” Brand said, “No.” He added: “My entire life has been consumed by these allegations. I have devoted myself to these matters.”

Winter took Brand through various statements from the complainants, some of whom he remembers meeting and others whom he says he has no recollection of. Winter asked Brand, “Is that something that you normally do? Speak during sex?” His client replied, “Yes… I believe I would have been saying: ‘Am I doing this right, do you like this, is this OK?”
Brand said when asked for his opinion on consent: “Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary, and in many ways more important than sex itself.”

The third complainant says Brand groped her breasts in a bar before pulling her to the toilets and forcing her to perform oral sex on him. He does remember meeting her, he told the court. “Is there any question you just grabbed her breasts?” Winter said to Brand. “Absolutely not,” he replied, saying the act does not turn him on because it’s “disgusting behavior.”

He remembers speaking to the complainant for less than a minute before going to the lavatory to “fool around.” Winter said: “As far as you’re aware, is there any question that she did not consent to going into the cubicle with you?” Brand told him: “There’s absolutely no question.”

items.title: How ‘NAZA’ and Avi Nesher’s ‘Our Loves’ May Have Swayed Israel’s Electorate Against Netanyahu
items.description: A pair of films may have played a critical role in moving voters to vote for the Change bloc over the bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Israeli elections held Tuesday.
items.author: Steven Zeitchik
paragraphs: A pair of films may have played a critical role in moving voters to vote for the Change bloc over the bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Israeli elections held Tuesday.
The first has become a box-office hit. The second didn’t play in the country at all.

As election results come in, the anti-Netanyahu “Change” bloc led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot’s center-right Yashar (Straight) party is notably behind the far-right government of Netanyahu, the leader of Likud and the longtime prime minister in power during and after the October 7 attacks. Netanyahu’s bloc has a 54-47 Knesset-seat advantage with more than 70% of the vote in. But he has no clear path to reach the 61-seat  majority threshold via a coalition government since five of the six parties outside his bloc are highly unlikely to join him (and the sixth is a toss-up). Gridlock and a new election in the coming months seem very possible.

The first of the two films that might have brought us here is Avi Nesher’s Our Loves. An action-tinged sentimental story of Israelis fighting to survive during the October 7 Hamas attacks, the movie does not wear politics on its sleeve.

But in showing an absent army and focusing on security failures, the film is, for all its undercurrents of unity and patriotism, at least implicitly critical of the Netanyahu government in charge at the time. Moreover, it’s a hit. Released purposefully two weeks before the election, the drama has garnered 150,000 admissions in Israel — a high tally for a non-Hollywood movie in the small country, and a number that could have given Netanyahu a few more key seats.

Nesher has been outspoken that he does not support the Netanyahu government and said he believes that its members wouldn’t like the film. “I do not share the government’s point of view at all. I’ll be one of those people who are not voting for this government,” he told The Hollywood Reporter at TIFF, and he has continued comments to that effect in the Israeli press.

Nesher’s words carry weight, not only because he is a beloved filmmaker but because he has made movies about finding one’s way out of previous eras of crisis (his Rage and Glory and Image of Victory are both set around the nation’s founding conflict in 1948) and he is seen as a form of artistic light in the darkness.

That Eisenkot, 66, lost his son fighting in Gaza also gives the movie a kind of heft on his behalf; it’s easy to watch the film and think of the candidate and what he went through. (Less so Netanyahu, whose own son has until recently been in Miami.) There’s even a tough military character in the film not much younger than Eisenkot.

The second cinematic wrench is NAZA, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary hit involving two dozen IDF whistleblowers revealing how Netanyahu’s government has conducted the war in Gaza. Though not released in Israel, word of it has been all over the Israeli press in recent weeks.

The effect is tricky — even many Netanyahu critics have criticized the movie for not telling the whole story; an anti-IDF film wouldn’t necessarily sit well with at least some Eisenkot supporters either. But the Netanyahu government tried to capitalize on this fact by making noise that they would attempt to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship (there is no known legal basis for them to do this).

While that move played to Netanyahu’s base, it didn’t seem to move the needle with the great swath of voters that Likud needed to win over — and in fact may have backfired, making it seem like the government was not open to any criticism, something Change voters absolutely feel should be in play.

Gauging the effect of a single doc on a complicated real world situation isn’t easy, of course. But mainstreaming the conversation about the war — newspapers have been filled with op-eds in the media-happy country since its Venice premiere last month — may have dinged the man who’s led it. (It’s worth noting that for all of Netanyahu’s political durability over the past three decades, his Likud Party these days is actually not a majority force on its own. It received fewer than 25% of the votes Tuesday and is reliant on a coalition-union with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties to approach a majority.)

Meanwhile, a film fixture ended up potentially moving the film needle herself Tuesday. Wonder Woman star Gal Gadot — the closest the country has currently to a national icon — released a video Tuesday of herself at the polls saying she was voting for Change. She flew in from Los Angeles to vote and in her Instagram post urged all Israelis to the same (some 80% did) before noting her anti-Netanyahu preference.

She then even appeared in a sketch on Eretz Nehederet (the Israeli SNL) that aired election night while the polls were still open, getting into an Uber and talking about living in Los Angeles as an Israeli.
She offered perhaps one of the greater unspoken truths about the region when the driver asked her if it was hard to be an Israeli abroad.
“I’m always explaining to people,” she said, alluding to the media ecosystem. “What you see there you don’t see here. And what you see here you don’t see there.”

items.title: In HBO’s 'War,' the Divorcees Go to Savile Row
items.description: In HBO’s punchy new legal drama War, billionaire tech scion Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) is nearly always dressed as though he’s on his way to a board meeting. Or at least that’s how costume designer Matt Price envisioned Henderson’s daily uniform. Set amid
items.author: Zack Hauptman
paragraphs: In HBO’s punchy new legal drama War, billionaire tech scion Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) is nearly always dressed as though he’s on his way to a board meeting. Or at least that’s how costume designer Matt Price envisioned Henderson’s daily uniform. Set amidst a thrilling and very British divorce between West’s Henderson and Sienna Miller’s Carla Duval, an A-list movie star who’s in the dark about what her husband’s net worth truly amounts to, the show and its costuming also offers a deeper look into the inner workings of the British establishment.

War is about divorce, first and foremost, but it’s also about class, something Price played with in crafting a variety of corporate costumes for the central cast. While Henderson occasionally wears a tie, his uniform style of dressing was critical for Price: “I don’t think you can necessarily cheat luxury on camera,” Price says. They agreed early on that he wouldn’t rely on neckties because “it didn’t feel like with his wealth and his position that he ever really needed to go there, to tighten up” in that way.

Henderson’s classic suits weren’t initially what the costumer had envisioned for West’s character. “We actually started with 1990s vintage Armani with him,” Price says. The simpler look was what stuck, albeit accented with rare orange detailing or a lilac shirt. “We wanted him to be formal yet kind of relaxed at the same time.”

It was also important to highlight the legacy of Savile Row, which is, in the world of the show, mere minutes away from the fictional law firms of Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts, where West and Duval seek out representation ahead of what inevitably turns into an incredibly messy divorce. “I’ve always been interested in the independence of Savile Row,” Price says. “It’s such a sort of short street and yet it holds so much heritage. It just felt kind of like a natural fit to be able to explore the Ede & Ravenscroft and the Thom Sweeneys and many others down there.”

When Price joined the show, the law firms’ spaces had already been designed, so it became his job to craft the outfits that would make sense inside those places. “We had the more traditional heritage space with Cathcarts: wood-clad, more compartmentalized,” he says. For certain characters, that meant classic three-piece Savile Row suits, nip ties, and a trilby hat. At Taylor & Byrne, the outfits couldn’t just be classic—they had to be elevated, modern.

For Price, the character of overconfident Johnny Warren proved an interesting challenge: as both a double agent and a striving outsider (he had a stint as a restaurant server between law jobs), he needed to fit in with both law firms and yet look slightly out of place at the same time. He had the idea that Warren would have “leftover [clothing] from his time in New York,” such as a classic American button-down, but with details that underlines his position outside the upper echelon of his clients—say, a mismatched striped shirt and a printed tie. “There’s little combinations that don’t necessarily feel exactly correct,” he says.“Maybe he’s got two or three suits that he can afford to buy, so his look doesn’t change that much.”

Halfway through the season, as Johnny cozies up to Sienna Miller’s Carla, she helps the young lawyer obtain a new black-tie ensemble, purchased from the same place where Morgan Henderson shops. Price wanted to ensure the look was as classic as possible, with a boxier fit than his everyday look at work. “It was kind of like, where would Morgan potentially go on Savile Row for something really classic for a black-tie event?” he says. They went with Ede & Ravenscroft.

Price, when he isn’t costuming within the parameters of Savile Row and British tailoring on War, is captivated by newer conventions of formal dressing. Outside of his day job, he’s, “really interested in softer tailoring. I love Kartik Research, for example, and [how the brand is] taking inspiration from different cultures and bringing it into suiting. I think suiting’s really changing drastically at the moment.” He also tells me the readers of this magazine shouldn’t necessarily emulate Henderon’s ultra-staid look when they’re seeking out their next suit. “[Suiting] is all to do with proportions,” he says. “Don’t be afraid to have some fun with tailoring.”

items.title: Cyndi Lauper on Auctioning Off Her Iconic Fashion Archive: "It's Only Stuff"
items.description: Cyndi Lauper is not a perfectionist. “I would call myself someone who either does it right or doesn’t do it,” she says as she adjusts one of the disco balls hanging from a mannequin in the Midtown Manhattan lobby of the Bonhams auction house. The room currentl
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: Cyndi Lauper is not a perfectionist. “I would call myself someone who either does it right or doesn’t do it,” she says as she adjusts one of the disco balls hanging from a mannequin in the Midtown Manhattan lobby of the Bonhams auction house. The room currently holds an array of Lauper’s iconic looks as part of the upcoming sale, Cyndi Lauper: Suitcase of Memories. Some are housed on disco ball-toting mannequins, others lined up in racks like you’re walking into Screaming Mimi’s, the famed NYC boutique where Lauper worked in the early ’80s. “We need way more disco balls,” Lauper looks around the room and exclaims, but not in a perfectionist’s tone.

The 73-year-old singer has decided now is the time to auction off her goods: over four decades worth of fashion, accessories, entertainment memorabilia, and personal mementos that trace the life and career of the “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” singer. “I hope this will inspire the older dames and people like me to remember how much fun it was to have that individual creativity,” she explains of the timing, which also happens to correspond with the 40th anniversary of her sophomore album, True Colors. “It’s also to inspire the young to look and go, ‘Yeah, I could do that.’”

The hero item of the sale is undoubtedly the hoop skirt covered in newspaper strips and Paper Magazine pages. The piece, worn with a blue and white tie-front blouse, was styled by Screaming Mimi’s founder Laura Wills and worn throughout the True Colors promotional cycle, including during an Annie Leibovitz photoshoot. “Laura just said, ‘Come on, we're going to do a paper skirt,’” Lauper recalled during a walkthrough of the space. “And we did not have a dress form. I was the dress form...We stapled it. I was good. A lot of the stuff that we did together, it was invention.”

There are many full designer looks on offer in the auction, particularly from the ’90s when Lauper had a more substantial budget and relationships with brands like Vivienne Westwood and Alexander McQueen. But a good portion of the ensembles are—like the paper skirt—comprised of vintage pieces and DIY projects. There is the pair of pajamas originally owned by her grandmother, accessorized with a homemade tulle bow, or the numerous looks that layer crinoline petticoats underneath voluminous skirts with corsets, vests, and button-downs on top. They’re draped in chains and jewels, accessorized with pins and hats that must sit just so. In fact, Lauper—while not a perfectionist—is very specific about the mannequins’ styling. While chatting, she frequently interrupts the flow of conversation to voice her displeasure at the displays.

“We didn’t wear it like that,” she says of a top and pants that should have been rolled up. “That’s backwards,” she comments on a skirt. A pair of suspenders spied in the auction’s catalog sends her into a tizzy. “Where are those suspenders?” she asks, though the answer is in front of her. “I’ve been looking for them.”

But now, they are out of her hands, on sale as part of the over 200 lots that make up the auction, which kicks off on October 22. At some point, Lauper will have to release control. Those who purchase her pieces are free to wear them however they wish, with sleeves rolled up or not. Below, the singer discusses her decision to put her entire archive up for sale, the one dress she might miss the most, and the contemporary singer who she feels is following in her chain-adorned, platform-booted footsteps.
Why did you feel like it was the right time to put all your clothes on display and to sell them?

I’m doing it now because we’ve all been corporatized so much that the individuality of creativity is getting squashed out. As big corporations buy up smaller companies, the creativity of those smaller companies eventually disappears. The color is drained and becomes beige. And there's nothing wrong with beige. The color of my skin is beige, but I think color is important. I think vibrancy and the individuality of creativity are very important.

Right now, we’re under this kind of weird dictatorship where they want to take away your vote and they want you to walk like sheep. And everything's for sale. That was never what this country was about. It'll go down in history as one of the more interesting times of this country if we can survive.
What was it like going through your archives to plan the sale?

It was pretty daunting, but I had to get rid of things. We sold our house and I’m glad because it was in Connecticut and that wasn’t great for us. When I first went there, I was so excited because of Pepperidge Farm, but it’s not like that. You think it’s going to be like that, but it’s not.
Do any specific stories come to mind as you look at these pieces?
This Pucci bathing suit [from a True Colors tour poster]. We shot that in Central Park. I remember standing in that shell, going “Ew, I don’t know what’s in this pond.”
Is there anything that was hard for you to give away?

Well, I wasn't sure about giving away the awards, but the truth is that I have a family and I have a kid with my husband and when you have all your awards up, it's a little oppressive for other people. You don't want that. And that's what happened. It was a mistake to have them up, so we took them all down.
But clothing-wise, you are OK with selling everything?

Oh, hun. I wanted to share, and I was excited to share. This dress [points to a floral strapless mini dress in the auction catalogue] I wore in Florida doing a movie, [Off and Running], as the mermaid with my husband, [David Thornton]. All these girls were chasing after him. After a while, I was looking at him and he was really cute. And I was like, "Why can't I chase after him? Maybe I don't have to. Where's that dress? Let me put on a Cindy Lauper dress.”
It’s a big deal to get rid of the dress you were wearing when you first started chatting with your future husband.
Why must I let it rot somewhere? I’d rather someone else wear it. It’s only stuff. What am I going to do? Hold onto it forever?
Do you look at any of this and think, “Oh my god, I can’t believe I wore that”?
No. Never. Because everything had a reason. I love Joan Rivers, but she didn't always understand my choices. But I didn't understand a lot of what she wore.
You mentioned wanting to inspire the next generation with this auction. Is there anyone coming up at the moment who you’re especially impressed with?

I think Chappell Roan is really great. I'm so proud of her for being able to be who she is and also to write songs about an alternative person in a natural way. I also think she has a wonderful voice. But listen, I also think Selena Gomez is an incredible young performer. She's a multimedia artist.

items.title: The Anthropic S-1 Filing Is Also an AI Doomsday Primer
items.description: Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might exp
items.author: Brian Barrett
paragraphs: Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.

While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.

“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)
Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.

The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.

Or, as the Anthropic filing puts it: “Risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models.”

The prospectus repeatedly makes the point that RSI could lead to AI models that develop faster than the company’s safeguards, and that the company may not even realize it has lost that race until it’s too late. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It also gets specific about what might happen after that. “As AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the prospectus says, “there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” This is Skynet territory.

Speaking of robots, Anthropic flags concerns about those as well. “When our models direct physical equipment,” the filing says, “errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible.”

You might think, given the apparently existential stakes, that serious consideration would be given to whether RSI should be pursued at all, much less embraced. In an industry as competitive as frontier AI, though, it’s become fait accompli. Here’s how Anthropic describes that same process elsewhere in the prospectus, this time in a section about the startup’s “core advantages:”
“We refer to this recursive dynamic as ‘closing the loop,’” the prospectus says, “and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.”

Failure to “close the loop,” Anthropic later says, could result in “falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities.” In other words, the same systems that are causing all that existential concerns are the ones Anthropic sees as critical to its success.

Every AI company is dealing with this same tension. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral for loudly resigning, he put curbing RSI at the top of his wish list for the industry. Employees at Google DeepMind and elsewhere have had similar revelations. There are multiple bills in Congress, including one cosponsored by Bernie Sanders, that propose a ban on RSI. At the same time, these are for-profit companies, and there are trillions of dollars at stake.
It’s a tricky dynamic to navigate. Recursive self-improvement could become a runaway train that destroys humanity. But until then, just look at how fast it can go.

items.title: Sauerkraut at Every Meal? These Fermentation Fanatics Tried That Long Before MAHA
items.description: Waking early, I put a small jar of my sauerkraut into my messenger bag, hop on my bicycle, ride to Seattle's King Street Station, and board a train heading to the Portland Fermentation Festival, the yearly gathering affectionately nicknamed “Stinkfest.”
items.author: Joe Ray
paragraphs: Waking early, I put a small jar of my sauerkraut into my messenger bag, hop on my bicycle, ride to Seattle's King Street Station, and board a train heading to the Portland Fermentation Festival, the yearly gathering affectionately nicknamed “Stinkfest.”

Usually the sheer existence of a festival like this is enough to get people revved up to come together and talk about their favorite ferments, but in an interesting twist, fermented foods are enjoying a popularity boost from a different crowd. The MAHA movement, and particularly the Donald Trump cabinet, are big into fermented food, eating meat, usually steak, with fermented sides like kimchi or sauerkraut at every meal.

I've come to Portland, Oregon, wondering if there was going to be any overlap in the Venn diagram between festival attendees and the MAHA steak-and-ferment crowd. I mentioned this to my cousin-in-law Erick, who's been part of the Portland food scene for years, and he laughed out loud.
“It'll be more like a Venn dumbbell,” he said, making a pair of thumb-and-forefinger circles and tracing a line in the air between them. “No overlap, but food will be the bridge.”
Still, I was curious. I’d check.

The festival is almost exactly what the fermentation-friendly might hope to find. Right inside the main door next to the check-in desk is a bacterial petting zoo—a common thing at this sort of event—and a table where attendees can drop off their own ferments to share. Further on, lining every wall of the main room, are exhibitors who have paid a grand total of 25 bucks for a table, handing out free samples of fermented foods.

The space quickly fills up–several hundred people flow through over the course of the evening–and it appears that there's both a line in front of each exhibitor and perhaps a more organic continuous line with people flowing clockwise from one exhibitor to the next. People are notably excited and happy. There's a kid walking around with a tray of handmade pickle pins he's giving people to wear and there's a collective gasp when 20 or 30 minutes in, Dillon T. Pickle, the mascot of the Portland Pickles West Coast League baseball team, walks into the room. At one point, a big baby crawls across most of the main floor, unhindered and happy.

In the middle of it all is festival co-organizer, journalist, and cookbook author Liz Crain. She explains that the Fest, now in its 14th installment, was started in 2009 by friends who love to ferment. There were members of a little company called Pickleopolis and a club called The Kraut Collective, and, with some help from author and fermentation rockstar Sandor Katz, they launched a Portland tradition.
When I ask how the festival has evolved since its first year, she gets a little philosophical.

“Cheap. Portland. Weird. People get excited,” she says in a tone where several punctuation options would be in the spirit of the festival. “People lined up on the sidewalk all the way around the building for the first one. I poured hard cider that I made from a tree in my backyard.”

“There's nothing for sale, and that gives it a potluck-y party style. Most big festivals have consumers and purveyors, but without those distinctions here, it makes conversations a bit deeper, a bit more personal,” she says. “There's no gatekeeping, no secret recipes. It's always been wacky and fun.”
She isn't sure how much MAHA crossover I'll encounter, but she has an openness to it.

“RFK is certainly infatuated with sauerkraut and steak. There's some good to be found in the overall MAHA tenets, but so much of it has been muddied by the anti-vax stance and ludicrous conspiracy theories,” she says, though she believes it's important to “look closely and critically at pesticides and favor less-processed foods.”

“But a diet that's based solely on meat, particularly beef, animal fats, and sauerkraut … well that's not a very diverse diet,” she says. “Let's just say I wouldn't want to sit next to that person on a plane or be stuck in an elevator with them.”
I pick up on these ideas with Chris Curtin, a fermentation microbiology researcher at Oregon State University.

“Historically, everything has shown that narrowing the scope of your diet misses some things. They don't turn out to be the best in the long run,” he says. An Australian living in the US for the last decade, he can clearly see the way trends are moving and notes that registered dietitians have consistently put fermented foods at the top of their superfood lists for the past decade.

Curtin describes his work as caring about what happens when we mess around with microbes to see what happens to the raw material. As he puts it, "I'm interested in tinkering if it involves microbe wrangling." He also gets the festival's popularity among those who ferment.
“Fermenting is such a readily accessible scientific experiment that you can do in your kitchen. People go, find foods they like and want to make in their own kitchens. It's accessible and tactile.”

This plays out at the festival as I begin to sample the merchandise. The first thing I taste is an “orange whey Julius” that includes whey and OJ and is pleasingly reminiscent of the Orange Julius I'd get as a treat as a kid at the Mall of New Hampshire.

Next to that is Nat West's booth with Peruvian corn beer called chicha. West has run a cider company, dabbled in politics, driven a TriMet city bus in Portland, and now runs the Vancouver, Washington, farmers’ market. In a chicha, the fermentation starts by the brewer chewing ground field corn. At the festival, attendees are drinking what West has chewed. As people in line joke about drinking this guy's spit, or at least the byproducts of it, West interjects, “nobody's died yet!”

“The ptyalin enzymes in the saliva kickstart the starch-to-sugar process,” he explains as I take a sip and gaze longingly at the draft beer in the hands of someone who's wandered into the show from the Hotlips pizza next door.
Further along, Portland's Jorinji Miso has a double booth with samples of miso soup with bonito flakes along with koji (rice fermented with Aspergillus oryzae spores) and amazake, a koji-based drink.

The couple who run Maypop Wine Co. have their hands full at the Fest. The company’s cofounder Vince Kelsea explains that they make “anything but pinot” in the Willamette Valley—a lush north-south valley in Oregon renowned for its pinot noir. Making unfiltered, low-intervention wines like Maypop in a region famous for its pinot sounds like they're making things hard for themselves, but the attendees maintain a several-deep line at the booth all night long.

In one corner is Kiyomi Hasagewa, a third-generation Japanese bean purveyor. She’s sharing tastes of a 15-year-old miso she dehydrated and ground so she could bring it from Hokkaido to the festival. She sprinkles it over the rice and tops it with a wedge of sun-dried daikon which her elderly mother fermented in a mashed pumpkin paste. It is easily the most interesting bite in the room.

Back in the entry hall are my personal favorites, the ferments that attendees have brought to share. Liz Crain has brought along plum and dandelion wines, pickle brine, a blackberry-blueberry-lemon water kefir, and a monster jar of sour dills. I note with pride that the jar of sauerkraut I brought is next to Liz’s pickles, near-empty. Nearby is another giant jar of “fermented carrot coins, cherry bomb, garlic, ginger, horseradish,” which I anticipate as a pleasant assault on my senses, but it's really just pleasant. A garlic blast for sure, but one with all of the harsh edges smoothed by time and beneficial bacteria into something lovely.
Also at the community table are Portland occupational therapist Eva Ortega and her fermentation buddy Letti Kittel who drove down from Seattle.
“I've only made unsuccessful ferments so far,” says Ortega, undeterred. “I'm here to learn.”

Kittel says she's been nerding out on fermenting for about a year and has brought a kombucha starter with its bacteria-and-yeast scoby for others to bring home and try. And while both of them have no comment about the MAHA connection, Ortega puts some of Kittel's starter in a little jar and drops it into her purse.

I'm expecting another round of “no comment” when the MAHA diet comes up with three other fermenting friends, Megan Andricos, Josh Monifi, and Desiré Demarest, but Andricos, aka DJ Sappho, followed a similar diet 20 years ago in what they call their “fermented-pickled food and protein phase,” which consisted of “mostly kimchi and meat.”
They're off that diet now, but they liked being on it. “Kimchi evens out my gut biome. I felt better. Not superhuman, but better.”
Also on the community table is something called “Higgins Kraut,” made with Napa cabbage, carrots, garlic, and ginger, which, with a lovely melding of flavors, won my personal Best-in-Show award.

Turns out it's made by one of the show’s other founders, George Winborn, who was involved for the first 10 years. He'd been farming in Dallas when he moved to Portland, to a place that had no yard and nowhere to farm.

“Doing the Fest helped scratch the itch,” he says. He's now getting Wellspring Farm in Gresham, Oregon, off the ground and noted how the festival has become a bit more commercial, a bit less homemade. But all that's relative, considering we're standing here over our jars of sauerkraut, and the exhibitors are very small businesses, if they're businesses at all.
“I still love the DIY and starter tables,” he says. “It reminds you that everyone can do this.”

items.title: Instagram Is a Streaming Service Now
items.description: I’ve never listened to a full episode of the Happy Wife Happy Life podcast, hosted by Jordan Myrick and Kendahl Landreth, but I’ve sure seen all the clips.
items.author: Reece Rogers
paragraphs: I’ve never listened to a full episode of the Happy Wife Happy Life podcast, hosted by Jordan Myrick and Kendahl Landreth, but I’ve sure seen all the clips.

My Instagram Reels algorithm recently served me, along with 5 million other viewers, a brief rant from Myrick about feeling bamboozled by the health care system. Then, I spent the next hour scrolling through the show’s other snippets on Reels, loving the couple’s snarky banter. Still, I never followed the duo to a different platform to watch the full-length podcasts.

On Monday, Instagram announced plans that might have turned me into a regular listener of the show. Instagram will expand tests in the US that let creators upload long-form content up to 90 minutes and flip a video’s orientation to horizontal. Creators can also link their short clips directly back to full-length videos.

“Our belief here is that entertainment and creativity are not limited to a three-minute video,” Tessa Lyons, vice president of product at Instagram, tells WIRED. She wants to build the “best place for social entertainment” with this overhaul of Instagram video. The social media platform may soon feel like a streaming service, as more viewers watch longer videos on their big screen.

Instagram is also expanding its creator tools for turning Reels into episodic content. “We want to be able to say, ‘Wow, Reece loved episode 3. So, as soon as episode 4 drops, we've got to make sure to show it to him,’” Lyons says. This Reels feature, called “Series,” is already available for some creators in the app, and it's being tested for TV viewing as well.

Instagram is focused on the experience of watching videos on your TV. It's hunting for ways to make that TV experience feel social, like showing your connections what you’ve been watching via the Friends tab. The company also plans to turn your smartphone into a TV remote.

Lyons sees the video-focused update as avoiding one of IGTV’s core mistakes—IGTV was the company’s previous attempt at more expansive content. In that instance, many viewers desperately wanted to flip the screen. IGTV failed to connect with users, in part, because it only allowed vertical videos. Meta discontinued the app a few years after its 2018 launch.

While Instagram’s latest changes challenge YouTube’s TV dominance, they also try to leverage its current strength as a platform for clips. Bite-sized clips, often of two people sitting behind podcast microphones, feel inescapable on social media right now, with many creators using them to boost visibility. Even WIRED’s own podcast now records videos for social media clipping.

Instagram is streamlining a viewer’s potential fandom journey. Rather than viral clips and long-form content existing on different platforms, Instagram is positioning itself as a centralized experience where I can stumble on Myrick’s health care rant in the morning and then open the app on my TV later that night and get a nudge to stream the full podcast episode.

“What we're seeing right now is that a lot of great short-form content is vertical, and a lot of great long-form content is horizontal, and we have the design challenge of figuring out how to make that all work cohesively in one product,” Lyons says. “TV becomes a great destination for watching long-form, horizontal content, and mobile becomes a great place for discovering that content.”

items.title: Unpacking the Gosselin Family Abuse Allegations
items.description: The Gosselin family is back in the headlines almost a decade after the hit reality-TV show Jon & Kate Plus 8 (later Kate Plus 8) went off the air. Last week, Collin Gosselin, one of the family’s sextuplets, published a memoir expanding on extensive abuse alleg
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: The Gosselin family is back in the headlines almost a decade after the hit reality-TV show Jon & Kate Plus 8 (later Kate Plus 8) went off the air. Last week, Collin Gosselin, one of the family’s sextuplets, published a memoir expanding on extensive abuse allegations against his mother, Kate Gosselin, that he first shared with the public in 2023. Many of the family members have been estranged from one another for years, but Collin’s memoir, as well as a forthcoming Netflix documentary, seems to have brought the tension further into the spotlight. Here’s what has happened so far.
The Gosselin children grew up on TV before their parents divorced in 2009.

You probably know the Gosselins from their TLC reality show, Jon & Kate Plus Eight, which premiered in 2007 and chronicled the lives of Jon, Kate, and their eight children: twins Mady and Cara, who were born in 2000, and sextuplets Collin, Aaden, Joel, Alexis, Leah, and Hannah, who were born in 2004.

Jon and Kate divorced in 2009 after ten years of marriage and five seasons on TV. Their split was messy and public — Jon faced cheating rumors when he began dating Hailey Glassman, the daughter of Kate’s plastic surgeon, though both he and Glassman denied they had been together before the separation. After the divorce, Jon was photographed spending a lot of time with Christian Audigier, the fame-hungry designer behind the Ed Hardy brand who was known to throw lavish parties attended by Michael Jackson and Madonna. Meanwhile, Kate received full custody of the couple’s eight children as well as their Pennsylvania home. She continued filming the reality series — which was retitled Kate Plus 8 — for six more seasons. The show aired its final season in 2017, when the twins were 17 and the sextuplets were 13.
Collin says he suffered years of abuse at the hands of his mother after his parents’ separation.

Collin first came forward with allegations against his mother in Vice TV’s 2023 documentary Dark Side of the 2000s, in which he talked about being isolated from his siblings and verbally abused. He expanded on those claims in an interview with The Sun in 2024, where he said Kate had kept him confined to a makeshift room in the basement that was “bolt-locked from the outside.”

In his new memoir, In the Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of my Childhood, Collin claims his mother mentally and physically abused him after Jon moved out, when the sextuplets were about 5 years old and Collin told her he didn’t want to be on-camera anymore.

He writes that Kate once yanked his ear so hard that his fourth-grade teacher noticed bruising and made a call to the local Children and Youth Services, which triggered an investigation. Kate removed Collin from school shortly after, telling him it was “for his own good,” he says. He claims that he then began spending most of his time in the basement room, which was monitored by two security cameras.

“Most days, I spent about 70 percent of my time locked in that room,” Collin writes, per E! “The rest was split between meeting with my teacher, eating alone without my siblings, cleaning up after everyone, or pretending to be happy when the cameras came around.” He says he would often attempt to escape his confinement, and on occasion his mother zip-tied his hands and feet together. He also accuses Kate of further verbal abuse, alleging she called him “crazy, dangerous, and other names nobody should ever call a child” and told his siblings he was a “bad kid.”

When Collin was 11, Kate checked him into Philadelphia’s Fairmount Behavioral Health System, a mental-health facility he describes in the book as an “institution,” where he stayed for 21 months. Kate said in a statement to People at the time that she had enrolled Collin because he had “special needs,” describing his diagnosis as “fairly fluid” but adding that “he needs to learn certain strategies to help him deal with things.” Collin claims in his memoir that he was given medication at the facility that made him feel “like a zombie” and was physically restrained at times. He says he was ignored when he asked questions about the duration of his stay, and throughout his nearly two years in the facility, Kate visited only once.

Collin, now 22, claims he was finally released from Fairmount after he smuggled a letter to his father asking for help. He says that his mother had led him to believe Jon hated him and that his letter was part of a last-ditch effort. After receiving it, Jon filed an emergency petition with the court to modify custody, Collin writes.

Jon gained custody of Collin and his sister Hannah in 2018, when they were both 16. Collin says he has not seen or spoken to his other siblings since being removed from their home. Hannah remained in contact with her siblings and her mother.
Collin’s sister Hannah initially stood by him before distancing herself from the allegations.

In the Vice documentary, Hannah corroborated Collin’s claim that he had been isolated from her and the rest of their siblings. In previous interviews, she said she moved in with Jon because she wanted to be closer with him.

However, Hannah has recently distanced herself from both her brother and her father, writing in a statement posted to TikTok that she has not lived with Jon in “over a year” nor spoken to Collin in “close to a year.” Her statement followed the news that Netflix will release a documentary about the Gosselin family featuring interviews with Jon, Collin, and herself.

“I have had a relationship with my mom and other siblings for quite a few years now,” Hannah wrote. “And that’s the only thing I’m clearing up. I will not be commenting on Collin’s behavior growing up or my experiences growing up with him.”

In response to his sister’s statement, which she published days before the release of his memoir, Collin told The View’s co-hosts that Hannah’s language “sounded like a lot of the words of my mother, especially the last part. What I do believe has happened is that Hannah’s caught in the middle — and nobody deserves that.” He added, “I know what it feels like to have to fight to have a relationship with your siblings. I don’t have one with my siblings, and I know how much that hurts. Not only is she caught in the middle, but I do believe my mom is either leveraging finances or Hannah’s relationship with our siblings over Hannah.”

He added that he thinks Hannah is also attempting “pre–damage control” — presumably to preserve her relationship with Kate — before the premiere of the Netflix documentary, which does not yet have a release date.

Collin’s other siblings have not commented on his latest allegations against their mother. After the Vice documentary aired in 2023, Collin’s older sister Mady defended her decision to cut ties with him.

“I do not owe my allegiance to any person(s) who has physically threatened me and every member of my immediate family (some incidents as recent as last year),” she wrote. “Further, I will never allow someone who has exhibited hateful and even violent behavior toward others based on their racial identity, gender identity, or religious beliefs to be in my life.”
She added that there was “no further conversation to be had about rebuilding relationships with anyone in my life after reaching the point of physical violence and hate speech.”
“I cannot speak any further on why Collin has done these things, just that I have witnessed them,” she said.

Jon responded to Mady’s post in a statement to People at the time, saying, “It took courage for Collin to sit down and speak about his past, and the last thing I would have expected was more abuse to come his way from a sibling that hasn’t seen or spoken to him since he was in sixth grade.”
Kate has denied Collin’s abuse allegations.

After Collin spoke out in 2023 about his experience of being institutionalized, Kate released an Instagram statement suggesting he had fabricated his claims. “My son Collin, whom I love with all my heart, has received multiple psychiatric diagnoses over the years,” she wrote. “For the safety of myself, his brothers and sisters and for his own well-being, he was placed in a facility following years of outpatient treatment which proved insufficient for his need. Collin’s distorted perception of reality is one of the many issues that he has always struggled with.” She insisted that “all measures that were taken in our home were at the explicit recommendation of [Collin’s] pediatric psychiatrist and/or his team of specialists and were put into place to safeguard every member of our family, our friends as well as our family pets.”

After Collin shared more details about the alleged physical abuse with the The Sun in 2024 — including his claim that Kate had zip-tied his hands and feet — Kate’s lawyer, Richard Puelo, told The Sun there are “always two sides to every story and when things take place in the past, it’s hard to determine because people have differing recollections and perspectives.”
“However, I think if Kate did the things that Collin is accusing Kate of, she would have been investigated by the authorities and prosecuted,” Puelo added.

Collin, meanwhile, has pushed back on the idea that mental illness drove him to make up allegations of abuse against his mother; he recently told TMZ that he had completed and passed “three independent psychiatric evaluations.”
Earlier this week, Kate, who has engaged in the comments sections of a few social-media posts defending her, addressed Collin’s claim that she had visited him only once at the behavioral facility.

“I visited EVERY single time the facility felt he was stable enough for a visit,” she wrote in an Instagram comment. “Sometimes a visit was planned but the facility canceled it because he was too unstable and it would have to be rescheduled.” In a separate comment under the same video, she wrote that she called her son “EVERY SINGLE TIME he earned phone privileges or was allowed to have or make a phone call.”
Jon has openly supported Collin.

Jon has remained supportive of Collin and Hannah, though he is currently estranged from his six other children. In a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight, Jon said he’s still interested in rebuilding his relationship with his other children. “Of course, I want to talk to them. It’s not about the book stuff. I just want to know how their life is going,” he said. “I mean, we’re perfect strangers now. It’s been a long time with Mady and Cara — about 13 years I’ve been estranged from them. I have no idea why.”

When asked if he had a message for the children he doesn’t speak to, Jon said, “I’ve tried to reach out to you publicly. In the early days, I tried to reach out to you privately. I hope you understand that I still love you.” He also encouraged them to read Collin’s book, adding that it will “explain a lot.”

items.title: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
items.description: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
items.author: Rachael Combe
paragraphs: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
As the third season of Nobody Wants This hits Netflix, the TV perennial, Frozen superstar, and modern-marriage poster girl reveals her secret sauce.

Kristen Bell appears on my computer screen eating a bowl of yogurt. She is backlit by a gauzy curtain in a corner of her California home, her blond hair in a top knot. She wears a black T-shirt and no visible makeup. She is 46, looks 16, and, almost immediately, is speaking with the wisdom of your coolest 76-year-old aunt.

“We all act like we’re not connected, but that’s the biggest joke. I see the world as a large family that f*cking fights a lot. I like that about myself, and I’m not planning on changing it no matter how much tribalism is presented to me,” she says. It’s a theme she returns to repeatedly in our conversation. “That’s what I love about Nobody Wants This. They’ve learned not just how to love, but how to fight and how to forgive and how to choose each other despite differences. I think that’s something the world could use more of.”

Bell speaks with her hands, fluttering and fanning her tapered pink nails, and expertly deploys eye contact — she’s not taking her eyes off of you, so you can’t take your eyes off of her. “I’m a feeler,” she says, her eyes welling up. “I wish I wasn’t sometimes. But I also know it leads me to a lot of my creative process. And I think creativity is one of the most important things in the world.” She sees her gifts — her ability to communicate emotion, her crystalline singing voice — as almost a moral imperative to improve the lives of those around her. “I do think thoroughly about how, hopefully, [a project] will land,” she says. “I could be in [viewers’] living room at night after they’ve had a hard day, and when they sit down, I could sweep them away into a world that is only imaginary, and for one hour, they forget that their hands and feet hurt.”

The third season of Nobody Wants This, Bell’s hit Netflix comedy, drops Oct. 22. The show, about agnostic, devil-may-care sex podcaster Joanne (Bell) falling in love with a careful, tradition-loving rabbi, Noah (Adam Brody), and the chaos it causes in each of their lives, is rom-com light. But it debuted in 2024 amid heightened antisemitism in the wake of the Oct. 7 attacks in Israel and the war in Gaza. Initially, the show was knocked by some for stereotypical portrayals of Jewish women — but it ended up being a huge win for Netflix, drawing 57 million viewers in its first three months on the platform. And as Joanne and Noah’s love story has developed, the series has blossomed into a surprisingly sweet treatise on tolerance, resilience, and the beauty of Jewish ritual and spirituality.
“Having people be disappointed in me is really hard for me. Like really hard. And with raising kids, that’s like a whole other level.”

Bell has made a career of making you root for other headlong women, rushing into danger (Veronica Mars), into the arms of oversexed rockers (Forgetting Sarah Marshall), into ice storms (Frozen), and into the afterlife (The Good Place). Though there are some Extremely Online People who don’t always manage to connect with Bell’s sense of humor on social media — the brouhaha about her tongue-in-cheek Instagram post to Dax Shepard on her last wedding anniversary comes to mind — she radiates likability even when she’s playing a next-level bitch (see her recurring guest roles in Party Down and Parks and Recreation). As Bell’s husband of 13 years, podcaster and comedian Shepard recently put it, “How on Earth could you hate this woman? She’s so lovely. If you hate this woman, clearly you’re bonkers.”

It’s true that in our stressed-out, maxed-out, polarized, atomized, rage-baited era, Bell is like a half-pint of lemonade: a sweet-tart all-American crowd-pleaser, able to take down the temperature and brighten the spirits of any room. Now that Dolly Parton and Betty White are no longer with us, Bell is probably in the running to take over their roles as America’s Most Beloved.
