items.title: Cupertino Recap: We Are the Robots
items.description: I have a question for you. Whenever Bo appears on Cupertino — and he appears an awful lot this week, even when people don’t want him to — how do you see him? Is he a machine? Or is he a friendly autonomous entity? Do you even see him as a “him”? Would “it” be
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: I have a question for you. Whenever Bo appears on Cupertino — and he appears an awful lot this week, even when people don’t want him to — how do you see him? Is he a machine? Or is he a friendly autonomous entity? Do you even see him as a “him”? Would “it” be more appropriate?

I’m going to stick with “him,” because that’s how Bo presents — and also to honor Rob McClure’s fully human performance as this sentient supercomputer. He’s so puckish! And have you noticed McClure’s many quirky facial expressions and hand gestures as Bo? These are the kinds of tics that AI-generated characters have gotten better at mimicking over the past couple of years. They coax us into thinking that the AI agents we talk to are real … ish.

This week’s Cupertino cuts to the heart of one of the biggest ethical and legal issues surrounding the tech industry these days. How much agency can we really ascribe to AI agents, and, by extension, how much responsibility for their behavior can we pin on their creators? It’s not just Bo who sparks this debate within the newly renamed Price, Siffre & Associates (or “PSA,” as I’ll call them). The lawyers’ case this week is a doozy, involving a chatbot who may or may not have convinced a teenager to stab his father 44 times.

This is the case that Natalia Boutella dropped into Michael and Olivia’s hands at the end of last week’s episode, to test their mettle and to see if they’re worthy of her investment. She described it then simply as “a motion to dismiss” and said that her involvement in the case wasn’t intended to vex her ex — or at least not entirely.

The truth is more complicated. As we find out over the course of several days of testimony, the man who wants this case tossed out of court is Kirk Boutella (Fisher Stevens), the outspoken tech billionaire behind Chatlike, an edgy AI chat service whose main attraction is Lady Marguerite, a sexy goth character whose conversations with users are designed to foster feelings of deep, intimate connection. That’s what happened with 13-year-old Daniel Mackenzie (Zachary Golinger), who responded to his father’s threats to disable Chatlike by killing him — after getting advice from Lady Marguerite on which body parts to stab.

The Cupertino writers are really cooking with this case, which once again sees multiple reversals of fortune, with Chatlike presenting airtight arguments that PSA punctures and vice versa. Courtroom dramas work best when we pull for our heroes while also seeing the opposition’s point. It’s tough to dispute Chatlike’s positions, which are threefold: (1) Marguerite’s more seductive qualities are supposed to be aimed at adults, but Daniel lied about his age. (2) Everything Marguerite told Daniel about how to murder a man is easily Google-able. (3) Daniel didn’t kill his father because of Marguerite; he did it because his whole family situation was messed up.

It’s here that Natalia’s insistence that this case isn’t entirely about hurting her ex-husband proves true. The title of this episode is “Juno,” which is the name of Daniel’s mother, the one suing Chatlike. To rattle Juno (Marin Ireland) and her new lawyers, the Chatlike attorneys pull a couple of sleazy moves. First, they bring in Nichole Ferebee (Renée Elise Goldsberry), an attorney who broke Michael’s heart years ago by accepting his marriage proposal and then leaving him for a partner at his dad’s firm. Then Nichole goes after Juno, who was at her “work flirt” friend Peter’s house when a desperate Daniel called her three times in the hour before the murder.

This week, we start to see Natalia as more than just a rich, vengeful divorcée. She has a law degree from the University of San Francisco. She helped Kirk build his company when he was a struggling Valley newbie. And she hates seeing a woman’s reputation get dragged through the mud. She wants Michael to protect Juno and eviscerate Kirk. So he does just that, using some old Chatlike emails (provided by Natalia) to show that Kirk specifically asked his team to target 12- to 15-year-olds with Marguerite. He also finds an email where Kirk insults a nephew with multiple sclerosis, after he used that nephew’s MS to curry sympathy from the judge. Ouch.

This whole case is ultimately about something that is emerging as Cupertino’s core question: Who bears responsibility for the terrible outcomes of emerging technologies? We’re just three episodes in, and already this show is shading in some of the nuances of how the tech giants operate, with nondisclosure and noncompete agreements obscuring the truth of what they’re doing and with financial shell games that hide where their money actually is. It’s not too surprising that PSA wins Juno’s case but receives no settlement, because Chatlike immediately declares bankruptcy. Instead, Michael and Olivia get their money from Natalia, who cuts them a check for six months’ worth of rent and salary. That’s how Silicon Valley runs: on rounds of funding, not traceable profits.

Which brings us back to Bo, and to Cupertino’s emerging MVP, Christy Palladino. The firm ends up taking Bo’s case, in part because he’s offering real money. (His retainer pays for a furnished conference room and hallway!) But also, this virtual guy is just so darned persistent, popping back up on PSA’s computers even after Michael hires their previous client Vik to scrub the network. While Michael and Olivia are working on Juno’s case, Christy swings into action to help Bo, making clever use of all of her connections to the IRL Silicon Valley: the cops, valets, waitresses, and construction workers AI can’t replace.

Bo needs to incorporate to be a legal entity? Fine. Christy calls a few friends — one of whom works at Hooters — to be Bo’s board. Bo needs someone from Colt AI’s recently fired safety team to sue on his behalf? No problem. Christy tracks down Calvin Settlemeyer (Andy Grotelueschen), the former team leader, now running a vineyard on land not far from where Christy’s grandfather once owned a chicken farm.

The Bo story line hits a couple of intriguing dead ends in this episode. First, Calvin surreptitiously directs Christy to look for a woman named Cokie Ficarra, who turns out to be the alleged leader of an anti-tech domestic terrorist organization known as the Enders — and therefore someone the authorities want PSA to avoid. Then later, a woman named Rosetta Lane (Erin Darke), who works in Colt AI’s public relations department (“Kind of,” she chirps), intimidatingly wanders into PSA’s secret unfinished backrooms (“Very deconstructionist,” she smirks) and offers to help the partners delete Colt’s rogue agent.

Now let me ask this: How do you see Rosetta? As played by Darke, she is clipped and cutting in a way that seems coldly robotic, even if she is always smiling a little. Bo is more “human” in his way, while Rosetta — a representative of Silicon Valley’s insular, unforgiving culture — comes off as casually cruel.
But make no mistake: Neither of these individuals is your friend.

• Jackie Earle Haley returns as Lincoln Cogswell, the folksy judge who handled the S-Talk case in the series premiere. He’s still making his rulings fairly and calmly (“Yuuup, overruled,” he says in very chill tones), though he also makes his own personal take clear. When Olivia tries to get a witness to speculate on what might’ve motivated Daniel, the defense objects and Judge Cogswell sighs, “Sustained … regrettably.”

• Before Michael and Olivia become the lead counsel on Juno’s lawsuit, Natalia expects them to work with her original lawyer, a civil rights legend named Austin Sullivan (played by a very funny Dakin Matthews). Sullivan never misses an opportunity to turn a case into a cause. His attempt to make Juno’s suit into an indictment of racist policing is misguided enough, but it’s when he tells Michael, “Tomorrow, you should wear a Kente stole,” that he gets fired. (Still … Wanna bet we see Sullivan again? The Kings do love to bring their wackier characters back.)

• Judge Cogswell patiently handles all of Austin Sullivan’s objections and exceptions, gently reminding him of the existence of the court reporter. “Even when you don’t say ‘exception,’ Nancy notes it. That’s why she’s waggling her fingers over there.”

• Put a pin in this: During Natalia and Michael’s heart-to-heart about their respective exes, they eye each other for a long time before hesitantly saying good night. I suspect we won’t have to wait too long for this particular Chekhov’s gun to go off.

items.title: ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts James Potter and Lily Potter, Plus Charlie Weasley in Character’s Screen Debut
items.description: The “Harry Potter” HBO series has cast another casting spell.
items.author: Ethan Shanfeld
paragraphs: The “Harry Potter” HBO series has cast another casting spell.

Harry Gilby, Jasper Talbot and Hannah Chinn have joined the cast as Charlie Weasley, James Potter and Lily Potter, respectively. The actors will appear in Season 1 of the series, which is dubbed “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone.”

James and Lily Potter, parents of the titular orphaned wizard, appeared in the “Harry Potter” movies in flashbacks, photographs and magical manifestations. Charlie Weasley is a minor character in the books and does not appear in the films, so the HBO series is straying from the movies regarding Ron Weasley’s older brother.

The first season of the “Harry Potter” TV show premieres on HBO on Dec. 25. The second season, based on the second book in J.K. Rowling’s beloved fantasy series, “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets,” is currently filming at Leavesden Studios outside London.

The logline for Season 1 reads, “There is nothing special about Harry Potter — or so his Aunt Petunia tells him. But when a mysterious letter of admission to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry arrives, it opens the door to a hidden world of magic, friendship and adventure. Yet behind Hogwarts’ enchanted walls lie dark secrets. Harry must find the courage to prove himself against the darkest wizard of all.”

“Harry Potter” stars Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid, Rory Wilmot as Neville Longbottom, Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy, Leo Earley as Seamus Finnigan, Elijah Oshin as Dean Thomas, Tristan Harland as Fred Weasley, Gabriel Harland as George Weasley, Ruari Spooner as Percy Weasley, Alessia Leoni as Parvati Patil, Sienna Moosah as Lavender Brown, Finn Stephens as Vincent Crabbe, William Nash as Gregory Goyle, Warwick Davis as Filius Flitwick, Sirine Saba as Pomona Sprout, Daniel Rigby as Vernon Dursley, Bel Powley as Petunia Dursley, Paul Whitehouse as Argus Filch, Johnny Flynn as Lucius Malfoy, Bertie Carvel as Cornelius Fudge, Luke Thallon as Quirinus Quirrell, Katherine Parkinson as Molly Weasley, Amos Kitson as Dudley Dursley, Gracie Cochrane as Ginny Weasley, Richard Durden as Cuthbert Binns, Louise Brealey as Rolanda Hooch, Bríd Brennan as Poppy Pomfrey, Leigh Gill as Griphook and Anton Lesser as Garrick Ollivander.

“Game of Thrones” favorite Kit Harington will join Season 2 as Gilderoy Lockhart alongside Bonnie Hill as Ginny Weasley, Lenny Rush as Dobby, Billy Barratt as Tom Riddle, Rafe Spall as Arthur Weasley, Molly Hewitt-Richards as Moaning Myrtle and Jasper Ambrose as Colin Creevey.

The “Harry Potter” series is written and executive produced by Francesca Gardiner. Mark Mylod will executive produce and direct multiple episodes of the series for HBO in association with Brontë Film and TV and Warner Bros. Television. The series is executive produced by Rowling, Neil Blair and Ruth Kenley-Letts of Brontë Film and TV, David Heyman of Heyday Films, Laura Neal and Jon Brown.
Gilby is represented by Independent Talent Group and Untitled Entertainment. Talbot is represented by United Agents. Chinn is represented by 42.

items.title: The NFL’s Biggest Dramas This Season Are in the Broadcast Booth
items.description: The NFL might be the undisputed king of TV content, but it is off-the-field drama that has dominated much of the conversation around the game this season so far.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: The NFL might be the undisputed king of TV content, but it is off-the-field drama that has dominated much of the conversation around the game this season so far.
In particular, it was a widely reported altercation before the Los Angeles Rams-Buffalo Bills game at SoFi Stadium this month … in the ESPN broadcast booth.

To recap: ESPN’s lead play-by-play announcer Joe Buck signed a rich new contract with the company, but his longtime analyst partner Troy Aikman has not, resulting in reported bad blood between the boothmates.

On-air, of course, viewers would have no clue (Buck and Aikman have continued to deliver a broadcast worthy of their decamillion-dollar contracts), but the dispute has become fodder, and Aikman has not been willing to shy away from discussing it.
The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback appeared on The Mike Fisher Show on Friday, where he was almost melancholy about what his future holds in media.

“I never had any interest in going into television, it was just by happenstance that I even got into it,” Aikman said, recalling the outreach from Fox Sports. “I don’t know that if they hadn’t hired me, I would have gotten an opportunity anywhere else. And here I am, 25 years later, and now as I’m into my last year at ESPN, I’m realizing that this is something that could very well be taken away from me, and so for the first time, I’m realizing how much I really do, and I’ve always enjoyed it.

“Until you risk having something taken away from you, I think sometimes you tend to maybe take things for granted,” he continued. “And so for the first time probably in my career, I’m realizing, you know, this is a great profession, it’s been a great ride for me, and I hope that it’s not over.”

As the faces of Fox and ESPN’s NFL coverage, Aikman and Buck have been staples on Sundays (and more recently Mondays) for years. The looming end of that is ripping through sports, media and the league itself. And the situation comes as Disney is set to host its first Super Bowl since 2006, with Buck and Aikman set to lead the game from the booth (they have also been a big part of its marketing). But with their rich deals, nothing can be assured, and in the TV business, any opportunity to get a better deal or sign talent that could make a difference is typically taken fast.
At a conference room in the InterContinental Barclay Hotel in Midtown Manhattan last week, NFL executive vp and chief media officer Hans Schroeder was asked about the Buck-Aikman ESPN impasse.
Schroeder, who is responsible for managing the league’s relationships with its media partners, said that it had “no concern” with the situation.

“I don’t know if you watched the game on Monday night. It was an incredible game. An incredible game, and incredible coverage by Joe and Troy, just like they always do,” Schroeder told assembled journalists in the room, adding that the league was proud of Disney’s coverage, including its numerous altcasts with the Manning brothers, Pat McAfee and Star Wars, and with all the effort going into the next Super Bowl. “I think the fans are deserving of first-class game production, which Joe and Troy have — I think going back to ’02 or something was their first year — a history of doing that as well as anyone, and I think you’ll continue to see them do that as well as anyone.”
Suffice it to say, it is not the story that the league or Disney want to be talking about right now.
And yet, the ESPN broadcast booth drama underscores what has been perhaps the most tumultuous and uncertain year ever for NFL broadcasters.

At CBS, Tony Romo’s preseason arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated (OWI) led to his ouster from the network’s broadcast booth. His replacement, J.J. Watt, was named the permanent successor last week when he was given a multiyear contract extension, with Skydance Sports chief David Berson praising him as “insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate.”

Greg Olsen is in the final year of his deal at Fox and is looking for a new home, while current NFL names like Travis Kelce and Sean McVay have bubbled up as potential TV talent in chats with agents and network execs.

A senior NFL source told THR that the league doesn’t micromanage the personnel decisions of its broadcast partners and that it isn’t involved in the calls being made when it comes to talent. But that doesn’t mean the league doesn’t have any say.

Sources at both the league and its rights partners paint the conversation around broadcasting as an ongoing conversation, with the league always interested in improving coverage of the game. More precisely, the league’s NFL deals require a quality of production from its partners that includes an A-team broadcast booth that can deliver a broadcast worthy of the league and its viewers (“first-class production,” as Schroeder said). It might be a mushy benchmark, but it does mean that more out there ideas like the Manningcast, the McAfeecase or animated altcasts remain secondary considerations, and that the main booth needs to have seasoned or otherwise A-list talent (like Tom Brady, who made his broadcast booth debut for Fox).

The drama matters, because the NFL matters. While no real fans will turn off their NFL games because of some broadcast booth drama, the entire situation is a rare speed bump for what is otherwise the most reliable bet in all of TV. And yet: The broadcast booths may change, but there’s no reason to think that the NFL will ever become less relevant, or less watched.

items.title: Kevin Bleyer, Emmy-Winning ‘Daily Show’ Writer, Dies at 54 in Car Crash
items.description: Kevin Bleyer, who won four writing Emmys for his work on The Daily Show, died Sunday in a car crash, his family announced. He was 54.
items.author: Mike Barnes
paragraphs: Kevin Bleyer, who won four writing Emmys for his work on The Daily Show, died Sunday in a car crash, his family announced. He was 54.
Bleyer was driving on a rural road in Millrift, Pennsylvania, where he had a home, when he was killed, his publicist told The Hollywood Reporter. No one else was hurt.

Bleyer worked on the ABC late night show Politically Incorrect, hosted by Bill Maher, from 2000 until its 2002 cancellation and wrote for Dennis Miller’s CNBC show during its lone 2004-05 season before he landed on Jon Stewart’s Daily Show at Comedy Central in 2005.

He spent nine years as a staff writer on the program through 2013 while also writing for the 2006 and 2008 Oscars that Stewart hosted. He and others shared Emmys for their work in 2006, 2009, 2011 and 2012 and were nominated four other times.
The Peabody and WGA award winner also served as a writer and producer on NBC’s Today show and as a supervising producer for MSNBC’s Ronan Farrow Daily; wrote a weekly column for The Daily Beast; and
recurred as a voice for The Onion Radio News.

For scripted television, he wrote on the Disney+ series The Right Stuff — an adaptation of the Tom Wolfe book — Fox’s Sleepy Hollow and Bravo’s Significant Others and created and executive produced pilots for Disney Television Animation, Comedy Central, Nickelodeon and Showtime.
Born in Bethesda, Maryland, Bleyer was raised in Seattle and attended Stanford University. He called New York City his home for the past 20 years.

He began his career as a dramaturg and assistant to Anna Deavere Smith at New York’s Public Theater and Broadway’s Cort Theatre before moving to London, where he worked for journalist David Brancaccio at the London Bureau of Public Radio International business affairs program Marketplace.

He was a co-author with Stewart and others on 2010’s Earth: The Book and the author of another best-seller, 2012’s Me the People: One Man’s Selfless Quest to Rewrite the Constitution of the United States of America.

He also wrote with former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations and New Mexico Gov. Bill Richardson the 2013 book How to Sweet-Talk a Shark, which recounted among other adventures their humanitarian mission to North Korea to negotiate the release of the hostage Kenneth Bae.

As a speechwriter, Bleyer wrote for President Obama, contributing to his addresses at the annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinners. He also served for a time as the deputy chief speechwriter for New York Mayor Bill de Blasio.

“Kevin Bleyer was a writer’s writer. From his many years on The Daily Show to writing Obama’s WHCD speeches to his many books and his work on numerous scripted dramas, Kevin could literally do it all,” actor and screenwriter Danny Strong said in a statement. “His immense talent was only outmatched by his kind soul. I am in complete shock that he is gone, and my sadness is overwhelming. I already miss him dearly.”

In 2013, Bleyer lived in Kyrgyzstan, where he executive produced Studio 7, the first political satire news show in Central Asia. Upon returning, he co-founded Pilot Media Initiatives, which launches civics-minded media programs in democratically challenged countries. And he produced and helped launch scripted, unscripted and political satire TV shows in North Macedonia, Nigeria, Moldova, Kenya, Jordan and Estonia in the past decade.

“I had the privilege of counting Kevin Bleyer as both a friend and a work partner,” producer Llewellyn Wells added. “Whether developing a series pitch or sitting around sharing stories, Kevin brought the wit, the funny, the satire. But underneath that rare talent lived a man with depth, love and a sincere desire to leave the world a better place than he found it.

“Whether working with the U.S. State Department in Central Asia to bring political satire programming to that part of the world or delivering biting and poignant takes on The Daily Show and many other programs, Kevin did just that. He left the world a better place than he found it. The heavens are shining brighter today, the earth lost an angel.”
Survivors include his wife, Nella; his father, Archie; his brother, Keith; his sister-in-law, Kelly; his nephew, Evan; and his niece, Lauren.
Donations in his memory can be made to the New York City chapter of the Alzheimer’s Association or to the ASPCA.

“Kevin spent his life finding the perfect words to make people laugh, think and see the world a little differently,” his wife said in a statement. “I was lucky enough to know the humor, curiosity, mischief and tenderness behind those words — and to be loved by a man who made my own world more joyful, more adventurous and infinitely more beautiful.”

items.title: ‘Minimum Wage’ Review: Netflix’s Format-Breaking Hangout Series Makes Good on the Promise of Short Episode Running Times
items.description: There were plenty of reasons Quibi, the shortform streaming platform, failed within eight months of its 2020 launch.
items.author: Daniel Fienberg
paragraphs: There were plenty of reasons Quibi, the shortform streaming platform, failed within eight months of its 2020 launch.

There was the poor timing, obviously: A streamer intended to offer viewers quick bites of programming perfect for wedging into a commute or office lunch break launched as a global pandemic was temporarily halting commutes and office lunch breaks.
Cast: Aidan Micho, Grace Reiter, Hyde Healy, Julia Dicesare, Luke Burke, Ryan Micho, Tommy Armstrong and Randall Park
Showrunners: Jeremy Garelick and Will Phelps
There was the silly, mispronounced name. (Though is “Quibi” actually sillier than “Tubi” or “Mubi”?)

Then there was the decision to offer a forward-looking format, which the streamer entrusted to a bunch of behind-the-curve showrunners who couldn’t distinguish between “actual microprogramming” and “traditional programming cut into 10-minute chunks.”

I made fun of Quibi and I’ll continue to, but one thing I won’t deny: The executives behind Quibi were probably right that shorter episodes were a key element of the future of storytelling, if not the entirety of the future.

Two weeks ago, Freeform released Coven Academy, a supernatural YA drama that aired on television with standard episodic lengths but then streamed with episodes running between 12 and 23 minutes. I won’t tell you that Coven Academy is a good show, but thanks to the length of episodes, it moves along like gangbusters, especially at a time when power players like HBO and Netflix still insist that hourlong dramas should be closer to 65 or 70 minutes per episode if they’re “prestigious.”
But longer isn’t exclusively better at Netflix.
Enter Minimum Wage, a streaming version of the web series of the same name from the production company American High.
The first season of Minimum Wage will be 28 episodes, premiering in two batches of 14 — I’ve seen the first batch — ranging between 12 and 20 minutes apiece.

Like Coven Academy — in this particular way, but not most ways — Minimum Wage is wedged somewhere between the past and the present. Episodes are short, but still frequently feel padded. Much of the young cast, who are also the creators of the format and the writers and directors of most episodes, have evident and immediate potential — Grace Reiter has already landed a featured slot on Saturday Night Live — but they aren’t all ready for primetime. And maybe this won’t be a problem for people watching on tablets, phones or fancy watches, but on a big TV, the series looks as conspicuously cheap as it presumably was.
Still, the episodes move along so fast and the bursts of talent emerge with enough frequency that Minimum Wage makes for an amusing, energetic, instantly disposable binge.

Stars Reiter, Aidan Micho, Hyde Healy, Julia Dicesare, Luke Burke, Ryan Micho and Tommy Armstrong play characters with the same names, the only employees at the Slice Club, part of a chain of pizzerias in upstate New York.

There are no evident shifts at Slice Club, even though most of the characters are high school students. Expanding the world in and around Slice Club might have allowed for a little additional diversity to be inserted between the web series and the Netflix series, but that clearly was not a priority in a show that’s very white, very heteronormative and probably a bit blander than was necessary. Oh well.

The only main character who isn’t underage is Burke’s Luke, a 20-something delivery guy who just started sleeping with the mother of Dicesare’s Julia, the homeschooled ingenue all the other guys might or might not be in love with (because when it comes to character relationships, Minimum Wage has only limited imagination).
Reiter’s Grace is the manager, which doesn’t really matter very much. Armstrong’s Tommy has a girlfriend who lives in “the city” — Albany — and with whom he’s constantly trying to break up.

I’d be hard-pressed to give descriptions for most of the rest of the characters, because traits wax and wane in importance. Ryan Micho’s Ryan is a little more serious-minded and hoping to go to college. Aidan Micho’s Aidan is introduced as somewhat dumb and credulous, though those aren’t consistent details.
Honestly, though, specifics barely matter for showrunners Jeremy Garelick and Will Phelps (Rolling Loud: The Movie).

The things you need to know about Minimum Wage are that these characters work close to full-time at Slice Club, with “work” probably deserving to be in quotation marks; that they have no additional outside friends; and that Slice Club is the center of their lives and their social circle. It’s less a job and more a likably dysfunctional family.

Hoping to make Slice Club function better is Terry Sylvester (guest star Randall Park), founder of the franchise. Terry is facing an ugly divorce, and his wife is getting all the other stores, each profitable, leaving him with just this one branch, the only money-loser in the portfolio. Terry has big and not-so-big ideas for turning around the fortunes of this story, but really, he just needs a basement to live in.

With a jittery mockumentary style that is never explained or justified — just add it to the list of questions you don’t ask when you’re spending five or 10 minutes on an episode but that begin to pop up when the running times double or triple — Minimum Wage has a lot of The Office in its DNA, along with traces of Party Down, hints of Superstore and a bit of the earliest DIY days of It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, minus the edge. There’s some Tires here, too. And maybe just a bit of the short-lived Special, one of the last times Netflix tried out the micro-comedy format.

I don’t know if it’s a show that feels like it’s made by people with extensive food service experience, but it definitely feels like it’s made by people who have watched a lot of shows about food service and general minimum wage work. Despite those hints of Superstore, it doesn’t have anything meaningful to say about the condition of minimum wage employment in contemporary America.

Some of the episodes have simply contained storylines, like the gang finding a pile of lottery tickets in an unoccupied booth and strategizing how to spend their modest winnings; the gang shooting a commercial for the restaurant; or, in the only episode that actually leaves Slice Club behind, the gang having a slumber party. Sometimes the plots are as simple as a small incident revolving around customers — an unruly high school drama club, a couple dramatically breaking up over dinner — and sometimes there are hints of decently constructed farce.

More than anything, though, Minimum Wage is a hangout show. Nobody’s really working very hard. Nobody’s the least bit stressed out about how many hours they’re working or how much money they’re making. Instead, they’re just goofing off and talking in rapid-fire, reference-driven bursts of dialogue filled with years of inside jokes and nods to things that happened earlier in the series.

The dialogue is silly-smart and grounded with just enough heart to make you believe that these characters like each other, even if the nature of their relationships is vague. I think everybody other than Luke has a crush on Julia at some point and that Julia has a crush on at least two or three of the guys in a wholly innocent, never-been-kissed sort of way. Grace and Ray appear to have a closer friendship based on one episode featuring their escalating celebration of each other’s birthdays, but it’s a friendship that’s almost never relevant otherwise.

Performance-wise, force-of-nature Reiter and likably loopy Dicesare have the most definition and are the most memorable. As for the guys, it’s an absolute blessing that they wear uniforms displaying their names the entire series; without that help, I’d have difficulty distinguishing between them and the characters they’re playing. Healy and Armstrong have the broader roles and don’t fit in as well when Minimum Wage tries to be naturalistic, but they get laughs. Ryan Micho flaunts well-utilized comic precision, and Burke delivers hints of too-old-for-this-shit pathos.

Park is the big addition here, and he pops up for a few minutes now and then, does something wacky and then goes unmentioned for an episode or two. It’s a good gig, and one to which he contributes a fair amount of his trademark unselfconscious energy. He’s a little bit too Michael Scott and not enough of an actual person, but that’s fine.

Loose and populated by talented people, Minimum Wage fits in with a lot of the more web-friendly programming that Netflix has been tiptoeing around recently with podcasts and medium-jumping formats. It has “This is how kids are watching TV now” written all over it, without the self-important Quibi aftertaste. Nothing lingers, and nothing is supposed to linger. Episodes would be perfect to watch on a short commute or during a lunch break.

items.title: The Hollywood Reporter Tops National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards With 96 Noms, More Than Any Other Outlet
items.description: The Hollywood Reporter is nominated for 96 National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards — more than any other outlet — including best publication, best website and two journalist of the year honors.
items.author: Kimberly Nordyke
paragraphs: The Hollywood Reporter is nominated for 96 National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards — more than any other outlet — including best publication, best website and two journalist of the year honors.

THR’s 96 noms also mark a personal record for the publication at the NAEJ Awards. Among them, THR’s Steven Zeitchik and Carly Thomas are up for print and online journalist of the year, respectively. Daniel Fienberg, Angie Han and David Rooney are nominated for best critic across multiple categories, and Scott Feinberg will vie for best anchor/host in the radio/podcast section. THR‘s other noms span the breadth of categories from cover art to photos to investigative stories to illustrations.

The 19th annual honors will be handed out at a gala ceremony on Dec. 6 at the Millennium Biltmore Hotel in downtown Los Angeles. The Los Angeles Press Club previously announced that this year’s ceremony will be dedicated to the late Dolly Parton, who received the organization’s Public Service Award for Contributions to Civic Life at the 60th Southern California Journalism Awards in 2018.

In addition, KCRW’s Madeleine Brand has been chosen as the Los Angeles Press Club’s 2026 Luminary Awardee for Career Achievement, while singer, songwriter, author and human rights activist Brandi Carlile will be honored with the Visionary Award for Humanitarian Work.
A full list of THR‘s NAEJ Awards nominations follows. See the full list of finalists here.

items.title: Nathan Fielder on Reality TV, Elizabeth Holmes, and the Curiosity that Drives Him
items.description: In 2023, Nathan Fielder, who is known for his unique style of reality-based comedy, invited the documentary filmmaker Lance Oppenheim to the Magic Castle. Fielder is a member of that exclusive Los Angeles institution—a private club housed in a mansion, which o
items.author: Lynn Hirschberg
paragraphs: In 2023, Nathan Fielder, who is known for his unique style of reality-based comedy, invited the documentary filmmaker Lance Oppenheim to the Magic Castle. Fielder is a member of that exclusive Los Angeles institution—a private club housed in a mansion, which only magicians are allowed to join. In Vancouver, Canada, where Fielder grew up, he had worked as a magician at birthday parties and bar mitzvahs. “I was doing magic, and I worked at a magic shop from when I was 13 until I was 20,” Fielder told me. “I had to stop, because if you don’t stop, people will forever say to you, ‘Show me a trick.’”

Fielder had initially met Oppenheim because he is a fan of Some Kind of Heaven, Oppenheim’s documentary about the Villages, a retirement community in Florida. The two started talking, and Oppenheim mentioned that he’d heard that Elizabeth Holmes, the notorious indicted CEO and founder of Theranos—the company that fraudulently maintained it had invented a machine that could diagnose many diseases with a single drop of blood—had approached A24 about a documentary. Holmes and her life partner, Billy Evans, wanted someone to film their lives together, theoretically to reveal a more human side of Holmes than the one that had been depicted in the media.

“We were both intrigued by the Holmes story,” Oppenheim recalled. “But initially, we were just spending an evening at the Magic Castle. Nathan loaned me a belt and a tie because there’s a dress code, and we were in the close-up magic room and they asked for a celebrity name from the audience. Someone shouted ‘Elizabeth Holmes,’ and we took that as a sign.” Within days, Fielder had contacted A24, which had produced his show The Curse, and met with Holmes and Evans at their home in San Diego. That was the beginning of a three-year project: the documentary You Can See Everything, which premiered in September at the Telluride Film Festival with a super-secret screening.

The film, which takes place largely in the Holmes-Evans household in the days before Holmes is set to go to prison in Texas, is remarkably intimate and revealing, but also confounding. Fielder moved into the couple’s guesthouse, and Oppenheim and Fielder and their crew worked up to 17 hours a day. Holmes is inscrutable, despite the fact that Fielder and Oppenheim, using three different cameras, captured scenes of the couple in bed and in the kitchen making breakfast for their two young children, William and Invicta. There’s even a striking moment in which Billy is brushing his teeth in the shower.

The intensity of You Can See Everything is amplified by Fielder’s interviews with Holmes. “When I started the project, Elizabeth seemed black and white to me,” he explained. “In my mind, she was guilty. But I was very interested in her and her situation. Curiosity drove me. I’ve always tried to find out the truth in any situation, even if there’s a lot of artifice involved. But when I met Elizabeth, she was so different than I thought she would be. She was disarming in real life. I told her right away that I believed everything that I’d read about her, but that didn’t frighten her.”

Fielder and Oppenheim, who codirected the film, retained creative control over the project and also the right to pull the plug at any time. “Every day, I’d say, ‘If this is too much for you, we’ll bail,’ ” Fielder recalled. “But Billy and Elizabeth always said, ‘We want you to stay.’ We didn’t want the film to relitigate the past. This was about their present moment, but we still had to reconcile with who Elizabeth Holmes is, and was.”

In one stunning segment, Fielder asks Holmes about her veracity; Holmes maintains that she’s never lied in her entire life. Fielder gently probes: not even a white lie to get out of a dinner obligation? Holmes says no, never, I can’t recall ever lying for any reason. “That was one of the moments when I realized the documentary was about something meaningful,” Fielder said. “When she said she’s never lied, she widened the gap so much. I realized there’s more going on here than I thought.”

Fielder appears in the film as a classic journalist, though there is a non-journalistic twist in the second half of the film, which he asked me not to reveal. His other award-winning TV projects have also combined journalism with a sense of the uncanny. The four seasons of Nathan for You, which premiered in 2013, were definitely funny, but the premise of the series was that Fielder would offer professional advice to struggling businesses. His more recent show, The Rehearsal, helps people navigate difficult life situations by gaming out scenarios in elaborately designed sets. For example, in order to investigate communication failures in aviation, Fielder actually became a pilot and flew a large passenger plane.

He had a similar level of commitment to You Can See Everything. “I felt conflicted at times, which was new for me,” Fielder said. “There was always more going on than I thought, and, even now, there are certain aspects of the film where I don’t feel I have a clear conclusion. I want the audience to help me understand the experience.”
Three Questions With Nathan
Do you watch reality television?

I was into The Bachelor for a period of time. I prefer The Bachelor to The Bachelorette. The dynamic between women is more interesting than the dynamic between men. Chris Soules [as the bachelor] was a good season of the show. He’s a total blank thing—there’s nothing from him—but the women were really interesting. When it works, I think The Bachelor has the best reality show format.
What chronological age do you feel?

Twenty-two. I’m 43 now, and sometimes when I’m with people in their 30s, I feel like they are older than me. I don’t know things that other people know. I always feel that everyone knows more than I do. So it’s very easy for me to ask people questions.
Did you feel that way with Elizabeth Holmes?

Yes and no. It was immersive: I was living there, at their request. I didn’t go out of their gated community because there were paparazzi everywhere, and we wanted to keep our project a secret. I think linearly—I always believe there’s a way to untangle any mess. My curiosity with Elizabeth was to understand her. And, in my life, I’ve never been so confused by a person.

items.title: The 8 Best Boot Trends for Fall 2026, Straight From the Runways
items.description: As the seasons shift into fall, boots are one of the first things we can’t wait to wear again. They’re a key part of cool-weather style, and in 2026, the runways have given us a range of exciting new shapes and styles to covet.
items.author: Christina Holevas
paragraphs: As the seasons shift into fall, boots are one of the first things we can’t wait to wear again. They’re a key part of cool-weather style, and in 2026, the runways have given us a range of exciting new shapes and styles to covet.

If you’re looking for boots that excel in attitude, this season has you covered with ultra-high over-the-knee (OTK) boots from Khaite and Chloé, prim, slim knee highs á la Marni and Gucci, and super-fitted styles that feel like a second-skin at Celine and Saint Laurent. On the more functional side, there are plenty of chic picks too. Miu Miu’s rubber-soled stompers, reminiscent of Prada Sport styles from the early 90s, are sure to be a huge hit this season. So too are low-key suede styles from Jil Sander and Dior, and Dries Van Noten’s spin on the buckle boot.
Shop all of our top trending boots for fall 2026 right here.
Cone-shaped heels, seen at the likes of Altuzarra and Celine, are cool, wearable, and tinged with ’70s nostalgia. Wear them with maxi skirts or high-waisted jeans.
Super slim boots in supple leather move with the body and are great for skirts and dresses. These leg-lengthening styles are more like pants or tights than pure footwear.
At Jil Sander and Dior, menswear-inspired suede boots gave suiting and eveningwear a low-key edge.
Heavy buckle boots anchored ornate looks at Dries Van Noten. Our Legacy and Chloé put spins on the style, too. And you can never go wrong with a classic pair from Frye.
Slouchy boots continue to gain momentum. Khaite’s Clive boot has become a runway hit, while at Chloé, rumpled leather shapes enhance the brand’s bohemian sensibility.
Knee-high boots are nothing new, but this season they took on a stiff, structured attitude. The clean, sharp shape feels distinctly ’90s.
Miu Miu brought back the bubble-soled boot this season, recalling cult vintage Prada Sport styles.
At Prada and Marni, lace-up boots struck a fresh balance between punk and office siren.
Super-high over-the-knee boots made a dramatic statement at Chloé and Khaite. Worn with short hemlines or beneath longer layers, the exaggerated shapes bring a sexy, subversive edge.

items.title: African Street Photography Gets the Anthology It Deserves
items.description: How do you select 33 artists from the hundreds of young African photographers who are working across the continent and sharing their images everywhere from museum exhibitions and fashion pop-ups to WhatsApp groups and Instagram projects, at a moment when Afric
items.author: Siddhartha Mitter
paragraphs: How do you select 33 artists from the hundreds of young African photographers who are working across the continent and sharing their images everywhere from museum exhibitions and fashion pop-ups to WhatsApp groups and Instagram projects, at a moment when African photography is more abundant and vibrant than ever?

First, if you’re Nadine Barth and Azu Nwagbogu, coeditors of the dynamic new anthology Street Photography Africa (Thames & Hudson, 2026), you embrace the abundance. You posit that broad access to photographic tools and the global circulation of images, far from diluting the purity of the art, has made photography more relevant than ever—as a way of documenting, but also of shaping and empowering, self-representation on the continent. You remind readers that it wasn’t so long ago that photography functioned, for most people in Africa, as an “apparatus of enclosure,” as Nwagbogu writes. It was wielded by colonial administrators, ethnographers, and, later, a certain breed of Western photojournalists parachuting into crises to control, classify, or pathologize African life.

And then you jump into the vibrant, tumultuous now, with a compilation that presents photographers as participants and actors. This is not the street photography that lurks in surreptitious wait for the candid “decisive moment” that distills pathos or paradox. It’s something overt and mutual, in which photographer, subject, and setting activate the street, the editors write, as a “laboratory of social transformation…where global influences merge with local sensibilities and where communities assert their right to be seen on their own terms.”

Divided into six thematic sections, Street Photography Africa has its share of cityscapes. Studies of Lagos, by Daniel Obasi, for example, or of Johannesburg, by Sabelo Mlangeni or Guy Tillim, convey both the congestion of city life and, more movingly, quieter moments: people gathered in doorways, or figures passing through the streets lost in thought. What develops across the 33 practices is a kind of expanded portraiture that breaks the silos of fashion, documentary, conceptual, and street photography in pursuit of an active force that traverses them: style.

Take the figures standing in front of minibuses or transport vans—a familiar sight in African cities that’s become a common trope—in two photographs: one by Hamza Rochdi, made in Casablanca, Morocco, and the other by Kenya Tay, made in Ho, a dusty regional capital in Ghana. The man in high-top dreads and extra-wide jeans with sunglasses and a carryall in Rochdi’s image, part of the series “Youth Mosaic of Casablanca” (2024), is clearly a model. The van, in a bright blue that matches his outfit, carries a mountain of boxes on a scaffold on its roof, with more visible through its side door. A subtle sociology is at work, to do with labor, commerce, and also race and immigration. The photo’s subject is either Black Moroccan or likely part of the country’s migrant population; the picture, ostensibly a style study, manifests and scrambles analysis all at once.

In contrast to Rochdi’s blues, the image by Tay, 66th Independence Day (2023), is a study in reds, vibrant over the brown earth of an unpaved bus park in Ho. Three young girls wear simple matching smock-like dresses with narrow red stripes, which might be school uniforms; behind them is a utilitarian bus typically used to transport workers at public agencies, in this case the fire department. As the title indicates, it is Independence Day, and one of them holds a small flag of Ghana to wave; another carries an umbrella against the sun. The strong sense is that Tay (who is Ghanaian-Dutch and based in Paris) has come across these teenagers and asked permission to “snap” them. It is this moment of mutuality—more than a courtesy, an energy—that turns the image into a social document even as it imbues the scene with allure.

It’s common to assert that Africa brims with style, a generalization across 54 countries and 1.5 billion humans that, when deployed without care, can slide toward fetishization. But there are certain common elements across the continent that are not only economic and ecological, structured by colonial histories and the geopolitical present, but also representational and aesthetic. Put basically, it’s hard to come away from cities like Dakar, Abidjan, or Lagos unmoved by a certain ambient fabulousness—in pattern, gesture, and poise—that transcends social barriers and manifests most vividly in the street.

For Nwagbogu, what makes African street photography so dynamic is how in these cities “the ordinary and spectacular continuously interpenetrate in public space.” He traces this effect to deep-seated, relational conceptions of identity: for instance, the Nguni Bantu philosophy of ubuntu (often rendered as “I am because we are”), or the Akan notion of “personhood as comprising multiple, fluid aspects” known as okra, sunsum, and mogya. “The street accommodates this multiplicity,” Nwagbogu writes. “One can be trader and mother and church member and fashionista simultaneously, performing different aspects of selfhood as context demands.” It’s this moral outlook that links people of the city—say, the Dakar designer and fashion maven Khadija Aisha Ba, as seen in a hyperstyled portrait by Trevor Stuurman—with the vendors and repairers in Tantolohun Ayanda’s bluesy Lagos scenes.

The intersection of African fashion and visual art is rich these days with crossover practices, notably among networks of millennial and Gen Z artists and designers connecting local and diasporic scenes. For curator and fashion historian Tosin Adeosun, who contributes an essay to Street Photography Africa, “present-day African photographers documenting through a sartorial lens are creating and steering a new archival practice.” Photographers Stephen Tayo and Sarah Waiswa, also featured in the book, appeared in the exhibition “Africa Fashion,” which originated at London’s Victoria and Albert Museum in 2022 and traveled to the Brooklyn Museum. They and others extend a legacy that Adeosun traces back to the great studio photographers of the 1960s–70s independence era, like Seydou Keïta or Paul Kodjo, who opened space for self-expression and self-invention, and that continued through pioneering magazines of the 1990s.

African photography is the subject of deepening study and gatherings driven by African practitioners. A photo biennial has been held in Bamako, Mali, since 1994; Nwagbogu founded the LagosPhoto Festival in 2010. Other events take place in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia; Cairo, Egypt; Marrakech, and elsewhere. The London-based curators Ekow Eshun and Osei Bonsu and the New York–based Oluremi Onabanjo are among those organizing major African photo exhibitions at key Western museums. The African Gaze (2024), by the Senegalese-American scholar Amy Sall, and Tender Photos, an innovative online platform for African photography founded by writers Emmanuel Iduma and Ayòbámi Adébáyò, are important new contributions. Into this rich milieu, Street Photography Africa brings its own vital proposition: that the old boundaries of photo practices blur to especially productive effect in the cities of the continent—where, as coeditor Barth writes, “true satisfaction from real or imagined self-staging is only ever found in the streets.”
