No Insider Knowledge: Joe’s point about having, in fact, eaten the apple was solid. I vote for Victor.
Yes Insider Knowledge: [Glowers at Victor in his current purgatorial state] You better stay banished, sir.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Orange County Recap: Mi Casita, Su Casita
items.description: This season doesn’t seem to have story lines so much as little things that pop up here and there and then disappear quickly. It doesn’t have story lines so much as it has warts. Oh, look, there’s one! Everyone scurries off to check it out and diagnose it, and
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: This season doesn’t seem to have story lines so much as little things that pop up here and there and then disappear quickly. It doesn’t have story lines so much as it has warts. Oh, look, there’s one! Everyone scurries off to check it out and diagnose it, and then, with a few applications of Compound W, it’s gone again and we’re just standing around waiting for the next dermatological event to take place. The most concerning of all the warts is the call Shannon gets from her dog Archie, who I believe is fully capable of initiating his own FaceTime because he is a very good dog — yes, he is. Shannon gets a call from her assistant saying Archie is a little low energy. Later, back in the OC, she tells the ladies she took Archie to the pet-cancer doctor, who said if Archie didn’t get radiation, he’d only live another four to six months. Sadly, he died this May, and I don’t think I want to relive any of it on reality television. It’s just too sad.

But, as wart inspectors, here we are, diagnosing a different disease. This week, all the warts are on Gina. The gang goes to Harajuku, which is a high-end neighborhood in Tokyo that Gwen Stefani made famous with some cultural appropriation. B-A-N-A-N-A-S. To be clear, I think what Gwen did — stripping the culture of the place for her own gain, both financially and creatively — is much different than what the women are doing, which is just a little bit of Japanese cosplay. As the woman in the shop explained to them, and the editors dutifully left in the episode to exonerate them, part of the aesthetic is bridging international ideas of cuteness (or kawaii in Japanese). Harajuku is not just full of these types of girls but all sorts of global luxury brands and, as Gina demonstrates, vintage stores selling those designers.

Heather Dubrow goes into a vintage store and says she doesn’t like clothes that have other people’s energies in them. What is she worried about, being haunted by a parka? She bought Lana Turner’s house in Beverly Hills, but she’s afraid someone else carried her pocketbook? Come on. Gina is going a little buck wild in the store, and the women bring up that she seems to be spending a lot more money lately. Heather says it reminds her of actresses who would get a show, buy a fancy car, then the show would get canceled. They also bring up that Gina and Emily got a stylist and each paid $12,000 for four borrowed outfits. Heather points out that she could own four $3,000 outfits for that price. Sure, but how often do these women get to rewear their clothes? A strange part of their job is that if they’re filmed in it once, either for the show or their social media, fans will make a stink if they see it again. What’s the point in owning that outfit if they can’t rewear it? I’m not defending the expense; I’m just saying I don’t entirely buy Heather’s logic.

Gina, however, buys a lot. But as they’re worried about her putting herself in the poorhouse, she’s buying a leather jacket that is only $800. That’s, like, half of what Heather pays for house slippers — that is a single designer slipper. Yes, a vintage store is more expensive than Goodwill, but it’s not like she’s dropping 20 bands at Gucci on two coats. And Gina has what seems to be a thriving career. Shannon doesn’t have a job (other than the show), is worried about her finances, and has an assistant. Why is no one worried about Shannon’s money? This whole thing seems wild and arbitrary to me.

Tamra tells Emily what Heather and the others were saying, and Emily brings it back to her bestie, Gina, who doesn’t take kindly to them counting her paychecks. She says Heather’s actress analogy is inept because it means she’s not going to keep having the same success she’s currently having. I get Gina’s point: No one wants to be told they’re bad at their job. However, Heather is a little bit right. While real estate isn’t as volatile as acting, the market shifts, mortgage rates rise, and there are all sorts of factors that might keep her from doing as well tomorrow as she is doing today. Just as even the best actresses go through their fallow periods (remember when two-time Oscar winner Dianne Wiest couldn’t pay her rent?), the same is true of Realtors. I do think Heather had good intentions with what she is saying, but the delivery wasn’t great.

They all get dressed up as Harajuku girls, covered in bows and plush toys and bright colors and lace and so many platforms — more platforms than we’ve ever seen on this “platform,” as they always call it. They walk through the world’s largest crossing (which really is overwhelming), all holding hands with a bunch of cameras. They then get mad when the commuting locals, dressed all in black, are pissed off being confronted by this impenetrable line of crazy white women, two dressed like the twins from The Shining after they got really into Hello Kitty.

At dinner, Gina brings up the group’s previous comments and says she didn’t like them. Jenn tries to compliment her, saying she’s gone from living in the casita to being a badass, but Gina cuts her off mid-sentence. Gina wants us to know she never lived in the casita. Guys, I know we’ve been calling her “casita” since her first season on the show and it is in the “universal chatter” about her, but Gina wants us all to know she only spent weekends there and her kids were never living with her in the casita. Okay, sure. Got it, Gina.

The problem is she is never going to escape “casita.” This is now part of her brand, just like the shitty clothes and the terrible hair during her debut seasons. (Yes, that is plural because it lasted longer than it should have.) In the great Housewives tradition, she might as well just own it. Yes, she was in a casita. Yes, she used to look like shit. Yes, she worked very hard at forming a real-estate career. Yes, she is doing a lot better now and she can afford designer (secondhand) bags, ski jackets that don’t zip in the front, and getting a real professional to take care of her hair. That is her journey and part of what makes us love Gina. (Well, most fans don’t love Gina, but they love her more than they love Emily!) Trying to erase the casita is telling us she wasn’t a mess when she joined the show even though she totally was. We know. We saw it!

With that, the Gina wart seems to clear up. What other warts are there? Oh, Jenn wants to be just as successful as the rest of the ladies and is trying to figure out how to make more money. She decides it’s going to be fitness classes online, so she comes up with SexyFit, a fitness class to help you look more sexy but also more fit. I want to make so much fun of this very silly and quite obvious title, but I’m sure someone made fun of Billy Blanks for Tae Bo and that made him shit tons of money. She films the class, and Gretchen and Slade show up because nothing in the world makes Slade harder than a camera. Ugh, talk about warts.

Shannon is trying not to get warts from Steve Guttenberg. Apparently, she saw a reel of his on Insta and told Jeff Lewis she thought he was cute, and he hammered on and on about it on his radio show, and now Steve Guttenberg is liking Shannon’s social-media content. Shannon, marry this man! What is she waiting for? Has she seen Steven Guttenberg? He is fit as hell and still strangely famous. Plus he’d make a great addition to this cast. We need to band together to make this happen.

Carmella thinks her boyfriend, Danny, is a wart and knows she needs to lance him but can’t figure out how to do it yet. Carmella is overwhelmed that she didn’t go on the trip, that she’s behind at work, that her kids are growing up and demanding nose jobs. It’s all too much for her. Maybe she can have a corn instead. Maybe a bunion.

There are a bunch of lesser warts that keep coming up — the ladies think Tamra’s friendship with Jenn is fake and she’s using it to annoy Heather, who is no longer looking for a buddy in the group and just wants to be on her own. I don’t know. These all make little sense and even less impact. Maybe they’re not warts, just pimples.

The wart that refuses to go away is whatever is up with Vicki and Tamra. They gather for dinner with a day-drunk Heather Dubrow, and Tamra apologizes for saying Vicki and her daughter, Briana, aren’t talking right now. I get that this is preemptive: Vicki will eventually see the season and not like her comments, but Vicki didn’t even know she’d said it yet. Tamra could have gotten away with this one. Vicki again apologizes for her comments about Tamra and her daughter, but it doesn’t sound like she means it. It seems like Vicki (who almost brained herself passing out in a Tokyo shop) doesn’t want to be there and doesn’t like a single one of these women, even Shannon. It’s like she is at dinner with Tamra and Heather, picks up her margarita (They’re so much better at Andale’s, she thinks), and looks down at her hand. She doesn’t know where she is; she doesn’t know how she got there. All she knows is that she is not at work — her happy place — and her hand is covered in mysterious bumps. Are they hives? Are they lesions? Psoriasis? Dermatitis? Herpes? A rash? No, none of the above. They’re just warts, and they’ll be gone in no time.

items.title: Macklemore Calls for Unity During First ‘Free Palestine’ Show as Hozier, Kneecap and Mark Ruffalo Support: ‘Those Two Words Are So Threatening to Some People’
items.description: Macklemore dedicated his first “Free Palestine” tour date in Dublin, Ireland to “love and liberation,” just over a month after he was dropped as an opener for Ed Sheeran following a political speech on stage.
items.author: Ellise Shafer; Steven J Horowitz
paragraphs: Macklemore dedicated his first “Free Palestine” tour date in Dublin, Ireland to “love and liberation,” just over a month after he was dropped as an opener for Ed Sheeran following a political speech on stage.

3Arena was dotted with keffiyehs and Palestinian flags on Monday night as Dubliners young and old gathered to back the “Thrift Shop” rapper at the start of the three-show stint, which will also see him play Paris and London this week alongside special guests. All proceeds are going to charities supporting Palestine, and Macklemore also donated his $1 million salary from Sheeran’s tour to the cause.

To recap, on Sept. 14 Macklemore was dropped from the remainder of Sheeran’s U.S. “Loop” tour after he said “free Palestine” on stage and gave political speeches over two concerts at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium on Sept. 4 and 5. His remarks went viral, sparking backlash from pop star Pink and a petition from the Israeli American Council calling for his removal and criticizing him for using the platform to “advance a political agenda.” At the time, promoter Messina Touring Group said they had been “notified by venues” that “they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup.” Macklemore claimed that it was Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft who had pushed him out of the tour, and Sheeran also posted a lengthy statement explaining why he doesn’t wade into politics, which generated backlash against him. In solidarity with Macklemore, Sheeran’s other opening acts — including Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe — and his backing band, Beoga, also dropped out of his tour.

Beoga was there to support Macklemore on Monday, alongside surprise guests including Hozier and Kneecap and a passionate Irish crowd that hooted and hollered for the duration of the nearly four-hour event. During his set, Macklemore took a moment to share what the evening meant to him in the wake of the controversy. “Six weeks ago, it was two words. Two words is all that it took. Two words that are rooted in love and liberation,” he said. “Not against anybody, not divisive. Not a call for hatred. But a call to recognize our shared humanity. Free Palestine. I said, free Palestine! The same thing that I want for all of us, freedom, dignity, the right to exist without fear. Being able to raise our children in the homes that we grew up in, not having to prove our humanity to the rest of the world.

“And yet,” he continued, “those two words are so threatening to some people. They would rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean. Because freedom that requires another person’s oppression is not freedom at all. And while the world debates those words, we see the videos, we see the footage, we see parents pulling their children out of the rubble. Families erased. Devastation beyond our imagination. And somehow, those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary. That’s why we are here tonight. That is why we are here, because throughout history, music has given people a place to resist, to come together as a collective, to share our grief, to share our stories, to move from the heart, to mobilize people with the frequency of love. The heartbeat in our drum that makes us feel alive, that makes us feel connected.”

But before Macklemore took the stage, the night kicked off with an introduction from Liam Cunningham of “Game of Thrones” fame. “Tonight, we celebrate life. We honor resilience. We stand with Gaza!” he said. The music then began with Palestinian-Israeli singer Lina Makoul, who delivered a powerful song without words “because anything she said could have severely affected her freedom,” as Cunningham noted. Beoga was next, performing several traditional Irish jigs after percussionist Eamon Murray told the crowd, “Don’t fuck with the Irish!”

The first heavyweight guest was none other than Hozier, who got the crowd crooning along with “Too Sweet,” “From Eden,” and “Work Song.” The Irishman said he is “so proud of my country and the way they’re showing up,” and highlighted that 55 students in Gaza are waiting to have their visas approved by the Irish government so that they can study there. “This has happened before. It happened last year, and this can be solved with ministerial discretion,” he continued. “It’s an absolute wonder, it’s baffling how it hasn’t been solved yet.”

Seeming uncharacteristically nervous, Hozier then announced that he was going to perform a tune that he’d “never sang live before.” It was “The Prayer of Shields,” an 18th-century folk song written by John Shield that hoped for equality for all people. “The Jew he is me fellow man/ The Muslim the same indeed, sir,” he sang in a haunting tone. “To the infidel I’d wish him well/ And help him in his need, sir.”

As the stage was reset, the crowd was treated to a series of video messages from celebrities who couldn’t be there but wanted to show their support. “Thanks to Macklemore for doing this,” The Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas said. “Take care of each other and the innocents, and continue standing up in this struggle towards a just world system.”
Added “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, “We are all together in this fight to help free Palestine. Keep speaking up and using your voice, it’s working.”

“Keep fighting for a free Palestine and humanity all over the world and amongst the people. There will be no peace until there’s equality,” Mark Ruffalo said to enthusiastic applause throughout the stadium. “Lots of love, have a good show. Keep fighting the good fight.”

Irish rap trio Kneecap then stormed the arena, injecting a dose of energy by getting mosh pits going in the crowd as they ran through fan favorites like “Fenian” and “H.O.O.D.” “We wanna thank Macklemore for organizing this concert. We wanna thank Ed Sheeran for helping to organize this concert,” member Móglaí Bap cheekily said as the crowd erupted in cheers.

It was then finally time for Macklemore’s set. The rapper was greeted with enormous applause as he emerged in a green-and-orange keffiyeh to “Chant,” with Australian singer Tones and I joining him to sing the chorus. Supported by a six-piece band, Macklemore rapped with conviction: “This is my moment/ They can’t take my talent/ They can’t take my stripes.” He addressed the crowd for the first time as the song finished, looking overwhelmed and wiping tears from his eyes. Before he could begin to speak, a “free Palestine” chant broke out in the audience.

“It has been a crazy six weeks,” he said. “We took my shortest tour of all time, which was two nights at MetLife Stadium, and we turned that shit into this right here.” He added, “We’re gonna start with an anti-capitalist anthem,” as his hit “Thrift Shop” rang out and a pair of peppy dancers two-stepped on stage.

A run-down of Macklemore’s greatest hits ensued, including “Same Love” with Mary Lambert joining him; “These Days”; “Glorious”; and “Good Old Days,” with Tones and I reemerging to sing Kesha’s part on the track. He then surprised the audience with a new song that “he wrote this last week,” titled “Where Is Our Love?” In the political yet soft-spoken rap, Macklemore says “free Palestine” and speaks about “America being terrorized by ICE agents” as well as mentioning Congo and Sudan.

The set ended on a high note with his 2012 hit “Can’t Hold Us,” during which Macklemore climbed into the crowd and had them literally hold him up. As confetti exploded in the air, Macklemore left the audience with one last message: “I am proud to stand here on stage in solidarity with the Palestinian people. We will continue to fight for collective liberation until our last breath,” he said before leading one final “free Palestine” chant.
Macklemore’s “Free Palestine” tour continues in Paris on Thursday and London on Friday.

items.title: Netflix Docuseries ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Is a Tragic, Mournful Portrait of Addiction: TV Review
items.description: There are not a lot of famous people in “The One About Matthew Perry.” None of the late actor’s “Friends” castmates sat for an interview for the three-part Netflix docuseries; neither did Perry’s longtime friend and “Simpsons” star Hank Azaria, who knew Perry
items.author: Alison Herman
paragraphs: There are not a lot of famous people in “The One About Matthew Perry.” None of the late actor’s “Friends” castmates sat for an interview for the three-part Netflix docuseries; neither did Perry’s longtime friend and “Simpsons” star Hank Azaria, who knew Perry as a striving young actor in L.A., or later collaborators like Bradley Whitford and Aaron Sorkin.

One could take this notable absence as an indicator of the access director Mary Robertson (“Quiet on Set”) and her team were, or were not, able to secure. But whether a matter of intention or circumstance, what emerges in place of star power is a more intimate portrait of Perry and his decadeslong struggle with substance abuse, leading to his death from a ketamine overdose in the fall of 2023. Through friends, family, fellow addicts and former partners, what emerges is a straightforwardly told, crushingly sad story of a man whose talent, humor and success were not enough to overcome a chronic disease.

The unofficial protagonist of “The One About Matthew Perry” is Perry’s younger half-sister Mia Perry Bowick, a therapist who narrates what it’s like to share a loved one with the world at the peak of the monoculture. Bowick is joined by Perry’s close friends Roger Castillo and David Pressman, who recall frequent pre-fame nights with Perry and Azaria at West Hollywood’s Formosa Cafe, as well as multiple ex-girlfriends and even a member of Gen Z who met Perry in one of his many rehab stints. (She says they partly bonded because, not in spite, of their age gap: “I was born in 1997; you’re not that big a deal to me.”) Some of these voices, like “The Whole Nine Yards” director Jonathan Lynn, can speak to Perry’s artistic ability. Most, however, are there to testify to what the public didn’t see, at least until Perry chose to share his start-and-stop road to recovery in venues like his 2022 memoir.

Because of such late-in-life disclosures, which Perry made after embracing his platform’s potential to help others with similar issues, there aren’t any bombshell revelations in “The One About Matthew Perry,” or even much new information. An introductory title card positions the series as “the story of Matthew Perry’s life, as told by his family and friends — and by Matthew himself.” Though recent events made me read that last clause and fear AI-assisted necromancy, Robertson’s approach is formally straightforward and free of such ill-advised techniques. Interviews are supplemented with archival clips of Perry’s screen work and interviews, and some of the show’s most searing material is conveyed in the actor’s own (previously recorded and publicized) voice.

“God, you can do anything you want to me; just please make me famous,” Perry freely admits to praying in his youth. (He got “Friends” shortly afterward, but ruefully notes that “God didn’t forget” about the first part.) “The One About Matthew Perry” is more a collation of established facts about Perry’s battles, including a sepsis-induced coma in 2018 resulting from his use of opiates, and an unveiling of new ones. What the project adds are personal testimonies about witnessing said battles up close, plus memorable observations like “intimacy was his greatest fear and his greatest wish.” Though the most memorable lines — “Reality is an acquired taste,” say — fittingly belong to Perry.

“Friends” has a couple of representatives in Robertson’s cast of talking heads, namely writer Jeff Strauss and former NBC Entertainment president Warren Littlefield; it wouldn’t be possible to tell Perry’s story without dwelling on his most famous role. What “The One About Matthew Perry” does is situate the sitcom’s run, which concludes by the docuseries’ halfway point, within Perry’s broader life: after a childhood feeling adrift between his remarried parents’ respective family units, before attempted follow-ups like “Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip” and addiction interfering with his work. The 2021 “Friends” reunion is presented as a source of great anxiety for Perry, who was hurt by online comments picking apart his mannerisms and appearance. Unbeknownst to viewers at the time, he was still recovering from his coma and the attendant complications.

The series’ length allows “The One About Matthew Perry” to communicate the protracted, start-and-stop nature of Perry’s addiction, from first taking prescribed painkillers after an on-set injury while filming the 1997 film “Fools Rush In” to the many cycles of relapse, detox and sobriety. Eventually, the actual circumstances of Perry’s death — which resulted in multiple criminal convictions for Perry’s dealers and live-in assistant Kenneth Iwamasa, who administered the fatal drug dose — are quickly addressed in the show’s closing minutes. After so much emotion, the detour into factual legal territory via interviews with a former U.S. Attorney is abrupt, if necessary. Bowick grounds these data points with an impassioned condemnation of Iwamasa’s enabling, arguing that he should’ve tipped off family members to Perry’s ketamine abuse. Such is the function of “The One About Matthew Perry”: well-known headlines, reframed through the lesser-known perspective of those deeply affected.
All three episodes of “The One About Matthew Perry” are now streaming on Netflix.

items.title: Errol Morris Is Sitting on a Secret Elizabeth Holmes Interview (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: “I have this problem,” shares Errol Morris, the Oscar-winning documentary filmmaker behind “The Thin Blue Line,” “The Fog of War” and countless other renowned docs. You see, the 78-year-old can’t seem to screen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s docu-phenome
items.author: Marlow Stern
paragraphs: “I have this problem,” shares Errol Morris, the Oscar-winning documentary filmmaker behind “The Thin Blue Line,” “The Fog of War” and countless other renowned docs. You see, the 78-year-old can’t seem to screen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s docu-phenomenon on Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything.” He claims to have contacted the appropriate parties but has thus far been rebuffed. “Can you get me a screener?” he pleads. (I cannot.)

What Morris did do, however, was finally watch Alex Gibney’s 2019 documentary on Holmes and her sham blood-testing company Theranos — “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley” — for the very first time.

Morris, who’s directed “probably 1,000” commercials for various companies, was hired by Holmes in 2015 to shoot a series of ads for Theranos that depicted the “founder” staring wide-eyed into the camera that have attracted criticism for contributing to her mythmaking. Morris says he doesn’t know how Gibney got ahold of extra footage from the ads to use in “The Inventor,” but that’s not all: Morris exclusively revealed to Variety that he actually conducted a two-hour Interrotron interview with Holmes that he’s contemplating releasing in light of the renewed interest around the infamous grifter.
So, I understand you have not seen “You Can See Everything,” but recently watched Alex Gibney’s documentary on Elizabeth Holmes, “The Inventor,” for the very first time.
I never really wanted to see it until recently for a variety of different reasons, and I was quite surprised to find out that I was in it.
He used outtakes from your Theranos ads, right?

Well, what’s really not known about any of this is, yes, I did all the advertising for Theranos, but I did it at a time when Elizabeth Holmes was on the front cover of Forbes and many other magazines. She was riding high, and this was before everything collapsed. Did I have any reason to believe that she was a fraud? I did not. Did that change as time went on? It did. I had tried very hard, over a number of years, to do a documentary on Elizabeth Holmes and it would have happened except that she was under indictment. There was massive litigation going on.
You wanted to interview Holmes for a documentary?

I asked her, at a certain point, if I could film an interview with her — and this is at the height of her success — and I did film a two-hour interview with her, which is not very well-known if it is known at all. And I just watched that. I am sincerely interested in putting that out as an unedited film.

If anything, it gives you a comparison of Elizabeth before and Elizabeth after, which I think is interesting in and of itself. I noticed that the Gibney film begins and ends with my interview with Elizabeth Holmes.
This two-hour interview you conducted with Holmes has not been seen by anyone other than yourself?

Well, myself and the people in my office, but yes, for all intents and purposes, it has not been seen by anyone. Let me ask you a fast question: Why do you think [“You Can See Everything”] has proven so popular?

I think it touches on a lot of different things that fascinate the culture — grifters, self-delusion to the point where the person created a persona that incorporated a fake Yoda voice, true crime and Silicon Valley megalomania channeled through the prism of Nathan Fielder’s brand of awkward comedy that pits, to borrow from John Ganz, a neurotic against a psychotic.

Well, it’s hard for me to tell you about the film having not yet seen it, but I can tell you what I think about Elizabeth Holmes having spent a considerable amount of time with her. I was interviewed by John Carreyrou recently for an article that subsequently appeared in The New York Times, and he was questioning me about something I’d said to him many, many years ago when I was considering making a documentary about Elizabeth Holmes and had asked him if he would participate in that documentary. Some people see these stories as an on/off switch of she’s innocent or she’s guilty, she’s lying or she’s telling the truth. And when you’re investigating a crime, part of that investigation has to be if the person is guilty or innocent, since the criminal justice system works in such a way that you are looking for some kind of result. But what interests me is: To what extent was she self-deceived? To what extent did she believe in her own bullshit? Carreyrou understandably wants to tell you that she knowingly committed fraud, is guilty, should have been convicted and is in prison, as she should be. I keep wondering about the psychology of self-deception because part of me believes that she believes in Theranos and that she could achieve the results as promised.
Aren’t there, say, serial killers who are convinced that what they’re doing is right and just? And isn’t it more about the people you hurt along the way?

Yes, it is. You could say that lots of people in Silicon Valley misrepresent or out-and-out lie about what their technology can achieve, but in this case it involved medical results and people whose lives are directly affected by those medical results, and that in itself makes it different.
One example of a lie would be that she’d claimed Theranos had a Department of Defense contract and its blood-testing technology was being deployed on the battlefield, none of which was true.

Now, we can get into a philosophical discussion of the nature of lying and what is a lie, and did she lie in a very clear sense? Yes. Many, many times. Did she see them as lies? That is of interest to me.

I want to ask you about something you’d said during a Reddit Q&A after Holmes’ house of cards collapsed: “When everything fell apart, I was shocked because I believed in Elizabeth Holmes. I feel, rightly or wrongly, that most of the television programs and movies about her have missed the mark. Did she do bad things? Most assuredly. The question remains, why?” You then drew a comparison between her and Joan of Arc.
Probably the Robert Bresson “Joan of Arc,” which is one of my very favorite films.
But Elizabeth Holmes wasn’t burned at the stake. She’s serving some time in prison for defrauding people.
The nature of her punishment is not similar to being burned at the stake, and if you thought that’s what I meant by it, I did not.
You were drawing that comparison in regard to their self-deception.

One thing I can say about Joan of Arc: Do I think that God was speaking to her? I have a confession to make: I don’t believe in God. Do I think that God exists? No, I don’t! Do I think that God was directly communicating with Joan of Arc? I don’t! Do I think she thought that God was directly communicating with her? She did! She went to the stake on the basis of it. That’s your comparison.
Going back to those Theranos promos you shot with her—

—Don’t call them promos! I was hired as a commercial director, and I’ve shot probably 1,000 commercials. In the Gibney documentary, it is mentioned that Elizabeth Holmes and Patrick O’Neill, who was her CCO, had hired me because of the many Apple commercials I’d directed for Steve Jobs. If I had known how much of my interview was being used [by Gibney], or even if it was being used at all, I’m not sure what I would have said. I knew it was being used, but I never really wanted to watch [“The Inventor”]. Maybe I’d just had enough of it.
How did Gibney get ahold of the footage?
This I do not know. I really don’t know. And I’m not being coy or cagey. I do not know.

I know the commercials you shot for Holmes and Theranos have garnered quite a bit of criticism for contributing to her mystique, but I found Holmes quite creepy in those commercials. How do you feel about people’s perception of those commercials?

People have never seen my long interview that I did with Elizabeth Holmes. I’ve heard that I have been accused of representing a fraud — knowingly — and this is just not true. I’ll join a lot of other people who were on the Theranos board at the time that I was doing this series of commercials.
Are you sure you want to join Henry Kissinger? I’m joking.
I actually interviewed Henry Kissinger just before he died.
Is that going to go anywhere?
It might. I have so much stuff that I do nothing with.
I’d heard a very funny story about how BP approached you to direct an ad for them following the Deepwater Horizon oil spill and that you proposed a wild idea that they turned down.
You tell me and I’ll tell you if it’s real!
That Mel Gibson would be standing on a BP oil platform and say something to the effect of, “If anyone knows about a public relations disaster, it’s me.”

That’s it! And of course, they said no. Fortunately, enough people have said yes over the years, but I can’t tell you how many people have said no. I once said to my producer for commercials, “You know, I get all these commercials, but I’ve never gotten diarrhea or erectile dysfunction commercials. What’s wrong with me?” I once got a Depend commercial, and my ideas for incontinence/Depend commercials were by and large rejected.
What was one of those ideas that you really liked?

Thank you for asking. I had just done a long interview with Janis Karpinski, who’d just been demoted in connection with Abu Ghraib — and this interview has never seen the light of day — so there’s this lady general inside a tank in a war zone. Shells are exploding all around. The tank is on maneuvers. We see the face of the lady general inside the tank. She has an enormously pinched expression. She is fidgety, edgy. And then, you hear the sound of running water, and the expression on her face changes to one of total relaxation and pleasure. And then we cut outside and we see the artillery exploding. Depend.
The guy who was producing the commercials to Depend put his face two inches away from mine and said, “THERE IS NOTHING, NOTHING FUNNY ABOUT INCONTINENCE!” And I said, “I guess I beg to differ.”
I’m with you on that one. By the way, why did your two-hour Elizabeth Holmes interview never come out?

Because the company fell apart and she was prosecuted… but I can’t really answer it. The clearest answer is that I’d moved on. But now I feel pretty strongly that this is an interesting document — not because I’m trying to prove something about Elizabeth Holmes, but it does provide some kind of evidence of what she was like when everything was going her way.
And what is your takeaway after watching the interview?
That she was a true believer.

items.title: ‘One of Them Days’ Filmmaker Lawrence Lamont to Direct Ice Cube’s Newest ‘Friday’ Comedy (Exclusive)
items.description: Lawrence Lamont is about to find out that a lot can go down between Thursday and Saturday.
items.author: Borys Kit
paragraphs: Lawrence Lamont is about to find out that a lot can go down between Thursday and Saturday.
Lamont, who made a splash last year with One of Them Days, has been tapped to direct Last Friday, the first installment of New Line’s buddy comedy movie franchise in 25 years.
Ice Cube, who co-created the movie series, is writing the script and producing, and will also star in the feature. Also producing are Bob Teitel and CubeVision’s Michael Gruber.

The first Friday was directed by F. Gary Gray and featured Cube and Chris Tucker as slacker Craig Jones and small-time drug dealer Smokey respectively as they faced increasing problems with jobs, girlfriends, exes, family, death threats, all in the streets of South Central Los Angeles. Cube wrote the script with DJ Pooh.

The movie was released in 1995, became a cult hit, and spawned sequels Next Friday, released in 2000, and Friday After Next, which came out in 2002. Cube wrote the sequels solo and starred in all three movies (Tucker only starred in the first one.) There was also an animated series, Friday: The Animated Series, which briefly aired on MTV2 in the aughts.

The new feature will be shot in Southern California and is part of the California production incentive program. New Line received $11.4 million to shoot Last Friday in state, with the project planning for 40 filming days and expecting 43 cast members and 150 crew.
Jeff Kwatinetz is executive producing.

Lamont first gained recognition directing music videos for longtime collaborator Big Sean, including “I Don’t F*** With You,” “Twenty88,” and “On Up.” He went on to work with artists such as J. Cole, Jhené Aiko, Snoop Dogg, and Nas. He received an MTV Video Music Award nomination for best hip-hop video for “I Don’t F*** With You” and won an MTV Video Music Award for his video “Light.”

He made his directorial debut with One of Them Days, which has thematic cross-over with Friday as it too was a buddy comedy set in an glamorous part of L.A., with this story centered on two female friends.

Starring Keke Palmer and SZA, the $14 million TriStar Pictures film grossed more than $51 million worldwide and later reached No. 1 on Netflix, holding the top spot for four consecutive weeks. Lamont received the AAFCA Breakthrough Director Award for the film and earned an NAACP Image Award nomination for outstanding directing in a motion picture.
Lamont is repped by WME, ColorCreative and Johnson Shapiro.

items.title: Yes, You Can Still See ‘Musk’ — Here’s What’s Happening With the Film’s Release Plan
items.description: Musk, Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary about the titular mogul and his growing power, is coming to VOD earlier than expected — but hardly being disappeared from the landscape.
items.author: Steven Zeitchik
paragraphs: Musk, Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary about the titular mogul and his growing power, is coming to VOD earlier than expected — but hardly being disappeared from the landscape.

While some headlines this weekend had suggested the movie was being “pulled,” distributor Bleecker Street is simply preparing to announce a new plan that will give the movie a somewhat shorter runway in theaters and a longer one on VOD.

Originally scheduled for a Nov. 24 debut on paid platforms, the movie will now come to paid VOD on Nov. 6. It will continue to play in theaters until then; after playing on 60 screens last weekend, it will be in an as-yet-undetermined number this weekend. Simultaneous plays in theaters after the VOD release are also possible, a company representative said.

Bleecker Street also reports that preorders on VOD are strong; indeed, Apple’s top 50 VOD orders for the current week include just two movies that have not been released yet: The Odyssey at No. 10 and Musk at No. 24. Those films land at No. 1 and 2, respectively, on the company’s preorder chart.

The film has grossed $650,000 in theaters since its release on Oct. 9, which works out to about 40,000 tickets sold — a number certainly small by many theatrical expectations, but hardly unexpected for a four-hour investigative documentary. A 28-day theatrical window for a documentary before it moves to VOD is also not unusually truncated.

The film remains on course to debut on HBO platforms this winter, even as Musk associate David Ellison has now acquired the network. The VOD move-up also extends the amount of time many Americans can see the film should any attempt to censor or stop that release materialize.

Gibney’s movie looks at how its subject came to amass so much power and how he has expanded it in the Donald Trump era via DOGE cuts, surveillance, media and broadband takeovers and donations to the Republican Party. With the news that he is investing $1 billion in Skydance and with unprecedented levels of contributions to swing midterm races to Republicans, Musk has become a figure increasingly central to the American political and media landscape.

As it has rolled out to theaters, Musk has also been hit by social media bans as well as theater-screen competition from the doc phenom You Can See Everything, though comparing the two films would be like comparing a smoothie to a Hershey bar; each provides a different kind of benefit.

items.title: Lego Has Hired a Hollywood Whisperer
items.description: The Lego Group is bringing on an in-house Hollywood whisperer.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: The Lego Group is bringing on an in-house Hollywood whisperer.

The Danish toy giant has hired WME veteran Kelsey Gray Sherman as head of celebrity talent and brand first partnerships, where she will work with Hollywood talent (and their agents and managers) and develop opportunities for Lego in entertainment projects and brand campaigns. She will also be tasked with developing relationships with brands that stretch beyond licensing and product collaborations.

Sherman joins Lego from WME, where she had been vp in the agency’s entertainment marketing & advisory group, leading talent partnerships and strategies for major global brands including McDonald’s, Visa, Amazon and Lego.
She will report to Jill Wilfert, senior vp entertainment, partnerships and content at Lego.

“Kelsey brings deep relationships across the talent and entertainment communities, along with a strong understanding of the Lego brand,” said Wilfert. “She knows how to bring together the right talent, partners and ideas in ways that feel fresh and authentic, and her experience and instincts will be invaluable as we continue to grow our work in entertainment and culture.”

“Having worked closely with the Lego Group for many years, I’ve seen firsthand its unique ability to bring together entertainment, experiences and culture,” added Sherman. “I’m excited to build on that strength through ambitious, distinctive partnerships with exceptional talent and brands. Together, we can create new ways to inspire creativity and play and connect with audiences around the world.”

items.title: R.J. Mitte’s Mother Shares Tribute After His Death: “We Are Lost Without Him”
items.description: Dyna Mitte is paying tribute to R.J. Mitte 15 days after discovering her son at his Texas home after he took his own life at age 34.
items.author: Jackie Strause
paragraphs: Dyna Mitte is paying tribute to R.J. Mitte 15 days after discovering her son at his Texas home after he took his own life at age 34.

“We are lost without him, yet we know he wouldn’t want us to be,” Dyna wrote about the Breaking Bad actor and activist in a social media post on Tuesday. “He would want his message heard and the work we were doing with The Mitte Foundation in Brownsville to continue.”

In her touching tribute posted to Instagram, Dyna wrote, “What can I say about my precious child? From the day we got RJ at 3 days old, he has been inspiring and sharing his heart with everyone he met. Whether he was learning to manage and later thrive with cerebral palsy or finding his way in the acting community, it required hard work, but he succeeded and was always ready for the next challenge. It became a joy watching his way with people, the way he naturally lit up in every room he entered and instantly charmed his way into people’s lives like they were family.”

R.J. Mitte was remembered earlier this month during an Oct. 16 Celebration of Life ceremony at the Mitte Center in Brownsville, Texas, where hundreds filled the seats and an overflow building to share tributes. The family was working on another celebration of life in Los Angeles at the end of the month, Dyna recently said in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter around that time, where she said she was speaking out in hopes of reaching anyone else who might be struggling.

“It’s important for parents to realize that there may be big signs or small signs. If you notice, even in conversation, that there are struggles or questions, be really in tune with your children and take the steps you can to help,” she said. “I thought R.J. was in a place where we had gotten over the hump and that he was OK. It wasn’t until he didn’t answer the phone that I recognized it as a red flag, because we talked regularly.”

She also clarified that her son was doing well in his career, quieting speculation suggesting otherwise. “R.J. had three movies that have already come out this year. He has two more coming out,” she told THR. “He has already signed deals on several new movies that he was going to be filming. There were talks of different things. He had a book coming out. He had a food truck he was starting. He had a lot going on.”
Read her full tribute below.

What can I say about my precious child? From the day we got RJ at 3 days old, he has been inspiring and sharing his heart with everyone he met. Whether he was learning to manage and later thrive with cerebral palsy or finding his way in the acting community, it required hard work, but he succeeded and was always ready for the next challenge. It became a joy watching his way with people, the way he naturally lit up in every room he entered and instantly charmed his way into people’s lives like they were family.

Life with RJ was a constant adventure. The places we traveled for his acting and appearances, though for work, he always made them fun. From Florida to Lithuania, he knew all the historical facts and places we should see, and we would always go just to satisfy his neverending curiosity. I can never express how proud I was of everything he overcame to become the man the world was just beginning to know. The years he spent advocating developed a deep empathy for those who needed him to be their voice and it was never a burden, but a role he loved to play. We are lost without him, yet we know he wouldn’t want us to be. He would want his message heard and the work we were doing with The Mitte Foundation in Brownsville to continue.

In time, I will get back to everyone who has reached out and shared their stories about RJ. Please know I’m seeing them and appreciate how much he meant to you all. My son was an incredibly special and sensitive soul who did so much for his family, his community, and the world, and we will mourn him for the rest of our days.

items.title: ‘I’m Addicted to Buying Loose Diamonds on TikTok’
items.description: When I open TikTok on a Wednesday afternoon, a young woman with a bejeweled nose ring is yelling at me to buy the three-karat diamond she’s holding between pliers. “Chat, this is a $3,000 stone. Someone better snipe this. It looks like crushed ice.” She introd
items.author: Emma Childs
paragraphs: When I open TikTok on a Wednesday afternoon, a young woman with a bejeweled nose ring is yelling at me to buy the three-karat diamond she’s holding between pliers. “Chat, this is a $3,000 stone. Someone better snipe this. It looks like crushed ice.” She introduces herself as Katie from True Carat Jewelry. Behind her are headless busts wearing sparkly necklaces, and Rae Sremmurd’s “No Flex Zone” plays on a speaker out of view. “Let’s run it,” Katie says. A box pops up at the bottom of my screen indicating that bidding starts at $1, and the battle begins in three, two, one … go. There’s a frenzy of usernames placing bid after bid, racketing the price up, up, up, until it’s over 20 seconds later and someone named Kira from Alabama wins at $317. “We can’t do any more steals like that,” Katie says. “Congrats, Kira, it’s yours.”

TikTok Shop live auctions stream at almost all hours of the day, with viewer counts in the low to high hundreds, and lately the most talked-abouts ones are happening in the DiamondTok corner of your FYP. “They’re the girl version of fantasy football,” says Chloe, a 33-year-old woman who’s scored over 20 diamonds on the clock app and requested to use her first name only. “Only they’re more addicting: With fantasy leagues, you have to wait until the end of the game to know if you win; this is gambling in 30 seconds.” Mia Rae Vorburger, 35, doesn’t gamble — “I don’t like the feeling of losing the money” — so she compares winning a TikTok diamond auction to opening a Pop Mart Crybaby blind box and discovering it’s the one you wanted.

Sometimes a celebrity like Jordyn Woods is in the mix, outbidding a regular person by a few bucks. Sellers present papers from the International Gemological Institute, the world’s largest laboratory for certifying diamonds, but offer no information on where their boatloads of stones come from. (They’re all lab grown, by the way.) The most you get is an offhand note that “new shipment from India just dropped.” That the stones are synthetic is of no concern to shoppers. “There are only, like, 20 natural red diamonds that have ever existed, and they’re almost all under a karat and sold at Sotheby’s auctions for millions and millions of dollars,” says Ryan Roth, a 28-year-old content creator who has been posting about his “loose-diamond addiction” since August. “Now you can buy one on TikTok for 200 bucks.” Roth owns 22 lab-grown stones: Some he won at auction himself; others were gifted by TikTok Shop sellers.

Every aspect of these livestreams is designed to get you to bid with abandon, of course. At best, the auctioneer’s vibe is high-spirited QVC host; at worst, the smarmy dude from high school offering to “hook you up with a special deal.” They toss around marketing lingo and blast high-bpm music to get your heart rate bumping. They use bright lights to make their gems extra sparkly and rave about how beautiful the stone will look on a gold band, conveniently leaving out that setting is a separate process that’ll cost you, at the very least, $1,000 at a jeweler. And they certainly don’t remind you that all purchases made via a TikTok’s live-auction feature are final sale.

“With some of the stones I’ve purchased, I’m not even looking at them,” says Vorburger. “The auctions show up on my ‘For You’ page, I get overcome with excitement, and I bid, not expecting to win. But then I do and I’m like, Oh, shit. Now I have all these loose stones.” So far, she’s had one TikTok diamond set into a 14-karat-gold-plated pinkie ring through an Etsy company. (Coincidentally, the night before our call, she dropped the ring and the diamond popped out of its setting: “It’s fine. I just have to go get it fixed now.”) Vorburger plans to set her other stones as “future projects” but isn’t in a rush. “I’m not looking to make them into items I’ll pass down to children, grandchildren, nieces, nephews. I’m just having fun,” she says.

Some buyers aren’t interested in setting their stones at all. In a DiamondTok group chat Chloe belongs to, members discuss the best display cases to display their loose stones. “I’ve seen somebody say, ‘Oh, I created an Excel spreadsheet to log my inventory.’ I’ll ask, ‘What have you set, or what are you looking to set?’ And they’re like, ‘I’m just collecting for now.’’’ Roth regularly gets comments from people who say they are “buying 50, 75, 100 stones” and are “4k down the hole.” Other shoppers, like 30-year-old designer Leslie Levis, go into auctions with the jewelry they want to make in mind. “Humans like shiny objects,” says Levis, who set a 1.43-karat marquise diamond, won at $235, into a stunning gold pinkie ring for $1,257. “I imagine it’s fun to feel like a little dragon with your big pile of diamonds. But my soapbox hopes are that people are discerning with their bidding and feel a creativity spark in terms of setting a stone, as opposed to having a hoarding mind-set.”

For others, though, it’s now time to log off of DiamondTok entirely. “The shine is wearing off the penny very quickly,” says Laurie, a retired 63-year-old woman using a pseudonym, who bought 15 TikTok stones and has had six made into jewelry. She requested anonymity in part because her husband doesn’t know the full extent of her hobby: “If he knew I bought them all through TikTok, he’d think I was crazy.” Laurie recently removed her credit-card information from TikTok and plans to give her remaining nine diamonds out as Christmas gifts. “I’ve reached the point of saturation,” she says. “I mean, how many pieces does one person need? I can’t buy any more loose stones.”

items.title: Blood, Sweat, Tears, and Ink: Tite Kubo, Creator of "BLEACH"
items.description: Blood, Sweat, Tears, and Ink: Tite Kubo, Creator of "BLEACH"
items.author: Hypebeast Newsroom
paragraphs: Blood, Sweat, Tears, and Ink: Tite Kubo, Creator of "BLEACH"
Blood, Sweat, Tears, and Ink:
Tite Kubo, Creator of “BLEACH”
Over a decade after the manga and anime’s conclusion, BLEACH remains a global pop culture touchstone.
For our cover story of Hypebeast Magazine Issue #38, we spoke to its creator, Tite Kubo, about what it takes to create one of the most successful series of all time.

What does it take to create one of the most successful manga and anime titles of all time? Near-insanity and not a lot of sleep, it seems. Just ask Tite Kubo, the creator of the 130-million-copy-selling series BLEACH, who prefers to show rather than tell through his thrilling hand-inked panels. It also doesn’t hurt that Kubo has a keen eye for gory theatrics, character complexity, an iron-clad work ethic, and knows when to give fans what they want… and when to make them wait for it, too.

Over fifteen years of its print serialization, BLEACH became such a cultural touchstone that even the manga-averse came to recognize the series’ orange-haired protagonist Ichigo Kurosaki’s menacing glare. It’s the blueprint for the modern fighting genre, influencing successors like Demon Slayer and Jujutsu Kaisen, which both picked up its mantle and sales popularity since BLEACH’s manga run ended in 2016. In Kubo’s words: “The creators of those series have told me they were influenced by BLEACH… I don’t think influence is something that flows in only one direction. It’s something that’s passed from one generation of creators to the next.”

Following the success of the manga, the original anime adaptation of BLEACH debuted in 2004 and ran until 2012. It was followed by the Thousand-Year Blood War series which premiered in October 2022. Now the series is back with BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War – The Calamity, a ten-episode rollout, primed to tie up any loose ends for fans still needing closure and another taste of Kubo’s iconic storytelling.

But first, a little context for the less familiar: BLEACH chronicles the adventures of Ichigo, a punk-with-a-heart-of-gold high schooler who can see the spirits of the deceased. He begins work as a death god (called a Shinigami, a profession somewhat similar to the Grim Reaper), after another reaper named Rukia transfers her powers to him. Shinigami purify souls called Hollows, then send the purified souls to Soul Society (aka the afterlife), usually through an intense showdown. They guide ordinary departed spirits to Soul Society, too.

Aside from satisfying the tropes of the shōnen genre (manga intended for young boys but popular today with everyone) — a fearless protagonist who always wins, a pantheon of muscular villains, the triumph of good over evil, plus a lot of schoolgirls, demons, boobs, and swords — BLEACH is unique in that it dips into the existential.

In Kubo’s words: “Originally, I was actually more interested in depicting people’s emotions than action.” Beyond the immediate satisfaction of battle sequences, many have analyzed the series as a retelling of the Buddha’s path to enlightenment, with Ichigo as a Buddha figure fighting it out in different realms. While others have also noted that the series draws upon imagery from traditional Japanese and Mexican folktales. Regardless of the inspiration, Ichigo is not your typical happy-go-lucky protagonist. If anything, he is an anti-hero who reluctantly heeds the call to bring spirits out of misery, with a dash of hot-headedness and detachment, mixed with unwavering loyalty to his loved ones. If you take away any lesson from this explanation of why this series hits, it would be that BLEACH satisfies both highbrow and lowbrow motivations. Essential when attempting to devour a 686-chapter manga.

Also, simply put, BLEACH looks cool. The series functions less like a straightforward action series and more like a pop-culture mood board referencing what Kubo loves: music and fashion. General telltale Kubo-isms include sparse backgrounds, intense shadows, angular linework, and some very good fits. Unlike other popular shōnen, there’s an emphasis on each character’s styling, with punk and Y2K streetwear fashion cues. Kubo says he finds inspiration from street style as well as things he’d like to wear in real life, but couldn’t find — coupled with inspiration from runway shows from Maison Margiela and Dior. Music runs through the series just as visibly; chapters are titled after songs and albums by bands like AC/DC, Oasis, and the Rolling Stones, which makes sense as rock is Kubo’s soundtrack of choice when drawing.
“Once I truly love something, I’ll continue loving it for the rest of my life.” – Tite Kubo

Being a mangaka in Japan is a highly idealized profession for school-age kids. In Kubo’s case, he decided to pursue the path in elementary school and followed through with it shortly after high school. But once your prefrontal cortex develops and the realities of the job set in, many drop out. It’s a vocation with one day off a week and a new chapter due every seven days, forcing creators to frequently sleep in their offices overnight. Pressure from devoted fanbases alongside publishers to deliver something bankable, lest the series be pulled, has historically caused a fair share of burnout for mangaka and even some premature deaths.

In our interview, Tite Kubo (also known by his birth name, Noriaki Kubo) doesn’t take the stance of complaining about it, though. The 49-year-old remains equanimous. He subtly remarks on the hazards of the job and how, at times, its demands make it difficult to continue. “It wasn’t a particularly healthy lifestyle,” Kubo says with a placid grin. “I would stay awake until late at night, go to sleep around four or five in the morning, and wake up at about eleven.” His drafting schedule for BLEACH was equally demanding. Kubo elaborates: “I would spend about three days developing the story and creating the name, or storyboard, then another three days drawing the finished pages, and take the remaining day off.” This August coinciding with BLEACH the manga’s 25th anniversary, Kubo and the anime’s separate team regroup and elaborate where the serialization left off, with BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War – The Calamity, to give fans something new after years of waiting.

BLEACH’s reach goes beyond manga and anime into other art forms, with cultural crossovers that prove Kubo is a titan, not just a bestselling author. In the realm of fashion, Kubo worked alongside John Galliano to create original illustrations and store display graphics for Maison Margiela’s Artisanal 2024 Collection, presented at Dover Street Market. PUMA marked the series’ 20th anniversary with an Ichigo and Grimmjow sneaker collection, and ASICS made a limited-edition sneaker inspired by the series that same year. Hip-hop artists like ZillaKami and Denzel Curry have referenced the series in their music. Combined with commercial tie-ins like limited-edition Coca-Cola packaging, these crossovers have cemented Kubo’s work as something even non-readers can identify on sight.

Kubo’s Tokyo studio is filled to its breaking point with sketches, books, and an entire wall-sized shelf of CDs, sprinkled with Bon Jovi and Gorillaz memorabilia. He sits quietly confident amid this organized chaos, with a youthful appearance perhaps a result of long hours spent out of the sun and in the studio. Throughout our interview, Kubo speaks with an ease that suggests fame hasn’t dented his humility or overwhelmed him in the slightest. Against a cityscape befitting of one of Manga’s most successful creators, he further spills creative juice on why the series endures, the mechanics of bringing a manga to life, and why reviving BLEACH felt necessary.
HYPEBEAST: BLEACH was serialized weekly for many years. How did you decide what would happen in each chapter? Which elements were planned far in advance, and which were decided week by week?

Tite Kubo: I had a long-term plan for the overall story. I had also decided on the ending very early in the series. BLEACH begins with Ichigo and Rukia meeting, and ends with Ichigo’s child and Rukia’s child meeting. I structured the entire story so that everything would gradually converge toward that ending. Each week, I would make sure to include at least one scene that I genuinely wanted to draw, and then construct the rest of the chapter around the path leading to that moment.
Did the production team become much larger as the series progressed? What are the difficulties involved in expanding a manga production team?

The team never became particularly large [laughs]. The original three assistants worked with me from almost the beginning of the series all the way through to the end. Later in the serialization, we added a fourth assistant, so we became a team of four. This person changed a few times over the course of the serialization. Other than that, very little changed.

When you add another person, you first need to prepare a workspace for them. There is also the question of whether the assistants get along with one another [laughs]. From a technical standpoint, someone also needs to have reached a certain level before you can immediately entrust them with the work.
“I don’t think influence is something that flows in only one direction.” – Tite Kubo

For many readers, the daily reality of being a manga artist is difficult to imagine. What did a typical day or week look like during serialization? Did your working style change as BLEACH became more successful?

It wasn’t a particularly healthy lifestyle. I would stay awake until late at night, go to sleep around four or five in the morning, and wake up at about eleven. That said, I’m someone who needs sleep, so even during serialization I always made sure to get at least six hours. I think I would have struggled much more mentally if I hadn’t slept properly.

I wasn’t drawing continuously for every hour that I was awake. I’m not someone who can maintain concentration for long stretches, so I would focus intensely for a short period, draw as much as I could, and then rest my mind for a while. I repeated that cycle throughout the day.

Even after BLEACH became successful, my basic routine didn’t really change. But as the series became more popular, I received more requests for things like color pages and cover illustrations, so gradually I had less and less free time.

As a general weekly schedule, I would spend about three days developing the story and creating the name, or storyboard, then another three days drawing the finished pages, and take the remaining day off. At my fastest, I could ink around 15 pages in a single day. I think most artists would manage around five, so I was probably quite fast.
Was there a period during the fifteen-year-long weekly serialization that you found particularly difficult?

The hardest times were when I was physically unwell but still had to keep drawing. Back then, Weekly Shonen Jump wasn’t the kind of place where you could easily take a break just because you had a cold. I imagine things are different today, but in my time, taking a hiatus simply wasn’t something that happened very often.
I remember catching the flu once and telling them, “I really can’t do it this time.” Even then, the editor-in-chief called me and asked, “Are you sure it’s actually influenza?” [laughs].

Emotionally, I also found it difficult whenever Ichigo was going through particularly dark moments. During the Lost Agent Arc, just before the final storyline, Ichigo was pushed to his emotional limits. It happened to be around that same time that my own health started to decline.

Until then, I didn’t think I was the type of creator who absorbed my protagonist’s emotions. But that experience made me realize that I was far more affected by Ichigo’s mental state than I had ever imagined.

During the long serialization of BLEACH, you received an anonymous letter from a seriously ill child that urged you to continue the series and end it the way you wanted to, without compromise. How did that letter affect you?

After many years of serialization, I was going through a period when my health had deteriorated. The letter arrived during that time, and it gave me a reason to keep pushing forward and continue drawing until the end. It became a major source of support. I believe the letter arrived sometime during the final arc.

Three months after the serialization ended, I publicly asked for information, and that was how we were eventually connected. Later, I was able to get in touch with one of the child’s friends, and I was also able to send a message in return to his family.
BLEACH really stands out for the fashion the cast wears. When designing the characters’ clothing, what kinds of styles, subcultures, brands, or fashion influences did you draw from?

Because the series ran for such a long time, the things that influenced me naturally changed from one era to another. But I tried not to consciously chase any particular brand or trend. It was more about combining things I saw on the street with things I saw in fashion shows. I would take elements I came across in everyday life, mix them with things I personally liked, and then filter everything through my own sensibility.

There was no particular city or neighborhood I always looked to for inspiration. I wanted to combine grounded, everyday clothing with the kinds of pieces you might see on a runway — things that do not necessarily exist in ordinary life. And when something did not exist exactly as I imagined it, I would redesign it in my own way and put it on the character.
People often say that Ichigo and the other characters’ personal style reflects your own taste in fashion. Is that true?

Yes, definitely. Sometimes I would put a shirt on a character that I had actually bought for myself as the basis for a design. Other times, I would see something and think, “This is great, but it probably would not suit me,” so I would let one of the characters wear it instead. In that sense, the characters became a way for me to express both the things I wanted to wear and the things I admired but could not necessarily wear myself.
“Inspiration can come from the most ordinary things.” – Tite Kubo
Which fashion brands or designers are you particularly drawn to at the moment?

Right now, I like Maison Margiela, Dior, and LOEWE. I tend to follow designers rather than brands. So when a designer moves to another house, I often find myself following them there. The reason I recently started buying Dior again is because Jonathan Anderson moved there.
And the reason I originally started buying LOEWE was because Jonathan Anderson was there. Then, before I knew it, he had moved on [laughs]. I still like LOEWE, of course, even after his departure.
In your everyday life, what inspires your creativity? And how do you avoid burning out after creating for so many years?

I’ve never really thought about it consciously. Books were actually the first medium I ever fell in love with as a child. I’m the kind of person who believes that once I truly love something, I’ll continue loving it for the rest of my life, so I still enjoy reading today.

Music has always inspired me, as well. But inspiration can come from the most ordinary things — something I notice while shopping, or even something I happen to see on social media. If I had to name one influence, I’d say Gorillaz. I loved their music, but I was equally inspired by Jamie Hewlett’s artwork.
Looking back, why do you think BLEACH became such a distinctive series compared to other manga of its time?

The most important thing to me when creating characters is giving them multiple dimensions. People are inherently complex. Even cheerful people have darker sides, and even those with a strong sense of justice experience doubt and weakness.
Ichigo was never intended to be a simple, straightforward hero. From the very beginning, I wanted every character to feel like a real person with different layers to their personality.
Many readers believe BLEACH established a blueprint that has influenced a new generation of manga. Do you see it that way, and if so, what do you think that blueprint is?
People often say that the captains of the Gotei 13 influenced the Hashira in Demon Slayer, or that concepts like Bankai inspired aspects of Jujutsu Kaisen.

The creators of those series have told me that they were influenced by BLEACH, so I think it’s fair to say that influence exists. But I don’t think influence is something that flows in only one direction. It’s something that’s passed from one generation of creators to the next.

When I was a child, I absolutely loved the anime Saint Seiya. The Gold Saints left a huge impression on me, and the Gotei 13 captains were my own interpretation of that kind of powerful ensemble cast.

That’s how creativity evolves. Every generation of creators absorbs ideas from the works they admire, reinterprets them through their own perspective, and transforms them into something entirely new. That’s what influence has always been.
Since your debut in 1996, how do you think the manga industry has changed? In particular, how do you view the rise of self-publishing and online platforms?
I think it has become much easier for new artists to enter the industry and compete, and I see that as a very positive development.

Ten or fifteen years ago, when people began posting their work online for free and using social media to build an audience, I remember thinking, “Is that really a good idea?” or “Isn’t it a waste to give your work away for free?”

But that was simply based on the way I thought at the time, and looking back, I was completely wrong [laughs]. Now there are far more ways for new creators to share their work and find readers. I think it has become a much more accessible environment.
What advice would you give to someone who wants to become a manga artist?

Compared to the past, it is much easier to pursue a career as a manga artist now. So I would encourage people to keep trying and take as many opportunities as they can. Manga artists can actually earn a more stable living than people might think [laughs].

Nearly a decade passed between the end of the original anime series and the adaptation of the final arc, Thousand-Year Blood War. Why did you decide to add new material that had not appeared in the manga?

Around ten years passed between the end of the previous anime series and the beginning of the new one. There were fans who had been waiting throughout that entire period, so I didn’t want to simply adapt the manga exactly as it was. I wanted to give them something more.

For that reason, we added parts that I had omitted when drawing the original manga, as well as elements that I hadn’t been able to fully depict at the time. There are new developments in every episode that even readers of the manga don’t already know, so I think they’ve been enjoying that.
What do you see as the biggest difference between the manga and anime versions of BLEACH?

The biggest difference is that anime has sound [laughs]. The pauses between lines and the rhythm of a scene inevitably feel different in animation than they do when you are reading manga. That is why I have remained closely involved in supervising the latest anime series, BLEACH: Thousand-Year Blood War, so that those differences do not become too pronounced.

items.title: Drake Gifted Rare 1986 Ferrari Testarossa Monospecchio for 40th Birthday
items.description: Drake celebrated his 40th birthday in New York City with a rare 1986 Ferrari Testarossa Monospecchio delivered curbside to Casa Cipriani
items.author: Joyce Li
paragraphs: Drake celebrated his 40th birthday in New York City with a rare 1986 Ferrari Testarossa Monospecchio delivered curbside to Casa Cipriani
The vintage red supercar was reportedly gifted to the artist by rapper Loe Shimmy with vehicle logistics coordinated by Pole Position Classics
The private Manhattan celebration hosted over 400 attendees alongside an impromptu stage performance by the Backstreet Boys

Ferrari took center stage for Drake’s milestone weekend as the artist received a vintage red 1986 Ferrari Testarossa Monospecchio outside Casa Cipriani in New York City. The rare collector’s car served as the centerpiece surprise during his 40th birthday celebration.

The iconic vehicle was reportedly gifted to Drake by rapper Loe Shimmy outside the party venue. Sourced and hand-delivered directly to Manhattan by classic car dealership Pole Position Classics, the 1986 Testarossa “Monospecchio” stands out as a prized collectible defined by its high-mounted single driver-side wing mirror and factory single-bolt knock-off wheels. Dressed in a sparkling black tuxedo jacket with wide-leg trousers, Drake posed alongside the red vehicle on the street before heading inside.

The automotive delivery highlighted a star-studded event that gathered more than 400 guests at the private club. Attendees were treated to a surprise stage appearance by Backstreet Boys members Nick Carter, Kevin Richardson, and Howie Dorough, who brought Drake on stage to perform “I Want It That Way”. Touching on the milestone during the night, Drake remarked to the crowd that “tonight is just about being alive, staying alive.” Alongside giveaways of Chanel and Hermès handbags, the evening featured a game show cash competition with prizes scaling up to $1 million USD.

items.title: Черника и голубика могут замедлять старение клеток
items.description: Северные ягоды могут замедлять клеточное старение и развитие фиброза
items.author: Виолетта Ефимова
paragraphs: Северные ягоды могут замедлять клеточное старение и развитие фиброза

Международная группа учёных с участием специалистов Сургутского государственного университета изучила свойства полифенолов северных ягод. Эксперименты показали, что эти вещества могут замедлять клеточное старение и препятствовать развитию фиброза — замещению нормальной ткани рубцовой. Результаты опубликованы в журнале Biomedicines.
Исследователи использовали ягоды, собранные в районе Сургута. Самый заметный эффект обнаружили у черники и голубики, однако изучали также клюкву и бруснику.

Основное внимание учёные уделили полифенолам — соединениям, которые растения вырабатывают для защиты от ультрафиолета, вредителей и болезней. Они также влияют на окраску и вкус плодов. Ранее исследования уже выявляли у полифенолов антиоксидантные и противовоспалительные свойства. Теперь учёные проверили, могут ли эти вещества влиять на процессы старения клеток и рубцевания тканей.

«Именно наши исследования установили возможность регуляции процессов сенесценции клеток и процессов фиброзирования ткани при воздействии полифенолов из черники, голубики, клюквы и брусники», — рассказала директор медицинского института СурГУ Людмила Коваленко.

Фиброз возникает, когда нормальная ткань замещается рубцовой. Он может развиваться в лёгких, печени, почках, кишечнике и сердце, в том числе на фоне хронического воспаления или повреждений. Особое внимание исследователи уделили фиброзу лёгких, который может возникать после пневмонии, при аутоиммунных и профессиональных заболеваниях, а также по неустановленным причинам.
По словам Коваленко, полифенолы северных ягод потенциально могут помочь контролировать развитие фиброза и снизить вероятность его возникновения.

В ближайшем будущем исследователи рассчитывают использовать изученные соединения при создании функциональных пищевых продуктов. В дальнейшем они надеются разработать на их основе препараты для лечения фиброза.

items.title: How Macron Destabilized France
items.description: Last weekend, mass riots erupted across France after weeks of protests by lycée students over underfunding and poor conditions in their schools. As the demonstrations grew, they expanded to include other groups, including those upset with the cost of living an
items.author: Isaac Chotiner
paragraphs: Last weekend, mass riots erupted across France after weeks of protests by lycée students over underfunding and poor conditions in their schools. As the demonstrations grew, they expanded to include other groups, including those upset with the cost of living and the Presidency of Emmanuel Macron, and rioters looting property and setting fires around Paris and other French cities. Macron’s second term ends next year, and even before the violence of last weekend, Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right party known as the National Rally, was, according to polls, his most likely successor. That appears to be even more true now, with Le Pen’s final-round opponent now likely to be Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a left-wing politician who has associated himself with the protest movement but who is also radically unpopular in the country at large.

I recently spoke by phone with Julian Jackson, an emeritus professor of modern French history at Queen Mary University of London, and the author of a number of books on French history, including the definitive biography of Charles de Gaulle, about the situation in France. During our conversation, which has been edited for length and clarity, we discussed what the riots mean for the political future of the country, why Macron’s Presidency is ending disastrously, and whether the riots will be understood as a hinge point of French history.
How much are the youth protests important in and of themselves, and how important are they because of what they symbolize about the state of the country?

That is a good way to think about it, because some events become important for what they represent, and these events are important because of what they reveal about a whole mass of anxieties and discontent in France today. But I think their importance has now become qualitatively metamorphosed, or changed, by what happened on Saturday with the rioting. So I think that’s created a qualitative change. We have moved from a protest that is revealing a lot of anxieties of the younger generation—and not just them, but also older generations—into a whole questioning about the functioning of the state or the government. I remember reading something saying that there will be a “before October 17th” and an “after October 17th.” And I think that may be slightly overdoing it, but it certainly transformed the political landscape.
You are referring specifically to the amount of violence that night?

Yes. But not just the violence. There was also the sense that the state was completely taken unawares and just had no control. It was like there was almost a void. There was a similar mood in 1968, actually, when de Gaulle’s No. 2, Édouard Balladur, described how he just had a sense that the state wasn’t able to do anything. And so I think there was that sense of a sort of void on that night, because people do need reassurance that they can be protected—their property and their lives. I was at a dinner party that evening just by chance, in Paris, and they were all, I think, fairly centrist, maybe slightly right of center, but totally not extremist people. And it was striking how one of them in particular was in a state of almost apoplectic fury. It was a bit like the way that some people wrote, after the Paris Commune of 1871, that this was a kind of Saturnalian, orgiastic, obscene uprising. And he talked in the same sort of language, that these people should just be shot. He meant the rioters, not the students, but what it showed me was a sort of class panic, a social panic, that that night created. And everywhere you go in France, people are terribly worried now about what’s going to happen next.
