You are suggesting that this could be seen as a hinge moment, and my first thought was that you meant it will be the moment when everyone looks back and says that this was when they knew Le Pen was going to come to power.

And then, when you were just describing that dinner party, I thought to myself, this is also going to be a reason, perhaps in their own minds, for people like that—centrist to right-of-center—to justify taking this giant step and voting for Le Pen.

Whether or not it’s pulled down the last obstacle to a lot of people accepting the idea that they could vote for this party or not, I think you’re right. I still won’t say that Marine Le Pen is definitely going to be elected. They’ve got six months to go, and a lot of things can happen. But obviously if you’re putting money on it, she will be elected, and the chances have obviously increased hugely as a result of what happened, not only because it will frighten people into voting for her but also because the only other person who’s been audible, really, in this moment is Mélenchon, on the extreme left. He had lost a bit of traction over the last two years, I think because of a number of things, partly because of antisemitism and partly just because he did seem to be slightly losing it and slightly a figure of the past. But this has definitely reinvigorated him.

And he obviously can’t defend the pillaging and looting on Saturday night, but he’s very clever. He says when he’s asked, Well, I’m not the government. It’s not for me to make a comment on that. I’m going to say that I think the students are at least legitimate in their demands, and I’m completely with them, and I will demonstrate with them. And it’s not for me to comment on the violence because that’s something the state should deal with. And it’s obviously a completely devious answer.

But what’s very interesting is that what you might call the centrist politicians have almost been completely inaudible over the last few days. They just don’t know what to say. So, yes, I think it is a radicalizing moment, but in both directions. I think it will win Mélenchon new support and win Marine Le Pen new support. So I agree with your skepticism. Who knows whether it’s a turning point, but it sort of feels like that at the moment.

And the way the French election works is that there’s a first round for the Presidential contenders and then the two front-runners go forward. And Le Pen is polling well against the centrist candidates in a possible final round, with small to medium leads. But she beats Mélenchon by over thirty points.

Absolutely. And all I would say about that is that if, and it is an if, a centrist candidate does get to the second round, at that point there’s a chance they could be in a position to actually win six months down the line, but we don’t know how long the impact of what happened on Saturday is going to go on because there are more demonstrations coming up, obviously. I had the sense, talking to people, that they’re living on a volcano and they’re sort of tiptoeing around, knowing that the government’s paralyzed, and it can’t do anything, so they just wait till the Presidential election. And there’s this sort of strange, ghostly expectancy, which is quite weird, a mixture of apprehension and fear.
You said the centrist candidates, from the socialist center-left to the center-right, seem somewhat paralyzed. Why?

Well, Mélenchon has been with the lycée a hundred per cent from Day One, they love him, and Le Pen basically says, We need order. Meanwhile, the centrists are not sure where to situate themselves. If they go too close to the school protesters, they seem to be legitimatizing disorder, but then if they go too close to supporting everything the police does, that is a problem, too. It is the classic problem of centrism when the two extremes are so voluble and actually convincing to their own constituencies, and also some of the centrists were in Macron’s government, so that is also a problem for them, and it is difficult for them to find their voice.

And the reason for that is that the one thing you cannot underestimate at this moment is the cold contempt everyone has for Macron. I have not met a person who has anything good to say about Macron. Actually, I had lunch with one of his ministers the other day who obviously did say good stuff about him. But beyond that, it’s almost impossible. And, of course, the picture people have of Macron at one level is a rather authoritarian figure telling people what to do, a sort of vertical President. But then another, a vertical President who simply has no power. He’s the worst of both worlds.
I was about to say he seems helpless, but people also think he’s a top-down–
They’re right; he is. But unfortunately, without being able to do anything, because there are no levers to pull any longer, which is a very sort of strange situation.
Saying the only person you met who likes him is a minister of his reminds me of the Onion headline, “Dukakis Wins 80 Percent of Dukakis Family Vote.”
Yes, absolutely. I remember that actually.

I remember something people were saying four or five years ago, maybe around the second time that Macron fought off Le Pen, in 2022, that basically Macron has had incredible political success, and he will have been President for ten years, but at the same time, he’s killed off the center right and the center left and not provided any alternative. And so you’ve had this chasm that, when he leaves, is going to exist. I remember political analysts saying that five years ago, and it seems like sometimes political analysts say things that turn out to be true and sometimes it turns out to be not true. But it turned out to be exactly right.

I completely agree. I have written something along those lines myself in various pieces about Macron. And I think I must have written five years ago myself that the tragedy of Macron, really, who did seem to offer something, was that he either seemed indifferent to or incapable of thinking about the succession. If you want to take a contrast with a President who he resembles, Valéry Giscard d’Estaing, who was also a centrist liberal, but who really did make efforts to build a center party between the Gaullists and the left. And Macron simply has either not bothered to do it or failed to do it. I don’t think he’s particularly bothered to do it. And what’s so striking is that whenever he’s had a prime minister, he immediately sets out to undermine that person who should be a credible successor.

Macronism was always going to be strange because it does move from the center left to the center right. Some of the people under the Macron umbrella are really very far right, and the people on the left are not very far left, but they’re certainly not far from the Socialists. So he had succeeded, but he only succeeded in bringing over individuals. He was never interested enough in a structure. You know what people jokingly said about how his movement was originally called En Marche? And people said, typically, that the initials of the movement were his own initials.

I think Macron both profited from the weakness of the political parties, first the Socialists and then the Gaullists on the right, and also hastened it, as it were. And he created no alternative future. He also really did show too much contempt in the early days for what the French call intermediary organizations. He sort of thought it was just him and the people. So, trade unions, local mayors, local associations—he was terribly dismissive of those sort of civil-society organisms that can actually make it possible to get things done. Admittedly, I started off as an admirer, and I had great hope, like so many people. I think he’s politically been brilliant at exploiting the possibilities of coming to power and then disastrous at knowing what to do with it.

We have talked a lot about Macron, and almost all of the things you’ve said about his failures are essentially character flaws or political errors based upon his character flaws. How would you define what his agenda was, and to what degree his policies were failures or not failures, too? Because France is obviously facing what a lot of people think is a pretty calamitous budget situation going forward. And you do hear some people blaming him for it. You say other people say, No, he tried his best; he raised the retirement age. But I’m curious how much you think his failures were, in fact, mostly personal and how much they were also policy-based.

Well, I think it seems to me incontrovertibly the case that the French need to deal with their issue of the pensions and that he was absolutely right in what he wanted to do. I think he was a liberal, he was a left liberal, a liberal in the European rather than the American sense, and he wanted a degree of deregulation, but with slightly leftist social rhetoric. It was a kind of Blairism, you might almost say. So there was something attractive and plausible in the agenda. But the Yellow Vest movement started after a gasoline-tax increase. And then it was done for good.

He had framed the gasoline-tax increase as an environmental policy. But of course, he wasn’t prepared for the reaction in any kind of way. And what he never thought of was that the people who were going to be most hit were not the sort of urbanites who believe in environmental protection in Paris but people living in deprived areas who desperately needed their cars to get to work. And so it’s almost as if he has this sense of detachment from what France really was. I also think he made a very big error at the very, very beginning. He said, Well, it’s going to be a regime. I’m going to encourage entrepreneurialism and a “startup nation,” all that kind of thing. But one of his first measures was to abolish a redistributive tax, and that was a really bad symbol that announced, I’m the President of the rich.

And it was so badly judged because it wasn’t going to liberate the economy. It was a handout, really, to the richer segment of the population. And so I think he had some perfectly good ideas. People of the socialist left would not agree with that, but I, as a centrist Social Democrat, think that he had perfectly good ideas. But the problem isn’t the ideas. The problem is his disconnectedness. Remember, he had never been elected to anything before becoming President. He didn’t have that feel for France. I don’t know whether you saw, but he made a very revealing comment to the French writer Emmanuel Carrère a bit of time ago. He said, “I was never a teenager,” which is an extraordinarily revealing comment, actually.
Also slightly disturbing given his romantic history, but we can leave that alone.

I want to ask you about de Gaulle because you wrote a really astonishing biography of him. There are obviously a lot of differences, but there are a lot of similarities: rising above the established parties; coming to power as this figure above politics, in some way; staying for ten years in Macron’s case, eleven in de Gaulle’s case; student uprisings at the ten-year mark. So anyone can come up with the similarities. But what struck me especially from your book is that de Gaulle was also just a very strange figure who would try to make these, in the Macron phrase, Jupiterian decisions. De Gaulle could be almost dictatorial. He could be authoritarian. He would sometimes remove himself from politics in strange ways and make decisions that no one could understand. And it almost felt to me, after reading your book and watching Macron, that Macron was sort of self-consciously trying to do this, but it just didn’t work in his case.

I think you’re right. I think that is how he pitched himself. Each President has an official photograph of themselves, and Macron’s has him with de Gaulle’s war memoirs in the back. Macron came after the failed Presidency of François Hollande, who said he wanted to be a normal President. And in a way, the problem is the Fifth Republic doesn’t really quite allow normal Presidents, and you’ve got to somehow inhabit the role. He did want to reëstablish the idea that the President of the Fifth Republic needs to have a certain weight and so on. He talked about verticality and about being Jupiterian. That’s all Gaullist. And what I said about ignoring intermediary institutions, very Gaullist. But of course what he didn’t have is what nobody could have really, which is that de Gaulle could do this with all the history that went with being de Gaulle in 1958, when he came to power. Macron arrived with a history of being a palace special adviser and a Rothschild banker. De Gaulle could do this because he had all the weight of legitimacy that came from being de Gaulle. I don’t say that Macron’s a lightweight, but he simply couldn’t do that. He couldn’t be that.

I’m quite lucky you haven’t asked, but usually people ask me the question, What would de Gaulle do now? And I always say to them, it’s such a stupid question because he was a man of his own time, and what de Gaulle would think about #MeToo or A.I. or the environment, who knows? But the great thing about de Gaulle was his extraordinary pragmatism. He was very adaptable despite his strangeness. But with Macron, I think he was preparing himself to reinvigorate the institutions that de Gaulle created, but failed. ♦

items.title: The Unlikely Friendship Behind the Knicks’ Title Run
items.description: Running an NBA team had never been part of his plan, but now, not long after news broke that he’d be doing exactly that, Leon Rose was on the phone with a friend, outlining how he intended to save one of the most embattled franchises in sports. It was February
items.author: Yaron Weitzman
paragraphs: Running an NBA team had never been part of his plan, but now, not long after news broke that he’d be doing exactly that, Leon Rose was on the phone with a friend, outlining how he intended to save one of the most embattled franchises in sports. It was February 2020, and after 25 years as an NBA agent, he knew the snake pit he was walking into.

These, after all, were the New York Knicks. In the previous 20 years, they had endured three times as many losing seasons (15) as winning ones (five), dumped one franchise icon (Patrick Ewing) and fought with another (Charles Oakley), and regularly filled the tabloids with the kinds of scandals typically reserved for reality TV. Even Phil Jackson, just three years after being welcomed as a savior, had been run out of town a few years before. The Knicks were the first NBA riddle the legend was unable to solve.

All of which was why Rose was now telling Mike Dunlap, a longtime coach and one of his earliest clients, that he’d start with the simple stuff. He’d be patient with his roster. Build a relationship with team owner James Dolan. Come in asking questions and being ready to learn. And there was one more thing, Rose told Dunlap. Something he could bring to the table that no one before him could.

“He thought Wes would be really important,” Dunlap said. Wes was William Wesley, a fellow South Jersey native known in sports as “World Wide Wes.” “Maybe the greatest connector I’ve met in my 50 years in the business,” said David Falk, Michael Jordan’s longtime agent. Whether you were a veteran general manager trying to defuse tension between a coach and a star, a rookie needing career advice, or a shoe executive wondering whether a kid was worth an investment, Wes was likely one of your first calls.

Rose understood this better than most. Over the previous four decades, he and Wes had built one of basketball’s most successful and unlikely partnerships. Neither had played college ball at a high level, let alone in the NBA, but together they’d climbed to the top of the sport.
“They’re like Batman and Robin, except they’re always swapping those roles,” said Lynn Merritt, a longtime Nike executive.

That June, with the NBA paused due to COVID, the two sat outside Rose’s Jersey Shore home and mapped out their plan. “Family is how we’re building this thing,” Wes told a friend soon after. At times, that approach seemed destined to fail. The members of their family didn’t all get along. Some had to be traded or fired for the good of the group. Others were given chances, or contracts, they might not have deserved. Over the years, rival executives and agents — and even some employees within the organization — would joke that the true genius of Rose and Wes was that in Dolan they had suckered a billionaire into handing over his checkbook so they could line their friends’ pockets. Many of these insiders, along with NBA reporters (including, it should be said, the one writing this story), believed they were in over their heads.

Yet six years after their chats at the Shore, there were Rose and Wes standing side by side, tears streaming down their cheeks, watching the team they’d built celebrate the snapping of a 53-year-drought.

Jalen Brunson may have been the catalyst, and OG Anunoby’s game-four tip might be the moment fans remember most. But the true story behind the Knicks’ magical title run is one of two outsiders — a Black kid from Camden and a Jewish kid from Cherry Hill — coming together and conquering the sport. And it’s a story that doesn’t begin in a glamourous gym but in a run-down shoe store on a nondescript stretch of South Jersey road.

It was the late ’70s, and Leon Rose wanted a pair of Julius “Dr. J” Erving’s signature shoes. So he did what most athletes in the area did at the time: He went to The Pro’s Shoe — though most in the area referred to it as Pro Shoes — in Cherry Hill. Known for its rare models and hard-to-find large sizes, the store drew ball players of all levels and ages. The owner rang up customers on an old crank register and strolled around with an unlit cigar dangling from his mouth. The heart of the store, though, was an enterprising teenager who, at around age 13, had started walking over every day after school. Most customers didn’t know his full name. To them, he was simply Fresh Wes, the kid who always outfitted them with the perfect pair of kicks.

Quick-witted and sharp, Wes had the people skills of a professional twice his age. He was a worker too — sometimes, to fund the high-school parties he and his friends liked to throw, he’d borrow a truck and go searching for old washers and dryers around town to bring to a scrapyard.

Pro Shoes became Wes’s second home. He’d talk up anyone who walked in, no matter their religion or race — an ability he’d picked up in middle school, after his family moved a few miles east to Merchantville, where “he was the only Black kid in our class,” said Jeff Selverian, one of his closest childhood friends.

By the late ’70s, the store had become a local hot spot with Wes making new friends every day. Some, like Milt Wagner and Billy Thompson, were high-school basketball stars from Camden. Others were just regular kids who needed shoes. On this day, it was a point guard from Cherry Hill High School East.
Wes made his way over to the customer.

Rose’s first dream was to become a coach. This concerned his father. “I said, ‘What you should do is go to law school first,’” Zev Rose, a commercial-real-estate lawyer, recounted. They compromised: Leon became an assistant at his old high school while enrolled at Temple’s law school. After graduating in 1986, he became a Camden County prosecutor and moonlighted as an assistant coach at Division III Rutgers–Camden.

Wes, meanwhile, was carving out a path of his own. South Jersey had become a wellspring of athletic talent with future pros seemingly on every corner. College coaches flocked there; one of the first was Wade Houston, a Louisville assistant. “On my first trip to the gym, everyone told me that if I wanted to really learn about these kids, then I had to go see this guy at the shoe store by the mall,” Houston said. Wes was in the stockroom when he heard someone asking for William Wesley. His first instinct was to hide. “At least until he realized I wasn’t someone looking to hurt him,” Houston said. Houston was impressed by Wes’s eye for talent, but what he liked most was how much Wes seemed to care about the recruits: “He was almost like their protector.”

Little by little, Wes’s roots spread. He organized parties, worked doors, and by the end of the ’80s was managing Sixers big man Rick Mahorn’s Cherry Hill nightclub. By then he’d also gotten close with David Falk, whom he’d first called after Billy Thompson hired Falk as his agent in 1986. “I never met him, I didn’t know who he was, and he told me he was Billy’s cousin,” Falk recalled. “I learned later on that Wes is everybody’s cousin.” Falk had introduced Wes to his biggest client, Michael Jordan, back when Jordan was just a few years into his NBA career. The two hit it off, giving Wes the ultimate endorsement.

Rose wasn’t yet hanging with basketball royalty like his friend, but his career was moving forward. By then, he had left the prosecutor’s office for a firm where his father was partner. He also made partner and worked on cases like a class-action suit over a toxic substance in Guam. With his law career secure, he started edging back into sports.

Rose and Wes (neither of whom the Knicks made available for an on-the-record interview) had stayed close over the years. First, there were sporadic meetings at Pro Shoes, then more frequent run-ins during pickup games at gyms around Cherry Hill, something they’d do multiple times a week. Then Wes started calling Rose whenever he or a family member needed legal advice, even for mundane issues like parking tickets. Wes viewed Rose as a mentor, someone he could lean on for all sorts of advice. Rose saved Wes on a few occasions, too, like the time an agent offered to pay $500 for every player he referred. Thinking he had hit the jackpot, Wes was ecstatic and shared the news with Rose over a meal at Houlihan’s in the Cherry Hill Mall. Then Rose laid out the math: Even if the agent signed only one of those players to an NBA contract, he pointed out, Wes would still be getting robbed.
Wes realized two things that day: that he still had a lot to learn and that the man sitting across the table would always have his back.

As Rose took on more sports work, he found his niche. In a world of Jerry Maguire aspirants, he was the agent who drove around in a Nissan Altima, favored baggy sweats, and started every other sentence with “Yo.” More than that, he was the agent players could turn to after being burned. He signed two Temple alums whose previous agency the players union had charged with improperly withdrawing client funds. And his first client was another kid from Temple whose agent had dumped him after he went undrafted. His name was Rick Brunson.

Rose gave everything he could to Brunson. He would rebound for him in the morning and work the phones during the day. When Brunson (who declined an interview request) was playing in Australia, Rose regularly made the 22-hour flight to see him. When Brunson had trouble getting and keeping NBA contracts, Rose stuck with him. Rose’s son, Sam, and Brunson’s son, Jalen, were of similar ages and often played together.

Word of Rose got around the Philadelphia area. That he had Wes’s seal of approval — and was often seen hanging with Wes before Sixers games — only boosted his credibility. In spring of 2002, Sixers superstar Allen Iverson signed with Rose, in part because “he told us he’d take care of Allen as if he was his own son,” said Iverson’s longtime manager, Gary Moore. Iverson wasn’t just a basketball star; he was a cultural icon revered by NBA players — and the kids trying to become them. Rose was now a made man.

Around the same time, Dajuan Wagner, the son of Milt Wagner, became a high-school phenomenon at Camden High. When it was time to enter the NBA, there was no question whom he’d pick as his agent. The Cleveland Cavaliers drafted Wagner sixth overall in 2002. This proved fortuitous. LeBron James, then entering his senior year of high school, was spending a lot of time around the Cavs, and he grew close with Wes, who had rented an apartment in the area to be near Wagner. “He’s been a great role model to me,” James told GQ when asked about Wes in 2007.

LeBron had hired a different agent before entering the draft but made the switch after his second season. In about a decade, Rose had gone from working on a class-action lawsuit in Guam to managing the careers of two of the biggest stars in the world.

Rose and Wes had become about as powerful as anyone in the sport. Their circle included many of the NBA’s top players, as well as elite coaches like John Calipari, whom Wes had first met in the early ’80s, when Calipari was a young Kansas assistant on a recruiting trip to Camden. Calipari had since become one of college basketball’s most successful recruiters and coaches, turning Memphis and then Kentucky into pipelines to the pros. Rose and Wes were also tight with “the Seals” at Nike — the term the company’s top NBA decision-makers used for themselves — and well liked in Reebok’s boardroom too.

By this point, Wes had become a subject of intrigue. Flip on a random game at night and there was a solid shot you’d see him, whether he was sitting next to an owner courtside or — as was the case during the infamous 2004 Malice at the Palace brawl in Detroit — jumping into the middle of the floor to keep one player from swinging at another. Put on a Drake or Jay-Z song and you might hear his name shouted out. All of this added to the mystique. In 2005, NBA reporter Henry Abbott began a series about Wes’s influence, first on his widely read blog, then for ESPN. Two years later, GQ asked in a headline, “Is This the Most Powerful Man in Sports?”

With fame came the whispers. That Wes’s relationships were the result of him lavishing kids — or, as he referred to them, his “nephews” — with Nike gifts. That Rose’s client roster was merely a product of his relationship with Wes, whom, these cynics believed, Rose must have been paying so he’d have a Black face recruiting players. How else could Wes be funding his jet-setting lifestyle? (Whenever asked about how he made a living, Wes said he was a mortgage broker for a firm in South Jersey.)

I spent months reporting this story and asked everyone I spoke to about these allegations. “All I can say is if that were the case, I think I would have heard something from someone at some point,” said Chrysa Chin, who spent 34 seasons in the NBA world, at the league office, the players’ union and Nike, and was so close to players that she became known as the “NBA Mom.” “Because in those situations, when you inject money or anything, at some point, a relationship with a player falls apart or gets ugly, and I’ve literally never even heard a player complain about either one of them.” Moore, Iverson’s manager, stressed that he was the one who asked Wes for an introduction to Rose, not the other way around.

Maybe, NBA insiders say, there were times when Rose benefited from having a Black friend like Wes. “But once you get past that initial introduction with people, that stuff doesn’t usually matter,” said a longtime union executive. And despite their relationship now entering its fifth decade, no one has ever gone public with an on-the-record complaint about how the two have done business.

Around 2006, Creative Artists Agency decided it needed a basketball division under its newly formed sports umbrella. Rose’s client list made him an obvious fit. “And from the first time we met Leon, we didn’t have a conversation with him without talking about his friend Wes,” said Howie Nuchow, who has been co-head of CAA Sports with Mike Levine since its inception. It took a bit, but in 2010, Wes came out of the shadows and joined Rose.

Early in his tenure at CAA, Wes approached his new bosses with a plea. “He’d tell us, ‘You gotta get to know Jim Dolan,’” Nuchow said. At the time, no one at CAA Sports had much of a relationship with the Madison Square Garden owner. The firm’s leadership didn’t know much about him beyond his reputation, which was, and remains, less than stellar. “But Wes kept on us, saying, ‘You guys gotta spend some time with him. He’s a good guy,’” Nuchow said.

Wes and Dolan (who declined an interview through a Knicks spokesperson) had met years earlier thanks to one of Wes’s original connections. In 1996, Wade Houston’s son, Allan, a six-foot-six guard with a sweet shooting stroke, signed as a free agent with the Knicks, becoming a star in New York and a pillar of the beloved turn-of-the-century teams. He also, according to people with close ties to the organization at the time, became a favorite of Dolan’s, who would soon be named chairman of MSG. That relationship brought Wes into Dolan’s orbit. Frank Isola, the Daily News’ longtime Knicks beat writer, remembers flying to Louisville in May 2001 for a golf event Houston was hosting and finding Wes outside the clubhouse, regaling Dolan and others with stories.

Now at CAA, Wes believed there was more business to be done. He started bringing Dolan to the company’s All-Star Weekend parties and connected him and Rose. In February 2011, Rose helped orchestrate a megatrade that landed his client Carmelo Anthony with the Knicks, who were coming off nine consecutive losing seasons.

Around the 2020 New Year, with the Knicks mired in their seventh straight losing season, Dolan decided it was time to make a change at the top of the organization. “And it’s hard for Jim to trust people who he doesn’t have some sort of personal or historical relationship with,” a longtime Garden insider said. Dolan called Rose to gauge his interest. Rose huddled with Levine, the CAA Sports co-head, at the agency’s midtown offices; met with Dolan at the Garden; then huddled with Levine again that night. Within two weeks, he told Dolan he was in. Wes told him he’d join him, and a few months later received the official title of executive vice-president and senior basketball adviser.

The calls from friends came in fast. Some were hired. Others — like Eddy Curry, the former Knicks center who thought he could get a job because his “uncle” and former agent were taking over — were told it wasn’t a fit. “Wes was like, ‘Nah, we gotta figure this thing out first,’” Curry said. “It showed me how seriously they were taking the job.” Later that summer, an acquaintance asked Wes whether he and Rose were worried about working for a boss as tempestuous as Dolan. “Don’t worry about that,” Wes responded. “We’ve got five-year deals.”
The person on the other end of the line asked if that would be enough.
“It’s going to be,” Wes said.
Two years into their new jobs, the pair was at a crossroads.

The Knicks had ended their playoff drought in Rose and Wes’s first season at the helm — largely thanks to the defense-first culture instituted by new head coach Tom Thibodeau, who had previously been a client of Rose’s — but took a step back in year two. They’d yet to nab a star, something that, after Rose and Wes were hired, many assumed would be imminent given their vast networks. Some colleagues in the building and executives outside of it felt that, at times, the job was getting the best of Rose. A number of his moves had backfired. Thibodeau was complaining about the front office’s pragmatic approach. Wes, according to reports at the time, was blaming the team’s struggles on Thibodeau. The train looked to be headed off the rails. The roster needed an injection of talent. It also needed someone who could lead the group into the future.
The time had come for Rose and Wes to push in all their chips.

Rose spent the offseason clearing salary-cap space. The Knicks then hired Rick Brunson as an assistant coach and signed his son, an undersized former second-round pick who’d never made an All-Star team to a $104 million four-year deal.
Upon hearing the news, many pundits were aghast.

“Jalen Brunson isn’t the answer!” Stephen A. Smith shouted on ESPN. Brian Windhorst, the network’s longtime reporter, was more clinical in his analysis. “It is not going to be the type of player that elevates them into contender status,” he declared.

But Rose and Wes believed there was more to the younger Brunson than he’d shown during his four years with the Dallas Mavericks. It would prove to be one of the best bets in NBA history. The following season, the Knicks won a playoff series for the first time in a decade. Brunson, it turned out, wasn’t just a star but a generational leader. Years after Rose stuck by Rick Brunson, karma had found its way back through his son.

“It could have been a complete disaster, and that would have been the end of it,” the MSG insider said. “But the bet on Jalen was the right one, and it changed everything. It gave Jim the confidence that there was something being built.”

With an alpha in place, Rose and Wes were free to do what they did best. Rose had traded for Josh Hart, a jack-of-all-trades role player and, perhaps more importantly, Brunson’s best friend. Later, he’d add Karl-Anthony Towns, an All-Star big man who, not coincidentally, was a former client of Rose’s, a Kentucky alum and one of Wes’s “nephews.” Wes did Wes things, whether that meant serving as a sounding board for Rose, connecting with Dolan, spearheading the organization’s alumni program, or taking a disgruntled player to dinner on the road.
“They created a family atmosphere,” one former Knicks assistant coach said.

But loyalty, they learned, had its limits. In December 2023, Rose pulled the trigger on a deal for OG Anunoby, a big, athletic wing perfectly suited to play alongside Brunson. Doing so, however, meant parting ways with Immanuel Quickley, a “nephew” of Wes’s who had played for Calipari at Kentucky.
“This is a fucked-up day for me,” an emotional Wes told a friend after the deal.

Rose’s test came in the summer of 2025. Thibodeau had just led the Knicks to their first conference finals in 25 years. His intensity, however, was grating on players and colleagues, and after the loss to the Pacers, many in the organization, Dolan among them, believed the team needed a new voice. Rose could see it, too. That June, he fired his longtime friend. Family still mattered. But it needed to fuel winning, not come at the expense of it.
“That was really hard on Leon,” said a person close to Rose. “He knew it would change the relationship.”

Rose replaced Thibodeau with Mike Brown, whom he and Wes grew close with in the mid-2000s, when Brown was coaching LeBron’s Cavaliers. But there were times during the 2025–26 season when it looked like that bet might not pay off. Towns clashed with Brown over his role in the offense and, according to people around the team, Anunoby often felt the same way.
Wes stepped in. He built a relationship with Anunoby. “That was huge for us,” said a Knicks source. “Because OG was the person who needed the most massaging.” Wes also stayed close to Towns.
“Uncle Wes, man, he’s everybody’s uncle,” Towns said recently. When asked what Wes does around the organization, Towns replied, “Think about an uncle, man — he does everything.”

Midway through the first round of the playoffs, the Knicks found their stride, clicking in a way few teams ever have. The group, assembled by Rose and Wes piece by piece over six years, became dominant and unflappable, setting records for comebacks and scoring margins. This was not the star-studded product most expected when the pair first arrived, either. This was something different, a web of individuals — all with various historical connections to Rose, Wes, and one another — coming together to form a whole greater than the sum of its parts.

It all coalesced in game four of the Finals. With nine minutes and 40 seconds left in the third quarter, the Knicks trailed by 29 points. Little by little, though, they hacked away at the deficit. With less than two seconds on the clock, Anunoby soared through the air to tip in Brunson’s miss, giving the Knicks the lead. Towns then deflected an inbounds pass to save the game. The final buzzer sounded. The Garden erupted.
Watching from his suite in the stands, Rose screamed and fell into Wes’s arms.

A week later, after another come-from-behind win in Game 5, this one sealing the series, a sea of fans clad in orange and blue — about 2 million in total — flooded downtown Manhattan to toast the Knicks’ magical run. Mike Breen, the team’s legendary announcer, stood at a lectern outside City Hall. Boxes holding keys to the city sat on a table nearby. In the months ahead, fights over contracts and bruised feelings over who in the organization deserved a championship ring would dampen the mood. But those were problems for the future. This was a day for celebrating.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” Breen declared to a plaza stuffed with fans, some of New York’s most famous faces among them, “your 2026 NBA champion New York Knicks!” The starting lineup’s usual introduction song blared out of the giant speakers stationed around the stage. The crowd, eager to welcome its heroes, roared.

But first out of the tunnel wasn’t the team’s star. It wasn’t the owner either. It was a former shoe salesman from Camden followed by the kid from Cherry Hill who, nearly 50 years earlier, had come into his store. The two longtime friends took their seats on the stage side by side.

items.title: 7 Ways Trump Lost His 2024 Coalition
items.description: Though the results could yet surprise us, it’s very likely the key story of the 2026 midterm elections will be the Republican Party’s loss of support from non-MAGA elements of the electorate who temporarily backed Donald Trump in 2024. To that extent it’s not
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Though the results could yet surprise us, it’s very likely the key story of the 2026 midterm elections will be the Republican Party’s loss of support from non-MAGA elements of the electorate who temporarily backed Donald Trump in 2024. To that extent it’s not just a matter of the White House party predictably losing ground in a midterm, which happens far more often than not. It’s a tale of trends reversing themselves that robbed Trump and his cohort of what many thought might be a political realignment making the GOP the majority party for years. So it’s worth a closer look: How, exactly, did Trump alienate these onetime supporters? Here are some tentative answers.
Trump’s 2024 coalition was never as big as he claimed

The president has incessantly exaggerated his winning share of the electorate in 2024. On Election Night, he claimed an “unprecedented and powerful mandate.” Shortly after taking office, he told supporters he had “achieved the most epic political victory our country has ever seen” and “the biggest mandate in 129 years,” and one of his spokespeople boasted he had “decisively won every battleground state and became the first Republican to win the popular vote in 20 years,” lines he would repeat often on Truth Social. In fact, he narrowly won the popular vote by 1.5 percent, far short of the usual 10 percent threshold for a “landslide,” which was smaller than the margins of victory for Joe Biden in 2020, Barack Obama in 2012 and 2008, and George W. Bush in 2004 (and smaller, for that matter, than Hillary Clinton’s popular-vote margin over Trump in 2016). Winning all seven battlegrounds is no big accomplishment, either; these were very close states, which is why they were called battlegrounds. Suffice it to say that Trump’s victory was legitimate but no great shakes by any historical standard.
Some of Trump’s gains were circumstantial, not a realignment

What had some Republicans buzzing about a “realignment” were the gains Trump posted among Hispanic, Black, and under-30 voters. The size of these gains varied by sources, but probably the most reliable, Pew’s “verified voters” analysis, showed Trump gaining 12 percent among Hispanics compared to 2020 (and 20 percent compared to 2016); 7 percent among Black voters (and 9 percent since 2016); and 4 percent among under-30 voters (and 11 percent since 2016). Considering how aggressively reactionary Trump had been in the intervening years, these were indeed impressive numbers in those demographic groups and cause for concern among Democrats, who had arguably taken them for granted. But Trump has now squandered these gains by every measurement we have.
The high price of breaking cost-of-living promises

Hispanic, Black, and under-30 voters are on average more economically vulnerable than other Americans, and there’s not much question a big part of their pro-Trump trend in 2024 involved unhappiness with Joe Biden’s record on inflation and Trump’s promises to lower the cost of groceries, fuel, and housing. He was not able at all to keep those promises, which were not realistic to begin with. While this isn’t the only reason he’s lost ground with these voters, it is clearly important, and it’s hard to overstate the depth of his failure. According to the latest high-quality New York Times–Siena survey of likely voters, Trump’s job-approval numbers on “the cost of living” are 20 percent approval and 79 disapproval (with 65 percent strongly disapproving) among Hispanics, 3 percent approval and 91 percent disapproval (with 88 percent strongly disapproving) among Black voters, and 13 percent approval and 86 percent disapproval (with 73 percent strongly disapproving) among under-30 voters. There is no way to sugarcoat these numbers on the most important issue of the midterms.
Latinos are unhappy with mass deportation

It was reasonably clear that the Latino/Hispanic voters who trended Republican in 2024 supported Trump’s border-control policies (most still do) and believed his claims that he would deport only violent criminals. But again, Trump broke his promises. A March 2026 Equus survey of Latinos found that by “a wide 65-30 margin, Latinos believe Trump’s actions on immigration ‘are going too far, and instead of deporting criminals, he is targeting the types of hardworking immigrants who strengthen our nation.’” The same survey showed 72 percent of Latinos weren’t happy with ICE, “whether that means they support reforming ICE to prevent violence and ensure accountability (37%) or abolishing ICE because it is out of control and no training or accountability could reform it (35%).” The Times-Siena poll showed 60 percent of Hispanics “strongly disapproving” of Trump’s immigration policies overall.
Trump has offended Black voters as much as possible

If you are a Republican who wants to increase your party’s fragile beachhead with Black voters, here are some things you should probably avoid doing: (1) devoting all the civil-rights organs of the federal government to a fight against alleged discrimination against white people; (2) virtually criminalizing diversity efforts in federal or federally supported hiring; (3) successfully encouraging the U.S. Supreme Court to atomize the Voting Rights Act of 1965; (4) successfully encouraging southern state legislatures to dismantle congressional and state legislative districts that elected Black people to office; and (5) making white Afrikaners from the former apartheid state of South Africa the one remaining recognized beneficiary of refugee status. That the Trump administration has done all these things helps explain why in the Times-Siena survey only 7 percent of Black voters gave the president a positive job-approval rating while 78 percent strongly disapprove.

Aside from being very sensitive to living costs, young voters are famously disinclined to support wars of choice (i.e., those that aren’t a matter of national self-defense), perhaps because they are often of the same generation as those who are dying or risking their lives in such wars. Trump’s war of choice against Iran is generally unpopular; according to the Times-Siena survey, 33 percent of likely voters support the war while 66 percent disapprove (57 percent disapprove strongly). Young voters really hate it, with only 9 percent supporting it (and just one percent supporting it strongly) and 86 percent disapproving of it (75 percent strongly). No wonder 79 percent of under-30 voters disapprove of Trump’s overall job performance (71 percent strongly).
Trump is now only focused on his base, because it’s all he has left

No wonder the president is traveling from red state to red state to rally his most loyal MAGA supporters to show up at the polls and mitigate his party’s losses. He has deliberately chosen to alienate everyone else, including voting groups that were open to changing sides. At this rate, Trump will leave the GOP in worse shape than he found it.

items.title: On the Front Line of the Vaccine Wars
items.description: O N A CRISP DRY DAY in Beckley, West Virginia, last September, 35-year-old litigator Chris Smith wore his lucky purple tie to court. With a wry smile, round face, and piercing blue eyes behind metal-rimmed glasses, Smith enjoyed a hard fight. But as he slid in
items.author: Katherine Eban
paragraphs: O N A CRISP DRY DAY in Beckley, West Virginia, last September, 35-year-old litigator Chris Smith wore his lucky purple tie to court. With a wry smile, round face, and piercing blue eyes behind metal-rimmed glasses, Smith enjoyed a hard fight. But as he slid into his seat for defense counsel in a courtroom crowded with lawyers, luck did not seem to be on his side.

Smith’s client, the West Virginia Board of Education, faced an uphill battle to save the state’s compulsory-vaccination law, which for 89 years had helped thwart the spread of infectious diseases. The state’s ambitious Republican governor, Patrick Morrisey, was aiming to allow parents a religious exemption to school vaccinations. He had powerful outside allies in his fight, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and one of his close confidants, a lawyer now seated to Smith’s right, Aaron Siri.

Siri, 48, bald and compact with lively dark eyes, looked ready to spar. While most of the lawyers in the courtroom were native West Virginians, Siri is a New York City plaintiff lawyer who’d relocated to Arizona and had spent more than a decade aiming to dismantle any law or regulation that mandated vaccination. As he’d put it in a 2022 tweet: “Mandates are the tool of bullies, criminals, and dictators.” His firm, Siri & Glimstad, has litigated state by state to loosen vaccine laws.

Schoolchildren in West Virginia can only skip required vaccines for medical reasons. In a state with roughly 235,000 kids in school, the health department issued only 203 full medical exemptions from 2015 to 2025. Siri was representing Miranda Guzman, a mother battling the education board so she could exempt her child from school vaccinations.

Siri now confronted Dr. Jacob Kilgore, the Raleigh County Board of Education’s expert witness, sitting placidly on the witness stand. Kilgore, medical director of the Marshall Health Network – Hoops Family Children’s Hospital and one of only seven pediatric infectious-disease doctors in West Virginia, was so well-known to those present that even Judge Michael Froble had waived the need to establish his expert credentials. Kilgore was courteous and mild-mannered to a fault. The left side of his face bore a large hemangioma birthmark, a lifelong challenge that had partly inspired his commitment to medicine.
Siri ticked through diseases, asking Kilgore: In a less-densely populated state like West Virginia, would religious exemptions really impact the level of immunity to measles?
“I think it depends on what you mean by ‘densely populated,’” Kilgore responded.
“Well, how about West Virginia versus New York City?” Siri asked.
“What part of West Virginia?” Kilgore replied. “Name a city in West Virginia. Any.”
“I don’t know,” Siri said, eliciting laughter in the courtroom.
“Just name a city in West Virginia.”
“Sure,” Siri said. “The biggest city in Raleigh County.”
“Can you name it for me?” Kilgore continued. The correct answer, which eluded Siri, was Beckley — the city they were in.
“You got me,” Siri acknowledged, telling the judge what was already obvious. “He got me, your honor.”

Aubrey Sparks, legal director at the West Virginia ACLU, who was in the courtroom that day, says, “There’s a real assumption sometimes that bringing people in from out of state means more firepower or better attorneys.”
But to her, the exchange encapsulated West Virginia’s unique go-it-alone ethos. “You might specialize in this type of case,” she says of Siri, “but you don’t specialize in West Virginia.”
In an era of partisan rage over public-health mandates and growing antipathy to scientific expertise, vaccination in America is on a knife’s edge.

For almost a century, the public has largely agreed on a social compact: We should vaccinate our kids not only to prevent individual harm, but to also shield the more vulnerable among us, whether the immune-compromised or infants too young to be vaccinated.

The public school system has stood at the center of that compact, with the requirement that children be vaccinated to attend, all but guaranteeing that our communities reach herd immunity, the level of protection that makes it harder for frightening infectious diseases — whether polio or measles — to take hold. A 1905 U.S. Supreme Court ruling, Jacobson v. Massachusetts, affirmed the right of states to require vaccination.

But fighting in the name of religious, medical, and personal freedom, an array of lawyers, state and federal officials, and President Donald Trump himself are seeking to break that compact. And though their progress has been slowed by federal courts, painstaking local resistance, and the sheer complication of dismantling existing vaccine policy, a change is clearly afoot.

Since Kennedy became the nation’s health secretary in February 2025, vaccination rates for kindergartners have dropped more than two percent, parental requests for religious or philosophical exemptions to vaccinations for school entry have climbed to four percent, and infectious diseases once vanquished have ticked up. Measles — declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000 — has surged to more than 3,600 cases this year alone, more than a twelvefold increase from 2024. A widespread outbreak in Pennsylvania this year led recently to four deaths, including two infants, according to state officials. (HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard says “attributing the measles resurgence to President Trump or Secretary Kennedy fundamentally misrepresents when and why” it began — “pandemic-era disruptions” to routine vaccination started “years before they took office.” She says HHS remains committed to an “effective public-health response while respecting informed choice, parental rights, and religious liberty.”)

None of this is by accident. While Kennedy has sown parental doubt from his federal bully pulpit, it’s his legal confidant Siri, an expert in the circuitry of vaccine policy, with his hands on the motherboard, despite having no formal government role. Internal emails obtained by Rolling Stone show Kennedy offering to take departmental action to “be helpful” with certain private legal cases of the type Siri’s firm has pursued, and Siri advising Kennedy on departmental actions he can take to weaken liability protections for manufacturers without congressional approval. Siri says in an email to Rolling Stone, “I do not provide the secretary with legal or regulatory advice.”
Says a former HHS official, “What gets Aaron Siri up in the morning is to try and figure out every possible, conceivable tool to make it harder to vaccinate people in America.”

In the hydra-headed attack on vaccinations playing out across the country, only four states besides West Virginia — Connecticut, California, Maine, and New York — do not allow religious or philosophical exemptions. In August, Trump issued an executive order directing the U.S. attorney general to take legal action against them.

West Virginia is the only state among the five that has never permitted any exemption other than for medical reasons. Its compulsory-vaccination law has stood since 1937, an outgrowth of activism linked to coal-miner health and safety. “It’s hard to prevent the spread of pertussis in a coal mine,” says Dr. Joshua Hess, a pediatric hematologist-oncologist at Cabell Huntington Hospital.

Still, Siri had good reason to believe he could topple West Virginia’s vaccine law. In 2023, he prevailed in Mississippi, winning a lawsuit that allowed families to cite religious reasons to opt out of school-entry vaccinations. Since then, Mississippi’s vaccination rates have dropped by more than two percent, enough to allow a return of some infectious diseases. Last year, a baby there died of whooping cough for the first time in 13 years.

But in West Virginia, what began as a seemingly winnable campaign evolved into a complex legal showdown, with a number of intertwined court cases pitting West Virginia’s governor against the Department of Education, legislators within the Republican supermajority against one another, and locals against outsiders. The fight has even divided families, with one pediatrician testifying as a plaintiff to save the law, while his sister, a far-right state legislator, works to bring it down.

With Kennedy aiding his cause from inside HHS, Siri isn’t stopping there. Del Bigtree, the founder and chief executive officer of the anti-vaccine group Informed Consent Action Network (ICAN), which has funded Siri’s litigation in West Virginia and other states, says that bringing a case to the U.S. Supreme Court is “absolutely the goal.” He says they are looking for a “more modern decision” than in the 1905 Jacobson case.

If the U.S. Supreme Court takes a case on vaccinations for school entry, the decision could drastically impact public health. It could be “potentially as earthshaking as the reversal of Roe [v. Wade],” says Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal, who in 2019 as a state senator helped tighten New York’s vaccination law to remove religious exemptions, after a widespread measles outbreak began in several under-vaccinated Orthodox Jewish communities.

Siri told me this summer, “The only position my firm takes on vaccines is that everybody should be free to get as many vaccines as they want, but at the same token, everybody should be free to be able to decline a vaccine.”

In West Virginia, though, Siri’s opponents are fighting for a long-held value in their state, where getting a shot comes as second nature if it means protecting neighbors, even those you don’t know. West Virginia is the kind of place, as Kilgore later puts it, where “y’all means all.”
‘All You Had to Do Is Write It on a Napkin’
The road to Smith’s faceoff against Siri began in the state capitol, a grand building with a gilded gold-leaf dome and taxidermied bears along the marble hallways.

Almost every year, some faction within the legislature has taken aim at the state’s vaccination requirements, only to meet with defeat. But on Jan. 14, 2025, the newly elected governor, Morrisey, a former pharmaceutical lobbyist who had aligned himself firmly with Trump and Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, issued an executive order on his second day in office. He directed the state health department to allow religious exemptions. In doing so, he leaned on a West Virginia law passed in 2023, the Equal Protection for Religion act, to claim that families could circumvent vaccine requirements if they didn’t align with their religious beliefs.

“It was really a philosophical exemption,” says Dr. Tom Takubo, a Republican state senator and pulmonary critical-care physician who is a vaccine defender and foe of the governor. “He called it a religious exemption, but all you had to do is write it on a napkin and have your child take it to school.”

Morrisey’s move signaled a new kind of threat. “We’d never heard of executive orders in the state, except to lower the flag half-staff or give state employees a Christmas Eve ball,” says retired lawyer Robin Godfrey.
A spokesperson for Morrisey says, “The governor’s position remains that West Virginia can protect public health while respecting the religious-liberty protections provided under state law.”

Godfrey formed the pro-vaccine volunteer group Stand for Kids, which now has coordinators in 44 of West Virginia’s 55 counties. By February, a handful of parents formed West Virginia Families for Immunizations, with backing from the national group American Families for Vaccines, which receives some funding from vaccine manufacturers.
With Republicans holding a supermajority in the West Virginia Legislature, Senate Bill 460 — which would have inscribed Morrisey’s executive order into law — seemed like a foregone conclusion.

A month after Morrisey’s executive order, the Senate Health and Human Resources Committee held a hearing. While three local pediatricians got about five minutes each, Siri was brought in virtually for nearly an hour. “West Virginia sits as an outlier in not respecting people’s individual and civil rights to be able to affirm their religious beliefs,” Siri testified.

“In one of the areas where we lead the country, people relied on a lawyer from out of town who came in on a Teams meeting,” says Joey Garcia, who sits on the health committee and is one of two Senate Democrats. “He kept talking and talking,” but the gist “didn’t make a whole bunch of sense for West Virginia.”

The bill cleared the Senate and went to the House of Delegates, seemingly on a fast track to pass. But activists deluged legislators with calls, emails, and visits that flipped votes. Last March, the bill was defeated 56-42. “That’s the power of the advocate voice in West Virginia,” says Jessie Ice, co-director of West Virginia Families for Immunizations.
But the fight wasn’t over.
What Makes West Virginia Different

On April 24, 2025, in Lowell, Indiana, Liam Dahlberg came home from school with a headache so severe he was “crying in excruciating pain,” his mother, Ashlee, recalls. After a trip to the ER, the eight-year-old was transferred to a Chicago hospital, where he was treated for a rare bacterial infection, haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib).

Within two days, he went from delirious to sedated to life support, and died on April 28. Liam was fully vaccinated, and the Hib vaccine has reduced more than 99 percent of cases in the U.S. since its introduction in 1987.

But as Liam’s family came to learn, his use of a steroid inhaler for severe asthma had weakened his immune system. In a school where almost 10 percent of students have opted out of vaccination for religious reasons, he was likely exposed. In the county where the Dahlbergs live, only 44 percent of children are fully vaccinated.

“Indiana allows religious exemptions, and because of that, my son lost his life,” says Dahlberg, who has become an advocate for vaccination. In the absence of stronger state requirements, she is considering whether to homeschool her other two children, one of whom also has severe asthma.

Historically, children whose parents decide not to vaccinate them have been the ones homeschooled. But as vaccination rates drop across the country, more parents like the Dahlbergs weigh whether to homeschool their vaccinated but medically vulnerable children. This year alone, more than 200 measures to undermine vaccines were introduced in 34 states, with nine of them passing, according to a New York Times analysis.

As neighboring Ohio, Kentucky, and Pennsylvania have struggled to contain measles and other infectious-disease outbreaks, West Virginia resembles a “halo,” says Takubo. The last measles outbreak there, defined as three or more related cases, occurred in 1994.

Since 2009, there have been only two reported cases of measles in West Virginia, both in adults. Neither case turned into an outbreak. “Because of herd immunity, it didn’t spread like wildfire,” says former public-health officer Dr. Matthew Christiansen.

The resistance to weakening the state’s vaccination law springs not just from a sense of community, but from a practical accounting: the view that overwhelming rural poverty could greatly amplify the harms of an infectious-disease outbreak.

In the wake of the opioid epidemic, there are counties where close to half of the children are no longer being raised by their biological parents. Many of those children don’t even see a doctor until they’re five and must get vaccinations. The law has a transformative effect, says Takubo: “It gets these kids in front of a doctor for the first time.”
Ask Chris Smith how he’s doing, and he’ll invariably say, “Livin’ the dream,” in a laconic drawl without a trace of optimism.

A partner at the Bailey & Glasser law firm, he works out of a storefront office on Capitol Street in downtown Charleston. The surrounding streets offer a mixed picture of espresso outposts and consignment stores.

Seated in an office conference room, Smith tells me his state is dying: “Every year we shrink. We’ve had sustained population loss. We’re one of the oldest states in the country” age-wise, “and they’re going to turn us all into a bunch of data centers and coal-slurry pits. We’re not going to be habitable much longer.”

Despite his bleak outlook, Smith owes everything to West Virginia, where his father worked as an engineer for local power companies. In high school, he loved chemistry and wanted to be a pharmacist. A 12th-grade mock trial changed his life. He graduated from both undergrad and law school at West Virginia University.

In 2024, Smith ran as a Democrat for the West Virginia House of Delegates, but lost in the general election, leaving him to wonder how best to make a difference. Saving the vaccination law would soon become his top priority, and what kept him up at night.

In the wake of Morrisey’s January 2025 executive order, the West Virginia Department of Health began to issue religious exemptions, the number of requests climbing to more than 570 within nine months. But on June 11, the Board of Education voted 9-0 to enforce West Virginia’s law as written and refused to allow the exemptions.

Within two weeks, Siri’s firm brought a lawsuit against the Board of Education on behalf of Miranda Guzman, a widow and neonatal ICU nurse, and one of the many West Virginians who had been granted a religious exemption for her child by the health department, only to find it blocked by the education board. Citing ongoing litigation, Siri declined to make Guzman available for an interview. But the complaint describes her longstanding Christian faith and “profound religious objections.” It states, “When Plaintiff is under conviction from the Holy Spirit, she is careful to obey, knowing that to do otherwise will entail eternal consequences.”

At a press conference announcing the lawsuit, Siri flanked Morrisey at the podium, as the governor declared there wasn’t “one shred of evidence” linking exemptions to negative public-health outcomes in other states. That very month, a measles outbreak in southwest Utah had been linked to the climbing number of religious exemptions, which had reached more than 25 percent in some counties. (A spokesperson for Morrisey says that Utah officials had identified unlinked cases at that time and were investigating.)
Siri says of his relationship with Morrisey: “As with many politicians, we share a common interest in protecting the religious liberty of all Americans.”

Siri then took to the microphone, citing how “millions of pieces of cellular and DNA debris” from fetal cells linked to aborted fetuses in two of the required vaccines were an affront to his client’s religious beliefs.

Siri’s claim, though vivid, is misleading, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics and other infectious-disease experts. Both the cell line and the virus used in the rubella component of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine were derived in the 1960s from aborted fetal tissue, but have been grown in a lab ever since. The finished vaccine is purified and contains no intact cells. Even the Vatican has stated that it can be used in good conscience.

The Guzman case was ultimately assigned to Froble, who ran for the judgeship on a platform of “In the beginning God.” He wore a tie with a cross on it while hearing the case. “I thought that was a little odd, when you’re the arbiter of a case where religion is central,” says Robin Godfrey of Stand for Kids.

Smith assumed loss was inevitable and shaped his strategy to create the “best record we could for appeal,” as he recalls, with the only outstanding question being how long the death march was going to be.
A Nineties-Style Ransom Note
On Sept. 10, 2025, Dr. James Robert Neuenschwander took the witness stand in Froble’s courtroom, his manner confident, silver hair swept off his forehead.

Dr. Neu, as he was known, an integrative-medicine doctor from Michigan who sits on the board of the anti-vaccine group ICAN, was Siri’s first expert witness, and he’d submitted a report concluding that “a handful of religious exemptions” would present “no material risk” for vaccinated students.

Neu confidently posited that unvaccinated children would be likely to feel sicker, therefore be more likely to stay home when sick and, as a result, be less likely to spread disease. By contrast, vaccinated kids might pose the real threat, Neu testified, claiming that because they may remain asymptomatic, and because some vaccines do not block transmission, they could spread a disease like pertussis to unvaccinated students.
Siri then went further, asking if there are “any benefits” to children becoming infected.

“Yes. There’s some evidence,” Neu said, claiming that a study from Japan showed that getting measles and mumps reduced death from heart disease. Citing additional studies, he posited that high fevers from infectious diseases, particularly measles, could induce the remission of various cancers. “There does appear to be some benefit to actually having the disease itself,” he said, triggering scoffing in the courtroom.

Three infectious-disease experts say that Neu’s claims distort the truth: that infected children can spread disease long before they have symptoms, and that the risks of being infected far exceed any purported benefit. “In the 18th century, if people were sick, you quarantined,” says Dr. Yvonne Maldonado, the Taube Professor of Global Health and Infectious Diseases at Stanford University School of Medicine. “We don’t need to do that anymore because we have 17 diseases that we have essentially controlled” through vaccination.
“The studies [Aaron Siri] was citing are not accurate. Take time to examine it, it all falls apart.”

When it came time to cross-examine Neu, Smith’s co-counsel, Benjamin Bailey, a former federal prosecutor and a founding partner of Bailey & Glasser, asked about his qualifications. Neu acknowledged he had failed to complete his surgical residency, was not board-certified in pediatrics, epidemiology, virology, or immunology, had no formal training in vaccines, and had never practiced in West Virginia. In 2004, he’d been hit with a $400,000 judgment after being accused of wrongfully prescribing medication that had caused a patient’s death. “I chose not to fight it,” he said, and settled it through a bankruptcy proceeding.

Then Bailey explained that the California Board of Medicine had rejected Neu’s expert testimony as not credible. He read aloud from the board’s 2021 judgment: “The court says, and I quote, ‘He does not believe any children should be vaccinated.’”
Siri’s co-counsel jumped in: “Your honor, we’re beating a dead horse at this point.”

Two days earlier, Smith and other lawyers had filed an unsuccessful motion to strike Neu’s testimony: He’d been disciplined in Michigan in 2015 for improper medical treatment of a cancer patient, and numerous medical boards and other courts had found his expert testimony unreliable.

“The studies he was citing are not accurate,” says Smith. “Take time to examine it, it all falls apart.” He adds that Siri’s message is “driven by a bunch of pseudoscience. It very much reminds me of a Nineties-style ransom note where we take apart newspaper clippings.”

Reached by phone, Neu says his expertise lies in treating vaccine-injured patients: “I understand what’s going into the kids. I understand what the vaccines do. I understand how they can create the injuries we see.” He adds that he is not against all vaccinations. “We’re at a place right now that if we stopped vaccinating for measles, I think we’d be in big trouble.”

Siri says in an email, “Dr. Neu was chosen as an expert witness because he has the moral and ethical fortitude to state what the evidence actually shows regarding vaccines, even in the face of what mainstream journalists will write about him, rather than parroting mantras about these products.”

In 2011, at age 34, Siri left the prestige and long hours of the law firm Latham & Watkins to strike out on his own, boasting a CV that included a law degree from UC Berkeley and a clerkship at the Israeli Supreme Court. Among the few cases he inherited from former colleagues, he represented a nurse who’d become disabled after getting a flu shot.

The case was his first exposure to the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, the specialized vaccine court first established in 1988, which lets plaintiffs seek damages for vaccine injuries, while shielding vaccine makers from the kind of liability claims that, if pursued in open court, could drive them from the market.

Siri bridled at the limits of the program, which pits plaintiffs against the Justice Department but does not allow for typical rules of procedure and discovery. For Siri, the case was the ultimate underdog fight.

In 2015, in a pro bono case, he successfully challenged New York City’s rule that required preschool children in city daycare programs to get an annual flu shot. Though his victory would later be reversed by the New York State Supreme Court, it got the attention of Del Bigtree, a television producer who was launching a national campaign to end vaccine mandates and needed a knowledgeable attorney. The two men joined forces.
Bigtree’s organization, ICAN, which he founded in 2016, became a mainstay client for Siri & Glimstad, paying the firm more than $28 million for its legal services over eight years.

The relationship also brought Siri into Kennedy’s orbit. In 2018, the two men served as co-counsel, representing ICAN in a lawsuit seeking federal vaccine safety records from HHS. Siri went on to serve as the lawyer for Kennedy’s presidential campaign.

As ICAN grew, so did Siri & Glimstad, which today employs some 70 lawyers, half of whom work on cases representing the vaccine-injured, the largest such practice in the country. Since 2015, the firm has filed more than 1,000 vaccine-related lawsuits, with over 208 of those on behalf of ICAN, according to Siri.

Before long, Siri was bombarding federal health agencies with Freedom of Information Act requests and citizen petitions, in search of proof that the federal government had willfully concealed vaccine dangers, and aiming to have the FDA pull vaccines long proven as safe from the market.

“He and his law firm were very aggressive in challenging almost any public statement suggesting a vaccine was safe,” says Sam Bagenstos, who served as HHS general counsel under President Biden. “We had this constant set of letters from [Siri], demanding that tweets, speeches, get taken down.”
He adds, “He was behind such a massive set of FOIA requests and litigation, he was bringing lawsuits to grind FDA to a halt in service of anti-vax ideology.”
Siri says of his efforts, “The civil rights work for our clients seeks to increase individual rights, vaccine safety, transparency, and accountability.”
A Conveniently-Timed Letter

On Sept. 11, 2025, the second day of the Beckley trial, Siri took to the podium and tried to torpedo Smith’s expert witness, Dr. Catherine Slemp, a public-health expert who had served multiple roles in West Virginia government, including as health commissioner. From the witness box, she regarded Siri warily.
“Doctor, what is the federal Vaccine[s] for Children Program?” he began. The program helps states cover the costs of purchasing vaccines, a lifeline to immunize poor children.
“Everybody should be free to get as many vaccines as they want, but everybody should be free to decline.”

Once Slemp described it, Siri then brandished a document that he had not yet entered into evidence. “Are you familiar with this letter?” he asked. The letter had been sent three weeks earlier by the director of HHS’ Office for Civil Rights to West Virginia’s health departments, and leveled a threat. It directed the state to allow a religious exemption for school vaccinations or risk losing its $1.3 billion in federal funding from the Vaccines for Children program.

Siri asked Slemp whether the prospect of losing that funding would lead her to change her testimony. The exchange troubled Slemp. Siri was “so definitive about what the letter meant,” she wondered, was he acting “as attorney in this case or as an adviser to HHS, either directly or indirectly?”

It was a reasonable conjecture, given the close, almost decade-long association between Kennedy and Siri, one that had helped catapult him from an unknown sole practitioner to a key tactician behind the U.S. vaccination schedule’s deconstruction.

To knowledgeable observers, the conveniently-timed letter appeared to be the result of coordination between HHS and Siri — which Siri denies. Says former HHS general counsel Bagenstos, it is “extraordinary and irregular” to have “the federal government telling the state how to interpret its own laws” or pay the price.

On Nov. 5, 2024, 10 months before the Guzman trial began in West Virginia, at an election-night watch party at a Palm Beach, Florida, hotel, Siri laid out his vision for Kennedy’s tenure as health secretary, according to a person present, describing how lifting legal protections for vaccine makers could set up a cascade of consequences that might force them from the marketplace.
Siri was “ready to burn the place to the ground,” as the person puts it. Siri denies that he has “ever spoken toward any goal of forcing vaccine makers out of the marketplace.”

As Kennedy prepared to become health secretary, Siri played a central if unofficial role helping to run the transition while working out of the Palm Beach home of Dr. Mehmet Oz, who would become the administrator of the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Siri tapped nominees for key staff posts, and grilled them about their positions on vaccines. Siri and his legal partner Elizabeth Brehm also screened potential members for the federal Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), which is supposed to be independent of HHS.

items.title: Walter Koenig, Chekov on Original ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
items.description: Walter Koenig, who memorably played Chekov in the original “Star Trek” series and seven “Star Trek” feature films, died Sunday in Los Angeles, Variety has confirmed. He was 90.
items.author: Carmel Dagan
paragraphs: Walter Koenig, who memorably played Chekov in the original “Star Trek” series and seven “Star Trek” feature films, died Sunday in Los Angeles, Variety has confirmed. He was 90.

His reps said in a statement, “Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world. He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece.

“Best known for his iconic role as Pavel Chekov in ‘Star Trek: The Original Series,’ Walter helped inspire audiences with his optimism, humor, and adventurous spirit. Beyond ‘Star Trek,’ his long and distinguished career showcased his versatility as an actor and his genuine love for his craft. His remarkable talent continued to shine in his later years, most recently with his performance in the short film ‘Mr. Fleischmann,’ for which he received the Platinum Award for Best Actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards — a fitting recognition of a lifetime devoted to his craft.

“Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.
“On behalf of all of us, we extend our deepest condolences to Walter’s family, friends, colleagues, and the millions of fans whose lives he touched over the decades.
“Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”
Koenig’s Chekov, an arrogant young navigation officer in the original series, was introduced to the series to appeal to teenage viewers — his hairstyle recalled that of the Monkees’ Davy Jones.
The Russian-born Chekov was also used to poke fun at the Soviet way of falsely taking credit for every important human invention.

Koenig played Chekov in the 2015 TV movie “Star Trek: Renegades,” set at a time in which the character has been elevated to admiral. The film, aimed as a backdoor pilot for a new “Star Trek” television series, was funded through crowdsourcing.

The Chekov character was not included in “Star Trek: The Animated Series” in the early ’70s because of the show’s limited budget, but Koenig penned an episode of the series entitled “The Infinite Vulcan.”

Koenig’s Chekov was central to the plot of 1982’s “Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan” and consequently the actor enjoyed considerable screen time in the film, generally considered the best of the “Star Trek” movies.

Koenig was also associated with another sci-fi franchise, J. Michael Straczynski’s “Babylon 5,” in which he played the evil Psi Cop Alfred Bester (named by the show’s creators after the science fiction writer). He appeared in 12 episodes of that show from 1994-98.

Walter Marvin Koenig was born in Chicago. The family of Russian Jewish heritage was originally named Koenigsberg, and he attended Fieldston High School in Fieldston, N.Y., where he did some stage work, before starting at Grinnell College in Iowa, where he was initially pre-med; he transferred to and graduated from UCLA with a degree in psychology. After a professor urged him to pursue a career in acting, he began studying at the Neighborhood Playhouse in New York; there his classmates included Christopher Lloyd, with whom he would be reunited on “Star Trek III: The Search for Spock,” in which Lloyd played the villainous Klingon Commander Kruge, as well as James Caan and Dabney Coleman.

Koenig made his small-screen debut with an uncredited role in an episode of “Combat!” in 1962, followed by guest-starring roles on “The Untouchables,” “General Hospital,” “The Alfred Hitchcock Hour,” “Ben Casey,” “Gidget” and “I Spy.” After the original “Star Trek” series went off the air in 1969, he worked occasionally in TV, guesting on “The Virginian,” “Ironside” and “Columbo” (in an episode that had William Shatner as the special guest star). He played a deputy sheriff in an unremarkable low-budget film called “Nightmare Honeymoon,” starring Dack Rambo.

During the 1980s, when he was busy with the “Star Trek” movies, he appeared as Pompey in a 1984 TV adaptation of “Antony & Cleopatra” that also featured Nichelle Nichols and future “Star Trek: Enterprise” actor James Avery.
