The actor appeared in a string of low-budget science fiction movies over the years, including “Moontrap,” in which he starred, and “Deadly Weapon,” both in 1989; as well as Cynthia Rothrock martial arts vehicle “Sworn to Justice” in 1996 and independent horror film “Mad Cowgirl” in 2006.
A one-character film that Koenig wrote and performed, “You’re Never Alone When You’re a Schizophrenic,” was screened at the 1996 New York Film Festival.
He voiced Chekov in a variety of “Star Trek” video games, including 1998’s “Starfleet Academy: Chekov’s Lost Missions.”

The actor guested on an episode of the CBS sitcom “Almost Perfect” titled “Where No Woman Has Gone Before” in 1997 and voiced himself on a 2002 episode of “Futurama” titled “Where No Fan Has Gone Before,” which also featured the voices of William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy, among other “Star Trek” regulars. He also guested on “Diagnosis Murder” (in an episode that featured several other “Star Trek” actors) and “Son of the Beach.”
He penned the 2008 sci-fi legal thriller “InAlienable,” in which he also appeared (the tagline was “From the mind of Walter Koenig”).
Koenig also had a stage career that spanned three decades.

In the early 1990s he toured with Mark Lenard (who played Spock’s father Sarek on “Star Trek”) in “The Boys in Autumn,” in which Koenig played a middle-aged Tom Sawyer reunited after decades apart with Lenard’s Huckleberry Finn.

Koenig also directed theater, including “Hotel Parsadiso” for Company of Angels, “Becket” for Theatre 40, “America Hurrah!” at Oxford Theater, “Twelve Angry Men” at the Rita Hayworth Theatre, “Matrix” at the Gascon Theatre Institute and “Three by Ten” at Actors Alley in Los Angeles.
Koenig taught acting classes at UCLA, at Actors Alley and elsewhere.

His satiric fantasy novel “Buck Alice and the Actor-Robot” was re-released in 2006; he created the comic book “Raver” published by Malibu Comics. In 2013 Bluewater Comics published the graphic novel “Walter Koenig’s Things to Come.”

Koenig penned the memoirs “Chekov’s Enterprise: A Personal Journal of the Making of Star Trek — The Motion Picture,” published in 1980, and “Warped Factors — A Neurotic’s Guide to the Universe,” published in 1998.
Anton Yelchin portrayed a much younger Chekov in the rebooted “Star Trek” films.

Back in the days of the original “Star Trek” series there was a period of tension between Koenig and George Takei, who played Sulu, but the two came to be close friends, and in September 2008, Koenig served as best man at Takei’s wedding to Brad Altman.
Koenig a daughter, actress-writer Danielle Koenig. A son, actor and editor Andrew Koenig, died in 2010.

items.title: Russell Brand Trial: Judge Reduces One Charge to Attempted Indecent Assault as Star Says “I Led a Very Promiscuous Life”
items.description: The court heard from Russell Brand on Tuesday in the disgraced star’s ongoing rape and sexual assault trial, where the judge also reduced one of his charges.
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: The court heard from Russell Brand on Tuesday in the disgraced star’s ongoing rape and sexual assault trial, where the judge also reduced one of his charges.

At London’s Southwark Crown Court, the actor, presenter and comedian (St. Trinian’s, Forgetting Sarah Marshall) was initially accused of three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault, with six women alleging offenses dating from 1999 to 2009. He denies all of the charges, which The Hollywood Reporter has looked at in depth, as they were presented by prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones in the trial’s first week.

But on Tuesday afternoon, Justice Bennathan reduced the indecent assault charge to attempted indecent assault. After a delay in court, the judge told the jury there was “insufficient evidence” to support the original charge and that they should find Brand not guilty of this particular allegation. The charge relates to a claim from one complainant who said, while she was working at MTV with Brand in 2001, he grabbed her by the arm and attempted to drag her into a nearby toilet.

Among the other claims are a woman who says Brand raped her in a Bournemouth hotel room in 1999 following a comedy gig of his. Another, whose emergency services call was played to the jury on Tuesday morning, says he grabbed her breasts and pushed her into a toilet in a bar in Soho, where he orally raped her, in 2004. A separate woman alleges Brand anally raped her at his home in Hampstead in 2009, after consensual vaginal sex. He maintains every encounter was consensual.

Also on Tuesday, after weeks of testimony from accusers, co-workers and Brand’s former personal assistant, the court heard from the defendant himself. His Nov. 16, 2023, police interview was played, in which he read out a prepared statement, according to Sky News.

“As I have repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I have spent years openly denouncing,” Brand told the authorities. “I have never engaged in nonconsensual sexual activity.”

Referencing a documentary made by Channel 4’s Dispatches and allegations in The Sunday Times in which Brand was accused of rape and assault — the reports that prompted the police to begin investigating Brand — he said: “On September 16, 2023, a defamatory and fictitious documentary was broadcast in conjunction with the publication of two national newspapers containing false, anonymized allegations, which led to unprecedented media reporting. Subsequently, both the media and the police publicly invited additional allegations to be made, which has resulted in further encounters to be invented or reimagined.”

In another prepared statement given to police by Brand in December 2023, he says he kissed “hundreds” of people in public in an attempt to be “friendly, consensual and warm” with fans. He added: “There was often physical contact. At live shows, press events, junkets and book signings, I did my best to be accessible, nondiscriminatory and loving. I spent a lot of time at these events.”

He says photographs from these encounters are available online. “Everything I did in public once I was famous could be photographed or recorded and end up in the tabloids — I was aware of this,” continued Brand. “I routinely made provocative jokes or comments both with members of the public and during live performances and broadcasts.”

He goes on to say in that same statement that he did “on occasion find reasons for leaving, or for asking partners in casual sexual encounters to leave, shortly after the experience had concluded.” He told police: “I had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios, often with people I had just met.”

This way of life, combined with the “magnitude of the promiscuity deceptively rendered in recent media attacks, accompanied by advertisements for complainants,” has caused “consensual encounters to be unfavorably reframed decades later.”
The trial could last up to six weeks.

items.title: ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Review: Netflix’s Intimate and Sincere but Overly Padded Docuseries
items.description: Perhaps it’s most helpful to begin a discussion of Netflix‘s three-part The One About Matthew Perry with an acknowledgment of the things that it is not.
items.author: Daniel Fienberg
paragraphs: Perhaps it’s most helpful to begin a discussion of Netflix‘s three-part The One About Matthew Perry with an acknowledgment of the things that it is not.

Directed by Mary Robertson (Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV), The One About Matthew Perry is not a salacious documentary about Perry’s death and the subsequent criminal investigations. Peacock already did one of those, and if you skipped it, you’re better off.
The One About Matthew Perry
The One About Matthew Perry also isn’t a definitive celebration of the life and comic genius of Matthew Perry, as related by those who worked with him most closely.

That is to say, it’s not a documentary designed to spawn “10 Fun Things We Learned From…” listicles and — despite the pandering title, with its borrowing of Friends episodic nomenclature — it’s only a documentary about Matthew Perry and his hit NBC sitcom insofar as you can’t tell Perry’s story without reciting nostalgic talking points about Friends. Even if it might be better if you could.

Literally none of Perry’s Friends co-stars appear in the documentary — nope, not even Janice or Gunther — nor do any of the key creative forces from the show. Unless you count Warren Littlefield, NBC’s entertainment president at the time, as a creative force from the show. Otherwise, one writer from the first season (Jeff Strauss) is included, but nobody with a high enough profile is there to say anything that might be interpreted as sensational or sensationalistic.

The same is roughly true of the rest of the A-listers whom Perry worked with over the years. Fools Rush In is represented by producer Doug Draizin, Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip (and Mr. Sunshine) by Nate Torrence, The Whole Nine Yards by director Jonathan Lynn.

I can’t say whether or not Robertson reached out to the various big names in Perry’s celebrity sphere, but it’s my instinct both that she did not and that none of them would have agreed to participate anyway. The bigger the names you get, the more the focus of the documentary becomes what Lisa Kudrow or David Schwimmer or Aaron Sorkin have to say about Matthew Perry, rather than Matthew Perry.

Plus, the truth is that The One About Matthew Perry almost isn’t about Matthew Perry at all, which I don’t really mean as a criticism, though it will leave some viewers disappointed. Yes, it contains a lot of the biographical details and memorable clips that you expect from a documentary about Perry. But The One About Matthew Perry might have been better if it had skipped the basics entirely, because it treats that stuff in a manner that feels perfunctory rather than even remotely inspired. It surely would have been more sharply focused.

What, then, is The One About Matthew Perry? It’s a sincere, generally non-exploitative examination of addiction and celebrity — but not from Perry’s perspective, since Perry wrote a bestselling memoir that covered all of that. Instead, it’s about addiction and celebrity as viewed from slightly outside the celebrity bubble.

If Robertson had been able to trim The One About Matthew Perry down to a 100-minute feature-length doc that didn’t find the basics so necessary to include, it probably would have been a better project. I’m not sure I learned anything at all about Perry here, but the documentary’s heart is with the people still struggling with what they did or didn’t know and what they could or couldn’t do when it came to Perry’s life and death.

Sure, it would be flashier if Netflix could boast that it had reunited the surviving cast of Friends, but most of The One About Matthew Perry is recounted by people you don’t know, starting with Mia Perry Bowick, Perry’s younger sister. Matthew Perry was 14 when she was born, and she did much of her growing up with an already famous sibling. The latter fact adds poignancy to her decision to become a psychotherapist, inspired by watching Matthew’s decades of struggles. Her memories of learning about Matthew’s first rehab stint from a tabloid headline, or of the day of her brother’s death, are heartbreaking — and not the sort of thing that will get aggregated in entertainment news stories. That’s why they cut through.

The same is true of the recollections shared by Roger Castillo and David Pressman, friends going back to Perry’s earliest days struggling as an actor in Hollywood. I don’t know if Robertson reached out to Hank Azaria, part of the same group that hung out at Formosa Cafe and in various cheap Hollywood apartments. But again, it’s savvier to present this chapter of Perry’s life without the distraction of big names.

Perry dated plenty of famous women, but the ex-girlfriends featured in the documentary aren’t the Lizzy Caplans or the Julia Robertses, but rather the René Ashtons and the Romes — women who knew Perry intimately but can speak without added distraction. (Actually, this stuff is already close to distracting. Ashton, in particularly, gives the impression that she’s trying to add sizzle to a documentary that doesn’t need it, but I’m glad she and Perry had sex on a private plane.)

Instead of offering viewers a line-up of flashy tributes, Robertson wants viewers to come away thinking of Tim Harrington, who met Perry in recovery and ended up living at Perry’s house for a year; or West Huddleston, who worked with Perry on drug court advocacy campaigns.

The thing viewers are supposed to take away from The One About Matthew Perry isn’t really that it’s hard to become famous and discover that fame (and $7 million) can’t cure the pernicious demons of addiction, but that it’s hard to do everything you can for a person and love them as best you’re able and still not be able to do enough. It’s hard to watch and painful to listen to, but Robertson handles the documentary’s key moments with subtlety and intimacy.

There’s so much good stuff in The One About Matthew Perry that it’s unfortunate how often it’s lost underneath so much less interesting stuff. With all the people telling Perry stories that have never been heard before, do we really need the talk-show footage of Perry telling stories he told repeatedly? Probably not. Does Littlefield add anything that he didn’t say in his own book and that hasn’t been said in various documentaries about Friends? No. Are the general platitudes about Perry’s talent and why Friends was successful — courtesy of a single cultural critic — really necessary? Maybe in principle, because you don’t want to just approach Perry in terms of his tragic end. But there had to be better ways of approaching the familiar side of things.
There’s an original and insightful feature-length documentary that could have been chiseled out from under all the generic padding here. You can’t have the former without the latter, apparently.

items.title: Susan Saint James, ‘Name of the Game,’ ‘McMillan & Wife’ and ‘Kate & Allie’ Star, Dies at 80
items.description: Susan Saint James, the Emmy-winning actress who delighted TV viewers with her light-hearted turns on The Name of the Game, McMillan & Wife and Kate & Allie before quitting at the peak of her powers, has died. She was 80.
items.author: Mike Barnes
paragraphs: Susan Saint James, the Emmy-winning actress who delighted TV viewers with her light-hearted turns on The Name of the Game, McMillan & Wife and Kate & Allie before quitting at the peak of her powers, has died. She was 80.
Saint James died Monday of pancreatic cancer, her family announced.

Survivors include her third husband, Dick Ebersol, the former Saturday Night Live executive producer and head of NBC Sports whom she married in November 1981. The couple soldiered on after losing their youngest child, 14-year-old son Teddy, in a 2004 plane crash.

Saint James was someone who was “generous with her time and energy, which she valued more than money, and instinctively drawn to whoever needed lifting up,” her family said. “She taught her children to pause, be kind and look out for other people.”

On the big screen, she went on the run with Peter Fonda in Outlaw Blues (1977); played the lustful target of Dracula in Love at First Bite (1979), starring George Hamilton; executed a heist with fellow suburbanites Jessica Lange and Jane Curtin in How to Beat the High Cost of Living (1980); and portrayed George Segal’s wife in Carbon Copy (1981).

A contract player at Universal, Saint James portrayed the frequently kidnapped editorial assistant Peggy Maxwell for three seasons (1968-71) on the stylish 90-minute NBC drama The Name of the Game. (THR took a look back at the series in 2018).

Peggy worked at Howard Publications for all three of the rotating characters on the “wheel” series — Tony Franciosa as hotshot reporter Jeff Dillon, Gene Barry as kingly publisher Glenn Howard and Robert Stack as FBI agent turned magazine editor Dan Farrell.

Six months after The Name of the Game’s final episode, Saint James was back on another 90-minute wheel series, McMillan & Wife, which began in rotation with Columbo and McCloud as part of the NBC Mystery Movie franchise.

Like Peggy, Saint James’ Sally McMillan also got into trouble and helped solve crimes, here with her husband, San Francisco police commissioner Stewart “Mac” McMillan (Rock Hudson). She appeared on the show for five seasons through 1976, when she left in a contract dispute (Hudson stuck around the final sixth season).

Saint James returned to series television in 1984 by reuniting with Curtin for the CBS sitcom Kate & Allie. On that show, two childhoods friends now divorced — Saint James’ free-spirited Kate McArdle and Curtin’s more by-the-books Allie Lowell — raise their kids (three in all) in a Greenwich Village brownstone they share.

When Kate & Allie was canceled in 1989 after the sixth season — it was nominated three times for the Emmy for outstanding comedy series — Saint James decided to pretty much shut down her acting career.
She told People magazine in 2002 that she was tired of being “one of those people juggling knives and melons and then [saying], ‘Toss me in a razor blade.’”

Saint James received an Emmy in 1969 for her work in the first season of The Name of the Game, then added noms in 1970 and ’71. She also was nominated for McMillan & Wife in 1972, ’73 and ’75 and for Kate & Allie in 1984 and ’85.

One of four kids, Susan Jane Miller was born in Los Angeles on Aug. 14, 1946. She and her family moved in 1958 to Rockford, Illinois, after her father, Charles, was named president of The Testor Corp., maker of tools and accessories for model kits, and the Hobby Industry Association of America. Her mother, Constance, was a schoolteacher.
Saint James attended the Woodlands Academy of the Sacred Heart for high school and lived and modeled in France for about three years.

Inspired by Paula Prentiss, she moved back to California to try acting when she was 20 — she lived at the Hollywood Studio Club — and quickly scored a part alongside Franciosa in the 1966 NBC/Universal TV movie Fame Is the Name of the Game. Directed by Stuart Rosenberg, who would soon helm Cool Hand Luke, it served as the pilot for The Name of the Game.

Created by Jennings Lang, the series sported a budget of $400,000 an episode, the largest of its day (Universal’s Black Tower stood in for Howard Publications headquarters). It was canceled after its third season, during which the temperamental Franciosa was fired.

In 1967, Saint James appeared in a failed pilot for a crime show called Ready and Willing that starred Jack Weston and Joe Flynn and in the George Peppard feature P.J. A year later, she showed up on the pilot episode of ABC’s It Takes a Thief, starring Robert Wagner, leading to a recurring role as the crook/love interest Charlene “Charlie” Brown.

She also made three other films at Universal that were released in 1968: Jigsaw, starring Bradford Dillman; What’s So Bad About Feeling Good?, starring Peppard and Mary Tyler Moore; and the sequel Where Angels Go … Trouble Follows!, starring Rosalind Russell.
When McMillan & Wife, created by Leonard Stern, bowed in September 1971, Saint James had just turned 25 while Hudson was closing in on 46.
In a 1971 interview with Bobbie Wygant, Saint James described Sally McMillan, the daughter of a cop, as “Peggy Maxwell grown up.”

“She’s still just as nutty and just as goofy, but she’s married to Rock Hudson, and they live a very sophisticated life, they have a very nice house,” she continued. “She can’t get anything done, she doesn’t do anything right, she gets him involved in all her terrible happenings. It’s kind of a comedy mystery.”
At the start of the final season, Sally is killed in a plane crash with her and Mac’s never-seen son.

Saint James moved to Connecticut in 1983 to star in Kate & Allie, which taped in New York City. The sitcom, created by Sherry Coben, debuted in March 1984 as a six-episode midseason replacement series but was quickly renewed for a full season in the fall.

She and Curtin went head to head for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series at the Emmys in 1984 and ’85, with the former SNL star winning both times. As The New York Times wrote in 2007, “Jane Curtin’s Allie, the ex-wife of a cheating Connecticut doctor, is truly miserable, and so the better character.”
When the sitcom ended after 122 episodes in March 1989, Saint James was 43 and would soon become pregnant with Teddy.

She didn’t quit acting entirely, appearing on episodes of The Drew Carey Show, Law & Order: SVU, Suits and Upload and onstage in Connecticut in The Miracle Worker, but she focused on being an active volunteer with the Special Olympics and launching a business selling baby-gift baskets.
Saint James, who had dated rocker Stephen Stills in the late ’70s, got together with Ebersol when she was about to host Saturday Night Live in October 1981.

“She comes to New York, we met on a Sunday, I was in love with her by Monday, we were living together in a hotel by Tuesday, and she did the show on Saturday,” Ebersol said in a 2009 interview. “We were married six weeks later.”

After she hosted, Ebersol took her out to dinner that night, and their photograph while kissing soon appeared in The New York Daily News with the headline, “When Dick Ebersol Books a Host, He Doesn’t Fool Around … On Second Thought, He Does.”
When Kate & Allie became a hit, Ebersol left Saturday Night Live in April 1985 to raise the kids.

On Nov. 28, 2004, a private plane carrying Ebersol and he and Saint James’ sons Charlie and Teddy crashed in snow and fog during an attempted takeoff from Montrose Regional Airport in Colorado (the Ebersoles owned a home in nearby Telluride).
Charlie pulled his injured dad through a hole in the middle of the plane, but Teddy was killed — his body was discovered underneath the wreckage 24 hours later — as was the pilot and steward.
Less than three weeks after the crash, Saint James recorded an interview with Tim Russert for the Today show to thank those who had reached out to her and her family.

“If you know anybody that loses somebody, call them on the phone,” she said. “People always say, ‘I know you don’t want to be bothered.’ You can’t be bothered enough. It’s just fantastic, and I just want them to know that.”

Her family on Tuesday called what she did in the immediate aftermath of Teddy’s death her “defining act … she delivered his eulogy as a note to each of her other children and her husband, giving them words to heal. Even in the deepest grief of her life, she put everyone else first.”

In addition to her husband and Charlie, survivors include another son, William, whom she also had with Ebersol; her son and daughter, Harmony and Sunshine, whom she had with her second husband, makeup artist (and manager) Tom Lucas; her sister, Mercedes; a niece, actress Christa Miller (Shrinking); seven grandkids; and her beloved service dog, Lola.
Her first husband was screenwriter Richard Neubert; they were married from 1967-68.

“She never met a stranger,” her family noted. “Every person she met became the most important person in the room at that moment, from a fellow board member to the clerk at the shoe store, who usually walked away knowing her entire life story.”

items.title: We Linked 150 of Ikea’s $10 Speakers to Make a Wall of Sound
items.description: When Ikea launched its super-cheap $10 Bluetooth Kallsup speakers in April, aside from the rock-bottom price and bright, white/green/pink colors, the claim that really caught WIRED’s ear was that the Swedish furniture brand said it was possible to chain 100 of
items.author: Jeremy White; Chris Haslam
paragraphs: When Ikea launched its super-cheap $10 Bluetooth Kallsup speakers in April, aside from the rock-bottom price and bright, white/green/pink colors, the claim that really caught WIRED’s ear was that the Swedish furniture brand said it was possible to chain 100 of these 2.75-inch sonic cubes together, should you so wish.

Now, because it’s highly unlikely any one household will ever own more than a handful of mini Bluetooth speakers, this is one of those consumer-tech statements that rarely gets tested. So we asked the good folks at Älmhult in Ikea headquarters if they’d let us do just this. To our surprise, Ikea not only agreed, but it also upped the ante, saying it might be possible to link up to 150 without breaking the connection, so that’s exactly how many it sent us. “No one has ever tried this, though,” an Ikea spokesperson said. “We haven’t.”

That is how we ended up building a literal wall of sound at our London office, stacking 150 Kallsups carefully on top of one another to test how many would chain-play from a smartphone. Sadly, one casualty during shipping from Sweden—a single Kallsup—despite lighting up correctly and looking ready to chain, made an ominous rattling sound as if its innards weren’t entirely secure. Sure enough, it refused to play ball (or anything else), so we ended up with 149 speakers.

The chain process itself is simple. Once you have paired a single Kallsup with your music device—in our case, an iPhone 16 Pro—and it’s up and running, simply power on another cube while playing and hold down the Play button until a chime tells you it’s in “multi-speaker” mode. It should then immediately start playing whatever the Bluetooth-connected Kallsup is playing.

Thanks to this near-effortless chaining process, linking up all these Kallsups took much less time than we'd expected, about 30 minutes. We stopped at 100 to test how loud the “system” sounded at that stage before resuming the build and moving on to the maximum amount. As the music continued while we chained the speakers, it would be obvious when the collective refused to add more cubes. But this didn’t happen, and the plucky Kallsups joined forces without grumbling right up to the full 149.

It’s tempting to preface the next few paragraphs with the phrase “for a $10 speaker,” because, despite Ikea’s vast buying power, experienced research and development team, and global presence, the ability to produce a tiny speaker that doesn’t sound absolutely horrible for less than a pint of half-decent craft beer is pretty incredible.
Each Kallsup has a single 1.8-inch, full-range driver powered by a 3-watt amplifier, with Bluetooth 5.3 support. No separate tweeter or woofer, just the one tiny driver.

On its own, the Kallsup speaker sounds fine. Yes, it lacks anything resembling the deep rumbling bass people talk about in audio reviews, but did we mention it’s a $10 speaker? It is a bit tinny, and you won’t want to push the volume very hard, but as a little desktop speaker, one by the side of the bed, or to throw in a suitcase, the Kallsup does the job. It doesn’t match the performance of one of our best Bluetooth speaker recommendations, but keep the cost in mind, and it’s hard to be disappointed.

Even at low background volumes, the Kallsups worked surprisingly well together, especially playing acoustic tracks. As we paired more speakers, the sound gradually grew nicely in scale. Nothing was overpowering or dominating, just the cumulative effect of all those tiny drivers moving small amounts of air.

With 149 individual 1.8-inch drivers, the combined surface area is roughly equivalent to one enormous 22-inch driver. Each Kallsup also has its own 3-watt amplifier, giving our wall a combined rated output of 447 watts. That doesn’t mean it behaves like a giant subwoofer or a conventional 447-watt speaker, but it explains why things got so loud.

But before we turned these up, if you will, to 149, we listened at 100, and when we pushed the volume, the collective Kallsups were seriously loud. But for the record, loud like a fire alarm, not a hi-fi system. With the wall complete, we worried the collective vibrations might send the whole thing crashing down. Disappointingly for the socials, it stayed resolute. Instead, we played Trans Lunar by Twin Dimensions (WIRED director of consumer tech and culture Mike Calore’s excellent band) and slowly increased the volume to maximum.

We almost wish we hadn’t. The noise was brain-numbingly loud as we blasted, somewhat appropriately, Richard Strauss’ Also Sprach Zarathustra. We couldn’t hear each other speak, and we could feel our internal organs vibrating. Any sense of fidelity disappeared, but—all power to the Kallsups—it worked. We’d successfully linked 149 Bluetooth speakers, though sadly we’re well short of the world record of 1,500 speakers set by Majority Audio in March 2026.

At more modest, realistic volumes, everything sounded considerably more composed, even if the music lacked levels of depth and detail. The overall lack of clarity could also be due to minor timing differences between the individual drivers.

At $1,490, a wall of Kallsups is quite an investment, and not one we’re recommending, but it is extremely impressive that we managed to sync and play music wirelessly through so many small, cheap speakers.

We also tested the wall alongside WIRED’s choice for best overall party speaker, the $500 LG Xboom Stage 501. Cranked up, both reached similarly ear-splitting, frankly uncomfortable volumes. But with two 5.25-inch woofers, two 2.5-inch full-range drivers, and clever digital signal processing, the LG delivered understandably fuller, deeper bass and a considerably more musical experience, as expected.

What’s remarkable about this experiment is that so little went wrong. Only one of the 150 speakers shipped didn’t work, clearly broken in transit. We managed to get all 149 sound cubes chained easily and quickly. And when we weren’t blasting the wall of sound at max volume, instead keeping levels moderate, the speakers sounded surprisingly competent as a collective.

However, there were hints of the Kallsup chaining capacity reaching its limit, as Ikea suspected. As we got beyond 100 units linked together, the incidence of failing to chain on the first try increased. Still, no speaker refused more than twice as we got toward the end of the build.

We also would have preferred indentations on the tops of the speakers, which would have given us a bit more confidence that the whole stack wasn’t going to collapse in a heap as volume ramped up (which it didn’t). Such a simple design feature would help whether you’re dealing with just a couple placed on top of each other, let alone 149—but this is splitting hairs.

Lastly, although this setup was impressively loud, no one in their right mind would do this in their own home. Ikea has been a good sport letting us try this out, but the ultimate, unsurprising lesson is: If you want high-quality audio, spend your money on a better speaker. As for the Kallsup? Simple to use, easy to chain, with approachable sound and clean design. You really can’t ask much more for $10.

items.title: I Like the Fitbit Edge. I’m Still Keeping My Air
items.description: The Edge brings Fitbit’s screen-equipped offerings up to speed with better health tracking, a brighter display, and improved durability. After testing it, I’m still not ready to give up my Fitbit Air.
items.author: Boutayna Chokrane
paragraphs: The Edge brings Fitbit’s screen-equipped offerings up to speed with better health tracking, a brighter display, and improved durability. After testing it, I’m still not ready to give up my Fitbit Air.
Google’s first repairable tracker. A bigger screen with adjustable brightness. More advanced health metrics and workout tracking.
Band fastening can be finicky. Auto-pause can be overly sensitive. No Google Wallet.

Earlier this year, the Google Fitbit Air won me over and made me wonder why I ever wanted a display on my fitness tracker in the first place. Of course, not everyone is ready to quit the screen cold turkey, especially if your wearable doubles as your everyday smartwatch. Google Fitbit hasn’t introduced a new tracker with a screen since 2023, and the older models are starting to fall behind on health features and hardware. That deters both newcomers who want a screen and longtime users who have to choose among aging models.

At $180, the new Google Fitbit Edge costs $20 more than Fitbit's Charge 6 ($160) and $80 more than the screenless Air ($100), but far less than Google's Pixel Watch 5 ($400). After 12 days of testing, I’d recommend it to Fitbit owners looking to upgrade. Personally, though, the Edge hasn’t given me enough reasons to give up my Fitbit Air.

The Edge is comfortable enough to wear throughout the day and overnight. Its dimensions are slightly larger than the Charge 6’s (39.2 x 25.5 x 11.5 mm versus 36.73 x 23.09 x 11.20 mm), but I found the capsule shape sat more naturally on my wrist than its predecessor’s rectangular build. It feels like a better option for people with slimmer wrists and those who might find the Pixel Watch or Apple Watch too bulky to sleep with.

As with any smartwatch, comfort also depends on the band. The Edge comes with Google’s Active Band, which is fine for workouts but isn’t my favorite of the available options. Google also offers the HNBR (high-performance synthetic elastomer) Active Sport, the breathable Performance Loop, the silicone Magnet band, and the Metal Links band.

I found myself alternating between the Metal Links and Performance Loop. I love the look of the former for a night out or a more formal setting, and the latter is best for everyday wear. The Performance Loop’s micro-adjustable fit makes it easy to get a precise fit, but it's just as easy to pull it a little too tight. I also noticed that the band occasionally popped loose while I was adjusting it. The tracker was still attached from one side, so I wasn’t worried about losing it, but the fastening mechanism didn’t feel as secure as it should. I eventually noticed that the locking button was stuck and had to fiddle with the mechanism to fix the issue.

The 1.34-inch display is the Edge’s obvious advantage over the screenless Air. I noticed the difference most during workouts. On outdoor runs, I could check my metrics and control my music without slowing down. The display also reaches roughly twice the Charge’s maximum brightness, making it easier to read in direct sunlight. With Google Maps integration, I could follow turn-by-turn directions from my wrist while running or cycling, without having to pull out my phone.

I do prefer Wear OS’s more colorful interface; Fitbit’s watch faces also feel a little elementary by comparison. But Fitbit’s software offers up to seven days of battery life, which is a feature the Pixel Watch can’t match. The Edge is also compatible with both iOS and Android, unlike the Pixel Watch. Plus, in a first for Fitbit, the Edge is Google’s first repairable fitness tracker, with modular construction including a replaceable battery, matching the Pixel Watch. This is likely due to battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union, which will require removable and replaceable batteries in smartphones, smartwatches, and similar devices starting February 18, 2027.
Two Steps Forward, One Step Back

The Edge is a significant upgrade over the Charge 6 when it comes to health and fitness capabilities. Google has added more detailed workout metrics and a few hardware upgrades that make the Edge a more capable fitness tracker.

Some of the additions are aimed at long-term health tracking. Like the Pixel Watch 5 and the Air, the Edge offers monthly blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Its SpO2 readings now include nightly averages, ranges, and changes over time. There’s also 24/7 heart rate tracking, cardio load metrics, and an updated ECG app with atrial fibrillation (AFib) detection. Alongside nutrition logging, if you use a continuous glucose monitor (CGM), you can view glucose insights.

Like any Google wearable, most features are locked behind Google Health Premium, which costs $10 per month or $100 annually. Without the subscription, you still get the core metrics and scores, but the deeper analysis and AI coaching are inaccessible. In other words, the Google Health Premium membership is essential to the experience. (Buying any new device gets you a three-month trial.)

The hardware has also caught up to Google’s latest models. A barometric altimeter measures elevation changes and floors climbed. The Edge also finally gets an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. Its display brings more of these metrics to your watch face, including live workout data and visual guidance.

Google adds a gyroscope that improves automatic activity recognition, but it may have overcorrected a little. During outdoor runs, the Edge auto-paused when I stopped and resumed when I started moving again. At times, it was too sensitive; even taking a single step forward while catching my breath sometimes restarted my workout. It’s not a major downside, but worth noting that I sometimes had to correct the Edge’s decisions.

The Charge 6 supports contactless payments, but the Edge doesn’t, which feels like a regression for a newer model. If you want to use the Edge as a smartwatch, the lack of NFC technology is disappointing. I didn’t miss it much myself because I rarely leave home without my phone, but it’s a beloved feature that shouldn’t have disappeared without good reason.

The Fitbit Edge is a robust smartwatch, and Charge 6 owners will be happy with the improvements. I’m less convinced it’ll win over newcomers. The Fitbit Air remains the most appealing value in Google’s lineup, and the Edge doesn’t offer much more to change that. Without NFC for contactless payment, it feels like a smartwatch with one too many compromises.

Boutayna Chokrane is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering consumer wearables, wellness tech, and online trends. She specializes in smartwatches, fitness trackers, beauty tech, and more. Before joining the Gear team, she was a music editorial fellow at Pitchfork. She also worked as a freelance journalist, covering fashion, ... Read More

items.title: LG’s Cheapest OLED Struggles to Keep Up With the Pack
items.description: It’s amazing what can happen in just one year. The LG B6 is the cheapest LG OLED model around (priced lower than the LG C6 and LG G6), but it also has some stiff competition. New art televisions like the Amazon Ember Artline (which costs under $1,000) use a ma
items.author: John Brandon
paragraphs: It’s amazing what can happen in just one year. The LG B6 is the cheapest LG OLED model around (priced lower than the LG C6 and LG G6), but it also has some stiff competition. New art televisions like the Amazon Ember Artline (which costs under $1,000) use a matte display that renders masterpiece paintings in convincingly realistic glory. RGB televisions like the LG Micro RGB Evo and those from Samsung and Hisense have also burst onto the market, making a convincing argument for choosing an RGB screen over an OLED one.

Last year around this time, we reviewed the LG B5 and ranked it a solid 8/10, but there was less competition. The LG B6 is still a good budget OLED TV, it’s just beset on all sides by better, brighter options, including from LG’s own LG C6.
Sleek Angles, Less Sleek Remote

The first thing that struck me while setting up the LG B6 is that it’s incredibly thin—just 1.8 inches at the base and about a quarter-inch at the top and around most of the bezel. The OLED panel doesn’t need any backlighting like most LED or RGB televisions, so it can be extra thin. The lower portion of the TV is thicker because of the four HDMI ports (all of which support a 120-Hz refresh rate), an optical audio out, two USB 2.0 ports, and one LAN port. The TV only supports Wi-Fi 5, certainly not the latest standard.

items.title: Lykyn Turns Growing Mushrooms Into a Spectator Sport
items.description: If your online algorithm detects your having even the slightest interest in growing mushrooms, you will, at some point, probably see an ad for the Lykyn. It looks like something out of a science fiction movie—a clear box with theatrical lighting, fog, and a gi
items.author: Kat Merck
paragraphs: If your online algorithm detects your having even the slightest interest in growing mushrooms, you will, at some point, probably see an ad for the Lykyn. It looks like something out of a science fiction movie—a clear box with theatrical lighting, fog, and a giant mushroom displayed like an otherworldly specimen.

After trying the Lykyn myself for a month, I can confirm that it really does look like that in real life, and as someone who has tried many different mushroom-growing methods, I was impressed by how well the Lykyn worked as a legitimate fruiting chamber. The thing you’ll have to decide for yourself is whether it’s worth $300 to showcase a process that lasts only a week or two.

Even though the company is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, Lykyn manufactures all fruiting chambers in Turkey and ships them straight from Istanbul for free. I worried about a delay, but my unit arrived in just 11 days, with none of the duty fees or other customs weirdness that seem to plague many overseas shipments these days. The speed was even more impressive given that I had the custom wood handle engraving add-on ($15), which puts your own text on the handle instead of “Lykyn.” (Mine had my name.)

The 13 x 13 x 15-inch unit, available in white or black plastic, arrives mostly disassembled—you will need to peel the protective film off both sides of each acrylic panel, slide them into plastic tracks on the base, add the corner posts, and fill the unit with distilled water. One panel doubles as a sliding door, and installing it was fiddly on my unit; I had to open and close it a few times to loosen it, and even now it still takes two hands to wrench it open. The Lykyn must be connected to 2.5-GHz Wi-Fi and a power source with its 5-volt USB-C cable (there is no provided brick), and the light—a little LED pad that sits on top—plugs into the base.

The only troubleshooting I had to do was with the ultrasonic humidifier, which emits an occasional cloud of fog (and is audible, but no louder than a typical humidifier), with extra humidity being pulled out by a fan. Despite my following directions, the mister produced no mist, and I kept getting notifications from the Lykyn app that the unit was out of water, despite the reservoir being visibly full. I eventually had to push the preinstalled wick farther down into its slot and “prime” the membrane on top with a little bit of water. (I later verified the Lykyn app’s humidity reading against my own hygrometer; the readings were similar within a couple of percentage points.) Other than refilling the water reservoir, the Lykyn needs no maintenance.
Brief but Spectacular Blooms

The Lykyn is a “smart” fruiting chamber, which means the humidity, airflow, and light schedules are controlled by settings for your specific species in the easy-to-use Lykyn app. There are also options to control these variables manually. (Note also that though the app shows the temperature, the Lykyn is not able to heat or cool.) While you can use any brand of fruiting block in the Lykyn up to 6 pounds, I tested my unit with the brand’s own 5-pound shiitake and pink oyster blocks, which came separately—no fruiting block is included with your Lykyn purchase. There are also no instructions on or with the blocks themselves, so be sure to check online for how yours needs to be prepared—some, like the shiitake, need to be taken totally out of their packaging, while others simply need an X cut into the side of the bag.

Having the block in versus out of the bag had a dramatic effect on the overall aesthetic of the Lykyn, which sat front and center in my dining room during the test. The bare shiitake block looked like a moon rock or quirky scientific specimen under the colorful lighting (which is customizable, but the default indicates the mushroom's “emotions," from green for “happy and thriving” to red for “stressed and worried”), while the black-bagged oyster mushroom block looked like … well, a black plastic bag. With the precisely controlled lighting and humidity, both mushroom blocks fruited within several days, compared with several weeks with other methods I’ve tried. This is especially impressive for shiitake, which are notoriously fussy in their requirements.

items.title: Grok Says Its AI-Generated Version of ‘The Odyssey’ Is ‘Not Historically Accurate’
items.description: You don’t hear the defenders of so-called Western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.
items.author: Miles Klee
paragraphs: You don’t hear the defenders of so-called Western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.

Maybe that’s because their rabid denunciations of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of Homer’s epic were buried in an avalanche of money. The July blockbuster has grossed nearly $1.8 billion worldwide, silencing the right-wingers who predicted a massive flop due to diverse casting and deviations from the source material.

Perhaps the loudest of these preemptive critics was Elon Musk. The world’s richest man spared no vitriol for what he considered a desecration of the ancient Greek narrative; four days after its release, he vowed to produce a superior version. “Before this year ends,” Musk wrote on X, “Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

A little more than three months later—long after the discourse moved on—the public finally has a first glimpse of what we might call the Grodyssey, an Odyssey rendered through prompts fed into xAI’s video and image generation model. Rather than a “full-length movie,” it’s a seven-minute “episode” of an apparently ongoing series, depicting how Odysseus, king of Ithaca, resists a call to war against Troy but is ultimately compelled by an oath of loyalty to sail there with his army.

“Odyssey with Grok Imagine,” Musk announced Friday on X when sharing the clip, produced by AI entertainment company Wonder Studios X. The subdued post received just 18,000 likes, notably less engagement than other recent posts in which Musk cast doubt on the results of Brazil’s elections, complained about pronouns, and disparaged “legacy news.”

Grok’s introductory episode bears many hallmarks of AI slop. The movements of faces don’t match the dialog, which is further undercut by stilted and unnatural delivery. Besides Odysseus, none of the principal characters are introduced by name, and the pacing issues are laughable: The Ithacans arrive on the shores of Troy immediately after leaving their homeland, for example. Even the blue checks on X were harsh in their assessment. “Someone actually watched this and still decided to post it?” wrote one user. “Fire that person.”

But Musk’s stated goal wasn’t to deliver a better-looking or more narratively cohesive version of The Odyssey. He and his culture war comrades dubiously claimed that they were against Nolan’s casting of Black and trans actors, the Americanized English spoken by the characters they played, and various designs of ships and armor in the film because they were “historically inaccurate.” Hence Musk’s guarantee of a “historically accurate” corrective.

So, did Grok Imagine succeed on that front? Asking Grok for a self-evaluation yields an interesting answer. “No,” the chatbot says when queried about whether this Odyssey snippet is historically accurate. “Grok Imagine’s Episode 1 (and the broader promised series) is an adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey, not a historically accurate reconstruction of real events.”

The AI model further notes that the characters have no basis in the historical record, and that the poem is dominated by “myth” and “invention” rather than confirmed events. “Homeric society mixes possible Bronze Age elements (palace-centered kingdoms, certain warrior practices) with later Iron Age features,” it also states. “Many details are anachronistic or literary.”

In laying out the reasons that the episode “does not meet a strict historical standard,” Grok points out that the characters speak modern English with British accents, “not Homeric Greek or any reconstructed Bronze Age language.” Visually, it says, the production reflects “modern cinematic tropes and AI training data,” not “primary archaeological evidence.” (The bot cites the appearance of cavalry in a battle scene as an error when compared with standard reconstructions of the period.) Grok concludes that “the Odyssey itself is not a historical document, and the production makes no serious attempt at archaeological or linguistic fidelity beyond a general ‘ancient Greek epic’ aesthetic.”

Of course, the creative license that comes with adapting a millennia-old legend swarming with gods, witches, magic, and monsters was understood by just about everyone but Musk and a handful of cranks insisting that Nolan had contradicted some fundamentally true account of heroic adventure. Even Grok can tell you that its master’s fit of pique led him to promise the impossible—as he so often does.

items.title: The Year I Learned to Live Alone by Living With Everyone
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Erin Chack
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

I remember the exact moment I realized I would never live with my husband again. I was standing in our kitchen, holding on to the back of a chair for support — both physical and emotional — while he explained that he would be staying with friends for a few nights before driving from California, where we lived, to New Jersey, where we grew up. He called it a trial separation. He told me it was temporary. Maybe he believed that. I didn’t. A few months later, our marriage was over, and I suddenly faced a problem I’d never anticipated I’d have at 36: Where was I going to live?
This happened a year ago. That chair is in a storage pile in my parents’ basement now; both the chair and I still haven’t found a permanent home.

Before this year, I had only ever lived with my ex. We met as teenagers, moved in together right out of college, then 20 years breezed by. Back in January, to stem some financial bleeding during the divorce process, my ex and I decided to rent out the house we owned together in Los Angeles. I realized then I’d have to get a roommate — something I thought I’d conveniently avoided all these years, something that felt lightly mortifying at my big-girl age.

So with my heart so broken I could hear it jangling around in my chest like loose change, I moved to New York to crash with my new friend Lindsey in Crown Heights. For years, Lindsey and I had orbited each other without somehow ever meeting while mutual friends insisted we would really get along — and they were absolutely right. We are in every way alike: tall, jockish, (mostly) straight girls with an almost perverse compulsion to do comedy bits all day long.

Living with Lindsey was like living in a network sitcom. I was newly single; she was newly in love. She let me borrow clothes and makeup; I cried in the closet to keep noise levels to a minimum. We began every day standing in our underwear around her kitchen island while eating yogurt out of the container and giving each other advice on our reversed romantic situations. I imagined a laugh track every time I kicked open her bedroom door to tell her my newest revelation about Where It All Went Wrong.

Because we share so many similarities, our dating algorithms do, too, which we quickly discovered when I downloaded Hinge for the first time. Lindsey and I spent many nights sitting shoulder to shoulder on her millennial-gray couch while she coached me through Brooklyn’s most eligible bachelors.
“Oh, I dated that guy,” she would say, pointing at my phone. “Shit, I dated that one too!”

I really could not have dreamed up a better person to initiate me into the world of dating. Lindsey told me exactly what to do (be myself; act normal) and what not to do (call men “brother”; talk about my divorce the entire time). And she always shared in my joy for these new-to-me-but-old-to-her milestones. The first time I had sex with a man who wasn’t my husband — a momentous second coming-of-age, two decades in the making — Lindsey recorded a video of me walking into her room at 2 a.m., announcing, “We freaked,” and then performing what can only be described as a touch-down dance as she giggles in the background. Afterward, we laid in her bed and recorded a 13-minute voice memo to send to the group chat. Girlhood at its absolute peak.

I was still very much in the pits of despair regarding my divorce, but Lindsey took good care of me. One night, while getting ready to go on a date with a man I found devastatingly attractive (mostly because he looked like my ex but taller), I realized halfway through blow-drying my hair that I didn’t leave enough time to eat dinner. I figured I’d have to pop into a bodega, grab a dusty Powerbar, and pray the first-date drinks wouldn’t drown me. I emerged from the bathroom with half-wet hair to find Lindsey had cooked an entire chickpea stew. I felt so relieved I almost ruined my mascara.

As we dined, something occurred to me: If I outsourced sex to random men on dating apps and let Lindsey coddle me like this, maybe I didn’t need a husband after all? She was a better cook than he was, anyway. I told her this between mouthfuls of stew.
“See?” she said, ladling a second bowl for me. “It’s fun being a hag!”

By March, living at Lindsey’s Halfway Home for Divorced Women rehabilitated me enough that I felt ready to strike out on my own. I reasoned that working as a writer for a giant tech company that didn’t care where I was in the world meant I could pretty much go anywhere that had Wi-Fi. I booked a flight to Costa Rica.

When I landed in the jungle, I realized I had never been this alone in my life: 2,000 miles away from everyone I knew in a country where I only grasped enough of the language to speak like a baby. And maybe that should’ve scared me, but it didn’t. He’d already left. What could be scarier than that?

My studio in Costa Rica contained only a kitchenette, a bathroom, and a bed, which felt like a castle because it belonged wholly to me. I spent the days surfing, cooking, writing, napping, and trapping bugs the size of my thumb under drinking glasses. I would’ve happily stayed there all month by myself, listening to the same three albums on repeat and perfecting my fried plantains, but I befriended a surfer named Sam who rerouted my plans.

One night, Sam called me to tell me he had contracted not one but two parasites and would need to return to the States. “You should take my apartment,” he said. I assured him I was happy in my bug castle. “Yeah … You should really take my apartment,” he insisted.

Sam’s place turned out to be an impeccably decorated two-bedroom, two-bathroom luxury apartment with a double-tiered balcony overlooking the ocean and a private pool. I decided the bugs could have the studio. There was a catch though: His younger cousin Charlotte would be arriving in a few days. Would I mind sharing the place with her? I wondered if it was worth sacrificing my solitude, this newfound thing that granted me a serenity I once thought only accessible to practicing Buddhists, or, like, Oprah. But he told me there was an outdoor shower and so my hands were tied.

Charlotte and I got along so fast and furiously that I think it surprised both of us. She was 24, 12 years younger than I am, but she felt like instant family, a kid sister on loan. The first day she arrived, I cleared out of the primary bedroom for her, figuring her kinship to Sam gave her dibs on the big room. But we quickly learned that the bugs in Costa Rica don’t know the difference between a studio and a luxury apartment; flying ants infested the second bedroom, emerging at exactly 10 p.m. like some sort of nightmare alarm clock. Charlotte, mercifully, invited me to sleep in the king-size bed with her.
“The bed’s freaking huge,” she reasoned. “We could both stretch out our arms and still not touch.” We tested it; she was right. So much for my solitude.

From that first day on, we lived like the millennial–Gen Z Bert and Ernie: sleeping together, eating together, sometimes brushing our teeth side by side. Every day we would wake up at 5 a.m., split a smoothie, and walk barefoot to the beach down dusty dirt roads with our boards on our heads. She surfed better than I did, and so I found myself paddling over waves that I had no right riding. I’m coming home from this trip in a coffin, I thought to myself with surprising detachment as I dodged an overhead set.

My lifelong anxiety had pretty much disappeared at this point. For years, I felt a constant need to monitor, a low, simmering impulse to look out for my husband at all times. I considered him always. I could eat a very good sandwich and think to myself, He would like this. I’ll save him the other half. And so I would stop eating the sandwich, even if I wanted the sandwich, so that he could enjoy the sandwich. After he left, I suddenly had to consider only myself. And with that mental load gone, I never felt so present in my entire life.

Now, even fighting for my life in monster swells, I found myself thinking, Well, I’ll probably be fine. Haven’t died yet, right? A mountain of water would roll through and I’d laugh in complete disbelief of the size of the thing, paddle over the top, make it out back by some miracle.

Surfing with Charlotte emboldened me. Watching her casually ride giants in her pink bikini made me want to take waves I’d normally pass on. But these weren’t the waist-high, rolling point breaks of California that I knew. These were overhead, powerful beach breaks, detonating on shore like liquid bombs. And so to keep up with Charlotte — a better, younger, stronger surfer with an unformed prefrontal cortex — I’d paddle into those big waves, but I didn’t always make it out of the explosion. I still have a scar on my back where my own fin sliced me. How did my fin, a thing on the bottom of my board, connect with my back, a thing at the top of my body? I have no idea; it happened while literal tons of white water pinned me under and rolled me around like driftwood. Surfers call it the washing machine; I hate the washing machine. I told Char this.

“Oh, the washing machine is the fun part,” she said. Huh. I had never considered this. And so I paddled into another wave, this time deciding that getting worked within an inch of my life was fun, actually.
I didn’t recognize myself. Why wasn’t I stressed out? Why was everything suddenly so easy? Was my heart so broken that I could no longer feel? Was this some kind of passive suicide attempt?

I emailed my therapist, Lisa, telling her I thought I might be experiencing some kind of manic episode because I seemed to no longer fear death. Lisa emailed me back telling me that it sounded like I was experiencing emotional regulation for the first time. Because my ex and I had gotten together so young, I’d never known life without him. I’d never known myself without him. Maybe, just maybe, I wasn’t actually an anxious person. Maybe I spent the last 20 years worrying about someone else’s happiness, and now I only had to worry about my own. I could eat the whole sandwich.
The Costa Rica trip awakened some kind of magic. From March onward, every time I needed a place to stay, one appeared in a poof! of pink smoke and glitter. And the roommates followed.

I lived with many cats: two identical ginger littermates I could not tell apart in Prospect Heights, a giant hissing Maine Coon who bullied me in Oakland, and an impossibly tiny black cat with a puking problem in Rockaway Beach. I spent a not insignificant time with a man I was seeing in Los Angeles, splitting time between his bungalow in Echo Park and his truck in Ojai. I roomed with my parents in a trailer on their property in the Hudson Valley, convincing myself that trailers are chic because that’s where actresses wait to go on set. I lived in my 1985 Volkswagen Vanagon along the California coast for a few weeks, sharing the small space with my surfboard, a nine-foot-tall companion who always got in my way. Then it was couch surfing with friends in the Bay, crashing with skateboarders in Greenpoint, cohabitating with a lesbian couple in Bed-Stuy.

I never worried where I’d sleep next or who I’d be sharing a space with, figuring it would always work out because it somehow always did. And I kept waiting for it to catch up to me, to wake up one day completely freaked out that I didn’t really live anywhere, that I had no permanent home, but the feeling never came.

By my conservative estimates, I’ve lived with 1 million roommates this year — some human, some feline, one canine, but all an illuminating peek into the intimate lives of near-strangers. I shared bathrooms, I shared bedrooms. I lived with single people and couples. Night owls and early birds. Neat freaks and the organizationally challenged. I watched their TVs; I used their shampoos. I accidentally dropped acid for the first time, mistaking it for a homeopathic stress reliever. I ignored the sex handcuffs in their bedside drawers and disregarded the pill bottles in their medicine cabinets. I let them care for me, show me a new intimacy, even love me. I cried at a lot of their kitchen tables with their hands on my shoulders.

And in return I did my best to honor the unspoken roommate code: to always do the dishes, to never eat the leftovers. To not colonize the shared space, but to leave the door open for consensual socializing. To pick up the tab at dinner as often as I could manage. I imagined myself as the platonic ideal roommate. Invisible yet ingratiating. Aloof yet amenable.

It made me wonder if I was a good roommate to my husband when we lived together. Sure, I made the bed, but I chastised the beard hairs in the sink. I cooked almost every night, but I expected him to clean the dishes after. I cheered whenever he came home from work, but I grumbled when he woke at 3 a.m., some demon driving him to sit at the kitchen table and think and think and think until the sun came up. I realized too late that the demon was him working up the courage to leave.

When we lived together, I felt very much swept up in his tides, even when they started to drown me. I was often late to work because I walked with him to get a coffee every morning despite the fact that I don’t drink caffeine. I would’ve gone anywhere he asked.

Without him around, I noticed new habits developing, habits that belonged to me and not us. I stretched every day; my hip pain went away. I listened to music constantly; my catalogues expanded. I journaled for hours; my prose found its rhythm. And with no partner to share my thoughts with, I started talking to myself out loud. I became my own companion. I enjoyed my own company.

This entire time — for a calendar year — I’ve lived out of a carry-on suitcase. I learned to dress with a capsule wardrobe, to whittle down my skin-care routine to whatever can fit in a ziplock. I worked my laptop job from a thousand cafés. I rehearsed creative answers to my least favorite question of all time, “So … where do you live?” And I fielded texts from my husband, who refused to speak to or see me but kept writing to ask when we were going to sell the house.

The house. The last symbol of our life together. What would selling the house mean? Sure, I had no place to live — but in the whimsical way. If we sold the house, I’d have no place to live in the concerning, my-life-is-in-shambles way.

In September, my friend Thomas offered to let me stay at his loft in Greenpoint while he traveled out of town for a bachelor party. Thomas and I had met on Hinge in January but remained friends after going on a few dates. He had tossed me the keys to his place before, but I especially appreciated the timing of this offer — despite my reluctance, my ex and I managed to sell the house without ever speaking to each other, and I knew I’d receive a call from the real-estate agent any day telling me that I had to move everything we owned before the deed changed hands. I needed a safe place to wait.
On my way to Brooklyn, Thomas texted to apologize for the state of the place; he hadn’t anticipated that he’d have a visitor and so he hadn’t cleaned.
“King Thomas,” I texted back. “Forever in your debt.” And I meant it.

When I arrived, I impulsively started tidying up the place, washing his dishes and folding his shirts — a meager payback for his boundless kindness. While I worked, I thought about all the people who had caught me while I fell through the floor of my marriage. Like Thomas, most of them were people I had met only this year, people I thought of as the season-two cast. They didn’t know my ex, and they didn’t know me as a married person. They knew only this chaotic, vagabond version of me — and still they accepted me. They rushed in to fill my empty, echoing ribcage during one of the weirdest years of my life. But why? What did they owe me? That’s what I couldn’t understand.
I once said to my therapist, “I don’t get why everyone’s being so nice to me.”
She said back, “Why do you think you don’t deserve it?”

I held up one of Thomas’s shirts mid-fold. The graphic featured a logo for a band we’re both fans of. Thomas and I have a lot in common: We both like jam bands and surfing and mixing peanut butter in our yogurt. It feels impossible that we hadn’t known each other before this year — and yet we could’ve only met this year. The marriage had to die for the friendship to live. It grew like a shimmering green tendril out of the rubble of my exploded life. I felt so overwhelmed with emotion then, so thankful for all the helpers — Thomas included, who showed up every time I needed him and never asked for anything in return. I hugged Thomas’s shirt to my chest and then I said out loud, “Oh my God, do I love Thomas?”
Immediately I got a text from Thomas. “I see you,” it said.
“You can unplug the dog cam,” he texted.
“No way …” I texted. “Does it have sound?”
The three dots went on for infinity and then he wrote back one word.
So I guess my heart is healing after all. And I need to learn to stop talking to myself.

items.title: ‘My Roommate Made a 30-Part TikTok Series Dragging Me’
items.description: In late May, a 30-year-old TikToker named EK went viral for her 30-part series about the drama brewing at her sublet in Bushwick. The videos — which EK often filmed on the apartment fire escape, speaking into tiny microphones — detailed a twisty saga between h
items.author: Bindu Bansinath
paragraphs: In late May, a 30-year-old TikToker named EK went viral for her 30-part series about the drama brewing at her sublet in Bushwick. The videos — which EK often filmed on the apartment fire escape, speaking into tiny microphones — detailed a twisty saga between herself, a full-time artist, and a woman she called her “horrible roommate.” In EK’s telling, the roommate had gone back and forth as to whether or not to re-sign the lease together before she ultimately decided to move out at the last minute. That left EK, who wanted to stay, searching for a way to keep the apartment.

EK told her followers she’d already moved multiple times that year, and now the rent had increased. The landlord had told her she needed to quickly find a new roommate or a personal guarantor if she wanted to stay — and she wanted to. Other than her roommate, the place was “absolutely wonderful,” she said, with its massive (by New York standards) bedroom with its own bathroom and the view of the backyard where the birds chirped. It had all become so stressful, she told followers, that she couldn’t plan her shop drops for the polymer clay worry stones she made.

EK’s “fuck-ass roommate situation” series quickly went viral, and she set up a GoFundMe with a $5,000 goal for rent. “I know the life that I signed up for being a full-time artist in New York City,” EK says in a tearful fire-escape video. “Mamdani gave a speech after the Knicks won. I don’t have all the words memorized, but he was like, ‘What is New York if not your back up against the wall?’”

In an emailed statement to The Cut, EK says the video saga came at a “very intense, confusing period of time” in her life. “The uncertainty led me to oversharing on social media, when I should have just kept it private. I recognize I made a bad situation worse by doing so, which is why I’m focused on moving forward and channeling my energy into my small art business and filmmaking.”

Another person who found the situation stressful? EK’s now ex-roommate Marlyn Rodriguez, a 20-something hospitality worker, aspiring actress, and TikToker herself who unwittingly became the subject of online rage after EK’s saga blew up. She tells The Cut about what happened from her perspective.

It all started when my roommate before EK — let’s call her Annie — and I fell out. I lived in that apartment in Bushwick for three years with her. We met on an app and became friends. But toward the end of 2025, I found out Annie lied to me about the ConEd bill, which was in her name. I’d ended up paying more than I was supposed to cover, on her end as well as mine. I confronted her, and — I regret this, I don’t think it’s morally correct — I ended up posting a “story time” about it on TikTok. We had an argument and decided to stop living together.

Shortly before the lease renewed, Annie told me she found an apartment and was going to move out, but she’d still pay her half of the rent until our lease was up. I didn’t think that was fair to her and suggested she find someone to sublet. She posted on one of those Facebook subletter groups. That’s where she found EK.

The first time EK and I met up in the apartment living room, Annie was present. EK was kind and bubbly; I was kind and bubbly back. Annie told me EK was a full-time artist — she showed us the clay trinkets she made — but I had no idea she was a TikTok creator or even had social media. I know Annie had told her about my accounts (in addition to social media, I work in hospitality and audition for dance and acting roles). I told her the plan was for her to sublet for two and a half months until the lease renewed, and we’d go from there.

The morning after EK moved in, I went out into the kitchen and saw all these things she added to the living room, like fairy lights and stuffed animals. She made and sold these little clay cat trinkets called worry stones. There were also little cars for the clay cats and TVs for them to watch. She also put her rugs out, one of which was very dirty. I didn’t mind it. She was paying half the rent; it was her apartment too. We were mutually respectful of each other.

We hung out a lot, usually in one of our rooms or on the couch, where we’d watch music videos. She’d ask me about fashion and vlogging and say she really wanted to get into that. I was like, “You definitely can, girl!” She told me she’d moved around a lot and had yet to find a place that made her feel safe, that her last roommate was a nasty and evil man who made her feel small, and she’d had to stay in her room all of the time. Throughout those early interactions, any conversation we had ended with her emphasizing that she needed to stay in the apartment and re-sign with me. “This is my first time ever feeling comfortable in an apartment,” she’d say. “This feels like I need to stay here. I just want something stable.” I understood she’d been moving around, but the fact that she kept repeating it and slipped into therapy-speak raised a red flag on my end.

At this point, I didn’t know what my plan was. I was going through a breakup and was considering either subletting out a new place — I posted videos about my apartment hunt on TikTok — or re-signing this lease. Those conversations made me feel like I had a responsibility to re-sign with her. I felt so much pressure. I should have made it clear I was undecided, but I saw how excited she was about it, and I didn’t know how to drop the bomb. That’s when I started telling her yes, and then no, and then yes, and then no.

The first real incident we had was over a dish rack. I’d had the same Amazon dish rack for three years with no dishes breaking. One morning, she texted me that she broke my wineglass and said we should get a new rack. The dish she broke was one my friend had gotten me on a trip. I was upset and told her I’d had the rack for three years without anything breaking and asked her to please be more considerate and mindful. Over text, she told me she was sorry. She offered to pay me back, but I didn’t want the money.

Another time, I was deep-cleaning the kitchen when I heard her moving things around in the fridge. She told me she’d prefer if our foods didn’t touch, and she didn’t want to share any condiments, including salt, pepper, or ketchup. I was fine with that and showed her the two sections in the fridge and pantry that would be mine and the two sections in each that would be hers. That same week, she started putting her things — double ketchup, double mayonnaise, we had triple of everything — on my shelf. I started moving her things back and texted her: “You literally wanted our stuff separated. Please keep it as such.” She responded saying that she didn’t know this would be a problem.

Then there were the lights. Our building upcharged us for electricity, so my thing was always leaving the lights off. I didn’t want to pay extra. But she left them on constantly. Over text, I told her we couldn’t keep doing that, and she started responding saying she felt unsafe and uncomfortable with how I was talking to her. I was like, “Hey, girl, you never told me any of this in person.”

I acknowledge I could be one foot in and one foot out about the lease, but it was genuinely me thinking out loud when I’d text her about it. I 1,000 percent never would have said yes to re-signing if we’d had the disagreements first. Through it all, I wanted to have an in-person conversation with her in the living room and say, “I don’t want to leave you out of the blue, but I don’t know what my next steps are.” But things had broken down to the point where she didn’t want to speak with me in person. If I was in the living room and she came home, she immediately went to her room. If she was cooking and I came into the kitchen, she’d look at me with so much hate. She only wanted to text. I don’t know if that was intentional or not, that she wanted the messages for her videos.

One night in the beginning of June, I was coming home at 1 a.m. after my work shift. I showered and was doomscrolling TikTok on my burner account when she popped up. I didn’t know she had TikTok or that she was even on social media. I checked on my regular account and saw she’d blocked me, and I discovered she’d blocked me on Instagram too. When I found the videos, I think she’d posted 28 different parts. I watched them all like a show. She called me a mooch, evil, and a bitch. She talked about how I was the shittiest roommate, how she was a struggling artist, and often tied it up with a neat little bow about her art. She’d say, “By the way, I have a drop coming soon,” or, “By the way, I’m going to be selling so-and-so in September.” Her marketing skills were ten out of ten, honestly, but Black Mirror vibes. I was like, Oh my God, is that not my roommate? Is that not the fire escape that we have? What the fuck? I thought we’d been buddy-buddy in the beginning when she needed something from me. Now I’m a mooch and a bitch? I texted my best friend, “She’s making videos about me.”

It was funny, but I was disappointed and pissed. After I found them, I’d see her pretty much every day in the living room, where I liked to chill after work, but before I could say anything to her, she would huff, ignore me, walk to her room, and lock the door until I left. So we never discussed them. I wish we had. She was confrontational on social media and dodged me in real life, which was okay with me because I would have dragged her and said, “You played in my face, and on social media.” Our walls were thin, but I’d never heard her recording the videos, even the ones filmed in her room. Maybe she made them when I was out.

Eventually, we got to a point where I didn’t want to be home and would wake up, get ready, and leave the apartment even if I didn’t have plans. I was like, Fuck this. She thought she was getting away with it, and the one-sided, silent beef on her end became a thing in real life. Over text, I sensed her passive aggression and decided to be mean back to her. I was being fucking evil, telling her, “I’m not going to re-sign, oh … yes I am.” My friend encouraged me to address it on TikTok, but I didn’t want to drag EK. Commenters already were writing things on her videos like, “Okay, girl, why don’t you just leave? Why don’t you talk to your roommate?” My friend pointed out she was the one who’d brought it to social media, but I still felt like it was pointless.

Toward the end of the month, about a week and a half before the lease was up, I told her I’d found a new apartment and that she could keep this one, which was petty on my end. I felt bad about leaving her without a plan, and I wish we could have just communicated like grown women, but I was so over it. She asked for photos of my room, which I didn’t want to give out. “Hey, can we please talk in person?” I asked her, over text, again. And she just kept saying, “No, I don’t want to talk in person.” And I said, “I feel like there’s so much I need to say and be vulnerable because texting is not helping me.” She said, “There’s literally nothing to talk about. I just need a few photos.”

Then I saw she’d made a GoFundMe to afford the apartment. That’s when I got pissed off and decided to post my own video addressing the situation, a week before I moved out. She was subletting, and that doesn’t give her the power to just stay or re-sign. I gave her plenty of time to make arrangements to find another person; in one video, she even said she did find someone, but that they backed out. She’d talked so ill of me in every video and was mad I chose what was best for me, but she would have done the same. There’s people who need GoFundMes for real-life issues and emergency situations, people who work full-time jobs. She always told people she couldn’t get a full-time job because she’s an artist, but all artists still have full-time jobs, even me. My following went from 45,000 to 80,000. I didn’t expect it to blow up — it wasn’t like her videos weren’t blowing up — I just wanted to state facts.

It all blew out of proportion on social media when it could have easily been resolved in person. I got positive responses as well as a lot of hate. I’m Mexican, and some of her supporters DM’d me to tell me they’d call ICE on my family. Someone DM’d me saying this was why EK was thriving in New York and why “my kind” would always struggle. “I hope you get run over,” someone else said. An older woman, judging from her profile photo, told me to go back to my country. “This is why President Trump is here, to remove people like you,” she wrote. I got death threats, people telling me I was fucking horrible and to kill myself. I cried a lot. I had never received so much hate in one sitting. I’m still a human being, and so is EK. The backlash she was receiving popped up on my “For You” page. It sucked to see people dragging her. The dead horse was already dead.
